title: 15 barodan tahliye başvurusu: "Kobanê davasında AİHM kararları uygulansın"
content:
Halkların Demokratik Partisi'nin (HDP) eski eş genel başkanları Selahattin Demirtaş ve Figen Yüksekdağ ve diğer HDP'li siyasetçilerin tutuklanmasıyla başlayan 4 Kasım operasyonlarının onuncu yılında, 15 bölge barosu ve Kobanê davası avukatları Ankara Bölge Adliye Mahkemesi 22. Ceza Dairesi'ne tahliye başvurusunda bulundu.




Başvuruda Demirtaş ve Yüksekdağ'ın yanı sıra Ali Ürküt, Alp Altınörs, Nazmi Gür, Pervin Oduncu, Dilek Yağlı, Aynur Aşan, Zeynep Karaman, Günay Kubilay, Bülent Parmaksız, Zeki Çelik ve İsmail Şengül'ün serbest bırakılması istendi.




Başvurunun temel taleplerini Avrupa İnsan Hakları Mahkemesi'nin (AİHM) kesinleşmiş ihlal kararları, Avrupa Konseyi Bakanlar Komitesi'nin 16 Eylül 2026 tarihli kararı ve Anayasa'nın 19 ile 90. Maddeleri'ne dayandırıyor. 




Avrupa Konseyi: "Demirtaş ve Yüksekdağ derhal serbest bırakılsın"




Avrupa Konseyi Bakanlar Komitesi, 15-16 Eylül 2026 toplantısında Demirtaş ve Yüksekdağ hakkında verilen AİHM kararlarının uygulanmasını yeniden ele almıştı. 



















Avrupa Konseyi, Demirtaş ve Yüksekdağ için ‘derhal serbest bırakma’ çağrısını yineledi




19 Eylül 2026










Komite, Avrupa İnsan Hakları Sözleşmesi'nin 46. Maddesi uyarınca kesinleşmiş AİHM kararlarının uygulanmasının devletler için koşulsuz bir yükümlülük olduğunu hatırlatmıştı.




16 Eylül tarihli kararın dördüncü maddesinde, Türkiye makamlarına Demirtaş ve Yüksekdağ'ın mevcut bütün hukuki imkânlar kullanılarak derhal serbest bırakılmalarının sağlanması çağrısı yinelenmişti. 




Komite, kararında Türkiye'de barış süreci kapsamında kabul edilen Ulusal Dayanışma ve Toplumsal Bütünleşmeyi Güçlendirme Kanunu'nun da kullanılabilecek araçlardan biri olabileceğini belirtti. Ayrıca söz konusu düzenlemenin AİHM kararlarından etkilenen başvuruculara uygulanıp uygulanamayacağı konusunda Ankara'dan açıklama istedi.




Ancak Komite'nin tahliye çağrısı yeni düzenlemenin uygulanmasına çıpalanmadı. Kesinleşmiş ihlal kararlarının gereğinin yerine getirilmesi, başlıbaşına Avrupa İnsan Hakları Sözleşmesi'nden kaynaklanan bir hukuki yükümlülük olarak vurgulandı.




Komite'nin doğrudan ve açık tahliye çağrısı Demirtaş ve Yüksekdağ'a ilişkindi.Barolar başvurusu Kobanê davasından hüküm giymiş diğer 11 siyasetçiyi de kapsıyor.




AİHM kararında siyasi gerekçeler nasıl değerlendirildi




Demirtaş ve Yüksekdağ hakkındaki AİHM kararları, tutukluluk süreleriyle sınırlı ihlaller tespit etmedi.




AİHM Büyük Dairesi'nin 22 Aralık 2020 tarihli Demirtaş kararı ile 8 Kasım 2022 tarihli Yüksekdağ Şenoğlu ve Diğerleri kararı, tutuklamalara dayanak gösterilen olguların makul bir suç şüphesi oluşturmakta yetersiz kaldığını ve siyasetçilerin özgürlüklerinden yoksun bırakılmasında siyasi amaçların rol oynadığını ortaya koydu.




Mahkeme, ifade özgürlüğü ve seçilme hakkı bakımından da ihlaller tespit etti.




Demirtaş hakkında 8 Temmuz 2025'te verilen ve 3 Kasım 2025'te kesinleşen bir diğer AİHM kararında ise 2019'da başlayan yeni tutukluluk dönemi değerlendirildi.




Mahkeme, tutukluluğun devamını haklı gösterecek yeterli gerekçelerin sunulmadığına ve özgürlükten yoksun bırakılmanın siyasi tartışmaları sınırlandırma amacı taşıdığına hükmetti.




Demirtaş'ın ilk tutukluluğuna ilişkin ihlal kararından sonra farklı bir dosya üzerinden sürdürülen tutukluluğu da AİHM denetiminde hukuka aykırı bulunarak iptal istemine konu oldu. 




Anayasa'nın 19 ve 90. Maddeleri ne diyor?




Baroların başvurusunda Anayasa'nın iki hükmü özellikle öne çıkarıldı.




1. Madde kişi özgürlüğü ve güvenliğini koruyor; 90. Madde, temel hak ve özgürlüklere ilişkin uluslararası anlaşmalar ile kanunlar arasında aynı konuda uyuşmazlık bulunması halinde uluslararası anlaşma hükümlerinin esas alınmasını öngörüyor.




Türkiye'nin taraf olduğu Avrupa İnsan Hakları Sözleşmesi'nin 46. Maddesi, kesinleşmiş AİHM kararlarına uyulmasını zorunlu kılıyor.




Baroların başvurusu, Kobanê davasındaki tutukluluğun bu hükümler ve AİHM'nin tespit ettiği ihlaller karşısında sürdürülebilir olup olmadığı sorusunu yeniden istinaf mahkemesinin önüne getiriyor.




Hüküm verildi, istinaf incelemesi sürüyor




Kobanê davasında Ankara 22. Ağır Ceza Mahkemesi, 16 Mayıs 2024'te Demirtaş'a toplam 42 yıl, Yüksekdağ'a ise 30 yıl 3 ay hapis cezası verdi.




Davanın gerekçeli kararı 25 Haziran 2025'te açıklandı. Dosya halen Ankara Bölge Adliye Mahkemesi 22. Ceza Dairesi'nde inceleniyor.




Türkiye hükümetinin Avrupa Konseyi Bakanlar Komitesi'ne 5 Ekim 2026'da sunduğu bilgilendirmede, Demirtaş ve Yüksekdağ'ın istinaf incelemesi sırasında hükmen tutuklu bulundukları da belirtildi. Hükümet, daha önce yapılan tahliye başvuruları hakkında henüz karar verilmediğini bildirdi.




4 Kasım'daki yeni başvuru, bu hukuki durum sürerken yapıldı.




Onuncu yılda Diyarbakır Adliyesi önünden çağrı




Tahliye başvurusunun yapıldığı gün Diyarbakır'da da barolar, insan hakları örgütleri ve meslek kuruluşları adliye önünde ortak açıklama düzenledi.




Diyarbakır Barosu Başkanı Sertaç Buluttekin, AİHM kararlarının uygulanmamasının yalnızca hukuk sorunu olmadığını, barış ve demokratik toplum sürecine duyulan güveni de etkilediğini söyledi:







“Kobanê Davası’nda devam eden tutukluluk halleri ve AİHM kararlarının uygulanmaması toplumsal çözüm noktasında güven duygusunu zedeliyor.”







Ortak açıklamayı okuyan İHD Diyarbakır Şubesi Eşbaşkanı Ercan Yılmaz, 2016'da HDP milletvekillerine yönelik başlayan operasyonların 2020'de yeni tutuklama dalgalarıyla genişlediğini hatırlattı.




Yılmaz'ın verdiği bilgiye göre Kobanê dosyasında halen 14'ü tutuklu olmak üzere 108 kişi yargılanıyor.




Açıklamada, AİHM kararlarının gereği olan tahliyelerin gerçekleştirilmesinin hukuki güvenlik açısından zorunlu olduğu, aynı zamanda kalıcı bir barışın kurulmasına katkıda bulunacağı vurgulandı.




Barış süreci ve uygulanmayan kararlar




On yıl önceki operasyonlar, 2013-2015 çözüm sürecinin sona ermesini izleyen siyasi ve hukuki ortamda gerçekleştirilmişti. Bugün aynı dosyanın yeniden gündeme gelmesi ise yeni "çözüm" girişiminin devam ettiği bir döneme rastlıyor.




TBMM'de sürece ilişkin yasal düzenleme kabul edilmiş ve AİHM ile Anayasa Mahkemesi kararlarının uygulanmasının önemi parlamentoda da gündeme gelmiş olmasına rağmen Demirtaş ve Yüksekdağ'ın tutukluluğu sürüyor.




Avrupa Konseyi Bakanlar Komitesi'nin Eylül kararında dikkat çekilen hukuki ayrım burada önem kazanıyor: Barış sürecinin yeni düzenlemeleri tutukluluğun sona erdirilmesi için kullanılabilir; ancak kesinleşmiş AİHM kararlarını uygulama yükümlülüğü bu düzenlemelerin sonuçlarına bağlı değil.




(AEK)

author: Daniel Hunter
title: Voters repudiated Trump. Grassroots momentum will shape what comes next.
content:
This article 

Voters repudiated Trump. Grassroots momentum will shape what comes next.

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.







The broad strokes of the midterms are clear: a massive repudiation of MAGA’s fascist wave has ended the Trump 2.0 era of congressional complicity with his authoritarian takeover. Trump’s lame duck presidency now begins. 




This lopsided electoral rejection is historically rare: Flipping control of both the House and Senate in a midterm has only occurred 

three times since World War II

 (1946, 1994 and 2006). The breakthroughs are astounding: 

the first Native American governor and senator

, 

five Black governors

, the first 

majority of Democratic governors in 16 years

, and critical downballot wins like the first Democrat to win as 

Texan oil regulator since 1990

 and the 

first openly transgender state legislator in Alabama

.




Authoritarians do not do well when trapped — and with a famously norm-busting president, anything is possible. But, critically, election deniers like 

Darline Graham

 and 

Greg Abbott

 are conceding their races. Donald Trump is already saying he’s 

“absolutely willing”

 to accept the results and 

told CBS

, “Congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country.”




So what do we do now?




1. It’s OK to exhale




These midterms have left me, like many, with abundant free-floating anxieties. The 

“what if” scenarios

 have been abundant — and while some of the most extreme versions did not happen, the federal government was weaponized against the election system like never before.




Because the times have been so rough, it can be hard to exhale and accept a win, especially since elections are not material changes — they are promissory notes that the future may be different. Until Jan. 3, we live under the same dangerous authoritarian government, even if the atmosphere has changed.










Sign Up for our Newsletter




We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.
































































 










Before I advocate for you to breathe, let’s affirm all the many hard reasons to not exhale. The wins were not universal, as some big losses cut deep. There’s a reality that all of this is ephemeral if Democrats cannot govern a policy of change — if we only manage an economic status quo it will disillusion and likely result in yet another whiplash election in the other direction. And it’s hard to breathe in a dizzying moment.




Further, the attacks on elections were treasonous. I won’t list the complete litany of federal assaults — but we have a Department of Justice captured by authoritarian forces using its power nakedly for partisan goals. The far right openly prepared 

sham legal theories

 to refuse certification of Democratic representatives. While we did not get systematic federal law enforcement terror at polls, we saw National Guard throughout 

Washington, D.C.

 We still have too many election officials committed to the Big Lie. And ongoing structural impediments to a fair election are consequential: In Mississippi, the Senate margin remains tiny while any win may be marred by 

equipment trouble, poll changes,

 and 

voters unexpectedly removed by data purges from the voting rolls

.  




Notably, the election maps themselves have been gerrymandered by racists to ensure power — though their greed rebounded 

multiple losses

 in these redistricted seats. (Groups like Black Voters Matter deserve a huge shout-out for fighting in the South and in races Democrats had abandoned.)




Despite all that, we managed a pro-democracy win that was too big to rig. The country delivered a shellacking to MAGA politics — an encouraging sign for all of us who are hoping for a better future. Ultimately, the election proceeded with voters refusing to be intimidated.




Buddhists remind me we can take a breath anytime. But this moment seems as good a moment as any, especially when we remind ourselves exhaling isn’t signaling that things are over. Exhales are how our body gets in tune with this moment and releases the latest tension. Bracing doesn’t make us wiser, just tenser.




So really, take five breaths right now. As you breathe, read in a poem by 

Jarod Anderson

: “

You can be still while the world is whirling. / You can be silent while your heart is thundering. / You can be alone while your memory is teeming. / You can live forever in the span of a moment. / You can grow kindness in the soil of hatred. / You can decide purpose. You can decide victory.”




2. Celebrate our unsung heroes




As we breathe in — exhale and inhale — it’s worthwhile to remember the overwhelming number of people standing up to authoritarianism right now.




Previous Coverage

 

Will historic protests against ICE shape the midterms?




Media have focused on tariffs, affordability and the Iran war as the defining issues of the midterms. But, as usual, they’ve skipped over the resistance that has taken root in this country. People lost their livelihoods exposing this regime’s corruption and 

risked their lives resisting ICE

.




We got to this moment thanks to many unsung people.




Here we could begin listing thousands upon thousands of names. The list would include top election officials in all 50 states who refused to be cowed by the DOJ’s threats to arrest them for doing their jobs. (Some of them are quite hilarious, like 

Oregon’s Secretary of State Tobias Read

, who mocked the DOJ hacks who misspelled his name: “my name is spelled R-E-A-D, as in ‘read the Constitution.’”) But those names extend deep through the electoral ecosystem, with many officials running extreme training scenarios steeling themselves against federal overreach, like 

Boulder’s County Clerk and Recorder Molly Fitzpatrick

, and others coming up with creative solutions, like Georgia’s 

Irwin County Election Supervisor Ethan Compton

 who added “panic buttons” for poll workers to get immediate back-up support.




Recognizing how election officials remain under attack, Protect Our Election 

set up

 a way to thank them online, and the National Conference on Citizenship created 

Election Hero Day

 as a “national celebration recognizing the tremendous contributions” of election officials.




But, of course, credit extends beyond officials. It goes to people like 

Keith Odom

, a 62-year-old forklift driver, who joined 

over 5,000

 at the “All Roads Lead to the South” rally in May, pushing back against the Supreme Court’s 

Callais

 decision undoing civil rights legislation. Credit is due to organizers like 

Chanae Jackson of Florida for All

 and 

Bill Hogseth

 of Grassroots Organizing Western Wisconsin, and 

Cassandra Welchlin

 of Mississippi Black Women’s Roundtable who collectively trained thousands of election defenders.




All that worked mattered greatly to avoid the worst scenarios. 




When the FBI raided the Ohio Organizing Collaborative — a get-out-the-vote community group in Ohio working primarily with people of color — it could have broken. Instead its director, Prentiss Haney, struck a defiant public stance, naming the raid for what it was: “a political act to try and intimidate people from voting.” The Ohio Organizing Collaborative kept going — and were backed by allies across the nation under the banner of “

Hands Off Ohio

.”




Despite all the threats, voters voted. And that’s thanks to Tobias, Ethan, Molly, Keith, Chanae, Bill, Cassandra, Prentiss, and the tens of thousands who fought to keep the election more fair 

despite

 the authoritarian attempts to subvert them.




Civil resistance researcher Hardy Merriman developed a helpful 

framework

 for understanding the full election cycle in authoritarian times. It’s four steps: Fight, Win, Prove, Enforce. Fight for every legal voter to vote. Win pro-democracy electoral victories. Prove what actually happened and expose manipulation. And finally: Enforce the will of the voters — and stop any attempt to overturn it. 




We don’t get to where we are right now without successfully moving through these early phases — Fight and Win. Take a moment to consider how you’ll appreciate those unheralded heroes — because you can be guaranteed the punditry class largely won’t do them justice.




3. We are entering Prove phase: count every valid vote




The election was decisive, but it’s not over. The current phase of battle includes wrangling over ballot counts — and making sure those counts are understood as significant 

despite

 all the shenanigans.




Anyone in or near a closely contested race can help in this phase by volunteering to cure ballots — the process of helping fix ballots with minor imperfections like a missing signature. Rules vary widely, so contact a local election or campaign office or find efforts at 

We Are Ground Control

.




As of writing, Mississippi is one of the hottest of these races, with Scott Colom on track to win narrowly if a clean election process unfolds, a challenge given the state’s messy, rickety election verification process. The Colom campaign 

feels confident

 that they will win.




Our job remains to be grounded in facts. Turn to trusted, verified reporting, like 

Votebeat

 or 

Brennan Center for Justice

. 

Pause

 before sharing any election information and try to verify its authenticity. And we must remind ourselves that this win was not inevitable, it was “despite” — despite DOJ lawsuits, despite ICE threats, despite gerrymandering, despite consistent attacks on voters, and despite the many ways the federal government tried to keep voters from voting.




While Trump, Vance and MAGA will make up lies, what happens next will depend in part on what their potential 

accomplices

 will do. Some groups like May Day Strong are wisely 

pressuring corporate targets now

, knowing that corporate accomplices make disenfranchisement much easier. They’ve notched some important wins: For example, the entire city of 

Culver City, California

 approved the 

Business for Democracy Pledge

, pledging public business opposition to any post-election shenanigans.




Which reminds us that proving the results doesn’t just happen in courtrooms and elections — it happens in the streets, too.




4. Don’t be scared of taking to the streets




A key lesson here comes from the 2000 presidential contest between George W. Bush and Al Gore. Folks who are old enough remember that it came down to Florida, which was decided by a margin of a few hundred votes out of the six million that were cast. As the recount began, paid Republican operatives screamed and pounded on doors of the Miami-Dade counting office, intimidating staffers and causing a halt to the recount. A history-changing moment unfolded: Democratic operatives told activists to 

not

 go into the streets and protest — 

trust the courts

, they said. The courts sided with Bush, cleared the way to never count the ballots, and the legal coup was cemented. (Three members of 

today’s Supreme Court

 were part of that Republican effort to halt the recount.)




The No Kings movement just proved the value of going to the streets. They experimented with gathering folks for Vote Early Day, to help surge turnout. Indications are this was very critical for the win. A TargetSmart 

analysis

 compared places with and without the No Kings Early Day mobilizations. The results were remarkable: 

a 19 percent increase in turnout for early voting where they had activations

.




So coupling street heat with elections boosted energy and turnout.




Previous Coverage

 

How Serbian students toppled an authoritarian




The pattern affirms what we learned from Serbia and Brazil — in both countries, an unprecedented number of people voted and overcame huge challenges with a drumbeat of protests leading up to the elections. Serbia experienced a record 

70 percent turnout

 and Brazil’s Lula won the 

largest number of votes in Brazilian history

.




A recent 

detailed review

 concludes that anti-ICE/pro-immigrant actions have reached historic levels, even in Trump-won counties. They cite research linking bases of support activated by protests and how they translate into previous midterm outcomes. The authors ask the question: “

Will historic protests against ICE shape the midterms?

” It appears they did.




So while our election infrastructure appears to be holding, our readiness to take to the streets only strengthens our hand. Local Indivisible and 50501 chapters have plans to hold upbeat “Count every vote” rallies (you can 

find ones in your area on Mobilize

). This is wise because it creates a narrative counterweight — especially as MAGA is expected to fill the narrative field with garbage.




Famously, in 2024, Philadelphia responded to Trump’s outrageous threats against the people counting the vote by holding an upbeat dance party outside of the Philadelphia Convention Center — a visible demonstration of countering ugly fear and threats with joy and life.




5. Get ready if we need to Enforce




Trump and Vance have developed a narrative about fraud that they could use to discredit selective election results. We know the DOJ is captured completely by Trump and subject to his whims.




We know Trump is too impulsive not to do something. Reading exactly what he’ll do and where is an exercise in reading tea leaves, but it appears more likely he’s following the path of victimhood, attacking Republicans for their lack of loyalty. Alongside telling the 

New York Times

 that he “look[s] forward to working with” Democrats, Trump has 

posted furiously on TruthSocial

 attacking Greg Abbott for losing because he was a Republican In Name Only, or RINO, writing “FoxNews bears responsibility for these losses” or asserting that the Republican Party as a whole would have won if 

he

 was on the ballot.




Alaska remains another state to watch, given MAGA’s claims that Alaska was stolen. For now the courts have rejected the DOJ’s Alaska gambit to force the state to refuse certification if the Republican candidate for Senate loses. And the drumbeat to stop Alaska’s certification has been dulled underneath the electoral avalanche that has descended on the Republican party.




Losing appears to be 

growing Republican in-fighting

. That’s understandable, since Trump is clearly no longer the mighty savior he once appeared to them to be. They, too, need to adjust to the new reality of the end of Trump 2.0 and discover what life under lame-duck Trump is like.




Part of the Enforce phase also means getting the message of the elections right. The most dominant message needs to be: the country looked at fascism and fully rejected it. This door must remain closed — and now we turn our attention to debating how we solve people’s pocketbook issues such that we don’t have a return to fascist populism.




Here are three actions to stay prepared:







Each person in a state with yet-to-be-called races or candidates who have not conceded should find if there are local ways to help with ballot curing and tracking their own state’s 

certification dates

. If you’re not in one of those states, get ready to act in solidarity with other states.




Circle Jan. 3 as a key date to anchor our planning — that’s when Congress is seated and our “end date” of the election cycle.




Get your list of people that you would want to go into the streets with. There likely are local groups you can connect with. 







So if you haven’t already: Write down the names of three or four people you would be willing to go into the streets with if something happens. Talk now about how you will contact one another, how you will make decisions, and what kinds of actions you are prepared to take. Agree on basic commitments: stay nonviolent, check information before acting on it, look after one another, and do not let a rumor become the plan.




To get plugged into national response, 

No Kings has set-up an election pledge

 to join mass nonviolent action in rapid response to election disruption and subversion if needed. Mass calls are already prepped for nationwide updates and mobilizations: Nov. 4 a 

No Kings Mass Call

 and Nov. 5 a 

Working Families Party Mass Call

. If you’re looking for more guidance on forming election-protection groups, 

Hold the Line

 and 

Strike Ready

 offer trainings and resources.




6. And then there’s the Sustain phase




Activist Nadine Bloch has helpfully added a fifth phase to Hardy’s model: Since the elections are not an endpoint, we must Sustain — 

which is about sustaining the energy and movement for the long-haul pressure campaigns that come after. We still have a whole body of work in front of us.




One tempting mistake is to waste the bulk of our ammunition against each other. We are not out of the authoritarian woods and the big tent attitude that got us here is still required, even as tensions are going to fray over strategy and direction. 




Still, some reckonings are overdue. In Florida, mainstream Democrats were shocked by Angie Nixon’s primary win and 

canceled their planned unity rally

. Her loss in the general election stings, especially because her organizing juggernaut defied centrist expectations and lifted turnout and downballot wins across the state. Running progressives did not, as some folks worry, result in devastating losses — quite the opposite.




Still it’s unhelpful for anyone to get cocky and claim the American public has embraced their entire platform. This was less a blue wave and more a red repudiation. 




This period of lame-duck Trump presidency remains precarious as progressives, centrists, populists, and anyone at all still have the chance to prove they have ideas that help people’s pocketbooks. Regular folks still want practical problem-solving, but know the system needs more than tweaks to get there.




With Democrats locked out of the executive branch, some policies remain out of reach. We have to communicate that often — so people do not lose sight of the need for a 2028 win and get needlessly discouraged that this moment does not result in faster change.




That means constantly telling a compelling story about the structural problems we face so that the solutions become more evident, while also showing that government can work. Think of Mamdani’s constant videos about the big challenges we face, paired with solving everyday problems like 

fixing potholes

. We got into this authoritarian mess because of much bigger issues than Trump. The social isolation. The drive of capitalism to pull wealth from the Earth and our own pockets. The way politics drives wedges between communities. 
















Support Us




Waging Nonviolence depends on reader support. Make a donation today!




Donate













All these problems require big structural fixes and strengthening local civic relationships. There is work everywhere and, as Nadine reminds us, the election is not an end but a beginning.




It’s important that we be ready to advocate for new policies that get us out of the forever gerrymandering wars. Restoring the Voting Rights Act, for a start. Protect Democracy is pushing for 

proportional representation

, both because it provides a pathway to meaningful alternative parties, which we desperately need, and because it also allows states to be more representative of their population. Plus, it can be implemented without a change in the Constitution.




We’ll need these kinds of bootstrapping solutions that move us closer to the democracy we have always deserved. Thankfully a range of groups are trying to help us fill this need: 

Issue One

 has been gathering policymakers to create legislation to steer money out of politics and reduce executive overreach — which 

did not start

 with the Trump administration. 

Go From Here

 is aiming to grow multiracial working class power using new rights, legal rules and governing strategies. 

Democracy Revival Center

 has been offering trainings called “How to Fix Our Broken System.” They offer a set of options on what we can do to get out of the authoritarian doomloop, echoing ideas like proportional representation, expanding the courts and subjecting judges to actual ethical guidelines.




These are important structural fixes that need to be joined with policies that directly speak to the “affordability” crisis. This crisis, just newly discovered by the media, has been around for my entire lifetime — folks struggling to get by on wages that are too low and health care costs that are too high. Pollsters tell us 

“Medicare for All”

 and other ways of saying guaranteed health care for everyone in the U.S. keep growing in popularity. 




This Sustain work isn’t just big national policies. There is a lot that needs to be done in our local communities to reengage civil society and experiment with new versions of community to rebuild trust and repair. I’ve been inspired by many groups, like Michelle Alexander and Nyle Fort’s 

Spirit of Justice

, which is experimenting with new religious formations; or 

Common Justice

, which is modeling alternatives to incarceration in New York City that are victim-centered and result in a stronger community — not the diminished one offered by the carceral state.




All this to say, it took a lot to end this devastating chapter of Trump 2.0. Now let’s exhale, appreciate the unsung folks behind this historic win, and roll up our sleeves — there’s much work to be done in this next chapter.




This story was co-published with Truthout.

Voters repudiated Trump. Grassroots momentum will shape what comes next.

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.

title: Bangladeş'teki eylemlerde yaralanan bir işçi hayatını kaybetti
content:
Fotoğraf: Wasiul Bahar/Wikimedia Commons CC BY-SA 4.0

Bangladeş'te tekstil işçilerinin aylık asgari ücretin artırılması talebiyle düzenlediği protestolara polisin müdahalesi sürerken, Gazipur'da yaralanan bir işçinin kaldırıldığı hastanede hayatını kaybettiği açıklandı.

Polis, işçileri dağıtmak amacıyla göz yaşartıcı gaz, ses bombası ve plastik mermi kullanırken, şu ana kadar eylemlerde onlarca kişi yaralandı.

Bangladeş'te süren protestolar sonrası Gazipur'da 150'den fazla, Savar ve Ashulia sanayi bölgelerinde ise 264 fabrikada üretim faaliyetlerine ara verilmişti. Yaklaşık 4 milyon işçinin çalıştığı Bangladeş hazır giyim sektörü, ülkenin ihracat gelirlerinin yüzde 80'inden fazlasını karşılıyor ve gayri safi yurt içi hasılasının (GSYH) yaklaşık yüzde 10'unu oluşturuyor.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Andrea DiP
title: “Em nome do Pai”: evangélicos se afastam de Flávio porque nunca gostaram do filho de Jair
content:
“Esses filhos de Bolsonaro são uns jumentos. Só se aconselham com gente errada! Faz carta, fala bobagem, depois corrige (…) Um bando de amadores babacas”. A frase, 

revelada pela coluna de Malu Gaspar para O Globo

 no último dia 28, foi enviada em um grupo de WhatsApp pelo pastor e influenciador político Silas Malafaia, um dos maiores líderes evangélicos do Brasil e aliado de primeiro escalão de Jair Bolsonaro durante seu governo. O comentário foi feito após a fuga de Flávio Bolsonaro aos Estados Unidos e da publicação da carta (ou seria das cartas?) em que o candidato derrotado se apresentava como o verdadeiro presidente do “Brazil”. 




As trapalhadas do 01 têm levado pastores das mega-igrejas protestantes a se posicionarem publicamente em uma tentativa de se distanciar de vez do nome da família Bolsonaro e de sua trilha de escândalos.

 No dia seguinte à eleição de Lula no segundo turno, o bispo Alessandro Paschoall da Igreja Universal publicou o trecho de um culto realizado por Edir Macedo em que ele criticava o lema “Deus, pátria e família” usado pelos Bolsonaro. “Na Universal, nós priorizamos essa hierarquia: primeiro Deus, depois família, e depois o resto. Não concordo com essa teoria “Deus, pátria e família”. Porque se não houver família, vai haver pátria? Impossível. Só há pátria se vier da família, que vem de Deus”, disse Macedo na manhã da votação do segundo turno. 




Curiosamente, o lema – que, vale lembrar, foi usado no Brasil na década de 1930 pela Ação Integralista Brasileira, movimento nacionalista de inspiração fascista liderado por Plínio Salgado –só incomodou o bispo agora. Macedo, que é pragmático e costuma se aliar a quem estiver no poder, foi um apoiador de Jair Bolsonaro em 2018 e em 2022, mas se manteve distante nas eleições deste ano. 




Outro bispo, Abner Ferreira, da Assembleia de Deus, que apoiou Flávio no segundo turno e chegou a participar de um mega culto promovido por seu irmão Bispo Samuel Ferreira, presidente da Convenção Nacional das Assembleias de Deus no Brasil no Maracanãzinho com direito a pedido de voto e a presença de Flávio, reconheceu rapidamente a vitória de Lula e publicou um texto em suas redes sociais na semana passada dizendo que a democracia “exige maturidade, equilíbrio e respeito às decisões populares, independentemente das convicções e preferências individuais”.




Outros bispos e pastores evangélicos também têm se manifestado na mesma direção, como o bispo JB Carvalho, da Comunidade das Nações, igreja de Brasília onde Flávio foi batizado em 2024 e o Líder da Igreja Fonte da Vida, Apóstolo César Augusto, também aliado de Flávio. Ou estão em silêncio.




Mas essa tentativa de afastamento por parte de líderes das principais igrejas evangélicas não começou após a carta golpista. É um movimento que vem se anunciando e que reflete também o desgaste desse apoio descarado entre os fieis. 

Parece haver uma avaliação de que o saldo positivo desse apoio incondicional aos Bolsonaro ficou só para a família, enquanto as igrejas tiveram cada vez mais sua reputação atrelada a golpes, violência, escândalos de corrupção, etc. 




Em conversa com a coluna, a professora do Programa de Pós-graduação em Sociologia e coordenadora do LePar (laboratório de estudos em Política, Arte e Religião da Universidade Federal Fluminense) Christina Vital, que é pesquisadora do campo evangélico de longa data, faz uma reflexão sobre esse reposicionamento: 




“O afastamento de líderes evangélicos em relação ao bolsonarismo tem a marca das eleições de 2022. De lá para cá só vimos crescer esse afastamento com críticas veementes como tentativa de se limparem moralmente em relação à truculência e corrupção associadas ao bolsonarismo. 

Nas eleições de 2026 isso se agravou e não vimos um investimento continuado e intenso em torno do nome de Flávio Bolsonaro por parte de muitos líderes evangélicos e, logo após a derrota, vimos as críticas públicas se avolumarem. A fuga para os EUA foi o estopim de uma relação que já não se sustentava

”, diz ela. 




Segundo ela, 

Flávio Bolsonaro não era um nome desejado por ninguém. Líderes religiosos não viam nele a força e maturidade suficientes.

 Michelle Bolsonaro também não foi uma apoiadora de primeira hora, e chegou a jogar contra com o vídeo de 27 minutos, revelando que as críticas que ela faz ali não são tudo o que ela sabia. 




“Quando o nome de Flávio se consolidou para a presidência, ela passou a apoiar o nome dele, assim como Damares Alves e outras parlamentares e candidatas, não em defesa dele próprio, 

mas porque sua vitória favoreceria à libertação do pai. 

Não era por ele, mas ‘em nome do pai’”. 




Para ela, 

a movimentação de Silas Malafaia “ está fazendo um aceno ao que pode se fortalecer neste momento: a direita dita liberal e democrática”. 




Ela diz que boa a eleição demonstrou que parte da sociedade ansiava por algo que fosse diferente do bolsonarismo e do petismo. 




“Tarcísio parece ser aquele político capaz de capturar, neste momento, esse anseio em torno de si e reorganizar uma direita e um centro que foram engolidos pelo bolsonarismo nos últimos anos”, aposta.  




Ou seja: parece que em nome do pai e do filho, o espírito santo não vai mais operar milagres eleitorais para a família Bolsonaro. Amém.

title: Mekke Anlaşması TBMM Genel Kurulunda görüşülüyor
content:
TBMM Genel Kurulunda Türkiye, Pakistan ve Suudi Arabistan Arasında Ortak Savunma İçin Mekke Anlaşmasının Onaylanmasının Uygun Bulunduğuna Dair Kanun Teklifi'nin görüşmelerine geçildi. CHP ve MHP anlaşmaya destek vereceğini açıklarken İYİ Parti ve DEM Parti karşı çıktı. Yeni Yol Grubu, Türkiye’nin hangi koşullarda askeri sorumluluk üstleneceğinin ve Meclis izninin ne zaman gerekeceğinin açıklanmasını istedi.

CHP Grup Başkanı Faik Öztrak, Türkiye’yi Yemen savaşı başta olmak üzere bölgesel çatışmalara çekme riski taşıyan Mekke Anlaşması’nın Ankara'ya NATO dışında bir bölgesel güvenlik yapısı kurma imkanı sunduğunu savunarak anlaşmaya destek vereceklerini söyledi.

Öztrak, işbirliğinin savunma ve caydırıcılıkla sınırlı tutulmasını ve İran’la güvenlik diyaloğunun sürdürülmesini istedi. Anlaşmadaki tehdit tanımının açıklığa kavuşturulması gerektiğini belirten Öztrak, TSK'nin yurt dışına gönderilmesinde Meclis’in yetkisinin korunması gerektiğini ifade etti.

CHP Yalova Milletvekili Tahsin Becan ise anlaşmanın ortak tehdidi ve ittifakın hangi coğrafyada devreye gireceğini açıkça tanımlamadığını söyledi.

İYİ Parti Kocaeli Milletvekili Lütfü Türkkan, Pakistan ve Suudi Arabistan’la savunma sanayisi, askeri eğitim ve istihbarat alanlarında işbirliğine açık olduklarını söyledi. Türkkan, süresiz yürürlük öngören anlaşmanın taraflara ilk 10 yıl boyunca olağan çekilme mekanizmasını kullanma imkanı vermemesini eleştirdi. Bölgesel ittifakların ve Türkiye’nin güvenlik önceliklerinin bu süre içinde değişebileceğini belirten Türkkan, ilk genel sekreterin Pakistan vatandaşı olmasının sonuçlarının da yeterince tartışılmadığını söyledi.

İYİ Parti Muğla Milletvekili Metin Ergun, askeri konuşlanmadan terörle mücadeleye kadar geniş bir alanı kapsayan teklifin neden Millî Savunma Komisyonu’nda görüşülmediğini sordu. Ergun, Türkiye’nin hangi koşullarda askeri destek vermekle yükümlü olacağının ve bu desteğin sınırlarının belirlenmesini istedi.

Yeni Yol Grubu adına konuşan İstanbul Milletvekili Hasan Karal, teklifin Dışişleri Komisyonu’nda değişiklik yapılmadan kabul edildiğini, Millî Savunma Komisyonu’nun ise teklifi görüşmeyeceğini yazılı olarak bildirdiğini söyledi. Karal, Dışişleri Bakan Yardımcısı’nın askeri yardımın otomatik olarak devreye girmeyeceği yönündeki açıklamasını hatırlattı ve uygulamanın anlaşma metninde açıklığa kavuşturulmasını istedi.

Karal, Anayasa’nın 92’nci maddesi uyarınca hangi görevlerin doğrudan anlaşma kapsamında yürütüleceğinin ve hangi durumlarda yurt dışına asker göndermek için TBMM iznine başvurulacağının belirlenmesi gerektiğini söyledi. Bir tarafın kendi çatışmasını tırmandırmasının Türkiye açısından peşinen askeri destek yükümlülüğü doğurmaması gerektiğini de belirtti.

DEM Parti Diyarbakır Milletvekili Ceylan Akça Cupolo, Yemen, Sudan, Gazze ve Ukrayna’daki çatışmalara işaret ederek yeni askeri paktların savaşları derinleştirebileceğini vurguladı. Anlaşmanın olası insani bedelini en çok yoksulların taşıyacağını söyleyen Cupolo, “Gözümüz kapalı bir şekilde savaşa gitmeyi reddediyoruz” dedi.

MHP Erzurum Milletvekili Kamil Aydın, anlaşmanın üç ülke arasında güveni ve dayanışmayı artıracağını, ortak tehditlere karşı caydırıcılığı güçlendireceğini söyledi. Aydın, kolektif savunma hükmünün uygulanmasına tarafların istişare ederek karar vereceğini belirtti. Anlaşmanın herhangi bir ülkeyi hedef almadığını savunan Aydın, belirlenen koşulları karşılayan diğer bölge ülkelerinin de ileride anlaşmaya katılabileceğini söyledi.

Taraflardan birine yönelik silahlı saldırıyı tüm taraflara yapılmış sayan anlaşma, ortak askeri faaliyetler, istihbarat paylaşımı ve lojistik destek hükümleri içeriyor. Süresiz olarak yürürlükte kalması planlanan ve ilk 10 yıl çekilmenin mümkün olmadığı anlaşma, Türkiye’yi ABD ve İsrail’in çıkarları doğrultusunda Suudi Arabistan’a destek için Yemen savaşına sürükleyeceği eleştirileriyle gündemde.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Marianne Lavelle
title: Activists Hope Midterm Wins Set the Stage for Renewed Energy and Climate Policy
content:
Environmental advocates point out voters are angry at Big Oil, which is making record profits while families struggle.

Environmental advocates point out voters are angry at Big Oil, which is making record profits while families struggle.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Democrats on Tuesday won control of both houses of Congress and a decisive mandate to put a check on Donald Trump’s tumultuous presidency, a victory propelled by voter anger over high prices, corruption and the unchecked spread of data centers.

Some of the same concerns helped to lift Democrats to victories in statehouses, where they gained a majority of the country’s governorships for the first time in more than a decade.

Voters in Ohio, South Carolina and Texas — states Trump won by double digits two years ago — put Democrats over the top in the U.S. Senate. And the Democratic wave surmounted a seawall of money: the unprecedented spending the GOP’s tech industry allies poured into the races in recent weeks to protect the status quo and their freedom from regulation.

Activists believe the result sets the stage for renewed environmental and climate policy, even though candidates seldom mentioned those issues by name in their campaigns. They argue that any action Congress takes on voters’ top issues — soaring energy prices, undue industry influence and the surge of artificial intelligence infrastructure — will curb the upward trajectory of U.S. fossil fuel consumption that Trump has encouraged.

“Voters rejected the Trump administration’s failing energy policies, which have pushed electricity bills higher,” said David Kieve, president of EDF Action, the political arm of the nonprofit Environmental Defense Fund, which invested $18 million in the midterms. “Families know that blocking clean energy raises rates. Paying companies to abandon wind projects, canceling grants meant to lower rural utility bills, and using emergency orders to keep coal plants running when cleaner, cheaper options are available all moved us in the wrong direction.”

A president’s party typically loses seats in Congress in midterm elections, and in the face of that history, Trump urged voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot.” The results indicated that voters listened. Trump’s sagging approval became a millstone Republicans were forced to carry, as opponents attacked them for their complicity in an unpopular war that had caused U.S. energy prices to soar. (The decision to unilaterally join Israel in airstrikes against Iran on Feb. 28 resulted in “incalculable political damage for Trump’s party,” political pundit Charlie Cook wrote on the eve of the election.)

In unfortunate timing for Republicans, the U.S. oil industry last week reported its profits — $130 billion over the past six months, or triple the earnings of one year ago, all due to the war-related run-up in prices. On the campaign trail, Trump tried to frame the oil industry’s boon as a blessing for Americans.

“They’re making hundreds of billions of dollars — our country is — on oil,” Trump said at an Oct. 26 rally in Georgia. Trump said his advisers warned him not to mention that “because people are paying a little bit higher,” but he said he didn’t care how his words would be portrayed. “I don’t give a damn,” he said. “We’re making a freaking fortune!”

But Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) seemed to better capture the mood of his state’s voters in his last days of campaigning for reelection: “Under failed president Donald J. Trump, it costs more than ever in American history to fill up your truck, stock your fridge, visit the doctor or power your home.” Ossoff coasted to re-election as expected, and former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated Republican Rick Jackson to win the Georgia governor’s race.

Opposition to data centers helped Democrats in many races, such as in Ohio, where Democrat Sherrod Brown staged a political comeback and defeated Republican Sen. Jon Husted. Brown dubbed his opponent “the face of data centers,” and sought to tie Husted to tax breaks and other policies that have attracted the giant computing centers to Ohio.

Trump’s foes — including environmental groups — blanketed the airwaves in swing states and districts with ads tying the pain of high gasoline and electricity prices to cozy Republican relationships with oil and utility companies, tech giants and the insurance industry. “Voters are not simply frustrated, they’re angry at monopoly utility companies, Big Tech, and Big Oil, who are making record profits while families struggle,” said Sara Schreiber, senior vice president of LCV Victory Fund. The super PAC of the League of Conservation Voters became one of the leading outside issues groups supporting Democrats on both state and federal ballots, with a $110 million investment in the midterms.

Cabinet members like Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin and U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins fanned out into states like Iowa where Republicans were in deep trouble. They touted Trump deregulatory policies and offered aid to farmers. But pre-election polling showed key Trump administration messages on environmental protection fell flat. More than 70 percent of likely voters in Iowa, Ohio and Texas felt rollback of environmental regulations would have either no impact on making their lives more affordable or would make things more expensive, according to early October polling by The Cook Political Report, New River Strategies and GS Strategy Group.

And the polling showed voters were more worried about the inflationary impact of Republican energy policies than Democratic climate policies. About 60 percent blamed “Republicans’ support for the war with Iran, trade wars, and billions in giveaways for data centers” for high energy prices; only about 40 percent said they were more concerned about “Democrats’ radical environmental policies like the Green New Deal.”

James Talarico overcame a fusillade of tech industry money to become the first Democrat that Texas will send to the U.S. Senate in 33 years. The world’s richest man, Elon Musk, alone contributed an unprecedented $445 million to super PACs, much of it to bolster Talarico’s scandal-plagued Republican opponent, Attorney General Ken Paxton. Talarico made Musk’s effort to buy the seat an issue in the campaign, which resonated in a state that has been convulsed over the spread of Big Tech facilities.

Across the country, 56 percent of voters said data centers were a crucial or major factor in their picks for Congress, according to polling by The Wall Street Journal. Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, seeing the tidal wave of opposition grow, imposed a temporary moratorium on new facilities in Texas. But his moves were not enough to win him re-election. State Rep. Gina Hinojosa will become the first Democratic governor of Texas since Ann Richards left office in 1995.

After pulling off her surprise victory in the South Carolina Senate race, Democrat Annie Andrews spoke of the moment as a rebellion against the status quo. “You have shown the nation that in this era of partisan divides, of vitriol and name calling, in a politics dominated by billionaires and special interest groups and insiders in Washington, D.C., that we will not bow down, that we will not back down, and we will chart our own course,” she told her supporters.

As Washington enters a period of divided government, governors and state legislatures will have an opportunity to lead on climate and energy policy in ways that the federal government won’t or can’t.

Democrats retained governors’ offices in Arizona, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, flipped control from Republicans in Iowa, Georgia, Ohio and Texas, and were on track to add other wins in closely watched races.

“Because of your hard work, Ohio has chosen unity and decency over division and hate,” said Ohio Governor-elect Amy Acton, a former director of the state public health agency.

Democrats also won the two open seats on the Georgia Public Service Commission, a utility regulator, giving the party a 3-2 edge. The panel had been controlled by Republicans for decades and the new majority has an opportunity to address consumer concerns about rising utility bills.

A key win for climate came early in the night with the re-election of Rep. Kathy Castor (D-Fla.), despite Florida Republicans’ failed efforts at redistricting to favor the GOP. Castor, who represents storm-prone Tampa, served as chair of the House Select Committee on the Climate Crisis during Trump’s first term and has been leader of a project to develop a legislative agenda on the economy and environment for the new Congress. The so-called Thriving Economies Project unveiled a menu of 800 policy recommendations in September designed to win bipartisan support, many of them tapping into the concerns that animated voters in the midterms. (One example: Creating a Strategic Energy Affordability Reserve, drawing from windfall oil and gas profits.)

Although Democrats were on track to exceed projections and net nearly 30 House seats, they won’t be able to pass legislation without Republican support. There simply were not enough seats in play to give them a veto-proof majority. The most immediate and concrete change they can force in Washington is the kind of oversight of the Trump administration that has been missing for two years. Democratic House leaders already have signaled plans to call Zeldin and other cabinet members to task over their deep cutbacks in staff and science investments. And investigations are expected to examine the growing influence of the tech industry in reshaping American landscapes, life and even foreign policy. A leading target is the man who invested more money than anyone else in a failed effort to fend off Tuesday’s Democratic wave: Elon Musk.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Las políticas represivas desplegadas en 1000 días del gobierno de Milei
content:
El Monitor de respuestas represivas estatales o paraestatales a la protesta social en Argentina del IEF-CTAA presentó un informe que analiza en profundidad los datos vinculados a las represiones y detenciones registradas en todo el país desde el comienzo del gobierno de ultraderecha de Javier Milei.




La represión a la protesta contra la regresiva reforma laboral el 19 de febrero de 2026. Foto: Indymedia Argentina




Compartimos los puntos salientes del informe titulado “Argentina reprimida”, y al final del artículo, el PDF con el trabajo completo.




Informe del IEF: Los 1000 días de Milei







El balance de la política represiva sobre la protesta social bajo el Gobierno de Milei da cuenta de un uso intencionado, planificado y sostenido de la violencia como mecanismo de disciplinamiento social.




Los datos relevados por el Monitor de respuestas represivas de la CTA contabilizan al menos 147 represiones estatales a la protesta en todo el país, en las cuales intervinieron tanto fuerzas federales como provinciales con una fuerte presencia de represiones en la Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires.







El conjunto de los eventos represivos analizados se reportan al menos 5141 personas heridas con distintos grados de gravedad. La evolución anual muestra un crecimiento sostenido toda la serie con un marcado incremento en los primeros 8 meses de 2026.




Entre los casos que a resaltar por su gravedad, se encuentran 6 personas que han perdido la visión de uno de sus ojos producto del uso de balas de goma y/o lanzagases en las siguientes protestas: Matías Aufieri, Ley Ómnibus, Congreso de la Nación, febrero de 2024; Claudio, en un reclamo de movimientos sociales por la entrega de alimentos, en la avenida 9 de Julio, en abril de 2024; Jonathan y Rodrigo, durante la protesta de hinchas y jubilados, en marzo de 2025; Marcelo, en una protesta de municipales de Hipólito Yrigoyen, Salta, agosto de 2025; y el caso de Lucas, quien perdió la vista de uno de sus ojos durante la protesta contra la reforma laboral el 11 de febrero de 2026.







Por último, se destaca el caso de Pablo Grillo, que aún no cuenta con una resolución judicial que determine los responsables que pusieron en juego su salud y su vida durante las jornadas del 12 de marzo de 2025.







La represión a los/as jubilados/as fue una política sostenida contra una población en situación de mayor vulnerabilidad, que reclama por sus ingresos y sus medicamentos. La agresión de las fuerzas de seguridad ha sido casi una constante en las protestas de los miércoles en el Congreso de la Nación, semana tras semana, con una presencia siempre desproporcionada de efectivos en relación con la cantidad de manifestantes.




Entre septiembre de 2024 y julio de 2026 se registraron 35 jornadas de represión a movilizaciones de jubilados y personas de la tercera edad, con un saldo acumulado de 1603 personas heridas y 164 detenidas.




Si se observan los casos de mayor cantidad de heridos en las represiones a las protestas de jubilados y jubiladas, vemos que en seis jornadas, ocurridas entre el 11 de septiembre de 2024 y el 28 de mayo de 2025, se concentran el 70% de las 1630 personas heridas.




En los 1000 días del Gobierno de Javier Milei se registraron al menos 762 personas detenidas por protestas y/o por estar organizadas. El 20 de diciembre de 2023, 10 días después de la asunción, se relevaron las primeras detenciones en el marco de una protesta social. Este tipo de hecho se repitió a lo largo de casi todos los meses en todo el país, con claros eventos de detenciones masivas en algunas protestas y un incremento sostenido de las detenciones totales durante el último año y medio.




Otro rasgo de los hechos de detención es que la amplia mayoría (78%) se desarrolló en el marco de 72 represiones a la protesta social.




En materia de la distribución geográfica de las detenciones, nuevamente existe una fuerte presencia en el territorio de la CABA, que es donde se desarrollaron los episodios más extensos y en donde se dieron detenciones masivas. En estos 1000 días fueron detenidas al menos 395 personas en 48 episodios.




En el resto del país, se registraron 367 detenciones en 19 provincias que ocurrieron en 77 eventos.




Otro dato saliente es el registro de casos de extensión en los tiempos de detención de manifestantes o militantes por participar de protestas o pertenecer a una organización popular. En este sentido, el Monitor de respuestas represivas registró al menos 13 casos de personas que fueron detenidas desde 10 hasta 450 días, tres de ellas hoy no están en libertad.







Resulta fundamental hacer una mención especial a las detenciones de Milton Tolomeo y Eneas Gallo, presos por luchar contra la reforma laboral. Ambos llevan más de 7 meses detenidos en el penal de Marcos Paz. Sus detenciones se dieron en el marco de una campaña mediática de la Ministra de Seguridad, Alejandra Monteoliva, en donde difundió el rostro de distintas personas acusadas de terroristas. Medidas similares las de la ex ministra de seguridad, actual senadora, Patricia Bullrich que acusó de terroristas a decenas de manifestantes.




Ambos detenidos se encuentran en permanente acompañamiento de distintas organizaciones del campo popular que reclaman su libertad; desde la Comisión por la Libertad a lxs presxs por luchar, se tejen redes de colectas de alimentos y otros productos para poder acercarles a Marcos Paz, así como visitas a Milton y Eneas. La exigencia de la liberación de ambos es también una forma de defender el derecho a la organización y a la protesta que el Gobierno atacó en forma sistemática, motivo por el cual los acusa de terrorismo en pos de deslegitimar cualquier acción de resistencia y rebeldía frente al ataque de las condiciones de vida de la clase trabajadora.







Monitor IEF CTA 1000dias B

Las políticas represivas desplegadas en 1000 días del gobierno de Milei

Indymedia Argentina Centro de Medios Independientes (( i ))

.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Los jubilados de la mínima perdieron un 30 por ciento de su poder de compra desde que gobierna Milei
content:
Según el informe mensual del Mirador de la Actualidad del Trabajo y la Economía (MATE), los jubilados y jubiladas que cobran el haber mínimo perdieron un 30% de su poder adquisitivo desde diciembre de 2023, cuando asumió el gobierno de Javier Milei. La pérdida acumulada alcanza los 6,5 millones de pesos por persona y afecta al 63% del total de jubilados y jubiladas, de acuerdo con el relevamiento elaborado en base a datos oficiales.







En diálogo con Informativo FARCO, el economista Lavih Abraham explicó que la mayor caída se produjo durante los primeros meses de 2024, luego de la devaluación y el fuerte aumento de los precios. En ese período, las jubilaciones llegaron a perder hasta un 35% de su poder adquisitivo, sin que el gobierno aplicara una compensación.




La posterior modificación del sistema de actualización permitió recuperar una parte de lo perdido, pero no alcanzó para recomponer los ingresos. Abraham señaló que la pérdida inicial se ubicó en torno al 23%, pero el congelamiento del bono que acompaña a la jubilación mínima profundizó el deterioro.




“El bono se actualizó un par de veces y hace un año y medio que dejó de actualizarse y está en 70 mil pesos”

, explicó. Mientras los haberes se ajustan de acuerdo con la inflación, el bono permanece congelado, lo que genera una pérdida adicional que se acumula mes a mes.







“Si decimos cuántos pesos son los perdidos por un jubilado de la mínima, estamos hablando de 6 millones 500 mil pesos a lo largo de todo este tiempo”

, precisó el economista.




Y agregó que se trata de dinero que cada mes deja de estar en el bolsillo de las personas jubiladas.




Lavih Abraham




El informe del MATE también advierte sobre el deterioro de los ingresos de quienes trabajan. Los salarios reales del sector público se encuentran un 21% por debajo del nivel que tenían al asumir Milei, mientras que los del sector privado registran una caída del 7%. En términos acumulados, el estudio calcula que cada trabajador estatal perdió alrededor de 17,5 millones de pesos y cada trabajador privado, unos 3,3 millones.




Otro de los datos preocupantes es la caída del empleo registrado. Desde diciembre de 2023 se perdieron 375.016 puestos de trabajo formales: 265.765 del sector privado, 89.620 del sector público y 19.631 de casas particulares.




Abraham explicó que estas cifras surgen de las declaraciones juradas de los empleadores registradas en el Sistema Integrado Previsional Argentino (SIPA). Aclaró que la pérdida de puestos formales no significa necesariamente que todas esas personas hayan dejado de trabajar, sino que muchas pasaron a desempeñarse en actividades informales o por cuenta propia, con menores ingresos y condiciones laborales más precarias.







De acuerdo con el informe, en cinco de los primeros ocho meses de 2026 la evolución de la actividad fue negativa. Los sectores vinculados al mercado interno, como la industria, la construcción y el comercio, continúan entre los más afectados. En agosto, la industria registró una caída del 13,7% respecto de 2023; la construcción, del 19,3%; y el comercio, del 12,6%.




Por último, el MATE sostiene que el modelo económico necesita recurrir al endeudamiento para sostenerse. Abraham explicó que, aunque el país genera dólares a través de las exportaciones agropecuarias, petroleras y mineras, una parte importante de esas divisas se destina al pago de intereses de deuda y a la dolarización de activos por parte de grandes empresas y sectores de altos ingresos.




“Los dólares que la economía real genera no son suficientes para atender la demanda de la economía financiera”

, plantea el documento. En esa línea, Abraham sostuvo que el esquema depende de conseguir financiamiento externo y que, cuando ese endeudamiento se encarece o deja de estar disponible, aparecen las dificultades para sostenerlo.

title: Missouri Voters Reject Effort to Overturn Their State’s Abortion Protections
content:
The measure would also have banned gender-affirming care for transgender minors, which is already illegal in the state.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Missouri voters rejected an effort to overturn their state’s abortion protections, according to a projection by Decision Desk HQ, ensuring that the procedure will remain legal and enshrined in the state constitution despite dedicated efforts by Republican leadership.

Amendment 3 would have reversed the results of a 2024 vote that enshrined abortion protections into the state constitution and made Missouri the first state with a constitutional ban on the procedure. It would also have banned gender-affirming care for transgender minors, which is already illegal in the state.

The measure’s failure offers a rebuke to efforts by Missouri’s Republican leaders, who largely oppose abortion. Amendment 3 was put forth by Republican lawmakers who, troubled by the 2024 vote’s results, hoped a second vote might result in the undoing of abortion rights. The state’s first lady, Claudia Kehoe, served as treasurer for the campaign to pass Amendment 3.

Polling conducted this summer suggested that while Missouri voters largely supported abortion rights, they opposed keeping gender-affirming care legal for trans minors, a point emphasized by Amendment 3’s backers.

“We’re trying to do everything. We’ve had canvassers knocking on thousands of doors,” Tom Estes, a Republican state Senate staffer working on the pro-Amendment 3 campaign, told The 19th earlier this year. “There are several pieces of this that resonate really well, that we may not have gotten last time. The number one piece of that is the trans issue.”

The campaign also argued that the abortion protections enacted two years ago had made the procedure unregulated and dangerous, suggesting that the new ban would protect women and children.

The reality, according to abortion providers in the state, has been different: Abortion has been highly regulated and only sporadically available. Even prior to the fall of Roe v. Wade in 2022, abortions in Missouri had become almost impossible to obtain, the result of a maze of restrictions enacted by the state’s conservative legislature. By 2022, only one clinic in the state offered abortion, in St. Louis.

“I would love to provide abortion services four to six days a week in Springfield,” Dr. Margaret Baum, the chief medical officer at Planned Parenthood Great Rivers, told The 19th at the end of August. “I think the demand is there.”

author: Harriet Williamson
title: Google UK Signs ‘Sweetheart Deal’ With Employer-Friendly Union
content:
Google UK has been accused of signing a “sweetheart deal” with an employer-friendly union to undermine workers’ ability to organise within the tech company. 




Google 

signed an access agreement with Prospect union on Monday

 to make inroads among its 7,000 UK workers – excluding DeepMind staff – after 

new rights for unions to access workplaces

 in Britain came into force last week.




However, critics say Prospect lacks a strong record of organising with Google employees – known as Googlers – in the UK. The two largest and most active unions in Google UK are Unite and the Communication Workers’ Union (CWU) via their United Tech and Allied Workers (UTAW) branch. 




Prospect was granted access to the Google UK workforce over Unite and the CWU, despite the latter two unions applying for access as soon as formally possible. This means Prospect can now 

communicate with non-unionised workers

 and encourage them to join. 




In a joint Unite and CWU statement to members seen by Novara Media, the two unions warned that Prospect’s agreement with Google is only for “occasional meetings and an internal page, falling far short of the legal minimum requested by your unions”. 




A Google UK software engineer and UTAW rep, speaking to Novara Media on the condition of anonymity due to fear of professional reprisals, called the deal “a huge slap in the face for me and all UTAW and Unite organisers in Google”.  




The software engineer said: “We have worked diligently over the past few years to represent our fellow Googlers’ needs through collective action. We fought to keep as many jobs as possible during redundancies, we demonstrated against Google’s military contracts, and we demanded a stronger, worker-led regulation on Google and DeepMind’s AI direction. 




“For all of our fastidious work, our request for a right as basic as access has been ignored and given to Prospect, a union with laughably low membership in Google which has not participated in a single one of our aforementioned struggles.”




Unite and the CWU are asking why Prospect, which has not engaged in member-led unionising activity at Google, was granted access so quickly and alleging that the Prospect deal was pre-planned because Prospect may be considered a “tamer” or more employer-friendly union.




The Google software engineer added: “This conduct by Google is an insidious way to undermine worker organisation while veiling themselves in the guise of a benevolent, pro-union company. It is telling that this deal was conducted by Google UK’s current senior labour relations consultant, Philip Bickerstaffe, an ex-national officer at Prospect.”




Bickerstaffe worked at Prospect as a national officer from 2004 to 2011, according to his LinkedIn profile, before going on to roles with BT, Boeing, Amazon and Google. 




The Prospect-Google deal follows 

a similar agreement

 between Prospect and Meta, the parent company of Facebook, Instagram and Whatsapp. Meta employs roughly 5,000 people in the UK. 




Right of access to workplaces in the UK – even where employers are hostile to trade unions organising onsite – was included in the Employment Rights Act 2025, and came into force on 30 October. 




Unite and the CWU say they put in an access request at the stroke of midnight on 30 October, and received a formal acknowledgement from Google on 3 November, which said their request would be considered and responded to “within the appropriate time frame”.




Employers then have 15 days to respond and a further 25 days to negotiate. The Prospect deal was announced on 2 November, suggesting that little, if any, time was spent negotiating the terms of the deal, which has added to the impression that the deal is favourable to the employer.




Unite, the CWU and Prospect are all members of the Trade Union Congress (TUC), which means they must 

respect the principle

 that a union shouldn’t organise at a workplace where another union already has the majority of workers as members or is actively engaged in significant organising activity. 




Unite and the CWU say Prospect has violated this national cross-union agreement by signing the access deal with Google UK. 




A Prospect spokesperson said: “These allegations are false and seem designed to undermine union organising at Google. Our access agreement with Google was agreed in accordance with the TUC principles and does not include Google DeepMind where other unions are making a recognition bid.” 




A spokesperson from Google UK said: “To comply with new UK workplace legislation, we have established a structured access agreement with Prospect union for Google’s UK employees, but not including Google DeepMind. This step builds on our established work with internal employee representative groups, allowing us to fulfill these new requirements while preserving the respectful, direct dialogue our culture is built on.” 




Unite and the CWU have assured members that they are escalating the matter through the appropriate channels.

author: Erin Reed
title: Republicans Spent Nearly $200 Million on Ads Attacking Trans People — and Lost
content:
The election was a stunning rebuke of anti-transgender politics, and Democrats should take note moving forward.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

By now, you have likely seen the results of the 2026 midterms: a wave election for Democrats the likes of which we have not seen in years. Republicans and their allies spent nearly $200 million on anti-transgender ads alone, bankrolled in part by billionaires like Elon Musk. Virtually every Democrat in a highly contested race was the target of these kinds of ads. And what did it buy the Republican Party? An earth-shattering loss, and a stunning rebuke of anti-transgender politics.

A blue Texas in the face of the biggest anti-trans ad spend of any race this cycle … a victory in Michigan from a Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate who forcefully defended trans people at every step of the race … a western Montana smokejumper who will go to Congress after telling voters the government has “no business sticking its nose into our personal lives” when it comes to transgender health care and sports … and an Alabama trans Democrat who won her race running on bread-and-butter issues in a conservative district in the Huntsville suburbs. These are just a small handful of the dozens of races we will remember as proof that anti-trans politics simply no longer works for the Republican Party, and that Democrats need never fear such attacks again.

I started writing about anti-transgender politics back in 2022 after the extreme efforts of Texas Gov. Greg Abbott and Attorney General Ken Paxton to sweep the state for transgender kids. In that dark time, they ordered child abuse investigations into the parents of transgender youth, and many of those families fled the state. Now, not only does James Talarico win in the face of ads built around him saying “God is nonbinary,” but Gina Hinojosa, who waved a trans flag on the Texas House floor after Democrats ran out the clock on a sports ban in 2021, wins the governorship. Vikki Goodwin wins the lieutenant governorship after being endorsed by Equality Texas and after voting no on every anti-trans bill that reached the House floor. And more than that, it appears the Texas House is going to go to Democrats for the first time since 2003. The dark era of horrific anti-trans targeting of trans Texans is over, and there is hope that one day, some of the trans people who fled may get to return to the state, despite the millions Elon Musk poured into Texas trying to prevent it.

The positive results for transgender people were not limited to Texas — they were seen across the board. If you were a Democratic consultant who believed that you had to moderate on transgender issues to win an election, the results in places like Montana’s 1st Congressional District make it clear that such capitulation is not necessary in the slightest. Smokejumper Sam Forstag, a Democrat running in a stubbornly Republican House district, won his election handily. When asked whether he supports transgender participation in sports or gender-affirming care for transgender youth, his answer was that the government has no place banning any of it, and that the issue is an attempt to distract voters while Republicans “pick our pockets.” Trump campaigned in Montana for Aaron Flint, his opponent, who ran anti-trans ads. It wasn’t enough. Western Montana will have a Democratic congressman who supports transgender people, and he won one of the toughest races in the country handily.

Several Democrats who championed transgender people won in major swing races, and the most notable was probably Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed. El-Sayed was the target of millions in anti-transgender ads on one side, and drew the ire of centrist Democrats on the other for not moderating on many progressive causes, including transgender people. When asked in a hostile CBS “60 Minutes” interview about trans people and other “social cultural issues,” his response was that “a failure to show up and fight for that right is a failure to show up and fight for your own.” Then, when asked specifically about schools, he called the fight over what kids learn in school a manufactured “cultural flash point.” It cost him nothing in a state Trump won in 2024. El-Sayed won Michigan’s U.S. Senate race by about 6 points as of the early morning hours.

It was also a big night for transgender candidates. Washington state will have the first out Black transgender woman elected to a state legislature in Jaelynn Scott, and Michigan will have a trans woman legislator as well in Joanna Whaley. But perhaps the most stunning result when it comes to transgender people winning their elections was Allison Montgomery, who won in a relatively conservative suburban Huntsville, Alabama, district. She ran on bread-and-butter economic issues. In 2022, the last time the seat was on the ballot, Republican Phillip Rigsby won it by 16 points. Now, she has beaten Rigsby by more than 6 points, a major swing for any Democrat, much less a trans Democrat running in Alabama. “I know the headlines tomorrow are gonna be provocative and catchy, but let’s focus on the most important part of this victory: we showed that a truly grassroots campaign that stands on its policies and its principles has a real shot in Alabama. We the people are tired of attempts to distract us with culture war issues, whether we’re in a minority group or not,” she posted to her campaign site after her victory.

The victories for transgender people didn’t stop there. Of 160 races being tracked by Erin In The Morning with transgender implications, 107 races went for the side supportive of transgender people while 53 went for the side that was not supportive. These races range from school board fights such as the Wake County board of Education going to trans-supportive candidates in North Carolina, to Wisconsin likely carrying a Democratic trifecta, allowing for real protections for transgender people to pass in the state. Meanwhile, candidates like Peggy Flanagan win in Minnesota, even after drawing the ire of Republicans for wearing a Protect trans kids t-shirt with a knife on it. In Mississippi, anti-transgender ads failed against the Democratic candidate for US Senate, who was within striking distance as of this morning. And even in Tennessee, there were victories against anti-transgender politics to be found: Victoria Broderick, a LGBTQ+ woman who has made supportive statements about transgender people, is likely to win her election against Scott DesJarlais in what was supposed to be a safe Republican Seat. “Any politician talking about men in women’s sports is a lazy politician,” Broderick said in the leadup to the election. “They are deflecting from questions about the war in Iran, the gas crisis and what is going on in our country.”

The results were not unanimously good for transgender people. Some anti-transgender democrats such as Josh Turek won, though their influence will be diluted in a party that sent many pro-transgender Democrats from swing states as well. Meanwhile, Anti-trans ballot measures look likely to pass in Colorado and Washington, although the forced outing measure in Washington is trailing, and the same was true in Arizona. But even in these results, the anti-trans side was winning by only 52-48 in Colorado and 57-43 in Arizona and Washington as of the early morning, with plenty of votes left to count. No longer can Republicans claim that even trans sports, the issue they have pegged as the most polarizing of trans-related issues, is an “80-20 issue.” Given the razor-thin margins in Colorado and the incredibly protective state courts in Washington and Colorado, it seems likely that these measures will end up in court, where they could be overturned or defanged. And in some states, transgender people won on ballot measures, such as Vermont, where gender identity will be enshrined in the state constitution, only the third state to do so.

Now, Democrats will hold significant power in state legislatures and nationwide, and they can present a real check on Trump’s power, including his attacks on transgender people. They may be able to stymie Trump’s trans military ban, or use the budget process to hinder the investigations of hospitals and schools that support transgender people. They can ensure that no new national anti-trans policy makes its way into budgets or law. The congressional bathroom ban will likely fall soon, and multiple states could pass protective legislation for transgender people that they could not before. And all of this happened in a national environment where Republicans put more effort into anti-transgender attacks than ever before, only to suffer one of the most devastating results any party has seen in a generation. The election was a stunning rebuke of anti-transgender politics, and Democrats should take note moving forward: it costs nothing to defend transgender people, and it may even lead Republicans to waste their time and money attacking us for virtually no gain.

author: Joshua Carroll
title: Illegal Iran War Helps Boost Oil CEOs’ Personal Fortunes by Millions
content:
The CEO of Shell is among oil bosses who have raked in millions of pounds as the value of their shareholdings soared amid the illegal US war on Iran.




Wael Sawan saw his shares in Shell gain £4.7m since the US and Israel first attacked the country in late February, 

research by Greenpeace

 shows. 




He cashed out £1.3m worth of shares on 22 May, the day before Donald Trump said a deal to cease hostilities had almost been reached. 




Bosses from TotalEnergies, Harbour Energy and Equinor also raked in millions as oil prices surged due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a major global transport route for oil and natural gas.




North Sea oil CEOs have added a total of £19m to their personal fortunes via share price increases since the war began, Greenpeace said.




The windfalls come as 

oil giants report a bumper set of financial results whilst

 households in the UK and across the world struggle with rising energy bills.




Equinor CEO Anders Opedal has seen his shares rise by £1.03m amid the war, while TotalEnergies’s Patrick Pouyanné enjoyed an £8.4m boost to his shareholdings, selling £3.1m in shares and savings one month after the war began. 




“Cashing out millions in personal shares while the market drives millions of people into energy poverty – all while their companies’ operations supercharge climate breakdown – is crisis profiteering at its most cynical,” said Rudy Schulkind, political campaigner at Greenpeace UK.




Equinor and Shell were recently granted permission by Andy Burnham’s government to start new drilling in the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea. Both are also set to benefit in the event that Rosebank oil field is approved.




Oil companies in the US have earned more than $130bn in profits during the war, according to 

an analysis last week

 from the New York Times. 




Trump’s decision to capitulate to Israel and attack Iran appears to have lost him a lot of support –  and is believed to have played a key role in the Republicans’ resounding defeat in the midterms on Tuesday. 




The US president campaigned on an anti-war platform while promising to lower people’s bills.
