author: Darío Aranda
title: Del cautiverio doméstico al tráfico de especies: “La fauna silvestre no es mascota”
content:
Por Ivonne Guevara




Una tortuga en un patio, un loro en una jaula o un animal exótico dentro de una casa pueden parecer escenas inocentes, hasta pintorescas. Pero detrás del mascotismo de fauna silvestre hay pérdida de biodiversidad, riesgos sanitarios y un tráfico ilegal que se cuenta entre los mercados ilícitos más lucrativos del mundo. Claudia Nigro, activista y veterinaria, aclara: “Bastaría con decir que sin vida silvestre la especie humana no podría sobrevivir en el planeta”.




A veces la relación entre las personas y la fauna silvestre comienza con una intención que parece buena, como cuidar, proteger, tener cerca, darle “hogar”. El problema aparece cuando ese vínculo se transforma en apropiación.

El ser humano domesticó algunas especies y las convirtió en animales de compañía hace miles de años. Sin embargo, aquella relación construida a lo largo de generaciones suele confundirse todavía con otra muy distinta, la de querer tener cerca, poseer o encerrar a un animal porque resulta bello, exótico o entrañable.




El problema excede largamente al ejemplar encerrado en una jaula. 

El comercio ilegal de vida silvestre mueve, 

según Interpol

, hasta 20.000

 

millones de dólares

 por año a escala mundial y se encuentra asociado con otras formas de criminalidad organizada. Detrás de muchos animales que terminan en una casa existe una cadena previa de captura, traslado, comercialización y muerte.

Nigro es médica veterinaria de la Universidad Nacional de Rosario, especialista en salud animal con orientación en epidemiología, cofundadora y coordinadora académica de la Cátedra Libre de Fauna Silvestre. “Debemos conservar nuestro patrimonio natural y cultural no solamente porque las generaciones futuras también tienen derecho y necesidad vital de ello, sino además porque es una cuestión ética. Consiste en 

considerar a 

la naturaleza como sujeto de derecho

”, enfatiza.




Foto: Cátedra Libre de Fauna Silvestre




Animales de compañía, no mascotas




Férrea defensora de la fauna y de la naturaleza en todas sus formas y especies, pone en relevancia que 

cada ser que está vivo merece su vida

 y existe una razón para esa existencia. Reflexiona, entonces, sobre esta convivencia entre seres humanos y no humanos en un planeta “preparado a lo largo de millones de años para proporcionarnos, sin pedir nada a cambio, lo que necesitamos para seguir presentes como especie y ser felices”. Propone como tarea “amorosa, estratégica y futurista” 

repensar nuestra manera de cohabitar la Tierra

.




Al hablar del mascotismo, principalmente cuando involucra especies silvestres, Nigro se detiene incluso en la 

palabra mascota, ligada en su origen a la idea de amuleto o talismán. “Nada más lejano a un ser vivo”

, exclama. Por eso sugiere hablar de animales de compañía cuando se trata de especies que pueden efectivamente convivir con los seres humanos.




Pero para que exista esa convivencia hay una historia anterior. Un animal doméstico es el resultado de un proceso de domesticación desarrollado a lo largo de miles de años. Ese proceso se dio a través de la selección de características generación tras generación, con transformaciones genéticas, fisiológicas y comportamentales que permitieron que determinados animales se adapten a la vida junto a las personas.




Pero un animal silvestre no deja de serlo porque haya nacido en cautiverio, porque coma de una mano o porque haya aprendido a tolerar la presencia humana. “A lo sumo se podrá amansarlos de alguna manera y esto está muy ligado a métodos crueles en muchos casos, pero no domesticarlos porque eso llevaría demasiado tiempo”, indica Nigro.




Foto: Claudia Nigro




Una historia de miles de años




La pregunta sobre si alguna especie nació para ser domesticada resulta inevitable. Hoy convivimos con perros, gatos, caballos, vacas, ovejas o cabras con tal naturalidad que resulta difícil imaginar que detrás de esos vínculos existieron alguna vez poblaciones silvestres.




La respuesta de Nigro es clara: “Fue una decisión tomada por el ser humano que aprovechó un agriotipo, que es una especie silvestre ancestral, la hizo atravesar un proceso de domesticación y originó así nuevas especies como perros, gatos, vacas, ovejas, cabras, cerdos, caballos, conejos”.




Con respecto al perro, quizás el compañero más estrechamente asociado a nuestra especie, la veterinaria analiza que la intervención fue tan exitosa que los seres humanos podemos expresar afecto sabiendo que el animal es capaz de interpretar buena parte de esos gestos y establecer con nosotros un vínculo social extraordinariamente cercano.







“

Como casi todos sabemos, el perro deviene del lobo y a pesar de que los últimos hallazgos fósiles señalan que hubo no menos de 35.000 años de domesticación, se cree que podrían ser muchísimos más, hasta 150.000 años”, revela.







La investigación genética siguió avanzando desde entonces y hoy obliga a poner esa cifra en discusión. Distintos estudios sitúan la separación entre los linajes ancestrales de perros y lobos en decenas de miles de años, aunque sigue sin estar resuelto exactamente cuándo, dónde y de qué manera comenzó la domesticación. Separación genética y domesticación, además, no necesariamente ocurrieron al mismo tiempo. Lo que no cambia es la diferencia fundamental: “Un ejemplar silvestre amansado continúa siendo silvestre”, asevera.




Foto: Argentina.gob.ar




El lugar que ocupa cada animal




Para Nigro, el rol de la fauna silvestre dentro de los ecosistemas es uno de los fundamentos más importantes para impedir la extracción de ejemplares de su ambiente. “Sin vida silvestre la especie humana no podría sobrevivir en el planeta. Conservar la biodiversidad es esencial para estabilizar los procesos evolutivos que sostienen el funcionamiento de los ecosistemas”, manifiesta.

La activista deja en claro que cada ejemplar pertenece a una población y forma parte de una trama mucho más compleja. Las especies intervienen en relaciones de alimentación y reproducción, dispersan semillas, polinizan, regulan poblaciones, transforman materia y participan del reciclado de nutrientes. Por lo tanto, sacar un animal del monte, del pastizal o del humedal no significa solamente trasladar un individuo, sino también intervenir sobre relaciones construidas a lo largo de miles de años.




En ese punto, introduce otro concepto relevante: el de “Una Salud”. La perspectiva reconoce 

la interdependencia entre la salud humana, la de los animales y la de los ecosistemas

. En Argentina, el Senasa (Servicio Nacional de Sanidad y Calidad Agroalimentaria) trabaja bajo 

este enfoque en la vigilancia y prevención

 de enfermedades, articulando con organismos de salud, ambiente, universidades y distintas jurisdicciones. “Los disturbios provocados por las intervenciones antrópicas pueden dañar momentánea o definitivamente el delicado y necesario equilibrio de los ambientes naturales y sus componentes, lo cual, más temprano que tarde, se vuelve un búmeran muy peligroso que podría afectar en última instancia a nuestra propia subsistencia”, alerta.







En mayo de 2026, la Organización Mundial de la Salud

 

(OMS)

 

volvió a reforzar esta mirada. Advirtió

 

que alrededor del 

60 por ciento de las nuevas enfermedades infecciosas

 que se registran en el mundo proceden de animalessilvestres

 

y domésticos.

 

Entre los factores capaces de favorecer su aparición y propagación aparecen el comercio de animales, la agricultura, la ganadería, la urbanización, el cambio climático y la fragmentación de los hábitats. La fauna encerrada en una casa también forma parte de esta discusión.







Foto: Cátedra Libre de Fauna Silvestre




Legislaciones, avances y pendientes




“La educación, sin lugar a duda, sigue siendo la herramienta más potente para intentar desactivar el tráfico clandestino de vida silvestre. Educar en todos los niveles, sin olvidar al público en general, deviene imprescindible porque entre otros logros permite que se construya un sentimiento de pertenencia hacia nuestros bienes naturales”, destaca.




Propone transversalizar contenidos relacionados con la Biología de la Conservación dentro de las distintas materias curriculares. La 

Ley Nacional 27.621 de Educación Ambiental Integral

, sancionada en 2021, establece la educación ambiental como una política pública nacional permanente y tiene como principal instrumento la Estrategia Nacional de Educación Ambiental Integral.

Nigro también considera fundamentales el establecimiento y sostenimiento de áreas naturales protegidas, reservas y parques que permitan conservar poblaciones silvestres frente al avance de las fronteras agropecuaria y urbana, la deforestación, los incendios, diferentes formas de contaminación, la caza furtiva, la sobreexplotación de especies, las especies exóticas y la 

crisis climática

.




La protección de la fauna en Argentina se sostiene sobre distintas normas y jurisdicciones. Al caso, la 

Ley Nacional 22.421

 de Conservación de la Fauna fue sancionada en 1981 y continúa vigente. Allí se declara de interés público la protección y conservación de la fauna silvestre y regula, entre otras actividades, su captura, tenencia, posesión, tránsito y comercio.




Esto requiere una precisión respecto de una idea bastante extendida. La legislación nacional no establece que cualquier tenencia de un animal silvestre constituya automáticamente un delito. La legalidad depende de la especie, su procedencia, la documentación correspondiente y las normas de cada jurisdicción. La legislación contempla, bajo regulación, criaderos y otras formas de mantenimiento de fauna en cautiverio. En la provincia de Buenos Aires, por ejemplo, existen establecimientos habilitados que crían y comercializan determinados animales nacidos en cautiverio y cuya procedencia legal debe estar respaldada por documentación. La 

Dirección de Flora y Fauna bonaerense

 advierte, al mismo tiempo, sobre el mascotismo y su relación con el tráfico ilegal.




Tandil, ciudad del sudeste de la provincia de Buenos Aires, cuenta desde 1988 con la 

Ordenanza 4548

, que prohíbe la comercialización, el obsequio y la simple tenencia de especies animales silvestres, además de su utilización en espectáculos circenses, exposiciones o sitios de entretenimiento. La propia normativa contempla excepciones para ejemplares provenientes de criaderos debidamente autorizados y para entidades con fines proteccionistas o conservacionistas. Mientras tanto, el tráfico de fauna comenzó a ser abordado cada vez con mayor claridad como algo más que un problema de conservación.




Por otro lado, en agosto de 2026, la Policía de Seguridad Aeroportuaria (PSA) presentó 

el primer Protocolo Nacional

 de Actuación para la Prevención, Detección y Abordaje del Tráfico Ilegal de Vida Silvestre en Aeropuertos. La iniciativa estableció criterios comunes de actuación ante el traslado ilegal de ejemplares, piezas y productos de fauna en las terminales aéreas del país.

Un mes después, el Ministerio de Justicia y la organización Wildlife Conservation Society Argentina 

firmaron un convenio

 para fortalecer la prevención, investigación y persecución de estos delitos. El acuerdo contempla asistencia técnica, capacitación, intercambio de información y análisis de posibles reformas normativas.




Foto: Juan Matín Mastropaolo




Llevarlo a casa no es rescate




Detrás de un pájaro en una jaula, una tortuga en un patio o un animal exótico ofrecido en una red social puede haber mucho más que una decisión individual. Puede haber captura, comercio ilegal, sufrimiento animal, 

pérdida de biodiversidad

, riesgos sanitarios y organizaciones que encontraron en la vida silvestre otro negocio.




Nigro repasa que un animal silvestre puede alojar bacterias, virus, hongos, ácaros, protozoos y otros organismos con los que ha coevolucionado. “Cuando aparece un factor que altera ese equilibrio, algunos de ellos pueden provocar enfermedad en el propio animal o transmitirse a otras especies”, insiste.




Cuando se extrae un ejemplar de su hábitat pierde buena parte de las condiciones que necesita para desarrollar las estrategias de vida para las que evolucionó. Además, el estrés puede afectar a su sistema inmune y favorecer la aparición de enfermedades. La psitacosis, por ejemplo, es una enfermedad bacteriana que puede transmitirse desde distintas aves, particularmente psitácidos como loros y cotorras, hacia las personas. De hecho, si se trata de aves puntualmente, dejan de volar libremente. Muchos ejemplares quedan aislados de sus congéneres, reciben una alimentación incorrecta o insuficiente y permanecen en espacios donde no pueden expresar sus comportamientos naturales.




Tortugas dentro de cajas, aves de gran porte en jaulas pequeñas o animales sociales condenados a vivir solos forman parte de una realidad que muchas veces comienza con la intención de cuidarlos. “En realidad, amansados, algunos podrían perderle miedo a las personas, pero jamás dejarían de ser silvestres y por tanto, son diametralmente opuestos a los domésticos”, distingue Nigro. También pueden ser atacados por perros o gatos o sufrir accidentes domésticos.




Encontrar un animal lastimado o fuera de su ambiente no significa que llevarlo a una casa y conservarlo sea necesariamente rescatarlo. “Los animales silvestres que requieren asistencia necesitan evaluación, rehabilitación y, cuando es posible, una estrategia adecuada para regresar a su ambiente. Aun cuando un ejemplar coma de nuestra mano, reconozca nuestra presencia o lleve años viviendo en cautiverio, esa diferencia permanece”, aclara. Y enfatiza que “amansar no es domesticar, y quizás querer tampoco debería ser sinónimo de poseer”.




Foto: Juan Martín Mastropaolo




La entrada 

Del cautiverio doméstico al tráfico de especies: “La fauna silvestre no es mascota”

 se publicó primero en 

Agencia de Noticias Tierra Viva

.

author: Donald Zrebiec
title: She Was Here: Finding My Grandmother After Willard
content:
I

 often mention that I was the only one of Catherine Smoral’s grandchildren to see her alive. I was six years old, and the visit to Willard State Hospital was a bad experience for all four of us who were there: my mother Anna, my Uncle Tony, me, and my grandmother Catherine. The three of us who came from Syracuse were all shocked at the physical and mental condition of our mother and grandmother. Our visit upset her, and we spent a very short time there before being asked to leave.




My grandmother was born in Poland in 1884. She emigrated to the U.S. in 1900, and in 1902 she married my grandfather, Karol Smoral. They were married at Sacred Heart, a beautiful Polish church that still stands on the west side of Syracuse. They were a happy couple who went on to have nine children, a happy and healthy brood. Karol bought his own home on Morgan Avenue, and a family burial plot at Sacred Heart Cemetery not far from it. In the early 1920s, disaster struck the household.




I received, I believe from Ancestry.com, a copy of an article from the Syracuse Herald from the early 1920s. This is how it read:




SMORAL FAMILY WOES CULMINATE IN COMMITTAL OF EIGHT TO INSTITUTIONS. Mother and Son Are Sent to Willard. Six Younger Children to Various Orphanages. Father Died in December.




Mrs. Catherine Smoral and son Stephen, 15, were committed to Willard. Until death delivered its first blow at 107 Morgan Avenue, the family of Karol had something resembling happiness. The mother, who had been in a State Hospital before, had been returned to her family apparently cured. Stephen, then the oldest child, was of working age at 16. The children were sufficiently nourished and progressing. When Karol died, his wife became melancholic, and their son Stephen succeeded her as both mother and father of the household. The burden of being both mother and father broke him down. An investigator from the International Institute found the family nearly destitute. The son Stephen had been employed in a laboratory, but conditions for work were made impossible.




Awaiting his transfer to his new home, Chester drugged himself [he was a year and a half old at the time] with some chocolate he was given by someone in the courtroom. He smeared himself with the chocolate . . . Welfare workers are working to find him a home in a Polish family. The four girls had been all dressed up for the trip and were quiet. They had been weeping.




No matter how many times I see or read this article, I get emotional. It encapsulates the reason I wrote the book. I have a lot of trouble with it. First, it is inaccurate, and it tries to make those kids into clowns instead of marveling at their courage. Perhaps what bothers me most is the comment early on that the family had “something resembling happiness.” Who in the hell was that reporter to make a judgment like that? That’s my family he is talking about. How did they make this family tragedy a front-page story, and why did they try to turn it into some semi-comic farce? Every time I reread it, I would like to hit that reporter right in the face. But at the time, maybe mental illness and sudden death were subjects for fun and light-heartedness.




His name was never Chester. His given name was Vincent, and his nickname was Chet. I get upset about his “drugging himself” on chocolate when he was a year and a half old. He may never have had chocolate until that day. I always admired him. He became a scholarship athlete who went to college and was the first member of the Smoral family to graduate, and he was an excellent role model for his children.




Then there is the way they described the girls, all dressed up but weeping. Those girls were about six, eight, and ten years old. They had just lost both parents, their home, and probably each other, and the newspaper noticed that they had been crying. This was my family they were talking about. They should have had the sense to commend those children for holding up so well. A lot of children could not have, and I wouldn’t have blamed them. This article encapsulates all of the sadness in this whole story.




Zrebiec family photo. Courtesy of Don Zrebiec




I got over the visit to Willard pretty quickly. My picture of my grandmother faded after a short time, and I became immersed in the process of growing up. I talked to my mother about her mother at times, but she always seemed reluctant to go very deep in these conversations and often changed the subject. She had been hurt by something that happened with a family of distant relatives who used her as their housekeeper, but she was happy remembering her mother’s love of singing Polish songs to and with her children.




It was a long time before the subject came back to us with any depth. My father died of cirrhosis of the liver in 1956, and in 1957 my mother learned that her mother, Catherine, had died at Willard State Hospital. I was living at my mother’s, preparing to go back to Syracuse University after three years away in the Army. I have no recollection of my mother or any of her siblings going down to Willard for a burial service, but I may have been too tied up with my own concerns. I do know my mother began to make inquiries about how to bring Catherine’s remains back to Syracuse.




I found out later, in my own inquiries, that burials of patients at Willard were unceremonious. The remains were buried in an open field near Willard and identified by a small numbered aluminum cap placed in the ground where the person lay. The field was not maintained very well, so finding a grave could be very difficult. This became a major point of contention for Willard families, and several years later the New York State Assembly passed a law making it much easier for families to look for their deceased loved ones. What exactly that bill did, I do not know.




In 1975 the company I worked for, Xerox, transferred my family and me from Rochester to its corporate headquarters in Stamford, Connecticut. In one of my biweekly phone calls with my mother, she told me she had successfully moved her mother’s remains from Willard to Syracuse. I was amazed. It had to be a difficult and expensive process. I didn’t ask her about the details, but she was very happy it was done. The burial plot Karol had bought at Sacred Heart Cemetery had passed to my mother.




In 1979 Xerox transferred me back to Rochester, and a short time later I drove into the cemetery to visit the Smoral plot. It was a little run down, to say the least, and I couldn’t find a gravestone for my grandmother. As soon as I got home, I called my mother to ask about it. She started crying and told me she had used all her money moving her mother’s remains, but she was saving her spare money and would buy her a stone as soon as she could. My heart fell, and I cried too. I asked why she hadn’t called me for help. She said she didn’t want to bother me; she was trying to do it herself. I quickly convinced her it was our problem and that I would help.




The following week I took a day off, drove to Syracuse, and bought a new gravestone for my grandmother, and one for my sister Betty, who had died at six from a ruptured appendix. Betty was two years older than me. My mother had had her mother’s name engraved on the back of Betty’s stone. That is why I couldn’t find it.




Today, in the Smoral plot in Syracuse, all with legible gravestones, lie my grandmother and grandfather, my mother and father, my older brother John and his wife Kay, my sister Betty, and my uncles Steve and Joseph, both children of Karol and Catherine.




I know how much this meant to my mother. She started working outside the house when I went into first grade and worked until she was 64, most of that time on the assembly line at G.E. She worked extremely hard and never complained. She never had an extra dime, partly because of my father’s drinking, but when I first started college, if she had a dollar she would give me half of it. She was kind, soft-hearted, and intelligent, and anyone who knew her loved her. I was lucky to have her as my mom, because I would have gone nowhere without her.




The next big event in my grandmother’s story and mine came after I had retired from Xerox and joined the faculty of the Rochester Institute of Technology. There were always old newspapers around, and sometime between 1995 and 1998 I picked one up. The first article I looked at said that Willard was closing, and that a trove of residents’ personal belongings had been found in the attic of one of the buildings. They were going to put the items on display, and if you could prove a connection, you could take an item home.




I immediately ran to my office to call Willard. I wanted something of my grandmother’s to keep and to remember her by. A rosary, a prayer book, an umbrella; my mind started racing. When I got through, they told me the attic exhibit had closed a week earlier. I called again the next day to ask whether there was any way to go through what remained for something, anything, of Catherine Smoral’s. A very nice young man who had worked on the exhibit told me there were few things left, but he would carefully go through them and call me within a week. He did call. He had found nothing, and he was sorry, because it seemed to mean so much to me. It did mean a lot to me, and so my quest for information on Catherine through New York State began.




I never thought it would be so difficult and frustrating. Probably the hardest part of the whole journey was dealing not only with the Office of Mental Health but with the entire political structure of the state. I was directed to the New York State Office of Mental Health in Albany. Many of the calls I made and the letters I wrote are included in She Was Here. Almost from the first call, I noticed an adversarial tone in our exchanges on every subject. The Office of Mental Health seemed to have a separate department for saying no, and I believe I was misled by them several times.




I wanted to know the reason for her hospitalization. I always thought it was a bad case of depression, considering the disasters in her personal life, but I don’t think her death certificate mentions depression. Perhaps it had a different definition and meaning back in 1920. More importantly, I wanted to know how she was treated while she was at Willard, and that was almost impossible. Asking where her treatment records could be found produced a lot of answers, none of them accurate. I eventually found out through the internet that the records had been sent to the state hospital in Binghamton. I called the records section there and spoke to a helpful young woman who said she would look them up and let me know when she had sent them. I heard nothing for almost three weeks, so I called again. A less friendly woman told me the first had left, with no mention of my earlier call, and no, she didn’t know where she had gone or how to reach her.




After giving up on the Office of Mental Health, I started writing to every New York politician I could find: Governor Cuomo, Lieutenant Governor Hochul, Senator Gillibrand, Senator Schumer, and my local representatives, State Senator Funke, State Senator Brouk, and Assemblywoman Lunsford. Out of all of them, I received one letter, from Kathy Hochul when she was Lieutenant Governor, telling me she had forwarded my letter to the Office of Mental Health. One of my state senators’ aides did listen. She sounded ready and willing to help, said she would call back in ten days with a progress report, and kindly gave me her personal phone number to call anytime. After three weeks I called, and the number had been disconnected. I never heard from that office again. No one else replied in any way.




Someone at the Office of Mental Health mentioned that there was a statute on the books sealing the records of Willard patients. I never chased that one down. But suffice it to say, New York State makes it very difficult to get information about relatives who were sent to Willard. When I first started collecting what little I could from the state, I came across a website run by a woman who had a close relative at Willard, just as she was announcing that after six years she would no longer continue it, because of her problems with the state.




I retired after thirty years at Xerox. I was lucky enough to have a very successful career, and I really enjoyed my job and the people of Xerox. Then I joined the faculty of the Rochester Institute of Technology and spent another ten good years in its College of Business. During my time in Rochester I was asked to serve on at least nine community boards, all not-for-profit organizations, among them Highland Hospital, Rochester Blue Cross/Blue Shield, the Rochester Institute of Technology, the Memorial Art Gallery, and St. John’s Senior Communities.




When I retired from RIT in 2000, I really did want to retire. I had a good friend at RIT named Jim Papero who thought otherwise. He was on the board of an organization called East House, which I had never heard of, and for six months before I retired he ran a campaign, sometimes a little hard to take, to get me to join him. Almost to quiet him down, I agreed to have lunch with Jim and the CEO of East House. Greg is a hard guy not to like. When he told me about their mission, which was to help people recover from a mental illness, a substance use problem, or both, and that their mission statement was to MOVE LIVES FORWARD, he had me.




I was on that board for several years and was chair for a period. It was my most meaningful and worthwhile board experience. We treat our clients as people who have temporarily fallen off track, and we help them back on. I met several of our clients and heard their stories of recovery, and I couldn’t help but think of my grandmother as a client of East House rather than of Willard. We have made a lot of progress in dealing with mental illness, but we need a lot more, a lot sooner.




My lovely wife Susan and I were married for 63½ years. She died in September 2024. We were blessed with a long and loving relationship. She was always supportive of my attempts to learn more about Catherine Smoral and to find a way to honor her. She never saw or read my book about Catherine, 

She Was Here

, but I know she would have loved the book and would be proud of how I have it displayed in our living room.




My oldest grandson, Matthew, an entrepreneur in Brooklyn, and I have always been close. He came up to spend a weekend in Rochester about a year after Sue’s passing, when I had been thinking about selling the house we had lived in for 28 years. Sitting on the kitchen table was a sheaf of papers I had collected in my search for Catherine’s background. I didn’t mean to leave it there. Naturally, he asked me what was in the folder. “My grandmother’s history,” I replied. When I told him I hadn’t figured out what to do with it, and that I might have to destroy it, he jumped up and said, “You’re going to forget her like everyone else.” I asked him what he thought I should do. His immediate response was, “Write a book for her.” As soon as he said it, I committed to doing it.




Thank you again, Matthew.




The post 

She Was Here: Finding My Grandmother After Willard

 appeared first on 

Mad In America

.

title: Oufti c'est les jeunes qui dissipent les ténèbres !
content:
C'est une information déterminante et pourtant largement négligée, le mouvement lycéen français a déjà largement débordé le cadre national. En tant qu'écho lui-même d'un soulèvement de la GenZ éparpillé dans le temps et l'espace, il est crucial d'en scruter toutes les résonances. Le 1

er

 octobre 2026, à Liège, des jeunes qui en avaient peut-être marre de jouer aux colibris sont sortis de leurs écoles et ont allumé des feux de trottinettes et de poubelles. Ces premières lueurs ont donné le coup d'envoi d'une séquence politique dans laquelle, traversant l'espace public comme des vols d'étourneaux, les jeunes des écoles montrent qu'il est encore possible de refuser le monde comme il va (dans le mur) et d'habiter politiquement les rues et les places de la métropole.




Flashback




Une odeur de fumée a traîné dans nos narines l'été dernier. Ce n'était plus l'hallucination olfactive liée à la Covid-19, mais les forêts et les fagnes wallonnes qui (après les rivières à l'été 2021) entraient en fanfare dans l'Anthropocène. Jusque-là relégués à un ailleurs lointain, les mégafeux de la canicule ont cette fois joué à domicile. À l'ici-et-maintenant devenu apocalyptique, nos responsables politiques n'ont rien répondu – rien de décent en tout cas. Darons et daronnes sidérées et anesthésiées par la succession des désastres humains et environnementaux, comme par la morgue et la brutalité de ceux qui auraient dû en répondre, nous-mêmes n'avons rien répliqué – rien d'adéquat en tout cas. Aucune de ces répliques n'a infléchi la situation d'un iota. Le train du monde a continué d'aller comme il va, sans frein et à l'abîme. Nous sommes restés assis dans notre compartiment, dépossédés de notre capacité d'agir dans l'exacte mesure où nous étions dépossédés de notre capacité à ressentir pleinement ce que nous éprouvons – tristesse, colère ou joie. Tristesse de la perte de ce à quoi nous tenons, colère face aux irresponsables et à la somme de leurs irresponsabilités, joie de peut-être agir ensemble pour y répliquer.




L'été est passé, les mégafeux se sont éteints. Nous sommes « rentrés » – de vacances, à l'école, au turbin. Nous nous sommes rendues à toutes ces choses qui n'attendent pas, apparemment plus urgentes qu'un monde qui brûle. Sans l'irruption des quelques lueurs qui, depuis ces poubelles de l'histoire du monde, ont commencé à faire événement, notre rentrée n'aurait été qu'une gesticulation de morts-vivants. Si elle a finalement été autre chose, c'est parce que l'action des jeunes des écoles a réouvert le champ du possible.




Révoltes férales




Virevoltant dans le centre de Liège par nuées aussi organiques et synchronisées qu'erratiques et spontanées, les jeunes des écoles et leur mobilité ont déconcerté. Personne n'y a d'abord rien compris, ni la police, ni les vilains gauchistes censés les « manipuler ». (Comme si ces jeunes avaient besoin de nous pour se mettre en mouvement, alors que ce sont précisément eux qui sont en train de nous rendre le sens et le goût du mouvement, l'audace et la joie de reprendre la ville, d'initier un cortège sauvage, de bloquer hier un rond-point ou une autoroute, demain peut-être une raffinerie ou une usine d'armement.) C'est qu'ils passent du concours de danse aux feux d'artifice en plein jour, de la battle d'aura à l'assaut des grandes enseignes. Sur la Place Saint-Lambert, certaines sont costumées en sorcières, en animaux kawaï, en superhéros. D'autres en cailleras. D'autres encore, nettement plus âgés, sont costumés en robocops et en brouillards toxiques. 

Èt qwè chal, carnaval ?

 Certes oui, avec toute l'ambivalence de ces moments où l'ordre symbolique vacille, où la fête peut impromptu virer à l'émeute.




Dès les premiers bris de verre et feux de poubelles, une frange non négligeable de l'opinion publique (et de la presse de caniveau qui l'amplifie) a employé un lexique opérant une animalisation des jeunes, et en particulier des jeunes racisés. La stratégie rhétorique est connue. Elle opère à peu de frais une relégation hors de la sphère du sens et de la raison (opération d'autant plus facile qu'elle vise des mineurs). Elle légitime aussi d'avance toutes les violences destinées à mater les « pulsions » et « instincts primaires » de cette « horde encapuchonnée (sic) ». En comparant les jeunes des écoles à des nuées (ou 

murmurations

) d'étourneaux, nous entendons prendre cette stratégie d'animalisation à revers. Des vols d'étourneaux qui peuplent la Place de la République française et ses environs, nous retenons le plaisir et l'ardeur, la beauté chorégraphique, l'appel d'air du possible. Nous retenons aussi la féralité, cette forme de vie sauvage ou de seconde nature qui s'épanouit au sein des infrastructures capitalistes et les met parfois en déroute. Comme les pigeons féraux, les étourneaux sont à la fois dans et hors la ville. Ils habitent autrement la métropole, ils la traversent avec une liberté synchronisée et une spontanéité organique – en lui chiant quelquefois dessus au passage.




Recouvrer le sens et la raison




Nous voulons remercier ces jeunes étourneaux à qui l'on reproche d'avoir quitté la sphère du sens et de la raison, parce qu'ils nous l'ont en réalité doublement restituée. Ils nous l'ont restituée en nous offrant des assemblages de gestes, de mots et de signes tout à fait inédits. Choses vues les samedi après-midi : Glatigny

 [

1

]

 t'es foutue Harry Potter est dans la rue ; un blocage d'autoroute improvisé et presque aussi débonnaire qu'une Marche Adeps ; « Ne nous regardez pas, rejoignez-nous » : à l'arrêt de bus, une dame âgée appuyée sur une béquille sourit en montrant sa jambe ; un lapin blanc géant ampli d'air crie « ACAB » à plein poumons devant l'hôtel de ville de Liège. Ces assemblages de corps et de signes initient une nouvelle circulation du sens et nous appellent à la prolonger – par des gestes et des mots hérités des luttes antérieures, mais aussi par un travail d'explicitation du sens que ces nouveaux assemblages charrient. La séquence politique qui vient de s'ouvrir nous rappelle qu'un événement historique ne se réduit pas à son avoir-lieu, mais inclut la signification qui s'en dégage. Ce qui fait de la prise de la Bastille l'événement historique que l'on sait, c'est que le sens d'un évènement qui pouvait jusqu'à un certain point être lu comme une émeute est devenu celui d'un acte de souveraineté populaire

 [

2

]

. Dans cette optique, le commentaire de l'événement fait encore pleinement partie de l'événement.




D'où l'importance – et en l'occurrence la défection ou la capitulation – des médias de service public. Plutôt que de chercher à expliciter de manière plurielle le sens des événements, ces médias ont majoritairement choisi d'en siphonner le sens en dépossédant les acteurs de leurs capacités d'agir, selon deux stratégies complémentaires : complotisme et sociologisme. Chercher qui tire les ficelles ; chercher dans les aléas d'une trajectoire individuelle l'explication d'un acte qui restera isolé. Chercher qui pousse à « casser » ; chercher par quelle fatalité sociale on devient un « casseur ». Mais ne jamais s'interroger sur les multiples significations que pourrait charrier le geste de la « casse », dans le contexte du démantèlement brutal de l'État social postcolonial, de l'apocalypse climatique désormais éprouvée dans la chair et de la continuation d'un génocide au vu et au su de la planète entière.




Si les étourneaux des écoles nous ont restitué la sphère du sens et de la raison, c'est peut-être aussi, et avant tout, en reconnectant ce qu'on nous avait trop bien appris à séparer : le sentir et l'agir, le sens et la matérialité. Beaucoup des mobilisations récentes en Belgique ont convoqué le lexique de la colère. Pour exprimer cette colère, on a défilé pendant des mois de manière paisible, comme si la signification de la colère pouvait cohabiter avec la matérialité de corps et de socialités apaisées. L'inflexibilité de la coalition Arizona atteste que ces manifestations de colère paisible(s) s'effectuent en pure perte. Pragmatiquement, la répétition rituelle de ce type de protestation n'a plus grand-chose de rationnel. En nous rendant le goût de la manifestation sauvage, les jeunes étourneaux des écoles nous aident à recouvrer un peu de raison.




L'inefficacité de la protestation paisible serait toutefois un moindre mal, si elle ne contribuait pas simultanément à miner les affects qu'elle est censée rendre manifestes. Qu'est-ce qu'une colère qui n'explose pas ? Pour s'éprouver colère, la colère (que nous sommes raisonnablement en droit de ressentir face à l'état du monde) ne doit-elle pas d'une façon ou d'une autre – sous peine d'atrophie et d'anesthésie – trouver à exploser ? En lui permettant d'enfin exploser (de façon somme toute assez mesurée, compte tenu de l'ampleur des désastres qui peuvent la susciter), les jeunes des écoles ont reconnecté le sens et la matérialité de la colère, qui n'auraient sans doute jamais dû être séparés. En ce sens, la parade sauvage de ces étourneaux est thérapeutique. Elle nous restitue les affects – de tristesse, de colère et de joie – que des « politiques de la cruauté » (qui nous exposent impuissant

·

es à une accumulation de violences traumatiques ici et ailleurs) avaient progressivement confisqués en les anesthésiant

 [

3

]

.




Proclamer les solidarités




Mais le pouvoir est obtus. Liège devait retrouver son calme, les touristes devaient pouvoir manger leurs gaufres et les forains réinventer le vigilantisme avec des barres de fer et la bénédiction du procureur du Roi

 [

4

]

. Après avoir inondé le centre-ville de gaz lacrymogène, multiplié les arrestations au faciès et les violences sur mineurs (et sur leurs témoins), après avoir réactivé la « bulle de trois » (voire de deux pour les sorties de gardes à vue) et les arguties théologiques du bon vieux temps pandémique, les autorités politiques de la ville ont proclamé le 19 octobre dernier l'efficacité de l'autoritarisme et la victoire sur le mouvement des casseurs. Ce que nous voudrions pour notre part proclamer, c'est l'ampleur de la solidarité avec le mouvement des étourneaux.




Des enseignantes sont venues soutenir les élèves puis les étudiants sur les blocus de leur établissement. Des parents et adultes alliés ont rejoint les manifestations d'élèves et d'étudiantes des hautes écoles et de l'université. Des travailleuses ont informé les jeunes sur leurs droits. Des infirmiers ont soigné les blessées en première ligne. Des activistes ont distribué du sérum physiologique et des masques, mais aussi des crêpes et du réconfort. Des médecins ont ouvert leur cabinet à des personnes qui ne faisaient pas partie de leur patientèle pour établir des constats de coups et blessures. Des psychologues se sont mis à disposition pour recueillir les traumatismes à vif. Des avocates ont investi les commissariats pour défendre le droit des mineurs. Des dizaines de personnes ont fait le pied de grue devant le commissariat central de la rue Natalis, pour accueillir les jeunes arrêtés arbitrairement, relâchés souvent en pleine nuit, pour les ramener en sécurité chez eux, écouter leurs témoignages et leur dire merci pour tout vous n'êtes pas seuls

 [

5

]

. Des travailleurs sociaux et des éducatrices ont orienté celles et ceux qui se trouvaient déboussolés par les coups et blessures reçus. Un bureau des plaintes s'est mis en place pour établir des archives de la répression, conduire une enquête indépendante et travailler à un contre-récit.




Suivre le lapin blanc de la jeunesse dorée




En 2021, Liège avait déjà connu des émeutes suite à une agression raciste de la police sur fond de répression de la jeunesse durant la période Covid

 [

6

]

. Les moyens judiciaires considérables alors déployés pour punir et faire payer lourdement un maximum de contestataires, faire taire les plaintes ainsi que continuer à nier les violences et le racisme systémique au sein de la police de Liège, n'ont rien résolu. Au contraire, ces choix politiques ont contribué à l'escalade des événements récents. Plus largement, le contexte inédit de perte d'influence géopolitique européenne et de dégradation des conditions d'habitabilité de la Terre est aussi celui du surgissement mondial d'une autoproclamée « jeunesse dorée », prête à sauver la mise en contestant pied à pied, dans la rue, un devenir mortifère – sans que personne ne l'ait vue venir. Des révoltes de la Gen-Z ont éclaté au Népal, au Maroc, en Indonésie, en Inde, au Chili, en Albanie, Serbie, France, Espagne, Italie, … et aussi en Belgique. La tâche de cette génération est immense, mais elle apprend très vite.




Nous nous réjouissons de la jonction entre la jeunesse dorée et des aînées décidées à faire autre chose que l'abandonner à la brutalité des forces de l'ordre. Cette jonction intergénérationnelle s'opère autour d'une relation émotionnelle forte, basée sur l'attention, la reconnaissance et des gages d'appui mutuels. La jeunesse dorée mérite d'être célébrée : née sans cuiller en or dans la bouche, mais dorée par son audace et la lumière qui en émane. Quand Alice voit passer un lapin blanc portant gilet et montre à gousset, et répétant qu'il est « en retard », elle le suit. En suivant le lapin blanc de la jeunesse dorée, nous ne pourrons que nous retrouver sur le chemin du pays des merveilles – le seul chemin qui ne soit pas celui de la dépression perpétuelle et des catastrophes infinies.

title: Landlord Forced to Cut Rent by £210 After Demanding £17 Increase
content:
A corporate landlord’s attempt to raise rent by £17.92 a month has backfired spectacularly after a tribunal forced the firm to instead charge its tenant £210 less.




London-based buy-to-rent firm Get Living was 

ordered to cut the monthly charge

 from £2,560 to £2,350 in August after tenant Davide Martinelli took his case to a first-tier tribunal.




Martinelli’s contract had a “rent review clause” under which rent could be increased with inflation, but such clauses were abolished under the Renters’ Rights Act, the tribunal noted. It then went further and ruled that the amount he was already being charged was above market rates. 




It is the eighth time a landlord has been made to reduce rent after trying to increase it since the act came into force in May. On average, tribunals have ordered a reduction of £58 a month, according to industry advisory firm LonRes.  




In one case in September, a landlord in Manchester 

was ordered to reduce the rent

 on a two-bedroom flat by £200 after trying to raise it by £50. 




Landlord Qi Cao requested an oral hearing and a property inspection ahead of the decision but a legal officer refused on the grounds it would be disproportionate.  




Housing minister Matthew Pennycook highlighted the Manchester case last month. “We’re standing up for renters and our reforms are working,” 

he wrote on X

.




The new rights have prompted the National Residential Landlords Association 

to issue a “warning”

 to its members about raising people’s rents.




“We are now reminding you how vital it is to do your due diligence before proposing increased rents,” the association said. ”Tenants can and will challenge proposals at tribunal, even for relatively small amounts.”




As well as making it easier to challenge rent increases, the new law bans no-fault evictions and fixed-term contracts, while also making it harder for landlords to start bidding wars between prospective tenants.




In August, London Centric revealed that landlords had been 

artificially increasing advertised rents

 in order to get around the new rules on bidding wars.

author: Shan Kenshin Ecaldre
title: Rights groups slam PNP double standards over ‘Bato’ wanted notices
content:
While activists and government critics are publicly vilified through wanted posters and terror-tagging, the Philippine National Police (PNP) sees no need to put up similar notices for Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa who has an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court (ICC) for crimes against humanity.

Human rights groups KARAPATAN and Hustisya criticized the PNP’s double standards. They asked why the police readily resort to public shaming and vilification against ordinary Filipinos but exercise restraint toward a former police chief facing international charges.

In a statement on October 30, Atty. VJ Topacio, national board member of Hustisya and a relative of victims of killings under the Rodrigo Duterte administration, pointed to the police’s practice of putting up posters, streamers, and banners targeting activists, critics, and marginalized communities.

Dela Rosa served as PNP chief during Duterte’s presidency and was among the principal figures behind the administration’s bloody war on drugs. Thousands were killed in police operations and other drug-related killings, leaving families demanding justice and accountability.

KARAPATAN Secretary-General Cristina Palabay said that the former police chief should not be treated differently simply because of his political position and connections. “Bato dela Rosa is a fugitive from justice, a former PNP chief with an outstanding arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court for crimes against humanity. He has evaded arrest and remains in hiding instead of facing the charges against him.”

For the groups, the PNP’s reluctance to put up wanted notices exposes the unequal application of state power, particularly when those being pursued are ordinary people versus former government officials.

“The irony is glaring: a former police chief who once wielded the authority of the State now refuses to submit himself to legal process,” Topacio said.

Palabay questioned why people exercising their democratic rights are readily subjected to state vilification while a former high-ranking official facing an international arrest warrant is treated with extraordinary restraint. “People exercising their rights should not be treated as enemies of the State, while a powerful former official wanted under an actual arrest warrant is afforded extraordinary restraint.”

With ICC proceedings moving closer to trial, families of victims and human rights defenders continue to demand dela Rosa’s immediate arrest and accountability for the killings committed under the Duterte administration.

Palabay said that no political position or former government title should place dela Rosa beyond the reach of justice. “No position, political connection, or former title should shield him from accountability. A man who once commanded the police and now serves as a senator of the Republic cannot be allowed to place himself beyond the reach of justice.”

For families who continue to mourn their loved ones, the demand for justice extends beyond the victims of the drug war. Topacio called for accountability for slain activists and other victims of human rights violations perpetrated by state security forces under Duterte and dela Rosa.

“As we, families of victims of killings remember our departed loved ones during this time, we reiterate our demand for the immediate arrest of Bato dela Rosa and for justice to be served,” Topacio said. (RTS, DAA)

Ως μοναδική απάντηση, η εξουσία φαίνεται να οχυρώνεται ακόμη περισσότερο πίσω από την καταστολή και τον έλεγχο.

. Η πρακτική του Υπουργείου Εσωτερικών, που δοκιμάστηκε ήδη στις 24 Οκτωβρίου, να εκδίδει αποφάσεις κατ’ οίκον περιορισμού, βασισμένες στις διατάξεις για την καταπολέμηση της τρομοκρατίας, εναντίον ακτιβιστών που μερικές φορές δεν έχουν κανένα ποινικό μητρώο τέθηκε σε εφαρμογή και μαζικά αυτό το Σάββατο. »




 




Η δικτατορία προχωρά μάλλον, όχι;




Στο μεταξύ, στις 28 Οκτώβρη η Γερουσία ενέκρινε σε πρώτη ανάγνωση, με 229 ψήφους υπέρ και 105 κατά, το νομοσχέδιο 

«όποιος καταστρέφει, πληρώνει»

«

Πρέπει πραγματικά να μην έχει πατήσει κανείς το πόδι του σε διαδήλωση εδώ και αρκετά χρόνια

»

 για να προτείνει κάτι τέτοιο, ανταπάντησε η οικολόγος γερουσιαστής 

M

é

lanie Vogel

, η οποία υπογράμμισε την αδυναμία στην οποία βρίσκονται πολύ συχνά οι διαδηλωτές να εγκαταλείψουν τον χώρο ή να απομακρυνθούν από τις ταραχές, ακριβώς λόγω της δράσης των δυνάμεων επιβολής της τάξης.




Άλλες διατάξεις του νομοσχεδίου προβλέπουν την αφαίρεση περιεχομένου από τα μέσα κοινωνικής δικτύωσης ή ακόμα και τη χρήση αλγοριθμικής βιντεο-επιτήρησης (τα γνωστά 

dr

nes 

, με άδεια που εγκρίθηκε σε πειραματικό στάδιο στο πλαίσιο των Ολυμπιακών Αγώνων του 2024 και έκτοτε παρατείνεται τακτικά.) Το νομοσχέδιο πρέπει τώρα να διαβιβαστεί στην Εθνοσυνέλευση σε ημερομηνία που δεν έχει ακόμη καθοριστεί.

. δεν τίθεται καν υπό κράτηση, εξετάζεται σε «ελεύθερη ακρόαση» για να δηλώσει την ταυτότητά του πριν αφεθεί ελεύθερος. Έπρεπε να κληθεί ξανά για μια άλλη «ακρόαση» την ημέρα της επίθεσης, τη στιγμή που είχε ήδη τραυματίσει σοβαρά έναν άνθρωπος για ρατσιστικούς λόγους. Την ώρα που η καύση ενός κάδου σκουπιδιών τιμωρείται με μέρες άμεσης κράτησης, συνοπτικές δίκες και μερικές φορές με πραγματική φυλάκιση.




 




Πλέον προφυλακισμένος για την επίθεση, ο 

K

é

vin T

 δικαιολόγησε το έγκλημά του, λέγοντας ότι «το 

Trappes

 είναι ένα κρησφύγετο ισλαμιστών». Μάλλον επανέλαβε όσα ήδη διαδίδουν τα ειδησεογραφικά τηλεοπτικά κανάλια και ένα μέρος της πολιτικής τάξης. Ήδη από το 2022, ο Μπαρντελά (του ακροδεξιου 

RN

) δήλωνε ότι «το 

Trappes

 είναι μια ισλαμική Δημοκρατία σε μικρογραφία, η ευρωπαϊκή πρωτεύουσα του τζιχάντ. Αυτό είναι το μέλλον όλης της Γαλλίας αν δεν ανακτήσουμε τον έλεγχο!». Στο 

Cnews

, ο Ζεμούρ υποστήριζε με έμφαση ότι «το 

Trappes

 είναι μια μουσουλμανική πόλη που διέπεται από τον μουσουλμανικό νόμο». 




Ο εισαγγελέας επιβεβαιώνει την ανακάλυψη ενός αντιτύπου του

 

Mein

 

Kampf

 

στην κατοικία του 

K

é

vin T

, αλλά και δεκάδων αυτοκόλλητων που φέρουν τις επιγραφές «Ζητώ η Γαλλία, 

RN

, περήφανος που είμαι Γάλλος», «100% Γάλλος, ζητώ η Γαλλία» και «υποστήριξη στις δυνάμεις τάξης». Τώρα, ο δικηγόρος ενός θύματος της επίθεσης του 

Trappes

 καταθέτει μήνυση εναντίον της Μαρίν Λε Πεν, του Μπαρντελά και του καναλιού 

Cnews

, για 

«συμμετοχή σε εγκληματική οργάνωση με σκοπό την προετοιμασία εγκλήματος κατά προσώπων».

 




 

Φοβάμαι άρα είμαι εδώ










Στη Νίκαια

, στις 24 Οκτώβρη, κατά την απαγορευμένη διαδήλωση, μια 

οργανωμένη ομάδα με γκλομπ, γάντια, μαύρες κουκούλες, επιτέθηκε βίαια

 εναντίον διαδηλωτών

. Αρκετά από τα μέλη αυτού του κομάντο που συνελήφθησαν, έχουν ποινικό μητρώο για ενδοοικογενειακή βία, βία από κοινού, φθορές… κι όμως, όλοι αφέθηκαν ελεύθεροι από τη δικαιοσύνη, ως την ακρόαση τους στις 26 Νοέμβρη. Σε 

βίντεο που δημοσιεύθηκε

 στο 

instagram 

ένας ακροδεξιός ακτιβιστής, με το όνομα 

Lexweights

, 

ανέλαβε ανοιχτά τη συνεργασία

 

μεταξύ των αρχών και των ακροδεξιών κατά της κινητοποίησης. 







 










Α

ς τρομάξουμε την κυβέρνηση_Παρίσι εξεγέρσου










 




Ο Γαβριάς και η 

Cosette

 είναι στο δρόμο, γράφει στο πανκάρτ.




Τα τραγούδια και πειράγματα προς την αστυνομία, αυτές τις μέρες θυμίζουν όντως τον Γαβριά, τον γνωστό ήρωα του 

Βίκτωρα Ουγκώ.

 Τον Γαβριά του οποίου η ίδια η καθημερινή του επιβίωση στους δρόμους του Παρισιού ήταν μια πράξη εξέγερσης, τον Γαβριά που βρίσκει την αξιοπρέπειά του στο οδόφραγμα, που πεθαίνει γιατί όταν οι επαναστάτες ξεμένουν από σφαίρες, βγαίνει μπροστά από το οδόφραγμα, για να μαζέψει φυσίγγια από τους νεκρούς.




Ο συγγραφέας των Αθλίων

, κάποια στιγμή γράφει για την κατάσταση των φοιτητών και των φτωχών του Παρισιού λίγο πριν βρεθούν στα οδοφράγματα της εξέγερσης του 1832: 

“Όποιος φέρει μες στην ψυχή του μια κρυφή εξέγερση ενάντια σε κάποιο δεδομένο του κράτους, της ζωής ή της μοίρας, αγγίζει την εξέγερση και, μόλις αυτή ξεσπάσει, αρχίζει να ριγεί και να νιώθει ότι παρασύρεται από τον στρόβιλο.

»




Nube




Στο εξεγερμένο Παρίσι!

title: Am 03.11.2026 vergibt die Bundesnetzagentur (BNetzA) Zuschläge zu 4,5 GW an Kraftwerkskapazitäten,...
content:
#Ende-Gelände #Ende-Gelaende #Ende_Gelaende




Am 03.11.2026 vergibt die Bundesnetzagentur (BNetzA) Zuschläge zu 4,5 GW an Kraftwerkskapazitäten, die das Stromnetz stabilisieren sollen. Statt auf neue Technologien, wie Batteriespeicher zu setzen, sollen neue fossile Gaskraftwerke gebaut werden. Das ganz wird massiv subventioniert mit Steuergeldern. Wie kommt Wirtschaftsministerin #Reiche darauf mitten in der Klimakrise neue fossile Kraftwerke zu bauen? Ganz einfach: Lobbyismus durch die großen Energiekonzerne. Die werden nämlich auch den Zuschlag für die Gaskraftwerke bekommen.




Hier ein Auszug aus den Verbrechen der großen Kraftwerksbetreibern.


EnBW: Ermittlung wegen Untreue und Steuerhinterziehung.


LEAG: Betreibt die Braunkohlereviere in der Lausitz. Neben riesigen Mengen CO2 werden auch weitere Schadstoffe in die Luft und das Wasser abgegeben. Der Konzern soll Schweigegelder an Kommunen gezahlt haben, damit diese die Verschmutzung nicht weiterverfolgen.


UNIPER: Hat jahrzehntelang Kohlekraftwerke mit Blutkohle aus Kolumbien betrieben. In Kolumbien geht der Kohleabbau mit Menschenrechtsverletzungen und Umweltzerstörung einher. An Reparationskosten beteiligt UNIPER nicht.


RWE: Betreibt Europas größte CO2-Quelle, das Rheinische Braunkohlerevier. Unzählige Dörfer wurden abgebaggert und mit dem Hambacher Forst ist ein einzigartiger Naturraum vernichtet worden.




Das Muster ist immer das gleiche Konzerne streichen Gewinne und hohe Subventionen mit den Kosten für Umweltzerstörung und Klimakatastrophe bleiben wir allein.




Mit unseren Aktionen haben wir uns schon letztes Jahr gegen die neuen Gaskraftwerke gestellt. Nächsten Sommer machen wir weiter… Stay tuned!

author: groundxero
title: Where Women Make History: Reclaiming Agency in History and in Movements
content:
Gargi’s book is a historiographical recovery of the junctures when women fought and moved another inch towards occupying half the sky. 




 




By

 Vertika Mani 




 




The first intriguing thing to notice about V. Gargi’s 

No Women, No History

 is the cover page of the book itself. Published by Virasam Books, the cover depicts women holding guns, marching with axes and also hugging trees. The image with its wide range of contrast yet a commonality of women as marchers and fighters interacts with its readers to convey the larger argument that this book seeks to make. The book was initially written as a collection of notes by V. Gargi, a revolutionary activist who dedicated this book 

“To all the women who fought against overwhelming odds, made great sacrifices to the extent of even laying down their lives to make this place better for all of us…”







 




The first edition of 

No Women No History: Women in Indian Movements (19th century – 2004)

 was published last year in August, at a pit stop, when the mainstream feminist discourse in India and abroad mostly associate women with power of intellect and pen, which are all quite a matter of privilege and can therefore be politically disabling at times. In that context, reading 

No women No History

 is refreshing as it takes us down the road of history of women’s struggle, almost on a rampage to discover the truth of the fighting spirit that Indian women have always stood for.




 




An extraordinary range of political histories 




 




The book covers an extraordinary range of political histories and geographical contexts from 19th Century to the year 2004 covering histories of peasant and Adivasi uprisings, anti-caste struggles, labour movements, revolutionary politics, autonomous women’s organisations, ecological movements, struggles in the North-East, cultural organisations and contemporary campaigns. Its approach is broad and, for the most part, non-sectarian. Rather than treating “women’s issues” as a separate political category, Gargi locates women within the wider structures of social and political struggle, as peasants, workers, artisans, Dalits, Adivasis and members of minority communities.




 




This method of writing makes gendered oppression therefore appear not as an isolated structure but is seen in relationship with caste, class, feudal relations, economic exploitation and political power. This is among this book’s most important methodological contributions which allow the history of women’s liberation to be read as history of movements rather than that of organisations. A history of movements in which women fought over land, wages, labour, caste hierarchy, food, displacement, forests, political representation and state power. The breadth of the historical canvas is therefore significant to explore beyond conventional boundaries of women’s history.




 




Beginning with women’s participation in tribal and peasant rebellions, Gargi moves between the histories of Ranis and Begums and those of ordinary women who participated in the political ferment of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The juxtaposition prevents women’s history from becoming a gallery of exceptional female figures. It takes a dive into the political labour of ordinary women, particularly peasant, working-class, Dalit, Adivasi and other marginalised women, who have so frequently remained outside the central narrative of political history.




 




One of the salient feature of discussions around movements is the notable references made to the women pioneers, for instance, of Self-Respect Movement which is mostly associated with Periyar but more often than not misses to speak of Maniyammai, the woman who went on to lead the Kazhagam after Periyar’s death. Similarly, Gargi talks about Ambedkarite and Dalit movements including women’s role at length. Other such references include the distinctive forms of women’s participation in movements like Jail Bharo Satyagraha of 1960–65. The histories of women in the freedom struggle, women revolutionaries and communists are similarly placed alongside organisational histories that are less familiar in mainstream accounts.




 




Similarly, the book discusses collectives which are again, less talked about. For instance, The Mahila Atmaraksha Samitis (MARS), which emerged as an important form of women’s mobilisation before Partition. The further chapters trace the experiences of women during and after Partition, discovering a phase in history where despite political upheavals, women liberation struggles were negotiated and resisted by its women participants through gendered forms of collective action. In the facet of organised women militia, the book digs into the history during the Tebhaga struggle by the formation of The Nari Bahini which was one of the early attempts to organise women into a militia. It provides the readers another striking example of women’s participation, this time, in agrarian politics. The history then extends into working-class movements under colonial rule and to women workers’ struggles across regions, from Tamil Nadu to Chhattisgarh.




 




The geographical movement across these histories is itself an important intervention. Women’s political history does not belong exclusively to metropolitan centres or to organisations explicitly identified with feminism. It is in factories, villages, forests, agricultural fields, working-class neighbourhoods and Adivasi regions. The movement across Tamil Nadu, Bengal, Telangana, Chhattisgarh, the North-East and Uttarakhand reveals a political geography in which gender cannot be separated from land, labour, caste, community, ecology and livelihood.




 




Participation is not the same as power




 




The chapters on Naxalbari and subsequent revolutionary movements extend this book into one of the most contested terrains of Indian political history. Gargi here brings into view women whose participation has often been overshadowed by the more familiar histories of male revolutionary leadership. Women appear as organisers, couriers, political workers and, in some instances, combatants. Their presence challenges the assumption that revolutionary politics was primarily a male domain.




 




But the histories gathered in the book also open a more difficult theoretical question, making us question if women’s participation in a radical movement necessarily transforms the gendered distribution of power within that movement?




 




The distinction between participation and political authority is crucial here. Women may be indispensable to a movement while remaining underrepresented in its strategic decision-making. They may organise, mobilise, carry messages, sustain underground networks and endure repression, while political authority remains concentrated elsewhere. The history of revolutionary movements thus becomes relevant not only for demonstrating women’s courage and agency but also for asking how organisational structures themselves reproduce or challenge patriarchy.




 




This question runs through the broader history that Gargi reconstructs. The participation of women in the Tebhaga movement, for instance, demonstrates both the possibilities and contradictions of radical mobilisation. Women could become central to agrarian struggles while encountering assumptions about physical weakness, domestic responsibility and the supposed disruption that women’s political participation could cause within families and communities.




 




The implication is not that progressive politics is necessarily patriarchal, but that progressive political ideology by itself cannot be assumed to dissolve patriarchy. Political movements have their own institutional cultures, hierarchies and divisions of labour. The question of women’s emancipation therefore has to include the question of who exercises political authority within emancipatory movements.




 




Women’s participation in Gandhian politics 




 




Women’s participation in Gandhian politics undeniably expanded the terrain of political action available to them. Yet the terms of that participation can be a subject matter for discussion.




 




The spinning wheel and khadi, for example, could bring political activity into the domestic sphere and make participation possible for women who could not enter public political spaces on equal terms. But the very possibility of political participation from within the household also raises a question: when does the inclusion of women in political life alter the gendered division of labour, and when does it simply assign political meaning to labour women were already expected to perform?




 




Gargi’s historical approach is valuable precisely because it allows such contradictions to remain visible.




 




The 60s and 70s




 




The book’s account of the political transformations of the late 1960s and 1970s marks another important shift. Gargi follows women’s participation in the Nav Nirman movement, resistance to the Emergency and the emergence of autonomous women’s movements around rape, dowry and sex determination.




 




This period altered the vocabulary through which women articulated their experiences. Violence within the family, sexual violence, dowry and reproductive control increasingly came to be understood not as private or secondary concerns but as political questions involving law, institutions, social power and the state.




 




The emergence of autonomous women’s organisations was therefore not simply a new organisational development. It represented a redefinition of the political system itself. The question of women’s emancipation could no longer be deferred to a supposedly more fundamental transformation that would occur elsewhere, in the economy, the state or class relations. Women were asserting that the structures governing intimate life, sexuality, reproduction and family relations were themselves sites of political power.




 




At the same time, these movements remained connected to wider struggles over class, caste, communalism, labour and state power. The history that Gargi reconstructs consequently resists an easy opposition between “class politics” and “women’s politics”. It instead reveals the continuing negotiations between different political priorities and different understandings of emancipation.




 




Revolutionary movements and the question of emancipation




 




The book’s sustained engagement with communist and Maoist movements is particularly important in this context. Gargi documents the extraordinary participation of women in revolutionary struggles, including their organisational, political and, in some cases, armed roles. These histories are significant because they challenge the persistent representation of women in revolutionary politics as merely supporters of male revolutionaries.




 




Yet the historical material also raises questions that extend beyond the question of representation. What constitutes emancipation for women within a revolutionary movement? How are autonomous demands negotiated against larger political objectives? Does participation in a movement committed to transforming class relations necessarily transform gender relations within the movement itself?




 




These are not questions that can be answered by measuring the number of women who participated. They concern the relationship between political agency and political authority, between formal commitments and everyday organisational practices, and between women’s autonomous demands and the priorities of broader movements.




 




The significance of Gargi’s historical recovery is that it makes these questions possible which in itself is rare.




 




Going beyond the familiar contours of women’s movements




 




The later chapters further expand the geographical and conceptual field. The discussion of the Shah Bano case brings questions of gender, law, religion and citizenship into the history of women’s political mobilisation. The chapters on women’s movements in the North-East and ecological struggles in Uttarakhand demonstrate how questions of land, environment, community and livelihood become gendered political questions.




 




The history of women affected by the Bhopal gas disaster provides another important example in this regard wherein women survivors formed the Bhopal Gas Peedit Mahila Udyog Sangathan for medical assistance, relief and access to information. Such instances are rarely discussed in books around women’s struggle. In most narrations around the tragedy, women were victims of an industrial disaster, but in reality, they were not confined to the political identity of victims. They became organisers and claimants, transforming the experience of disaster into a sustained struggle for relief and rights.




 




It makes it difficult to speak of a singular trajectory of Indian women’s movements. The political experiences of a factory worker, an Adivasi woman resisting displacement, a Dalit woman confronting caste hierarchy, an urban feminist confronting sexual violence and a woman participating in an underground revolutionary organisation cannot simply be collapsed into one category. But the book tries to encompass it all and instead of understanding them in isolation, makes an attempt to connect each other’s struggle with the other through commonalities in terms of structures of power.




 




Post economic liberalisation 




 




The historical trajectory assembled by Gargi also invites attention to the transformations in women’s political life after economic liberalisation. The terrain of struggle has changed substantially with the expansion of informal and contractual labour, migration, the growth of the service economy, the fragmentation of workplaces, the increasing significance of unpaid and care work, and new forms of commodification and social insecurity.




 




These transformations do not make the earlier struggles irrelevant. Rather, they complicate the organisational forms through which women can exercise collective political agency. The factory floor, the agrarian field and the neighbourhood remain important sites of struggle, but they now coexist with fragmented workplaces, informal employment, domestic labour, platform-mediated work and increasingly individualised forms of economic insecurity.




 




Viewed from this longer historical perspective, the question of women’s emancipation remains inseparable from the question of organisation. The forms through which women collectively acquire political voice have always changed with the economic and political structures around them. Gargi’s history provides the longer genealogy necessary to understand that changing terrain.




 




Women at the Centre of History 




 




Though the book suffers from scholarly limitation because of lack of footnoting, making it difficult for its reader to trace or verify the historical claims. This is perhaps understandable given its notes-like, underground origins, but the good part is that even that does not diminish the force of its intervention asking us to reconsider the very architecture of political history that we have been taught.




 




Gargi through her work demonstrates that to write women into history is to alter the categories through which political history is understood. The women Gargi brings into view carried messages, organised workers, confronted landlords, challenged caste hierarchies, sustained underground networks, fought for land and wages, built women’s organisations, resisted state repression and, in some struggles, took up arms. In the light of such an incredibly wide range of women’s contribution to history, the central achievement of 

No Women, No History

 lies in its challenge to the writing of history itself. In conclusion, as a reader I would like to thank Gargi for this attempt to challenge the grammar of history to restore us all from its making.




 







Vertika Mani

 is a feminist writer and legal practitioner at the Supreme Court of India, currently serving as the Organisation Secretary of the People’s Union for Civil Liberties (PUCL).

author: Dinah Gardner
title: The Other China We Need to Talk About
content:
WHAT IF I told you that there was a chance—not a very high chance, but a real chance nonetheless—that if you visited the People’s Republic of China today you might be kidnapped, blindfolded, driven to a specialized facility and subjected to six months of psychological torture. All on the orders of the state.

It sounds unbelievable, doesn’t it?

But this is what happened to at least several dozen foreign citizens in recent years. It is what happened to American scholar Min Zin this past June, when he landed in Yunnan province on the invitation of a Chinese academic institution to attend a conference. And it is also what happened to half a dozen people who appear in the latest edition of the book The People’s Republic of the Disappeared, which we just published on 28 October.

This important book is a collection of mostly first-person stories that expose the psychological horrors of being held in the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) feared secret detention system called Residential Surveillance at a Designated Location (RSDL). The system permits police to hold an individual in complete isolation, no contact with family or lawyers, to be interrogated for hours at will.

The individual is under 24-hour guard: this includes being watched all day every day, all night every night, whether you are asleep, sitting quietly in your cell or even on the toilet. The CCP intentionally uses RSDL to strip away every last shred of human dignity. RSDL is designed to break a person’s will to extract a confession for crimes imagined by the state

For more than a decade, the CCP has used RSDL against its own people, in particular human rights defenders. It is now increasingly using it against foreign citizens to exert its will across borders and as a kind of hostage diplomacy. Michael Kovrig, a former Canadian diplomat who wrote the foreword to this edition, is one of its most well-known examples.

In editing the stories for this book, I was struck again and again by how similar everyone’s experience was. This speaks to the uniformity of the RSDL system:

The removal of the temporal world. “There are no clocks in RSDL” is the title of Australian TV anchor Cheng Lei’s chapter. She would guess and count breaths to keep track of time.

The removal of the physical world. There are no windows in RSDL or they are covered in thick blackout curtains. Japanese scholar Hideji Suzuki cried when he was granted 15 minutes of sunlight, the only time in his seven months’ incarceration when he was allowed to see the sky.

The removal of yourself. Michael Kovrig noted: “There are no mirrors—not even the reassurance of seeing your own face.” Chinese activist Li Qiaochu writes how she was simply called “target”.

Filling the space left by these absences was a current of fear. Endless rules, the lack of privacy yet total isolation (guards were forbidden from talking to prisoners), reduced nutrition, sleep deprivation, lack of fresh air, and the padded suicide-proofed walls. Several of the detainees wrote while they could never see outside their RSDL facility, at nighttime they would often hear gunfire or the barking of dogs.

“In my mentally exhausted state, the sounds of gunfire would constantly startle me and even cause me to imagine that I was about to be executed,” wrote Taiwanese human rights activist Lee Ming-che.

But something else struck me as I read through their testimonies. However harrowing these stories of suffering are, they are also evidence of human resilience in the face of horror.

Cheng Lei writes about how she would escape into her mind, translating poems, reliving her former TV interviews and making up stories in her head. Similarly, Michael Kovrig meditated, sang songs to himself, and remembered past moments in his life, as if it was a recording playing in his mind.

“I learned to meditate on the movies I had watched and the poems and novels I had read,” wrote Li Qiaochu. “Those precious memories allowed me to gradually filter out the brainwashing, to preserve my vitality and to keep myself from being transformed into their machine.”

Feedback from earlier editions informed us that rights activists use the Chinese editions of The People’s Republic of the Disappeared to prepare for and strengthen their mental resolve and courage in case one day they too are taken into RSDL. Knowing that others have gone through this and come out the other side can be an immense help. It’s for this reason that the Chinese edition of this book will be available free to download as a PDF from our website.

In a world where influencers and media wax lyrical about the futuristic cities, advanced technologies and amazing sights in China, in a world where it’s a desirable goal to be Chinamaxxing, we need to remember that there is another side to China, a much darker side.

That is why we are publishing this third edition of The People’s Republic of the Disappeared in English, focusing this time on foreign citizens as targets. Foreigners who never imagined they would be kidnapped by the CCP.

We cannot let the world forget that this is how the world’s second superpower behaves or we will all lose our human dignity in the end.

The English version of the book is available in multiple formats from Amazon. All money raised goes into our urgent actions and advocacy work.
