author: Hilde Marie Rekstad
title: The Process: Helen Wesnes Fights for Her Rights
content:
Editor’s Note: This piece was originally published on our affiliate site, 

Mad in Norway

.




Helen Wesnes took control of her own case from the beginning and has already won several victories in the legal system. She does this for all those who lose their lives in psychiatry. Photo: private




H




elen Wesnes was 19 when she sought help from the health care system. It cost her 15 years, followed by a 12-year legal process. She has already won millions in damages and is ready for the next round. Now she explains how she built her case.




Few people know that in Norway there is a society within a society, full of paradoxes and with no known way out. This is the Norway offered to psychiatric patients once they fall under the Mental Health Care Act. “Someone must have slandered Josef K., for one morning, without having done anything wrong, he was arrested,” writes Franz Kafka in his world-famous 

The Trial

, and what follows is a nightmare about the individual’s powerlessness against the arbitrariness of bureaucracy. Josef K. and Helen W. don’t have a great deal in common, since she walked out alive and victorious. Otherwise, the process was much the same.




“The media are failing their mission when they don’t raise this case to a systemic level. The practice itself is the problem, not whatever diagnosis the patient may have.”




Helen Wesnes speaks out about her 15 years of confinement, and the legal process that followed




I have invited Helen Wesnes to a conversation in which she shares reflections on the 15 years she was locked up in psychiatry, cut off from both physical and emotional contact with other people. This was the consequence of seeking medical help after a collapse brought on by a critical life event. Her story is an almost unbelievable process, and so is the battle Helen is now fighting in the Norwegian legal system. It is a battle she is fighting for everyone who loses their lives to psychiatry. She holds hard-won experience of what health care should have been, but isn’t, for those who need it most.




There has been limited media interest in covering the legal process Helen Wesnes has pursued for 12 years, and which is still ongoing. This despite the fact that it is historic for a psychiatric patient in Norway to be awarded damages for human rights violations. The articles that have been written have focused on the fact that she was misdiagnosed. Helen says the media are failing their mission when they don’t raise this case to a systemic level. The practice itself is the problem, not whatever diagnosis the patient may have.




Helen has unique expertise in how to prevail against the system once mistakes have been made. She has acquired these skills through what has so far been a more than twelve-year war against state bodies, along with insight into what goes on behind closed doors. In this in-depth interview you can read about a Norway that very few people know exists. She is now asking for deeper understanding from the media and others. “They tend to focus on how terrible it is that I was misdiagnosed, back when trauma was interpreted as schizophrenia. They don’t ask the fundamental question: Should any human being be treated like this?”




Above the entrance to Reinsvoll hospital, the sign reads “Emergency care.” When Helen needed two weeks of rest after a crisis, the consequence was 15 years of confinement and inhumane treatment. Photo: Helen Wesnes




There are events in this story that reveal eugenics thinking, and this is Norway in the 2000s. The sum of what she has been subjected to can also be understood as misogyny. The mechanisms meant to detect and correct problems in the many locked wards in our country have proven to fail. Helen herself says she believes she got out at the last minute, when medical tests showed alarming values.




What began as a patient injury case in 2015 has become an insane process in which the State is doing everything to crush a patient, where the hospital had admitted its mistakes even before the case began. This shameful story should have been compensated many years ago. Instead, the state has dared to appeal.




A brief outline of the Norwegian system




Patients subjected to compulsory treatment must turn to the Control Commission to complain, or to the County Governor (Statsforvalteren) if the complaint is unsuccessful. Once treatment has ended, patients can claim compensation from NPE (the Norwegian System of Patient Injury Compensation). If the claim is rejected, or the patient disagrees with the amount awarded, the case can be appealed to the Patient Injury Compensation Board under the Norwegian Board of Health Complaints (Helseklage). If the case is still not resolved, the patient must turn to the courts by suing the state, represented by NPE. In doing so, one also risks having to pay the state’s legal costs if one loses. Norway has three levels of court: the District Court, the Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court. The final avenue for human rights violations is to bring Norway before the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg.




Background to Helen Wesnes’s case




The pathologization process




What triggered Helen’s crisis was a rape in her late teens, something she did not talk about until a year into her admission at Sykehuset Innlandet Reinsvoll (SIR), by which point she had already been labeled seriously mentally ill. When she sought help, it was because she had stopped sleeping, was burned out and had broken down. She had tried to work hard to forget the rape, and she had stayed awake at night to avoid the nightmares. Eventually she saw a psychologist, who recommended two weeks of rest at Reinsvoll hospital. Fifteen years later she got out.




Helen describes herself as a child who always found her own way. She wasn’t concerned with following the crowd, and her family supported her when she chose a Steiner school and violin lessons, which was unusual in the working-class community where she grew up. She was strong-willed, curious and exploratory, and she learned quickly. Activities and sports were an important part of her upbringing.




The hospital’s treatment plans state that all staff were to avoid talking with Helen about anything other than practical matters, and this became the young woman’s daily life for 15 years. Friends were turned away at the door, and relatives and family were only allowed visits of 30 minutes, with staff present. Mechanical restraint was part of the treatment of a girl who was never violent, aggressive or suicidal. It was carried out to calm her down, which is illegal. The treatment approach was to reject all of the patient’s attempts at human contact.




The treatment was to limit human contact to a minimum, use restraints to make the patient compliant, and stop all communication of a personal nature. Photo: Helen Wesnes




Over the course of the “stay,” the ball rolled from one brain-disorder diagnosis to the next, until she ended up with a long list of diagnoses and an even longer list of medications. The diagnosis that would set the course for the inhumane treatment she was subjected to was schizophrenia, written in her chart by a summer substitute after a few meetings and without any in-depth knowledge of the patient. She never received a proper assessment, because with that word in the chart, the course was set, in a system built on authority and hierarchy.




In the hunt for brain disease, the hospital paid no attention to the fact that Helen gained 50 kilos and slept 16 hours a day. On the contrary, she was given sleeping pills when she had barely woken up. Since then, Helen has sought out a handful of former staff to hear their view of what she was like, and why she was treated so harshly. The answer was that she was “too smart” for them, and that it was challenging to be met with argument and Helen’s quick comebacks.




In 2012 she was rushed to hospital with dangerously low blood pressure, fainting and questionable ECG results. Helen now says she would have died from the overmedication if they had been allowed to continue much longer, and that she got out at the last minute.




The NPE process




It was the hospital itself that told Helen about NPE, after realizing it had mistreated her for 15 years. When Helen filed her claim in 2015, she therefore assumed the case shouldn’t take more than a couple of years, but the NPE process would end up taking more than ten years before she received the first compensation payment.




In 2022 she sued NPE because she disagreed with NPE about the extent of the injuries she had suffered and how much she had lost in earnings. Helen also argued that she had to be compensated for non-economic losses in the form of deprivation of liberty, torture and the loss of the right to family life. Because NPE considered itself the wrong party for this part of the case, the State, represented by the Ministry of Health and Care Services, was sued for violations of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR). Because the case is so extensive, it was split into two parallel proceedings. The trial concerning the ECHR violations was held in June 2026. The case against NPE, however, has been postponed to February 2027.




NPE’s first expert reports were based on an incomplete medical record that was missing nearly a thousand pages from the first eight years of the admission. These reports therefore concluded that Helen was schizophrenic and in need of treatment, and that she had received the correct treatment. They also claimed she would have recovered had the treatment been allowed to continue, and gave no weight to the fact that the hospital had backtracked and admitted its mistakes.




Helen argued and documented thoroughly in her correspondence with NPE for years, before she and her lawyer discovered, just before the trial was due to begin, that NPE had not obtained the full medical record. That NPE did not discover this itself can only be explained by their not reading the responses they themselves had requested, but carrying on undeterred toward a rejection.




Lawyers Emma Dahl Grammeltvedt and Gorm Are Grammeltvedt have worked with Helen because they believed in the case. Here at Romerike og Glåmdal District Court, June 2026. Photo: Helen Wesnes




Once the error was on the table, the impending trial had to be halted, and NPE appointed a new expert. This expert found in Helen’s favor, but NPE’s caseworkers have since expressed dissatisfaction with his report and stated that they do not agree with all of his conclusions. (These are people with one year of training in case processing and no medical expertise.) The NPE expert who found in Helen’s favor has never been given another assignment by NPE.




The court proceedings




Helen Wesnes is the first person in Norway to be awarded damages for human rights violations following psychiatric treatment. This happened at Romerike og Glåmdal District Court in June 2026. The State has appealed the ruling, and the next round will take place in 2027 at Eidsivating Court of Appeal. The District Court had already awarded Wesnes damages for misdiagnosis and mistreatment in 2024, in an amount of more than NOK 7,700,000. The 2026 round was therefore about whether the treatment she was subjected to violates human rights, and if so, what it should cost the state.




Helen says that a few years ago she did a quick calculation of how much the mistreatment has cost the state, by adding up the daily rates in specialist health care, the supported housing and her disability benefits. The total came to about NOK 130 million. Had the system had its way, Helen would still be in this costly treatment. But the reckoning is about something far more important than money: namely, how reality is to be defined.




At Romerike og Glåmdal District Court in June 2026, Helen Wesnes and her lawyers Gorm Are Grammeltvedt and Emma Dahl Grammeltvedt won what is a historic ruling, in which she was awarded damages for human rights violations during psychiatric treatment. (Inger-Mari Eidsvik had already become the first person in Norwegian law to have a human rights violation in psychiatry recognized in 2025, but because of earlier decisions on the statute of limitations in that process, Eidsvik was denied compensation. She has appealed to Strasbourg.)




Treatment principles during Helen Wesnes’s confinement:







Rejection of all conversation beyond the practical




Prolonged mechanical restraint at any signs of an emotional life (she was never aggressive or suicidal)




A requirement to behave exactly the same toward all staff




Rotation of staff at signs of a relationship with the patient




A ban on writing about herself in her own diary




Limited time allowed for writing in her diary




Restrictions on/refusal of taking photographs (the patient’s hobby)




Seclusion with elements of isolation for weeks at a time




Disregard for her need for safety and care after a murder attempt by a fellow patient




Forced medication




Friends turned away at the door




Visits from parents and relatives monitored and reduced to a few minutes per week







“How can health care workers do things like this? Is this treatment? There were plenty of beds, time and resources, so that wasn’t what it was about.”




Interview with Helen Wesnes: on isolation and its consequences, on how to win a compensation claim, and on the paradoxes




The rest of this article and the interview that follows are in Helen’s own words, from a conversation that was open and without many direct questions. The conversation was audio-recorded, and the written text has been tidied somewhat where the spoken version was not clear enough as text. The interview has been read and approved by Helen. It took place on August 21, 2026.




Reflections after fifteen years in a locked regime




It was totalitarian and oppressive




Will these outrageous stories even be believed, and would I have believed them myself? That I was put in restraints as part of the treatment? That they left me lying there in my own urine? That I was the victim of an attempted murder by a fellow patient, and the message was that I should just “rise above it,” with an expectation that we would barbecue and eat waffles together shortly afterward? How can health care workers do things like that? Is this treatment?




There were plenty of beds, time and resources, so that wasn’t what it was about. It’s about individual acts by individuals, and choices they made, like coming into my room on my birthday just to say, “We don’t sing birthday songs or give hugs on 3A!” I will never forget the female staff member who just patted me condescendingly on the restraints when I asked why I had to lie in them, before ignoring me completely. It was so disrespectful! It made a huge impression. It was a deeply inhumane and callous culture.




I never got help with what the problem actually was, not even after they learned about the rape. The hospital had no interest in it whatsoever. All they cared about was the schizophrenia diagnosis, and so they followed a treatment theory holding that it was harmful to talk with the patient about anything interior. All you were supposed to talk about was the weather and practical things.




Helen has now found support in her family. Here she stands with her mother, Christine Ann Wesnes. Her brother Jan Nicolai Wesnes stands behind, with her father Kjell Wesnes on the right. Photo: private




My closest family were also instructed to relate to me in this way, so not only was I consistently rejected by staff, but they thereby isolated me from everyone else, not just physically but emotionally, too. Being so alone created enormous wounds.




Individuals had all the power – no one knew




Clinicians I had later were shocked to hear what had happened on the ward where I had been at Reinsvoll. These were their colleagues, but they knew nothing. I have also spoken with staff who left after working there a while, and they say the place was toxic. The ones who stayed were the ones who adapted to the culture. Boundaries shifted, and violations and exercise of power were gradually normalized. It was reminiscent of a kind of Stanford experiment, in a closed society with no outside correction. The senior physicians were there three hours a week. Power corrupts, and that is what happens in psychiatry. Petty evil takes root when individuals are given unlimited power in a totalitarian system. The Control Commission came by in 2008 and checked coercion decisions, but where were they all the other years? Besides, staff carried out almost all coercion without any formal decision, and then there’s nothing to check.




Mechanical restraint – effective for producing compliant patients




Restraint was used as treatment, but that is not legal. I ran into one of the nurses by chance and confronted her about all the restraint I had been subjected to. She laughed nervously and replied, “Well, I hope we did everything by the book!” But which book has she been reading, I wonder? I was never violent. I didn’t trash the room. I wasn’t dangerous, and not suicidal either, even though the Attorney General’s office tried to claim so, because then they can call it necessity. No, it wasn’t like that. The Control Commission even approved restraint decisions that describe how cooperative I was in the situation. Then necessity is not a valid justification, and it’s illegal. They used restraints because it was effective. And it was, because you give up and become compliant. I really liked what one of the witnesses said in court: that the court had to understand the difference between voluntariness and resignation. Not resisting doesn’t mean it’s voluntary. It’s like freezing during a rape. That witness was one of the staff from when I was admitted.




“There’s a place in hell for those people.”




The patients were not human beings




“You shouldn’t have children,” I was told while I was admitted, and the chart says: “must have a serious talk with pt about contraception due to e.g. heredity.” This is racial hygiene and eugenic thinking, and it’s happening in the 2000s. Information is fine, but when the goal is contraception, it means that a child with my genetics is not wanted in society. Ergo, they don’t want patients like me in society either.




This hurt more than any restraint, because it was an attack on my person and my human dignity. So we’re not human beings. The attitudes are frightening, and these people are still in their jobs. My treating psychiatrist has apologized since, so I have been able to make peace with him. I have forgiven many, but not those who defend themselves and cannot say sorry. There’s a place in hell for those people.




Despite being locked up, sedated by medication and restricted from pursuing her interest in photography, Wesnes is soon to graduate as a photojournalist. Photo: Helen Wesnes




The hard road back to life




I didn’t know how to be in the world




People who know me now say they never understood how completely destitute I was when I got out. I didn’t know how to be in the world and interact with ordinary people. I had been on a high-security ward with drugged and violent men. I knew nothing about what normal functioning requires, having been institutionalized and helpless since I was 20. I was 35 when I got out. It was worse than being in prison: you don’t get put in restraints or poisoned in prison because you look a bit sad one day. You can get an education, have visitors, and actually have a bit of privacy, like going to the toilet alone. And nobody stands watching you while you shower. You can make a private phone call.




How are you supposed to behave, quite simply, and what is expected? And how do you vote in an election and pay bills? What are Spotify and Netflix? How do you finish upper secondary school and get a driver’s license? How do you make new friends when you don’t have a job or aren’t a student? I just had to show up at clubs and activities and throw myself into things. It was really scary, but it worked out. I can’t expect people to understand, and I can’t talk about it. People are afraid to touch the subject. And I camouflage, presenting myself without showing how things have marked me.




I’ve been very hard on myself in the process since. Taking your life back requires daring. Can you give a talk, people asked me. Yes, absolutely, I replied, but I had never done it before! Then I put on my theater hat and play a confident person, while thinking about who can help me. Because how does PowerPoint actually work? I don’t ask myself whether I want to, because I’m going to! “Think of Reinsvoll! You’ve been through worse,” I tell myself. I’m not actually confident when I say I can do something. I learned something very useful from a TED Talk by a social psychology researcher named Amy Cuddy (YouTube): “Fake it till you become it.” Eventually you’ll be able to.




I bet it felt like being on acid




I had no methods for regulating the emotions that came up as I tapered off the medications. All sensory impressions hit me as if they were being used for the first time. Smells, tastes, sounds: everything was switched on, and the impressions were extreme. The medication bubble that had muted everything was suddenly gone.




When the drugs were taken away, everything changed. Everything was beautiful, and also very sad, she recalls now. Photo: Helen Wesnes




I sat in the park for 5–6 hours every day and thought everything was just amazing. My God, how beautiful! It was the world’s most beautiful sunset every day, every single damn day! I imagine that’s what being on acid must be like. I lay down and touched the grass! Because what did it actually feel like? And what does the bark on trees actually feel like? That’s the kind of thing I did! I smelled, felt and looked around me for hours every day. Everything was so wonderful, and at the same time very, very sad. I cried at the slightest thing during that time.




Doing well now – in spite of psychiatry




I’ve tried to make up for a lot of what was lost, and it has been incredibly demanding. How you’re doing has a lot to do with how you take it. Life is what it is, and there are things you can’t do anything about, that’s just how it is. You can’t let yourself be overwhelmed by the losses, because then they’ve won. I’m doing well now, and I created that myself. I managed it, not because of psychiatry, but in spite of it. The loneliness I feel isn’t because I’m alone, because I’m not anymore. The loneliness is about being pretty much alone in what I’ve been through.




Claims to protect patients – protects itself




A lack of logic – NPE reveals that the system protects itself




I requested extended access to records and checked NPE’s statistics. The majority of those whose claims were upheld won on grounds of lack of treatment, not because psychiatry had given the wrong treatment. Suicide tops the list, followed by delayed diagnosis. You see examples of inadequate safety measures or suicide assessments, or poor follow-up of medical problems in psychiatric patients, which places them under the psychiatry statistics at NPE. Over the past five years, NPE has found only 12 cases of misdiagnosis in psychiatry that resulted in a decision in the patient’s favor. That’s just over two cases a year.




If these statistics reflect reality, then this subjective, opinion-based field is the most accurate discipline in all of medicine. But, is psychiatry really the most accurate health service there is? NPE is a body meant to look after people after injuries in the health care system. The truth is that psychiatry decides the NPE cases too; those who provide treatment are the same people who assess the treatment. The system has a collegial mentality, a guild mentality, that protects the profession as well as NPE’s coffers.




How she built her own case




The first thing I did when I got out was sit down and read: pharmacology in psychiatry. The Mental Health Care Act. The old guidelines from the Norwegian Board of Health Supervision for the treatment of schizophrenia. The old guidance documents on schizophrenia. What is good treatment? What is an assessment? I read everything!




At first I didn’t have a lawyer and I did everything myself. And I did a thorough job: I wrote 35 pages of comments on NPE’s first expert statement (which was 16 pages). “This is missing…”, “This has not been done…” and so on. I pointed out every failure there was and backed it up with references to the professional literature as well as to the medical record. I found the weaknesses in the reports and the record, and commented and argued point by point. “This is wrong, and this is wrong… And this can’t be right, because if he believes this, then why does it say this…?” I referred to research and to the knowledge of the time, and the laws and regulations of the time.




I also did a lot of networking. The hospital understood that I had been mistreated, and I chose to seek out the senior physician who was responsible for the mistreatment and insisted on occasional meetings with him. Instead of going to war against Reinsvoll, I decided that they would understand what had happened, and that we would do this together. I also gathered several written statements from staff who had worked at the hospital during the years I was admitted, as well as from health professionals outside the institution. Collecting all these witness statements shortly after the mistreatment ended has been decisive for my court case.




She has unique expertise in winning against a system that protects itself. Photo: private




When everything comes down to luck, there is no legal protection




Suing the state costs millions, and if I had lost, I would have risked having to pay the state’s legal costs as well. I didn’t have the money for that, so I just took the chance. My lawyer has put in an enormous amount of work and has been willing to share the risk with me. Colleagues he consulted reportedly told him he could forget about winning this case, that we didn’t stand a chance, but both he and I believed in the case, because we knew we were right.




We can’t have a system where you depend on who you happen to meet, and whether you’re lucky enough to meet lawyers willing to work pro bono. At NPE it’s a matter of luck which expert and caseworker you’re assigned, and the same goes for the National Complaints Body for the Health Service/Patient Injury Compensation Board. It depends entirely on what the experts think, so it’s completely dependent on the individual. In my case, the Board’s experts were one from the Asthma and Allergy Association, one with expertise in women’s health, one specializing in cardiovascular disease, along with two lawyers. How were people with no expertise in psychiatry or pharmacology supposed to assess a case like this? Of course I lost there.




A high price, but she can’t give up




The case I’m fighting now concerns human rights violations (ECHR), and it’s a matter of principle. Should people be able to be locked up for years without being compensated? Why am I taking on this case, one might ask. It demands an enormous amount. You need health and finances, and it’s more than a full-time job. The fight has come at a high personal cost. When I started, I believed the systems worked. I believed we had legal protection, and since the hospital had already admitted its mistakes, I thought this was an open-and-shut case. I thought it would go straight through when I filed with NPE, but I was very naïve. I would probably have filed anyway, even if I had known in advance what this process would demand, because I’m far too stubborn to give up. But it has cost too much. The system has now almost taken another 15 years, on top of the 15 they had already taken, and the case isn’t over. And they have damaged me so much.




Lawyer and former head of legal affairs at NPE Gorm Are Grammeltvedt was the one who contacted Helen when he heard about the case. He thought the process must be based on misunderstandings. But the state meant business. Photo: Helen Wesnes




Pitfalls, paradoxes and the risk of asking for help




Dangerous to seek health care while tapering




By the time I had almost finished tapering off one of the medications, the hospital had understood that I had been mistreated and that I should never have been on these drugs. But quitting abruptly went to hell. If you’re a staff member meeting a patient in that kind of chaos (which is what tapering off psychiatric drugs is), you’ll naturally think the person has lost it.




It’s very risky to seek out the health care system while tapering, because withdrawal reactions (physical reactions to reducing or stopping medication) can be interpreted as anything at all. Withdrawal symptoms can show up in all sorts of strange ways, and then it’s dangerous to tell anyone, because it can be interpreted as a sign that the illness has returned. Then you quickly get more medications slapped on you, and that happened a couple of times in my history. In my case, my withdrawal reactions were interpreted as depression, which it absolutely wasn’t, and so they gave me the maximum dose of antidepressants. You should try to stay away.




Every time I needed to talk, the health care system felt a strong need to act




I had a lot of feelings and struggled a great deal in the years after I got out, so I did seek out health services to ask to talk to someone. You’re “drilled” to think that if there’s a crisis, you have to talk to someone in the health care system, but you actually don’t! (Laughs.)




The risk of ending up back in endless isolation was always present. Photo: Helen Wesnes




As soon as I had feelings and asked to talk to someone, the response was: “We have to do something here! Now we have to call Reinsvoll hospital.” But that wasn’t what I needed; I just needed to talk. I needed someone who could listen. Sometimes they could just have listened, and they could just have let me have my feelings, but instead it turned into discussions about whether I needed to be admitted. Fortunately, I had clinicians I knew well, who protected me from health workers who might potentially decide to admit me.




You can’t be sad or angry if you’re a psychiatric patient




I was just having a hard time, but you can’t express strong emotions when you’re a psychiatric patient. Because then you’re sick, and then someone has to intervene. You can’t be sad or angry if you’re a patient in psychiatry, because feelings are interpreted as you being acutely ill. In general you can’t have feelings in psychiatry, and what a paradox is that? What they’re doing is acting on their own fear.




Without a diagnosis, she could finally get help at a DPS




Eventually I got a fantastic psychologist, an experienced woman in her sixties. Once the diagnosis had been removed, I could finally get talk therapy. I didn’t get that as long as I was “sick.” Is that a paradox, or what? (Laughs for a long time.) I asked for a psychologist at the DPS (district psychiatric center) for years, but I didn’t get one. The reasoning was that what I needed was “stabilization” in supported housing, and to learn to live with the illness. But once I had been discharged and was off medication, then I could get treatment! It’s good to have a psychologist to talk about what you’ve been through. For me it’s mostly about understanding what I was subjected to in psychiatry, and why people act the way they do, more than understanding myself.




Never fill in a form!




I once filled in a form, right after I had discontinued my medication and was completely off balance. I had just realized that I had lost 15 years of my life, and on top of that the withdrawal reactions were producing a whole range of symptoms, so I scored sky-high on the depression symptom form. Then they wanted to put me on the maximum dose of antidepressants, me, who had finally gotten free of medications. I’m never filling in a form again! It’s a trap.




I have encountered shocking treatment in the health care system, even after I was awarded compensation for misdiagnosis and mistreatment. The stigma that comes with it leads to suspicion of everything from dangerousness to being mentally disturbed or abusing drugs. This happens even though I have never been violent, and the only intoxicants I have ever used were given to me by the health care system. I no longer contact the health care system if I’m in a crisis.




“I’m going to live a life, not win a war.”




The best revenge is living well




My psychologist quoted me back to myself: “Do you remember, Helen, what your driving force and your goal was? It was revenge!” There’s a lot of power in anger and the desire for revenge, so I got a lot done! (Laughs for a long time.) They don’t understand what they’ve created; I’ve become the ultimate opponent (laughs again). But I’m going to live a life, not win a war. The best revenge is living well, and taking your life back. But I’m not done with the fight, and I hope people can use the ruling for something. I want it to benefit others.




Hilde Marie Rekstad




The post 

The Process: Helen Wesnes Fights for Her Rights

 appeared first on 

Mad In America

author: Jen Fifield
title: Voting Rights Experts Are Monitoring These 5 Issues as the Midterms Unfold
content:
Courts have thwarted most of the administration’s plans to assert federal control, but Trump has kept up the pressure.

Courts have thwarted most of the administration’s plans to assert federal control, but Trump has kept up the pressure.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

As Americans head to the polls on Tuesday, voting experts are watching to see how the Trump administration’s unprecedented efforts to assert more federal control over elections will play out.

Since President Donald Trump retook the White House, his administration has tried to force states to turn over their unredacted voter rolls and to restrict mail-in voting. The Department of Homeland Security has used its resources to identify and prosecute noncitizen voters, an effort that has unfolded alongside the agency’s massive crackdown on immigrants.

The president has justified these steps by claiming, without evidence, that American elections are beset by fraud and that illegal voting is tipping the scales in favor of Democrats.

Courts have thwarted most of the administration’s plans to date, but Trump and his top deputies have kept up the pressure. Most recently, they’ve threatened to prosecute election officials who don’t reject ballots from people that the federal government has identified as likely noncitizens.

The administration hasn’t explicitly ruled out sending federal agents to the polls or seizing ballots or voting machines.

Election experts say the cumulative effect has been to ramp up anxiety about the midterms and to erode voters’ trust in the system.

“The administration has been creating a lot of noise, a lot of confusion, a lot of doubt,” said Ben Hovland, whom Trump fired as a commissioner for the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission earlier this year. He said he worries that this will make voters “sit it out” and “throw their hands up.”

In an emailed response to questions, a DHS spokesperson said Immigration and Customs Enforcement “is not planning operations targeting polling locations,” adding that the agency would only arrest people at the polls to address a safety threat as part of “intelligence-driven targeted enforcement.”

The DHS and the Justice Department “are laser focused on identifying, prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens,” the spokesperson added. “Our message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences — including criminal charges and deportation.”

Before and on Election Day, it’s typical for the major political parties to mount poll-watching operations, but both Democrats and Republicans say they’ve expanded these activities in this pressurized midterm.

Republicans will focus on issues such as voter eligibility and voter-roll accuracy, according to Ally Triolo, the Republican National Committee’s election integrity communications director. Democrats will concentrate on voter intimidation and other hurdles to voting, Angelo Fernández Hernández, a Democratic National Committee spokesperson, said.

Here are five issues that voting rights experts say they’re watching as this year’s election unfolds:

An incident in Leon County, in the Florida Panhandle, illustrates the widespread anxiety about law enforcement at the polls.

Mark Earley, the county’s supervisor of elections, told ProPublica he was “furious” when two marked U.S. Customs and Border Protection vehicles parked outside the county’s busiest early voting location last month, after he’d been repeatedly reassured by the administration that agents would not do this.

He reported the sighting to the FBI, then learned that the agents, who were headed out of state, had just stopped by to try to vote themselves. The episode generated a flurry of news coverage.

“Given the negative media coverage regarding federal agents at the polls, it shows pretty bad judgment that they showed up in their official vehicles,” Earley said.

It’s against the law for federal law enforcement to be near polling places.

Nick Brown, Washington’s attorney general, leads a group of Democratic state officials and voting rights advocates who have been planning how to respond if, indeed, there is real federal interference. The group has “war-gamed” how to react if government agents attempt to commandeer voting equipment or ballots.

“We’ve seen the tension and chaos that’s in the air,” Brown said. He called the federal government “the biggest challenge to smooth elections right now, which is not the way it’s supposed to be.”

A DOJ spokesperson said “the best preparation for any election official is following federal law.”

It’s routine for DOJ monitors to watch over polling places, and the agency has assured states that, in the midterms, its observers will follow the law and not interfere with voting or election administration. Still, state officials remain concerned. During Wyoming’s primary election, poll workers said they felt uneasy when DOJ monitors asked about their training and to inspect voting systems. The state’s governor criticized these actions as “a bit aggressive” and “irregular.”

The Trump administration’s multipronged effort targeting alleged noncitizen voters has already led to eligible voters being improperly removed from the rolls. Voting rights groups fear this will block some U.S. citizens from being able to vote when they show up on Tuesday.

Federal officials have made clear they plan to go after anyone they think is committing voter fraud.

On the first day of early voting in Texas, Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, posted a YouTube video announcing his intentions. “If you violate federal election law,” he warned, “I will hunt you down and prosecute you.”

This threat came days after the DOJ sued California, seeking to block the state from counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 voters it claims are “likely” noncitizens. The administration had obtained the state’s public voter rolls, which the DHS had blended with its own immigration information and third-party data.

In a court filing, California called the claim that there are 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls “specious.” Los Angeles County analyzed a sampling of the likely noncitizen voters that the federal government claimed were registered there. Many weren’t registered in the county or had never voted, the analysis showed. Some said on their voter registration forms that they were born in the United States.

Asked about the case, the DOJ told ProPublica, “Federal law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections, and the Department has a duty to enforce it.”

A federal judge has rejected the DOJ’s motion for an emergency order that would have barred California from counting the 20,000 voters’ ballots. (A federal appeals panel later backed that decision.) On Thursday, the administration sent grand jury subpoenas to California officials demanding records about their response to allegations of noncitizens on the state’s rolls. Late Friday, a federal judge issued a restraining order blocking the DOJ’s demands, calling them an “intimidation plan” that would interfere with legal voting.

Last week, the DOJ wrote a letter threatening to sue Washington state if officials there refused to review a list of 400 voters it believes to be noncitizens within 24 hours. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters late last month that the department was considering additional actions, saying there were “a number of states that we’re looking at.”

In a letter responding to the DOJ, Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs called the government list of 400 names “not reliable,” saying it included U.S. citizens, people who aren’t registered to vote and duplicate entries. “Time and time again,” Hobbs wrote, “DHS claims about noncitizen voter registration turn out to be greatly exaggerated or false.”

Sam Trepel is Rule of Law program director at States United Democracy Center and a former attorney for the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division. She said the agency’s actions involving California and Washington were a “disturbing use of prosecutorial authority.”

Trepel worries that the DOJ may try to seize ballots cast by voters identified as likely noncitizens, before or after the election, which would “put their votes at risk and undermine trust more broadly.”

Voting rights advocates also worry that the government’s efforts to target noncitizen voters could frighten eligible voters to the point that they won’t show up.

A federal judge recently put limits on a multistate effort by the DHS to go door-to-door in search of suspected noncitizen voters, at least through Election Day, saying it was illegally intimidating legal voters.

“A voter could say, ‘Well, maybe I don’t want to put myself on the target list here, maybe I won’t register, or maybe I won’t vote,’” said David Janovsky, acting director of The Constitution Project at the watchdog group Project on Government Oversight.

States often change laws and rules related to voting.

Since 2024, Republican-led states have taken a number of steps that experts say will make it more difficult for some of their residents to cast ballots and have them count.

A North Carolina law, for example, requires voters to provide proof of identification when sending mail-in ballots. Under new rules, ballots now come with two envelopes, both of which must be sealed. Ballot rejections have skyrocketed, Democracy Docket reported, because voters aren’t sealing the inner envelope.

Texas and other states have cut back on the number and location of polling places, especially in areas favoring Democrats. In hotly contested Tarrant County, which includes Fort Worth, the number of polling sites was slashed by almost a third. This could increase the risk of long lines and voter confusion on Election Day.

Voting rights groups such as the Texas Civil Rights Project are tracking two issues involving the state’s voter registration systems. A software error at the Texas Department of Public Safety stopped several hundred thousand new voter registrations from being forwarded to local election officials, preventing them from being added to the rolls. A separate state system for updating registration information wasn’t processing changes for several weeks, leading to more backlogs. Counties say they’ve been able to address these problems.

Every election features some issues with voting equipment.

So far, there have been isolated complaints involving touch-screen voting machines — including one from Dolly Parton’s sister in Tennessee — spawning fears that machines have been “rigged” to switch votes.

ES&S, the company that makes the machines garnering the complaints, told ProPublica that the company hadn’t received widespread reports. Election experts say occasional problems with touch-screen machines don’t signify tampering or manipulation. Any attempt to tamper with programming would surface during testing by election officials and be corrected, they said.

Incidents in the run-up to the midterms have ratcheted up election officials’ concerns about the potential for both cyber and physical attacks.

Last month, officials in several states, including Arizona, received envelopes with an unknown white powder. Arizona eventually deemed the material nontoxic, but Secretary of State Adrian Fontes said “the fear it caused was real.”

In 2024, false bomb threats, thought to be from foreign actors, caused widespread evacuations of vote-counting sites across the country. The disruptions were brief, however, in part because a message board funded by the federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA, alerted election officials that the FBI had deemed the threats not credible.

Trump, however, has dismantled CISA since retaking the presidency, leaving states and local election officials to grapple with both physical and cyber threats on their own. Election nonprofits have stepped up to try to fill the gap, and states, with CISA’s help, have enhanced their own cyber defenses.

Derek Tisler, counsel and manager for the elections and government program at the Brennan Center for Justice, said the federal government’s absence has weakened the defenses.

“States acting on their own just do not have the same power,” he said.

Election lawyers fear that actions by the Trump administration in the run-up to the midterms suggest the government will aggressively pursue postelection challenges if the results are not to the president’s liking.

Late last month, the DOJ sued Alaska, seeking to block the state from certifying the result of its Senate race if the Republican incumbent doesn’t win. A federal judge threw out that lawsuit on Sunday, but the administration is expected to appeal.

Trump has said he personally ordered the lawsuit to be filed. It claims the system is unfairly rigged against Sen. Dan Sullivan, because another Alaska man named Dan Sullivan also qualified for the general election ballot. The New York Times reported last week that campaign aides to Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola orchestrated the candidacy of the second Dan Sullivan after a monthslong, statewide search to recruit someone with the same name.

Nonetheless, the DOJ’s case is unusual, both because federal law prohibits the government from interfering with an active election and because challenges typically come after voting is complete. Postelection challenges are most often brought by losing candidates in state courts.

“This is using the federal government to interfere with our election process in a way that I think is pretty troubling on multiple levels,” said Brown, the Washington attorney general.

In response to ProPublica’s questions, the DOJ pointed to Blanche’s statement about the lawsuit on social media, which said the agency “does not seek to stop any ballot from being cast or to stop the certification of Alaska’s election.” (The lawsuit calls it “vital” that the state not certify “any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion” and asks the judge to prevent Alaska from doing this.)

Some election lawyers have suggested that if the GOP suffers significant losses, Trump could try to pressure Republicans in Congress to block new members from being seated. Several lawyers, including Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, say that the incoming Democratic majority would be able to fend off such an effort; courts, too, are likely to stymie it, though it might cause a short delay, according to Muller.

Brown said he and other attorneys general are also planning how to respond if local election officials or boards refuse to certify election results, based on their own claims of fraud or claims by the administration.

“I worry tremendously about what they might do,” Brown said.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. As Trump attempts to silence dissenting voices, we have no choice but to ask for your help.

We are fundraising today to fund our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: ROAPE
title: Africa on the map, but still off the table
content:
On 4 September 2026, the United Nations General Assembly adopted a non-binding resolution that might initially appear to belong to the relatively technical world of cartography. The resolution, “Correct the Map: Rebalancing Global Cartographic Representation and Promoting Equitable Representation of the World’s Regions, Particularly Africa,” was introduced by Togo on behalf of the African Group and adopted by 164 countries, with one country voting against and six abstaining.




In presenting the resolution, Togo’s Foreign Minister Robert Dussey argued that maps are not merely technical tools: their repeated use in schools, the media and digital platforms shapes how people understand and visualise the world. The African Group argued that the Mercator projection, designed for specific purposes—especially maritime navigation—had become a general-purpose image of the world that visually minimises Africa and other regions near the Equator.




The delegation framed the initiative around scientific and educational accuracy, cognitive justice, historical memory and the equal dignity of peoples. It also stressed what the resolution would not do: condemn the Mercator projection, impose a single map for every use, alter borders or take a position on territorial claims. Instead, it encouraged the use of projections such as Equal Earth when comparing the relative areas of continents, alongside better teaching about the strengths and limitations of different projections.




The resolution encourages the use of equal-area map projections, including Equal Earth, particularly when the relative size of regions matters. It also highlights the implications of existing representations for geographical and cartographic literacy. Importantly, however, it does not replace the Mercator projection, redraw international borders or alter the legal status of any territory. So why does a map matter? And why now?




These questions are more significant than the technical debate over which projection should be used. The UN resolution opens a much larger question about who has historically possessed the authority to represent the world, whose knowledge becomes universal knowledge, and what happens when previously marginalised actors begin to challenge that authority.




Mercator Map versus Equal Earth (wikicommons)




The map is not the territory—but it shapes how the territory is imagined




Gerardus Mercator’s famous projection was first published in 1569. It was developed primarily as a tool for maritime navigation, as its preservation of angles and constant compass bearings made it particularly useful for sailors plotting routes across oceans. The projection was never intended to provide an accurate comparison of the relative size of continents. Its distortion, however, has had a long afterlife.




Because the Mercator projection increasingly enlarges landmasses as they move away from the Equator, Greenland can appear comparable in size to Africa, despite Africa being approximately fourteen times larger.There is therefore an important distinction to make. Mercator was not invented as a deliberate attempt to make Africa smaller. Its original purpose was navigational. The political question emerges from what happened afterwards: how a projection designed for a particular technical purpose became normalised as a general image of the world.




A cartographic choice made for navigation became, through repetition, an educational and cultural convention. Maps entered classrooms, atlases, newspapers, television graphics, websites and digital platforms. In doing so, they did more than provide geographical information. They participated in producing a particular visual imagination of the world. This is where cartography becomes political. Can a two-dimensional map ever be neutral?




From geographical distortion to cognitive hierarchy




The significance of the new 

UN resolution

 therefore lies less in replacing one map with another than in recognising that representation itself has consequences. The resolution’s language is striking. It connects cartographic representation to education, perception and collective understanding, framing the correction of historical distortions as a matter of equitable representation. The UN Office of the Special Adviser on Africa has presented the initiative as an African-led effort to challenge the symbolic minimisation of the continent. But the tension remains.




If representation contributes to how societies imagine the world, then correcting representation can be understood as a form of cognitive or epistemic intervention. Yet cognitive correction is not the same thing as material transformation. Africa does not become politically more powerful because it appears larger on a classroom wall. Its borders do not change. Its economies do not automatically become less dependent on external capital. Its resources do not cease to be sites of extraction. Conflicts do not become more visible merely because the continent is represented more proportionately. This is precisely where the politics of the map becomes interesting. What does it mean to correct the image of Africa while leaving many of the structures that have historically shaped Africa’s position in the international system intact?




Why Africa, and why now?




The timing of the resolution is important. It comes amid a broader period in which African states have increasingly sought greater authority over how African histories, identities and political interests are represented internationally. In March 2026, for example, Ghana led a separate UN initiative recognising the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and racialised chattel enslavement as the “gravest crime against humanity”. That resolution was adopted by 123 votes to three, with 52 abstentions.




These initiatives are different in substance. One concerns historical enslavement; the other concerns cartographic representation. Yet they can be read together as part of a broader struggle over who gets to define historical knowledge and the terms of recognition within international institutions. This is not simply a demand to be represented more accurately. It is also a demand to participate in determining what counts as accuracy. That distinction matters.




For centuries, knowledge about Africa was frequently produced through institutions, categories and intellectual frameworks located outside the continent. Colonial cartography did not merely describe territories; it participated in ordering them. Colonial knowledge systems classified populations, territories and resources in ways that made them legible to imperial administration.




The contemporary map is not identical to the colonial map. Nor should Mercator’s projection itself be treated as a colonial conspiracy. But the history of mapping reminds us that knowledge and power have rarely been entirely separate.The question today is therefore not simply whether Africa has been drawn at the wrong scale. It is whether Africa is increasingly claiming the authority to participate in drawing the conceptual map of the world.




The paradox of symbolic recognition




Here lies the deeper paradox. The international system can recognise that Africa has been visually underrepresented while continuing to struggle with the structural inequalities that shape Africa’s position within that same system. The map can be corrected much more easily than the hierarchy. A classroom can replace one projection with another in an afternoon. Changing the global distribution of economic power, institutional representation and access to capital—and changing who controls natural resources or sets the terms of international decision-making—is considerably more difficult. I describe this gap as moral fragmentation.




By moral fragmentation, I mean a condition in which international actors can converge around the recognition of a particular historical or representational injustice while remaining divided—or unwilling to act collectively—on the deeper structures through which inequality is reproduced. The map provides a particularly revealing example. The African Union has also called for permanent African representation on the UN Security Council. This demand raises a related question: how should the continent’s political weight and interests be represented within global institutions?




There is now remarkably broad agreement that the relative size of Africa should not be visually distorted when size is what a map is intended to communicate. Yet there is no equivalent consensus about what a more equitable international political and economic order should look like. The correction of representation therefore raises an uncomfortable question: Can an international system correct the image of inequality without confronting the structures that produce inequality?




The politics of the classroom




The emphasis on education in the resolution deserves particular attention. The UN initiative is not only about producing a different image for diplomats or cartographers. It explicitly engages with educational and geographical literacy.




That matters because maps enter political consciousness long before most people encounter international relations as an academic discipline. Children learn the world through images. They learn which countries appear large, which appear small, which regions dominate the page, and which are visually peripheral. They learn spatial hierarchies before they necessarily have the vocabulary to question them.




This does not mean that seeing Africa at its correct relative scale automatically produces anti-racist or anti-colonial consciousness. That would be another form of determinism. But it does mean that representational choices form part of the environment in which political knowledge is produced. The classroom is therefore not politically neutral simply because the lesson is called geography.The question is not whether a map determines what a child thinks. It is whether repeated representations contribute to what becomes familiar, normal and imaginable.




The United States and the politics of disagreement




The vote itself adds another layer to the story. The United States was the only country to vote against the resolution, while Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia and Ukraine abstained. It would be tempting to interpret the American vote as evidence that Washington rejects the principle of more equitable representation of Africa. The vote alone, however, cannot establish that. The United States did offer an explicit explanation: its representative argued that the resolution formed part of what 

Washington characterised as a wider ideological project

, pointing specifically to references to reparations and “cognitive justice”.




The US delegation described resolutions of this kind as distractions from issues it considered more directly connected to international peace, prosperity and good relations, and argued that they undermined the UN’s credibility. This provides evidence for interpreting the vote: the objection was not presented as a technical disagreement over the mathematics of map projections, but as opposition to the resolution’s wider political framing. It does not, however, establish every motive behind the vote or mean that the United States opposed all efforts to improve cartographic accuracy.




The contrast is revealing: Togo presented accurate representation as a matter of dignity and educational fairness, while the United States treated the 

resolution’s links to reparations

 and cognitive justice as evidence of ideological overreach. Several delegations supporting the resolution emphasised that it should not be understood as changing borders, sovereignty or territorial claims. Mexico, for example, supported the resolution while stressing that different projections serve different purposes and that no single projection can represent every property of the Earth without distortion.




This disagreement is important because it prevents the debate from becoming a simplistic opposition between a supposedly enlightened South and an obstructive North. Politics are more complicated.




The real question is not whether one map is universally “correct”. Every projection involves choices and compromises. The question is who gets to decide which compromises are appropriate, for which purposes, and whose historical experience informs those decisions.




From correcting the map to questioning the world it represents




Perhaps the most provocative aspect of the resolution is therefore not that Africa will appear larger. It is that an African-led initiative has successfully placed a seemingly technical question of cartography onto the agenda of the world’s principal multilateral institution.  For a long time, Africa has frequently appeared in international discourse as an object of knowledge: a continent to be mapped, measured, developed, secured, rescued or extracted from. The “Correct the Map” initiative reverses that relationship, at least symbolically. Africa is not simply being represented; it is intervening in the politics of representation.




But symbolic intervention has limits. If the correction ends with a different image on the classroom wall, the transformation remains incomplete. The more difficult task is to ask what else must be corrected: whose knowledge is treated as authoritative, whose histories receive institutional recognition, who controls resources, who sets the terms of development, whose voices shape international institutions, and who gets to define what constitutes justice.




The danger is that the international system becomes very good at recognising injustice symbolically while becoming considerably less willing to redistribute power materially. That is the contradiction at the heart of the new map. A larger Africa on the map is not necessarily a more powerful Africa in the world. That is precisely why the map matters. The point of correcting it should not be to make Africa look bigger. It should be to make visible the question of why Africa has so often been made to matter less.

Africa on the map, but still off the table

 appeared first on

title: S. E. Parker - Krieg und Frieden
content:

Während der letzten zwei Jahrzehnte haben wir uns so daran gewöhnt in einer Welt des Krieges oder der Bedrohung durch einen Krieg zu leben, daß wir begonnen haben, eine solche Situation beinah als normal zu betrachten. In einer Atmosphäre dauernder Krisen, Kriege und heißer Vorfälle hat ein aktiver Widerstand gegen den Krieg eine deutliche Neigung schwach zu werden, sogar bedeutungslos zu sein, obschon es scheint, daß der Kessel auf dem Punkte ist, jederzeit überzukochen. Bis heute hat er es noch nicht getan, mag er uns auch dann und wann bange machen, wenn sein Deckel klappert.

Als eine Folge dieser “Normalität” der Krisen verlieren Warnungen gegen die Gefahr des Krieges, seine Übel und gänzliche Unverantwortlichkeit, ihre Dringlichkeit und werden ein Teil der täglichen Klischees. Es ist wahr, daß Explosionen der A- und H-Bomben hysterische Wellen und Spannungen auslösen, aber nachdem die Versammlungen gehalten wurden, die Bittschriften unterzeichnet, die Wissenschaftler sich gezankt haben, glätten sich diese Wellen wieder. Sogar auf der Höhe einer solchen Panik fühlt man, daß hier etwas fehlt. Die Phrasen vom Frieden und von den Übeln des Krieges scheinen unwirklich, abgenutzt und verblaßt zu sein durch andauernden Gebrauch und andauernden Verrat. Man muß an die Versammlungen vor dem ersten Weltkriege denken, mit ihren Beschlüssen von internationaler Solidarität: man erinnert sich der Debatten und Demonstrationen zwischen 1918 und 1939, und der Gelübde, das Kämpfen abzulehnen. Und dann erinnert man sich, wie alles praktisch zwecklos war, die Massen gehorsam die Uniformen anzogen und wie sie sich gegenseitig abschlachteten auf Befehl ihrer Herrscher: mit Beifall begrüßt von vielen derjenigen, die vorher so laut nach Frieden schrien.

Auf diese Weise gefangen in einer für den Krieg gerüsteten Welt, zwischen der falschen Hoffnung, daß der Krieg abgewandt oder auf unbestimmte Zeit verschoben werden kann und dem niederdrückenden Wissen von den Mißerfolgen aller Anstrengungen für den Frieden wird man oft in die Verzweiflung gestürzt.

Was können wir, die Anarchisten, darauf antworten?

Wie wir es sehen, kann das Problem des Krieges nicht isoliert von den anderen sozialen Fragen betrachtet werden. Die Wurzeln des Krieges liegen in der heutigen sozialen Anordnung. Der Krieg ist heute notwendig für die kapitalistische Ökonomie. Ohne Krieg oder der Vorbereitung für einen Krieg würde es dem Kapitalismus unmöglich sein, die erzeugten Waren unterzubringen und die Vollbeschäftigung für seine Lohnsklaven aufrechzuerhalten oder die unheilvollen Preisstürze und Krisen abzuwenden, die vor 1939 charakterzeigend für seine Existenz waren. Es gibt keine Märkte mehr zu erobern, keine neuen Quellen von Rohmaterial, die nicht direkt oder indirekt unter der Kontrolle irgendeiner Macht stünden; die kapitalistischen Nationen sind in Verlegenheit. Einziger Weg aus dieser Verlegenheit ist der Krieg. Durch einen Krieg kann der “Überschuß” an Waren untergebracht werden und brauchbare Quellen für Material und “Reichtum” werden gewonnen. Das heißt nicht, daß die einzelnen Kapitalisten ihre Zeit damit verbringen, Kriege anzuzetteln oder wissentlich darauf hoffen, aber Krieg ist dem Mechanismus der Profit-Ökonomie angeboren und dem Staate der dieses unterstützt. Sogar wenn der Staat aufhörte, das ausführende Organ einer herrschenden Klasse zu sein und der politische und wirtschaftliche Herr der Gesellschaft wird, so kann er doch nicht die Notwendigkeit eines Krieges vermeiden als das letzte Instrument im Kampfe um die Weltherrschaft.

Natürlich gibt es viele, besonders unter den Pazifisten, die im Grunde mit dieser Analyse einverstanden sind, aber die anführen, daß der Krieg das größte Übel unserer Zeit sei und darum mit allen Mitteln versucht werden müsse, einen Krieg zu verhindern. Deshalb ihre Verteidigungen der Zusammenkünft von Staatsmännern mit den Versuchen durch Verhandlungen die A- und H-Bomben zu ächten, Unterstützung der UNO und Forderung einer Weltregierung. Gewiß, auf den ersten Blick scheinen solche Vorschläge viel praktischer zu sein denn die Haltung der “Puritaner”, die den Krieg als eine Folge des Staats- und Eigentums-Systems ansehen und seine Abschaffung als untrennbar von der Abschaffung dieser Systeme. Schaut man unter das Flittergold dieser praktischen Pläne, dann kann man sehen, daß sie auf falschen Grundlagen stehen.

Wie schon bereits gesagt wurde, wurzelt der Krieg in dem heutigen Gesellschafts-System und er zieht seine Nahrung aus dem Grundsatz der Autorität und der Beherrschung und Ausbeutung die es erzeugt.

Es genügt nicht, daß man bei einem Unkraut bloß die Blätter abschneidet, man muß auch die Wurzeln ausrotten wenn man es vernichten will. Wiederum ist es die Höhe der Unwirklichkeit, von einer solchen Einrichtung wie dem Staat, der gegründet wurde um Krieg zu führen, zu erwarten, daß er ein Mittel zum Frieden sein könne. Von Staatsmännern erwarten, die nicht gezögert haben zwei Weltkriege zu führen und beschäftigt sind einen dritten vorzubereiten, daß diese den Grund ihrer Existenz beseitigen, der muß der größte Tropf sein.

Die naive Haltung derjenigen, die annehmen, daß der politische Leopard seine Flecken ändere, ist ebenso albern wie die jener, welche glauben, daß die furchtbare Zerstörungskraft der modernen Waffen einen Krieg verhindern wird. Dieses könnte etwas Glaubwürdiges haben, wenn die Menschen, die im Kommando der militärischen Maschine sind, vernünftige Menschen wären, aber wie ihr Betragen in letzter Zeit gezeigt hat, sind sie es nicht – sondern sie sind geistig Kranke.

Die Ursache der augenscheinlichen Unwirksamkeit der heutigen Anstrengungen für Frieden liegt in der Oberflächlichkeit der Einschätzung derjenigen, welche dem Krieg entgegentreten. Der Kampf für die Abschaffung des Krieges muß verbunden werden mit dem Kampf gegen das heutige unsoziale System. Individueller und kollektiver Widerstand gegen Militarismus und Staat müssen gegründet werden auf das Verständnis, daß Krieg die Natur des Staates ist und seinem Fortkommen dient. Widerstand gegen den Krieg kann nicht getrennt werden vom Widerstand gegen die Autorität. Im Verkehr und in den Beziehungen zwischen Menschen ist stets der Grundsatz der Autorität, daß Menschen zur Herrschaft kommen über ihre Mitmenschen und auf diese Weise den bösartigen Kreislauf des Konkurrenzkampfes in Bewegung setzen, der zum Kriege führt. Wir Anarchisten lehnen Vorrechte und Macht ab. Wir streben weder Herrenmenschen noch Massenmenschen zu sein, wir wollen freie Menschen sein. In der Gesellschaft, die wir uns wünschen, ist alle Autorität der Menschen über Menschen abgeschaft und die Befriedigung der menschlichen Bedürfnisse wird erlangt durch freiwillige Zusammenarbeit unabhängiger Menschen. Krieg, Produkt des konkurrierenden ökonomischen Systems, aufrechterhalten durch den Zwang der Regierungen und den Gehorsam der Massen, hat logischerweise keinen Platz in der freien Gesellschaft der Anarchie. Der Friede wird herrschen, wenn Menschen ablehnen weder Herrscher noch Beherrschte, weder Ausbeuter noch Ausgebeutete zu sein. In der Zwischenzeit ist es unsere Aufgabe sowohl dem Krieg als auch dem sogar Frieden genannten Ruhezustand der Autorität entgegenzutreten. Wir müssen mit unserem eigenen Ungehorsam die soziale Revolution beginnen, den grundsätzlichen Wechsel im menschlichen Verkehr und in den menschlichen Beziehungen verwirklichen, welcher allein Garantie ist für den Frieden und die Brüderlichkeit in unserer Welt.

title: Despidos masivos en IOSFA: más de mil trabajadores de todo el país quedan en la calle
content:
La liquidación y el desmantelamiento del Instituto de Obra Social de las Fuerzas Armadas y de Seguridad (IOSFA) avanzan con consecuencias devastadoras para sus trabajadores y sus familias, denunciaron desde la Asociación de Trabajadores del Estado.







En el marco de la lucha nacional que el gremio está desarrollando en defensa de las funciones de la Obra Social de las Fuerzas Armadas y del Personal Civil (IOSFA/OSFA), en el marco de la cual 

realizó una Jornada Nacional el último jueves

, la Seccional Rosario de ATE denunció hoy que el gobierno cierra la estructura de la obra social en Rosario, lo que afecta directamente a 60 estatales. En la ciudad de Santa Fe, capital provincial, otros 25 trabajadores enfrentan la pérdida de sus puestos laborales.




Esta situación se enmarca en un proceso que alcanza a más de 1.000 trabajadores de IOSFA en todo el país, muchos de ellos con décadas de antigüedad, que hoy quedan sin trabajo y sin reconocimiento por toda una vida de servicio a la institución.




Durante años, estos trabajadores fueron contratados mediante contratos sucesivos y renovaciones consecutivas que no les reconocían estabilidad laboral, pese a que en la práctica sostenían tareas permanentes y esenciales para el funcionamiento de la obra social. Hoy, esa modalidad de contratación se convierte en el argumento para desvincularlos, desconociendo décadas de trabajo y compromiso, denunciaron desde el gremio




Para ATE, no se trata solamente de una reorganización administrativa. Son miles de familias las que pierden su sustento. Son trabajadores que sostuvieron IOSFA durante años y que ahora enfrentan la incertidumbre y la desprotección.




Por eso el Sindicato exige respuestas, respeto por los derechos laborales y soluciones concretas para todos los trabajadores afectados.

author: Joshua Carroll
title: NHS Claims Palantir’s Tech Helps Hospitals That Are Not Even Using It
content:
The NHS claimed dozens of hospitals had benefited from a platform built by spytech firm Palantir despite the hospitals not even using it, an investigation has found.  




Medical charity Medact revealed that 29 NHS Trusts supposedly “realising benefits” from the AI-powered federated data platform (FDP) have either said the system is not live or that they are not using any of its applications.




The revelations, based on freedom of information requests, add weight to widespread calls for Andy Burnham’s government to cancel the NHS’s £330m deal with the US firm. 




Those calls are based on fears that patient data could be misused by Palantir, which has worked closely with Israel’s military amid its genocide in Gaza and also sells its services to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).




Labour MP Chi Onwurah, who chairs the parliamentary science and technology committee, said the government should exercise a 2027 break clause in the NHS contract. 




“If many NHS trusts don’t see the value of the FDP, serious questions need to be asked about whether the hype surrounding Palantir’s products matches reality,” she 

told the Guardian

. 




Analysis by the think tank Health Foundation 

found in July

 that a patient discharge tool from Palantir made “no meaningful difference” in discharge delays despite claims by NHS England to the contrary. 




In response to public 

pressure to exclude Palantir

 from UK government contracts, the company has ramped up lobbying efforts. In September, it appointed former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson as a senior vice president, and he has since said that 

“mob rule”

 should not dictate how public contracts are awarded.




Last month, 

Novara Media revealed

 that Palantir has sent “intimidating” letters to British MPs who have criticised the company. 




Former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn was among those to receive a letter from Palantir’s UK CEO Louis Mosley, who is the grandson of deceased fascist leader Oswald Mosley. 




“Their tactics of intimidation will not work and they will not shut me up,” Corbyn said.  




A spokesperson told the Guardian that Palantir’s software “is helping to deliver better care” including more operation and lower discharge delays.
