author: Publicación Abierta
title: Empresarios aplauden al presidente cuando pide una hoguera para quemar periodistas
content:
Sólo una Cámara empresaria salió a criticar los dichos del presidente Javier Milei.




Milei en la Fundación Faro




Por Mario Hernandez




Luego de que el viernes 23 de octubre, ante empresarios, el Presidente pidiera una hoguera para quemar a los periodistas, sólo una Cámara emitió un comunicado para alertar sobre el avance del mandatario sobre la democracia, y además lo hizo sin siquiera citar a Milei.




El resto, en tanto, se mantvo en una absoluta negación. La que se expresó sobre el tema fue IDEA. Las que no lo hicieron fueron la Unión Industrial Argentina (UIA), la Asociación Empresaria Argentina (AEA), AMCHAM (la Cámara de empresas estadounidenses en Argentina, el Grupo de los Seis (Sociedad Rural, UIA, Cámara de Comercio y Construcción, ADEBA, la Bolsa) y el campo en general.




Hace una semana, todos ellos emitieron un documento opinando contra un fallo de la Justicia sobre un bloqueo de camioneros a una empresa pyme. Fue una acción como ya ha ocurrido, años previos, con decisiones de política de Estado, discusiones del PJ con la Corte Suprema, críticas del kirchnerismo a los medios y cualquier otra cosa que ameritara marcar la cancha. En los años del macrismo, de hecho, se creó el Foro de Convergencia Empresarial, con el fin de tener una institución que defendiera al PRO y cuestionara a los opositores. Lo integraban dirigentes de todas las Cámaras.




El alineamiento de los privados con Milei, para conservar reformas de fondo, acumular poder y tener negocios, es prioridad sobre cualquier ataque al sistema democrático.




IDEA, el instituto que organiza el coloquio empresario en Mar del Plata, es un polo afín a las ideas liberales. Históricamente reacio a posiciones donde el Estado tiene más poder. Aún así, fue la única entidad que se expresó sobre los desbordes presidenciales.




En un comunicado, precisaron que “la libertad de prensa y el respeto por las ideas, aun cuando existan diferencias, son pilares fundamentales de la convivencia democrática. Desde IDEA consideramos que el debate público debe desarrollarse en un marco de pluralidad de opiniones, diálogo y respeto, sin agravios ni descalificaciones”.




En esa línea, evitaron pronunciar la palabra Milei al aseverar que “quienes fueron elegidos para gobernar deben actuar con responsabilidad y contribuir a un debate público respetuoso. Los agravios a periodistas en el ejercicio de su función contradicen ese deber”.




IDEA concluye que, “en un contexto en el que la ciudadanía realiza un esfuerzo colectivo para alcanzar la estabilidad y el desarrollo del país, desde IDEA insistimos en la necesidad de promover y respetar la libertad de prensa y de expresión, y de sostener un debate público basado en el respeto, la tolerancia y la responsabilidad”.




Los concurrentes al evento de la Fundación Faro aceptaron pagar 25 mil dólares por cabeza o 300.000 pesos por una mesa en el Yacht Club de Puerto Madero a los anfitriones, los Neuss, el grupo que se está quedando con buena parte de los negocios en la era libertaria. También estuvieron José Luis Manzano, Hugo Eurnekian, Bettina Bulgheroni (CICYP y PAE), Marcelo Mindlin, el dueño de Swiss Medical, Claudio Belocopitt y líneas medias de Techint. Se hizo ver, además, el hombre fuerte de Marcos Galperín en Mercado Libre, Juan Martín de la Serna. Todos ganadores y pocos “perdedores” del modelo, entre ellos Gustavo Weiss, titular de la Cámara Argentina de la Construcción.




Rubén Tchernaskovsky




Uno por uno los empresarios aplaudidores




Entre los primeros nombres mencionados apareció Rubén Tchernaskovsky, principal accionista de Newsan y con vínculos en el sector energético.




Damián Pozzoli




También Damián Pozzoli, propietario de Havanna. Además, se mencionó la asociación de Tchernaskovsky y los Neuss en Edison Energía y su participación en operaciones vinculadas con privatizaciones energéticas, entre ellas Transener.




Juan y Patricio Neuss 




Otro de los empresarios fue Marcelo Mindlin, presidente de Pampa Energía y del Museo del Holocausto de Buenos Aires.




Marcelo Mindlin (Pampa Energía)




La periodista Natalia Volosin, quien dijo tener un vínculo personal con él, cuestionó su presencia en el evento: “Yo me pregunto qué hubieras hecho y si hubieras aplaudido si hubieran llamado a quemar judíos”. Más adelante, insistió: “Sería importante que cuando llaman a quemar periodistas tampoco te pares a aplaudir”.




Hugo Sigman




En el repaso también aparecieron Marcelo Cielecki, socio de Mindlin en negocios vinculados con el transporte de gas, y Hugo Sigman, relacionado con Cielecki y con el sector farmacéutico.







Otro de los nombres mencionados fue Adrián Huerten, dueño de DirecTV y vinculado al sector de las telecomunicaciones. Durante el intercambio también se señaló su participación en el negocio de internet satelital y la adquisición de derechos deportivos.




Francisco De Narváez escuchó a Javier Milei en la Fundación Faro




El periodista Antonio Riccobene aportó que, después de que trascendieran las declaraciones presidenciales, algunos asistentes habrían intentado reducir su exposición pública. Según explicó, “intentaron, borraron muchísimas fotos en las que aparecían, pidieron que no se difundiera la lista de invitados”. También señaló que la Fundación Faro no quiso entregar la lista de participantes, porque, según la explicación que recibieron, así se había acordado.




Fabián Kon, ex gerente general del Galicia




Entre los asistentes figuró Fabián Kon, ex CEO del Grupo Galicia y presidente de IDEA. Después del encuentro, la organización difundió un comunicado sobre la libertad de prensa: “La libertad de prensa y el respeto por las ideas, aun cuando existan diferencias, son pilares fundamentales de la convivencia democrática”.




Martín Migoya, co-fundador y CEO de Globant




En el listado también se mencionó a Martín Migoya, CEO de Globant e integrante de la Asociación Empresaria Argentina (AEA). Uno de los asistentes que estaba en primera fila aplaudiendo.




Juan Martín de la Serna, Mercado Libre




Otro nombre destacado fue Juan Martín de la Serna, presidente de Mercado Libre en Argentina.







Movilización en defensa del Estatuto del periodista




El jueves 29 de octubre, numerosos sindicatos de prensa, carreras universitarias de comunicación de todo el país, ArGRA y sectores de la cultura y la comunicación se concentraron frente al Congreso a partir de las 12:00 para exigir que sesione la Comisión de Trabajo y Previsión del Senado y trate el proyecto de actualización del Estatuto del Periodista Profesional y del Personal Administrativo presentado en junio pasado.




Compartimos comunicado del Sindicato de Prensa de Buenos Aires:




Agustín Lecchi: “Los senadores no están haciendo su trabajo y tienen que tratar el Estatuto del Periodista”


El secretario general del Sindicato de Prensa de Buenos Aires (SiPreBA), Agustín Lecchi, sostuvo que “las y los senadores que hablan de regulaciones laborales no están haciendo su trabajo” y reclamó que al Comisión de Trabajo y Previsión del Senado “trate el proyecto de reforma” presentado por todos los sindicatos del país agrupados en la Federación de Trabajadores de Prensa (FATPREN).




“Desde la sanción de la reforma laboral, la Comisión de Legislación del Trabajo del Senado no se volvió a reunir ni una sola vez”, señaló Lecchi en declaraciones al programa “Pasaron cosas”, en 

Radio Con Vos

, y convocó a la concentración que se realizó este jueves 29/10 a las 12:00 frente al Senado para exigir a la comisión laboral que trate el proyecto de actualización del Estatuto del Periodista Profesional y del Personal Administrativo presentado en junio pasado.




La convocatoria se realizó junto las carreras universitarias de comunicación de todo el país, sindicatos de prensa, ArGRA y sectores de la cultura y la comunicación.




Al describir el comportamiento de las y los senadores ante la presentación del proyecto de modernización del Estatuto, Lecchi precisó: “El PRO actúa igual que la Libertad Avanza. En el radicalismo hay excepciones como la de




Maximiliano Abad, que no votó la derogación del Estatuto del Periodista, pero la mayoría del bloque sí lo hizo. Incluso Carolina Losada, que viene de trabajar en medios de comunicación”.




“Hay senadores como Eduardo Vischi, de la UCR, que es parte de la comisión del Senado, y podría promover que se reúna, como lo hacen otros senadores peronistas como Mariano Recalde, Juliana Di Tulio o Flavia Royón”, agregó.




Además dijo: “Lo que me preocupa es que, en un contexto de gran ataque a la libertad de expresión, donde el Presidente de la Nación dice que nos quiere quemar en la hoguera, los empresarios de medios aprovechan la política laboral de este gobierno para derogar una ley que protege la libertad de expresión, que nos protege”.




“Tenemos una propuesta en donde eliminamos un montón de artículos que quedaron viejos, pero sostenemos los derechos fundamentales como la protección de la libertad de expresión, la indemnización especial y algunos resguardos a la actividad periodística de carácter profesional e incorporamos nuevos elementos vinculados a las plataformas, a la inteligencia artificial, al teletrabajo y a la cobertura en exteriores porque la represión existió siempre pero nunca con tanta saña como ahora hacia el trabajo de los periodistas que cubren en la calle”, completó.




“No vendan el Estatuto”




Sindicatos de prensa de todo el país, representantes de las carreras de comunicación y organizaciones de la sociedad civil se movilizaron el jueves 29 al Congreso de la Nación para reclamar que traten los diversos proyectos legislativos para actualizar o prorrogar el Estatuto del Periodista Profesional (Ley 12.908), cuya derogación fue establecida por la regresiva Reforma Laboral del gobierno nacional de ultraderecha a partir del 1º de enero de 2027.




“Senadores, diputados: NO VENDAN EL ESTATUTO DEL PERIODISTA, la libertad de expresión y el derecho a la información”, pidieron dirigentes gremiales, periodistas y trabajadores y trabajadoras de prensa en la bandera que desplegaron en la puerta del Congreso Nacional. La acción de visibilización fue impulsada por el Sindicato de Prensa de Buenos Aires (SiPreBa) y la Federación Argentina de Trabajadores de Prensa (FATPREN).




En el marco de la protesta, se presentó una solicitud formal dirigida a la senadora Carmen Álvarez Rivero, presidenta de la Comisión de Trabajo y Previsión Social del Senado, y a los legisladores que la integran. El documento exige la inmediata convocatoria a reunión de comisión para evitar que la inacción parlamentaria decante en un vacío legal, que termine exponiendo al periodismo en una situación de vulnerabilidad mayor a las presiones políticas, económicas y judiciales.




La nota convoca a todos los miembros de la comisión a tratar los proyectos, pero puntualmente a los legisladores que se comprometieron a discutir una actualización de la Ley 12.908 en el marco de la prórroga, como los senadores Carolina Losada, Eduardo Vischi, Sonia Rojas Decut, José Carambia, Flavia Gabriela Royón y Carolina Moisés, entre otros.




“En un contexto de gran ataque a la libertad de expresión, donde el Presidente de la Nación dice que nos quiere quemar en la hoguera, los empresarios de medios aprovechan la política laboral de este gobierno para derogar una ley que nos protege y resguarda la libertad de expresión”, sostuvo Agustín Lecchi, secretario general de SiPreBA.




Durante el acto expresaron su apoyo los senadores Mariano Recalde, Marcelo Lewandowski, Jimena López, Ana Inés Marks y María Teresa González, junto al diputado Esteban Paulón y el legislador porteño Gabriel Solano.




Entre las organizaciones que acompañan el pedido al Congreso se encuentran la Federación Internacional de Periodistas (FIP), el Centro de Estudios Legales y Sociales (CELS), la Asociación de Reporteros Gráficos de la República Argentina (ARGRA), la Federación Argentina de Carreras de Comunicación Social (FADECCOS), Periodistas Argentinas, la Red de Carreras de Comunicación Social (REDCOM) y la Carrera de Comunicación de la Universidad de Buenos Aires (UBA).

title: Peace Mothers head to Ankara
content:
Peace Mothers from several cities in Northern Kurdistan have set off for the Turkish capital, Ankara, to hold a two-day vigil. They are demanding the physical freedom of Abdullah Öcalan, the release of political prisoners, and concrete steps toward implementing the peace and democratic society process. Before their departure, the women gathered at two meeting points in Van and Amed (Diyarbakır).




In Van, Peace Mothers from Tatvan and Hakkari joined local participants at Musa Anter Park. Chanting slogans such as “Long live the resistance in the prisons” and “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî – Freedom for the leader,” they set off for Ankara.




In Amed, Peace Mothers from Siirt and Batman, together with activists from local women’s groups, gathered at the Human Rights Monument in Koşuyolu Park. Chanting “Long live the resistance of the mothers” and “Long live the resistance in the prisons,” they reaffirmed their demands.




Speaking on behalf of the assembled women, Afife Kartal stated that the Peace Mothers were no longer willing to accept the continuation of the political process without concrete steps from the Turkish government.




“We are going to Ankara to demand the physical freedom of Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan and our children in prison. We do not want Öcalan to remain imprisoned on Imralı. We will fight for his physical freedom. We are going to Ankara to open the gates of Imralı and secure his freedom.”




Kartal called on the Turkish government to fulfill its responsibility to achieve a political solution to the Kurdish question: “We Kurds demand our rights. The state must take the necessary steps. For the process to succeed, we want the safe return of our children and the release of prisoners. To this end, we will intensify our struggle and take our demands directly to Ankara, where those responsible are based.”




The Peace Mothers then set off for the capital amid applause, chants, and the traditional ululations of Kurdish women.

title: People of Kobanê celebrate World Kobanê Day
content:
World Kobanê Day was marked with a public celebration in Kobanê on November 1. Under the slogan “In memory of the heroic martyrs – Long live World Kobanê Day,” large numbers of people gathered to commemorate the resistance against the terrorist organization Islamic State (ISIS) in 2014 and those who lost their lives. The event focused on the historical significance of the resistance, the leading role of women, and the defense of the achievements of the revolution in Rojava.




The celebration began with a minute of silence in memory of the martyrs. Ferhan Hec Îsa then addressed the gathering on behalf of the people of Kobanê. He paid tribute to those who had defended the city against ISIS attacks and made its liberation possible.




“November 1, World Kobanê Day, is not merely a day of remembrance on the calendar. This date represents the epic resistance through which the people of Kobanê rose up against the attacks of dark forces in 2014 and emerged victorious. Today, Kobanê is known worldwide as a city that has entered the history of resistance and dignity through its struggle against ISIS,” Hec Îsa said.




He called for the achievements won through the struggle to be preserved: “Kobanê is a city that belongs to all of us. We must defend the achievements of the resistance of Kobanê.”




Women paved the way for victory




Perwîn Yûsif, Co-Chair of the Democratic Union Party (PYD), spoke on behalf of the women’s movement. She highlighted the crucial role of the Women’s Protection Units (YPJ) and the People’s Protection Units (YPG) in the liberation of Kobanê.




“The resistance, which has continued under women’s leadership to this day, has brought about major achievements. The resistance in North and East Syria has become a symbol for the entire Middle East. ISIS mercenaries and their supporters had no regard for human values. They murdered women and children and destroyed entire cities. Yet thanks to the resistance of YPJ and YPG fighters, the fight to push back ISIS began in Kobanê.”




Yûsif emphasized that defending the revolution remained a central responsibility: “What is required of us today is to protect the achievements of our revolution, continue the struggle in the spirit of November 1, and achieve historic victories.”




The celebration then continued with a cultural program featuring performances by kamancheh player Zêrîn Ararat and musician Xelîl Can. The event concluded with slogans including “Long live the resistance of Kobanê,” “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî,” and “No life without the leader.”

author: Unknown
title: Women’s conference in Ankara criticizes stagnation in the peace process
content:
The stalled peace process in Turkey and the responsibility of politicians and society to achieve a democratic solution to the Kurdish question dominated the second day of the women’s conference in Ankara. Discussions focused on the lack of concrete political steps, the unequal conditions surrounding negotiations with Abdullah Öcalan, and how women from different social and political backgrounds could work together to achieve lasting peace. Participants made it clear that while they regarded an end to the armed conflict as a crucial step forward, they did not consider it sufficient in itself to guarantee peace in society.




The conference, titled “Women Discuss the Future Side by Side,” was initiated by 80 women and opened on Saturday with more than 500 participants. On the second day, female politicians, academics, and activists gathered at the Chamber of Civil Engineers to discuss political responsibility for peace, the role of parliament, and opportunities for grassroots organizing.




Buldan warns of deadlock in the peace process




Pervin Buldan, a DEM Party MP and member of the Imralı delegation, recalled the failed peace negotiations between 2013 and 2015 and the subsequent ten years of armed conflict. She emphasized that the most significant achievement of both the previous and current talks was the protection of human lives. At the same time, she pointed to the unequal conditions under which the political actors involved were operating. While President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and MHP leader Devlet Bahçeli are able to carry out their political duties freely, she said, Abdullah Öcalan is attempting to advance the process from a prison cell. She explicitly expressed her gratitude to him for his efforts.




However, Buldan expressed concern about the current state of the talks. T”he Imralı delegation last visited Öcalan on September 13. There has been no further meeting since that day. So, there is something of a deadlock. Overcoming this impasse should not be left solely to the political negotiators. Women in this room can decide today that we need peace. They can become an organized force that puts pressure on the government and the actors involved in the process to ensure that it continues,” she said.




Buldan also proposed establishing dedicated women’s committees within the structures responsible for overseeing and monitoring the peace process. She stressed that women must come together not only in conference halls but also in public squares and on the streets.




Criticism over the delayed implementation of the framework law




Gökçe Gökçen, an MP from the YENI Party, criticized the government’s approach so far. She emphasized that the Kurdish question and the democratization of Turkey were inseparably linked, arguing that limiting the process to disarmament alone would be insufficient. “One side says that this is exclusively a matter of security and therefore calls the entire process a ‘terror-free Turkey.’ We, on the other hand, speak of a ‘democratic Turkey,’” Gökçen stated.




She stressed that laying down arms was important but must be accompanied by democratic reforms. Lasting social peace, she argued, required equality to become a lived reality and public confidence in justice to grow.




Gökçen was particularly critical of the delays in implementing the framework law passed by parliament on August 10. She said the text of the law had been presented only at the last moment, without allowing for a broad political debate. Unlike other political groups, her party was not invited to participate in the discussions, she added.




“Distrust of the process is, in fact, distrust of the government,” Gökçen said. She argued that the government had had numerous opportunities to take confidence-building measures but had failed to do so. She stressed that making the implementation of the law dependent on a decision by the National Security Council (MGK), thereby postponing it indefinitely, was neither politically nor legally justifiable.




“Peace is too serious a matter to be left to men and governments”




Former HDP MP Filiz Kerestecioğlu emphasized society’s responsibility in the peace process. Peace negotiations, she argued, should not be treated as a technical matter reserved for political decision-makers. “Peace is too serious a matter to be left to men and governments. It is also too serious to be treated as a purely technical issue. Society must be convinced of the process and actively participate in shaping it,” Kerestecioğlu said.




Responding to the frequently asked question of how women could trust the government in such a process, she said: “We don’t trust the government at all. Nor do we have to. What matters is trusting ourselves. The question is: Where do we stand in this process?”




Using a photograph from Cizre, Kerestecioğlu recalled the curfews and military siege imposed on Kurdish cities in 2015. She recounted the story of a woman she had helped transport for medical treatment at the time. Rather than being able to rely on the support of other women, she had been forced to seek assistance from then-Education Minister Nabi Avcı. She described the experience as an example of the isolation in which many Kurdish women had been left during the attacks. “When we say that women stand side by side, we must also be able to understand and empathize with that loneliness,” Kerestecioğlu said.




Buldan: “We must not pit the suffering of mothers against one another”




Pervin Buldan also addressed the human consequences of the conflict. She displayed photographs of Ceylan Önkol and Eren Bülbül, two children who lost their lives under different circumstances in connection with the war in Kurdistan. “Ceylan’s mother and Eren’s mother shed the same tears. We must not pit the suffering of these two mothers against one another,” she said.




One could spend hours discussing the Roboski massacre, unsolved political murders, and the injustices suffered by the Kurdish population, Buldan said. At the same time, she added, it was necessary to acknowledge that the conflict had affected people from different segments of society. “The silence of the guns alone is not enough to build lasting peace. We also need democratization and freedoms,” she emphasized.




In Buldan’s view, a new constitution could only be drafted on the basis of a broad social consensus. The current constitution dates back to the 1980 military coup. However, she stressed that overcoming the present deadlock in the peace process must take priority.




Arzu Yılmaz: Peace process is the result of historical changes




Political scientist Arzu Yılmaz placed the current developments within a broader political context. She argued that the peace process had not emerged from a voluntary rapprochement between the Kurdish movement and the AKP government, but rather from changing historical and regional circumstances.




“After all, the Kurds did not choose to make peace with the AKP either. It was not a free choice. Rather, both sides found themselves in a historical situation in which change became inevitable,” Yılmaz said. In her assessment, the process was also driven by state interests. Faced with profound transformations, the state is attempting to prepare for necessary changes, minimize risks, and safeguard its own interests, she added.




Yılmaz pointed out that conventional political concepts and approaches were no longer sufficient to understand these developments. “The crucial question, therefore, is which social forces will be able to help shape the impending restructuring,” Yılmaz said and pointed to the widening gap between politics and society, as well as growing social inequality. “Whether the current changes will produce a new social contract benefiting the broader population will depend largely on the influence of the women’s movement and other social struggles,” she added.




Hatimoğulları calls for a broad peace alliance




DEM Party Co-Chair Tülay Hatimoğulları echoed these arguments, calling on women’s movements not to allow political and ideological differences to become obstacles to working together for peace.




“How can we women build a peace alliance despite all our differences? Women on the right and left, women who wear headscarves and those who do not, liberals, politically organized and unorganized women – how can we all come together to form an alliance for peace?” Hatimoğulları asked.




Rather than focusing exclusively on past shortcomings, she argued, participants should discuss what they could build and organize together in the future. For her, this was the central task of the conference.




Message from Figen Yüksekdağ in prison




The conference also received a message of support from imprisoned former HDP Co-Chair Figen Yüksekdağ. Her written message from Kandıra Women’s Prison was read aloud by journalist Gözde Şeker. Yüksekdağ drew attention to wars, violence, and growing uncertainty about the future. Under these circumstances, she emphasized, it was more important than ever to build a society based on peace, freedom, justice, and democratic rights.




“Cooperation among women can serve as a bridge that brings together and unites different social and political forces,” she stated. The women’s movement, she said, possessed the experience and capacity to mobilize people who had suffered oppression and injustice in the struggle for peace and a democratic society.




Actress Füsun Demirel, who was unable to attend in person, addressed the conference through a video message. She noted that while male-dominated politics was primarily concerned with who had won the peace, women were focused on how to shape a shared future after the violence had ended. She summed up her message with the words: “Peace is in our hands.”

title: TEV-DEM calls for guarantees for Kurdish rights and protection of achievements
content:
On the occasion of World Kobanê Day on November 1, the Movement for a Democratic Society (TEV-DEM) and its Women’s Council issued separate statements commemorating the historic resistance against the so-called Islamic State (ISIS).




While TEV-DEM emphasized Kobanê’s significance in the struggle for democracy and human dignity and warned against one-sided integration in Syria, the Women’s Council focused on the role of women in defending the city and safeguarding their political and social achievements.




‘Integration does not mean assimilation’




TEV-DEM described the resistance of Kobanê as a historic process whose significance extended far beyond geographical and political boundaries. The movement pointed out that the defense of the city had become a global symbol of freedom, social diversity, and the protection of human dignity. “The international solidarity shown by democratic movements, intellectuals, and numerous prominent figures demonstrated that the struggle for humanity transcended both national and religious boundaries,” it underlined.




Regarding the political restructuring of Syria, the movement warned against attempts to exclude Kurds from the process of building the new state or disregard their achievements. It cautioned that any attempt to impose integration unilaterally would pose significant risks. “Integration does not mean assimilating a people’s identity or demanding that they abandon their national identity, culture, and political rights. Instead, integration must be a collective process of state-building in which the distinct identities, rights, and achievements of all social groups are protected,” TEV-DEM stated.




The movement emphasized that those who defended Kobanê against ISIS deserved to live in peace, security, freedom, and dignity. It called on national and democratic forces, as well as intellectuals and prominent figures who had supported the resistance, to continue advocating for the rights of the Kurdish people.




Women’s Council pledges to continue the struggle




In its statement, the TEV-DEM Women’s Council described November 1 as a historic day symbolizing the collective resistance of peoples against terrorism and their determination to defend themselves. The Council emphasized that ISIS, through its ideology and violence, had particularly targeted the existence and freedom of women.




“The people of Kobanê, along with young men and women in the ranks of the People’s Protection Units (YPG) and Women’s Protection Units (YPJ), stood up against this threat. With the support of the Peshmerga, historic resistance emerged, sparking solidarity worldwide and leading to the declaration of World Kobanê Day.”




The Women’s Council highlighted the fact that Kurdish women had not only played a leading role in the military defense of the city but had also demonstrated their capacity for social self-governance and shaping a democratic future. The Council pledged to continue their struggle to defend the rights and achievements won through their resistance at the political, social, cultural, diplomatic, and constitutional levels.

title: İlk yarıda öne geçti, ikinci yarıya golle başladı: Beşiktaş farkı açtı
content:
Süper Lig'in 10. haftasında Beşiktaş, Kasımpaşa deplasmanında 2-0 öne geçti. İlk yarıyı Leandro Trossard'ın golüyle 1-0 önde tamamlayan siyah-beyazlılar, ikinci yarının ilk dakikasında Dusan Vlahovic'in golüyle farkı ikiye çıkardı.

Süper Lig'in 10. haftasında Beşiktaş, Kasımpaşa'ya konuk oldu. Recep Tayyip Erdoğan Stadı'nda saat 19.00'da başlayan karşılaşmayı hakem Reşat Onur Coşkunses yönetiyor.

Ligde geride kalan 9 maçta 6 galibiyet ve 3 mağlubiyet alan Beşiktaş, 18 puanla haftaya dördüncü sırada girdi. Siyah-beyazlılar, Kasımpaşa karşısında kazanarak zirve takibini sürdürmeyi hedefliyor.

Ev sahibi Kasımpaşa ise 16 puanla mücadeleye çıktı. Lacivert-beyazlı ekip, Beşiktaş karşısında galip gelerek üst üste üçüncü galibiyetini almak istiyor.

Kasımpaşa: Andreas, Arous, Ilie, Winck, Ayberk, Kerem, Mendes, Hajradinovic, Rak-Sakyi, Ali Yavuz, Benedyczak.

Beşiktaş: Nübel, Murillo, Agbadou, Emirhan, Rıdvan, Ndidi, Salih, Olaitan, Cerny, Trossard, Vlahovic.

6' Kasımpaşa kırmızı kart bekledi. Agbadou'nun kontrol edemediği topa hareketlenen Hajradinovic, Beşiktaşlı futbolcunun müdahalesiyle yerde kaldı. Kasımpaşalı futbolcuların itirazlarına rağmen hakem oyunu devam ettirdi.

6' Kasımpaşa'nın kart itirazının ardından Beşiktaş gole yaklaştı. Kaleciyle karşı karşıya kalan Trossard, fırsatı değerlendiremedi.

7' Hakeme yoğun itirazlarda bulunan Kasımpaşa Teknik Direktörü Emre Belözoğlu sarı kart gördü.

15' Beşiktaş gole yaklaştı. Cerny'nin ceza sahası içinden yaptığı vuruşta top, kalenin sağından auta çıktı.

28' GOL | Beşiktaş öne geçti! Rıdvan Yılmaz'ın pasında topla buluşan Leandro Trossard, fileleri havalandırdı: 0-1.

45' İlk yarının sonuna 1 dakika ilave edildi.

46' İkinci yarı başladı. Beşiktaş'ta Cerny'nin yerine İlhan Fakılı oyuna girdi.

title: Enes Ünal gol attı, Getafe Sevilla'yı 3-1 mağlup etti
content:
Fotoğraf: www.realvalladolid.es/Wikimedia Commons CC BY-SA 4.0

İspanya LaLiga'nın 11. haftasında Getafe, milli futbolcu Enes Ünal'ın gol attığı karşılaşmada Sevilla'yı 3-1 yendi. İlk yarıyı geride kapatan Getafe, ikinci yarıda bulduğu gollerle galibiyete uzandı. Sevilla'da Manu Bueno, 90+1. dakikada kırmızı kart gördü.

İspanya Birinci Futbol Ligi'nde (LaLiga) Getafe ile Sevilla karşı karşıya geldi. Coliseum Stadı'nda oynanan mücadeleyi ev sahibi Getafe 3-1 kazandı. Milli futbolcu Enes Ünal, Getafe'nin ilk golünü kaydederek takımının geri dönüşünde rol oynadı.

Karşılaşmada Sevilla, 19. dakikada Kike Salas'ın attığı golle 1-0 öne geçti ve ilk yarıyı bu skorla tamamladı.

İkinci yarıda baskısını artıran Getafe, 68. dakikada Enes Ünal'ın golüyle eşitliği sağladı. Ev sahibi ekip, 74. dakikada Martin Satriano'nun golüyle 2-1 öne geçti.

Sevilla'da Manu Bueno, 90+1. dakikada kırmızı kartla oyun dışında kaldı. Getafe, 90+4. dakikada Orel Mangala'nın golüyle farkı ikiye çıkardı ve sahadan 3-1 galip ayrıldı.

Bu sonuçla Getafe puanını 12'ye yükseltti. Sevilla ise 17 puanda kaldı.

title: Labour and the budget: same old same old (with a side of pickles)
content:
When Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey presented his budget on Wednesday October 28

th

 he said: “This is a Budget for the working people of Britain. For British businesses, big and small.”  Well, no. It offered little to working people, and plenty to businesses, to the military and to the defence industry.




We were offered the pittance of 86p a week off of electricity bills. In addition, there will be a £100 one-off winter fuel payment for 20 million households in council tax bands A to D. This will almost immediately be wiped out by a predicted rise by £276 in January, to just under £2,000 a year. Another forecast from the EDF energy company, predicted that it might rise higher than this.




Healey introduced a £2 cap on single bus fares in England from January 2027. But, for example, many workers and students in London cannot afford to live in inner London and must make long journeys by bus to get to work and study, because they cannot afford the rail and tube fares.




He also announced the end of gas standing charges, which will save a mere £45 a year, and then only for 60% of households. Healey had already announced that an extra £432 million would be spent on a programme to get rough sleepers in England off the streets. Unpaid carers would no longer lose all of their Carer’s Allowance if they earnt more than 1p over the £204 allowed and instead there would be a tapered payment.




On the other hand, Healey reassured the boss class by stating that he was committed to “prevent regulation from holding back investment by removing regulation and tariffs worth £800m to business.” The banks feared that the corporation tax surcharge would be raised by as much as 8 per cent. In fact, Healey only raised it by six per cent, and smarmed the banks by saying,” I celebrate and am grateful for the role you play”. In fact, this surcharge will only last for 15 months from January. As a result, share prices of the main UK banks increased, after the budget announcement.




The Financial Times, the bosses’ voice, enthusiastically noted that Healey and Burnham wanted to reassure business and the banks.




He promised an increase of £10 billion on economic and military support for Ukraine, in addition to the £25 billion already committed by previous Tory and Labour administrations. He would also make cuts in the budgets of various government departments by 1%to further fund defence spending. As a result, the Warm Homes Plan, would suffer a £1 billion cut. He promised a maximum amount of private investment in defence, including through public private partnerships.




Labour had promised to end discriminatory age bands and to increase the minimum wage for 18- to 20-year-olds to be the same as those over 21 years old. Healey broke this promise with the 18 to 20 years olds earning nearly £2 an hour less. scrapping “discriminatory” age bands, and to increasing the minimum wages for 18- to 20-year-olds so young workers are paid the same as those over 21. Healey broke this promise—18- to 20-year-olds will still earn nearly £2 an hour less. The rate for both age levels will rise by 3.9% but this will be cancelled out by rising inflation.




Labour will use these young workers as a cheap labour force, and is already pushing an unpaid work experience scheme at Sainsbury’s.




Labour is preparing for further attacks on welfare, and Healey promised, “As the Prime Minister and I have both said, we will bring down the welfare bill.” They are eying up attacking the Personal Independence Payment, the major disability benefit. All of this is in the pipeline.




Healey did not remove the Triple Lock on pensions, and this will not happen before the 2030 election, but made the menacing statement that Labour would adjust the Triple Lock after that.




All in all, the budget was low key, with a series of minor announcements. In addition to the above, there was the removal of import tax on some 100 products, meaning cheaper prices for things like, baked beans, gherkins, garlic and marmalade. This was derided widely in the media, as this would save around £21 a year, or £1.75 a month! Parental pay would be extended, so that 150,000 parents will receive two weeks of support of up to £194 a week. Again, this will be wiped out by rising inflation.




So, no real challenge to big business and a massive increase in defence spending, with looming attacks on pensioners, young workers and the disabled. But we never expected anything else from the Burnham administration.




When Burnham assumed the leadership of the Labour Party, earlier this year, he promised to “end 40 years of neoliberalism.” This budget underlines that he, Healey and the rest of the Labour leaders remain committed to fiscal policies, which are exactly what neoliberalism requires in order to function. Nothing then has changed, with lilliputian tinkering instead of the radical change that Burnham promised.

title: Humanitarian conditions deteriorate in Washokani and Al-Talae camps
content:
The humanitarian conditions of displaced families living in the Washokani and Al-Talae camps in Syria’s Hesekê Governorate have further deteriorated following recent rainfall and flooding. The Serêkaniyê Displaced Persons Committee has called for urgent shelter assistance ahead of winter season and for the process of returning families to their hometowns to be expedited.




Speaking to Shafaq News, committee spokesperson Mahmud Cemîl said that the tents in both camps had deteriorated and could no longer provide adequate protection against rain, cold weather and extreme heat. Cemîl said the committee had been requesting support and new tents from humanitarian organisations for seven years, but these requests had not been adequately addressed.




Returns should accelerate




Cemîl said that displaced families were facing administrative delays and various obstacles in returning to their hometowns. He called on the Syrian government to expand organised return convoys and increase the number of families able to return.




Cemîl also urged the Syrian presidential delegation overseeing the return process, international organisations and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) to support efforts to accelerate returns before winter conditions make life in the camps even more difficult.




3,278 families returned in six convoys




Since August, a total of 3,278 families have returned to their hometowns through six organised return convoys.




Some of the families returned to Serêkaniyê and its surrounding countryside, while others returned to settle in villages around Til Temir, Zirgan and Abu Rasin, north of Hesekê.

title: 7,000-year-old architectural model discovered in Soran
content:
The General Directorate of Antiquities and Cultural Heritage of the Kurdistan Region has announced a significant archaeological discovery at Banahîlk Hill in the Soran district, northeast of Erbil.




In a statement, the directorate said that a rare model of an ancient building's roofing system, dating back more than 7,000 years and belonging to the Halaf culture, had been discovered. Describing the find as a first in archaeological history, the statement noted that it demonstrates the advanced engineering and architectural skills of communities during that period.




The discovery was announced to the public at a press conference held on 28 October at the Scientific Research Centre of Soran University. The archaeological project was carried out in cooperation with the Soran Directorate of Antiquities and Culture, the Autonomous University of Barcelona (UAB) and Salahaddin University.




The Halaf culture, dating approximately from 6100 to 5100 BC, was influential mainly across the lands of Southern Kurdistan (Başûr), Western Kurdistan (Rojava) and Northern Kurdistan (Bakurê Kurdistan). Known for its distinctive pottery decorated with geometric patterns and animal motifs, this culture provides important archaeological evidence of the prehistoric history of Mesopotamia and the Near East.

title: DEM Party’s message on 1 November, World Kobanê Day
content:
The DEM Party’s Central Executive Board (MYK) issued a written statement to mark 1 November, World Kobanê Day. The statement said: "On 15 September 2014, ISIS, which is hostile to different faiths, identities, cultures and the will of peoples to live together, launched a major attack on Kobanê. In response to the ISIS gangs’ assault on Kobanê, the peoples of the world—particularly the Kurdish people—and internationalist resistance fighters who travelled to Kobanê from all corners of the globe waged an epic resistance against ISIS.




Faced with this historic resistance, which lasted 134 days, the ISIS gangs and the forces behind them suffered a major defeat. The victory won in Kobanê, embraced by peoples across the world and marking a turning point in the beginning of a new history in the Middle East, carries even greater international significance today."




The statement added: "Developed under the leadership of the women’s struggle, the Kobanê resistance laid the groundwork for the Kurdish people to secure their identity-related, cultural and historical rights. It also enabled the development of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, which today represents a hope for an equal and free life.




The devastating social consequences of the wars of interest waged by imperialist and regional powers, particularly in the Middle East, during this historic period we are living through have once again demonstrated just how vital Mr Abdullah Öcalan’s Call for Peace and a Democratic Society, issued on 27 February 2025, truly is."




The statement continued: "In the 12th year of the Kobanê resistance, we salute the struggle, led by women, through which a great victory was achieved against the order hostile to humanity that the ISIS gangs sought to establish. May 1 November, World Kobanê Day—proclaimed through the united struggle of peoples around the world against those seeking to destroy human values—be a blessed day for all the peoples of the world, especially the peoples of the Middle East.




We respectfully commemorate those who lost their lives in Kobanê, particularly women, who sacrificed themselves to protect humanity."

title: Kongra Star calls to continue to protect the city on World Kobanê Day
content:
Kongra Star issued a statement to mark 1 November, World Kobanê Day. The statement commemorated the historic sacrifices made in the fight against ISIS mercenaries in 2014, while highlighting the current and future challenges Kobanê is facing.




The statement paid tribute to the martyrs of the resistance, particularly Arin Mirkan. It stressed that the determination demonstrated by the resistance was no longer confined to the city's geographical boundaries, but had become deeply rooted in humanity's collective memory and conscience as a struggle for freedom and human dignity, placing an ongoing responsibility on everyone to preserve these values.




The statement noted that 1 November represents an "epic of resilience" by a people who refused to bow to darkness. It said that, through their unwavering determination and international solidarity from across the world, the resistance fighters managed to break the siege of the city and repel ISIS attacks, turning Kobanê into an international symbol of ISIS's defeat and a renewed source of hope for peoples worldwide.




Kongra Star underlined that what happened in Kobanê went beyond the military defence of a city, representing instead a defence of a model of coexistence, equality and solidarity that transcends political, linguistic and ideological boundaries. It noted that the experience demonstrated how local resistance can become a universal human value.




Kobanê still needs to be protected




The statement warned of the current threats surrounding Kobanê's future, rejecting any attempt to reduce its cause to mere "administrative arrangements, political calculations or pressure over borders."




Kongra Star said that any harm to Kobanê's social fabric and spirit would constitute an attack on the shared memory of the resistance. It called for the city's security concerns and future to be addressed with the utmost seriousness, while warning against any acts of revenge or settling of scores that could pave the way for terrorist organisations to regain strength.




Kongra Star ended its statement calling on "democratic, socialist and internationalist forces, as well as human rights defenders worldwide, to fulfil their responsibilities towards Kobanê's security and the will of its people. It stressed that protecting the city today is an extension of the spirit of international solidarity witnessed in 2014 and an effort to keep the light of freedom from being extinguished."

author: Unknown
title: Mining destroys Chaldean village's nature and heritage
content:
Aksu (Harbol in Syriac), a historic Assyrian settlement located at the foot of Mount Cûdî in the Silopi (Silopiya) district of Şırnak (Şirnex), is just one of countless places affected by the destruction of nature for the benefit of capital. 

Yeni Yaş

am

 said in a feature that mining operations established in the village's rural areas and on the slopes of Mount Cûdî over the past decade have completely transformed the landscape. The surroundings of the village, which were covered in greenery in 2015 and earlier, are now almost entirely devoid of vegetation. The mining sites are reportedly located on the village's former settlement area, and almost no trees remain in the region. Ecological destruction in Botan accelerated with the intensification of the war in 2015.




For years, Botan's natural environment, much of which has been declared off-limits, has been destroyed under military supervision and through the activities of village guards. The ecological destruction that began with forest fires has continued through tree felling, mining and oil exploration.




The mountain's silhouette has changed




Satellite images and photographs showing the surroundings of the village reveal terraced excavations and exposed layers of soil across much of the mountainous area. The mines, which threaten village life, are located just a few hundred metres from the settlement. The excavations have exposed successive layers of the mountainside, revealing different soil colours ranging from red to white. The mountain's silhouette has been visibly altered. Another striking aspect is that these operations have been carried out for years in an area where civilian access is prohibited. The extent of the destruction on one side of the mountain can be clearly seen by comparing it with the preserved vegetation on the opposite slope.




The village's historical remains have been destroyed




Satellite images of the mining area also show the remains of Harbol's former settlement. The mining operations have not only devastated the natural environment but have also destroyed the village's historical remains, erasing traces of its past. The large number of gendarmerie stations at the village entrance and in the surrounding area is reportedly linked to the provision of security support for mining operations. Soldiers are said to have prevented residents from filming or photographing the environmental destruction. This militarised dimension, in which extractivism operates alongside security-driven policies, is also examined in the 2025 position paper 

Militarisation Is Extractivism: From Mines to Missiles

, translated into Turkish by the Polen Ecology Collective. The paper explores the relationship between mining and militarism on a global scale.




The village was evacuated in the 1990s




Harbol, located on the slopes of Mount Cûdî in Şırnak's Silopi district, was forcibly evacuated between 1990 and 1993 on the grounds of "security". The village's entire population consisted of Assyrian-Chaldean residents. Those forced to leave migrated to major cities in western Turkey, as well as France and other European countries. Returns to the village began in 2014. Today, only seven families live in Herbol. Other former residents visit temporarily before returning to the places where they settled after being displaced.




Destruction across Mount Cûdî and the Euphrates-Tigris Basin




The Extractivism Map shows that intensive mining and other environmentally destructive projects are continuing across the Euphrates-Tigris river basin, which covers an area of 176,258 square kilometres, alongside active projects on Mount Cûdî. In Şırnak alone, 135 mining projects entered the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) process between the beginning of 2023 and 8 February 2026. The Extractivism Map illustrates the extent of these activities across Mount Cûdî and the wider Euphrates-Tigris Basin.

title: Özgür Sevgi Göral: France’s dilemmas also exist in Turkey - Part One
content:
Academic Özgür Sevgi Göral said that a strong voice had emerged against inequality in Paris, adding, "Reducing the revolt of the suburbs, which demands profound transformation, to presidential elections would dilute the movement's anger and enthusiasm." Göral said that all the dilemmas facing France were also present in Turkey.




The streets of Paris have witnessed some of the most intense social mobilisation of recent times. Protests that began in September, led by high school students, grew into a mass movement day by day.




ANF spoke to Özgür Sevgi Göral, who is currently in Paris and has participated in the demonstrations, about the historical foundations of the protests and their potential.




Academic Özgür Sevgi Göral emphasised that the protests were rooted in a historical accumulation of struggles, saying, "This history includes the inequalities created by racialised capitalism and the many different forms of violence it has spread throughout everyday life."  Göral stressed the importance of the struggle, saying, "The struggle truly is endless, and despite all the difficult conditions, millions of people around the world refuse to abandon the streets."




Göral argued that the protests should be understood less in relation to 1968 and more in the context of the political mobilisation and suburban uprisings that emerged in the 1970s and 1980s and continued strongly throughout the 2000s. Göral also warned that directing the anti-fascist stance solely towards the April 2027 presidential elections risked alienating young people from the suburbs in particular.




Göral also assessed what kind of political ground, language and methodology were needed today to address the Kurdish question. Göral emphasised the importance of convincing broad sections of society that the current process could provide a foundation for a shared life based on equality and freedom and said: "Since the state will not provide this foundation, it will have to be built by all movements for equality, freedom and liberation, particularly the Kurdish Freedom Movement, by drawing on their capacities and establishing the broadest possible alliances. In fact, all the dilemmas we have discussed in relation to France are also present in Turkey, although, of course, in different forms."




You also participated in the demonstrations in Paris. What were your observations on the streets? What were the differences between the official narrative and the situation on the ground?




The high school protests in Paris are actually rooted in a particular historical background. This history includes the inequalities created by racialised capitalism and the many different forms of violence it has spread throughout everyday life. The more immediate historical background to this movement includes the severe class inequalities experienced during last year's extreme heatwaves in Paris, which claimed thousands of lives, particularly in schools in the suburbs. Even when temperatures reached 40 degrees Celsius, secondary schools were not provided with fans. There are also the structural inequalities associated with Parcoursup, the university admissions system, which separates students attending privileged high schools from those attending schools in working-class neighbourhoods, and the experience of collapsing public services, including education and healthcare, in suburban neighbourhoods.




The mobilisation began after the teachers' strike held in Paris and its suburbs on 29 September, which demanded greater public funding for public services. One of my favourite slogans, "The suburbs influence Paname, and Paname influences the world" (Paname is another name for Paris), resonated strongly. The blockades of high schools, which first began in Seine-Saint-Denis, gained strong support first in Paris's privileged high schools and then in higher education institutions. Saturday demonstrations in Paris, led by youth movements, attracted enormous crowds. Despite the extraordinary level of police violence, participation did not decline but continued to increase. According to figures from the General Confederation of Labour (CGT), 250,000 people participated in the Paris demonstration on 24 October, while more than 800,000 people joined demonstrations across France.




From the outset, the official narrative framed the wave of protests within a security paradigm. It categorically refused to discuss the profound structures of inequality highlighted by the demonstrations, the class, racial and ethno-political hierarchies that racialised capitalism has spread much more intensely throughout the suburbs of Paris, but also in the city centre, or to recognise the issue as a social problem. Instead, it described the demonstrations in terms of "protester violence" and refused to acknowledge police violence, declaring that police officers faced the risk of death because of the protesters. Moreover, it called on everyone to condemn this violence, which it characterised primarily as "damaging public property, looting shops and destroying everything." It introduced a political discourse that is fundamentally right-wing, confines social and political problems within a security paradigm and erases their actual substance. This discourse calls on everyone to express remorse and submit to this security-oriented approach. It also seeks to label those who refuse to comply as "undesirable" or "dangerous" protesters, thereby legitimising the police violence directed against them. This appeal was partially effective. All the centrist parties were quick to condemn protester violence without a moment's hesitation.




Elements of the reformist or parliamentary left that stand further to the left, such as La France Insoumise (LFI, France Unbowed), partly challenged this language but also adopted aspects of it, albeit selectively. The government therefore pursued an aggressive political strategy of separating acceptable protesters and their demands from those it considered unacceptable. The protesters on the streets, however, are not a single bloc. They consist of different groups. This discourse had little significant impact on those coming from the suburbs, who experience the fundamental violence produced by racialised capitalism every day in their bodies, their lives and their political imaginations. Other groups partly resisted this discourse and partly acted through certain compromises. Nevertheless, among the groups taking to the streets, opposition to this narrative appears stronger for the time being.




How would you describe the profile of the students taking to the streets? Are their demands limited to local policies, or are you seeing a broader critique of the system and concerns about a future without prospects?




I can only answer this question in relation to the situation in Paris. From what I have observed, the leading group consisted of young people living in the suburbs. Young people from Saint-Denis, Aulnay-sous-Bois and Seine-Saint-Denis raised a powerful voice against the inequalities they experience. The blockades of high schools and the erection of barricades began there. These students constitute the first group within the movement. They face enormous inequalities not only in their schools but also in their homes, the public services they rely on, and the lives they are building both today and for the future. There are currently three million millionaires in France, yet in that same country, one in five children cannot eat three meals a day because of the class inequalities they experience. This is the reality of life for young people in the suburbs of Paris. Therefore, what mobilised this group was both the conditions in their high schools and a broader anti-capitalist anger. I believe this is essentially the group that offers the broadest critique of the system and expresses the strongest reaction and anger against racialised capitalism, even though it does not have a comprehensive anti-capitalist programme or a strong political organisation.




The wave of protests subsequently spread to high schools in Paris, including the prestigious schools known for their privileges. Universities and higher education institutions then joined the solidarity demonstrations. For this second group, I think the specific demands concerning high schools, namely greater public funding, better facilities and the abolition of Parcoursup, the university admissions system, played a more prominent role. Of course, the immediate consequences of capitalism and the brutal violence it produces, particularly through the climate crisis and class inequalities, also feature in this group's political discourse. However, it differs somewhat from the strong emphasis of the suburban movement and its repertoire of political action, which at times includes self-defence against the police. Nevertheless, leading figures within this group also expressed the need for a break with the existing system and for a left capable of organising a broader programme of transformation. This second group became the more visible face of the protests, particularly through its appearances on television programmes and its prominent presence at demonstrations.




Over the past two weeks, the Yellow Vests (Gilets Jaunes) have also begun participating in the Saturday demonstrations. This group encompasses different political tendencies, including activists who maintain links with left-wing groups as well as others who hold right-wing or even racist views, although the latter are increasingly in the minority. The issue of police violence is what holds these three groups together.




How did protesters on the streets respond to the violence and the methods of police intervention?




First, let me provide some figures illustrating the extent of state violence. As of 15 October 2026, the Ministry of Justice reported that a total of 7,950 people had been detained, 85 per cent of whom were minors. According to historian Vincent Lemire's calculations, this figure exceeds the total number of detentions recorded over an entire year during the Yellow Vests (Gilets Jaunes) movement, when 6,730 people were detained.




As I mentioned earlier, the streets do not consist of a single, homogeneous group. Generally speaking, although everyone participating in the protests opposed framing the issue as a security problem, the political language and radical content of that opposition differed between groups. For young people living in the suburbs, police violence has a long and deeply rooted history. The illegitimacy of this violence, which has made their lives a living hell, is much more apparent to them. Moreover, they understand this violence as part of a broader critique of the system and capitalism.




At this point, I would like to briefly discuss the history of this violence, particularly in the suburbs. Police violence is deeply embedded in everyday life in these urban areas. It not only continually deepens segregation in schools but also creates a broader experience of social and ethnic-racial discrimination. Here, class and race, or racialised categories, are intertwined. Children from working-class communities living in the suburbs, particularly Black and Arab children, experience both racialised violence and class-based violence in forms that are interconnected and reinforce one another. The state describes political mobilisation in these areas as "urban violence" (violence urbaine). Although young people living there have been French citizens for generations, they are not regarded as genuine citizens. Discussions about the suburbs are consistently linked to immigration and racialised. Of course, there is also a large population of poor migrants living in the suburbs. However, even young people whose families have held French citizenship for four generations are described as "French on paper" and told that they are not truly French. This language of French racism also finds widespread acceptance in mainstream discourse. Class-based violence operates alongside widespread and deeply entrenched patterns of racism, including anti-Muslim racism.




Research in this field has shown that the term "urban violence" emerged in the 1990s following the Mas-du-Taureau uprisings in Vaulx-en-Velin. According to many researchers, the term serves to politically discredit protests and political struggles by reducing them to acts of violence and categorising those acts as "vandalism". For example, Didier Fassin, who researched the Anti-Crime Brigade (Brigade Anti-Criminalité, BAC) in Bobigny, Seine-Saint-Denis, argues that the category of "urban violence" serves to legitimise a state of exception that has become routine in the suburbs. Police violence, particularly violence used to suppress uprisings, is legitimised through this framework. On 6 December 2018, during the Yellow Vests movement, clashes broke out between police and high school students at Saint-Exupéry High School in Mantes-la-Jolie. The students were protesting the government's education reforms, including the Parcoursup system and changes to the baccalaureate examination. Police detained 151 students aged between 12 and 21 in a mass operation and forced them to kneel in the mud for hours with their hands held behind their heads. The incident came to light when footage recorded by a police officer, who could be heard saying, "Now that's a well-behaved class," circulated widely on social media. For young people from the suburbs and working-class neighbourhoods, neither police violence nor the struggle against the unequal practices of capitalism is anything new. Therefore, rather than viewing their opposition to police violence as a reaction limited to the present moment, we must understand it as today's manifestation of resistance to a deeply entrenched practice.




What are the similarities and differences between the events taking place in Paris and the youth protests of 1968?




The most important difference between May 1968 in France and the current wave of protests is that the youth movements of 1968 were accompanied by a powerful wave of working-class strikes. Today, trade unions are not a force standing behind the youth movement or advancing alongside it, and the movement is not developing in conjunction with a powerful wave of general strikes. The General Confederation of Labour (CGT) has called for a strike on 5 November, but that is all for now. Beyond this, although student unions in particular are involved in the protests, it is difficult to speak of a broader wave of strikes or calls for strikes.




On the other hand, I believe it is more appropriate to understand this movement in relation to the political mobilisation and suburban uprisings that emerged in the 1970s and 1980s and continued strongly throughout the 2000s, rather than comparing it primarily with 1968. Working-class neighbourhoods, known as the suburbs, have served as laboratories for the two main elements of what we might call the doctrine of "maintaining public order": managing and controlling the masses, and police violence. For example, the Flash-Ball, the predecessor of the LBD (Defence Ball Launcher), which is widely used in today's demonstrations and causes permanent injuries and disabilities among young people, was introduced throughout the national police force in 2002 at the initiative of then Interior Minister Nicolas Sarkozy, primarily for use in the suburbs to suppress uprisings. Consider the 2005 uprising, which is also familiar to the public in Turkey.




In Clichy-sous-Bois, a suburb of Paris, two young people, Zyed Benna, aged 17, and Bouna Traoré, aged 15, were electrocuted after hiding in an electrical substation while fleeing a police identity check. The suburban uprising that followed lasted three weeks. The government declared a state of emergency under a law dating back to 1955, and more than 4,000 people were detained. The statements made by then Interior Minister Nicolas Sarkozy, who said he would clean these neighbourhoods with a high-pressure Kärcher washer and described young people from the suburbs as "rabble" (racaille), remain central elements in the memory of that uprising.




In 2023, the killing of 17-year-old Nahel Merzouk, of Algerian and Moroccan descent, who was shot at close range by a police officer during a traffic stop in the Paris suburb of Nanterre, triggered another major uprising, particularly as footage of the incident spread rapidly on social media. The demonstrations were not confined to Paris. Just as they have today, they spread to major cities such as Marseille, Lyon and Lille. As in the current protests, the demonstrators were very young. The anger of young people from the suburbs targeted not only police buildings but also other symbols of the established order, including municipal buildings and schools. It would therefore be more appropriate to understand the current wave of protests, particularly its initial phase and the anger it contains against racialised capitalism, in relation to this history of uprisings.

title: İpek Er’s mother: My daughter was killed a second time
content:
“My daughter was killed a second time today.” With these words, Hikmet Kılınç, the mother of Kurdish woman İpek Er, who died in 2020, protested the recent acquittal of former gendarmerie officer Musa Orhan at a women’s conference in Ankara. Six years after her daughter’s death, she has leveled serious accusations against state officials and announced her determination to continue her fight for justice all the way to the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR).




The protest follows a ruling issued on October 22 by a criminal court in Batman. Musa Orhan, who was sentenced to ten years in prison in 2021 for a serious sexual assault against İpek Er, was acquitted of the charge of incitement to suicide in a separate trial. According to Kılınç, the decision represents another setback in her years-long struggle to secure legal accountability for her daughter’s death.




Addressing more than 500 participants at the “Women Discuss the Future Side by Side” conference, Kılınç recounted her experiences since her daughter’s death. She accused state authorities of exploiting her hopes for justice and attempting to exert political pressure on her. “For six years, they told me: If you stay away from the Kurdish parties, we will ensure justice for your daughter. After six years, they acquitted him,” Kılınç said. She explained that she had sold all her possessions and moved to Batman. “Under the pretext of defending my daughter’s rights, they deceived me.”




The mother also directed her criticism at former Turkish Interior Minister Süleyman Soylu, accusing him of protecting Orhan and facilitating his acquittal. At the same time, she appealed to Kurdish members of parliament not to lose sight of the case. “My daughter’s blood must not go unavenged. As long as I live, I will fight for her rights. I will pursue this case all the way to the ECtHR,” Kılınç said. “My daughter was killed by someone who wielded state power. As long as the perpetrator walks free, there can be no talk of justice.”










https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/b62c3f26_20261031121003_2026-10-31-ankara-hikmet-kilinc-ipek-er-annesi-kadinlar-yan-yana-gelecegi-konusuyor-konferansi-cagri-1.mp4










Allegations of threats and abuse




In her speech, Kılınç also described the violence and intimidation her daughter had endured. According to her mother, İpek had been manipulated and subjected to pressure. She had been threatened with the killing of her father and brother, and there had even been an attempt to sell her. “İpek’s hair is evidence of the torture she suffered. I still have my daughter’s bloodstained clothes,” Kılınç said. She said she continues to preserve her daughter’s personal belongings to this day.




Kılınç made these statements at the two-day women’s conference held at the Chamber of Civil Engineers in Ankara. Since Saturday, journalists, academics, politicians, and activists have been discussing peace, justice, equal citizenship, and the struggle against patriarchal violence.




Six years of legal proceedings




On July 7, 2020, İpek Er filed a criminal complaint against Musa Orhan with the public prosecutor’s office in Siirt. Orhan was serving as a professional soldier in the district of Beşiri at the time. Er stated that he had been raped by him. On July 16, she attempted suicide after leaving a farewell letter. After spending 34 days in hospital, she died on August 18, 2020.




Orhan was initially detained but subsequently released under judicial supervision. Following public protests, he was remanded in custody on August 19, 2020, but was released just one week later after an appeal. He was later dismissed from the gendarmerie.




In December 2021, a criminal court in Siirt sentenced Orhan to ten years in prison for sexual assault, applying mitigating circumstances. Despite his conviction, he remained free. A separate criminal case was also brought against him in Batman on charges of incitement to suicide. That trial ended in an acquittal on October 22. The ruling concerns only this second charge and does not overturn his earlier conviction for sexual violence.

title: Shengal People’s Council call for the recognition of the city’s special status
content:
The Shengal People’s Council issued a statement regarding the democratic integration process underway in the city. The statement, which also marked World Kobanê Day on November 1, recalled that both Shengal and Kobanê were besieged by ISIS militants in 2014 and that a new phase of struggle had begun in both Rojava and Shengal after 12 years of resistance.




The Council welcomed the democratic integration process, describing it as the first time in more than a thousand years that a state had recognized the will of the Yazidi community and announced an agreement reached with the freely chosen representatives of the Yazidi people.




The Council further stated that democratic integration in Shengal encompassed not only the YBŞ-YJŞ and Êzîdxan Asayiş, but also all institutions of the Yazidi community.




“The integration of military forces into Iraq’s security institutions is not a project imposed from outside, but a process that has developed through the will of our people and guarantees the preservation of our achievements and lasting security for our community. Those who seek to portray this as a threat are themselves the ones attempting to profit from our community’s suffering and leave Shengal defenseless once again,” the statement said.




The Council pointed out that Shengal has been classified as a disputed territory for 23 years, yet the problems facing the Yazidi community remain unresolved. “We see addressing these historical and social issues together with the central government as the first step in this process,” it added.




The statement emphasized that the issue of Shengal concerns an entire community and its faith, and therefore cannot be reduced to a single armed force, nor can a solution be expected from any one force alone. It stressed the need to address the Shengal issue within the framework of the Iraqi Constitution and in cooperation with the Iraqi Federal Government.




Recalling that the Yazidi people have never accepted any agreement reached without regard for their will, the statement continued: “A genuine solution requires recognition of Shengal’s special status and local administration, as well as guarantees for our rights to self-governance and self-defense. These are the legitimate and natural rights of the Yazidi people. Shengal, the faith center of the Yazidi people, cannot be governed or protected against the will of the Yazidi community. We believe that a lasting solution lies in local self-government, and we demand recognition of this will. Our struggle for the recognition of local self-government will continue.”




The Council called on all relevant parties and individuals, particularly the KDP leadership, to respect the will of the Yazidi community and act accordingly: “The Yazidi cause is both a national and an international issue. No force or party has the right to downplay or distort this reality. They have attempted to frame the Shengal issue around whether or not Yazidis are Kurdish. This is a deliberate distortion and an agenda designed to obscure the truth. Through such agendas, they seek to divert attention from the will of the Yazidi community, create issues that do not serve the interests of the Yazidi people, and distract us from our fundamental demands.”




The statement further called on all Yazidi parties, organizations, women, and young people to set aside their differences and unite under one umbrella.




Amid these developments, the statement said, the 12-year period following the genocide against the Yazidis cannot be assessed without acknowledging the efforts of Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan and the Kurdish Freedom Movement.




“They came to our aid when we had been forgotten and saved our community from the most brutal genocide of the century. We have reached this stage through the philosophy of a free society. Today, the People’s Council, YBŞ, YJŞ, and all Yazidi institutions are products of these ideas and this philosophy. Following Leader Öcalan’s initiation of the democratic society process and development of the democratic integration project, negotiations with Iraq began. The stage we have reached today is the result of these efforts and initiatives. We call on all friends of the Yazidi people to continue supporting this process and contribute to a democratic solution,” the statement concluded.
