author: Solange Guimarães
title: Fuga de Flávio abre caminho para bolsonarismo abraçar políticos para além do sobrenome
content:
A derrota de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) para Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) nas eleições presidenciais e sua fuga para os Estados Unidos abriram uma disputa pela liderança da extrema direita brasileira que pode resultar em um bolsonarismo cada vez menos dependente dos membros da família do ex-presidente.




Para três pesquisadores que estudam a extrema direita, ouvidos pela 

Agência Pública

, o episódio pode representar o início de uma mudança mais profunda: a separação entre o capital político acumulado pelo bolsonarismo na última década e a família que deu nome ao movimento. A crise dos herdeiros de Jair Bolsonaro, entretanto, não significa necessariamente uma perda de influência da extrema direita, que poderá manter sua agenda política, sua capacidade de mobilização e sua atuação nas instituições mesmo sob novas lideranças.




Michelle Bolsonaro, o governador reeleito de São Paulo, Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos), e o deputado federal Nikolas Ferreira (PL-MG) estão entre os nomes citados pelos acadêmicos que podem ganhar espaço na reorganização do movimento, que perdeu a disputa pelo Palácio do Planalto, mas ampliou sua presença no Congresso Nacional.




“Acho que todo mundo, de uma certa forma, respira aliviado com a fuga do Flávio. Porque isso significa que há espaço dentro do bolsonarismo para além da família Bolsonaro”, afirma a antropóloga Isabela Kalil, pesquisadora especializada na extrema direita brasileira. Segundo ela, o senador não dispõe de capital político próprio suficiente para exercer, a partir do exterior, a liderança que seu pai construiu no país.
















Pesquisadora da extrema direita no Brasil, Isabela Kalil enxergar espaço no bolsonarismo sem os Bolsonaros




A avaliação é compartilhada pelo filósofo Rodrigo Nunes, professor da PUC-Rio e professor visitante da University of Essex, no Reino Unido. Para ele, a disputa pela sucessão já alcança o interior da própria família. “Parece que a briga pela sucessão está se abrindo dentro da própria família Bolsonaro, porque todo mundo percebe que o grande nome dentro da família agora é claramente a Michelle.”




A historiadora e cientista política Tatiana Vargas-Maia, professora de Relações Internacionais da Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS), aponta uma transformação ainda mais ampla. “Talvez a gente veja a morte do bolsonarismo como identidade, mas uma manutenção dele como estratégia”, afirma. Na avaliação da pesquisadora, o movimento pode abandonar gradualmente a dependência da figura de Jair Bolsonaro sem abrir mão das práticas políticas, eleitorais e de mobilização desenvolvidas nos últimos dez anos.




A reorganização foi necessária após a vitória do presidente Lula no segundo turno, com 51,79% dos votos válidos, contra 48,21% de Flávio Bolsonaro. O senador recebeu quase 60 milhões de votos, mas deixou o país dois dias depois, apesar de uma determinação do ministro do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) Alexandre de Moraes, para que entregasse seus passaportes à Polícia Federal.




Flávio chegou a Miami na quarta-feira (28), acompanhado da mulher e das duas filhas, após passar pela Argentina onde pegou um vôo particular com escala no Equador. Já nos Estados Unidos, divulgou uma carta em que se apresentou inicialmente como o verdadeiro presidente do Brasil, apesar da derrota nas urnas. Posteriormente, alterou o documento para se autodeclarar líder do país, mantendo acusações de fraude eleitoral sem apresentar provas.




Entre aliados, as decisões de Flávio provocaram reações que evidenciaram o seu isolamento. desde Tarcísio de Freitas defendeu o reconhecimento do resultado das urnas, enquanto Rogério Marinho (PL-RN), coordenador da campanha presidencial do PL, afirmou que não havia elementos para sustentar as acusações de fraude. O distanciamento reforça as dificuldades de Flávio para se apresentar como líder da oposição a partir do exterior.




Michelle e Tarcísio despontam na disputa pela sucessão
















Como senadora, Michelle Bolsonaro pode consolidar a sua liderança no bolsonarismo




Lideranças do campo conversador não demoraram a enxergar o espaço construído pela fuga de Flávio Bolsonaro. Para os pesquisadores, Michelle Bolsonaro e Tarcísio de Freitas são os nomes com maior destaque nessa reorganização até o momento, embora a disputa também envolva políticos mais jovens e movimentos que não se identificam integralmente com o bolsonarismo.




Rodrigo Nunes considera improvável que os filhos 01 e 03 de Jair Bolsonaro, dos Estados Unidos, consigam manter Flávio como sucessor político do pai. O filósofo observa que o enfraquecimento de ambos pode atingir também o poder de influência de Jair Bolsonaro, caso o ex-presidente deixe de exercer um papel decisivo na escolha de quem comandará o movimento. “Cada vez mais me pergunto se o Jair ainda é um personagem relevante nessa história”, afirma Nunes.




Na avaliação do professor, Michelle e Tarcísio surgem como os dois principais nomes da sucessão. A ex-primeira-dama, eleita senadora pelo Distrito Federal, mantém vínculos com a base conservadora e religiosa que apoiou o marido, mas também construiu uma trajetória política própria, inclusive em meio a divergências com os enteados.




Tatiana Vargas-Maia chama atenção para a atuação de Michelle à frente do PL Mulher e para sua capacidade de interlocução com setores evangélicos, 

como a 

Pública

 já mostrou

. A pesquisadora considera que a ex-primeira-dama já vinha demonstrando independência em relação a Flávio e pode utilizar essa posição para ampliar sua influência no partido.




Tarcísio, por sua vez, chega à disputa fortalecido pela reeleição ao governo de São Paulo. Embora tenha mantido alinhamento com o bolsonarismo durante a campanha, o governador se distanciou da contestação eleitoral promovida por Flávio. Para Tatiana, essa diferença é politicamente relevante: Freitas pode reivindicar parte do eleitorado bolsonarista sem carregar o sobrenome da família.




Nikolas Ferreira, que mantém forte presença nas redes sociais e mobiliza um público mais jovem, é apontado pelos especialistas como uma liderança com potencial de crescimento. Tatiana acrescenta Renan Santos, ligado ao Movimento Brasil Livre (MBL) e ao partido Missão, como representante de uma corrente da extrema direita que busca construir identidade própria, sem depender diretamente dos Bolsonaro.




A multiplicação de lideranças, entretanto, não garante unidade política. Kalil considera provável que o campo se fragmente em diferentes grupos da direita radical e da extrema direita, sem que uma única figura consiga reproduzir o papel exercido por Jair Bolsonaro.




Sobrenome Bolsonaro já não garante liderança




A antropóloga Isabela Kalil diferencia a capacidade de herdar votos da construção de uma liderança reconhecida pelos próprios apoiadores, no caso do senador derrotado nas eleições. “O capital que o Flávio conseguiu, e mesmo a votação bastante expressiva, foi por herdar o capital político do pai, e não por ter um capital político próprio”, afirma.




Kalil recupera pesquisas de campo realizadas no início do governo Jair Bolsonaro, quando o então presidente tentou indicar Eduardo Bolsonaro para a embaixada brasileira nos Estados Unidos. Na ocasião, a pesquisadora identificou desconfiança em relação aos filhos mesmo entre apoiadores fiéis do ex-presidente.




Segundo ela, havia eleitores que consideravam Jair Bolsonaro honesto e comprometido com uma agenda conservadora, mas não atribuíam as mesmas qualidades a Eduardo e Carlos Bolsonaro. Alguns questionavam a preparação dos filhos para o exercício de funções públicas.







Tatiana Vargas-Maia, da UFRGS, ressalta que o “patrimônio eleitoral” de Flávio estava muito ligado ao legado do pai e ao sobrenome







Para a antropóloga, essa diferença ajuda a explicar a dificuldade de Flávio em sustentar uma liderança autônoma. Jair Bolsonaro construiu uma relação carismática com sua base, enquanto o filho foi alçado à condição de candidato presidencial principalmente pela indicação do pai.




A pesquisadora avalia que o destino político de Flávio pode se aproximar do de Eduardo, que vive nos Estados Unidos e mantém interlocução com grupos conservadores e com a extrema direita norte-americana, mas tem dificuldades para exercer uma liderança significativa no Brasil.




As críticas aos filhos de Bolsonaro seguem vindo de apoiadores de primeira hora do pai. Em comentário a aliados obtido pelo jornal 

O Globo

, o pastor Silas Malafaia, um dos principais líderes evangélicos do país, ao comentar o episódio da carta golpista, se refere a eles como “jumentos”. Esses filhos de Bolsonaro são uns jumentos. Só se aconselham com gente errada! Faz carta, fala bobagem, depois corrige“, afirmou, completando: “um bando de amadores babacas”.




Para a pesquisadora Tatiana Vargas-Maia, existe uma diferença fundamental entre reivindicar a condição de herdeiro de um patrimônio eleitoral e conseguir exercer liderança efetiva sobre o campo político que produziu esses votos. A saída do país, segundo a historiadora, acelerou a erosão de uma autoridade que Flávio havia conseguido construir ao longo da campanha.




Extrema direita mantém força no Congresso e pode mudar de estratégia




Apesar da derrota presidencial, a extrema direita chega ao próximo governo Lula com representação expressiva no Legislativo. O PL elegeu 121 deputados federais, tornando-se a maior bancada da Câmara a partir de 2027, além de ampliar sua presença no Senado. O resultado cria condições para que o movimento continue exercendo influência sobre a agenda nacional, independentemente de quem ocupe a Presidência da República.




Concentrar a análise apenas na derrota de Flávio é subestimar a presença da extrema direita nas instituições na avaliação de Tatiana Vargas-Maia. Ela ressalta que o movimento também possui representantes em governos estaduais, assembleias legislativas e administrações municipais. “A nossa extrema direita contemporânea, no Brasil principalmente, não precisa conquistar o Executivo Federal para exercer influência política e para avançar o seu projeto”, afirma.




Isabela Kalil considera possível que o bolsonarismo presente no Congresso se fortaleça em torno de uma agenda própria, menos subordinada às decisões da família Bolsonaro. Já Tatiana identifica um possível movimento de moderação na apresentação pública de determinadas lideranças, especialmente entre aquelas que reconheceram o resultado eleitoral e passaram a defender uma atuação institucional da oposição. “Uma reorganização da extrema-direita, que vai se tornar menos bolsonarista, talvez desenvolva uma maior capacidade de atuação e interlocução institucional, mas que não significa necessariamente que ela vai se tornar menos radical”, afirma.




A historiadora considera possível que lideranças nacionais adotem uma postura pública mais moderada, enquanto grupos políticos nos estados e municípios mantenham ou aprofundem pautas ideológicas mais radicalizadas.Nesse cenário, o bolsonarismo poderia deixar de funcionar como uma identidade política unificadora, mas conservar estratégias de ocupação institucional, articulação partidária, comunicação digital e mobilização eleitoral.




Rodrigo Nunes acrescenta outro elemento à reorganização da direita: o papel do Centrão. Segundo o filósofo, o avanço da extrema direita nas eleições legislativas reduziu o espaço ocupado por partidos tradicionais, mas a capacidade de mobilização demonstrada pelo PT no segundo turno pode alterar essa relação.




Na avaliação do professor, o Centrão pode voltar a ocupar uma posição de equilíbrio entre o governo Lula e a extrema direita, em vez de continuar perdendo protagonismo para os setores mais radicalizados. “Se o PT mantém essa capacidade de mobilização, isso tem condições de mudar o jogo”, afirma Nunes.
















Rodrigo Nunes, autor do livro “Do Transe à Vertigem: Ensaios sobre Bolsonarismo e um Mundo em Transição”, destaca a importância das mobilizações sociais para equilibrar o jogo no Congresso Nacional




O fator Trump




A tentativa de Flávio Bolsonaro de estabelecer uma liderança política a partir dos Estados Unidos também depende das relações da família com Donald Trump e com organizações da direita internacional.




Para Isabela Kalil, Eduardo e Flávio apostam na proteção do presidente norte-americano, especialmente por meio de articulações com grupos conservadores ligados à Conferência de Ação Política Conservadora (CPAC). Essas conexões integram uma rede internacional que também aproxima lideranças, como o presidente de El Salvador, Nayib Bukele.




A antropóloga, entretanto, considera que Trump não teria dificuldades para retirar o apoio à família Bolsonaro caso essa aliança deixasse de atender aos seus interesses políticos ou diplomáticos.“O Trump não precisa da família Bolsonaro e a família Bolsonaro não acrescenta nada para o próprio projeto trumpista”, afirma.




Segundo ela, a relação dependerá também das negociações entre os governos brasileiro e norte-americano, especialmente diante dos interesses econômicos e diplomáticos envolvidos.




Rodrigo Nunes apresenta avaliação semelhante. Para o filósofo, um eventual afastamento de Trump, combinado à ausência de uma manifestação decisiva de Jair Bolsonaro em favor dos filhos, pode acelerar a perda de relevância política de Flávio e Eduardo. A situação abriria ainda mais espaço para a disputa entre 

Michelle Bolsonaro

, Tarcísio de Freitas e outras lideranças da direita.




Derrota nas urnas não encerra os riscos para a democracia




A reorganização da extrema direita também coloca em discussão os riscos de novas mobilizações contra as instituições democráticas, especialmente depois de Flávio Bolsonaro contestar o resultado eleitoral.




Isabela Kalil não descarta a possibilidade de ações extremistas isoladas, mas considera improvável, neste momento, uma mobilização semelhante à que culminou nos ataques de 8 de janeiro de 2023.




A antropóloga destaca que a mobilização anterior contou com tolerância e apoio de setores militares e que, desde então, as Forças Armadas têm procurado se afastar publicamente do bolsonarismo. Ela também avalia que os órgãos de segurança e inteligência brasileiros ampliaram sua capacidade de monitoramento de ameaças extremistas.




Tatiana Vargas-Maia, por outro lado, chama atenção para um risco político de longo prazo: a normalização de pautas autoritárias no debate público e nas instituições, mesmo sem uma ruptura democrática aberta.




A pesquisadora considera que a mobilização que levou à vitória de Lula no segundo turno demonstra a capacidade de reação democrática de setores da sociedade brasileira. Mas ressalta que a extrema direita permanece organizada, com representação eleitoral e capacidade de influenciar decisões políticas.




Para ela, o desafio não se encerra com a derrota de Flávio nem com o enfraquecimento dos herdeiros de Jair Bolsonaro. O movimento pode assumir outras identidades, construir novas lideranças e conservar parte de seu projeto político.




É o que Tatiana define como um possível processo de “despersonalização do bolsonarismo”: o afastamento progressivo da figura de Jair Bolsonaro e de sua família, sem o desaparecimento do capital político e ideológico construído em torno deles.




Assim, a disputa aberta pela fuga de Flávio pode determinar não apenas quem herdará os votos da família, mas de que maneira a extrema direita brasileira buscará exercer poder nos próximos anos.

author: Cierra Bettens
title: InFocus: What’s at stake for Indigenous Peoples in the U.S. as midterm elections draw near?
content:
On Tuesday, U.S. voters will cast their ballots in the country’s midterm elections. The elections come halfway through a president’s four year term.

A record-breaking number of Indigenous candidates–at least 355–are running in this year’s race.

This week on InFocus, Pawnee/Ponca lawyer Brett Chapman tells us about the candidates he’s following and how Native Americans are feeling the impact of Trump’s second term.

A recent study by the Brookings Institution reported that the Trump administration slashed $469 million in grants and contracts to tribal communities.

“I think a big problem with the administration, the second go around, is that because of the focus by them on DEI [Diversity, Equity and Inclusion], things of that nature, they have really tried to reduce Native American issues to [being] race-based,” Chapman said.

“What defines being Native American in the United States is not being a member of a race. It’s political sovereignty in the history of over 500 tribes having treaties with the government, and they’re having their own governments. And so you’re having a government-to-government relationship.

“You’re really seeing a weakening of that when it should be stronger.”

Covering elections is nothing new for Mark Trahant, a founding editor of Indian Country Today, now called ICT. The Shoshone-Bannock journalist has been in the industry for over 50 years.

However, with the Trump administration’s threats to press freedom, it’s a slightly different terrain.

“One thing I’ve been writing a lot about is how do we plan for life after Trump and start to build institutions again? And I think media is a big part of that,” Trahant said on InFocus.

“One that I would advocate for…is starting to think about government funding of media. You look at, particularly in Indian Country, how much people have to do with so little resources. Whereas, in other countries in the world, they have a steady stream of revenue that allows them to expand, and report, and do things that you would normally do in a media environment that’s healthy.”

Listen to this week’s episode for a closer look at how the U.S. midterm outcomes could impact Indigenous communities.

Cierra is the host and co-producer of the of the weekly APTN News InFocus podcast. She joined APTN in 2024 as a reporter-correspondent in Winnipeg after working in campus and city news. She’s currently completing her Master of Arts in Media Studies at Concordia University in Montréal. Cierra has mixed settler and Red River Métis roots and is a member of the Manitoba Métis Federation.

author: Dominique Gené - Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Kuujjuaq Greenhouse gets $1M in federal funding
content:
The Kuujjuaq Greenhouse has $1 million in federal funding to expand local food production and processing in the community.




Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty and Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Rebecca Alty toured the greenhouse Friday morning as part of a funding announcement from Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions. It’s a federal program that gives financial support to small and medium-size businesses and non-profit organizations.




The money will go toward the construction of a new service building connected to the existing greenhouses that were built in 1999 and 2012, said Roxane Archambault, a member of the four-person volunteer committee managing the Kuujjuaq Greenhouse. The project is operated by the municipality.




The new building will include an insulated space to help extend the gardening season, washrooms and improved facilities to provide more comfortable working conditions, Archambault said. The committee also hopes to integrate a seedling container into the new building.




It will also support the greenhouse’s food-processing activities, preservation equipment and workshops on growing fresh food.




The Kuujjuaq Greenhouse’s gardening season has wrapped up for the year, with community members expected to return to their plots when the season reopens in late May or early June. (Photo by Dominique Gené)




“We’re really glad to get this funding. We were not sure what we would do without it,” Archambault said in an interview in French.
















The project is expected to be completed by fall 2027, she said.




The Kuujjuaq Greenhouse currently has 46 gardening plots available to community members, Archambault said. Inuit beneficiaries and residents who have lived in Kuujjuaq for at least 10 years automatically qualify for a plot.




After Inuit and longtime residents get their plots, anyone else can apply for a plot, after living at least one year in the community.




The remaining plots are awarded by lottery if necessary. Organizations also automatically qualify.




Alongside individual plots, there are community plots with fresh produce, such as lettuce, spinach and herbs available to residents.




This gardening season has officially ended and is expected to resume in late May or early June next year.
















Gull-Masty congratulated the greenhouse committee on the project and said she hoped to return for another visit in the summer.

author: Unknown
title: In the Crosshairs of the Far-Right Advance : An Update on Anti-Fascists and Anarchists in Greece
content:
Anarchist graffiti from Athens, Greece (2026)




The anarchist movement in Greece faces a new wave of repression. Urged on by the US and its obsession with combatting “far-left extremism,” the Greek state has targeted anti-authoritarians with new legal charges and attacked demonstrations, while fascists carry out street attacks and plot their return to the halls of power. Amidst a landscape of ongoing austerity, terrorism designations, lethal prisons, and ferocious wildfires, anarchists nonetheless continue to forge a combative culture of revolutionary solidarity.




In this article, we present an interview with an anarchist comrade in Athens assessing the current situation among anarchists and anti-fascists in Greece, along with analysis of the US’s role in advancing state repression and fantasies of Western supremacy.







The US and Greece: A Right-Wing Alliance to Defend “The West”




Earlier this month, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio delivered a speech at the Pnyx in Athens. With the historic Acropolis and the Parthenon—that ancient symbol of Western democracy, constructed with slave labor—in the background, he delivered a warning message to Greece’s political and business elite.




“The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world or resigns itself to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline,” Rubio cautioned. “We will either choose to act now or lose the choice to act at all.” Lamenting how “nationalism became a dirty word,” he called for renewed militarism, praised Christian faith and martyrdom, and announced a new counterterrorism information-sharing program between the two countries. His statements were calculated to reinforce the colonial legacy of Western dominance over the rest of the world, while urging the worst of Greek society to imitate America’s current political trajectory.







 




US Secretary of State Marco Rubio constructs an elaborate photo op for his defense of nationalism, militarism, and “the West” (October 7, 2026).










The speech came in the wake of a conference Rubio convened in July that aimed to coordinate intensified repression against “far-left extremism.” The following month, the US government imposed a “global terrorist” designation on the Italy-based 

Autistici/Inventati (A/I) tech collective

, which operated the free publishing platform NoBlogs.org.




Greece’s right-wing politicians and business leaders benefiting from the country’s endless austerity measures are heeding Rubio’s call to preserve the hubris of the so-called West. Meanwhile, governments are collaborating to escalate repression against any truly revolutionary movements that challenge the world’s current status quo.




Greece’s strategic importance to Western powers is rooted in its symbolic status as the birthplace of “Western Civilization,” as well as its strategic location in the world today. The country offers the US access to four military sites, including a dedicated Navy base in Crete’s Souda Bay. Those with a longer memory have not forgotten how the US supplied napalm to Greece’s fascist forces, who worked with the Nazis during World War II and later with the British and US in a Cold War anti-communist alliance. Fascists dropped American napalm on Greek partisan resistance fighters during the civil war from 1946 to 1949, scorching bodies and charring forests, leaving the countryside scarred to this day.




More recently, the Greek people were pummeled by the 2008 global economic crisis, brought on in part by Wall Street firms such as Goldman Sachs that raked in immense profits while destabilizing the world’s economy and immiserating millions. The US then contributed to the austerity measures imposed on Greece in 2010 by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), leading to years of ferocious resistance to neoliberal capitalism and government complicity.




Today, Greece’s current New Democracy regime upholds 

the legacy of the brutal military junta

 of 1967-1974, promoting the image of Greece as a symbol European supremacy as invoked by Rubio. Despite its nationalist rhetoric, the government continues to lick the boots of the US, crushing opposition in the streets and enforcing a never-ending precarity on the majority of Greece’s increasingly exhausted and numb population.




This continuing legacy of US imperial arrogance and Greek state complicity can reach the point of absurdity. Recently, the US Ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, resigned following allegations of soliciting bribes—in the form of paying off credit card debt—from a wealthy Republican donor in exchange for promises to leverage her connections to the Trump family. One cannot ignore the hilarity of Greece’s elite lining up to lick the boots of this comically incompetent and corrupt American official.




The US Rages as an Anarchist Goes Free




However, before her resignation, Guilfoyle 

commented on the release of anarchist Nikos Maziotis

 after serving 14 years in prison, saying people like him “have no place in civilized society.” Maziotis was a member of Revolutionary Struggle, an armed guerrilla group listed as a foreign terrorist organization by the United States, and was arrested in 2014 while on the run following a shootout with police.







 




Banner in solidarity with Revolutionary Struggle prisoner Nikos Maziotis, just released from prison in September 2026.










Revolutionary Struggle emerged around 2003 after multiple attacks on the Evelpidon courthouse in Athens. They are also well known for an attack on the Athens Stock Exchange in 2009. Maziotis remained an uncompromising revolutionary while imprisoned. His co-defendant and partner Pola Roupa attempted unsuccessfully to free him from prison in 2016 by hijacking a helicopter. Shortly before 

his release

 in September, Maziotis released 

a statement

 in which he affirmed:







I would not change my political and activist choices in the slightest, even if I could turn back time.


From the bottom of my heart, I thank all my comrades, everyone who stood in solidarity with us in any way over all these years, with us, the members of Revolutionary Struggle, who remained faithful to the choices of struggle we made. 


NO RECONSIDERATION, NO REPENTANCE 


LONG LIVE REVOLUTIONARY STRUGGLE 


HONOR FOREVER TO COMRADE 

LAMBROS FOUNTAS

 







—Nikos Maziotis, Domokos Prison, September 2, 2026







 




Nikos Maziotis emerges from prison after 14 years into the arms of his comrades (September 2026). You can watch the video of his release 

here

.










The Resurgence of the Extreme Right




Maziotis’s release happened just one day before the release of convicted neo-Nazi and Golden Dawn leader Ilias Kasidiaris, who served just six years of his thirteen-and-a-half-year sentence for leading a “

criminal organization

.” His conviction stemmed from a token prosecution to calm anger over 

the murder of anti-fascist rapper Killah P

 (Pavlos Fyssas) by a Golden Dawn member.




Guilfoyle, of course, condemned only Maziotis’s release, remaining silent about Kasidiaris. That is no coincidence. And the Greek state will certainly try to compensate for his obligatory release by furthering its assault on the anarchist movement and other revolutionary struggles—no pun intended—in Greece.




Upon his release, Kasidiaris stated his intention to immediately resume his political activity. Whether or not he ends up back in Parliament, he will undoubtedly be a force behind Greece’s right wing in the streets, and a more subtle but tangible influence on those in the halls of power. At present, he is unable to restart his neo-Nazi organizing in Parliament under the banner of Golden Dawn without a court ruling to reverse their designation as a criminal organization and to allow them on the ballot. But he intends to start a new organization with the same goals under a different name. Similarly to Marine Le Pen in 

France

 with National Rally, he is attempting to clean up his reputation and pursue a more mainstream approach to achieving his fascist aims. His legacy continues to inspire right-wing youth, even though violent street actions must not be connected to him while he seeks political legitimacy and another career in Parliament.




His release has emboldened Greece’s institutional and grassroots fascist forces. Like Zionist settlers in the West Bank, groups such as the Golden Dawn enjoy the support of country’s police and military. This allows them to minimize risk when attacking immigrants, refugees, anti-fascists, anarchists, and other targeted groups. They often imitate the aesthetics of anti-fascists and anarchists, dressing in black and claiming to be “rebels” (like Americans who idolize the Confederate past). Yet their “rebellion” is mere cowardly cosplay, consisting primarily of attacking migrants, homeless people, squats, and other vulnerable individuals. They undertake their violence secure in the knowledge that it would require headlines and widespread discontent to prompt anything nearing the level of repression that anarchists and actual revolutionary groups face. Only when the Golden Dawn killed Killah P, a Greek man, did the state finally crack down on them; and despite their convictions, many have now been released and are free to continue their fascist organizing.




Neo-Nazis have been emboldened since the release of Kasidiaris, exemplified by the 

attack on a known anti-fascist

 walking his dog by two young fascists in the neighborhood of Elefsina, just a bit outside of Athens. The two youths approached their target screaming, “You are a leftist and we are fascists.” The anti-fascist succeeded in defending himself, humiliating the two youths who surprised him in the street. However, upon realizing that they couldn’t beat him, the cowards stabbed him in the thigh, hitting a critical artery. Fortunately, the anti-fascist was brought to the hospital and survived his wounds.




A massive 

anti-fascist demonstration

 happened in the neighborhood after the attack. It faced no grassroots opposition, but the uniformed opposition massed nearby with officers ready to pounce if given the order. The media at first immediately dismissed the attack as standard hooligan-on-hooligan violence, refusing to recognize the pervasive fascist influence Golden Dawn continues to exert in Greece to this day. It took a widespread outcry, multiple demonstrations, and the discovery by police of fascist paraphernalia in the two youths’ house, including an “Autonomous Nationalist Youth of Athens” sticker, for the state to admit that this was an attack by fascists influenced by the legacy of Kasidiaris’ Golden Dawn. Anti-fascist sources have established the connection of the two young fascists to the notorious Nazi street action group 

ProPatria

.




Had the anti-fascist been Roma or Pakistani rather than Greek, the attack likely would have been swept under the rug. The ruling 

New Democracy party

 refuses to acknowledge the suffering of marginalized peoples who have been assaulted, murdered, trapped by debt into forced labor, 

kidnapped by the far right in the streets

, or faced pogroms and indefinite detention in EU-funded 

migrant concentration camps

 across the country. Many such attacks by police and fascists remain unreported, deemed unworthy of recognition by the mainstream nationalist press.




Like the thugs of the military junta fifty years ago, Greece’s nationalists have always been a friend to the country’s ruling class, similar to Trump and his MAGA base in the US today. So neither Guilfoyle’s silence on Kasidiaris’ release nor the designation of Revolutionary Struggle as a terrorist group by the US is a surprise. Neither Rubio, Guilfoyle, nor New Democracy Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis take issue with political violence. They take issue with political violence aimed at revolutionary change or self-defense against oppression.




At the moment, Greece’s anarchist movement remains in the crosshairs of the Greek state. The movement is adapting to a modernized repression, inflicted to defend a society treated as a zoo for tourists with an educated population ripe for exploitation by customer service and tech firms from wealthier nations. This interview continues our efforts to offer English-language updates on the anarchist movement in Greece from comrades on the ground. Our priority is to develop a concrete understanding of the current situation in Greece, to cultivate resilience and solidarity that transcends borders and prison bars.







Repression and Resistance in Greece Today: Interview with an Anarchist in Athens




The following is an update from a comrade on the ground in Athens, Greece. For further background and context, see our previous coverage on the 

Solidarity Assembly for Imprisoned Fugitives and Persecuted Combatants

 (2026), state repression of 

the refugee struggle

 (2023), the 

Greek Wildfires

 (2021), 

the state of the anarchist movement at the end of the pandemic lockdown

 (2021), the state’s 

ban of the fascist Golden Dawn party

 (2020), and the right-wing 

New Democracy party’s crackdown on autonomous movements

 (2019).







“

Our passion for freedom is stronger than any prison cell.

”







—Felix Daspitilakis, Anonymous Publishing Union, Athens, 2026







We 

spoke a few months ago

, but for new international readers, could you introduce yourself and the projects you’re involved with?




I participate in the anarchist and anti-authoritarian space in Athens, Greece. I am involved in various open assemblies organized in response to multiple issues, such as solidarity with political prisoners in Greece and internationally, or state repression against the movement here. I also support the movement’s infrastructure, especially organized counter-information and the defense of squats.




Since we last spoke, the international press has widely discussed the 

recent arrests

 made sixteen years after the burning of the Marfin bank in 2010, which resulted in the death of three employees who had been 

forced to work by their bosses

 despite the unprecedented general strike. Could you explain what brought on these sudden charges, the details of the case, and its implications?




This case concerns the events of the 5th of May of 2010. During a massive, half-a-million-strong demonstration in support of a general strike, the building of the Marfin bank was set on fire and three employees who had been locked inside by the management died. This triggered a massive retaliatory repression attack by the state, both against the demonstration on the day of the strike and over the following days and years against the broader movement.




It is clear that the anti-memorandum movement of 2009-2015 [

a series of protests against government austerity measures, including pension and salary cuts and higher taxes, imposed by the International Monetary Fund

] had seriously threatened the Greek state. Masses of people participated in protests, massive 

general strikes

 and numerous 

clashes with police

 took place, and the belief that there is an alternative to the politics of the Greek state, the EU and the IMF became widespread. This remains an open wound for those in power. And although in the end this turned out to be political capital that the 

SYRIZA

 (a left-wing party in power from 2015 to 2019, known for its broken promises) government expended without achieving anything, the state wants to have the last word about this historical period.




This is especially true for the right-wing of this country. The Marfin bank arson offered them an opening to attempt to recover a moral high ground. Over the years since it happened, the right has consistently invoked it to elicit declarations of democratic submission from the left, almost with the same intensity as with the shooting of Bakogiannis by the revolutionary organization November 17th group (N17) in 1989.

1

 And, apart from a few exceptions, the left unfortunately did indeed offer concessions to the right following these events as a result of pressure campaigns arranged by New Democracy and Greece’s right-wing parties.




This is the third time that this case has been reopened. The first round of prosecutions ended in acquittals, while the second round didn’t even result in trials. Until this third attempt to use this tragedy against the anarchist movement, the only conviction was of the owner of the bank for forcing his employers to work on that day of general strike while neglecting fire safety standards and protocols, the main culprit for the death of the three employees.







 




Posters in solidarity with the three anarchists charged in the Marfin bank case.










Now, sixteen years after this tragic event, we face another government scheme that has nothing to do with offering justice to the victims of the fire. The evidence that led to the pre-trial imprisonment of the three arrested anarchists consists of anonymous email, sent sixteen years afterwards. It names random people—one of whom was actually in jail during the event—alongside photos that allegedly identify various individuals, using pictures of people on vacation compared with images of hooded participants in the demo with supposedly similar body types and punk band stickers on bags.




As usual in these cases, the mainstream media advances all kinds of fanciful stories to obscure the total lack of evidence. We read about AI systems that supposedly can magically reconstruct faces from photos of hooded people. The anonymous email is an almost comic attempt to modernize the anonymous phone calls historically used by police and the anti-terrorist unit to falsely incriminate people in earlier cases.




Such theatrics and flimsy evidence give the impression of a case that will again be voided by the first degree court. Nonetheless, even if this turns out to be the case, the state’s effort offers some important lessons.




Most importantly, pre-trial detention can last for up to eighteen months. Apart from the terrible conditions in Greek prisons—many states, including the UK, officially categorize Greek prisons as inhumane—the destructive effects this has on the lives of those arrested is evident.




Furthermore, being falsely accused, tried, and convicted by the media for killing other people imposes a practical and psychological burden that will not be relieved by dismissed charges or acquittal.




Finally, it is clear across all Western states that repression is on the rise on many levels: augmentation and modernization of police, harsher penal codes, etc. Regardless, as a movement, we will organize to put a stop to this persecution of our comrades. But the case shows that the Greek state is once again advancing its attack on revolutionary movements as a whole and against the anarchist space specifically.




To conclude, we should mention a new development which clearly shows the state’s intention with regard to this case. In October, our comrades faced another round of interrogation, concerning a new charge of “atomic/personal” terrorism. This makes the case file even more nonsensical: we now supposedly have three separate and independent terrorists that committed an organized triple murder together, along with multiple other attempted murders of the other employees that were trapped inside the bank by their bosses. Given that a murder conviction carries the heaviest penalty in terms of prison years under the Greek legal system, these additional charges do not add anything substantial in the way of sentencing.




This shift in charges reveals the state’s true intentions. Under Greek law, terrorism charges move a case from a jury court to a court with only “professional” state-appointed career judges, who are under more pressure by the state and have a clear incentive to convict, regardless of the actual evidence or lack thereof.




Prior to the reopening of the Marfin bank case, police made multiple arrests in connection with alleged attacks on Greek politicians’ homes in Salonika. Do you have details on these arrests, their potential use by the Greek state in cracking down harder on the anarchist movement, or their connection to this strange decision to reopen cases from long ago?




The Marfin case was reopened immediately following the Salonika case, making it obvious that the state wanted to use them together to create a strong effect in the media. For the Salonika case, our comrades’ position is that they are being targeted as known anarchists. The state needed to show a strong reaction since during the incident, the mother of a member of the governing New Democracy Party was killed. The government’s rhetoric targets the anarchist and anti-authoritarian movement as a whole. So the appearance of both of these cases at the same time indicates a hardening of the state’s position against us, and an indicator that things will probably get even harder.




How is the anarchist movement currently responding to escalating levels of repression?




The anarchist movement has accumulated many differences and divides over the years. This puts us at a disadvantage during a very difficult period in terms of repression. After each incident, whether it is an eviction of a squat, a fascist attack, or the reopening of the Marfin case we discussed above, the anarchist movement tries to overcome these problems and organize via open assemblies.




Our goal is to claim a portion of the public space with our voices and bodies, to counter the state’s propaganda and defend our comrades and our spaces.




Beyond judicial repression, we have learned about 

the killing of a boy on the spectrum in Argos, Greece

 by police. We watched one demonstration against the murder 

attacked brutally by police

. Are police becoming more emboldened to crush demonstrations without concern about public judgment? Does the background of the murdered boy help to explain why they are so emboldened to respond like this?




I think that there has been a shift in the political reality in Greece concerning repression, at least since 2019. First of all, the population of cops is much larger than before. Also, they are one of the few social groups that have continued to receive benefits from the state during these years of extreme economic austerity, making them a loyal and hardened “partisan army” for the government. This, combined with the decline of the left and social movements in general, as well as the extreme rhetoric of the government concerning its repressive ambitions, has given them the signal that they will be protected no matter what they do.




In response to this particular state murder, the current and former mayors of Argos both opted to cover for the cops completely. The government advanced all kinds of half-baked scenarios in the media to support the police’s version of events from day one. The attack on the demonstration follows this reality and the state’s attempt to silence the movement.




It should be noted, though, that the call for the demonstration in Argos and its support by so many comrades marks an important moment for the Greek movement. Despite the fact that it took place in a town largely dominated by right and extreme right-wing politicians, the feeling our comrades got from the people there was not hostile.







 




Protestors from disability justice and anarchist movements confront police in Argos (July 25, 2026).










Since we last spoke, have there been any updates on the well-being of 

Marianna

 and 

Dimitra

, the anarchists imprisoned in 

the Ampelokipoi Case

, or the arrests related to alleged bank robberies we discussed in

 the last interview

?




For Marianna and Dimitra, who were 

sentenced to long prison terms

 for supposed membership in a non-existent terrorist organization, the second-degree court has been arranged for March of 2027. They are both being held in the women’s prison in Thiva and are as well as can be expected given the situation. The same holds for the anarchists who have been pre-detained in prisons all around Greece for the Tithorea bank case. We still have no date for the court until now.




At a gathering of fascist diplomats this July, United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio 

referenced the alleged attack

 in Salonika. Do you see these accusations against the anarchist movement as a new opportunity for the Greek state to exploit? Do you think that America’s push for a global war on anti-authoritarian tendencies is catching on with the politicians currently in power in Greece?




The Greek state has historically been responsive to the United States’s demands, especially in matters of repression and anti-terrorism. I am afraid that these statements by Rubio will likely have an impact, at least in the Salonika case. Given the growing pressure the US is exerting in these matters globally, such as labeling “antifa” and 

Autistici/Inventati (A/I)

 terrorist organizations, Greece will follow the trend of repression that is now on the rise in most European states.




The Greek state has revised its penal and correctional codes three times since 2019. This has created legal chaos, with lawyers and courts not knowing which law is in effect with each case, and prisons overcrowded with people convicted of low-level offenses. But of course the state is always ready to make things even worse, especially in matters where the US shows a strong interest. We already have government officials talking about extending the maximum prison sentence to 30 years, in response to 

US pressure over the potential releases

 of some convicted N17 organization prisoners. According to the current law, their sentences cannot be extended beyond next fall. There is also talk of making it very difficult, or even impossible, to have a prison sentence suspended until the second-degree court makes a decision.




Greece also made international headlines late this summer for its catastrophic wildfires, an ongoing issue in the country that 

we’ve reported on here

. Do you have any comments about that?




These wildfires have unfortunately become normal in Greece over the last decades. The state always approaches this issue as a natural catastrophe that cannot be addressed effectively due to the climate crisis. And the only attention they receive within Greek society, if any at all, focuses narrowly on the loss of human lives and the economic toll from destruction of property.




Even as these extreme wild fires become ordinary in more and more regions, it is clear that the Greek state cannot pretend it has done the bare minimum to address this issue. Typically for this government, all methods for countering wildfires are outdated, when they are not completely ignored. The fire department remains understaffed, and no money has been allocated towards new technologies that are supposed to help.




I would add that it does not take much thinking to realize that capitalist development is behind many of these catastrophes. Regardless of discussions about what is or is not “natural,” it is obvious that the planet has reached a breaking point as a result of human technological advancement. The connection between these fires and capitalism’s extreme exploitation of human and non-human life has been made explicit in the past years.







 




The wildfires that raged through Greece this summer reflect the dire state of a planet ravaged by capitalism.










Considering the extreme heat waves facing the country and the underfunding of prisons in Greece, are prisoners facing harsher conditions than normal? Are prisoners organizing, or are solidarity efforts being organized from the outside?




There have been reports coming in from various prisons about the terrible conditions experienced during the heat waves. In some cases, such as in Domokos prison, water was not even available for prisoners,. There has been one case of a small-scale 

insurrection in the women’s prison of Thiva

, but it appears that nothing is really moving inside or outside of prisons.




Some of the most horrifying conditions exist in the Agios Stefanos prison of Patra, where we’ve seen nine consecutive deaths of prisoners since April of this year. While not directly caused by the heat waves, this horrifying death toll is a direct consequence of the way the prison system in Greece deals with drug users, along with the lack of effective medical care inside prisons. This number was big enough to attract the interest of the media, though the prison attempted to place all the blame on the prisoners and used cops to harass them daily. In the end, popular outrage forced the state to change most of the administration of the prison. Also, the “Solidarity Assembly for Imprisoned, Fugitive and Persecuted Combatants” called a gathering outside the prison on October 12.




I should also mention the recent 

insurrection of migrants at the closed camp of Sinitiki

. The conditions described there, before and especially after the insurrection, are nightmarish. Migrants were reportedly offered nothing but rotten food, when any food at all was available, and insufficient water. People were crowded into cramped containers, with guards who can act as cruelly and violently as they wish, since there is no public oversight. Information about these concentration camps for migrants is scarce, but what we do know reflects the extreme racist violence that is systemic in Greek society.




How can comrades best show solidarity with the movement in Greece?




International solidarity is always the best way for us to support each other. Our struggles and goals are common, whatever our differing circumstances inside the movements are. Each of us fights around the world in solidarity with a common struggle against the state and capitalism. The networks by which money can be sent to support judicial costs are absolutely indispensable, of course. But I would also argue that the strengthening of political relationships internationally could prove to be enormously beneficial for all of us.




Is there anything else you’d like to add?




I would like to state my concern about the 

A/I closure

, after the US government labeled them as a “Specially Designated Global Terrorist” and made it legally compromising to have any official, especially economic, relationship with their services. Terrorist lists have existed for decades now, especially originating from the United States, and have caused various difficulties for individuals who have been accused or convicted under anti-terrorism laws. But this case appears to demonstrate the successful realization of a new strategy for state repression on an international level.




I do not say the above as a criticism to the comrades of A/I for choosing to stop the project. To them I can only express my appreciation for all the years they kept their services open and their efforts to continue while under attack. But given that these states have in a way “socialized” terrorism accusations, and the influence the US has on anti-terrorist legislation in the European states, I am afraid we will see similar repressive moves in the future. Accordingly, we must find ways to deal with them.




The comrades from A/I have already indicated a path I’d also suggest: 
“

Go forth and multiply! May 10 - 100 - 1000 servers spark up.

”







 




Plaque in Athens commemorating anarchist Kyriakos Ximitiris, whose tragic death in a 2024 explosion led to the Ampelokipoi Case in which Marianna and Dimitra were imprisoned.













How to Support Anarchists in Greece against Repression




The main fund for economic solidarity is 

Tameio

, which provides financial support to political prisoners on a monthly basis. Over the years, it has become one of the most important structures of the anarchist movement in Greece. In addition, there are many specialized funds for specific cases, usually to cover the legal costs of arrested comrades. These funds can be found on websites such as 

Athens Indymedia

 and 

Firefund

.




How to Stay Up to Date and Learn More




CrimethInc.’s 

coverage of the anarchist movement in Greece

 will continue. 

Athens Indymedia

 is the most frequently updated site with relevant information, and can easily be translated using browsers such as 

Brave

.




We also suggest getting a copy of the book 

Anarchy in Greece: Resistance Reports

, published by 

Active Distribution

 and 

Detritus Books

. The book includes some articles that have appeared on CrimethInc, plus additional texts by anonymous anarchists on the ground in Greece as well as political prisoners such as 

Marianna Manoura

. Any and all profits from the book go to 

Tameio

.













On September 26, 1989, politician Pavlos Bakoyannis of the New Democracy Party was assassinated by members of the Marxist-Leninist guerrilla group Revolutionary Organization 17 November. Founded in 1975, N17 conducted a decades-long campaign against the Greek state and businesses, including at least 23 assassinations and numerous bombings, before the arrests of many group members in 2002. The potential release of some long-term N17 prisoners next year has catalyzed right-wing efforts to expand prison sentences and legal repression even further. 

↩

title: From France to Kurdistan: How well do we understand society in transition?
content:
France occupies a special place in the political memory of the modern world. The Enlightenment, the Revolution of 1789, and the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen gave freedom and equality universal significance. Yet proclaiming rights does not necessarily mean that all social groups can exercise them equally. The Republic’s promise of equality has repeatedly been put to the test by colonialism, class divisions, and discrimination against citizens with migrant backgrounds.




Against this backdrop, the words of jurist and statesman Robert Badinter, who lost his father during the Nazi occupation and played a key role in abolishing the death penalty in 1981, take on particular significance: “France is not the country of human rights, but the country where the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen was proclaimed.” The gap between the historical legacy of these rights and contemporary social realities continues to demand critical examination.




The new language of the streets




The protests by students at French secondary schools, which began in mid-September and continued throughout October 2026, offer valuable insights into contemporary French society. Teacher shortages, long school days, overcrowded classrooms, poor conditions in school cafeterias, and anxieties about the future are among the students’ concerns. Some protest signs also reveal a sense of humor: the irony of a student complaining that his overloaded timetable leaves him no time to see his girlfriend may seem trivial at first glance. Yet these young people are questioning not only the conditions of their education but also the way their everyday lives are organized.




After five weeks of sustained protests, the government announced a plan on October 26 that included changes to the Parcoursup* higher education admissions system, reductions in class sizes, and the creation of additional university places. School and university student organizations considered these measures insufficient. The fact that problems raised for years only make it onto the political agenda following mass mobilization by young people highlights the difference between merely listening to the youth and genuinely responding to their demands.




Taking to the streets is nothing new in France. The country has a deeply rooted culture of protest, stretching from the revolutions and May 1968 to workers’ strikes and demonstrations against pension reforms. Today’s Generation Z, however, has a different relationship with traditional institutions. Digital communication tools make it easier to mobilize around specific demands in a very short time. Yet this is not simply a matter of new means of organization. Young people refuse to let others determine their lives and futures. They demand that their voices, living conditions, and expectations be taken seriously, and they want to play an active role in shaping their own future.




How well do we, who are intimately familiar with May 1968 and the political struggles of the past, truly know today’s French youth and the social realities in which they live?




We live in an age when access to information is easier than ever before. Yet having access to information is far from the same as understanding society as it is lived today. Young people who do not carry the political memory of previous generations can still fight against the injustices they experience themselves. Rather than judging them by the standards of the past, we must listen to them and understand what they have to say today.




Between solidarity and racist violence




The social reality of France cannot be understood solely through young people’s protests and their search for solidarity. In a country where the ideals of freedom and equality have a significant historical legacy, discrimination, exclusion, and racist violence also persist.




After the protests by secondary school students had dominated public debate, an armed attack in Trappes and La Verrière on October 23 once again brought another, darker side of France into focus. One person was killed and five others were injured, including a twelve-year-old child. President Emmanuel Macron described the incident as a “racist terrorist attack.” Investigations are underway on suspicion of a racist motive and terrorist offenses.




No direct causal link can be established between the students’ protests against their educational conditions and this attack. However, the fact that both occurred during the same period illustrates how social tensions can manifest in different ways. The growing influence of the far right in Europe is another social reality that cannot be overlooked. Economic insecurity, migration, and anxieties about the future can, under certain circumstances, foster solidarity, while under others they can encourage exclusionary identity politics.




The key is not to hastily interpret social developments through existing ideological frameworks, but to understand them in terms of their own causes and contradictions.




Neo-nationalism and youth in Turkey




The anxieties about the future experienced by young people in France raise the question of what political orientations similar forms of social uncertainty might produce in other countries. The neo-nationalism emerging among young people in Turkey is particularly revealing in this regard.




According to a study published in December 2025 by researcher Selin Gücüm at the French Institute for International and Strategic Affairs (IRIS), a survey conducted by GoFor and KONDA in February 2024 among people aged 18 to 30 found that approximately 39 percent of respondents identified as nationalist, while 44 percent identified primarily as Kemalist. These figures refer to all young people surveyed, not exclusively to those holding neo-nationalist views.




Neo-nationalism is not merely a continuation of traditional conservative nationalism. It is also found among segments of urban, secular youth who are critical of authoritarian forms of rule. Some young people who express concerns about economic insecurity and restrictions on fundamental freedoms simultaneously perceive refugees or the political demands of Kurds as threats to national unity and sovereignty.




Why does someone who demands freedom for themselves fail to recognize the freedom of others as part of the same principle?




This political orientation cannot be explained solely as a spontaneous reaction emerging among young people. One of its key historical foundations lies in the homogenizing conception of national identity that the Turkish state has repeatedly reproduced through the education system, official historiography, and security-related discourse.




Selin Gücüm’s study highlights another important aspect: Some young people with neo-nationalist views do not regard the “father state” as a sacred and infallible authority, but instead criticize it for its inability to provide social and economic security. However, this criticism is not accompanied by an equal recognition of different identities. According to the report, Kurdish, Circassian, and Armenian identities are tolerated in these circles only insofar as they remain within the framework of “Turkishness.” This is therefore a political orientation that, while differing from traditional state nationalism, does not fully overcome its homogenizing conception of national identity.




No simple contrast can be drawn between young people in France and those in Turkey. Rather, the crucial question is why similar anxieties about the future foster solidarity under certain conditions, while under others they encourage a politics that denies other people their rights.




A shared future and social transformation




Can Kurdish and Turkish youth come together in a common democratic struggle in the face of poverty, unemployment, and anxieties about the future?




Shared problems do not necessarily give rise to a shared political consciousness. The experiences of Kurdish youth, shaped by language, identity, and historical memory, serve as a reminder that equality cannot be achieved solely on the basis of economic demands.




Moreover, shared problems are not experienced to the same extent everywhere. A report by the Center for Kurdish Studies comparing data from the SEGE-2017 and SEGE-2025 socioeconomic development indices describes 16 predominantly Kurdish-populated provinces as a “region of inequality.” After nearly a decade, none of these provinces had managed to move up to a higher level of development; all remained in the bottom 16 positions in the nationwide rankings. This does not indicate absolute stagnation, but rather that their relative position compared with the rest of Turkey has remained unchanged. While the region moved marginally closer to the national average, the gap between it and Istanbul actually widened.




Economic performance continued to improve in some provinces, but their rankings in education and healthcare remained virtually unchanged.




In the 2019/20 school year, the preschool enrollment rate in the region stood at 36 percent, compared with 46 percent in the other provinces. Understanding the lived realities of young people requires recognizing these conditions as well.




Kurdish youth may have a strong sense of patriotism and a deep identification with their origins. However, this should not be equated with adopting the political and organizational patterns of previous generations. Embracing Kurdish identity does not require rejecting other identities and can be reconciled with universal values of freedom and equality.




Everyone engaged with the Kurdish question and the cause of Kurdistan can make an effort to speak directly with the young people around them. Equally important, however, is listening to their answers without trying to change them. Young people’s political and ideological views may differ from our expectations. Interpreting these differences as a rejection of patriotism or the historical struggle would be an overly simplistic conclusion.




The living conditions of Kurdish youth in the four parts of Kurdistan, in cities outside Kurdistan in Turkey, Syria, Iraq, and Iran, in the Caucasus, and in other regions of the world are by no means identical. Education, working life, migration, women’s demands for freedom, and technological change are reshaping their relationship with politics.




One of the central challenges facing the Kurdish freedom movement is passing on the legacy of its historical struggle to future generations. Yet methods that brought success yesterday may become a weakness tomorrow if they are no longer sufficient to understand a changing society and its new dynamics. Passing on this legacy does not mean imposing the language and organizational forms of previous generations on young people, but enabling them to give meaning to that legacy within the context of their own lives and in their own language.




We are living through a period of polycrisis, characterized by interconnected crises in which wars, economic crises, mass migration, technological upheavals, and political tensions mutually reinforce one another. Wars are no longer fought solely on the front lines, but also in the realms of economics, technology, and information. It is as though we are living on a simmering volcano. Beneath the events we perceive on the surface, deeper tensions are building.




At such a time, political movements that seek to drive social transformation and change society must question not only their political discourse but also their established ways of listening and organizing. It is these young people who will live through the future. We, meanwhile, are increasingly the bearers of experiences from the past. These experiences are valuable. Developing visions for the future, anticipating developments, and exploring possible paths forward are also among the responsibilities of political movements.




Yet the experiences and insights of the past do not give anyone the right to determine alone how the future should be shaped. The real challenge lies in finding ways to envision and shape the future together, without imposing historical experience on new generations against their will.




How well do political movements that seek to transform society truly understand society in transition? Perhaps the question we must first ask ourselves is even simpler: How attentively do we actually listen to the young people to whom we say the future belongs?




*Parcoursup: France’s national online platform through which final-year secondary school students and other prospective students submit applications to universities and other higher education programs.

title: Hatimoğulları: Alevis should play an active role in the peace process
content:
DEM Party Co-Chair Tülay Hatimoğulları called on the Alevi community to actively participate in the peace and democratization process in Turkey. At a meeting with representatives of Alevi organizations in Istanbul, she criticized the exclusion of Alevis from parliamentary deliberations and warned against leaving the future of the process solely in the hands of the government. Lasting peace, she argued, could only be achieved on the basis of equal citizenship, legally guaranteed fundamental freedoms, and the democratic restructuring of the republic.




The meeting took place at the Kazım Karabekir Cemevi in Istanbul’s Ümraniye district. Alongside representatives of Alevi associations and institutions, numerous other guests attended the event. Speaking here, Hatimoğulları emphasized that the process initiated by Abdullah Öcalan must not be understood as a power struggle between political camps. “We do not view peace in terms of one side winning and the other losing. Peace means building a shared life and giving one another our consent to do so. Genuine peace can only emerge when all 86 million citizens of this country can live in justice, freedom, and peace.”




Criticism of the exclusion of the Alevi community




The DEM Party co-chair recalled the decades of persecution, massacres, and assimilation policies targeting Alevis. Despite these experiences, she said, the Alevi community expanded its social and political organization in Turkey and Europe. Rather than allowing the history of injustices it suffered to paralyze it, the Alevi community drew strength from these experiences for its resistance and self-organization, she underlined. Hatimoğulları also addressed the massacres of Alevis in Syria by the Islamist forces of HTS, which have ruled the country since late 2024. She noted that international solidarity actions against this violence was warmly welcomed by the affected population.




Regarding the peace process, she particularly criticized the Turkish parliament speaker’s refusal to hear representatives of the Alevi community. “We have repeatedly asked the government why Alevis are not being heard. A faith community to which millions of people in this country belong cannot be ignored. Peace cannot be built without speaking to Alevis.” Remarking that the DEM Party has repeatedly insisted on their participation, she described Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmuş’s rejection of this demand as politically unacceptable.




Peace process amid state repression




Hatimoğulları spoke at length about the contradictions between the government’s official declarations of commitment to peace and its continued policies of repression. She pointed out that restrictions on freedom of expression, the persecution of opposition politicians, the imprisonment of critical voices, and the appointment of state trustees to opposition-run municipalities stood in the way of credible democratization. She also addressed questions that Alevi organizations had raised with the DEM Party: How can a peace process be advanced under conditions of severe state repression? Is there a risk that the AKP will exploit the process for its own electoral interests? And does participating in the talks mean politically aligning oneself with the government?




“These are all legitimate questions. As a party, we raise them with the same clarity as you do. The concerns and objections of the Alevi community must be taken seriously and discussed openly, Hatimoğulları stated. In this context, she also criticized the political instrumentalization of ongoing investigations and the unequal treatment of alleged financial crimes. “While opposition figures and smaller businesses are being targeted with considerable severity, the names of politically influential individuals allegedly implicated in the major investment fund scandal remain undisclosed.”




“If these were names from the opposition, wouldn’t they have published them on every front page long ago? But now they won’t even reveal the names. Why? Because the matter reaches into their own ranks. Despite the contradictions between the peace process and government policy, the democratic opposition must not abandon the struggle for a political solution.”




“We do not need religious brotherhood, but equal rights”




One of the DEM Party’s central demands is the legal guarantee of equal citizenship, Hatimoğulları said, rejecting a conception of social coexistence based on shared religious identity while ethnic, cultural, and religious differences continue to be politically subordinated. “Despite all these concerns and criticisms, we have no choice but to establish peace in this country. We do not need brotherhood based on the ummah, but solidarity based on equal citizenship. Religious brotherhood is not enough for us. We need equal rights, and this equality must be guaranteed by law.”




According to the DEM Party co-chair, Alevis must therefore not merely observe the process from the sidelines: “Their active participation is also necessary to prevent the government from determining its course and outcomes alone. If we manage to stand together at the heart of this process, take ownership of it, and move it forward, those who are carrying it forward will not be left alone. Peace will then no longer be left to the goodwill of this government.”




A democratic republic as a shared vision




Hatimoğulları reaffirmed that the demands of the Alevi community are an integral part of the DEM Party’s political program. These, she said, include recognition of religious and cultural diversity, a science-based education system free from state-imposed religious homogenization, and guaranteed access to education in one’s mother tongue. “Education policy, in particular, demonstrates how deeply state assimilation policies are embedded in social institutions,” she said, noting that the DEM Party opposes a homogenizing education system that excludes different identities, faiths, and languages from public life.




On the occasion of the 103rd anniversary of the founding of the Republic on October 29, Hatimoğulları emphasized the need for fundamental democratization of the political system. “The Republic must be the common home of all 86 million citizens. To achieve this, it must treat everyone equally and deny no one’s identity. What we need most urgently in Turkey today is the democratization of the Republic and the establishment of a democratic republic.”




Following her speech, the meeting with representatives of Alevi organizations continued closed to the press.

title: Iranian security bodies block medical leave for Kurdish political prisoner
content:
Iranian security bodies have blocked medical leave and access to adequate treatment for Fahim Ebadi, a Kurdish political prisoner in Orumiyeh Central Prison who suffers from diabetes, high blood pressure and high blood fat levels, the Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN) has reported.




Iranian forces arrested Ebadi, who is from Orumiyeh and is serving a 45-month sentence, in the city around two years ago.




After several weeks of interrogation at the Ministry of Intelligence’s detention facility, he was transferred to Orumiyeh Central Prison, where he has remained since.




After several months in detention, a branch of the Islamic Revolutionary Court of Orumiyeh sentenced him to 60 months in prison on charges of “membership of opposition groups” in connection with membership of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK).




His sentence was subsequently reduced to 45 months after he waived his right to appeal and requested a sentence reduction.
