UK/Europe team

























ODNR spokesperson Andy Chow told DeSmog and 

Rolling Stone

: “When administrators were meeting with representatives in Washington County, they were discussing matters related to injection wells located in Washington County. ODNR stands by the comments made by its administrators.”




Concerns over polluted drinking water cross political and social divides, perhaps nowhere more so than rural Washington County. As intensely salty wastewater pushed below ground resurfaces, residents and officials have injected the issue into the already bitterly divided Ohio governor’s race. Susan Vessels, a Republican official in Washington County, recently appeared alongside Democratic gubernatorial candidate Dr. Amy Acton because of Acton’s pledge to pause new wastewater wells in this densely drilled area. “We have a chance to prevent the worst from happening, and we need to act now,” Acton told DeSmog and 

Rolling Stone

.




“Drinking water is not political and it is my hope Ohioans will come together across party lines on this issue.”

Susan Vessels, Marietta City Council President




Ohio ranks in the 

top 10 nationally

 for both oil and gas production. Fracking can occur within 100 feet of a school or rural home, and operators have been able to tap the gas-rich Marcellus and Utica formations by drilling directly beneath water reservoirs and state parks. But in order to maintain that production, the industry has to offload the tidal wave of toxic wastewater — rich in salts, carcinogens, heavy metals, and radioactive elements — that surfaces in the weeks and years that follow drilling an oil or gas well.




That wastewater gets pumped into injection wells deep below ground, where impermeable geological layers are supposed to keep it from leaking into oil and gas wells or drinking water supplies. Washington County, whose 19 injection wells 

outnumber all of Pennsylvania

, has received complaints of this wastewater, or brine, 

flooding nearby oil and gas wells

, according to the New York Times.




Now, an hour and a half drive north, in the town of Coshocton, Ohio, records show evidence of a family’s drinking water polluted by high levels of the same types of salts found in fracking wastewater.




“This is different”




In early November 2021, Bill Burgan, an eastern Ohio water well driller, called ODNR to complain about water from a 360-foot well he had drilled in 2017 for the Fisher family in Coshocton, 

according to ODNR documents

. At the beginning of 2021, their water had become salty and corrosive. Not only did it leave a salty taste in the mouth, but it caused their hot water tanks to rust out prematurely. The couple had replaced two tanks in four years. Within weeks, the newest one became coated in an unidentifiable white precipitate.




“Sometimes we drill through pockets of salt,” said Burgan, president of American Drilling and Pump Service, in an interview with DeSmog and 

Rolling Stone

 this summer outside his Stone Creek, Ohio, shop. “But this is different, it’s fracking waste.”




Burgan told DeSmog and 

Rolling Stone

, and, separately, 

ODNR according to public records

, that he expressed concern that the Fishers’ drinking water well became impacted by an oil and gas wastewater injection well located less than two miles from the family’s home and operated by a Texas-based company called Buckeye Brine. The local community vigorously opposed Buckeye Brine’s installment of the injection well, where since 2014 the company has injected over 400 million gallons of waste.  




After receiving Burgan’s complaint, ODNR swiftly launched an investigation that agency geologist Tamara Richards said “will focus solely on contaminants associated with oil and natural gas exploration and production,” 

according to public records

. 










The state’s results indicate signatures of possible drinking water pollution from oil and gas wastewater, according to independent experts who reviewed the findings. 

Ohio’s final report on the incident

, completed in January 2022, found two separate indicators of potential fracking wastewater contamination — total dissolved solids, and chloride —  in the Fisher family’s water. Both tested at more than five times the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) limits. ODNR also tested for sodium, which lacks a formal EPA limit but has a threshold, as high levels can cause unpleasant taste and health problems for diabetics. In the Fishers’ water, sodium was 17 times the EPA threshold.




According to Jeffrey, the Marietta College geologist, high levels of total dissolved solids, chloride, and sodium also are found in the sea of fracking wastewater pumped into injection wells like the one operated by Buckeye Brine.




However, ODNR concluded there was “no evidence of an oilfield related impact” and pinned the cause of the contamination on a sandstone layer called the “Big Injun” that the agency, without providing any data, stated “appears to be” naturally salty and surrounded part of the family’s water well.




But Jeffrey said testing done by the state did not look at enough parameters to determine that the contamination was natural and not from fracking wastewater. “It seems ODNR is either stonewalling, misdirecting, or just doesn’t know what they are doing,” he told DeSmog and 

Rolling Stone

.




In a separate case that would unfold over a year after ODNR tested the Fishers’ water, the 

agency was considering whether leaking injection wells

 or else the “Big Injun” sandstone formation might be contaminating conventional oil and gas wells in Athens County, just west of Washington County. This time, ODNR concluded the impacts “cannot be plausibly explained” by the sandstone formation due to its unique brine signature, citing a “June 2, 2020 technical analysis prepared by ALL Consulting.” The agency added that impacts from this natural layer would have been consistent from the start, and “it is unlikely” they would have appeared only after the injection well operator began working. ODNR ultimately suspended the permit for a set of three injection wells that were eventually shut in for leaking fracking wastewater. ODNR has not yet replied to questions regarding this case.










When asked about the state’s findings in Coshocton and their scientific evidence, Burgan was dismissive. “They are covering it up,” he said, “because they are making too much money off of this.”




Oil and gas companies pay Ohio five cents a barrel to dispose of in-state wastewater, and 20 cents for wastewater imported from other states. Much of the waste injected comes from neighboring West Virginia and Pennsylvania. With at least a billion gallons of waste injected every year, that income translates to an average of $2.4 million annually for state coffers, 

according to state documents

.




“The ODNR Division of Oil and Gas Resources Management uses evidence and facts, testing, and the latest technologies to evaluate complaints of brine migration” and “stands by the results of its investigation,” said ODNR spokesperson Chow.




The entrance to Buckeye Brine’s injection well facility in Coshocton, Ohio. Credit: Justin Nobel/DeSmog




But ODNR did not investigate the Buckeye Brine injection well, subject of the original complaint, or any other injection wells. It did investigate “producing oil and gas wells within a one-half mile radius” of the family’s home.




After Burgan’s company reached out, we “contacted ODNR and ODNR was not interested in any further efforts on the matter,” said Susie Patterson, the manager at Buckeye Brine, by email. Patterson said groundwater monitoring wells installed in 2019 and sampled quarterly showed “no indication of contamination by oilfield substances,” or that “the water was not fit for consumption due to contaminants,” and pinned issues with the Fishers’ well on the water well driller. 




“The wells were drilled much deeper than surrounding wells producing good drinking water,” said Patterson. “It is Buckeye’s opinion that the driller was trying to justify to the well owner the bad wells.”




The Fishers declined to participate in the story. 




The Oil and Gas Industry’s Trillion-Gallon Problem




Across America, over 

one trillion gallons of oil and gas wastewater

 are generated every year — enough to fill a line of waste barrels to the moon and back 28 times. Nearly all of this waste — 96 percent — will be injected deep into the earth at disposal injection wells.




Given the oil and gas industry’s reliance on injection wells as a critical means of disposal for a dangerous waste stream, analysts have referred to injection wells as a linchpin to the sound operation of the entire oil and gas industry. Disposal of oil and gas wastewater is the industry’s “Achilles’ heel,” said Ted Auch, a researcher at the oil and gas industry watchdog Fieldnotes. A 2021 

Rice University Center for Energy Studies report

 stated that if the industry did not have injection wells to rely on for waste disposal, the “resulting economic impacts would be profound — and likely, existential.” 




The United States has more than 181,400 oil and gas wastewater injection wells, but as industry leaders testified at the Texas state capitol in August, lack of space to store this toxic brine already is threatening to 

curtain oil and gas production in Texas’

 productive Permian Basin. Even where it has been stored, increasing evidence shows the wastewater is not always staying put.




Injection has proven particularly problematic in Ohio, where state regulators have halted operations 

at over half a dozen injection wells

, citing concerns that fracking 

wastewater has leaked

 and has 

traveled up to five miles

 underground to contaminate conventional oil and gas wells. ODNR noted in 

a 2023 letter to DeepRock Disposal Solutions

, a southeast Ohio company 

formerly run by the chair of the state senate’s energy committee

, that such incidents pose a risk to public health and drinking water too.   




In Texas, 

wastewater shot down injection wells

 has burst back to the surface at old oil and gas wells, at times generating 

100-foot geysers of brine in the desert

, and Inside Climate News reported that 

oilfield waste has contaminated drinking water sources

 in the heart of West Texas oil country. Reporting by ProPublica revealed the situation is similar in neighboring Oklahoma, where 

regulators have clashed over

 how far to rein in the injection industry, despite state evidence showing 

drinking water sources polluted with contaminants

 consistent with oilfield waste. 










Independent scientists raise the question of whether other oil and gas states may be facing similar problems.




“We have always been concerned as environmental scientists and geologists in this area that there is no underground containment in these [injection] wells,” 

said Jen Bowman, a water chemistry expert and the director of environmental programs at Ohio University, in Athens. “What so many folks in this area don’t understand, our underground layers are just rock layers so there is no magic underground lake where you are getting water from, and there is no magic underground storage container where the waste is going.” Injecting millions of gallons of waste at high pressure means contamination miles from the site of injection is inevitable, she said.




“This is not a good plan or disposal mechanism for potentially dangerous materials,” Bowman told DeSmog and 

Rolling Stone

, “especially given that people rely on groundwater in so much of rural Ohio.”




The concern about drinking water in Washington County is exactly what motivates Susan Vessels, the Republican president of the Marietta City Council. She has led the council in writing a resolution, passed last October, urging Ohio state legislators to introduce legislation imposing a three-year moratorium on new wastewater injection wells in Washington County. More recently she has crossed the political aisle when Amy Acton, the former state health director, came to Marietta last month as part of her gubernatorial campaign. Acton supports Vessels’ proposed moratorium and is facing an 

ugly, expensive race against billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy

. 




Acton told DeSmog and 

Rolling Stone

 that the fight over injection wells and drinking water contamination comes down to ensuring a better future for Marietta and all of Ohio. 




“That is why I am committing to a three-year moratorium on wastewater injection wells in Washington County,” said Acton. “I’m fighting against the corruption in our Statehouse and the cost of that corruption that we pay for. We must act to protect our resources and our drinking water.” Ramaswamy’s campaign has not replied to questions. 




“Drinking water is not political,” said Vessels, “and it is my hope Ohioans will come together across party lines on this issue.”




In an op-ed, she 

took to task

 the GOP contender 

Ramaswamy

, who called people “whiners” for raising concerns about clean water, energy use, and other issues as proposals for AI data centers arrive in Ohio.




“I think they are full of shit, and that is point-blank my opinion.”

Phillip Johnson, Washington County water well driller




Washington County water well driller Phillip Johnson said he has drilled hundreds of private water wells in the region. He disagreed with the state’s conclusion that brine from the sandstone formation caused the Fisher family well’s contamination.




“I think they are full of shit, and that is point-blank my opinion,” he said.  




Johnson said that if the sandstone formation was the cause of the salt contamination in the Fishers’ drinking water, then the salty taste should have been there from the beginning, and not strengthened over time as the couple reported, according to ODNR documents.




“Just because you drill 1,000 wells and everything works fine, it just takes one well to not work right for there to be a problem,” said Johnson. “It is nature, if you pump something down under pressure, the path of least resistance is up.”




“I am all for drilling oil and gas,” he added, “but fresh natural water is the most essential natural resource there is, in this country, the state, anywhere in the world, and if you contaminate it, you essentially ruin everything.”




Dominic DiGiulio, a retired EPA scientist with a doctorate in geoscience and decades of experience investigating the movement of underground fluids, provided another assessment of the state’s conclusions in the Coshocton case.




“The ODNR’s logic for stating that the domestic well is partially screened in the Big Injun formation is flawed,” said DiGiulio, who also previously consulted for government agencies and NGOs. “ODNR does not provide compelling evidence.”




The post 

Ohio Denies Evidence of Fracking Waste in Drinking Water. Its Own Records Show Otherwise. 

 appeared first on 

DeSmog

.

author: CMI Argentina
title: “No vendan el Estatuto”: el gremio de prensa reclamó al Senado que trate en comisión los proyectos para proteger el periodismo
content:
Sindicatos de prensa de todo el país, representantes de las carreras de comunicación y organizaciones de la sociedad civil se movilizaron este jueves 29 al Congreso de la Nación para reclamar que traten los diversos proyectos legislativos para actualizar o prorrogar el Estatuto del Periodista Profesional (Ley 12.908), cuya derogación fue establecida por la regresiva Reforma Laboral del gobierno nacional de ultraderecha a partir del 1 de enero de 2027.







“Senadores, diputados: NO VENDAN EL ESTATUTO DEL PERIODISTA, la libertad de expresión y el derecho a la información”, pidieron dirigentes gremiales, periodistas y trabajadores y trabajadoras de prensa en la bandera que desplegaron en la puerta del Congreso Nacional. La acción de visibilización fue impulsada por el Sindicato de Prensa de Buenos Aires (SiPreBa) y la Federación Argentina de Trabajadores de Prensa (FATPREN).







Presentamos una solicitud formal a su presidenta, @carmenAlvarezR , y al resto de los legisladores para exigir que cumplan su compromiso y traten los proyectos de actualización y prórroga del Estatuto.




No vamos a permitir que el silencio parlamentario y los intereses de las empresas de medios destruyan nuestros derechos ante un contexto de ataques a la prensa y grave precarización laboral.




#SiPreBA2026




— SiPreBA – Sindicato de Prensa de Buenos Aires (@sipreba) 

October 30, 2026







En el marco de la protesta, se presentó una solicitud formal dirigida a la senadora Carmen Álvarez Rivero, presidenta de la Comisión de Trabajo y Previsión Social del Senado, y a los legisladores que la integran. El documento exige la inmediata convocatoria a reunión de comisión para evitar que la inacción parlamentaria decante en un vacío legal, que termine exponiendo al periodismo en una situación de vulnerabilidad mayor a las presiones políticas, económicas y judiciales.







La nota convoca a todos los miembros de la comisión a tratar los proyectos, pero puntualmente a los legisladores que se comprometieron a discutir una actualización de la Ley 12.908 en el marco de la prórroga, como los senadores Carolina Losada, Eduardo Vischi, Sonia Rojas Decut, José Carambia, Flavia Gabriela Royón y Carolina Moises, entre otros.




“Desde la sanción de la reforma laboral, la Comisión de Legislación del Trabajo del Senado no se volvió a reunir ni una sola vez. Las y los senadores que muchas veces hablan de la regulación laboral no están haciendo su laburo”, sostuvo Agustín Lecchi, secretario general de SiPreBA.




“En un contexto de gran ataque a la libertad de expresión, donde el Presidente de la Nación dice que nos quiere quemar en la hoguera, los empresarios de medios aprovechan la política laboral de este gobierno para derogar una ley que nos protege y resguarda la libertad de expresión”, agregó Lecchi.







 NI UN DÍA SIN ESTATUTO DEL PERIODISTA




Mariano Recalde @marianorecalde , senador de Unión por la Patria, realizó un pedido de preferencia para que se trate de manera urgente los proyectos para sostener la vigencia y actualización del Estatuto del Periodista Profesional. 




Exigimos a la senadora @carmenAlvarezR que sesione la Comisión de Trabajo y Previsión. Denunciamos que desde la Reforma Laboral no se juntó ni una sola vez, bloqueando cualquier tipo de debate democrático.




— SiPreBA – Sindicato de Prensa de Buenos Aires (@sipreba) 

October 30, 2026

author: Daron Letts
title: NuBrew stops canning, blames regulatory changes
content:
Nunavut Brewing Co., the sole local brewer in the territory, has stopped canning its beer after the territorial liquor commission made changes to the way it prices alcohol.




The markup applied by the Nunavut Liquor and Cannabis Commission to NuBrew beer used to be 76 per cent less than what’s applied to beer imported into the territory. As of June 1, that difference was reduced to 40 per cent less.




“The difference between our markup and the big brewers like Anheuser-Busch has shrunk,” said Jordan Kennedy, interim manager of Nunavut Brewing Co.




“T

hose big brewers do not provide anything to this territory.

 They don’t pay payroll taxes. They don’t pay property taxes. 

They don’t employ people. They don’t contribute to the local economy like we do.”




Kennedy said he first learned of the the cost increase when a customer complained about an approximately $120 price hike to a keg of the company’s beer purchased through Iqaluit’s beer and wine store in late July.




Kennedy said when contacted the commission at the end of the summer, the response was a suggestion the brewery reduce the alcohol content in its products.




That’s because one of the changes Nunavut Liquor and Cannabis Commission made to its price structure is it started scaling its prices according to a product’s alcohol content. 
















Previously these markups were applied on a per-litre basis. Now, a 355-millilitre can of beer at 3.5 per cent alcohol by volume, such as a Corona Light, carries a standard markup of $1.46. A six-per-cent beer of the same size carries a $2.50 markup.




Nunavut Brewing Co. Ltd.’s core brands include Floe Edge and Aupaqtuq Red Ale, which are five per cent alcohol content by volume, and Frob Gold Strong Ale at 6.8 per cent alcohol.




Kennedy added he was disappointed that the brewery was not consulted in spring or early summer, in advance of the sealift season.




“That’s when you need to figure out what you need to bring up,” he said. “Then all of a sudden we’re hit with these changes.”




Lewis MacKay, director of the Nunavut Liquor and Cannabis Commission, said such consultation is not standard regulatory practice.




“Our key message is that this is a harm reduction initiative,” MacKay said in an emailed statement. “This encourages Nunavummiut who choose to drink to choose products with lower alcohol content.”
















For now, these changes limit Nunavut Brewing Co.’s ability to raise prices to cover the cost of inflation, further cutting into the company’s profit margin. Which means the brewery is sticking to its standard beer recipes and its decision to cease canning operations, Kennedy said.




“If the government comes back to us with an option that is equal to what we’ve previously had we’d certainly consider opening up the canning line again,” he said.

author: Neesha Powell
title: North Carolina Movement Urges Voters to Reject Corporate Tax Breaks
content:
Organizers say the ballot amendments won’t benefit working-class people, but rather corporations and the ultra-wealthy.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The affordability crisis is hitting people hard across the country, but it’s especially acute in North Carolina. For the sixth year in a row, North Carolina holds the distinction of being the worst state in the nation for workers based on its wage policies, worker protections, and rights to organize, according to Oxfam. Nearly half of renters in the state are struggling to afford their homes, while nearly a third of households are cost-burdened (spending over 30 percent of their income on housing).

North Carolina voters’ eyes may light up when they see two proposed constitutional amendments on their November ballots: one to cap the state personal and corporate income tax rates at 3.5 percent, down from a cap of seven percent, and another to limit how much local governments can levy in property taxes. On their face, they appear as if they might bring much-needed tax relief to North Carolina’s working class.

The amendments are deceptively framed as being beneficial to working people and homeowners, reading as if they would lower individual taxes when there’s no indication that they will, according to Todd Warren, statewide campaign strategist at Down Home North Carolina, a member-led organization that endorsed a “no” vote. Instead, Warren said, the measures would be a giveaway to corporations and wealthy individuals by limiting how much they pay toward the public good — and a “scam” for voters.

Since the passage of the two Republican-sponsored bills that placed the amendments on the ballot this past May, Down Home NC and over 20 other groups have come together as the NC Vote Against coalition to defeat them, as well as to oppose a third amendment that would enshrine voter identification requirements in the state constitution.

Each organization has its own expertise and its own tactics, but a common message: The amendments will not benefit working-class people, but rather corporations and the ultra-wealthy. Each group is playing its part in collecting a total of 100,000 pledges from North Carolinians who commit to voting against the amendments.

Down Home NC joined together with another coalition member, the Carolina Federation, to launch the Fund the Future campaign, deploying nearly 200 paid canvassers.

Jenn Frye, co–director of the Carolina Federation, spent part of this weekend canvassing at the poll at a Durham, North Carolina library, where she convinced an older couple to vote “no” on the amendments. After a member-led endorsement process that included political education on the amendments, a leadership summit and a vote at a statewide membership meeting, the Carolina Federation decided they wanted to deeply engage in the amendment fight. “We see more and more people in North Carolina who agree that corporations and the wealthiest individuals aren’t contributing what they owe when day in and day out, North Carolinians are working really hard,” Frye said. “We pay our taxes, and we contribute what we owe.”

Down Home NC and the Carolina Federation were founded in 2017 and 2018, respectively, in the wake of President Trump first taking office and Republicans winning control of both North Carolina’s state legislature and governorship in 2013 (for the first time since Reconstruction). The groups share a long-term goal of loosening corporate power’s grip on the state legislature and supplanting it with people power.

The Fund the Future campaign campaign is knocking doors, talking to voters at the polls, getting resolutions against the amendments passed by local governments and school boards, and placing signs in small businesses and in yards, among other tactics. So far, the Carolina Federation’s canvassers have knocked on over 600,000 doors across six counties, collecting over 33,000 pledges, while Down Home NC’s canvassers had knocked 500,000 doors across 20 counties and collected about 8,000 pledges.

“Whatever the outcome of this amendment fight, Federation’s members plan to launch a statewide campaign next year with other organizations like Down Home and Siembra to demand that the legislature pass fair tax policies that make corporations and the wealthiest individuals pay what they owe our communities in taxes,” Frye said. “That may be a multi-year fight. It is one our members feel is worth waging.”

North Carolinians deserve funding for real solutions, Frye said, such as property tax assistance programs, childcare tax credits, an increased minimum wage (it’s currently the federal minimum, $7.25 per hour), and protections against corporate landlords.

Todd Warren of Down Home NC said he has never seen such a robust response to a single issue in over 20 years of working and organizing in North Carolina.

Because Down Home NC’s chapters run organizing campaigns to make sure that local budgets go toward working people’s needs, members recognized immediately how the amendments would exacerbate the underfunding of local services. Like the Carolina Federation, its members endorsed a “no” vote in addition to endorsing political candidates who are supportive of its platforms.

Many voters don’t know about the amendments, Frye said, and if they do, they’re often not sure what to make of them or inclined to support them because they’re exhausted and stressed out due to the affordability crisis. But when they are engaged in conversation about how the amendments affect services they rely on, “then people are movable,” she said.

Frye gave the example of her own mother, who recently suffered a series of strokes. Fortunately she was living in a North Carolina county with adequately funded Emergency Medical Services, or EMS. But residents of counties with underfunded EMS operations could face a life-or-death situation during medical emergencies.

“Right now, people feel like ‘taxes’ is a dirty word,” said Warren, a former public school teacher. “But if they connect it to something that they care about, like, ‘Oh, in Johnston County, we have explosive population growth. We need to build a new high school. These amendments would limit our ability to [do that].’ Then they’re like, ‘I’m gonna vote “no” on it.’ We can do that in a five-minute organizing conversation. It doesn’t take much for people to see through the scam.”

North Carolina has lost out on almost $18 billion in annual tax revenue since Republicans began overhauling the tax system in 2013. Personal income tax reforms are so regressive that the state’s lowest earners pay more than 10 percent of their income in state and local taxes, while the highest earners pay only six percent. For corporations, the income tax has dropped from seven percent to two percent, the lowest in the nation, and will be phased out completely by 2030. As tax revenue shrinks, so does local governments’ ability to fully fund vital public services.

“Our public services, the things that are supposed to strengthen our communities and support all families in all counties in North Carolina, are being stretched to the limit by the tax cuts,” Frye said. “These amendments want to take that and enshrine it into the [state] constitution.”

Exploitation has marked North Carolina’s economy since the days of chattel slavery. Post-slavery, Black families like my own (in Bertie County) sharecropped for a living well into the 20th century — jobs now carried out by migrant workers who experience poor labor conditions. The Duke family once had a monopoly on the state’s tobacco industry and founded both Duke Energy and Duke University, two institutions notorious for not paying their fair share.

Now the state and some local governments are subsidizing data centers, of which over 60 have been built and at least 30 more are planned or under construction. Under pressure, the state eliminated some tax breaks for data centers in July, but three remaining sales tax subsidies are projected to rob the state of $250 million in revenue annually. Meanwhile, between 2017 to 2024, the average electricity bill of a North Carolina household rose by nearly 30 percent. The state is subsidizing wealthy corporations as regular folks struggle to keep their lights on.

On May Day this year, thousands gathered in the capital city, Raleigh, to rally for fully funded schools. Tax cuts have already contributed to the state being ranked last in the country in public school funding by GDP.

Isabell Moore, a coordinator at North Carolina Families for Public Schools (a project of Down Home NC) and a public school parent, said the amendments could be “catastrophic” for public education. North Carolina Families for Public Schools comprises countywide, districtwide and schoolwide teams of volunteer organizers who are calling for equitable, fully funded public schools. These teams are currently circulating a pledge to fund the future for children that includes voting against the amendments, along with measures like fair funding for special education; higher teacher pay; and safe, inclusive schools for all students, including those from immigrant families.

North Carolina Families for Public Schools had already voted on its 2026 platform when the amendments dropped in May but decided to incorporate them because they stand directly in the way of their goal to win fully funded schools. Their organizers have been tapping into their personal networks to turn people out to vote against the amendments, holding house parties and school-based parties to educate people on the amendments, and more.

“Everyday working people and public school parents are creative and tough and scrappy,” Moore said. “If we commit to not just voting ‘no’ but also organizing other people in our networks and in our school communities, that’s when we really start to build the power to defeat the amendments.”

Even public schools in wealthy counties like Durham, home to Duke University (which has a $14.3 billion endowment) and Duke University Health System (which made nearly $766 million in profits last year), are chronically underfunded. The riches of these two tax-exempt nonprofit institutions haven’t trickled down. Among other demands, the Durham Rising coalition—made up of workers, students, and community members—is calling for Duke University to help fund public schools and educator salaries by making a voluntary payment to the local government called a PILOT, or payment in lieu of taxes.

Since the summer, Christy Patterson, vice president of the Durham chapter of the North Carolina Association of Educators, or NCAE, and a middle school teacher for students with disabilities, has been knocking on doors to tell folks the amendments are for billionaires, not everyday people. The NCAE, which functions as a professional organization because North Carolina bans public-sector collective bargaining, is part of the NC Vote Against coalition and was one of the main architects of the “Kids Over Corporations” rally in May.

“Our voters and our community are engaging us in conversation on the doors,” Patterson said. “We’ve had some conversations that really made us think. Constructive friction on the doors is always good because everybody’s not going to say the same thing or think the same. They’re just so ready to open the door and talk to us, so we are grateful for that.”

In a September poll by Elon University, 67 percent of respondents were in favor of the income tax amendment, and 72 percent supported the property tax amendment. Organizers are working hard to turn that tide.

However, even if they don’t get their desired outcome, there is an entire movement that will continue holding North Carolina corporations and wealthy households accountable until they contribute their fair share to the public good. Organizations like the Carolina Federation, Down Home NC, and the NCAE have been engaging in this work for years and are in it for the long haul.

Warren hopes the Fund the Future campaign can help shift the narrative so that people understand that “taxes” aren’t inherently bad but rather a tool for improving quality of life for themselves, their families, and their communities.

“Through years of listening and campaigning, we know what working people across North Carolina want,” Warren said: well-funded, well-staffed public schools, healthcare access, transportation options and recreation programs for kids, infrastructure for effective disaster response. “When we talk to people about those things, even when they understand that it may involve an increase in taxes for them personally, they support funding those types of programs.”

As Trump cracks down on political speech, independent media is increasingly necessary.

Truthout produces reporting you won’t see in the mainstream: journalism from the frontlines of global conflict, interviews with grassroots movement leaders, high-quality legal analysis and more.
