title: Bir ayda ikinci emekli polis intiharı: Ekonomik koşullar karşısında hayatlar sönüyor
content:
Zonguldak'ta 2023 yılında emekliye ayrılan 51 yaşındaki polis memuru Baskın Pekmen, 21 Ekim'de babasının mezarı başında ölü bulundu. Üç çocuk babası Pekmen'in, yaşamını yitirmeden önce evinden ayrılırken bir not bıraktığı, borçlarının bulunduğu ve ailesine "Size iyi bakamadım" yazılı bir mektup yazdığı öğrenildi.

Sözcü'den Cengiz Karagöz'ün haberine göre, Yeni Parti Zonguldak Milletvekili Deniz Yavuzyılmaz, Baskın Pekmen'in ölümüne ilişkin yaptığı açıklamada, emeklilerin yaşadığı ekonomik sorunlara dikkat çekti. Yavuzyılmaz, "Emeklileri yoksulluğa, aileleri çaresizliğe mahkum eden ekonomik koşullar karşısında hayatlar sönmeye devam ediyor. Çok üzgünüm" dedi.

Birleşik Emekliler Sendikası da yaptığı açıklamada, emeklilerin yaşadığı geçim sıkıntısına tepki gösterdi. İktidarın seçim dönemlerinde emeklilere yönelik sınırlı düzenlemelerle oy desteği sağlamaya çalıştığı ifade edilen açıklamada, "Ama biz emekliler yapılanı unutmayacağız, sandıkta hesabını soracağız. Bizler oy deposu değiliz" denildi.

Emekli dernekleri ve sendikaların zam talebiyle Ankara'da AYM önünde yaptığı eylem sırasında "Geçinemiyorum" diyerek kendisini vuran emekli polis Ali Şekeroğlu hayatını kaybetmişti.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: Cyberlibel complaints vs journalists strengthen calls to decriminalize libel
content:
The criminal sanction for Philippine libel laws is “excessive” and is in violation of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) to which the Philippines is a signatory.

Libel complaints were recently filed against journalists and media company executives. For a journalists’ group, these validate the previous calls to decriminalize libel.

The GMA chapter of the National Union of Journalists of the Philippines (NUJP) stressed that libel laws silence journalism. “[C]riminalizing speech only undermines the public’s fundamental right to know,” the chapter said in a statement.

Davao City 1st District Rep. Paolo Duterte filed libel and cyberlibel complaints against GMA executives and broadcast journalists which stemmed from the network’s report about alleged cash deliveries to the Dutertes claimed by dismissed police officer Rodulfo Gracioso Jr.

Duterte filed the complaint before the Davao City Prosecutor’s Office on October 23, more than two weeks after his sister, Vice President Sara Duterte, made a joke about filing a multimillion-peso libel case against GMA Network. Her remarks happened during a press conference on October 6 while reading her affidavit which answers Gracioso’s claims.

Among the respondents were GMA executives Felipe Gozon and Gilberto Duavit, as well as journalists Mel Tiangco, Vicki Morales, Emil Sumangil, Darlene Cay, Marvin Parado, Joel San Luis, and other unidentified individuals.

In a statement released on October 23, the TV network said that they have not yet received the complaints.

Gracioso and National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) director Melvin Matibag were also named as respondents.

Meanwhile, veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr. was arrested on October 24 over a cyberlibel complaint reportedly filed by Mans Carpio, Sara’s husband. He was unaware of the complaint, according to his legal counsel. He was released on bail on the same day.

NUJP has been campaigning for the decriminalization of libel, echoing the views of the United Nations (UN) Human Rights Committee that the criminal sanction for Philippine libel laws is “excessive” and is in violation of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) to which the Philippines is a signatory.

Right(s) Up: Why journalists and advocates push for decriminalization of libel

On September 18, NUJP released its policy review on libel laws, stating that the high court has already identified the problem of these laws but reform requires legislation. The review, to name a few, cited Justice Marvic Leonen’s opinion in Disini, Jr. v. Secretary of Justice which stated that libel was unconstitutional as penal sanctions impose “an invidious chilling effect.”

It added that removing jail time alone, as proposed by some legislators, is not decriminalization because of limitations of a fine-only regime, saying that if the accused cannot pay, subsidiary imprisonment may follow.

The review cited the data obtained from the Office of Cybercrime of the Department of Justice (DOJ), indicating that 3,770 cyberlibel cases had been filed, as of May 2022, since the enactment of the Cybercrime Prevention Act. More than 2,500 cases remained pending in courts and before the prosecution level. There were already 12 convictions.

In the 2023 study by NUJP, 61.5% of the libel cases against 50 journalists from 2021 to 2023 were filed by politicians.

ML Party-list Rep. Leila de Lima said that filing a libel suit against journalists and media workers for doing their job sends a “chilling message” to other members of the press. Parties being accused can just respond to the allegations, she wrote in a Facebook post.

Under the Journalist’s Code of Ethics approved by media groups, journalists shall recognize the duty to air the other side and the duty to correct substantive errors promptly.

“Contrary to allegations of malice or unverified reporting, the report went through standard, multi-layered editorial and legal verification procedures,” the NUJP GMA Chapter said. “The team conducted due diligence—verifying information through official sources, law enforcement documents, and background checks—and obtained proper clearance from network leadership and legal counsel before airing the story.”

In the subject report, the reporter, Cay, and anchor Tiangco mentioned that they were trying to get the comments of the people implicated by Gracioso, including the Dutertes, but they did not receive a response when the report was aired last month.

Prior to the complaints filed against GMA executives and news personalities and Lustre, NUJP documented 16 incidents involving filing libel and cyberlibel against the media under the Marcos Jr. administration. (DAA)

author: Shannia Cabuello
title: Proposed foreign-funded wind projects threaten Bicol fishers
content:
Photo frrom Province of Camarines Sur

“If they say this project is for development, development for whom? This is not for us fisherfolk.”

Norberto Tobias of Tanggol San Miguel Bay (SMB) Network stressed this point as he and other fisherfolk from Bicol expressed opposition to the planned 1,000-megawatt San Miguel Bay Offshore Wind Farm.

They joined the Kampuhang Magbubukid (peasant camp) in front of the Department of Agrarian Reform from October 15 to 20.

The proposed wind farm covers 23,307 hectares of coastal waters across municipalities in Camarines Sur and Camarines Norte, including the fishing communities in Calabanga, Cabusao, Tinambac, Siruma, Sipocot, Basud, and Mercedes. This affects at least 6,000 small-scale fisherfolk.

Tobias said in a statement that the planned wind project is only for the profit of foreign companies and its local partner.

The project reportedly started its pre-development phase in 2023 but the fisherfolk communities countered that they only learned about it in 2025.

It is just one of the three Offshore Wind Projects of the Copenhagen Infrastructure New Market Fund Corp. (CINMF), the first 100% foreign-owned company to be granted a wind energy service contract (WESC) by the Department of Energy (DOE). It acquired exclusive rights to explore and develop SMB for wind energy in electricity generation.

The wind farm was developed under the partnership of CINMF-affiliated and Denmark-based Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) and local tycoon Ayala group’s ACEN Corp which has a 25% stake.

In 2024, the project was also granted Green Lane status by Philippine Board of Investments (BOI), a Certificate of Energy Project of National Significance (CEPNS), and pre-development Environmental Compliance Certificate (ECC) which expedited the project’s necessary licenses and permits processes.

The Kilusang Magbubukid ng Pilipinas (KMP) described the Marcos Jr. administrations’ promotion of large-scale renewable energy investments as aggressive, citing its insufficient protection for coastal resources-dependent communities.

The group condemned how the government opened the renewable energy sector in 2022 to 100% foreign ownership, streamlining approvals for strategic investments.

Since August 2024, a total of 91 offshore wind contracts nationwide has been approved by the Department of Energy.

Along the same coastline, six other planned offshore wind projects also raised concerns on combined impacts on marine resources and fisherfolk way of living.

Calabanga fisherfolk leader Norberto Harukhok said in an interview with Climate Change Network for Community-based Initiatives (CCNCI) that fisherfolk in coastal areas are united to stop the power plant from pushing through as they do not want the future generation to suffer.

“We don’t have a problem if they put it there as long as they follow our request to build it 15 kilometers away. Not by the shore,” Harukhok said.

“This is where we catch fish, earn a living, and get food for our families. If they prohibit us from fishing, where would we go?” Tobias asked, stressing that they may suffer from fishing access restrictions, marine habitat damage, and declining catches.

The CCNCI interview also highlighted that effects on ecosystems may result from the project’s regular operations. Coastal families may also face much lower incomes and worsen hunger.

“Once it is placed there, the fishes would not come closer because of the loud vibrations. Muds would go on the shore. Once they dug it up, the fishes would die from toxicity,” Harukhok said, adding that small-scale fishers with no motorized boats would struggle more as it would be difficult to go far to fish.

Harukhok said that only the government and capitalists would benefit from the project, leaving the fisherfolk without any benefits.

“So-called solutions to the climate crisis must not create another crisis for fishing communities already struggling with poverty, rising costs and impacts of climate change,” KMP Secretary-General Ronnie Manalo said in a statement. (DAA)

author: Lance Selfa
title: What to expect in the US midterm elections
content:
The Republican Party, also known as the GOP or Grand Old Party, controls both chambers of the US Congress, allowing President Donald Trump to pursue his far-right agenda with little legislative resistance. But that may soon change.

In the United States, federal elections occur every two years. The congressional midterms, so named because they occur in the middle of a president’s term, will be held on Tuesday. Polling suggests Republicans will be trounced. Voters will elect all 435 members of the House of Representatives, who serve fixed two-year terms, and about one-third of the 100 Senators, who serve six-year terms. A range of state-level races, including for governors in California, Michigan and Florida, will also take place.

The Democratic Party is expected to win back control of the House and possibly even the Senate. But just how much difference will that make? 

Lance Selfa

, author of 

The Democrats: A Critical History

 and editor of 

US Politics in an Age of Uncertainty

, previews the elections and what might come after them.

Multiple indicators point to a Democratic victory in the midterm elections. Trump is an historically unpopular president. Gasoline and diesel prices are at their highest in years because of Trump’s war in Iran. 

Consumer confidence is at a 73-year low

, and 

74 percent of Americans

 tell pollsters that the country is moving in the wrong direction.

So it’s no surprise that Democrats are favoured to win the House. In fact, Republicans have given up trying to forestall that. 

Data-driven forecasters like G. Elliott Morris

 and Nate Silver place the probability of a Democratic House higher than 90 percent, and the probability of the Democrats winning the Senate at 70 percent or higher.

The well-regarded 

New York Times

 poll

, published 21 October, estimated that, were the election held then, Democrats would receive 52 percent of the vote, compared to 41 percent for the Republicans. If that holds, it will be the biggest Democrat popular-vote margin in a midterm election since the Watergate scandal brought down the Republicans in 1974.

That result wouldn’t represent an endorsement for the Democratic Party, which remains as unpopular as the Republicans. But US midterm elections are classically “throw the bums out” elections. And the Republicans, who control all parts of the national government, are the bums this year.

Trump and his toadies declare the polls “fake” and promise a Republican victory. But their behaviour—Trump, Vice President Vance and other administration figures are campaigning almost exclusively in “red” conservative areas—suggests they know they are in deep trouble. Polls currently show that the Senate race in Kansas, where Democrats haven’t won since 1932, is a toss-up. And Democrat James Talarico is slightly favoured to win a Senate seat in Texas, where a Democrat hasn’t won statewide since the 1990s.

The last-minute campaign blitz and the truly obscene amount of money billionaires are spending to shore up Republican candidates may limit GOP losses. It seems clear, however, that the Democrats are headed for victory next week. The real question will be how high the Democratic wave will crest.

What will Trump do?

All the above assumes that 3 November will unfold as a “normal” midterm election. But Trump and his minions are talking openly about challenging or overturning the results. Given Trump’s attempts to overturn the 2020 presidential election, nothing is “off the table”.

Trump, his captive Supreme Court, and Republicans at all levels of government have conducted a years-long campaign to disenfranchise sections of the population and undermine democracy. This includes the Supreme Court’s evisceration of the Voting Rights Act, gerrymandering to lock in GOP majorities, and Trump’s so-far failed attempt to use the US Postal Service to make mail-in voting more difficult.

Trump and his Justice Department have continued to act on the lie that non-US citizens are voting illegally. The DOJ has tried to force state governments, constitutionally responsible for running US elections, to hand over their voter rolls. With voting data in hand, the Trump government says it can purge non-citizens from the rolls. So far, no state has complied, and the courts have ruled against Trump and the DOJ.

However, the DOJ has persisted. In late October, it indicted 28 individuals in California whom it claims voted illegally. Moreover, it sent lists of supposed non-citizen voters to each California county, threatening each with legal action if they didn’t set those voters’ ballots aside. The Trump DOJ has even filed a pre-emptive suit against Alaska—before a single vote is tallied—because it allowed two Republican candidates with the same name to appear on the ballot.

Trump has also increased the harassment of Democratic politicians, such as Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar and Virginia state Senator Louise Lucas, accusing them of crimes.

These tactics are meant to intimidate opponents of Trump, while threatening legal sanctions against thousands of election officials and government workers who are charged with making US elections free and fair. It’s also worth watching what sort of chicanery—from closing polling stations to dropping thousands from the voting rolls— Republican-controlled states will deploy to limit the vote.

There are other more far-fetched tactics Trump and his minions contemplate. They might declare that foreign governments are intervening in the election—which would require the federal government to seize state voting machines. They might deploy ICE thugs, police or the military to polling places to harass and intimidate minority voters who disproportionately vote for Democrats. MAGA hardliners are even calling on Trump to implement “martial law”.

Even though these moves are far-fetched, the 6 January 2021 storming of the Capitol should tell us that they are not beyond a desperate Trump or his lackeys like Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Still, to work, they depend on a disciplined and willing chain of command that doesn’t appear to exist currently. Remember, this is the same crew whose failure to make the most basic war preparations allowed Iran to knock out most US military bases in the Middle East.

Whether all of this will work to preserve Trump’s and the Republicans’ hold on the state is unknown, especially if the Democratic victory is as overwhelming as many expect. The Democratic Party is mobilising hundreds of lawyers and thousands of poll watchers to counter them. But if some of these dirty tricks succeed while Trump and the GOP are overwhelmingly unpopular, socialists should be prepared for street mobilisations. Democrats may want to fight it out in the courts, but the balance of social forces will matter more. And this is where Trump’s historic unpopularity has a material impact on events.

Follow the money

The 2026 midterm election is on track to be the most expensive of all time, with billions being spent on both sides. Open Secrets, a non-partisan monitor of campaign spending, noted that “outside groups”, i.e., groups not officially connected to candidates, had 

spent more than $2 billion by early October

. These spending levels would have been considered excessive for a presidential race only about a decade ago.

But as campaign spending—mostly 24/7 television and online advertising—spirals upward, the leverage a small number of billionaires gain over the political system increases as well. By some estimates, Elon Musk alone could spend as much as half a billion dollars to support Republicans. This is more than Trump’s campaign committee spent in 2024. But for Musk and his ilk, this is pocket change.

And even accepting that these are truly obscene amounts of money that amount to legalised bribery of politicians who set the legal framework for capitalist profit-making, they are a small price to pay for the capitalist class and its richest members. We are amid an unprecedented investment boom (

estimated at $10 trillion between 2025 and 2032

) to remake the US economy under the aegis of artificial intelligence “hyperscalers”. A few billion to shape the legislative and regulatory environment is a trivial expense in comparison.

While the liberal anti-Trump opposition has focused on the spending of right-wing billionaires like Musk or the Uihleins of Illinois, we can’t ignore that the candidates raking in the most money in this midterm cycle are almost exclusively Democrats! As 

Open Secrets’ analysis of early October reports to the Federal Election Commission pointed out

:

“Democrats dominate the top fundraising rankings in both [the House and Senate]. They hold the top nine spots among Senate candidates and nine of the top 11 among House candidates.”

The leading Senate candidates, Texas challenger Talarico and incumbent Georgia Democrat Jon Ossoff, hold huge advantages over their Republican opponents. And the leading House fundraiser, with the most cash on hand, is 

none other than “democratic socialist” Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez

! Many Democrats may say that they (mostly) reject corporate political action committee (PAC) money and depend on “individual contributions” from ordinary people. But it’s clear from Federal Election Commission data that most individual donors to Democrats are well-off people associated with the tech, higher education and health sectors.

And if you look at 

Representative Hakeem Jeffries,

 who is set to become Speaker of the House and third in line to the presidency, you will find that he doesn’t turn down corporate PAC money. About 85 percent of his funding comes from business interests. Moreover, corporations launder their contributions through “super PACs”, providing another source of support for candidates.

Democrats may be spineless and feckless, ineffective in delivering for their liberal base when they gain official state power. But the main reason goes beyond character and is better explained by 

Upton Sinclair’s admittedly gendered quip

: “It is difficult to get a man to understand something, when his salary depends upon his not understanding it!”

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC), the organisation charged with recruiting and funding Democratic congressional candidates, draws more than 60 percent of its war chest from corporate PACs and rich individuals who can afford $50,000 contributions, 

writes socialist Kim Moody

. Given that, is it any surprise why the vast majority of congressional Democrats are pro-corporate “centrists”?

Two of the most active sectors in political donations—cryptocurrency and AI/tech—have leaned toward Trump and the GOP since Trump retook the White House. But they remain “bipartisan” in their 

approach to winning support in the legislature

 and among state-level politicians. In fact, one leading AI Super PAC runs two divisions: one that 

donates to Republicans and one that donates to Democrats.

The northern Virginia suburbs of Washington, DC, are becoming as reliable a Democratic Party stronghold as New York or the San Francisco Bay Area. But the area also has the largest concentration of AI data centres in the US, 

and the region’s Democratic congressmembers receive

 hundreds of thousands in AI industry donations.

Despite huge bipartisan popular opposition to Big Tech and data centre exploitation of land, tax breaks, power and water around the country, don’t be surprised if a Democratic Congress and the Republican White House figure out a way to pass “reforms” on AI and crypto that will leave ordinary people wondering why they voted for “change” in 2026.

Will it stop the slide to authoritarianism?

In the event of a Democratic sweep, people who despise Trump and MAGA will alternate between celebrating and feeling relieved. But, just as in 2020, they shouldn’t assume that the threat of US authoritarianism is vanquished. This will be so for both specific, “conjunctural”, reasons, and for more general aspects related to our political era.

The first conjunctural reason is the most obvious. Trump will still have the White House and the administrative machinery of the federal government at his disposal even if the Democrats take the Congress. Trump is likely to increase his lawless and authoritarian behaviour while daring the Democrats and the courts to stop him. Even moderate legislation to limit Trump’s tariffs or to restore cuts to federal health care programs will face Trump vetoes.

The second conjunctural reason to keep up the fight is that Democrats may be the GOP’s only alternative on most ballots, 

but they are not an opposition party

. The Democratic Party is a corporate-backed entity dedicated to supporting American capitalism and US empire.

Democrats are campaigning on vague promises to bring “affordability” to ordinary Americans and “accountability” to the criminals in the Trump administration. If they do take one or both houses of Congress, they will become locked in a cage match with an administration that will not recognise Democrats’ authority.

On the “accountability” front, Democrats are already lowering expectations. Jeffries and even leading progressives are saying they want to avoid a 

“performative” impeachment

 of Trump. So, despite condemning the president’s corruption and lawlessness, they are already signalling they don’t want to use congressional power to hold him accountable. On affordability, they are promising legislation 

to reverse some Trump policies

 (back to the Biden 

status quo

), but they are also pursuing the fool’s errand of winning Republican support for them—in a Congress where Republican minorities will be hard-core MAGA zealots. This is a recipe for failure.

The third conjunctural reason is that a Democratic majority in Congress won’t change the fact that a small handful of billionaires exercise more power over policy and ordinary people’s lives than any “democracy” should tolerate. As author Hamilton Nolan told 

New Republic

 journalist Perry Bacon:

“[W]hen money buys influence, and you have these obscene, enormous, nation-level fortunes in private hands, it just at a certain point crowds out the ability of everybody else to influence politics in a way that you have any kind of balance of power.”

The American oligarchy may be in Trump’s circle now, but it can easily move its money and power to influence Democrats as well. Especially when they have willing Democrats like Jeffries or California Governor Gavin Newsom to attend to them. Newsom, a presidential hopeful for 2028, is opposing a referendum for a one-time tax on billionaire wealth to fund state health care programs. That’s how the “affordability agenda” crashes on the shoals of American oligarchy—or is watered down so much that no one even notices it.

The question of oligarchy leads into the general character of the “era” of politics that Trump has come to define in the US. A generation of neoliberal hollowing out of good jobs and government services in the service of oligarchy has 

left the share of wealth going to labour at its lowest level since the 1940s

.

This reality has undermined the legitimacy of the “centre-left” and “centre-right” parties that had dominated the politics of liberal democracies since the Second World War. The far right has surged into political spaces the old parties vacated, while labour and social movements have been weakened.

Lula's come-from-behind victory in Brazil’s presidential election and the landslide defeat of MAGA-friendly Vŭkic in Serbia show that far-right victory isn’t inevitable. But if fighting authoritarianism relies only on electoralism and leaves it to mainstream political parties, we are only one election away from the authoritarian consolidation Trump has so far been unable to accomplish.

So those who will welcome the GOP’s defeat next week shouldn’t look to manoeuvring in Washington. They should draw inspiration from 

mass movements

—like those in India, France, the Spanish state and Serbia, to name a few—for a strategy to put the right on the defensive.

author: Publicación Abierta
title: La impunidad de Machado
content:
Diez meses fuera y vuelve en caravana




El 25 de octubre, María Corina Machado regresó a Venezuela. Recorrió el país, de Barquisimeto a Caracas, entre banderas y vítores, como quien vuelve de unas vacaciones. Y, sin embargo, desde el propio Gobierno venezolano se la había calificado de prófuga de la justicia y se había advertido de que «tendrá que rendir cuentas» si pisaba el país. No ha rendido ninguna. Se pasea libremente, aclamada y sin que nadie le pida explicaciones.




El historial de la que vuelve




Conviene recordar quién es. La que llamó a las guarimbas. La que incitó a la violencia y al enfrentamiento entre venezolanos. La que pidió, una y otra vez, la intervención militar de los Estados Unidos de Trump y del Israel de Netanyahu contra su propio país. La que reclamó sanciones contra su pueblo y apoyó el sabotaje para rendir a Venezuela por hambre, sin medicinas, sin comida, sin lo más básico para la vida. Una venepatria de manual, que nunca dudó en poner su tierra en bandeja a las potencias extranjeras.




Su amo la despacha con un «muy agradable»




Y mírese cómo recibe su amo el regreso de su sierva. Preguntado por los periodistas, Trump respondió: «Es una mujer muy agradable. Me dio su Premio Nobel, así que ¿cómo puedo decir otra cosa? Y espero que esté a salvo». Ni una palabra más. Enseguida, a lo suyo: a Estados Unidos, dijo, le va «realmente bien en Venezuela». Ese es todo el pago por años de servicio y por regalarle hasta el Nobel. El 3 de enero, el día de la captura de Maduro, ya la había descartado para dirigir el país con la misma fórmula: muy agradable, pero sin el respeto necesario. Así pagan los imperios a quienes les sirven: los usan mientras son útiles y les dan una palmadita cuando estorban.




Una justicia para cada clase




Que nadie se engañe: esta impunidad no es un accidente; es justicia de clase. A quien se juega el sueldo defendiendo a sus compañeros en un centro de trabajo le piden cuentas por mucho menos. A quien trabajó para que el sufrimiento llegase a miles de familias venezolanas la recibe una multitud, con las cámaras de medio mundo apuntando hacia ella. Hay una vara de medir para el pueblo trabajador y otra muy distinta para quienes sirven a los poderosos.




No hay redención para quien traiciona a su pueblo




No hay perdón para quien ayudó a traer tanto dolor a Venezuela. Nunca pensé que llegaría a ver cómo quienes empujaron a la guerra, a la necesidad y a la muerte caminan tranquilos por la calle, sin pagar por sus actos. Con el Nobel de la Paz colgado, además: un premio concedido a quien se ha pasado la vida pidiendo la invasión de su propio país, convertido así en el Nobel de la vergüenza. Pero esa vergüenza palidece ante lo que hoy vemos en Venezuela. El pueblo venezolano sabe quién le hizo daño, y la historia no suele ser tan indulgente como un presidente con quien le hace un regalo.




¡Até á vitoria sempre!




André Abeledo Fernández







La entrada 

La impunidad de Machado

 se publicó primero en 

Indymedia Argentina Centro de Medios Independientes (( i ))

.

author: Jeff Rickertt
title: Phil Monsour’s ‘Time of Monsters’ is a call to action against Israel’s genocide
content:
Time of Monsters Phil Monsour October 2026 Pre-order the album and lyric book at: pozible.com/profile/phil-monsour. Listen now on Bandcamp.

In the mythical Anglo-Saxon poem Beowulf, an entire population is subjugated by a bloodthirsty and seemingly invincible monster, Grendel. He “ruled in defiance of right, one against all”. “Malignant by nature, he never showed remorse.” (Seamus Heaney, Beowulf: A New Verse Translation, New York, WW Norton & Co, 2000, p11.)

With the genocide in Gaza now into its fourth year, and with Israel extending its military savagery to Lebanon, Syria and Iran, and tightening its bloody grip on the West Bank and East Jerusalem, it is clear the peoples of the Middle East are also living under the sway of a monster, malignant by nature, never showing remorse.

Unable to resolve the crisis of legitimacy generated by its founding act of land theft and dispossession, unable to quell the desire of the land’s indigenous people for liberation, the Israeli state, like Grendel, lashes out in rage, resorting to ever-increasing violence to sustain its power.

Halfway across the planet, in Magan-djin/Brisbane, Australia, a new album by Phil Monsour foregrounds the trauma, resilience, courage, fears and hopes of those resisting this evil; first and foremost the Palestinians themselves, but also the millions who have mobilised globally in solidarity with them over the past three years.

This album, Time of Monsters, adds to Monsour’s already impressive body of music about colonisation and war in the Middle East. It comprises 12 songs written over the past three years, each a response to Israel’s latest genocidal escalation of its never-ending war of subjugation.

One track is a rousing cover of Macklemore’s “Hind’s Hall 2”, the only song on the album not by Monsour. Another track, “Song for Fatima Hassouna”, honours the Palestinian photojournalist murdered by the Israel Defense Forces, alongside six members of her family, in April last year. The other songs respond to the genocide and Western complicity thematically. They invoke the visceral monstrousness of it, framing their narratives around recurring motifs: barbarism, loss, grief, survival, love and hope. The style is acoustic rock, although closer to Bruce Springsteen than Billy Bragg.

Monsour’s music is inscribed with activism. He is a founder and coordinator of Justice for Palestine Magan-djin, the Palestinian solidarity organisation that, since October 2023, has spearheaded the movement in Magan-djin, organising hundreds of rallies, pickets, vigils and public meetings. The size and intensity of this mobilisation has surpassed anything before it in the city’s history, including the struggle against the United States war in Vietnam.

Monsour composes and sings as a partisan of this uprising, a musician-activist, rather than a musician-ally. Without ever assuming to speak for Palestinians, some of his songs on Time of Monsters adopt a Palestinian first-person perspective. “Free Me from the Dust”, for example, addresses the horror in Gaza from the viewpoint of a Palestinian survivor: “In this shroud I bury soon something inside of me, flesh that binds me.” In “One Day in the Sun”, Monsour describes a Gazan’s daily struggle for survival: “All I can do is breathe, all I can do is wait, wait for tomorrow, and one day in the sun.” In another track, “I Am Not a Number”, the narrator tells us, “I live beyond your pictures; this land and I, we are the same.”

The Palestinian persona of these songs, however, is not ubiquitous across the album. The lens of the title song cuts away to an ally watching the genocide in livestream: “I am staring at something, can’t look away, the past the future is haunting me this day, crimes that echo on a million screens.”

The effect of this shifting perspective from song to song is a reframing of the Palestinian “I” as a “we” of the global liberation movement, positioning the Palestinians as a universal subject and Monsour himself (and us) as part of that multitude. “Our world is in pieces,” he declares in “Long List of Lost Things”, speaking for all of us. Monsour’s own place in the struggle — his own authorial “I” — is never far from the surface: “I can’t say if I’m broken, I can’t say if I’m whole, I just keep walking, nowhere else to go.”

This positioning gives the lyrical content of Time of Monsters urgency and emotional immediacy that sets Monsour’s songwriting apart in the genre of protest music. Woody Guthrie, Pete Seeger and Joan Baez, to name just three of the luminaries in the political folk tradition, sang about the resistance of the oppressed, often joining them in song at picket lines and rallies.

Even Bob Dylan, in his early years, occasionally engaged directly with the subjects of his protest tunes. Today, the likes of Macklemore, Roger Waters and Irish rappers Kneecap sing in solidarity with the Palestinians, using their profiles to mainstream the cause and call out the complicity of so-called non-alignment.

Monsour occupies a different place in this tradition. His songs not only articulate the demands for liberation, they are infused with the temper of the liberation movement itself. They do not constitute — to invoke an old cliché — the “soundtrack” of a movement. They are not an appendage. They are the resistance talking to itself and the world at large in verse and chorus, guitar in hand, amp turned up. They register the intensity of the rally, the march, the picket. They stridently declaim justice, urging everyone to keep showing up, to fight the despair with active solidarity, to believe that the monsters of our time can be vanquished by our collective efforts.

And as these monsters keep going about their awful business, these songs also speak to our grief and doubt. “Can we repair what is broken, rebuild what is left?”, we are asked.

The pedigree of such resistance art can be found in the activist songs of the Industrial Workers of the World, in “Bella Ciao” and the European anti-fascists, in the African American spirituals transformed into anthems of perseverance by the underground, and of course in the poetry of Palestinians themselves.

It is a tradition with a deeply personal dimension. Monsour enacts resistance through his music, and that resistance is psychological as much as political. Confronting monstrous evil, this work of songwriting and performing serves as a metaphorical call to arms and an outlet for anguish.

This is art as politics and catharsis. And in both realms it lifts us up, prepares us to struggle another day, one step closer to liberation. “Revolution love will see us through,” Monsour assures us. In the end, Grendel was defeated by the warrior Beowulf. In Time of Monsters, Beowulf is all of us.

author: Cas Smith
title: Students, staff rally against proposed ‘mega university’ merger plan
content:
About 500 people, including students, academics and concerned members of the community, rallied at Western Australian Parliament in Boorloo/Perth on October 21 to oppose the shock proposal by the state Labor government to merge three major universities.

Organised by the National Union of Students (NUS) and student guilds of Curtin University, Murdoch University and the University of Western Australia (UWA), the rally came only a week after WA education minister Tony Buti unveiled details of the merger plan, which he said would allow the state’s tertiary education sector to remain “highly competitive, accessible and relevant”.

But, speaking to the crowd gathered outside Parliament, Curtin Guild President Dylan Storer said students and faculty had not been consulted. “We are not going to let you decide the future of our universities without us,” he said.

“Our universities do not belong to the government, they belong to the people of Western Australia, and we deserve a say in their future.”

The proposed merger is set to cost upwards of $1 billion. Storer said the money could be better spent addressing WA’s cost-of-living crisis, which is also having a profound impact on university students.

“New research has revealed that more than 456,000 West Australians are living in poverty: around one in six people in one of the wealthiest places on the planet,” he said.

“Students are skipping meals to afford rent and working multiple jobs just to stay at university.

“The state government has the opportunity to shelve this merger and instead invest in our students, our staff and our universities. To invest in affordable student housing, to invest in better teaching, better facilities and better student support.”

Instead of better, more-accessible education institutions, Labor has presented “a billion-dollar corporate restructure”. Storer said the state government-commissioned feasibility study is riddled with errors, likely introduced by the use of artificial intelligence.

UWA guild councillor Rojin Didari argued that the focus on corporate interests, rather than student needs, was obvious, given the language of the feasibility study, which used the words “competition” and “business” more than 100 times.

She said the plan was “about subordinating our future to the interests of the mining industry, the defence sector, militarism and AUKUS”.

National Tertiary Education Union Curtin branch president Barbara Whelan said if WA Labor was serious about addressing problems in higher education, it would call for a Senate inquiry into university governance, as has been done in NSW, or develop a statewide strategy, as the feasibility study itself had recommended.

WA Greens MLC Sophie McNeill told the rally the plan was an attempt to “erode academic independence, reduce choices in universities and entrench further the corporatisation of your education”.

She said that students and staff could not trust Buti when he said the final decision on the plan was yet to be made, because he had handpicked a steering committee full of people who support it.

An enthusiastic sentiment prevailed for much of the gathering, including chants of “the students, united, will never be defeated” and “our degrees, our say, no merger in WA”.

Liam Staltari, Liberal MP for Carine and shadow education minister, said his party also opposes the merger. He was met with anger from the crowd over the Liberals’ history of education funding cuts.

NUS WA branch president Rama Sugiartha said the NUS had also invited Labor to speak at the rally, but they refused.

“Students are asking, ‘Will my course still exist?’, ‘Will my campus still be there?’, ‘Will my lecturer still have a job next year?’, ‘Will my tutorial go from 20 people to 40?’,” Sugiartha said.

“These are not hysterical questions. And this Labor government cannot answer a single one.

“They paid their consultants to study this merger, and the consultants were told in black and white not to look at staffing, not to look at redundancies. They studied the buildings and ignored the people inside them.”

He said the “mega university” that would result from the merger would have more students per academic than any of Australia’s Group of Eight universities.

Steven, It's an idea you might like to consider.

Back in the Winter of Discontent of the late 70's we had a thriving COHSE branch in our hospital. All of us were reluctant to go on strike and threaten patient care.

We invented something we called "imaginative Industrial action". This worked from a core of shop stewards and activists. We ignored our trade union hierarchy and certainly the RCN (of whom we considered to be run by retired matrons and another branch of management).

Our actions included: ward and admin office occupation; an impromtu band in the foyer of a Health Authority building; the banning of catering staff serving tea to managers; using the press imaginatively; when nurses were told that in future they were to wear the old starched hat we had a couple of male nurses so attired; leafleting visitors; running managerial decisions up the grievance ladder, & etc.

The unions came down on us heavily. We learned not to trust any Marxist abbreviation. By winning visitors to our side and refusing to threaten patient care we won some useful press attention.

Anarchist need to step away from mainstream TU activity. Small groups using cunning and imagination are both inspiring and empowering.

If anarcho-syndicalists can cover the base of thoroughly, heavily + regularly distributing a newsletter all over the country, that is great. That is not all that is necessary. But that is what they are able to bring to the fight. Playing a serious part in one of these public sector disputes (right now) means having to not be purist or sectarian, + suppressing the political gag reflex from time to time.

That's not to say progress is not being made. By even having anarcho-syndicalism as any kind of featured player, workers will first have their eyes opened to a genuine alternative which they might have only imagined before, + then will be able to judge if they like that approach/way of organisation better than the current position of things...

It is very easy to say 'the unions will sell us out', but why let it happen, yet again, this time? If we do then more fool us. It's no cause to be smug + say 'told you so' if public sector workers end up forced to take a paycut - it is cause for shame. Forget your ideological hang-ups about different organisations + think about what will actually work right now in the real world.

At the same time as encouraging all union members to use their vote, we have to talk in depth about the best tactics for action, before public service workers are railroaded into more token one-day all out strikes. Then look at how to apply pressure so that those tactics are on the table as serious options for mass participation. Unfortunately we do not have the luxury of much time. That may mean making use of unsavoury + 'dirty' structures... But it has to all come back to what is best for the workers as a whole (not the personal political cause) in this particular fight.

Union members are not ignorant - so many are aware that casting a vote once a year is not anything like real democracy. They know that voting alone on this pay issue is not enough, + in my experience do think in a farsighted way about possibilites + outcomes.

The way things are at the moment, the majority of the response to this is going to be union-controlled, I think most of us recognise this regardless of our view of the unions. The postal wildcats show that this is always contingent however, although the recent ones weren't against the union of course, and were quickly brought back under its control. There's also been private sector wildcats around pay and redundancies this year which again are an encouraging sign. Overall the first thing which is going to prevent "sell outs" (although calling crap deals sell outs suggests the union leadership would act any other way) is that people are as well informed as possible about things going on both in their own sector and in others, and that there's direct communication between individuals involved. royalmailchat is doing a fantastic job on this - hopefully dispatch will encourage more discussion both face to face, on rmc and on here.

This doesn't mean that workers shouldn't go out on strikes called by the unions, or that communists should abstain from giving any opinion on whether people should go out on strike just because the union is calling a ballot. It means arguing for the maximum possible action to be taken, whilst making it very clear that the union's primary focus is maintaining it's place at the negotiating table more than the interests of the members. Effective action is always going to be outside the union framework in most cases, because really effective action threatens their ability to control disputes and deliver a deal, to both sides.

I think the term "sell out" is a misnomer. It's the trade unions' role within capital to negotiate for heir members as wage earners, and to maintain a position within the management structure that allows them to negotiate such deals - a position which is contingent on maintaining 'discipline' in return for a say in how things are implemented. When people talk about a 'sell out' it suggests that they expect the leadership and the union apparatus as a whole to act differently - contrary to their interests.

As such the unions shouldn't be seen as some kind of conspiracy - they just have to be recognised for what they are, so there's not the constant cycle of building hopes up for a successful all out fight within the boundaries set by disputes, then the calls of 'sell out' and demoralisation which follows when this doesn't happen. That focuses attention on a crisis of leadership rather than a crisis of the conflicting interests between workers and their union - which is a distinct institution with it's own particular needs. The 'sell out' cry usually leads to leadership challenges, calls for 'working class representation' (Trot parties), splinter-unions, doesn't deal with the systemic issues which cause them - i.e the actual relation of labour power to capital and the union's role in managing this relationship

title: Ephéméride des luttes : 28 octobre
content:
L'éphéméride des luttes du 28 octobre abhorre les fascistes, comme toujours, ainsi que les armées et les patrons. Elle se méfie toujours autant des faux alliés autoritaires et pose de nouvelles bases pour un mouvement féministe, tout en ne reniant pas sa culture émeutière.




1791 :

 Olympe de Gouges, militante "proto-féministe", présente la 

Déclaration des Droits de la Femme et de la Citoyenne

 à l'Assemblée nationale.




1893 :

 A Chicago (Etats-Unis), "

un individu qu'on dit être un anarchiste pénétra dans la résidence du maire de Chicago Mr. Carter Harrison et le tua de plusieurs coups de révolver. Mr. Harrison avait été plusieurs fois menacé par les anarchistes et un attentat avait été commis contre lui, sans succès, quelques semaines auparavant

".




Repris de l'éphéméride anarchiste.




1904 :

 La police apprend à utiliser les dépôts gras laissés par les doigts : c'est le début de l'utilisation des empreintes digitales à des fins policières.




1919 :

 Au Japon, sortie du premier numéro du journal "Rôdô Undô - The Labor Movement" (Le Mouvement Ouvrier), d'inspiration anarchiste.




1922 :

 En Italie, les fasciste commencent leur marche sur Rome. C'est de lébut de 22 ans de dictature.




1937 :

 Au cours de la guerre d'Espagne, le gouvernement républicain est transféré à Barcelone.




1938 :

 En Espagne, les Brigades Internationales sont démobilisées du front.




1938 :

 A Marseille, pendant un congrès radical-socialiste, un incendie accidentel ravage les Nouvelles Galeries sur la Canebière, gagnant l'hôtel de Noailles, le Grand-Hôtel et l'hôtel Astoria. Plusieurs dizaines de personnes y ont trouvé la mort. Le Grand-Hôtel abrite aujourd'hui le commissariat de Noailles.




 

 

 

 




1956 :

 A Budapest, on est toujours en plein dans l'insurrection Hongroise.




1968 :

 A Paris, des militants maoïstes et anarchistes attaquent au molotov le bar Relais-Odéon, qui accueille les meetings de l'organisation néofasciste Occident.




1974 :

 A Ballynkilar en Irlande du Nord, l'IRA fait sauter des explosifs contre une caserne de l'armée Britannique. Deux soldats trouvent la mort dans l'explosion.




1979 :

 - En Irlande du Nord, deux soldats sont abattus par l'IRA près de Belfast.




 Aux Etats-Unis, les Hopis et Big Mountain Dine déclarent leur indépendance vis-à-vis des gouvernements tribaux et du pays.




1986 :

 A Berlin, les Cellules Révolutionnaires (RZ) tirent dans les jambes du chef de la police des étrangers.




1988 :

 A Las Queñes, dans la cordillère chilienne, deux commandants du FPMR-Autonome, Cecilia Magni ("comandante Tamara") et Raúl Pellegrín ("comandante Rodrigo") sont abattus par les carabiniers de Pinochet après une attaque à l'explosif et à la mitrailleuse contre la caserne du village. Rodrigo et Tamara faisaient partie des principaux responsables de cette organisation de lutte armée contre la dictature.




 

 

 

 




1998 :

 A Vitrolles, destruction à l'explosif du transformateur du stade qui devait accueillir un concert de Rock Identitaire organisé par la mairie FN.




2001 :

 De grosses émeutes ont lieu à Belfast, des bombes artisanales sont lancées sur les officers du Royal Ulster Constabulary par les émeutiers. De nombreuses voitures sont incendiées et deux autres charges explosifs dans d'autres zones de la ville.




2011 :

 A Thessalonique, des manifestant-e-s parviennent à faire annuler un défilé militaire en bloquant les voies de chemin de fer et en attaquant la tribune officielle.




2013 :

 A Berlin, un véhicule de l'entreprise Sodexo est incendié pour protester contre la cogestion des prisons et des centres de rétention par l'entreprise d'alimentation de masse.

author: none
title: Censorship in the Education Department at FCI Allenwood Medium
content:
Casey Goonan

10/26/26




Casey offers here their reflections on the recent book drive they organized for the prison library, its popularity with everyone locked up, as well as how it has since been blocked and how Casey subsequently was fired from their library job.

Please share and repost.

– Casey Support Committee







AFFIRMATION

Thank you to everyone out in the so-called “free world” for contributing to our Summer Book Drive. On behalf of the Support Committee and every convict at FCI Allenwood Medium involved in this autonomous initiative, we send our revolutionary love and profound gratitude. From this self-organized prisoner initiative, we introduced a wide range of new, interesting, and relevant books into the prison’s official library collection. During my time as a library worker, many significant changes were made to the form and content of the library here at Allenwood Medium. Unfortunately, because of the Book Drive’s budding success and overwhelming popularity among the captives, i was fired from my job as librarian last week.

TERMINATION

On Thursday, October 1, i was fired as a library worker at FCI Allenwood Medium prison for no reason other than “ordering too many books” and “donating them directly into the library catalog” without the approval of the Education Department Supervisor, Mr. Williams. Although my boss, Ms. Ashton, knew about the plans for a mass donation and granted permission to do so, i was thrown under the bus once she learned her boss found out, and especially once she learned i was adding certain books into the catalog without her approval. There is nothing against policy within the books that were donated, even the ones i donated without Ms. Ashton’s knowledge. The Book Drive was successful in adding around one hundred brand new books to the library catalog, which transformed the library space from a realm of entertainment and distraction into one of pedagogy and critical study. By the first week of September, around seventy more books were delivered to the mailroom, yet staff deliberately let them pile up, before complaining to admin about the quantity of donations and returning them all back to sender. A few days later i learned of my termination.

It’s the overwhelming pettiness of the reaction that bothers me. There is no BOP policy that states we as prisoners cannot donate books into the library collection. There is an official process to do so however and i bypassed some of the red tape. Yet the only violation of policy i am “guilty” of is not showing my boss, Ms. Ashton, every single book that i was donating. My decision to not report donations wasn’t at all due to any intentional plot of deception. It was simply because whenever i gave my donations to Ms. Ashton, she would “never get around” to adding them into the catalog. They would just sit around and often disappear. I was frustrated by Ashton’s lack of enthusiasm regarding this rare opportunity to enhance the library collection, so i decided to just start marking, labeling, and cataloging the books myself. Basic direct action.

ACTION/REACTION

All who were involved in the Summer Book Drive (not only me as an individual) took direct action both to remedy the negligence of the correctional officers who oversee “education” operations at Allenwood Medium and to counter fascist anti-intellectualism, of which the official indifference to our depraved learning conditions is symptomatic. I am not exactly sure how the process occurred behind the scenes, but apparently a mailroom officer (who does not like me) contacted S.I.S. (the surveillance and investigative wing of the prison administration), who then contacted Mr. Williams, who in turn emailed Ms. Ashton ordering my termination as a library employee. I believe that the primary reason i was fired was politically motivated censorship, coupled with the fact that some of the COs already had an issue with me working in the library.

My termination as a library worker demonstrates how the administration at FCI Allenwood Medium will attempt to stifle any act of autonomous sufficiency and self-organization among us convicts, especially if activities aim to improve the conditions of life. The Summer Book Drive initiative was not only an attempt to counter the dehumanizing conditions of a neglectful Education Department but a demonstration of collective action to provide and (re)distribute resources in the face of (or rather in spite of) organized abandonment. Inadvertently, the initiative also illuminated a potential collective capacity that exists between concrete people across prison walls. Within a matter of weeks around 200 books were donated through a public wishlist. What other outcomes might result from a similar constellation of autonomous, informal organization? The purpose of this reportback, however, is not to address this question in particular. That must be the topic of discussion elsewhere. For now, i just want to catch everyone up to speed and explain just how the Summer Book Drive unfolded, and how our work in the library was demonstrably changing the atmosphere of learning in this prison.

REPORTBACK

When i arrived at FCI Allenwood Medium back in February, i was appalled by the lack of resources provided by the Education Department’s “library.” Barely any of the books were visible on the shelves. The shelves themselves were behind a desk, so no patrons could walk up and pull a book on their own. The content of the library catalog was almost entirely fiction, and none of the scarce non-fiction texts were visible at all. In fact, i was told by my boss Ms. Ashton that “this bunch are more of the fiction, fantasy kind of guys” — an assumption proven completely false once i conducted a survey and began offering fellow prisoners non-fiction books with social, cultural, and historical relevance. From what i’ve gathered, the library at Allenwood Medium is by far one of the worst libraries in the Federal BOP. The more time i spent in the library, i became intimately attentive to the inadequacies and intricacies of why this alleged library earned the reputation of “worst of the worst.”

In June 2026, when i was hired as a librarian, i began conducting a survey of each “car” in my unit and then across the entire compound, researching what the most popular books are among prisoners at Allenwood Medium. (For those who don’t know, “cars” are how we are collectively organized, prisoner-to-prisoner throughout the BOP; i.e. the Midwest Car, White Car, Gang Cars, Pennsylvania Car, and so on.) I made sure that all races and religious affiliations were considered in this survey, and i consolidated the results to a list of around 100 specific books, as well as dozens of authors, publishers, and topics of books that prisoners desired to read at this facility. From there my support committee and i created a wishlist derived from the survey findings and circulated the wishlist publicly using the incredible www dot bookshop dot org. The idea was to use the social platform that my support committee has worked so hard to maintain over the past two and a half years to organize a SUMMER BOOK DRIVE, where people on the outside can purchase the requested books from the public wishlist. The books then were to be delivered to me, which i would donate directly into the library collection.

As the Book Drive began, i was already involved in the process of rearranging the library stacks by subject and genre and had the support of Ms. Ashton to do this. In fact, she initially welcomed my consistency and enthusiasm. For FICTION i divided up the shelves to hold (with visible labels) ‘Fantasy’, ‘Western’, ‘Science Fiction’, ‘Thriller & Suspense’; ‘Mystery & Crime Drama’, ‘Deep State Fiction & Political Drama’, ‘Military Fiction’, ‘Historical Fiction (Modern)’, ‘Historical Fiction (Pre-Modern)’, ‘Historical Fiction (20th Century)’. As time went on my plan was to also create an section of the library for ‘Urban Novels’ and ‘African American Classics’. For NON-FICTION, i made the existing books in the library visible to patrons for the FIRST TIME EVER and then created various subject categories such as ‘US History (Pre-20th Century)’, ‘US History (20th-21st Century)’, ‘World History’, ‘Social Studies’, ‘Native Studies’, ‘Science & Nature’, ‘Geography’, ‘Music, Film, & Pop Culture’, ‘Sports’, ‘Health & Fitness’, ‘Business & Marketing’, ‘Self-Help’, ‘Survival & Uplift’, and ‘Resume & Job Search Resources’.

As i described above, around 100 books were successfully delivered to me. After receiving what books the mailroom *did* allow, i added those books into the library catalog. By “adding into the catalog,” i mean that my coworkers and i stamped, stickered, added check-out cards in the books, and shelved them. The feedback from fellow convicts regarding the Book Drive was wildly supportive and positive without a doubt. As the library collection progressed, regular patrons who entered the library would comment on how much better the selections were; how much easier it was to find books; how they felt more interested in going to the library; and most of all, i noticed a substantial interest in the non-fiction sections, especially Social Studies, US History, and Native Studies. The number of nonfiction books that patrons checked out increased markedly. Most importantly, in the days leading up to my termination, a new spirit of critical study and discussion seemed to be permeating the library and its users.

I have to remind myself that there is only so much you can do without greater organization of opposition to the prison regime from within and without. I am chalking this up as another experience, or maybe, rather, the marking of a new chapter in the Campaign Against Prison Censorship and Book Banning

[ see 

https://trueleappress.wordpress.com/2023/04/13/new-zine-campaign-against-prison-censorship-and-book-banning/

 ].

I’m not sure what my next moves will be, but one thing is for certain: There’s a growing number of convicts in this prison who desire a deeper grasp of the world beyond the false sense of “participation” shoved upon us by the TV screens, corporate newspapers, radio shows, remedial programs, and commercial-distraction novels sanctioned by the Federal Bureau of Prisons. The Book Drive could be blocked but the information that such literature instills in our convict class is something that fascists can never return to sender. One idea that my celly had was to simply order books on anti-prison activism, abolition, and prisoner movement history for every prisoner at FCI Allenwood Medium. All of our information is public access on the BOP website. Just pick a name on the BOP “Inmate Locator” and order a book. Brilliant!

Ever more obvious is the substantial mass of people beyond the wall in the so-called “free world” who are impacted by the regime and continue to express a desire to participate in collective anti-prison resistance. These are people actively searching for opportunities to support their own loved ones and others in captivity.  As Ruth Wilson Gilmore writes in her 1999 article ‘You Have Dislodged a Boulder’, by “organizing surplus labor into cages,” the state pulls our loved ones, especially mothers and other caregivers, into its “spheres of operation.” The regime’s gravitational pull on our families and communities creates opportunities where our people can find each other and cooperate together *against* the state’s interests. Gilmore writes, “The magnitude of imprisonment suggests the magnitude of possibility”; and that magnitude “starts small, over and over again.” The scale and dynamic capacity of formal and informal prisoner-support structures put on display by the Summer Book Drive suggests the embryo of such possibility. I know if i were on the outside right now, i would be dreaming and scheming of where to take this collectivity next. I send my blessing for anyone reading this to do the same. After all, it’s one struggle at base.




To write Casey:

Casey Goonan #24611-511

FCI Allenwood Medium

PO BOX 2000

White Deer, PA 17887




Casey Support Committee

email: 

cscommittee@proton.me

instagram: @freecaseynow

donations: 

https://chuffed.org/project/supportcasey

author: Maria Martha Bruno
title: Bolsonaristas fogem da Justiça e se espalham por ao menos quatro países
content:
Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) pode ser o mais novo integrante da lista de bolsonaristas que deixaram o Brasil. Caso confirmada a chegada aos Estados Unidos, o candidato derrotado nas eleições de 2026 se somará a parentes, influenciadores e ex-membros do governo de Jair Bolsonaro, que deixaram o país por condenações ou investigações. Sempre sob o argumento de perseguição política. 




A denúncia partiu do veículo argentino 

Infobae

, que publicou hoje, 27 de outubro, que Flávio estaria na cidade de Puerto Iguazú, que faz fronteira com o Brasil, pronto para tomar um voo rumo aos EUA. Ainda não se sabe como o senador teria saído do Brasil para o país vizinho. Em 26 de outubro, dia seguinte à derrota nas urnas, o ministro Alexandre de Moraes determinou que Flávio entregasse o passaporte à Justiça.




Um dos fundamentos da decisão de Moraes foi uma entrevista do irmão de Flávio, Eduardo Bolsonaro, dada dois dias antes do segundo turno, afirmando que o então candidato deveria deixar o país se perdesse o pleito. Também nesta terça, o blogueiro Paulo Figueiredo disse em sua live que, na noite de domingo, após confirmada a derrota, havia aconselhado o senador a ir para os EUA.




Flávio Bolsonaro é investigado em duas frentes pelo Supremo Tribunal Federal, mas, terminado seu mandato como senador, em 31 de janeiro de 2027, perderá o foro privilegiado. Sob relatoria do ministro André Mendonça, ele é investigado pela suspeita de evasão de divisas e de lavagem de dinheiro por conta do financiamento da produção do filme “Dark Horse”, sobre a trajetória de Jair Bolsonaro. A investigação mira repasses de Daniel Vorcaro, ex-dono do Banco Master, à produção do longa. 




Em outra frente, sob relatoria do ministro Alexandre de Moraes, Flávio é investigado pela suspeita de lavagem de dinheiro por meio de uma casa de apostas. A Polícia Federal (PF) quebrou o sigilo telemático do 

advogado Willer Tomaz

, amigo de Flávio, e encontrou e-mails que apontariam que o senador foi cadastrado como “usuário master” de uma conta bancária da empresa Alcazar Holdings, de propriedade de Tomaz.




Segundo a PF, há indícios de “vínculo de controle ou propriedade de fato de Willer Tomaz sobre a Rede Loto”, a primeira a obter autorização estadual da Loterj, no Rio de Janeiro, para explorar bets no estado.
















O senador Flávio Bolsonaro afirmou em seu Instagram ter sido intimado pela Polícia Federal (PF), nesta segunda-feira (26), a entregar seus passaportes.




Bolsonaristas nos EUA de Trump




Eduardo Bolsonaro mora no Texas (EUA) desde março de 2025. Ele foi condenado pelo STF em junho de 2026 por sua atuação para obter sanções americanas contra autoridades brasileiras. O ex-deputado teve a prisão decretada em outubro, entre o primeiro e o segundo turno das eleições.




Eduardo tem passaporte italiano e também 

conseguiu

 o 

green card

, documento que garante a residência permanente nos EUA. Desde que fugiu do Brasil, ele fez diversas viagens ao Oriente Médio e chegou a 

abrir uma empresa

 no Bahrein, conforme a 

Pública

 revelou.




Seu braço direito nos EUA, Paulo Figueiredo, mora na Flórida há dez anos. 

Ele

 é investigado no Inquérito das 

fake news

 e foi denunciado pela Procuradoria-Geral da República pela tentativa de golpe em 8 de janeiro de 2023. Seu caso nunca foi julgado porque o neto do ex-ditador João Figueiredo 

nunca foi intimado

, mas ele é considerado 

foragido

.
















Eduardo, Allan dos Santos e Alexandre Ramagem juntos, em 2026, em encontro nos EUA




Outro foragido que vive na Flórida é o blogueiro Allan dos Santos. Ele teve mandado de prisão preventiva decretado pelo STF em outubro de 2021 e 

reforçado

 em 2024, bem como o bloqueio de suas contas bancárias e perfis digitais no Brasil. O criador do extinto “Terça Livre” também é investigado no Inquérito das 

fake news

 e das milícias digitais por disseminação de conteúdo falso e ataques a autoridades.




Ainda na Flórida mora Alexandre Ramagem, ex-diretor da Agência Brasileira de Inteligência (Abin) e ex-deputado federal pelo PL. Ele foi alvo de pedido de extradição após ser condenado pelo STF a 16 anos de prisão pela trama golpista.




A fuga, em setembro de 2025, contou com a ajuda de Rodrigo Cataratas, condenado por liderar o garimpo ilegal na Terra Yanomami, conforme 

revelou

 a 

Pública

. O empresário do garimpo 

também está foragido

 por ter ajudado na fuga de Ramagem.




Em abril de 2026, Ramagem chegou a ser detido pelo serviço de imigração dos EUA (ICE), mas foi liberado dois dias depois. Hoje, ele é um imigrante ilegal no país, segundo o Departamento de Segurança Interna (DHS, na sigla em inglês) e está sujeito a detenção e deportação, como a Pública também 

mostrou

.




Bolsonaristas na Argentina, Itália e Espanha




Na Itália, a ex-deputada federal Carla Zambelli chegou a ser presa em junho de 2025. Em maio de 2026, ela foi solta pela Corte de Cassação de Roma, última instância da Justiça do país. Ela havia sido 

condenada

 pelo STF a dez anos de prisão por contratar um hacker para inserir um mandado de prisão falso contra o ministro Alexandre de Moraes, do STF, no sistema do Conselho Nacional de Justiça (CNJ).




Ainda na Europa, mas na Espanha, mora o blogueiro Oswaldo Eustáquio, considerado foragido da Justiça brasileira desde 2023. Em outubro de 2026, ele se tornou 

réu

 por associação criminosa no âmbito do inquérito que investiga a tentativa de golpe de 8 de janeiro. Em junho de 2025, o governo espanhol rejeitou o pedido de extradição do governo brasileiro por considerar que houve motivação política.




Leonardo Rodrigues de Jesus, o Leo Índio, é primo de Flávio, Eduardo e Carlos Bolsonaro. 

Ele

 é investigado no inquérito do golpe de Estado em 2023 e teve a prisão decretada em 2025. Ele mora na cidade de Puerto Iguazú, do lado argentino da tríplice fronteira, por onde Flávio Bolsonaro teria passado para tomar um voo para os EUA. A 

Pública

 mostrou que Leo é um dos investigados por desinformação e tentativa de golpe que 

seguem ativos

 nas redes em 2026.




Também na Argentina, estão cinco brasileiros condenados pelos ataques golpistas de 8 de janeiro de 2023 foram extraditados em dezembro de 2025: Joelton Gusmão de Oliveira, Joel Borges Correa, Rodrigo de Freitas Moro, Wellington Firmino e Ana Paula de Souza, segundo 

apuração

 da BBC Brasil.
