title: Gane quien gane el sionismo seguirá: Israel votó entre dos bloques que coinciden en perpetuar la ocupación palestina
content:
Con una elección ajustada y una fuerte participación de la población árabe, pese a las trabas y las denuncias de intimidación, Israel define su próximo gobierno. Al momento, Netanyahu estaría conservando una gran cantidad de votos pero menos que la oposición.  Pero advertimos que las principales fuerzas que disputan el poder comparten el rechazo a la creación de un Estado palestino soberano y retirarse de Gaza y Cisjordania. Las diferencias pasan por la conducción política, la estrategia militar y los métodos para sostener el dominio israelí. Por ANRed




Las elecciones legislativas de Israel se desarrollan este martes 27 de octubre en un escenario de fuerte polarización, con Benjamin Netanyahu buscando conservar el poder y el exjefe del Estado Mayor Gadi Eisenkot encabezando la principal alternativa. Pero detrás de la disputa por el gobierno hay un consenso que atraviesa a buena parte del arco político israelí: la negativa a reconocer la autodeterminación palestina y a poner fin a la ocupación de los territorios palestinos.




La participación de la población árabe israelí, mayoritariamente de origen palestino, adquirió un peso central en la jornada hasta el momento con un incremento del 80%, las mas altas desde 1965. Las largas filas en localidades árabes contrastaron con la campaña de Netanyahu, que presentó la concurrencia a las urnas como una amenaza política y advirtió sobre la posibilidad de que los partidos árabes adquirieran influencia en el próximo gobierno. Estas declaraciones fueron denunciadas como racistas e intimidatorias. También hubo controversias por los intentos de excluir a representantes políticos árabes, mientras referentes de la ultraderecha pudieron competir pese a sus declaraciones contra la población palestina.




La participación árabe podría incidir en la distribución de escaños y en las negociaciones para formar una coalición, aunque el bloque opositor también mantiene límites explícitos a una alianza con los partidos árabes. La disputa electoral, por lo tanto, no equivale necesariamente a una disputa sobre el fin de la ocupación.




Dos bloques, un mismo rechazo a la soberanía palestina




Benjamin Netanyahu, líder del Likud, representa la continuidad de un proyecto nacionalista y religioso que profundizó la expansión de los asentamientos en Cisjordania, reforzó el control militar sobre los territorios ocupados y rechazó abiertamente la creación de un Estado palestino. Durante la invasión contra Gaza, su gobierno sostuvo una ofensiva que provocó una destrucción masiva, desplazamientos de población y decenas de miles de muertes palestinas. Una comisión de investigación de Naciones Unidas concluyó que Israel había cometido 

genocidio

 en Gaza, una calificación que el gobierno israelí rechaza.




La alternativa encabezada por Gadi Eisenkot, exjefe del Estado Mayor de las Fuerzas de Defensa de Israel, cuestiona aspectos de la conducción de Netanyahu, pero no plantea una ruptura con los pilares de la política hacia Palestina. Eisenkot también rechazó la solución de dos Estados y cuestionó la idea de un Estado palestino. Su discurso pone mayor énfasis en la seguridad, la capacidad militar y la necesidad de una conducción política y estratégica diferente.




Las coincidencias no son menores. Ninguno de los dos principales referentes propone una retirada integral de los territorios ocupados, el desmantelamiento general de los asentamientos o un acuerdo que garantice la soberanía palestina. Tampoco existe, en el centro de sus propuestas, un compromiso claro con la reparación de la destrucción causada en Gaza y con el reconocimiento de los derechos nacionales palestinos.




En Gaza, la diferencia entre ambos sectores se expresa principalmente en cómo administrar la guerra, qué hacer con Hamás y cómo garantizar el control territorial y la seguridad de Israel. En Cisjordania, el rechazo compartido a la creación de un Estado palestino deja abierta la continuidad de la ocupación militar, la expansión de los asentamientos y las restricciones a la población palestina.




Esto no significa que ambos bloques sean idénticos. Netanyahu depende de una coalición que incluye fuerzas religiosas y ultranacionalistas que promueven la anexión, la expansión territorial y, en algunos casos, el desplazamiento de la población palestina. Eisenkot representa una alternativa con otra composición política y mayores diferencias respecto de la gestión del gobierno, la institucionalidad y la conducción militar. Pero esas diferencias no se traducen, por ahora, en una propuesta de descolonización ni en el reconocimiento efectivo de la soberanía palestina.




El sionismo como proyecto político colonial




Para comprender estas coincidencias es necesario analizar el sionismo no solamente como un movimiento histórico vinculado a la búsqueda de seguridad y autodeterminación del pueblo judío, sino también como una corriente política expansionista y colonizadora que, en su vertiente dominante dentro del Estado israelí, ha impulsado un proyecto de control territorial y de limpieza etnica sobre Palestina. El sionismo no es una corriente homogénea: existen tradiciones judías y sionistas con posiciones diferentes, incluso críticas de la ocupación. Sin embargo, la crítica anticolonial apunta a las consecuencias concretas del sionismo estatal y de sus expresiones nacionalistas y expansionistas, aunque su expresión es muy minoritaria.




Desde esta perspectiva, el carácter colonial del proyecto se expresa en la apropiación de tierras, la colonización mediante asentamientos, el desplazamiento de la población palestina y la construcción de un sistema que otorga derechos y posibilidades diferentes según la pertenencia nacional. La Nakba de 1948, cuando cientos de miles de palestinos fueron expulsados de sus hogares durante la creación de Israel, constituye un antecedente central de esta historia. La negativa al retorno de los refugiados y la continuidad de la expansión territorial muestran que el conflicto no puede reducirse a una disputa religiosa ni a una sucesión de enfrentamientos militares.




En Cisjordania, los asentamientos israelíes y las restricciones a la circulación fragmentan el territorio palestino. En Jerusalén Este, las políticas de ocupación y desplazamiento constante amenazan la permanencia de comunidades palestinas. En Gaza, la destrucción de viviendas e infraestructura y los desplazamientos masivos han profundizado una catástrofe humanitaria que sin dudas es un genocidio. La continuidad de estas políticas, bajo gobiernos de distintas orientaciones, permite analizar la ocupación como una estructura de dominación que excede a un solo primer ministro.




Criticar el sionismo como proyecto político colonial no significa responsabilizar colectivamente a las personas judías ni cuestionar sus derechos como pueblo. Significa discutir un orden estatal y territorial que subordina los derechos nacionales palestinos, incluso su supervivencia.




Un arco político desplazado hacia la derecha




El mapa electoral israelí muestra un desplazamiento sostenido hacia posiciones nacionalistas y militaristas. La ultraderecha que integra el gobierno de Netanyahu, con figuras como Itamar Ben-Gvir y Bezalel Smotrich, defiende abiertamente la expansión de los asentamientos, la anexión de territorios y distintas formas de desplazamiento de la población palestina. Sus posiciones no son marginales: participan del gobierno, influyen en las políticas públicas y condicionan el debate electoral.




Pero el problema no se agota en esa ultraderecha. El rechazo a la soberanía palestina atraviesa también a sectores que se presentan como centristas o como una alternativa institucional a Netanyahu. La negativa de Eisenkot a la solución de dos Estados constituye una expresión concreta de ese consenso. Mientras la disputa interna se concentra en la gestión de la guerra, la seguridad, la justicia y la formación de coaliciones, los derechos nacionales palestinos quedan relegados.




El espectro político israelí como ultraderechista es  hegemonico pero sería preciso mencionar la existencia de fuerzas árabes, judías y de izquierda que cuestionan la ocupación, la discriminación y la guerra. Pero el centro de gravedad parlamentario se ha desplazado hacia la derecha y las principales alternativas con posibilidades de gobernar no ofrecen, hasta ahora, una salida que garantice la autodeterminación palestina.




La continuidad del respaldo político y militar a la ofensiva contra Gaza, así como la persistencia de la ocupación y la expansión de los asentamientos, permite señalar que el consenso dominante ha sostenido políticas denunciadas internacionalmente como crímenes de guerra y, en el caso de Gaza, como genocidio. La responsabilidad política y jurídica debe establecerse a partir de las decisiones, los actos y las pruebas correspondientes, pero la discusión electoral no puede ocultar sus consecuencias para la población palestina.




Una elección sin voto para millones de palestinos




La participación de la ciudadanía árabe israelí puede modificar el equilibrio parlamentario e incluso resultar decisiva para la formación de un gobierno. Sin embargo, la mayoría de los palestinos que viven en Gaza y en los territorios ocupados de Cisjordania y Jerusalén Este no pueden votar en estas elecciones, pese a que las decisiones del Estado israelí determinan aspectos centrales de sus vidas: las fronteras, la circulación, la seguridad, el acceso a los recursos y la posibilidad de permanecer en sus hogares. Un verdadero 

Apartheid.




Esa desigualdad política es uno de los puntos centrales del conflicto. Mientras los partidos israelíes discuten quién debe conducir el Estado y cómo garantizar su seguridad, millones de palestinos siguen sin poder decidir sobre el poder que controla buena parte de su territorio y sus condiciones de existencia. En esta situación convive el estado sionista.




El resultado electoral puede cambiar la composición del gobierno, el peso de la ultraderecha y la forma de conducir las operaciones militares. También puede abrir disputas institucionales y modificar la relación de Israel con sus aliados internacionales. Pero, si no cambia la política de ocupación, la expansión territorial y la negación de la soberanía palestina, una alternancia en el poder no significará, por lo menos, un cambio sustantivo en la ocupación.

title: İranlı yönetmen Cafer Penahi'ye 5 yıl 1 ay hapis kararı
content:
Fotoğraf: Kacy Bao/Wikimedia Commons CC BY-SA 4.0

İranlı yönetmen ve senarist Cafer Penahi, Tahran Devrim Mahkemesi’nin 26. Şubesi tarafından görülen davada 5 yıl 1 ay hapis cezasına çarptırıldı. Mahkeme, Penahi’nin taşınır ve taşınmaz tüm mal varlığına el konulmasına, 2 yıl sanal medya faaliyetlerinden men edilmesine ve yurt dışına çıkışının yasaklanmasına karar verdi.

HRANA’nın Emtedad’a dayandırdığı habere göre, Penahi’nin avukatı Mostafa Nili, kararın müvekkilinin yokluğunda verildiğini açıkladı. Nili, Penahi’nin banka hesaplarının dondurulmasının ardından karardan haberdar olduğunu belirtti. Avukat Nili, müvekkilinin 30 Mart 2026’da İran’a dönmesine rağmen dava dosyasında ülke dışında olduğunun belirtildiğini ve duruşma tarihinin kendisine bildirilmediğini söyledi. Penahi hakkında 20 Mayıs 2026’da yakalama kararı çıkarıldığını da aktaran Nili, yönetmenin şu anda üç ayrı hukuki dosyasının bulunduğunu ifade etti.

Penahi, daha önce “rejime karşı propaganda” suçlamasıyla ayrı bir davada 1 yıl hapis cezasına çarptırılmış, 2 yıl yurt dışına çıkış ve siyasi ve toplumsal örgütlere üyelik yasağı almıştı. Yönetmenin yeniden yargılanma talebi Haziran 2026’da reddedilmişti.

title: İsrail ordusunun Gazze'ye düzenlediği saldırılarda 4 Filistinli hayatını kaybetti
content:
Filistin sağlık kaynaklarından alınan bilgiye göre, Gazze Şeridi'nin kuzeyindeki Cibaliya Mülteci Kampı'nda bulunan El-Hoca Caddesi'nde İsrail askerlerinin açtığı ateş sonucu 28 yaşındaki Filistinli Mahmud Semih el-Herş hayatını kaybetti.

Refah kentinin batısında yer alan Mevasi bölgesindeki El-Alem Kavşağı'nı hedef alan İsrail saldırısında kimliği belirlenemeyen bir Filistinlinin de cenazesine ulaşıldığı aktarıldı.

Önceki saldırılarda yaralanan 2 Filistinli öldü

İsrail ordusunun açtığı ateş sonucu Mevasi bölgesinde yaralanan 6 yaşındaki Tehani Muhammed Said Şelalife, müdahaleye rağmen kurtarılamadı.

Gazze kent merkezindeki Es-Sevra Caddesi'ne birkaç gün önce düzenlenen İsrail saldırısında yaralanan Ahmed Yasin Buseyso da tedavi gördüğü hastanede hayatını kaybetti.

Gazze'nin çeşitli bölgelerinde birisi çocuk yaşta olmak üzere 5 Filistinlinin de İsrail saldırılarında yaralandığı aktarıldı.

İsrail'in Ekim 2023'ten bu yana Gazze Şeridi'ne düzenlediği saldırılarda en az 74 bin 561 Filistinli hayatını kaybederken, yaralı sayısı 175 bin 759'a ulaştı.

title: Eğitim-İş'ten beslenme çantası tepkisi: "Bir ayda yüzde 6,20 zamlandı, maliyeti 2 bin 147 liraya çıktı"
content:
Eğitim-İş, beslenme çantasının maliyetinin yüzde 6,20 artarak 2 bin 147 liraya yükseldiğini açıkladı.

Eğitim-İş'in sosyal medya hesabından yapılan açıklamada, şu ifadelere yer verildi:

"Okulların açılmasından yalnızca bir ay sonra beslenme çantasının maliyeti yüzde 6,20 artarak 2 bin 147 TL’ye yükseldi. Bu tutar, asgari ücretin yüzde 7,65’ine, emekli gelirinin yüzde 9,12’sine, yeni başlayan öğretmenin maaşının ise yüzde 3’üne karşılık geliyor. Emekçilerin gelirleri temel ihtiyaçları karşılamaya yetmezken çocuklar okula boş beslenme çantalarıyla gidiyor. Aileleri yoksullaştıran ekonomik politikaların sorumlusu siyasi iktidar, çocukların beslenme sorununu görmezden gelerek kamusal sorumluluğu ailelerin omuzlarına yüklüyor. 15 Ekim 2026’da açıklanan bütçe gerçekleşmelerine göre Türkiye Maarif Vakfı’na yalnızca eylülde 2 milyar TL, yılın ilk dokuz ayında ise 4 milyar 58 milyon TL aktarıldı. Eylül ayında vakfa aktarılan kaynakla 931 bin 150 öğrencinin bir aylık beslenme ihtiyacı karşılanabilirdi. Çocukların beslenmesi kamusal bir sorumluluktur. Ücretsiz bir öğün yemek haktır."

Queer/Feminist Alternatives to Both Historical Anarchism and State Systems

Benevolent State Control vs. Community Care

Cindy Barukh Milstein. 2024. Constellations of Care: Anarcha-Feminism in Practice. London: Pluto Press.

Constellations of Care is an anthology of answers to a fundamental question: what do people do to survive and thrive from the margins of society? According to the volume’s editor, Cindy Barukh Milstein, the goal of state-based systems is not to provide prosperity and security for all. Rather, they strategically reserve material and political protections for those who conform to a masculine and heteronormative model of the ‘good citizen’. The various authors of this anthology, all members of various anarcha-feminist collectives, employ the praxis of anarcha-feminism to suggest that resistance to state-based exclusion depends first and foremost on the practice of care, sustaining and building relationships that give life to those without political and economic power or opportunities, who unwittingly or willingly do not conform to the standards desired by the state. Empowerment and social transformation are not driven by massive state projects, but by interpersonal and highly specific interventions managed by those who share the ontological experience of exclusion through inhabiting queer or feminine bodies.

What follows is a collection of histories, reflections, conversations, and artwork that reflect collective, anti-hierarchical, and locally organized efforts to care for a global network of the excluded. Whether written by underground abortion care providers in Poland, communal kitchen collectives that sustained anti-government protests in Colombia, or unhoused and precarious sex workers in Philadelphia who hold weekly needle exchanges, each of its thirty-seven entries offers an approach to creating communities by and for the marginalized.

In some ways, Milstein’s work sits at odds with a strictly academic style of writing. One of the first entries in the book, written by members of the Nightshade collective in Philadelphia, actively denounces the ability of formal academia to understand and advance anarchist theory, suggesting that academia is inherently hierarchical, focuses on creating grand universalist theory rather than accepting theoretical plurality, and gatekeeps legitimacy through economically restricting access to academic credentials (p. 24). Constellations of Care is based on the idea that theory is created, interpreted, and used not by researchers, but by the everyday stakeholders in the political processes that it analyzes. The book emphasizes alternatives to academic style in some of its editorial choices. For example, each section’s author biography veers away from listing degrees or institutional affiliations, and rather briefly chronicles the author’s skill sets and political positions, as well as their close relationships to both communities and geographies, often defined by a city or an Indigenous land designation, rather than a nationality. However, the main contribution of the book is to showcase/underscore/reveal both the vastness of anarcha-feminism’s theoretical considerations and approaches, as well as highlight the difficulties of living out radical politics on a day-to-day basis. The reader is constantly invited not only to explore the deep-seated reasonings that drive the book’s storytellers, but are also challenged to forget clean, academic theory and engage with the messy process of extending a hand to the people around them.

Anarchist organizing has often struggled with how to oppose hierarchical structures without simply reproducing their harms or coercive authority in less formalized ways. These anarcha-feminists often characterize state power with masculinized values and phenomena, including violence, individualism, and the influence of charismatic and ambitious political leaders who are willing or able to take public risks in the name of a cause. Two members of Food Not Bombs, a collective that gives away free meals to unhoused people and at protests, write that “emphasizing only the most visible, frontline, or confrontational forms of activism fails to acknowledge the massive amounts of labor carried out every day that…are part of the glue that holds us all together” (p. 348). This invisibilized labor is often only understood from the standpoint of those who are either doing the work of caring for the marginalized, a disproportionately feminine group, or who are outside of normative economic, familial, and domestic structures, a key part of the ontological experience of queerness.

This understanding offers a corrective course to both official marginalization and trends within social movements that prioritize direct action against a hostile authority over the daily needs of vulnerable people. What it doesn’t offer is a clear idea of where masculinity as a concept or masculine bodies reside in a framework of care. The book, like many of the collectives featured within it, is entirely the work of women and queer contributors, with a range of opinions from wanting to work in tandem with more ‘masculine’ political groups, to advocating for full autonomy of feminine and queer anarchists from cisgendered and heterosexual men as a strategy towards harm reduction. The argument is clear-cut that a theory of masculinity in line with the values of horizontal, communitarian care politics is the responsibility of men themselves, not women or gender queer people. At the same time, anarchism as inherently pluralist, inclusive, and non-hierarchical cannot simply condemn or disregard masculinities and move on. In presenting a gendered understanding of the division of roles in alternative and social movement spaces, Constellations of Care highlights the unclosed gap between a queer feminist politics of care and both institutional and radical politics that are understood to be masculine.

“Safety, however, is itself a problematic concept. First off, there is no way to ensure 100 percent safety. It’s all just harm reduction. Presenting a space as “safe” might actually make it less safe because if people walk in expecting to be shielded from any and all harm, they are defenseless.” – Corinne, Aurore, Éris and Tom, members of the Bibliothèque Anarcha-Féministe of Toulouse, France in their chapter Tea, Books and Thresholds (p. 63)

The question of whether or not to constantly reassert the validity of care work against a harmful masculinist anarchism raises another dilemma. How much care work is based around providing material or affective support, and how much is based on shielding marginalized people from harm? As the above quote from a self-managed library in Toulouse notes, the idea of total safety can be deceiving and utopian, as different individuals’ needs and expectations for safety come into conflict with each other. Furthermore, a collective that believes itself to be ‘safe’ based on its standpoint or on the identities represented in its membership may be less likely to take accountability or accept criticism when real damage occurs. Thus, several entries emphasize the importance of both anticipating and pre-empting both the external harm that their members openly face, as well as harms that may be committed within movement spaces. Collectives thus recount dedicating large amounts of time to understanding any instances or allegations of harm and determining what accountability and reparation measures are appropriate. More traditional forms of anarchist organizing have objected to the amount of dedication anarcha-feminists hold to addressing harm, arguing that it takes time and energy away from more ‘positive’ activities. However, as Benji Hart of the Chicago youth anti-war collective Dissenters explains, “Anarchist feminist politics do not teach us to reject all structure, they invite us to imagine structures that are shaped by and intended to protect the autonomy of the most vulnerable versus the interests of the most powerful” (p. 360). Redressing harm forms the basis for building new structures that address the needs of the most vulnerable and sheds light on the ways in which anarchists unwittingly reproduce coercive or authoritarian systems.

Ultimately, many of the authors conclude that some amount of plurality is necessary to be able to provide the care and protection that is required by diverse populations with divergent needs for safety. This calls up the metaphor of the constellation in the title, casting care networks as being widespread and just as diverse and loosely organized as the communities they serve.

“We ended it while we still appreciated each other, we ended it without being in debt, and in fact… and we ended by each of us moving toward other horizons.” – Cindy Barukh Milstein Stitching Together our Worlds (p. 228)

Anarchic collectives, Milstein notes, have several points of departure from more institutionalized organizations, even if both appear on the surface to do similar work. One key difference comes in the way that the temporality and impact of work are linked. For a state or non-profit organization, productivity is linked to temporality through quarterly goals, annual reports, and funding cycles, all of which carry the urgency of proving both effectiveness and efficiency. The longevity of such organizations is tied to their ability to consistently meet a standard of efficacy that is defined by funders.

Self-organized and funded groups are under no such obligation, thus tend to consider the best measure of whether their work is needed and should continue through relational and affective lenses. If the care provided is nurturing relationships, and the members of the collective maintain an intuitive sense that the work is sustainable and ‘worth it’, collectives carry on. Temporalities of anarchic care thus ebb and flow with the broader energy and demands of social movements, direct communication with communities, and the needs and limitations of caregivers. This places decisions about effectiveness and temporality out of the hands of funders, and into the hands of those directly doing the work. As a result, many of the authors actively celebrate the fact that they are not bound to an outside standard of productivity, and all the flexibility or joy of simply doing nothing once in a while that comes with it. The Bibliothèque Anarcha-Féministe of Toulouse, or the Pink Peacock, a “queer, Yiddish, anarchist feminist, anticapitalist cafe” in Glasgow (p. 151) relish in offering their services for free or on a pay-what you can basis, using community space and volunteer labor to make themselves available. Philadelphia’s Nightshade collective and OccupyICE, Colombian Community Kitchens, or members of the Mačjak squat in Ljubljana pointed out the importance of simply claiming public space for their use or enjoyment without asking permission.

“In Prison, we referred to health care as ‘health scare.’ It was such a dehumanizing process to submit a written application to see a doctor, wait for weeks, and then just be dismissed, patronized or put down during the two-minute consultation…my friend nearly died of cancer in prison after the authorities failed on nine separate occasions to take her to hospital appointments for lifesaving surgery.” – Nicole Rose/Solidarity Apothecary in the Chapter Solidarity Apothecary: Reclaiming Life (p. 179)

The other major distinction between institutional and anarchic forms of care comes in whether there are certain forms of control or coercion built into receiving care. This quote comes from Nicole Rose, an apothecary and herbal medicinalist who works with incarcerated people. While she makes no claim that herbal cures, especially ones that can be accessed from inside prison, are a match for conditions like cancer, she emphasizes her interventions are meant to humanize patients and come with no strings attached. The options offered by the state can be quite effective, but severe limitations in access communicate that institutional providers in this context do not prioritize the health or quality of life of specific individuals, leading to more dehumanization rather than its alleviation.

Other contributors, especially those working with unhoused communities, sex workers, drug users, and undocumented immigrants consistently noted the trade-off between receiving state-sponsored care and being subject to policing and surveillance. Anarchic care is focused on continuing to allow people to live outside of systems, such as housing markets, immigration laws, and minimum wage labor, without using access to care to guide vulnerable people into specific economic and social modalities. While this does not lead to a condemnation of many programs that vulnerable people are able to access through state care, anarchists such as Bayla (Bay) Ostrich of the Network for Reproductive Options, a grassroots abortion referral and funding network (p. 375) or the Philadelphia Nightshade Collective’s Raani Begum (p. 100), are critical both of the ways that healthcare housing, food distribution, and rehabilitation programs impose a mold of the ‘good’ and thus masculinized citizen, and also how failure to meet that standard can result in a loss of care or even criminalization.

“Creating spaces of joy has literally always been how Black and Brown people have sustained ourselves throughout history and fluctuating degrees of violence or being targeted” Claire Barrera of Brown Girl Rise in Brown Girl Rise: How We Take Care of Our Own (p. 119)

Perhaps the most consistent theme throughout the book is summed up by a sense of political pleasure, a certain form of happiness that comes with being in a trusted community, united by common ideals and sense of purpose. Over and over, the authors emphasize that the most important aspect of care is providing a space where people can simply enjoy themselves, be happy, and find community with people who might understand them. In reading Constellations of Care, one can sometimes tangibly feel the affection that the contributors hold for their respective collectives.

Thus, the next time you find yourself asking what is to be done in situations of hopelessness and marginalization, the answer might be to pick up this book, read an entry or two, and hopefully be inspired to show care to someone around you.

author: Unknown
title: İsrail'de çıkış anketleri: Netanyahu çoğunluğu sağlayamıyor
content:
İsrail'de 26. Knesset'i belirlemek üzere yapılan seçimlerde sandıkların yerel saatle 22.00'de  kapanmasının ardından yayımlanan çıkış anketleri, hükümet kurma müzakerelerinde Filistinli Arap yurttaşların partilerinin belirleyici konuma gelebileceğini gösterdi.




Netanyahu'nun bloku 61 sandalyeye ulaşamıyor




120 üyeli Knesset'te parlamenter çoğunluk için 61 sandalye gerekiyor. Üç büyük televizyonun güncellenen çıkış anketleri Netanyahu'nun Likud, Şas, Birleşik Tevrat Yahudiliği ve aşırı sağ partilerden oluşan blokuna 50 sandalye öngörüyor.




Eisenkot öncülüğündeki Netanyahu karşıtı partiler ise 52 sandalyede kalıyor. Böylece iki blok da tek başına çoğunluğun altında kalıyor.




Bununla birlikte, Netanyahu'ya yakın yayın çizgisiyle bilinen Kanal 14'ün çıkış anketi iktidar blokuna 60 sandalye veriyor. Bu projeksiyonda Likud 30 sandalyeye ulaşıyor. Ancak Kanal 14'ün tahmininde de Netanyahu bloku çoğunluk sınırının bir sandalye gerisinde.







Çıkış anketleri ile kesin sonuçlar geleneksel olarak çok yakın




İsrail’de çıkış anketleri genellikle kesin sonuçlara birkaç sandalyelik farkla yaklaşırken, 2022 seçimlerinde Netanyahu blokuna 61–62 sandalye öngörülmesine karşılık blok 64 sandalye kazanmıştı; dolayısıyla bu kez üç büyük kanalın ortak 50 sandalye tahmini, Netanyahu’nun çoğunluğu sağlayamayacağına ilişkin güçlü bir gösterge olmakla birlikte kesin sonuç sayılmaz.







Kamu yayıncısı Kan 11 ile Kanal 12 ve Kanal 13'ün ilk projeksiyonlarında Likud 24–25 sandalyeyle birinci, eski Genelkurmay Başkanı Gadi Eisenkot'un Yashar partisi 21–23 sandalyeyle ikinci sırada yer aldı.




Eski Başbakan Naftali Bennett'in B'Yachad (Birlikte) ittifakı 12–14, Yair Golan'ın Demokratlar Partisi 9–10 sandalye düzeyinde görünüyor.




Arap partileri 18 sandalyeye yükseliyor




Çıkış anketlerinin en dikkat çekici sonuçlarından biri, Filistinli Arap yurttaşların partilerinin parlamentodaki temsilinde öngörülen artış.




Hadash, Ta'al ve Balad'ın oluşturduğu Birleşik Liste'ye 11, Mansur Abbas'ın Ra'am partisine ise 7 sandalye öngörülüyor. Böylece Arap partilerinin toplam sandalye sayısı 18'e ulaşabilecek.




Bu sonuç, 2022 seçimlerinde toplam 10 sandalye elde eden Arap partilerin temsili açısından önemli bir artışı demek.




İsrail Komünist Partisi'nin de yer aldığı Hadash'ın Birleşik Liste içindeki temsili sürecek gibi görünüyor. Ancak Ofer Cassif dahil komünist adayların milletvekilliklerinin kesinleşmesi için resmî oy sayımının tamamlanması gerekiyor.




Koalisyonun anahtarı Arap partilerinde




Çıkış anketlerindeki dağılım, Netanyahu karşıtı muhalefetin parlamenter çoğunluğu sağlayabilmek için Arap partilerinin desteğine ihtiyaç duyacağını gösteriyor.




Eisenkot çevresindeki muhalefet partilerinin 52 sandalyesine Ra'am'ın yedi sandalyesi eklendiğinde toplam 59'a ulaşılıyor. Bu durumda Birleşik Liste'den en az iki milletvekilinin daha desteği gerekiyor.




Ancak Eisenkot ve diğer merkez sağ muhalefet liderlerinin Arap partileriyle resmî koalisyon kurmaya karşı tutumları, parlamenter aritmetiğin siyasal bir hükümet anlaşmasına dönüşmesini güçleştiriyor.




Bu koşullarda, Arap partilerinin dışarıdan desteklediği bir azınlık hükümeti kurulamazsa veya partiler arasında yeni bir koalisyon düzenlemesi yapılamazsa, yeniden seçim seçenekleri gündemde.




Katılımda büyük artış




Seçim gecesi açıklanan verilere göre katılım yüzde 77,7'ye ulaştı. Bu oran son yılların en yüksek katılım düzeylerinden biri olarak bildirildi.




Filistinli Arap seçmenlerin katılımına ilişkin ülke çapında kesinleşmiş ayrı bir oran henüz açıklanmadı. Arap partilerinin sandalye projeksiyonlarındaki artış ise bu seçmenlerin hükümet aritmetiğindeki ağırlığını ortaya koyuyor.




Resmî sayım bekleniyor




İsrail Merkez Seçim Komitesinin oy sayımı sürüyor. Çıkış anketleri kesin seçim sonuçlarını yansıtmıyor ve sandalye dağılımı resmî sayımla değişebilir.




Reuters'a göre sayımın 30 Ekim'e kadar tamamlanması, sonuçların ise 4 Kasım'da resmen yayımlanması bekleniyor.




Çıkış anketlerinin doğrulanması hâlinde seçim, Netanyahu'nun parlamenter çoğunluğunu yeniden elde edemediği, ancak muhalefetin de Arap partilerinin desteği olmaksızın hükümet kuramadığı bir tablo ortaya çıkaracak.

author: cnt.es
title: Comunicado de CNT sobre los incidentes en Bilbao
content:
Leer en

Castellano

Euskera







Castellano

Comunicado de CNT sobre los incidentes en Bilbao




Desde CNT queremos desmarcarnos y mostrar nuestra preocupación ante los incidentes registrados la noche del 26 al 27 de octubre en Bilbao tras la finalización del acto de protesta contra la presencia de un provocador de extrema derecha en nuestra ciudad. Diversas organizaciones, asociaciones y colectivos antifascistas secundamos la convocatoria, que en todo momento transcurrió de manera tan multitudinaria como pacífica.




La movilización se dio por terminada y quedó disuelta tras conocer la cancelación del acto ultraderechista.




Fue en ese momento cuando elementos desconocidos, que nada tenían que ver con los convocantes, comenzaron a provocar incidentes, con el resultado conocido.




Aún desconocemos con certeza quiénes fueron los instigadores e iniciadores de los disturbios, pero nos resulta llamativa la juventud, inexperiencia y actitud caótica de los participantes en los mismos. Nos preocupa la utilización política que se está haciendo de estos hechos, con la intención de criminalizar las legítimas y necesarias movilizaciones populares de la izquierda contra el fascismo y a favor de los derechos laborales y sociales. Observamos una clara intención por parte de la derecha mediática y política de trasladar la imagen de un clima de caos y violencia en las calles, con el objetivo de influir electoralmente para beneficiar a partidos defensores de planteamientos autoritarios.




Desde CNT, queremos alertar a la sociedad en general, a la juventud en particular y a las personas más oprimidas, del riesgo de ser manipuladas, instrumentalizadas y utilizadas por sectores de la derecha y la ultraderecha para favorecer sus intereses en contra de las libertades y derechos de la clase trabajadora.




La mejor manera de evitar este riesgo es la organización y militancia política, social, sindical y vecinal.




Unidad, organización, cabezas frías y claridad de ideas.







Euskera

CNTren komunikatua Bilboko istiluen inguruan.




CNT sindikatutik gure kezka adierazi nahi dugu urriaren 26ko gauean Bilbon izandako istiluengatik, gure hirian eskuin muturreko probokatzaile baten presentziaren aurkako protesta-ekitaldia amaitu ondoren. Hainbat erakunde, elkarte eta kolektibo antifaxistek bat egin genuen deialdiarekin, manifestazio jendetsu eta baketsua izan zen.




Ultraeskuindarrak bere ekitaldia bertan behera utziko zuela jakinarazi zuenean, mobilizazioa amaitutzat eman eta manifestazioa desegin zen.




Une horretan, deitzaileekin zerikusirik ez zuten pertsona ezezagunak istiluak sortzen hasi ziren, denok ezagutzen ditugun gertaerak sortuz.




Oraindik ez dakigu nortzuk piztu eta bultzatu zituzten istiluak, baina deigarria egiten zaigu parte-hartzaileen gaztetasuna, esperientziarik eza eta jarrera kaotikoa. Kezkatzen gaitu gertatutakoari buruz egiten ari den erabilera politikoak, faxismoaren aurka eta lan eta gizarte eskubideen alde beharrezkoak eta legitimoak diren ezkerreko herri-mobilizazioak kriminalizatzeko. Ikusten dugu eskuin mediatiko eta politikoak asmo argia duela kaleetan kaos eta indarkeria giroa dagoela erakusteko, hauteskundeetan eragina izateko eta planteamendu autoritarioak defendatzen dituzten alderdiei mesede egiteko.




CNTtik, gizarteari oro har, zapalduenei eta gazteei bereziki ohartarazi nahi diegu eskuinaren eta ultraeskuinaren sektoreek manipulatuak, instrumentalizatuak eta erabiliak izateko arriskuaz, langileen askatasun eta eskubideen aurka beren interesak bultzatzeko.




Arrisku hori saihesteko modurik onena antolakuntza eta militantzia politiko, soziala, sindikala eta auzotarra da.

Batasuna, antolakuntza, buru hotzak eta ideia argiak.




La entrada 

Comunicado de CNT sobre los incidentes en Bilbao

 se publicó primero en 

Confederación Nacional del Trabajo

.

author: Keelan Jacobs
title: Canada appeals landmark rulings that found it has legal duties on First Nations water and housing
content:
Chiefs from Shamattawa, St. Theresa Point and Sandy Lake First Nations return to court this week to defend landmark Federal Court decisions that recognized Canada’s legal duties to provide safe drinking water and adequate housing on reserve — rulings the Carney government is appealing.

“The Government of Canada continues to fight us in Court over one of our most basic rights as human beings,” said Chief Jordna Hill of Shamattawa First Nation. “But Canada knows what it has done to First Nations people is wrong.”

“Canada ships bottled water to reserves for their federal employees, while First Nations people living under long-term drinking water advisories are forced to use the contaminated tap water.”

The two court cases in question that the Federal Government is appealing are Shamattawa First Nation v. Canada [Water] and St. Theresa Point First Nation v. Canada [Housing].

The federal government is appealing two decisions released in December 2025 by Federal Court Justice Paul Favel. In those decisions, he ruled that Canada owes fiduciary duties, a common law duty of care, and Charter rights to equality, life, liberty and security of the person, and religion in relation to on-reserve drinking water and housing.

According to the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs, Canada continues to argue it has no legally enforceable obligations, attributes difficulties on reserves to First Nations themselves, and is seeking costs against the First Nations.

Chief Elvin Flett of St. Theresa Point Anisininew Nation said the federal government created and reinforced the housing crisis.

“The federal government put First Nations in an impossible position by creating and reinforcing our housing crisis. We are now living in a permanent state of emergency. We have had no choice but to turn to the courts for our survival,” he said.

“While we would have preferred to work with Canada as nation-to-nation partners, Canada has made clear that we will need to enforce our rights through the courts for anything to change.”

According to the Assembly of Manitoba’s Chiefs Favel’s water decision ran 59 pages. and rested on roughly 10,000 pages of evidence.

The housing decision was 122 pages and drew on about 12,000 pages.

The court found that many members live on reserves that are isolated and “lack a viable economic base,” making commercial and residential development impractical. In those circumstances, the judge wrote, Canada can either provide the resources needed or restore First Nations to a position where they can provide for themselves, but it cannot maintain the status quo.

The court also rejected Canada’s attempt to ignore the legacy of colonial policies and the Indian Act, which has controlled nearly every aspect of life on reserve.

Favel found that a structural deficit has left many First Nations unable to keep up with housing needs since the creation of reserves.

Chief Delores Kakegamic of Sandy Lake First Nation said the conditions would be treated as a political crisis anywhere else.

“For too long Canada has swept the housing crisis on reserves under the rug. Canada’s politicians and bureaucrats have been satisfied with doing the bare minimum while First Nation members were forced to live in decrepit and overcrowded homes that harm their health, safety, and community,” she said.

“If these on-reserve housing conditions existed elsewhere, it would be a political crisis.”

Grand Chief Kyra Wilson of the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs linked the appeals to the language of partnership heard at this week’s First Nations–First Ministers Meeting in Ottawa.

“At the First Nations–First Ministers Meeting, Canada spoke of partnership. This week, it will stand in a Winnipeg courtroom and argue it owes First Nations no duty to provide safe drinking water or adequate housing. Canada cannot have it both ways,” Wilson said. “Instead of spending undisclosed sums on lawyers to fight Shamattawa and St. Theresa Point, Canada should honour its Treaty obligations and put that money into water plants and homes.”

Court confirms Canada is liable for water and housing woes

The December 2025 decisions by Favel are the first contested rulings to hold that Canada owes First Nations legally enforceable duties to provide reliable access to safe drinking water on reserve and adequate housing on remote reserves.

The federal government has tabled the First Nations Clean Water Act while simultaneously arguing in court against it.

Until these judgments, the federal government largely treated water and housing on reserve as policy or funding questions rather than judicious legal obligations.

If the Federal Courts of Appeal upholds the decisions, First Nations gain a stronger judicial tool to compel action and remedies instead of relying solely on political commitments or discretionary funding programs.

The Federal Court of Appeal will hear the cases on Oct. 28 and 29. The case will also be livestreamed.

Keelan is Anishinaabe from Walpole Island First Nation (Bkejwanong Territory). He graduated with an Honours B.A. In Political Science from the University of Toronto and follows the stories where power, money and public policy meet. Keelan has a strong interest in economics and finance, and is a lifelong hockey and sports fan.

author: Unknown
title: Rising from the Ashes : The Yellow Vests Return as France Burns
content:
Helicopter hovering over Place de la République during the curfew implemented in Paris.




Over the past month, France has erupted in a nationwide rebellion that has shaken the ruling order to its core. As politicians of all stripes focus on polishing their brand image for the next 

presidential election

 in May 2027, high school students have 

organized

 on a grassroots level. Through occupations, blockades, and street protests, they have taken a stand against both the deplorable conditions of their schools today and the 

menacing future

 that looms ahead of them. They took France and the entire world by surprise with their determined mass resistance and their courage in confronting the police forces sent to repress them.




After weeks of daily actions and nationwide demonstrations, leading to an unprecedented wave of arrests targeting rebellious youth, the Macron government was reaching a political impasse. It desperately tried to buy time by opening dialogue with some student organizations, in hopes of blunting the force of the movement until the upcoming school break slowed its momentum.




However, the authorities had not anticipated several developments. First, the students multiplied their force by joining the national call to take the streets on Saturday, October 17 to reignite the 

Yellow Vests movement

, the popular mobilization against high gas prices and government austerity policies that emerged in 2018. Second, anger over the intense police violence of the previous weeks drew even more people in the streets. Third and most dramatically, the day’s protests snowballed into an insurrectionary situation that 

surpassed

 what we experienced eight years ago during the height of the Yellow Vests struggle.




This new wave of collective rage that swept over the cities of France last week has plunged the current government into a deeper crisis. Politicians scrambled to capitalize on the upheavals, while authorities responded by implementing more authoritarian policies on a national scale. In the following article, we describe how the dramatic events around October 17 unfolded, analyzing their significance and reflecting on what is at stake.







 




Burning barricades blocking a narrow street in the historical part of downtown Bordeaux (October 17.)













Glowing Embers of Discontent




In 2018, the Yellow Vest movement emerged into the French political landscape seemingly out of nowhere. This grassroots wave of protests formed a reaction against rising gas prices and worsening living conditions among the country’s lower and middle classes. After decades of economic crises, inflation, and harsh neoliberal austerity policies, a portion of the population was feeling isolated, disenfranchised, and abandoned. The capitalist dream of ease and opulence that successive governments had promoted was turning into a living nightmare for a growing number of individuals. The politically diverse movement, named after the fluorescent emergency vests drivers were required to carry in their vehicles, made visible the ongoing economic emergency that gripped more and more people across France.




Due to its open-ended form, the Yellow Vests initially attracted populists from the left and the right and autonomous participants with a range of grievances against the ruling order. From the beginning, an internal struggle unfolded within the movement as radical participants 

confronted

 far-right and fascist factions and attempted to prevent cooptation by reactionaries. Over time, the Yellow Vest movement gradually shifted to embrace more anti-capitalist and anti-state perspectives.




Since the initial wave of Yellow Vest protests died down in 2020, the economic situation in France has worsened. The gap between rich and poor has continued to 

widen

, while the Macron government accelerated its dismantling of public services. International conflicts from Ukraine to Iran have further impacted the French economy, worsening inflation and driving up prices on essential goods, energy, and gas.




It is no surprise that people facing such economic pressure would take to the streets to express their discontent. And what better way to threaten the current ruling order than to bring the Yellow Vest movement back from the dead?




It is difficult to know the exact source of this proposal, which began to spread on social media platforms such as Tik Tok and Instagram in September and rapidly went viral. However, veterans from the Yellow Vest struggle along with radical activists, leftist organizations, and student groups alike reposted this call on their own platforms. Unlike the more open-ended participation in the initial swell of populist rage in 2018, this combination of forces left no space for the far-right to try to infiltrate and co-opt this emerging movement.




These groups announced October 17 as a nationwide day of mobilization against the rising cost of living. In the days leading up to the demonstrations, the government remained unsure about what to expect and how to handle the upcoming demonstrations. Focused on defusing the student crisis via democratic tricks and judicial repression, they failed to gauge the looming popular anger that was rising.




Several student organizations issued statements online confirming that they would join the Yellow Vests during the day of action to broaden the base of their weeks-long struggle. Similarly, a range of leftist political parties and organizations called on their supporters to flood the streets to protest the economic situation and the planned budget cuts announced several days prior. On October 1, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu 

presented

 the government’s 2027 budget, which proposed to reduce public spending by €54 billion, including cuts to retirement pensions, family pensions, and state workers’ wages. If approved, this budget would plunge the French populace into even harsher austerity than we are already experiencing.




Nonetheless, the authorities seemed to have not understood the explosive political situation they faced, nor did they identify what was at stake. Did they really fail to see how the extreme violence students experienced at the hands of police over the previous weeks would provoke outrage and spur people to fight back? Did they really think that we would continue to silently bow down in front of their decisions as they made our lives more miserable day after day?







 




Police forces charging at protesters in the streets of Lille (October 17).










Already weakened by the student mobilization, the government did not have enough time to prepare properly to fight on another front. As a result, their clumsy and erratic response mirrored their handling of the student unrest over the past month.




The Paris Police Prefecture anticipated that between 20,000 and 40,000 protesters would converge in the streets of the French capital city on October 17. Fearing 

potential violence

 and public disorder, they decided to cancel the itinerary of the demonstration organized by university students. This march had intended to link Place de la République with Place de la Concorde, near to many symbols of power such as the 

Assemblée Nationale

 (the National Assembly) and the 

Palais de l’Élysée

 (the Presidential Palace). Instead, authorities allowed the demonstration to connect Place de la République with Place de la Nation. Meanwhile, a second demonstration organized by a revived Yellow Vest Movement and trade unions was also supposed to connect Place de l’Opéra with Place de la Bastille.




While Place de la République and Place de la Bastille are the usual gathering areas for social movements and demonstrations in Paris, the decision of the organizers to plan routes that would allow people to reach areas such as Place de la Concorde and Place de l’Opéra presented a clear message of defiance to authorities. These areas are located within some of the wealthiest and most tourist-heavy districts in Paris and contain numerous official buildings and symbols of capitalism and state power for protesters to target.




Before the day of action, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez announced that to maintain “peace and order” in the streets, polices forces would be allowed to use stun grenades. Only a few days earlier, following the 

horrific permanent injury

 of a teenager during clashes with police forces, the government announced that the use of these specific grenades against young protesters would be suspended until further notice. However, citing the involvement of other demographics of protesters in the upcoming actions, authorities revised their law enforcement strategy by reauthorizing the use of these weapons, voluntarily turning a blind eye to the fact that students would be heavily represented among the ranks of demonstrators that day.




Such announcements form part of a strategy to instill fear among potential demonstrators and discourage individuals from taking the streets. Yet the government’s efforts to intimidate the movements failed, and popular determination remained intact. All eyes turned to the streets of France as October 17 approached—and soon the government would have to face its own worst fears.




A Contagious Rage




October 17 saw actions of unprecedented number and intensity breaking out all over France. Many observers, including politicians, described scenes of chaos that surpassed the most memorable riots of the Yellow Vest movement years before.




As of this writing, it remains difficult to provide a full account of all of the cities that experienced the fury of this new Yellow Vest 

storm

 or to offer a comprehensive list of the actions that took place that day. However, government and media sources acknowledged at least 110 locations throughout France that were impacted by protests on October 17. These ranged from peaceful occupations of highway roundabouts to attacks against police, government, and corporate targets, encompassing an extraordinary range of tactics.




The following selection of actions, while far from exhaustive, illustrates the level of intensity of the day’s protests. The events of October 17 have been widely reported and discussed. Nevertheless, 

actions

 speak louder than words, and the rioters that unleashed hell in the streets offer living proof of our own agency to take back control of our lives and our future.







 




A map of France showing a partial list of cities where actions took place on October 17 as the Yellow Vest movement surged back to life.










Reports from Paris




Early in the morning, we learned that any gathering in the Champs-Élysées area was strictly forbidden. The legacy of fear in this wealthy district still remains strong years after the riots of the Yellow Vest era. Authorities also decided at the last minute to cancel the original 

itinerary

 of the afternoon demonstration. Instead of departing from Place de la Bastille, people would have to gather at Place de la République before marching through the northern districts of Paris towards Place de Clichy. By imposing this new route, authorities aimed to push protesters further away from the wealthiest districts of Paris and its symbols of power.




The morning began with a coordinated attack by around one hundred protesters against the headquarters of the television channel CNews. The demonstrators threw multiple projectiles at the building, breaking some windows, before dispersing as police forces arrived. Since its purchase by far-right billionaire 

Vincent Bolloré

 in 2016, the channel has become the major platform on French television for conservative, reactionary, and fascist ideologies. Today, CNews has become one of the country’s most viewed 24-hour news channels, playing a critical role in 

enabling

 the surge of the National Rally party of Marine Le Pen and normalizing its racist ideas within mainstream political debate. The action drew attention to the central role of corporate media in manipulating popular opinion and spreading harmful political agendas.




Before midday, authorities were already reporting multiple unauthorized gatherings in different areas of Paris. Some attempted to get as close as possible to the Palais de l’Élysée before being pushed back by police units ordered to defend the seats of power. Reusing a strategy that proved effective during the Yellow Vest movement of 2018, these groups refused to follow a specific planned route, understanding that speed, spontaneity, and freedom of movement remain critical assets during street confrontations. BRAV-M motorized police units took charge of stopping the progression of these unruly groups. Their response followed a specific pattern: arriving rapidly on site and reacting as quickly as possible to attack protesters and disperse them with tear gas, stun grenades, or rubber bullets. Their targets then retreated and regrouped elsewhere. This cat-and-mouse game between demonstrators and police would continue all day long, punctuated by moments of conflict at fixed points.







 




Intense riots unfolded at Place de la République on October 17, after law enforcement officers kettled the demonstrators before the official departure of the afternoon procession.










On the other side of Paris, people were already gathering at Place de la République before the official departure time of the authorized afternoon demonstration. The area was packed and police forces were also present on site, controlling access to the square in an effort to contain the crowd. Tensions increased rapidly, and clashes soon erupted between protesters and the agents of “peace and order.” Taking advantage of the layout of this main square, law enforcement successfully kettled the demonstration and blanketed the square with thick clouds of tear gas on multiple occasions. In response, crowds surged back and forth, as demonstrators fled the irritating gas while rioters counterattacked with projectiles thrown at police lines. At some point during these confrontations, some rebels set a car on fire.




Place de la République remained under police lockdown. Large crowds continued to arrive near the square but were prevented from joining the gathering. Soon, thousands of determined Yellow Vesters, students, activists, families, and rioters were surrounding the square, occupying the main boulevards and nearby streets behind police lines. Protesters seized the opportunity to launch different wildcat marches that set out from République in multiple directions. During these joyful wanderings, massive property destruction and looting took place. Small groups of highly motivated individuals attacked many kinds of stores, enjoying the simple pleasure of getting everything they wanted for free—a feeling long forgotten within our consumer capitalist society, where everything has a price. In some areas, looting and property destruction occurred on such a wide scale that not a single storefront remained intact.







 




Expensive clothing stores were targeted during the riots that spread throughout France on October 17. This picture was taken in Paris and the graffiti reads: “Arc’teryx for all!”










Riots spread throughout the city all afternoon. Thick clouds of smoke from flaming barricades billowed above the Parisian skyline, punctuated by explosions from fireworks or stun grenades echoing through the streets of numerous districts. Intense confrontations with police forces took place in the districts of République, Bastille, Châtelet-Les Halles, Madeleine, and Le Marais, among others. The outnumbered police forces were clearly overwhelmed by the insurrectionary situation unfolding the streets: burning barricades by the hundreds, cars set ablaze, numerous attacks on symbols of capitalism, and more. On multiple occasions, officers had no option but to retreat from confrontations as angry rioters got the upper hand and took control of entire streets. These moments showed plainly the powerlessness of the authorities to maintain their “peace and order” in the streets of France’s capital city.




As the sun set, demonstrators attempted to converge on the Champs-Élysées, building more barricades and confronting police forces in the neighboring streets. The deep darkness of the autumn night proved the perfect ally for rioters who wanted to continue raging until the early hours. Mobile groups continued to loot stores regardless of what they were selling: clothing, electronics, video games, pharmacy, tobacco, and other outlets all saw their goods redistributed outside the logic of the market. In some instances, multiple attacks targeted single stores on different occasions. Police forces continued to chase the remaining protesters throughout the night as the intensity of the upheaval gradually declined.




While some regions of the city saw widespread looting amidst flaming cars and barricades, others saw calmer mobilizations. During the afternoon, as offensive street actions broke out in some areas, other demonstrators joined the official march composed of students and leftist organizations, walking through the northern part of the city in a completely different atmosphere. During this more traditional march, demonstrators did not engage in property destruction or confrontations with police, sometimes remaining unaware that intense riots were happening just a few streets away. Yet the following morning, visible proof of these dual realities lingered in the remains of burned barricades, shattered targets, and looted stores.







 




A video-game store looted in Paris (October 17).










Beyond the Capital: An Overview of Resistance




Paris was far from the only city in France where protesters overcame police forces and freely expressed their rage on October 17. In fact, similarly to the Yellow Vest mobilizations years before, some of the most impressive actions of the day took place elsewhere. One of the major strengths of this day of action was its decentralized character, which allowed grassroot forces to gather locally and forced police forces to disperse throughout the entire country. The scarcity of law enforcement in specific cities combined with the unstoppable determination of rioters led to extensive 

attacks

 against institutions of power and their symbols.




Here

 is an overview of highlights from the day’s actions in other French cities:







In Marseille, confrontations between protesters and police forces began early in the morning and continued all day long. Angry demonstrators succeeded in keeping police forces in check. During the day, crowds attacked at least two police stations, stormed City Hall, and looted and ransacked numerous stores. Local authorities announced that at the height of the riots, some 30,000 individuals were engaging in looting, property destruction, and direct confrontations with law enforcement.










 




Rioters attacking a police station in Marseille (October 17).













In Bordeaux, protesters ransacked the Palais de la Bourse, the location of the Chamber of Commerce and Industry and the commercial court. Demonstrators also rampaged through the main shopping street, looting numerous stores and setting a sport retail store on fire after emptying all of its goods. Intense confrontations with police forces took place in front of the City Hall. A riot police vehicle was attacked and burnt. Some protesters also raided the private residence of a local government representative.







By the end of the day, the situation in Bordeaux had gotten so out of control that local authorities received assistance from the RAID, a specialized response unit of the national police. For example, the RAID took part of the assault at the Bataclan during the terror 

attacks

 of November 15, 2025.







 




The day after the storm, somewhere in downtown Bordeaux.













In Nantes, demonstrators experienced brutal police violence even before the departure of the authorized demonstration. Anger against these attacks led to hours of riots in the city. Police units were forced to back down on several occasions, allowing protesters to progressively retake control of the streets. Barricades appeared throughout the streets, the train station was vandalized, and several stores were invaded. At the end of the afternoon, confrontations continued to take place and law enforcement deployed armored vehicles in the streets.










 




A protester kicking a tear gas canister in Nantes (October 17.)
















In Rennes, demonstrators started the day with numerous blockades before converging to the main demonstration. Dozens of barricades were set on fire, some construction equipment found along the route was deployed to block the progress of law enforcement, and protesters engaged in various clashes with police. As in other cities, department stores were also looted.










In Lyon, protesters let their rage explode. Massive street confrontations with police forces took place in several areas, while rioters looted everything they could. The arson attack on the tourist office at Place Bellecourt exemplified the intensity of the day’s actions.













 




The Lyon tourist office burns to the ground (October 17).













In Lille, demonstrators attacked several entrances of the City Hall before finally succeeding in breaking in and rampaging through the mayor’s office. A movie theater was also devoured by flames.










 




Young protesters confront the real “agents of chaos” in Lille (October 17).










During this nationwide insurrection, protesters relentlessly attacked all kinds of symbols of power, from police stations and prefecture buildings to city halls, in cities such as Caen, Angers, Orléans, Brest, Avignon, and Grenoble, just to name a few. In one of the day’s most spectacular attacks, protesters burned down the city hall of Limoges, which authorities later 

confirmed

 is now “largely lost.”







 




The Limoges City Hall being devoured by flames, (October 17).










Besides the widespread confrontations with police forces in the streets, demonstrators also targeted key infrastructures to disrupt the flow of people and goods. In Montpellier, protesters shut down the train station, while Reims, Chambéry, Toulon, and Tours saw main roads and freeways blocked and gas stations targeted.




Reflections on an Insurrection




The events of October 17 overwhelmed all expectations of both the state and the movement. How did this happen? What does this explosion of insurrectionary energy across the country tell us about the political situation and the movement’s possibilities?




Since the emergence of the first Yellow Vest movement in 2018, its participants have come and gone as its character shifted over time. As noted above, after several months of unrest, the movement gradually evolved towards a more distinctly anti-capitalist approach and focused on active resistance to police violence and government austerity measures. Such political positions, as well as the more openly offensive tactics embraced by its more revolutionary participants, might have scared away some less radical demonstrators.




Nevertheless, Yellow Vesters remained massively present in the streets during other important moments, such as the annual 

May Day

 processions and the pension reform 

strikes

 of 2023.




Participants in the movement appeared less visibly as a force in the streets during the past few years, as many stopped wearing the symbolic fluorescent emergency vest to preserve anonymity. Nonetheless, they continued to organize on a local scale within groups that remain active to this day. It was exhilarating to see them return in large numbers for this nationwide call, as some played an important role alongside other radicals during street confrontations and riots.







 




Yellow Vesters in front of a burning barricade, somewhere in Rouen (October 17).










The number and intensity of actions carried out on October 17 was simply overwhelming and amazing. No single explanation can account for why events unfolded as they did, but several factors contributed to the day’s unprecedented explosiveness.




First, it is important to acknowledge that everything that happened on October 17 

was already happening

 during the student unrest, although on a much smaller scale. Several high schools had been vandalized or set ablaze, well-organized groups of teenagers had attacked police forces, and stores had been looted during this month-long mobilization. Protesters had been experimenting with militant tactics that generalized across the country on the day of action when the social forces engaged in the demonstrations broadened.




Moreover, the violent repression that specifically targeted teenagers from 

les banlieues

 and other low-income neighborhoods antagonized rebellious youth. The national day of action offered them an ideal opportunity to retaliate and avenge their comrades, even though some of these young rebels usually prefer to stay away from traditional social movements and political appeals.




Additionally, social media played a key role in spreading word about the day of action through different demographics of protesters. It is undeniable that these platforms helped people to organize and prepared them to gather 

en masse

 in the streets throughout France. Corporate media have reported on some so-called influencer who went as far as openly urging his followers to take the streets to riot and loot everything, as if in some real-life video game. While such instances serve more as an easy target for official condemnation than a plausible explanation for popular rebellion, the least we can say is that his words didn’t remain unheard.




On October 17, events were able to escalate rapidly due to the overall low number of police forces deployed to contain the waves of protesters present in the streets. Many people were furious and willing to act accordingly. Yellow Vesters, radicals, groups of teenage rioters—everyone wanted to participate in the festivities in one way or another and were determined get their part of the cake. As Mikhail Bakunin rightfully 

said

 in 1842: “

The passion for destruction is a creative passion, too

.”




Finally, amidst this beautiful raging chaos, anarchists, autonomous radicals, and other rebels did their part. Throughout France, we were able to seize the day and effectively attack the ruling order. From the messages left on the walls or in the streets, to the capitalist and corporate symbols targeted, to the multiple attacks against institutional buildings and police stations, the meaning was clear. We reminded those in charge that we are still here, and we will continue to relentlessly attack their world.




What happened on October 17 surpassed our expectations. The energy, determination and intensity unleashed in the streets will continue to inspire us through the challenges ahead. We were able to fight together for hours against police forces, to the point of literally defeating them. We created multiple spaces for other accomplices to develop their agency and engage in their own forms of illegal actions. Most importantly, we were able to show for an entire day that their power is nothing but a sham. It takes only courage and a brick to make it shatter.







 




Protesters building a makeshift barricade to protect themselves from police forces at Place de la Madeleine in Paris (October 17).










The Government Reacts




Around 9:00 pm, as riots were still raging across the country, the government began to construct its narrative about the day’s events through statements in the corporate media. President Emmanuel Macron stated that individuals who took part in property destruction and looting would be “prosecuted and punished” and insisted that the country would “stand united against the sowers of chaos who seek only to bring down our institutions.”




In numerous cities, mayors unanimously condemned the acts of violence that took place during demonstrations. Emmanuel Grégoire, the Mayor of Paris and member of the Socialist Party, lamented the “heavy” toll from the violence and the “immense scale” of looting in the capital, with “entire streets” having been “methodically ravaged.”




Indeed, the economic impact of the riots was extraordinary. In the following days, journalists 

claimed

 that “the extent of the damage in such a short period of time could be unprecedented,” with about 3,000 stores around the country destroyed, according to official estimates. So far, “the bill is expected to reach as much as 1.2 billion euros,” which could very likely increase if property destruction continues over the coming weeks.




Interior Minister Nuñez announced that 550,000 people had participated in the day’s protests throughout France, including 110,000 in Paris alone. Organizers estimated that between 800,000 and 1 million demonstrators had answered the nationwide call on October 17, 2026. Arrest totals were originally 

reported

 as 1,200, with almost 400 in Paris, and climbed to 1,800 the following day, with 

some sources

 claiming more than 2,300 arrests. By October 22, 

reports indicated

 that at least 2700 individuals were in custody and 217 were in pre-trial detention following the events of October 17.







 




Police forces arresting a protester during riots in Marseille (October 17).










The number of demonstrators injured during confrontations is almost impossible to estimate, with no official way of counting them. However, national media reported that in Saint-Étienne a demonstrator had his hand “

blown off

” by a grenade. This injury resulted directly from the government’s decision to reintroduce the use of this specific military weapon to repress protesters. Unsurprisingly, the state has more blood on its hands once again.




The Days After




The next morning, the people of France awoke in a haze, witnessing scenes of chaos and devastation in the streets and realizing the level of damages that had resulted from the protests. As usual following days of action, so-called “good Samaritans” and self-righteous citizens decided to help clean up their streets and neighborhoods, actively participating in the process of erasure that the ruling order implements to bring back the illusion of normality.




Owners and employees of stores that experienced lootings or property destructions on the previous day complained to corporate media outlets, using familiar arguments that stigmatized rioters and dissociated them from other demonstrators. They reinforced the narrative that such actions have nothing to do with the “legitimate” demands made by the movement. We see here how the official discourse has become ingrained within a part of the population concerned only with defending its own privileges, even as the political class and economic system the rioters fought to challenge renders those privileges ever more precarious.







 




After the riots, city workers and “good Samaritans” cleaned up the streets (Paris, October 18).










The Political Parties Attempt to Capitalize




It took no time on Sunday morning to hear official communiqués from across the political spectrum regarding the riots of the previous day. As the Ministry of the Interior 

cried

 about the nearly 1,000 officers injured the previous day, party leaders planning to run for president in the next election moved quickly to turn the events to their advantage. In unison, all sides criticized the Macron government’s handling of the unrest and management of law enforcement. However, their interpretations differed radically depending on their ideological position.




Unsurprisingly, far-right leaders focused on two of their favorite themes: national security and immigration. They emphasized on the government’s failure to maintain social order across the country or to ensure the safety of its “good citizens” and “hard workers” against the “hordes of rioters” who “disrespect and hate this country and want to destroy it by any means necessary.” According to 

them

, radical leftists and lower-class people living in 

les banlieues

 bore sole responsibility for the previous day’s violence, proving themselves to be the “enemy within” that must be eliminated. Such rhetoric echoes through the rhetoric of reactionary and fascist political leaders worldwide, exemplified by the image of 

Donald Trump

 in the US. In addition, some far-right reactionaries called on the government to implement a state of emergency without delay to restore control over the nation.




Members of the conservative right, centrists, and the liberal left also criticized the government’s law enforcement doctrine. They expressed their worries in terms of public safety and national security and requested investigations to understand how such events were able to unfold. They also reiterated their support for business owners whose property was destroyed and the families of injured officers. Finally, in almost all their statements, they accused 

La France Insoumise

 (LFI), the so-called radical left statist parliamentary party, of being co-responsible for—if not fully in control of behind the scenes—the violence in the streets. Indeed, since members of LFI had officially called on supporters to join the mobilizations on October 17, other politicians held them responsible for fomenting the rage in the streets. The Macron government also aligned with this narrative.




In response to these allegations, LFI leaders and other members of the parliamentary “radical left” publicly defended their positions. They 

attacked

 the Macron government’s decision to brutally repress any form of resistance in the streets, from the high school students of the previous weeks to the more diverse crowds of protesters present on October 17. They also refused to play the game imposed by journalists who asked them to pick a side between the Republic or rioters. Because they desire to one day hold power in France, LFI and its leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon continue to have an ambiguous political position, supporting protest in general while disavowing its ungovernable expressions. While they always take to the streets during social movement mobilizations, they commonly turn their back on demonstrators who act on their own terms outside of the state’s legal framework.




Throughout several official statements that saturated the corporate media, one concept came back in the political discourse: the “ultra-left.” The newly elected right-wing mayor of Limoges, Guillaume Guérin, emphasized this framework during his press conference following the arson that burned the City Hall to the ground. According to him, this action was the result of well-prepared members of the ultra-left who knew exactly where to attack the building.







 




Guillaume Guérin, the right-wing mayor of Limoges, during the press conference following the arson that burned the City Hall to the ground (Limoges, October 18).










The concept of the ultra-left gained traction within the French mainstream political discourse back in 2008, when the state launched its ultimately unsuccessful terrorism prosecution in the 

Tarnac case

. This concept lumps together all individuals considered by mainstream political forces to be on the left side of the radical left, from anti-statist communists and autonomists to anarchists. After the riots of October 17, anarchists and other rebels are once again in the crosshairs of the authorities and intelligence services. A couple of days later, several individuals were arrested in connection with the arson of the Limoges City Hall. So far, a 34-year-old individual linked to anarchist and radical environment circles has been 

indicted

 on three charges: “destruction as part of an organized group,” “criminal conspiracy,” and “attempted murder of a person holding public authority.”




Mayors from various cities announced that they would gather in front of city halls on Monday October 20 in defense of the French Republic and its institutions and to show support to all the “victims” of property destruction. During these so-called apolitical events, conservative politicians and defenders of the status quo assembled, and far-right activists in cities such as Lyon took the opportunity to spread their messages.




The Streets Attempt to Keep the Riots Alive




On Sunday afternoon, some determined and courageous individuals decided to push forward and riot anew in different cities. In Paris, small groups of protesters started to converge at Place de la République, but the unauthorized gathering faced an assault by police forces with tear gas canisters and stun grenades. Groups of rioters dispersed and spread through neighboring streets, creating confusion and increasing tensions in the area.




At the Quai de Valmy, near the canal Saint-Martin, people built makeshift barricades with self-service rental bikes before setting them on fire. Police forces arriving to “secure” the street were met by hostile protesters screaming, “ACAB.” In nearby Beaurepaire street, groups of young rioters looted a clothing store in front of awed bystanders who were simply enjoying a quiet sunny Sunday afternoon. Sporadic clashes with law enforcement continued until 

late at night
