En General Pueyrredón, la lista Multicolor de SUTEBA también convocó a 48 horas de paro, que incluyen a Mar del Plata

. En 

Marcos Paz, en cambio, se realizará paro este martes 27 y una jornada de protesta el miércoles 28

. Mientras que en 

Bahía Blanca, la convocatoria contempla jornadas de protesta durante ambas fechas, pero no anuncia un paro

 para esos dos días. La convocatoria también menciona a la minoría de Ensenada y a congresales y delegados de la lista Multicolor.




Para hoy, 

martes 27, la Multicolor también anuncia una movilización a las 11 en ART de CABA (Mitre y Pellegrini) y a las 13:30 a las Casa de Corrientes (Maipú 271) junto Ademys por la aparición con vida de la docente correntina Nanci Godoy, desaparecida desde el 7 de octubre y que desempeñaba como 

directora suplente de la Escuela Rural N°626 del paraje El Malezal

, en el departamento de Esquina.










 


































Ver esta publicación en Instagram






































































 




Una publicación compartida por multicolor suteba (@multicolorprovincialsuteba)













El rechazo se centra en el incremento del 6%, distribuido en dos tramos del 3% para octubre y noviembre, calculados sobre los salarios de septiembre, con una nueva discusión paritaria prevista recién para diciembre. Mientras la mayoría de los gremios del Frente de Unidad Docente Bonaerense (

SUTEBA

, 

UDOCBA

, 

SADOP

 y 

AMET)

 aceptaron la oferta – 

salvo la FEB, que rechazó la oferta y llamó a un paro de 24 horas el jueves de la semana pasada 

-, los sectores opositores la calificaron como una «

paritaria de miseria

» y 

reclamaron un salario de $1.700.000 por cargo testigo, con equiparación de módulos y horas cátedra

. También exigen que no haya docentes pobres, el cumplimiento pleno de los acuerdos paritarios y el cese de los descuentos aplicados por participar de medidas de fuerza.










 


































Ver esta publicación en Instagram






































































 




Una publicación compartida por multicolor suteba (@multicolorprovincialsuteba)













En las publicaciones de la Multicolor, 

el cuestionamiento se dirige además al mecanismo burócrata de aprobación del acuerdo mediante el voto de secretarios generales, sin una consulta suficiente a las bases escolares, y reclama que las decisiones sobre las medidas de fuerza se definan a través de asambleas y mandatos

. En esa línea, plantean: «

impulsemos asambleas de escuela para tratar la oferta salarial y votar el plan de lucha

«, remarcan desde la agrupación de La Plata, que refleja la posición del conjunto de la Multicolor.




La Multicolor también reclama 

respuestas frente a la violencia en las escuelas

, el 

cumplimiento del acuerdo paritario de resguardo y reparación

, 

mejores prestaciones de IOMA

 y la 

defensa del estatuto docente y del régimen jubilatorio

.




En este marco, la 

Asociación de Maestrxs de la Provincia de Buenos Aires mantiene una agenda propia y diferenciada de este paro de la Multicolor 

y anunció que 

se sumará el viernes 30 de octubre a una huelga nacional junto con el Frente Nacional Democrático por la Educación Pública (FRENDEP) y programó otra medida provincial para noviembre

. Mientras que 

la Federación de Educadores Bonaerenses (FEB), por su parte, si bien también rechazó la propuesta salarial y realizó un paro la semana pasadas, aún tiene pendiente definir la segunda jornada de las 48 horas de paro aprobadas por su congreso

.




«No es aumento, es ajuste»: docentes bonaerenses rechazan el 6% de aumento de Kicillof y convocan a paros, ollas populares y movilizaciones







La nueva jornada de lucha se produce después de la 

movilización del pasado jueves 22 en La Plata, donde docentes de la Multicolor, integrantes de la Asociación de Maestrxs, y residentes y becarios de la salud pública confluyeron frente a la Gobernación

, que unificó reclamos por recomposición salarial, mayor presupuesto, mejores condiciones de trabajo y rechazo a los descuentos por luchar. La continuidad de las medidas muestra que el acuerdo paritario no cerró el conflicto y que distintos sectores docentes buscan mantener abierta la discusión sobre los ingresos y las condiciones en las escuelas bonaerenses.

title: Şener: Flood disasters are not caused by heavy rainfall alone
content:
The floods that followed heavy rainfall in Istanbul last week have once again brought the destruction of the city's ecosystem and unplanned urbanisation into focus. The increasing spread of concrete development, the destruction of natural areas and the disruption of ecological balance are also heightening the risk of disasters.




At least four people lost their lives in the floods. The devastation in Ayazağa, where construction has expanded alongside the destruction of the Northern Forests, has renewed criticism of Istanbul's urban development policies.




Umut Şener from Polen Ecology spoke to ANF about the floods in Istanbul and the consequences of the destruction of the city's ecosystem.




‘The underlying problem is the city's lack of drinking water’




Umut Şener pointed out that ecological destruction in Istanbul has a long history and discussed the environmental problems the city has faced over the centuries.




Şener said, “In the case of Istanbul, it is possible to trace the transformation of nature as far back as antiquity. The environmental problems inherited by the Ottomans when they conquered Istanbul, following centuries of Roman and Byzantine rule, and the measures introduced to address them, demonstrate just how far back this history extends. The decrees concerning ecological matters issued during the Ottoman period, beginning with Sultan Mehmed the Conqueror, along with decisions made by the state bureaucracy and the legal authorities of the time, provide concrete examples of this.




The underlying problem is that Istanbul, surrounded by seas and with enclosed inland water basins, has faced a shortage of fresh water, particularly drinking water, since it first began to develop as a settlement. Over the centuries, population growth and expanding construction have added further problems to this shortage. Istanbul had previously served as the capital of the Byzantine Empire. When it became the capital of the Ottoman Empire, the existing problems were inherited, while the state's land-based system, implemented through conquest and settlement policies, contributed to the city's expansion and steadily growing population.




The destruction and pollution of wooded areas established to protect water resources, the discharge of rubbish and sewage into the Sea of Marmara, and the transformation of areas containing waterways and streams into residential neighbourhoods to meet housing needs were among the problems inherited by the Republic of Turkey from the Ottoman Empire. Of course, ecological problems that emerged with the development and acceleration of capitalism gradually turned into deliberate and increasingly intensive plunder of nature. Because the prevailing political outlook has never incorporated an ecological approach, these problems have become structural, compounded by new environmental problems, and continue to have devastating consequences.”




‘The effects of the Menderes era continue to this day’




Şener said that the plunder of Istanbul had been paved by the approach introduced during the Adnan Menderes era, which promoted the idea that “roads are civilisation”. 




He continued: “As is well known, Adnan Menderes is associated with roads. Roads were built recklessly to facilitate the spread of mechanisation, symbolised by cars in cities and tractors in rural areas. Of course, this must also be considered in the context of the Marshall Plan. Roads were presented as civilisation and development, but they also laid the foundations for the ecological problems that have become increasingly severe today. This was capitalist development that disregarded social needs.




A road was built along the Florya-Sirkeci-Sarayburnu route without any consideration for ecological, economic or aesthetic concerns in urban planning and architecture. Its construction involved expropriations that seriously damaged the cultural and historical fabric of the coastline, the building of seawalls and the creation of land reclamation areas.




The consequences continue today, from the disappearance of species in the Marmara ecosystem and problems such as marine mucilage to the destruction of public spaces inland, as seen in the Yedikule Gardens. These projects destroyed micro-ecosystems, disrupted water current patterns and caused pollution in water resources, including those flowing into the Sea of Marmara, to reach critical levels. The coastline was subjected to outright plunder, and that plunder continues.”




‘Artificial green spaces cannot replace lost marine habitats’




Şener also discussed projects implemented under the Justice and Development Party (AKP) government and the construction and environmental destruction associated with them.




He said, “The Yenikapı Project became one of the symbols of the depoliticisation of urban squares, coinciding with the period when the AKP was once again imposing restrictions on public squares. Of its approximately 715,000 square metres, 518,000 square metres were reclaimed from the sea. Maltepe Orhangazi City Park covers approximately 120 hectares. Figures released by the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality (IMM) administration at the time indicated that around 101 hectares consisted of newly reclaimed land. The first major land reclamation projects that altered Kartal's present-day coastline began in the 1980s and continued throughout the 1990s.




The fact that these areas are now used as parks, walking paths and venues for public activities does not erase the ecological cost of their creation. Natural coastal ecosystems are not simply empty spaces where people can walk. They perform vital functions in supporting life on the seabed, maintaining coastal currents and facilitating the exchange of matter and energy between land and sea. When the sea is filled in, these relationships change along with the coastline itself. Newly created artificial green spaces cannot provide an ecological equivalent to the marine habitats that have been lost.




The destruction caused by the Northern Marmara Motorway and the third bridge projects, which form part of the assault on the Northern Forests that began with the Third Airport and is now intended to continue through INRAIL, is not limited to the land occupied by the roads themselves. The Northern Forests are interconnected ecosystems that replenish the city's water basins, support the soil's capacity to retain water, regulate the climate and provide habitats for numerous species.




These projects fragment and damage natural habitats, while motorway connections create additional pressure for new construction. At the same time, these regions are treated as sources of raw materials and logistical hubs serving the extractive and imperialist policies of global capital. Our neighbourhoods, forests and water resources are being destroyed, while agricultural land is disappearing. This means that access to food and water is becoming increasingly difficult for the people of Istanbul. Studies examining satellite imagery clearly reveal the spread of concrete development and the transformation of the land in these areas. Kanal Istanbul, a project driven by land speculation and the pursuit of profit, is a plan for ecological devastation that will affect the entire Black Sea and Aegean region. The scale of destruction that would result from excavation waste, the enormous amount of energy required and the disruption of ecosystems caused by changes in marine currents is almost unimaginable. The loss of the Sazlıdere Dam, the destruction of agricultural and forest areas, the salinisation of groundwater around Terkos and Küçükçekmece, and changes to water circulation in the Sea of Marmara are among the principal risks. These would be irreversible losses.




Construction is now proceeding at full speed in Arnavutköy's Sazlıbosna neighbourhood, driven by the pursuit of profits from land development. Moreover, those who pocket the profits from land speculation are not the ones who suffer the consequences of flooding, water scarcity, rising rents and the loss of public spaces.”




‘Flood disasters cannot be explained by the intensity of rainfall’




Umut Şener also addressed the recent floods, stressing that the disaster could not be explained by the intensity of rainfall alone.




Şener said, “The first thing that comes to mind is that the climate crisis is already here and affecting us today. It affects everyday life in different ways throughout the year. We cannot ignore the extraordinary intensity of the rainfall. However, the fact that flooding turns into a deadly disaster is not simply a consequence of how heavily it rains. Thousands of people have seen their housing, working conditions and livelihoods affected. In a city surrounded by seas, urban development policies that prevent water from reaching the soil and the sea amount to a form of social murder carried out over many years. Urban crimes committed through excessively dense and unplanned construction are typical examples of ecological injustice. For example, according to a statement by the Istanbul Provincial Coordination Board (IKK) of the Union of Chambers of Turkish Engineers and Architects (TMMOB), nine shopping centres and 16 university campuses in Istanbul are located on streambeds.




The death of a child who was electrocuted after stepping into accumulated water in a park, or the death of a worker while draining water from a construction site, cannot simply be attributed to flooding. The class dimension of this destruction becomes decisive at this point. Poor working-class communities and lower-income groups are forced to live in areas close to streambeds, lacking adequate infrastructure and facing the highest risk of flooding. Property-owning classes, meanwhile, can live in ecologically safer areas at higher elevations or avoid the effects of disasters through privately provided protection measures during times of crisis. This is a reflection of deepening class inequality.”




‘The consequences of the climate crisis expose the true face of concrete development’




Şener also pointed out that ecological destruction is shaping Istanbul's future and that the consequences of the climate crisis are becoming increasingly visible.




He continued: “When considering Istanbul's future, we should not treat ecological destruction as a series of separate problems. Deforestation, the water crisis, flooding, rising urban temperatures, air pollution and biodiversity loss are all consequences of the same urban policies. As we discussed earlier, the consequences of the climate crisis expose the true face of concrete development. Infrastructure proves inadequate, water cannot reach the soil or the sea, urban heat islands create serious public health problems, and energy consumption increases. 




Given the risk of earthquakes, we cannot plan for the future by focusing solely on the structural strength of buildings. Urban transformation has so far served as a tool for generating profits from construction and pushing the urban poor towards the outskirts of the city. It has produced monstrosities such as Fikirtepe. The government has attempted to legitimise new opportunities for profit by accusing those who oppose this profiteering of being against earthquake safety measures. Yet the construction of enormous skyscrapers and densely built-up districts with no room to breathe proceeded without any difficulty. Now we are faced with an enormous problem of buildings at risk. 




As these buildings are being replaced, there is no comprehensive urban plan in place. Yet it would have been possible to take into account the infrastructure capacity of neighbourhoods, rainwater management, the need for green spaces and the right to housing. Instead, people have been forced to choose between earthquake safety and inadequate infrastructure.”




‘Stream rehabilitation is a solution, but not a cure’




Şener also commented on the minister's statements about stream rehabilitation, stressing that while rehabilitation is one possible approach, it cannot provide a solution on its own.




Şener said, “Stream rehabilitation is a method that has been considered and implemented throughout all the historical periods we have discussed. Of course, rehabilitation is one approach, but whether it leads to recovery or destruction depends on the perspective behind it and the methods used to implement it. Even a look at the most common rehabilitation methods and their consequences makes it clear that the current approach cannot offer a lasting solution.




Today, covering streams, narrowing waterways and streambeds, and enclosing streams within concrete walls are all described as 'stream rehabilitation'. Yet the fact that water has nowhere to go whenever it rains and overflows from streambeds clearly demonstrates that these methods do not work. Rather than integrating urban waterways into the city's culture, adapting infrastructure to their natural characteristics and prioritising public health, stream rehabilitation is carried out to create further opportunities for construction and profits from land development.




Throughout history, conventional stream rehabilitation in cities has been based on the logic of controlling and exploiting nature. In today's cities, the term 'stream rehabilitation' refers to confining waterways within concrete channels, narrowing streambeds to generate profits from real estate and covering streams to turn them into roads or car parks. Streams whose channels have been narrowed and enclosed by concrete walls direct water towards city centres at greater speed as soon as rainfall exceeds their capacity, increasing the scale of disasters.




Capital's desire for spatial expansion treats streambeds as potential vacant land in the urban property market. Rather than making waterways part of urban culture and social life, protecting public health and preserving biodiversity, priority is given to opening up new areas for the construction industry.”




‘Cities in harmony with ecosystems are possible’




Umut Şener emphasised that urban development in harmony with ecosystems is possible, but that cities must be planned on the right foundations.




He said, “Urban development in harmony with ecosystems is both historically and scientifically possible. The Earth is an enormous ecosystem in which organic and inorganic materials, along with mechanical, climatic and biological cycles, interact dialectically. Cities are an inseparable part of this ecosystem. Every step taken in urban space, every nail driven into the ground, enters into a dialectical relationship with historical and ecological factors and transforms the material world. The fundamental question, therefore, is not whether we possess the necessary scientific and technical tools, but for whom and for what purpose plans are made.




Achieving urban development in harmony with ecosystems requires spatial planning to serve social needs and ecological balance rather than capital accumulation. The greatest obstacle to ecological urban planning is the treatment of urban land and water resources as commodities for profit. Removing urban land from speculative market forces and bringing land ownership into public hands would pave the way for scientific and ecological planning based on watershed boundaries rather than property boundaries.




Planning decisions must be taken out of the hands of central bureaucracies and capital groups and transferred to local people's assemblies, neighbourhood committees and networks of ecological expertise and solidarity. As with the implementation of other social responsibilities, a model of participatory democracy must be adopted in which urban residents have a direct say in decisions concerning their own living environments and infrastructure needs.”

title: PJAK spokesperson Awdanan: Region preparing for new phase of war
content:
Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK) spokesperson Rêwar Awdanan commented on the course of the war between Iran, the US and Israel, as well as developments across the region.




PJAK spokesperson Rêwar Awdanan noted that the Islamic Republic of Iran had suffered devastating defeats in the 12-Day War, the 40-Day War and the Strait of Hormuz War. “Despite this, it continues to act stubbornly and ignores the advice of figures such as Karroubi, Khatami, Zarif and Rouhani. They even view agreements such as the Treaty of Turkmenchay as beneficial to the stability of the system. Negotiations and the Islamabad Agreement were not enough to extinguish the flames of war, because the concessions demanded by each side are unacceptable to the other,” he said.




Negotiations failed to prevent war




Stating that all indications point to preparations for a new phase in the US-Israeli war against the Islamic Republic of Iran, Awdanan said: “The Strait of Hormuz War and the naval and air blockade imposed on Iran demonstrate the reality of the full-scale and intense war we are facing. In the phase preceding the conflict, neither the Islamic Republic of Iran was able to impose on the US and Israel the share of power it wanted in the new Middle Eastern political system, security arrangements, and the region’s trade and economic routes, nor did the US and Israel succeed in bringing the regime under control and completely destroying it through military attacks and the targeting of Ali Khamenei and other leaders. Removing the Islamic Republic of Iran from its position as a dangerous power within the new Middle Eastern order is a fundamental part of the US strategy to contain China.”




This time, things will be different




Noting that the global economy would weaken, and the US would be unable to advance its agenda against China as long as the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb remained under the control of the Islamic Republic and its proxy forces, Awdanan said: “By easing pressure on Russia and reducing its support for Ukraine, Trump is effectively pressuring the European powers—Britain, France and Germany—not to stand in the way of the US-Israeli agenda in the war against the Islamic Republic. Neither the Islamic Republic nor the US had committed all its forces during the previous stages of the war. This time, however, things will be different.”




We may witness a new form of World War III




Awdanan stated that the war would intensify, and strategic infrastructure would suffer further destruction. “Current indications suggest that we may witness a new form of World War III. The scope of the war will encompass the areas surrounding Iran, particularly the countries of the Arabian Peninsula. The region is currently in turmoil, and the parties are ready at any moment to unleash a living hell upon one another,” he said.

title: Seventh denial of release for Nedime Yaklav
content:
In the fourth week of its ongoing protests against the blocking of women prisoners’ releases at Sincan Women’s Closed Prison, the Ankara Democratic Institutions Platform made a statement in front of the Ministry of Justice. The protest highlighted the seventh denial of release for Nedime Yaklav, who has been imprisoned for 34 years.




Speaking on behalf of the platform, Nesil Çifçi stated that although there were insufficient social and sporting activities available in the prison, Nedime Yaklav’s failure to participate in these activities had been cited as grounds for denying her release. “Postponing prisoners’ freedom on the basis of facilities that the institution itself fails to provide is not justice; it is oppression,” she said.




Nesil Çifçi stated that, according to data from the Lawyers for Freedom Association (ÖHD), the release of 90 prisoners had been blocked over the past three months. She called for an end to the arbitrary obstruction of prisoners who have become eligible for release and demanded that sentence enforcement practices be revised in accordance with human rights principles.




Mehmet Sıddık Akın, Co-Chair of the Health and Social Service Workers’ Union (SES), also drew attention to violations of the right to health in prisons. He called for the release of seriously ill prisoners, for reports from independent healthcare institutions to be taken into account, and for degrading searches to be brought to an end.

title: Bakırhan: 'Peace and Politicisation Council’ must be established immediately
content:
With Abdullah Öcalan’s “Call for Peace and a Democratic Society”, the process entered a new phase. The Kurdish Freedom Movement announced its decision to dissolve itself, burned its weapons and withdrew its forces. However, the state’s delays in taking legal and political steps in response to these moves have increased questions and concerns about the future of the process.




Speaking to ANF, DEM Party Co-Chair Tuncer Bakırhan said that trust must be established for the process to move forward and called on the government to take concrete steps. He stressed that the verification and assessment report must be published without delay, that the National Security Council (MGK) must adopt a decision, and that implementation of the Framework Law must begin. “Now it is the government’s turn,” he said.




At last week’s parliamentary group meeting, you pointed out that the government was ‘coming up with a new condition every week and a new pretext every month’. Why is the government dragging its feet? What arguments is it putting forward at the moment?




The way to build trust and establish a future through the “Peace and Democratic Society Process” is for both sides to take reciprocal steps. From Mr Öcalan’s call to the statement issued by the Movement’s Leadership on 8 October, very important steps have been taken since the process began. In response, significant steps were also taken, including the establishment of a parliamentary commission and a parliamentary delegation’s visit to İmralı. However, there has been a wait-and-see approach when it comes to taking the steps needed to advance these developments, provide the process with legal guarantees, and ensure Mr Öcalan has the freedom to work and communicate.




This delay is continually justified with various pretexts. That is why we sought to draw public attention to this inaction and the failure to fulfil the necessary responsibilities. The government must respond to each step with a corresponding step. The process should proceed through a “staircase” approach, with each successive stage being crossed through reciprocal steps.




When is the ‘verification and assessment report’ expected to be released?




In my view, there is no longer any reason to wait for the report. Look, the Movement’s Leadership has taken important steps. First, the weapons were burned, followed by the decision to dissolve the organisation. Now they have also evacuated the Metîna Camp, which they had regarded for years as one of their most strategic positions, along with other important bases, and withdrawn their forces from Turkey. No one should underestimate this. When an armed movement voluntarily abandons its own positions, it is the clearest possible way of saying, “We stand by our decision; there is no turning back.”




Now it is the government’s turn. The verification and assessment report must be published without delay, the MGK must adopt its decision, and implementation of the Framework Law must begin. If one side continues taking steps while the other keeps waiting, trust will erode. And trust is what this process needs most.




I want to emphasise one point in particular. It is Mr Öcalan who can accelerate this process and bring it to a conclusion. I am not saying this merely as a hope; I am saying it based on what has happened so far. At every critical juncture, it was his calls that opened the way forward. That is why a “Peace and Politicisation Council” must be established immediately under Mr Öcalan’s coordination. There is no requirement for this to be conditional on the verification and assessment process or on legislation. Let the council be established and meet with Mr Öcalan. The work we refer to as verification and assessment would then proceed much more quickly and on a firmer footing.




What legal reforms are needed to ensure that the process is lasting and irreversible? Specifically, what concrete steps do you expect the government to take to provide legal guarantees that will open the way for democratic politics?




To make the process lasting and irreversible, implementation of the Framework Law must be the starting point. Establishing the bodies envisaged under the law and beginning their work is important for overcoming this critical threshold. We must also reinforce the Framework Law with legislation on freedoms and democratisation to make peace permanent.




Legal guarantees are an indispensable foundation for democratic political activity. A legal framework must be established that enables Kurds and every citizen in Turkey to participate in democratic politics freely and on an equal footing. As you know, Turkey’s system of governance has historically approached the right to engage in democratic politics through restrictions and, since 2015, has largely denied people legal protection.




This long-standing trajectory must be reversed. That is why we call the new era a “Democratic Republic”. Putting an end to the Republic’s century of mistakes, addressing its shortcomings and strengthening its democratic character will help make peace permanent.




Does the AKP government have a policy of withdrawing its military forces from Iraq and Syria now that weapons are being laid down?




No policy has yet been announced with a clear timetable. But there should be one, because this is the natural consequence of the process. It would be incomplete to view this peace solely as an internal Turkish matter; we have never seen it that way. A significant part of the more than 40 years of conflict shifted to the Turkey-Iraq border. The border areas became filled with military bases and outposts. Villages in the Kurdistan Region were emptied, and people became unable to go to their fields and summer pastures. From the outset, the PKK was cited as the justification for Turkey’s military presence in Iraq. Now the weapons have been laid down, the organisation has been dissolved, and the camps are being evacuated. If the justification has disappeared, there is no longer any reason to remain there.




Moreover, this is in Turkey’s own interests. Withdrawing its military presence is not a concession. It would open the way for Turkey to build relations with Baghdad, Erbil and all Kurds on the basis of cooperation, trade, energy and shared development, rather than security. We say the same about Syria: at a time when the Kurds and Damascus are seeking a formula for living together, Turkey should exert political and diplomatic influence rather than military force. Peace must not remain confined to this side of the border; it must extend to the other side as well.




Does the AKP want to conduct the process with an eye on the elections? And when might the next election take place?




Any political party may develop policies with an eye on elections. There is nothing unusual about that as a political stance. However, there must be limits to this approach. For example, when it comes to resolving an issue with a history spanning more than two centuries, such as the Kurdish question, electoral considerations cannot be among the foremost concerns. Human life and fundamental rights stand above politics. The democratic resolution of the Kurdish question cannot be made contingent on elections. A party that delivers a democratic solution will, in any case, have done the right thing, and Turkish society will reward that through the ballot box.




Rather than making a direct prediction about when the election will be held, we need to remember that Turkey has more important and pressing priorities, foremost among them the democratic resolution of the Kurdish question. Instead of making the resolution of these problems dependent on an election or tying it to an electoral timetable, we must give them priority.




From what we can see, peace is not being discussed sufficiently in Turkish society and public debate. The issue is treated as though it concerns only the Kurdish side. Why has a ‘peace movement’ not emerged in Turkey?




You are right. This is one of the issues that concerns us most as well. Peace is still discussed as if it were “the Kurds’ problem”. But who has not paid the price of this war? Among the tens of thousands of people we have lost over 40 years are young people from the Black Sea region, the Aegean and Central Anatolia. Think about the money spent on this war. That money did not go towards schools, hospitals, pensioners or people earning the minimum wage. For years, the democratic space across the entire country was restricted under the pretext of “terrorism”. In other words, peace is as much an issue for a mother in Sivas or Bursa as it is for a mother in Diyarbakır.




Why is it not discussed enough? The government bears some responsibility. It is conducting the process but is not making sufficient efforts to explain it to society. Sometimes it becomes preoccupied with other domestic issues. At other times, it acts cautiously out of concern about losing votes. But peace that society does not embrace remains fragile. Look at the media: the language used on television still resembles that of the conflict years. You can hardly find reports explaining what peace would mean for people’s everyday lives.




As for the opposition, I need to speak more frankly. A significant part of the opposition still views this process from the outside. They should point out its shortcomings and criticise it; that is both their right and their responsibility. We, too, highlight these shortcomings every day. But they must accompany their criticism with a programme of their own. Do you want this peace to happen? If so, how should it happen? What are your proposals?




I ask this: why should calls for the government to “take action” always come from the DEM Party? Where is the verification report? When will the MGK adopt its decision? What has happened to the sentence enforcement reforms? When will the government-appointed trustees be withdrawn? Why does the opposition not ask these questions even more forcefully than we do? Do you know what would happen if it did? The government would no longer be able to drag out this process according to its own political timetable. Peace would cease to be the demand of a single party and become a shared demand of the country.




I know that pressure on the opposition plays a role in this situation. Mayors are being arrested, politicians are being prosecuted, and everyone understandably becomes preoccupied with their own problems. But the foundations for these pressures were laid during the years of conflict. The practice of appointing trustees to Kurdish municipalities eventually extended to Esenyurt. Remember the cases brought under the label of “urban consensus”. The laws expanded in the name of “combating terrorism” now stand in everyone’s way. When the guns fall silent, these justifications will disappear as well. Peace is what will give the greatest breathing space to social opposition movements.




We are working to establish a broad, cross-party peace movement in Turkey. We are visiting opposition parties, trade unions, bar associations, professional chambers, women’s and youth organisations, Alevi institutions, writers and artists, one by one. We are proposing that we work together on a common programme for peace and democracy. We want to organise peace assemblies and public gatherings not only in Diyarbakır and Van, but also in İzmir, Ankara and Trabzon. The DEM Party does not have to own this movement. We want all of Turkey to be its founder. If we can make peace a shared concern for the entire country, we can also make democracy a shared achievement. I see no other way forward.




Finally, under its foreign policy approach described as ‘regional ownership’, Turkey first joined the ‘Mecca Alliance’ and then the ‘Badr Alliance’. How does the DEM Party interpret Ankara’s efforts to establish these alliances in the region?




The global order and the dynamics of the Middle East are undergoing major upheaval. In principle, we understand that in this era of uncertainty, every country seeks to organise its moral and military defence through various alliances. However, throughout history, states have consistently sought security through these militaristic alliances, while humanity has endured immense suffering throughout that same history.




The solution, therefore, lies not in multiplying military alliances, but in establishing equality among peoples, democracy and justice in every sphere of life, particularly economic justice. For quite some time, we have been warning about a global storm and its regional repercussions. The wisest course for Turkey would be to establish social peace as soon as possible and avoid taking sides in regional tensions.

title: Besê Hozat: Abdullah Öcalan’s status must be formalized for the process to move forward
content:
KCK Executive Council Co-Chair Besê Hozat spoke to Medya Haber TV about the current stage of the process, the women’s freedom struggle, practices in prisons, and regional developments.




This is part one of the interview. 




25 October marked the 34th anniversary of the martyrdom of comrade Bêrîtan (Gülnaz Karataş), who played a pivotal role in the development of the Kurdish freedom struggle and particularly the women’s resistance movement. What impact did the change she pioneered have on Kurdish sociology?




To begin with, I commemorate all the martyrs of the revolution and the struggle for freedom represented by comrade Bêrîtan with respect, love, and gratitude. Comrade Bêrîtan holds a special place in our struggle. Her place and importance are particularly unique from the perspective of the women’s freedom struggle. Comrade Bêrîtan is a symbol of resistance and of the struggle for freedom. Comrade Bêrîtan’s stance, character, and her resistance – the noble stance she took against the impositions of collaborationists, traitors, and capitulationists, as well as against the line of surrender – have had a tremendous impact on organizing women and on the development of women’s self-defense. Her influence on Kurdish women, in particular, has been immense.




There is a deep-rooted culture of resistance in Kurdistan. Kurdish women play a decisive role in the development and formation of this culture. Comrade Bêrîtan was shaped by this culture. When she joined the PKK’s struggle, she surpassed herself both in terms of her character and the struggle she was waging. Today, comrade Bêrîtan represents a guiding principle for both the women’s freedom movement and the Kurdish freedom movement as a whole.




Comrade Bêrîtan played a very significant role in deepening this culture of resistance, internalizing it, and turning it into a guiding principle. Her personality, her stance, and the attitude of resistance she demonstrated against surrender, betrayal, and collaboration remain very powerful. And, of course, she did have a particularly profound impact on women and society in South Kurdistan. Especially in the face of impositions of surrender and betrayal, she fostered a resolute stance among Kurdish women. The most fitting tribute to our comrade Bêrîtan is to wage a strong struggle for freedom, to adopt a stance of freedom, and to stand strong against all forms of surrender, betrayal, and collaboration.




It is necessary to organize this stance of resistance, transform it into a force for struggle, and gradually turn it into a social system and way of life. This is the most appropriate and meaningful response in her memory. If we renew this stance and attitude for today, the most meaningful response would be the following: Kurdish women have to be able to transform this stance of resistance and this freedom-oriented line into a democratic, free Kurdish unity. This is of the utmost importance. Kurdish women must be able to take the lead in this democratic Kurdish unity. By establishing their own unity – and by securing their internal unity based on democratic and free principles – they must be able to lead the way toward a democratic Kurdish unity. This is an urgent necessity, both from today’s perspective and in light of the period we are currently experiencing.




This can only be achieved through organization, through a stance of self-defense, and through a spirit of resistance. In this sense, comrade Bêrîtan’s path of struggle and life serves as an example. It is inspiring and encouraging, both for Kurdish women and for women in general. She serves as a model in expanding organization and self-defense and in establishing a democratic women’s unity, a Kurdish women’s unity, and a democratic Kurdish unity.




In light of the legacy of resistance and struggle for freedom created by her, how would you assess the sociological reality of Kurdish women and their role in the freedom struggle within the Kurdish freedom movement today?




The Kurdish women’s freedom movement has already developed along this legacy. There is also the legacy of the prison resistance of Amed, which was pioneered by comrade Sara. Comrade Sara also played a leadership role for Kurdish women. This is the struggle of the Kurdish women’s freedom movement. And comrade Bêrîtan is also a continuation of this legacy. She is a continuation of this tradition of resistance. The comrades like Bêrîtan, Zîlan, Sema, Gulan, Viyan, and Şîlan are all continuations of this tradition and legacy. This has become part of our culture; it has become a tradition, a culture, a style, and a way of understanding. It has created a new mindset, and the struggle that has developed through it has brought about a very significant change and transformation in Kurdish sociology as well. The influence of this has been immense in the development of democratization among the Kurds, a culture of freedom, a culture of equality, and the mindset and understanding of living freely and equally alongside other peoples.




A significant sociological transformation is taking place. This democratization among the Kurds – this understanding of freedom, equality, and justice – is a level that has emerged through the struggle developing along this cultural line and this trajectory: the construction of a shared life with other peoples, cultures, and faiths – what we call the “paradigm of the democratic nation” – and the building of a system for living freely and democratically together.




Femicides and acts of violence across society have reached an alarming level. According to official numbers, on average, two to three women are murdered every day, and many more are attempted. The statistics from September show that 26 women and 6 children were murdered. Additionally, 10 women and 6 children died under suspicious circumstances. In a situation where violence against women has intensified to this extent, is the current women’s struggle sufficient? What can women do against violence against women, and how can they develop their self-defense strategies?




Physical violence against women is one dimension of violence against women. But one has to see that women are subjected to multifaceted, multidimensional violence. There are many dimensions to it, including psychological and economic violence. Today’s dominant culture itself is a sexist, male-dominated culture – a culture that has developed over the course of thousands of years. Life has been shaped accordingly, and gender roles have developed on this foundation. This is reflected in the media, in art and culture, in politics, and in the economy. We are dealing with a male-dominated and sexist culture that permeates every aspect of life to its very depths. This, in turn, manifests as violence against women in every sphere of life. There is a profound exploitation of women.




In response to this – especially throughout the past century – there has been a significant awakening among women, and a rising struggle is taking place worldwide. The gender contradiction is becoming the primary contradiction. And everywhere, a serious solidarity among women and a shared struggle are developing. Against the male-dominated system – the most concentrated and institutionalized form of which is the system of capitalist modernity and the nation-state system – the system of capitalist modernity is experiencing a deep crisis, alongside the struggle of women, the peoples, and all social dynamics in general.




The intensification of violence against women – to the point of physical massacres and the genocide of women – is also linked to the deep crisis and chaos experienced by the mindset of capitalist modernity and the patriarchal system. To keep the system afloat, it is escalating violence, expanding its scope, and deepening its impact. But, there is also a strong and genuine women’s struggle against this.




The system of capitalist modernity is a system of war and a system of violence. There is war all over the world. Also in this region, the war has intensified, and the war centered on Kurdistan has deepened. There is also a policy of genocide targeting the Kurds. This spans a century, or maybe even longer. If one pays attention, one can see that many massacres against women in Kurdistan are being carried out directly by the state. These are being carried out as part of the attacks stemming from an organized, planned policy of genocide. Violence of every kind is intensifying in this way. There is a growing awareness of this. As I said, a process of raising consciousness, building resolve, and organizing is developing among women. Solidarity is also growing, as are collective actions and the struggle itself. However, this still remains insufficient.




It is important to strengthen this, and in order to make it stronger, it is necessary that we organize. Women must strengthen their organization everywhere, in every sphere of life. They must strengthen their self-defense. Self-defense comes through organization. The more you organize, the more that organization becomes your self-defense. It also becomes your collective strength in the struggle. When a collective struggle, a strong fighting force, and an organized stance emerge, the patriarchal system – and the manifestations of male violence that permeate society and even the family – naturally recede and weaken in the face of organized struggle. If this organized struggle and self-defense continue to grow, it will accelerate the collapse of the patriarchal system. It will also gradually eliminate this sexist culture. Women’s education, organization, self-defense, and collective struggle push back against the patriarchal system and culture and, over time, ensure their eventual eradication.




Two years have passed since the process began on October 22. As the freedom movement, you have taken significant steps. Turkish state officials have also made statements to a certain extent. Parliament has become active, and a commission has been formed. A law has also been passed. However, it appears there is a stalemate in the process. Where is the process at the moment?




Over the past two years, the Kurdish freedom movement has taken some historic steps. We have halted the armed struggle against Turkey, and many other steps followed. All guerrilla forces within Turkey’s borders have been withdrawn. Units in the cities have been withdrawn. Tunnels and caves near the border and some in more remote areas have been evacuated to diminish the risk of conflict. These are very concrete examples that demonstrate our sincerity, determination, and stance regarding this process. And, like I said, they are truly historic steps.




In contrast, there has been no serious movement on the part of the state. You asked if there is a stalemate. It might not be appropriate to put it exactly that way. But there is indeed a state of stagnation. There is a state of pause and stagnation. You could call it a deadlock, but there is a state of paralysis. The reason for this lies in the attitude of the state and the government. It is a state of paralysis on that front. They are not taking any steps. They are not taking steps toward democratization. The political and legal groundwork is not being laid. First and foremost, there is the situation of our leader. The isolation has not yet been lifted. Our leader is not enabled to steer this process. And that was our fundamental condition at the PKK dissolution congress. We ended the armed struggle, but for this to be put into practice – for all the decisions made at the congress to be implemented – Rêber Apo [Kurdish people’s leader Abdullah Öcalan] needed to be enabled to freely steer this process. Democratic, political, and legal steps needed to be taken. The groundwork needed to be laid for waging a democratic political struggle. To achieve this, the state needed to implement very serious legal reforms. But there has been no progress on this front. Consequently, there is a state of stagnation, a freeze caused by the state. We can put it that way.




Most recently, there was a statement of your movement, announcing that you also emptied your remaining positions in the area of Metîna. After that, reports appeared in the Turkish press claiming that the tunnels and caves in Xakurkê, Xinêre and Garê had also been evacuated, and that weapons had been surrendered. Within the Kurdish community, a perception has formed that the state is using pressure to conceal what it itself should be doing. What is the current situation?




All of this is part of a strategy of special warfare. Since the state has not changed its mindset or policy, it is not taking any steps on this issue; instead, it is playing for time and buying time by creating agendas and shaping different perceptions. If they were serious and took steps – if the groundwork were laid politically and legally, starting with the freedom of Rêber Apo, and if an environment for democratic politics were created and that opportunity were granted – then, forget about Metîna, Xakurkê, and Xinêre – in all areas, the guerrillas would lay down their arms, come down from the mountains, and join democratic politics in an organized manner. That issue would be resolved, rather than focusing on this or that specific area. If the state were to take a serious step, we would naturally enter such a process as a whole. But it is not taking any steps. Its insistence on the current stance and policy of intransigence is leading to the emergence of these kinds of special war, made-up agendas. There are no concrete steps being taken.




Every day a different area is being debated, and attempts are being made to create a different perception. These are special war agendas. One must not give them any credence. Everyone needs to turn their attention to the state. Is it taking a step, or isn’t it? As I pointed out, there is currently a state of stagnation and paralysis. If the state takes a step, nothing will remain. That process will unfold on its own.




In an article he wrote a few days ago, Mehmet Uçum stated that even if Kurdish people’s leader Abdullah Öcalan were given a role, there would be no change in his legal status. This gave the impression that they were approaching him as a tool to dismantle the freedom movement. How do you assess this evaluation?




Mehmet Uçum is a representative within the state of the tendency that insists on intransigence, on war policies, and on denial. He is a full-fledged agent of special warfare. There is a significant circle in Turkey that feeds off war and intransigence, and there are serious factions within the state. Mehmet Uçum acts as one of their representatives and spokespersons. It is appropriate to put it that way.




Rêber Apo is the leader of this people; he embodies the will of this people. Rêber Apo’s freedom is synonymous with, and inextricably linked to, the democratic resolution of the Kurdish issue. It is clear and unequivocal that the guerrillas will not take a single step forward unless Rêber Apo is freed, his status is formalized, and he is able to freely lead this process. Because this is the litmus test. The approach to our leader is the approach to the Kurds. However, they approach our leader, that is how they approach the Kurdish issue. If there is no progress regarding our leader’s freedom and the conditions for freedom, if his status has not been formalized, and if an official dialogue has not been established – this means that this state will approach the Kurdish issue in the same way. It will continue its policy of non-resolution and denial. That is what it means. From that perspective, everyone’s eyes and attention are, and should be, focused on Rêber Apo’s situation.




Mehmet Uçum’s remarks of this kind directed at Rêber Apo reveal his approach to the Kurds and his stance on the Kurdish issue. They reveal just how frivolous this approach is. And in a way, Mehmet Uçum is confirming and validating those who make such assessments. If this is the case, of course, this process will not develop. This process will not move forward. For this process to move forward and proceed successfully, the status of our leader must be formalized. Rêber Apo must be able to freely lead this process. Otherwise, it is not possible for this process to proceed successfully.




There are still quite a number of comrades who have been in prison for over 30 years. They are not being released even though their sentences have expired. Among them are some who are seriously ill. Reports indicate that the conditions in prisons remain very harsh.




The fact that this process continues in this manner – including the dimension of the prison situation – stems from the mindset we discussed a moment ago, exemplified by figures like Mehmet Uçum. Prisons are the most concrete expression of this mindset and worldview – one that insists on the absence of a solution, that insists on a kind of war, that insists on hostility toward Kurds, and that perpetuates this policy.




According to Turkish law, according to state law, they have served their sentence. Their 30 years are up. Yet, despite this, their sentence is being extended, and they are being held inside. They are seriously ill. Some have cancer, and some have heart problems, and the like. Despite all this, they are being held inside, and their sentences are being extended. A law of hostility is being enforced. This is unprecedented. They are not even applying their own laws. They are trampling on their own laws. It is unlawful, unethical, and politically irresponsible. And when I say “politics,” I am referring to the ethics of politics. Beyond all of this, an inhumane “law of hostility,” a “law of war,” is being enforced. One of the most striking and obvious places where this law of hostility and war is applied is, in fact, the prisons. It’s as if they’re taking revenge, trying to break one’s will. They have served 30 years, 32 years. They have devoted their entire lives to the cause of freedom, to the freedom of their people; yet they’re forcing them to repent, trying to break their will, trying to make them surrender. There is only one way to describe this: it is hostility. It is hostility toward the Kurds. It is a persistence in hostility toward the Kurds. It is a persistence in war. There is no other meaning to it. Over the course of two years, so many steps have been taken. Such a strong will has been demonstrated in pursuing democratic politics, and the armed struggle against Turkey has been halted; yet, despite this, a law of hostility is at work in prison – a law of war is at work.




Obviously, this generates immense anger. It fosters a profound lack of belief and trust both towards this process and toward the state and deepens anxieties. Consequently, the process is failing to gain societal traction. There are serious concerns and anxieties among the Kurdish people regarding this issue. They look at the situation of Rêber Apo; there is no change. They look at the prisons; a regime of outright oppression and hostility is in full force there. How can this possibly foster trust in society? How can it inspire faith in this process? So of course, the situation in the prisons is another factor that negatively impacts the process in a major way.
