author: Robert Narai
title: Days of hope and rage in France
content:
At the centre of Paris, the Monument à la République looms over a square that has hosted every great mobilisation of the French left in modern history. The bronze statue of Marianne, symbol of the Republic, holds an olive branch above the words: 

Liberté. Égalité. Fraternité.

 During mass demonstrations on 17 October, dozens of young people scaled the monument while tens of thousands looked on. Some flew Palestinian and red flags. On the statue of 

Egalité

, someone had scrawled “jeunesse dorée” (“gilded youth”, an old term for the idle rich). Marianne herself was draped in a giant yellow vest bearing the words: “The police mutilate high school students”.

For almost a month now, a mass student revolt has been rocking France, in one of the deepest political crises seen in the country in decades. The state that claims to embody liberty, equality and fraternity has answered 

lycéens

 (high schoolers aged 15 to 18) demanding better conditions in schools with tear gas, rubber bullets and mass arrests. That the Republic’s police are maiming young people in the streets is an indictment of the capitalist system the Republic protects.

Days of rage

In response to a national day of action on 17 October, in which an estimated 800,000 people protested across France, the government of Emmanuel Macron unleashed a flurry of violence.

Police fired tear gas into the crowd gathering at Place de la République before the march had formed. Riot police armed with batons, shields and armoured vehicles charged into crowds in Paris, Lyons, Bordeaux and a string of provincial cities, attacking protesters and bystanders alike. According to the Interior Ministry, almost 1,800 people were arrested and more than 500 police were injured, with 855 arrests in Paris alone. A teenager lost a hand in Saint-Étienne and another lost an eye in Mulhouse. Street medics were dragged along the ground by police.

The new element on 17 October was the return of the Yellow Vests, the leaderless movement of rural and provincial workers against fuel taxes and the high cost of living that erupted in 2018, until it was crushed with brute force by the state. After weeks of watching 

lycéens

 face down riot police, the Yellow Vests called their own day of action protesting the cost of living. The Yellow Vests blocked roundabouts and fuel depots from the morning and declared their support for the student revolt. Among them was Pierre, a retiree from Bandol: “I’ve been gassed five times since this morning”, he told 

La Provence

. “[Macron’s government] is declaring war on the people.” The return of the Yellow Vests raises the possibility of the student revolt becoming a rallying point for broader working-class grievances.

Nurses, teachers and firefighters joined the Yellow Vests demonstration. In Lille, 20 rail workers marched together in their SNCF vests. Most of the working class support the movement (55 percent of the French population support the student-led protest movement, according to an Elabe poll) but are not yet part of it.

Whose Republic?

The Macron government’s strategy has been to paint the victims of violence as its perpetrators. Prime Minister Lecornu blamed “far-left groups”, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez targeted “ultra-left individuals”, while Macron declared that “nothing can explain, nothing can excuse” the violence. They pointed to a handful of burnt buildings, such as the town hall in Limoges, to paint a movement of hundreds of thousands as a mindless mob. “The perpetrators directly targeted the institutions of the Republic and the authority of the State”, wrote Bordeaux mayor Thomas Cazenave.

It is worth asking what sort of Republic the mayor of Bordeaux is defending: one in which a burnt town hall causes enormous outrage, but a sixteen-year-old losing an eye to a police grenade prompts hysteria about the need for more law and order.

The ruling class never calls the conditions that produced this revolt violence. Students in France’s poorest schools sit in classrooms infested with cockroaches and rats, in classes of up to 35. Outside school, the police stop, search and arrest young Black and Arab men from the 

banlieues

 (working-class suburbs) for the colour of their skin and the estate they live on, and their operations now cause more than one death per week. Fuel and food prices keep rising, while, according to Oxfam, 53 billionaires own as much as the poorest 48 percent of the population. This is the systematic violence the working class is subjected to every day under French capitalism.

“A riot is the language of the unheard”, as Martin Luther King Jr said. The looting that broke out in some cities is not senseless. It comes from people with little money who have been demonised for years and told that their lives are worthless.

Yet riots are not a way forward for the movement. They invite more repression and hand the right the story it wants to tell, of mindless “casseurs” (wreckers) to be answered with curfews and soldiers. And they push away workers whose strikes could win what the movement wants.

The right has also racialised the riots. Government spokesperson Maud Bregeon blamed 

racaille

 (“scum”) and “

that 

type of population”, while fascist Éric Zemmour, leader of the far right Reconquête, described “a horde of Maghrebi and African barbarians entering the cities”.

The impact of this racist backlash can be seen in the 

banlieue

 of Trappes. On 23 October, a gunman drove through the Parisian suburb for around fifteen minutes, shooting at black and brown people. He killed a 26-year-old and wounded several others, among them a 12-year-old girl who was shot eight times. 

Le Monde 

reports that he “congratulated himself, in essence, on having ‘avenged the shopkeepers’” by attacking “Blacks and Arabs”. Politicians across the spectrum, Macron included, have professed their horror, but these are crocodile tears from the people responsible for the climate of racism. For years, they have backed laws against migrants, refugees and Muslims and echoed the politics of the fascist National Rally. 

Polarisation

This is not the first time that working-class youth from the 

banlieues

 have rebelled against the French state. In 2005 and again in 2023, after police killings of teenagers, the suburbs rose without the workers’ movement: much of the left abandoned the rioters in 2005, and in 2023 the union leaders offered only statements, not strikes.

What has changed in 2026 is that the youth have learned lessons from previous struggles. This revolt began in the schools, not as a riot, and its first act was to create mass assemblies through which students can democratically direct their movement. And it has been shaped by two experiences less evident before. The first is the Palestine movement, which taught a generation about state repression and the moral vacuum at the heart of the Republic. The second is the fascist National Rally, who, if they come to power in next year’s presidential elections, pose a mortal threat to the interests of all workers and the oppressed.

The threat of a fascist-led Republic gives the student revolt a sense of urgency and a sharper political edge: students are not only demanding a better future, but defending the right to have one at all. And years of mass strikes have taught them where the power to win lies: with the workers who can shut down production.

The revolt is also radicalising the capitalist class. “A wave of shock has swept through the business world”, writes Martine Orange in 

Mediapart

. “We have a useless, unworthy, incompetent political class”, an investment banker told Orange. “Retailleau, Attal, Philippe, Glucksmann [leading politicians of the centre and right]—there isn’t one of them worth anything.”

Many capitalists are looking for an iron fist that can restore profitability and order. France’s public debt is well above 100 percent of GDP, and the ruling class want workers to pay the bill: first, the budget cuts the students are blocking, then further attacks on pay, pensions and public services. That will require defeating the unions and the left. While many capitalists do not entirely trust Marine Le Pen (presidential candidate and leader of the RN), Orange concludes, “some believe she alone will be able to ‘restore the authority’ they crave”.

The fascist Le Pen is ready to do the job. Her party has spent years courting big business and presenting itself as the party of order. An RN government would not have to build the repressive machinery for a confrontation with the unions and the left, because the centre has already built it: bans on demonstrations, the power to dissolve left-wing organisations, and riot police and soldiers normalised and ready to be deployed against the population. Macron is currently wielding it against high schoolers and youth from the 

banlieues

. A Le Pen presidency could wield it against unions and the left.

For decades, the French establishment has told voters that the “Republican Front” of the centre is all that stands between the Republic and the fascist RN. They say that the only way to keep out the fascists is to vote for the establishment candidate and accept their austerity and racism. Macron and his allies have used this argument repeatedly to bludgeon the left into voting for them. In 2024, the New Popular Front, an alliance of the left including France Unbowed that challenged this logic, won the most seats only for Macron to refuse to let the left form a government. The defenders of so-called “Republican values” are throwing open the doors of the Élysée to the fascists.

In the days after 17 October, the Macron government set about building a de facto state of emergency without openly declaring one. Lecornu gave mayors the power to impose curfews “where they need to”. Curfews on minors followed in Paris and other major cities. Protests were banned, and the army’s Sentinelle patrols were deployed. “If necessary, clearly we could”, said Lecornu when asked about declaring a state of emergency. At the same time, he invited the RN to meetings on the government’s crisis response. By the eve of 24 October, the ban had spread to nearly every city, and the government had mobilised 70,000 police, special forces and armoured vehicles.

Days of hope 

Since 17 October, the student assemblies have spread from the high schools to the universities. In Bordeaux, about 1,000 students packed each of two campus assemblies. In the Paris region, delegates from 32 campuses voted to join the days of action on 22 and 29 October and the march on 24 October, and to prepare for a general strike from 5 November.

On 22 October, the national coordination of student assemblies called a day of action in Paris, but the police turned the march into a static rally. 

The state could stop them marching on 22 October. But it could not stop them on 24 October. In a massive show of strength, hundreds of thousands of demonstrators defied the Macron government’s intimidation tactics. Hundreds of thousands of students and workers stretched over four kilometres in Paris. Tens of thousands marched in Marseilles where they held a minute of silence, hands raised, for the victims of Trappes and against fascism. In Bordeaux, more than 10,000 braved driving rain and defied a ban on demonstrating in the city centre. The cops responded with tear gas. In Lyons, around 20,000 marched in the face of armoured vehicles, as the police fired volleys of tear gas. In Nice, the police used water cannons to try to smash the demonstration. An estimated 800,000 people mobilised across the entire country. One placard in Paris summed up the contempt for the ruling-class hysteria over broken glass: “I would have liked to be a shop window, so I would be taken more seriously”.

24 October was a humiliation for the Macron government and a significant victory for the movement: the show of force was meant to intimidate people. Instead, it has only emboldened them. Macron’s government no longer knows whether it can contain the fury from below.

The day also saw tens of thousands take on the fascists in Orléans, where the RN held its congress to launch Le Pen’s presidential campaign under heavy police protection. More than 30,000 people marched, about twice as many as expected: trade unionists, young anti-racists, undocumented migrants, women’s and LGBT+ groups, and the revolutionary left. This is not enough on its own to stop the fascists winning state power, but it sent a clear message: the RN may be winning at the polls, but it cannot hold the streets.

In a major step forward for the movement, the country’s second-largest trade union federation, the CGT, has been pressured to call a general strike for 5 November. The intersyndicale, the coalition of France’s main union confederations, spent the weeks before 24 October asking the government for concessions on the budget and school funding, even excluding high school representatives from the negotiations. But Lecornu offered nothing, and now, deprived of their mediating role, they are calling for a general strike. “Workers must hold general assemblies everywhere, in all workplaces, with all their colleagues, in every administration, to generalize the November 5 strike and after”, CGT general secretary Sophie Binet said in a statement.

Macron’s dilemma is that if he continues to use repression to keep the students off the streets, he risks a social explosion. But if he relaxes his grip, the crisis of the budget and the school system returns, and the revolt continues to grow. 

The movement has its own dilemma. The state has shown it will make an example of anyone who steps out of line, and the threat of prison and curfews is enough to keep many demonstrators at home. At the same time, the union leadership holds the keys to the workers’ strength and uses them cautiously. Union leaders speak boldly while preparing for a bureaucratic one-day strike. A one-day strike would let off steam; it would not break the government. (In 2023, the union leaders called fourteen separate one-day strikes over five months, and Macron waited them out.) The answer is for workers to shut down production and halt the flow of profits by going on indefinite strike in their millions.

The Yellow Vests have called “Acte III” for 31 October, and high school and university students will keep pushing for national days of action on 29 October and use the school holidays to take the argument to hospitals, railway stations and workplaces to build their own assemblies. Anti-racist organisations and trade unions defied bans on demonstrations on 26 October in response to the racist attack in Trappes.

Students and workers have shown that the Republic’s iron fist can be defied through mass action. As 5 November approaches, the ability of the organised left to carry the students’ militancy into the workplaces, and to win workers to the rank-and-file action that can take a strike beyond a single day, will decide how far this rebellion goes.

author: Ming-Yeh T. Rawnsley
title: Women and Taiwan’s Next Economic Transformation
content:
IN 2015, ECONOMIST Elliott Fan (樊家忠) encountered a result that his collaborators found difficult to believe. An experiment involving 450 residents of Taipei and New Taipei City showed no statistically significant difference between men’s and women’s willingness to compete. Studies elsewhere had frequently found men more inclined to enter competitive situations. In his Taiwanese sample, that familiar gap was absent.

Fan checked the procedures and sample but found no mistake that explained the result. The finding prompted a larger inquiry: what had shaped women’s opportunities and expectations in Taiwan?

Women’s participation in work, business and politics helped shape Taiwan’s transformation even as economic change opened new possibilities for them. That relationship matters again as the semiconductor economy enters the AI boom. Access to technology careers will influence who shares in its rewards and who helps direct its development.

In a podcast interview released in October by the NTNU International Taiwan Studies Center, in collaboration with the International Journal of Taiwan Studies, the National Taiwan University professor explored how agriculture, business, migration and electoral politics had changed women’s lives. His research suggests that gender expectations respond to economic opportunities and institutional rules. The same attention to those conditions is needed as technology reshapes careers.

TAIWAN, JAPAN, AND SOUTH KOREA share aspects of a Confucian heritage, including traditions assigning women responsibility for care. Yet their gender outcomes differ. Fan points to women’s visibility in Taiwanese politics and business as reasons to question explanations that treat culture as a fixed constraint. His experimental finding invites scrutiny of the circumstances in which gender differences emerge.

One explanation begins in colonial Taiwan. Sugar production expanded under Japanese rule, requiring substantially more labor than rice cultivation. Women became more deeply involved in agricultural production, increasing their contribution to household income.

Women’s contribution to household income could strengthen their bargaining position within the family. Yet they continued to cook, clean and care for children while taking on more fieldwork. Greater economic importance came with a heavier workload. That tension remains relevant to technology careers, where access to paid work may expand without a corresponding redistribution of unpaid care.

Nevertheless, demand for women’s labor could unsettle established restrictions. In research published in 2022 with Nora Cheng and economic historian Wu Tsong-min, Fan links expanding sugar-cane cultivation to the abandonment of foot-binding in early twentieth-century Taiwan. In the NTNU podcast, he also describes higher postwar female labor-force participation in former sugar-growing areas than in rice-growing areas, suggesting that changes in women’s productive roles could influence later generations.

These consequences do not make colonial exploitation a project of emancipation. They show how economic demands could alter household relations, with effects extending beyond the intentions of those directing development.

FAN’S SECOND EXPLANATION concerns Taiwan’s small and medium-sized enterprises. In a small firm, an owner may know employees’ capabilities directly. A capable woman may gain responsibility without passing through numerous layers of management dominated by men.

Family succession creates another route: daughters may take over when there is no son, when a son does not wish to continue the business, or when a daughter is better placed to lead. Across an economy with many family businesses, these decisions can create substantial opportunities for women to exercise authority.

Fan’s work on firm size and gender equity remains in progress, and small firms are not automatically fair. The important question is how business structures affect access to leadership. Applied to technology careers, this means examining how people are recruited, recognized and promoted, alongside encouraging women to gain technical qualifications.

His third inquiry concerns postwar migration. Military dependents’ villages, known as juancun (眷村), brought mainland Chinese migrants into contact with surrounding Taiwanese communities. Fan describes comparisons associating proximity to these settlements with greater female labor-force participation, later marriage and weaker son preference among local Taiwanese residents.

This research also remains in progress. Fan suggests that everyday contact transmitted different expectations about women and family life, without implying uniform attitudes within either population. Gender norms may change through encounters between neighbors as well as through changes in the workplace.

POLITICAL REPRESENTATION offers a more direct example of institutional design. Taiwan’s local electoral quotas reserve seats for women according to the number of seats in a district. Fan and his co-authors use variation generated by these rules to examine the effects of exposure to female political leadership.

Their findings, published in the Journal of Development Economics in 2025, extend beyond elections. They found evidence of weaker son preference, greater participation by married women in household decisions, and increased interest among female students in studying law and political science.

The results are consistent with a role-model effect. Seeing women exercise public authority can expand other women’s sense of what is possible. For a student choosing a university subject, political leadership becomes a career she can imagine pursuing.

This suggests a question for technology employers and educators: who is visible as an expert or leader, and whose ambitions receive support? The political findings do not establish that identical interventions will work in technology. They do show that institutional changes can influence career aspirations beyond the people who benefit directly.

FAN WORRIES that the expansion of a male-dominated AI industry could concentrate access to highly paid jobs among men, making further progress toward wage equality harder. His warning concerns who captures the gains from growth; it does not establish that AI has already reversed Taiwan’s progress.

The historical lesson is that participation depends on how opportunities are organized. Encouraging girls to study science and technology is part of the task. Access also depends on recruitment, promotion and working arrangements that allow people with caring responsibilities to build careers. Women need opportunities to acquire authority and shape decisions as well as enter the workforce.

Following Fan’s argument means asking practical questions. Can women enter technical fields through retraining as well as university education? Are promotion criteria transparent? Can workers take parental leave without losing access to career-building assignments? These are ways to examine whether the promise of opportunity reaches beyond recruitment campaigns.

Technology careers could reproduce the uneven bargain of the sugar fields if access expands without changes to the organization of work and care.

Asked which university major will offer the best prospects in the AI age, Fan answers: ‘I don’t know, because nobody knows’. Uncertainty about future jobs need not prevent action on the barriers that already restrict people’s choices.

Taiwan’s next economic transformation will be shaped by decisions about education, employment and authority as well as technological advances. Its success should be judged partly by whether women gain secure careers, share in the rewards and help decide how new technologies are used. Women helped build the economy that made this transformation possible. They should have a full part in shaping what comes next.

author: Unknown
title: Ephéméride des luttes : 27 octobre
content:
Le 27 octobre de l'éphéméride des luttes est une dure journée, parfois triste. Elle ne fait que marquer toujours plus profondément à quel point le monde qui nous entoure vit de notre tristesse et de notre souffrance, et donc toutes les raisons qui nous poussent à lutter.




1889 :

 A Gouliaï-Polié en Ukraine, naissance de Nestor Makhno, anarchiste Ukrainien qui mena une insurrection libertaire armée contre les prétentions bolcheviques, juste après la révolution Russe de 1917.




1962 :

 A Milan, au cours d'une manifestation en soutien aux révolutionnaires Cubains, l'étudiant Giovanni Ardizzone meurt renversé par une camionnette de police.




1968 :

 A Londres, 120.000 personnes manifestent contre la Guerre du Vietnam.




1969 :

 A Pise, au cours d'une manifestation organisée par 

Potere Operaio

 contre le régime fasciste des Colonels en Grèce, des affrontements ont lieu entre les militant-e-s d'extrême-gauche et des néofascistes. La police intervient et une grenade lacrymogène tirée en plein visage tue le jeune Cesare Pardini, militant d'extrême-gauche.




1971 :

 En Irlande du Nord, l'IRA abat deux membres de l'armée anglaise à Rosemount, près de Derry et un troisième est tué par une mine de l'IRA à Kinawley. Le même jour, un membre du Royal Ulster Constabulary est tué à Toome par l'IRA.




1977 :

 - En Allemagne, funérailles de Baader, Ensslin et Raspe, militant-e-s de la Fraction Armée Rouge (RAF). Plus d'un millier de personnes sont présentes et sont bloquées par un triple cordon de police.




 A Gênes, les Brigades Rouges incendient les voitures de cinq responsables de la Démocratie Chrétienne, le parti au pouvoir.




1980 :

 En Irlande du Nord, les prisonniers de l'IRA revendiquent le statut de prisonniers de guerre en commençant une grève de la faim.




1982 :

 En Irlande du Nord, l'IRA abat trois membres des l'armée royale anglaise.




1991 :

 Au Pérou, arrestation de l'anarchiste Andrés Villaverde pour sabotage, qui sera maintenu longtemps en prison sans que rien ne soit possible de prouver contre lui.




1994 :

 A Berlin, le K.O.M.I.T.E.E attaque un bâtiment de l'armée à l'aide de plusieurs engins incendiaires.




1997 :

 En Ontario, c'est la plus grande grève de l'histoire de l'université et des écoles aux Amériques : plus de 2.1 millions d'étudiant-e-s y participent.




2005 :

 A Clichy-sous-Bois, Zyed et Bouna, deux jeunes poursuivis par la BAC, se réfugient dans un transformateur électrique et y meurent. S'ensuivront de grandes émeutes et une déclaration de couvre-feu, tandis que l'état d'urgence sera déclaré en région parisienne.




 

 

 

 




2006 :

 A Oaxaca au Mexique, lors de la répression contre le soulèvement de la ville contre le gouverneur, le journaliste anarchiste d'Indymedia Brad Will est abattu par la police.




 

 

 

 




2013 :

 A Nijni-Novgorod en Russie, un centre de recrutement de l'armée est attaqué au cocktail molotov. L'anarchiste Ilya Romanov, blessé, sera arrêté par la police.




2018 :

 A Titz en Rhénanie-du-Nord, dans la nuit, quatre bus de la société autocariste « Tirtey » 

sont incendiés

 près de la mine à ciel ouvert. Il y en aurait pour plus de 400.000 euros de dégâts. L'attaque incendiaire n'est pas revendiquée, mais elle parle d'elle-même, dans un contexte local de lutte directe contre un projet d'extraction de charbon et de répression.




Voir aussi 

l'éphéméride anarchiste

 du 27 octobre, qui offre notamment une biographie conséquente de Makhno.

author: Alfons Bech, Dick Nichols
title: International convoy seeks to boost solidarity with Ukraine from the bottom up
content:
Alfons Bech is the International Network for Solidarity with Ukraine (INSU) trade union coordinator and a member of the Coordination Group of the International Solidarity Convoy to Ukraine, organising its southern route from Barcelona to Kyiv.

Green Left’s Dick Nichols spoke to Bech about the convoy’s goals and organisation.

Where did the idea of the convoy come from?

It emerged on the second anniversary of Russia’s full-scale invasion [February 22, 2024], when the European Network for Solidarity with Ukraine (ENSU, now INSU) proposed organising a large international delegation of trade unionists to an event in Kyiv that the Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine (FPU) and the Confederation of Free Trade Unions of Ukraine prepared with the support of the European Trade Union Confederation.

Trade unions participated in very large numbers, but online. Only one delegation went to Kyiv, representing the Catalan affiliate of the all-Spanish General Union of Workers (UGT).

The UGT delegation was very shocked by what they saw, but very pleased to have been there in person. They saw the devastation Russia had caused in Bucha and in the neighbourhoods of Kyiv, took part in the distribution of some material aid and got to know a little about Ukrainian culture.

From this, a sort of twinning has developed between the UGT and Ukrainian trade unions, which has been key to our understanding of this war and to the aid effort for Ukraine in Catalonia.

Many aid convoys have already gone to Ukraine. What makes this one different?

This convoy is building on what has already been done at the grassroots level in terms of aid to Ukraine. Nonetheless, this convoy takes place at a crucial moment for Ukraine and Europe.

We are entering the fifth year of a brutal war, and it is not clear how much further attacks the country’s already heavily damaged infrastructure can withstand.

The experience of the past four years shows Ukrainian workers will continue to suffer greatly from always having to repair infrastructure under enemy fire. Russia, conscious of this situation, is preparing to attack even more forcefully what is essential to the survival of the population: energy, cities, hospitals, schools, the bridges of Kyiv, the water supply and the sewerage system

It is a genocidal plan. But it is not being implemented because Russia is doing well in the war or economically. [Vladimir] Putin’s regime faces many difficulties, and these are translating into savage attacks on Ukraine’s civilian population and more repression within Russia.

In this situation of extreme need, we know that any help the convoy can provide, while useful, will be a drop in the ocean.

That is one potent reason why the convoy must have an extra, political, dimension, as a public and visible show of support from the working people of the rest of Europe to their sisters and brothers in Ukraine.

It repeats the cry of the Spanish Civil War, ¡No Pasaran! (They shall not pass) against today’s enemies of human and democratic rights and their chief guarantor, the majority of working people.

We, in Catalonia, cannot bear to see in Ukraine a repeat of the Spanish Republic’s fate, which was abandoned in the face of international fascism. That treachery by great “civilised” powers intent on appeasing [Adolf] Hitler and [Benito] Mussolini cost the peoples of the Spanish state forty years of fascism.

So, the stakes could not be higher…

It is why we in INSU see the need for the sort of sharp expansion of solidarity action that the convoy represents — it is not enough for us to just carry on doing what we have been doing up to now.

What the convoy offers is not only humanitarian or material aid. It is also an instrument for showing that boosted solidarity with Ukraine starts from the bottom up.

This is not just a message about getting more and bigger donations, but of raising awareness about what the overall effort of solidarity with Ukraine must involve.

One critically important example: it is urgent Ukraine receive the €210 billion in frozen Russian assets held by Western financial institutions, such as Euroclear, to fund its defence effort.

While most European governments are looking for ways to cut social spending and increase military spending, these same governments are reluctant to declare the kind of financial war on the Kremlin that would be involved in releasing these assets to Ukraine.

The convoy will be a platform for this and other important messages.

What organisations are supporting the convoy?

As of early October, a growing number of trade union organisations, social movements and elected representatives from 20 countries have officially supported the convoy.

Trade union support includes the FPU, the Swiss Trade Union Federation, the Brazilian Trade Union and Popular Centre Conlutas, the General Labour Federation of Belgium, the Belgian Confederation of Christian Trade Unions, the UGT of Catalonia, the Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation, the University and College Union of the United Kingdom and the Theatre and Performing Arts Trade Union of Norway.

It is also supported by more than 20 political organisations and parties spanning Europe, the Americas, Asia and Oceania, and more than 40 MPs and public representatives, including 18 Members of the European Parliament.

More than 50 solidarity associations, NGOs and independent media outlets have also expressed support. All of this can be found on the convoy’s website, which we update weekly as the number of organisations and volunteers grows.

The convoy has launched its own fund appeal. Where is it at?

The convoy’s central fund appeal “Generators and Stoves to Ukraine” is now [October 19] approaching 30% of its €100,000 target, after a bit more than a month of serious effort.

This shows the initiative is reaching a broader audience of people who want to do something for Ukraine.

What is the convoy planning to take to Ukraine?

The main “cargo” will be generators, wood-burning stoves, medical supplies, electrical equipment that cannot be sourced in Ukraine and vehicles.

We will provide humanitarian aid, supplying whatever we can of the requests received from Ukrainian organisations.

What impact, if any, do you expect the convoy to have inside Ukraine?

The convoy, while supporting Ukraine’s rights and its resistance in general, also looks to help strengthen trade unions and civil society organisations inside Ukraine and make them more visible in the rest of Europe.

That is why we stand with workers’ unions, student unions, nurses’ unions and railway unions when the Ukrainian government attacks their rights.

We hope the arrival of the convoy will demonstrate that there is support from workers in the rest of Europe for Ukrainian workers and trade unions.

Can solidarity with Palestine go with solidarity with Ukraine?

The convoy does not require participants to take a position on Palestine, but my personal response is: “Yes, it should.” Both peoples are victims of ruthless attacks by aggressive colonialist powers that want to lay hold of their wealth and, moreover, root out their very culture.

The key difference is that Ukraine has a real state while Palestine does not. That is why Ukraine can defend itself much better than the Palestinians. But the underlying problem, which is the right to self-determination of nations, is identical.

By being passive or indifferent about either oppressed nation, you effectively offer support to their oppressor. That is why we in INSU go to demonstrations for both Ukraine and Palestine with a banner that says: “From Ukraine to Palestine, occupation is a crime.”

What final message would you give to anyone reading this interview? Why should they support this convoy?

This convoy is an opportunity for everyone who wants to do something to end a horrendously cruel invasion on just terms.

For everyone who has no trouble recognising that this aggression was started by Putin, not NATO, and who want to do something to support Ukrainians’ just resistance.

For everyone who does not want to be on the wrong side of history or have their conscience scarred by the thought of having done nothing until the war was over.

[Abridged from links.org.au. Donations to the International Solidarity Convoy to Ukraine Fund Appeal can be made here.]

author: Albashir Dahab
title: Delayed Rains and Broken Routes: War and Climate Crisis in North Darfur’s Jebel Issa
content:
All names of individuals interviewed for this article have been changed their safety and privacy. 




The Fatal Rain of Wadi Saleh




In mid-September 2026, when rain finally touched the parched soil of Jebel Issa in North Darfur’s Al-Malha locality, it did not bring life, but rather severe ecological and economic devastation.




Under normal conditions along this fragile Sahelian belt, the rainy season begins in mid-June or early July and extends through late September This predictable precipitation serves as the ultimate lifeline for rainfed millet and sorghum farming, as well as the primary water source for livestock grazing across the northern Darfur plains. This year, however, unprecedented climate variability left the skies dry until 12 September.




When a sudden isolated downpour finally struck the western sectors of Jebel Issa livestock already severely weakened by months of starvation, scorching heat, and gruelling treks between depleted pastures and distant wells suffered immediate thermal and physical shock. Over three consecutive days, from 12 to 14 September, more than 420 head of sheep perished in Wadi Saleh alone, with additional unrecorded livestock deaths reported across neighbouring valleys.




Local livestock that have died from thermal shock after delayed rain. Photo credit: Albashir Dahab / Local Reporting Network.




‘The animals had been walking exhausting multi-kilometer distances every day searching for withered pasture left over from the previous year just to reach the few functional water points,’ 

explains Hassan Ahmed (name changed), representative of the Jebel Issa Emergency Response Room. ‘They arrived at the wells severely malnourished and dehydrated When the sudden downpour hit, accompanied by an abrupt steep temperature drop their weakened bodies simply could not endure the extreme climatic shock.’




In rural Darfur, livestock ownership carries a deeply collective social weight. ‘These 420 sheep were managed collectively by 16 caretakers, but under our traditional social structure, each caretaker manages a combined herd belonging to extended families brothers and kin’ Ahmed adds: ‘Wiping out these herds means destroying the entire financial safety net and accumulated wealth for dozens of vulnerable households in a single weekend’.




Regional Climate Anomalies and Sahelian Pressure




The crisis in Jebel Issa is not an isolated weather anomaly. It reflects a broader accelerating climate shift across the northern Sahelian belt. According to regional climate assessments and data from international bodies like the 

Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change

 (IPCC), this zone is experiencing extreme rainfall variability characterised by shorter highly erratic rainy windows interspersed with prolonged, intense dry spells.




In Jebel Issa where subsistence farming relies strictly on rainfall without irrigation machinery or artificial reservoirs these delayed rains have disrupted the delicate ecological balance. According to estimates from the 

Food and Agriculture Organization

 (FAO), regional cereal production across vulnerable belts in Darfur has plummeted sharply due to the convergence of delayed rainfall and conflict. Furthermore, the localised nature of the recent rainfall left the northern and eastern sectors of Jebel Issa completely dry, creating stark disparities where some farming councils received a single downpour while adjacent areas received not a single drop.




Weaponised Geography: Blocked Routes and Economic Siege




Jebel Issa sits roughly 35 kilometers from the administrative centre of Al-Malha. Jebel Issa serves as the central economic agricultural and water hub for a vast cluster of surrounding village councils including Wadi Hora, Jabra, Wadi Bisha, Wadi Tandis, and Del Sari. Neighboring areas such as Wadi Akhdar, Al-Har, Um Saro, Aito, Ashar, and Abkran face identical climatic conditions and rely entirely on Jebel Issa’s central infrastructure.




Wells in Jebel Issa are a source of water for a much wider region. Some currently stand empty. Photo credit: Albashir Dahab / Local Reporting Network.




Historically, communities in North Darfur weathered severe dry spells through vibrant cross-border trade and commercial supply lines moving along three major trade arteries: the Al-Dabbah route connecting to Northern Sudan, the Mellit route leading deeper into Darfur, and the northern Triangle (Al-Muthalath) border highway linking Sudan to Libya and Egypt.




However, the ongoing armed conflict between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has transformed these trade routes into active battlelines and militarised checkpoints. The total closure of these three commercial arteries has effectively placed Jebel Issa under an economic siege As noted by food security monitoring networks like 

FEWS NET,

 supply blockades have crippled regional markets, causing staple grain and fuel prices to surge far beyond the financial reach of rural families living below the poverty line.




Collapse of the Groundwater Network




The destruction of state infrastructure, public services, and municipal funding due to the war has turned the daily retrieval of drinking water into a desperate struggle for survival.




The water supply grid across Jebel Issa relies on nine deep groundwater wells powered by diesel generators or solar energy systems. Today, the network is in a state of advanced collapse: o

ut of the nine deep groundwater wells supplying the region, only four remain operational.

 Three solar-powered wells have completely shut down due to damaged inverters, broken solar panels, and electrical component failures. Due to the total blockade of commercial routes, replacement spare parts cannot be imported or transported into North Darfur. 

Two government-owned diesel wells sit idle due to a total lack of fuel supplies.




The remaining two government wells are operated solely through voluntary community pooling where impoverished residents contribute their remaining cash to buy overpriced fuel on the black market. The only other functional points are two privately owned solar wells operating at maximum capacity.




Queues outside some of the few function wells in the region. Photo credit: Albashir Dahab / Local Reporting Network.




This severe contraction from nine operational wells down to four has created dangerous chokepoint conditions Thousands of residents and tens of thousands of livestock are forced to congregate around fewer water points, drastically increasing the physical distance herders must travel and intensifying the physical exhaustion that proved fatal during the September rains.




With international and national humanitarian organisations entirely absent from this remote zone, the Jebel Issa Emergency Response Rooms voluntary body organised by local youth remains the sole entity managing water distribution, emergency maintenance, and limited relief efforts.




Voices from the Ground: Farmers on the Brink of Famine




Communities across Jebel Issa practice traditional, low-input rainfed agriculture using hand tools. Without tractors, modern fertilizers or commercial reserves, any single crop failure translates directly into immediate widespread food insecurity.




‘In previous years, by mid-September, we would have finished clearing weeds from our fields and begun preparing for the early harvest’ says Mona Khalid (name changed for security reasons) a 28-year-old mother of three who cultivates a 2.5-acre plot 




‘Last year, seeing someone ask for grain in the street was an unusual sight. Today with hundreds of displaced families fleeing active conflict zones into our villages mothers begging for a small bowl of millet or sorghum has become an everyday reality’.




Mohamed Omer , a 35-year-old father of five who planted his 3-acre plot before the rains arrived shares a similar story of loss. ‘Nothing I planted has germinated or survived’ Omer says ‘Half the agricultural season has already slipped away. Even if late rains fall now, the crops will not have enough time to mature before the heat dries them out. My heart sinks knowing our harvest has completely failed’. 




For rural households in North Darfur, food security is tied directly to millet, the primary grain used to make Aseeda (a traditional thick porridge) ‘We do not rely on wheat bread here; millet porridge is our daily life’ explains Yousif Issa a 37-year-old father of four ‘Today, millet is completely absent from the markets. Neighbors frequently come to my door asking if I have anything left to feed their starving children. Even though my own family has almost nothing left, I divide whatever small portion of grain we have remaining’.




A Race Against Time




As the dry pasture left over from the previous year is rapidly consumed, livestock face an inevitable starvation crisis long before the arrival of the next rainy season. The threat is further amplified by the total collapse of public veterinary services. Without vaccines antibiotics or veterinary personnel, minor treatable livestock diseases are turning into fatal outbreaks across North Darfur 




Historically, families survived failed agricultural seasons by selling a portion of their livestock to purchase grain or through mutual community aid. Today both safety nets have dissolved: livestock are dying or too emaciated to sell at market, grain is unavailable for purchase, and the entire population has been reduced to equal levels of poverty.




The crisis in Jebel Issa illustrates a stark reality across the Sahelian belt climate shocks do not occur in a vacuum In North Darfur, extreme weather variability has collided with an escalating war and severe supply blockades, stripping vulnerable communities of their traditional coping strategies and pushing an entire region toward an unprecedented compound human and ecological catastrophe.




The post 

Delayed Rains and Broken Routes: War and Climate Crisis in North Darfur’s Jebel Issa

 appeared first on 

African Arguments

.

author: Unknown
title: "Lula'yı zafere toplumsal taban, kitle seferberliği ve demokrasi taşıdı"
content:
Aralarında “Toplumsal Cinsiyet ve Eşitsizlikler: Brezilya'da Demokrasinin Sınırları” başlıklı kitabının da yer aldığı birçok yapıtın yazarı Brasilia Üniversitesi (UnB) Siyaset Bilimi Profesörü

 

Flávia Biroli başkanlık seçimlerini ülkenin popüler gazetelerinden

 Folha de São Paulo'da "Lula'yı zafere toplumsal taban, kitle seferberliği ve demokrasi taşıdı" başlıklı makalesiyle değerlendirdi. Biroli, Lula'nın kampanyasının 

Brezilyalıların irkilerek baba ve oğul Bolsonarolar'ın pandemi günlerine geri dönüşü temsil ettiklerini hatırlamalarına yardımcı olarak başarıya ulaştığına dikkat çekti. 




Siyaset bilimci, tarihçi ve feminist kuramcı Biroli, 2005'ten bu yana Brasília Üniversitesi'nde (UnB) ders veriyor ve halen Siyaset Bilimi Enstitüsü'nde profesör olarak görev yapıyor. 2018–2020 arasında Brezilya Siyaset Bilimi Derneğinin (ABCP) başkanlığını üstlendi; 2009–2017 arasında Revista Brasileira de Ciência Política dergisinin editörlüğünü yürüttü. Araştırmaları özellikle demokrasi, toplumsal eşitsizlikler, feminist siyaset teorisi, neoliberalizm ve yeni muhafazakârlık üzerinde yoğunlaşıyor. Önemli eserleri arasında Feminizm ve Demokrasi (Luis Felipe Miguel ile, 2014), Toplumsal Cinsiyet ve Eşitsizlikler: Brezilya'da Demokrasinin Sınırları (2018) ve Toplumsal Cinsiyet, Yeni Muhafazakârlık ve Demokrasi (Maria das Dores Campos Machado ve Juan Marco Vaggione ile, 2020) de yer alıyor.







Bu pazar (25 Ekim) tanık olduğumuz şey, son iki haftada giderek büyüyen bir dalganın sonucuydu. Lula ikinci turu kazandı, çünkü İşçi Partisi (PT) hâlâ geniş bir toplumsal tabana sahip. Bu taban, tarihsel olarak örgütlü kesimlerin, 2013'ten bu yana daha güçlü bir örgütsel varlık kazanan toplumsal hareketlerin ve o ana kadar potansiyeli bilinmeyen bir gücün birleşiminden oluşuyor: Bu ülkenin dört bir yanında sokaklara çıkan, aralarında oldukça genç öğrencilerin de önemli bir yer tuttuğu gençliğin gücü. Bu toplumsal taban aşırı sağı durdurmaya kararlı olduğu için Milletvekili André Janones'in sosyal medya atağı karşılık buldu.




PT'nin zaferi, bir siyasal programa sahip olmanın fark yarattığını da gösteriyor. Flávio Bolsonaro (Liberal Parti - PL), PT karşıtlığına bel bağladı; halk karşıtı tutumlarının artık savunulamaz hâle geldiğini anlamıştı. Ancak yeterince açıklanmayan bir “büyük kesinti” programıyla bir tür sağcı Lulacılığı birleştirmeye çalışan, inandırıcı görünmeyen bir taklidin ötesine geçemedi. Bu kez geniş cephe aşağıdan kuruldu. Birleşik Sağlık Sistemi'nin (SUS), asgari ücrette reel artışın, iş dışında bir yaşamın, kamusal eğitimin, Bolsa Família aile yardımı programının ve altyapı yatırımlarının (elektrik, su sarnıçları) savunulması, somut bir içeriğe sahip demokrasi savunusu olarak yaygınlaştı. Soyut bir kavramın ötesine geçti.




Demokrasiyi kitle seferberliğiyle savunurken, nelerin söz konusu olduğunun kavranması, hep bir arada oy kullanmayanların oranını ve geçersiz oyları azaltarak seçim sonucunu değiştirdi. Birinci ve ikinci tur arasında boş oyların oranı yüzde 1,84'ten yüzde 1,12'ye; geçersiz oyların oranı yüzde 2,93'ten yüzde 2,12'ye geriledi. Asıl etki, sandığa gitmeme oranının yüzde 21,08'den yüzde 19,21'e düşmesinde görüldü. Ancak Lula'nın oylarındaki artış bu farkı da aşıyor; bu da seçmenlerin oy tercihlerini değiştirdiğini gösteriyor.




Evet, ülke bölünmüş durumda. Ulusal Kongre de aşırı sağın gücünü ortaya koyuyor. Ancak nispi temsil sistemiyle belirlenen parlamento üyelikleri için kullanılan oylarla cumhurbaşkanlığı için kullanılan oylar arasında önemli bir fark var. İnsanların günlük yaşamlarını etkileyecek bir tehdidin açıkça ortaya konması, baba Jair Bolsonaro hükümetinin keyfî uygulamalarını yeniden hatırlattı. Haberler, halkla yapılan söyleşiler ve internet mizahı, pandemi felaketini yeniden gündeme getirdi. Baba Bolsonaro'nun gerçek ve olası şiddet örnekleri olarak hafızalarda yer etmiş kabalıkları, oğulun alaycı davranışlarıyla yeniden canlandı.




Öğleden sonra ülkede, seçmenlerin oy kullanmasının engellenmesine yönelik girişimlere tanık olundu. Bu son derece ağır bir durum ve seçim suçu oluşturuyor. Bu yazıyı bitirdiğim sırada, Bolsonaro yanlısı kesimden seçilmiş bazı parlamenterler, bir kez daha seçim sonuçlarını kabul etmeyeceklerinin işaretlerini veriyor. Önümüzde hareketli günler var ve demokratik kurumlar bir kez daha sınanacak.




Ancak bu kez iş başında, son haftalardaki sokak gösterilerinden güç alan, solda seferber olmuş bir siyasal hareket var.




(FB/EK)

author: Sara Connors
title: First Nation of Na-Cho Nyäk Dun says it’s up to citizens to decide how to move forward on Eagle mine
content:
The First Nation at the centre of the Eagle gold mine disaster in north-central Yukon says it will ultimately be up to its citizens to decide how it plans to support the sale of the mine to a foreign mining company.

The First Nation of Na-Cho Nyäk Dun, on whose traditional territory the mine is located, indicated in an Oct. 23 news release that while negotiations with Singapore-based mining and acquisitions company Boroo are in the early stages, the relationship appears positive.

“Boroo has approached our Nation with openness, respect and good faith, and we recognize the positive foundation that has been established,” it says.

“We are not turning away from mining. We believe the answer is to do it better,” it adds.

The release says the First Nation is not granting any interviews for the time being.

A failure at the mine’s heap leach facility in June 2024 saw more than 300,000 cubic metres of cyanide-contaminated water released into the surrounding environment on the First Nation’s traditional territory. The mine subsequently went into receivership.

The Yukon government and PricewaterhouseCoopers, the mine’s receiver, announced last week that they had reached an agreement to sell the mine for up to $140 million, a process they said will include input from Na-Cho Nyäk Dun.

Officials said any potential buyer is required to have an agreement with the First Nation in order for the sale to proceed and mining operations to restart.

Yukon, Canada, ask for dismissal of $150M mining lawsuit launched by First Nation of Na-Cho Nyäk Dun

Singapore-based company chosen as potential buyer for Yukon mine after collapse

According to the release, the First Nation wants its citizens to have “the full picture” before it decides whether to support the sale. It notes that citizens “hold the highest authority” through its assembly process.

It says that includes understanding the environmental, technical, economic and long-term implications of the sale, as well as having the opportunity to ask questions before it makes an “informed decision.”

It also notes that the First Nation doesn’t want to be rushed during the process, either.

“Our administration, Lands Department, technical experts, negotiators and Council are working hard to understand the risks, strengthen protections and secure the strongest possible agreement for our people, our lands and the Yukon,” it states.

“If we get this right, Eagle Gold can become a story not only of what went wrong, but of how we learned, rebuilt trust and chose a better path for the generations who will inherit the consequences of our choices.”

The sale is not a done deal, at least not yet.

It still requires court approval and other conditions before Boroo can take possession of the site.

With the sale expected to close before year’s end, the release indicates it is a critical time for the First Nation.

“The most important work for our Nation is still ahead,” it states.

Sara Connors is originally from Nova Scotia and has a journalism degree from the University of King’s College in Halifax. After graduation she worked in South Korea for two years as an English language teacher and freelance journalist. After she returned home in 2019 she worked behind the scenes at CTV Atlantic in Halifax before joining APTN's Yukon bureau in July 2020.

author: labor4pal
title: Motown and the Making of Working-Class Revolutionaries: an Interview with Jerome Scott and Walda Katz-Fishman (UAWD Daily Struggle)
content:
Anthony Stoner October 26, 2026

Jerome Scott and Walda Katz-Fishman, authors of Motown and the Making of Working-Class Revolutionaries: The League of Revolutionary Black Workers, share their reflections on the UAW’s Black radical tradition, the tactic of the wildcat strike, and the importance of unions fighting for the working class as a whole.

In the 1960s, Chrysler—the only Big Three corporation whose operations remained largely in Detroit at the time—began to hire Black workers, many fresh from the U.S. South. They had the worst and most dangerous jobs, and Chrysler frequently fired them before they obtained UAW contract protections after a 90-day probation. In 1968, these conditions and the lack of representation by the white-dominated UAW—at that time led by Walter Reuther, whose “Administration Caucus” dominated the union then and for decades after his death led to a wildcat strike in the Dodge Main plant initiated by the Dodge Revolutionary Union Movement (DRUM) (A wildcat strike is a strike not officially authorized by a union). A number of other RUMs were then created around Detroit, and in 1969 the League of Revolutionary Black Workers (LRBW) was founded by Black militant labor organizers to help unite and aid struggles around the city. Among those organizers was Jerome Scott, who, along with Walda Katz-Fishman, has written an account of the LRBW, based on extensive interviews with surviving members of the League, their families and comrades. Their book, Motown and the Making of Working-Class Revolutionaries: The Story of the League of Revolutionary Black Workers, is available from University of Georgia Press.

—Anthony Stoner, UAW Local 4811

Anthony SToner: Why were wildcat strikes the tactic both DRUM and then the LRBW focused on? What’s the role of a wildcat strike for today?

Jerome scott: The wildcat strike became our principal tactic mainly because it was a two-edged sword. We could attack the company as well as struggle with the union. The company of course was and is the major enemy, but back in the day, and in some unions even today, the collaboration between the union and the corporation is not good for the workers themselves. And so we realized after the first wildcat strike (for us, and the first in the country for about fifty years) at Dodge Main that that wildcat strike really did attack both of our struggles. What we didn’t realize when we started it was that it was also a very offensive tactic. We were making the decisions; and the corporation and the union had to respond and defend against that, rather than the workers always being on the defensive. So the wildcat strike was a hell of a weapon.

AS: How did Doug Fraser [then head of UAW Chrysler Department] and the UAW International use the “flying squadron” during the 1973 wildcat?

JS: A little bit on the history of the flying squadron. It started with the United Mine Workers movement in Appalachia because of the rolling strikes that happened in the organizing of that union. It was an organized group of union members that they would take from strike event to strike event and try to make sure that nobody crossed the picket line. They were an apparatus that actually really backed up the picket lines in the strikes that were held in the heyday of organizing the UAW, the United Mine Workers, and so on. And the purpose was really to let the workers know that the International was part of this strike. So the concept of the flying squadron had a long tradition of respect from the union movement.

In our case, in our strike at Chrysler in 1973, we were able to shut down the entire Chrysler corporation for about a week; and that was because of the strategic nature of the Detroit Forge plant where I worked. There was only one other plant in the world that made the same parts that we made and it was a forging plant in [apartheid-era] South Africa. The corporation had done all it could do to try to break our strike, and try to break the picket line, but the picket line was going on 24/7.

What we learned later is that the corporation had called Solidarity House and said, “you have to do something about this strike.” And it was then that Fraser organized the historic flying squadron to come break our picket line rather than support it. And it was a pitched battle—it wasn’t like we saw them coming and laid down our picket signs—it was a big struggle. But eventually they were able to break our picket line and end our struggle after a week. Now the company decided that they would permanently fire three of us. But later on we learned that the company didn’t decide who to fire—the company left it up to the union to decide. They fired two Black workers and one white worker, two production workers and one skilled trades worker. The two Black workers were in the League of Revolutionary Black Workers leading up to that strike, and the skilled trades person was someone we had worked with in our plant over the previous two years. So not only did they bring out the flying squadron to break our strike, they also collaborated with the company to decide who would be permanently fired.

Now, that permanent fire for the three of us sort of backfired on them, because one of the skilled tradesmen who was out on the wildcat strike was also in the process of buying a bar across the street from the plant we had just shut down, and across the street from six other Chrysler plants up and down that block. So he hired the three of us as bartenders, and that became the best job we had ever had. Because once you shut down the corporation and people knew you were in this fight with the union and the company, they wanted to talk to us. So we had a constant flow of workers coming into the bar, having political discussions, trying to figure out how they could have a wildcat strike at their shop.

AS: Why do you think the International was acting this way—was it mostly racism, was it also their investments in the company?

JS: The 70s was a period when the unions were really trying to collaborate with corporations to have these “Joint Work Committees” on the shop floor with the foremen and the workers. They were promoting this whole idea that we could have peace in the working-class battle between the owners of the Chrysler corporation and the workers. So it was this notion, I think, that we could have this “peaceful” period, where they wouldn’t have to strike, they wouldn’t have to do the real fight for workers, but the corporation would somehow allow them to make advances.

I think there’s one other thing that played into this: early on in the 50s, unions made a decision that they would only represent their members, and not the working class as a whole, and so they saw this peaceful coexistence with the corporation as a way to support their members and separate themselves from the struggles of the working class as a whole and concentrate on just the relations between their members and the corporations as opposed to the struggles between the working class and the corporations.

WALDA katz-fishman: The workers also did some investigation, and they found out the union was actually invested in the corporation and was making more money from its investments than from the actual dues from its members. So it was not just a political collaboration, it was really an economic merging of the interests of the “union hierarchy” and the corporation. And that’s pretty extraordinary: Y’all should do some investigation today.

AS: Your book discusses the idea of union organizing for the working class as a whole rather than just representing the members of the union. Why is that important? What can we do with that today?

When you struggle for higher wages in a shop, that really does affect the whole community around it. And so if you fight and bring in the communities around the shops and bring in whatever motion around police brutality or the fight against poverty or any of those community-based fights, they’re all working-class fights.

JS: It’s more important today than it’s ever been. When the trade union movement was developing in this country, it developed on the basis of representing the working class. Back in the 30s and 40s, there were at least 9 or 10 international unions that demanded the end of capitalism as the way for workers to actually get and hold what they were fighting for. So the trade union movement has a revolutionary guts to it that they’ve been trying to stomp out ever since. I think it was during the McCarthy era in the early 50s, one of the demands that the ruling class made on the union movement—well of course, one of them was to rid itself of any communists that existed in the leadership and try to scorch its membership as well. But one of the other demands was that they had to stop trying to mobilize the working class as part of the union struggle and only concentrate on their members. And the corporations would then back off on the struggle around contracts and give them easier access to making contracts. So the leadership of the international trade union movement made that agreement. They agreed that they would concentrate on their membership.

The reason it’s so important is because when you struggle for higher wages in a shop, that really does affect the whole community around it. And so if you fight and bring in the communities around the shops and bring in whatever motion around police brutality or the fight against poverty or any of those community-based fights, they’re all working-class fights. And a trade union struggle in the middle of that can add a lot of power and prestige to those struggles as well as provide the trade union with support from the community that will also have an effect on their battle in the shop.

We have got to understand that we’re in a much more powerful position if we approach it from the standpoint of a broad-based front of struggle to organize a shop. Not just the workers in it, but their families, the community that it sits in, the drivers that service it, the whole shebang. And more or less a working-class strategy for organizing a union rather than a membership-based strategy for organizing a union.

WKF: Huge sections of the working class, the academy, professors and scientists and doctors and nurses and the whole tech industry that has not been historically unionized, are losing jobs. They’re losing jobs, job security, certainly benefits, and so we’re in a class war. And so to develop that class consciousness when the trade union movement is such a small percentage of the working class, it’s really important for us to think about the working class as a whole, and it’s really important for that section that is more highly organized to help broaden out the understanding of who we are, what our interests are in society, and how do we help lift up and help organize the working class as a whole. And I think some of the unions have played an important role—in May Day Strong, or in the call for a 2028 general strike—so we can see that they have a capacity to take some important “leadership roles,” because they do have resources and organization.

AS: How important was organizing around health and safety issues to expanding League contacts with the non-Black workers in the factory, the white workers, the skilled trade workers, and so on?

JS: Health and safety was a lot bigger than anybody thought, when you think back on it. There were two major things that were really the impetus for wildcat strikes. One of course was the way management treated workers. The whole question of white supremacy in the plants back in the 60s was just as bad as anyplace else. The foremen thought they could treat Black workers any way they wanted to, and treated us like, I’ll fire your ass in a second, if you don’t do as I tell you to do and not argue with me, not discuss with me whether or not it’s legal for me to treat you this way. The other reason was health and safety. Somebody was always getting hurt in the plant, every day. Once we began to reach out to white workers to try to figure out how to build those kinds of relationships, we realized the connecting factor was health and safety, and skilled trades workers were just as concerned that they might get injured on the job as we were as production workers.

WKF: As I recall, it was a white worker whose hand was cut off; that was the provocation for the ‘73 wildcat strike.

WKF: And what the white workers said to you all, the Black workers, we’re really glad you all have been carrying forward this fight. So once they were able to work together, it was better, the wildcat was more powerful when it was a multiracial wildcat.

There has always been multiracial struggle—there’s been Black working-class struggle but also multiracial struggle—in the South against the conditions of life there.

JS: The difference between the wildcats that happened prior to our ‘73 wildcat, which was mainly Black workers that went out and were able to shut down the process of that particular factory for a while. Our ability to shut Chrysler down for a whole week was the difference between having the vast majority of the workers in that shop support the strike versus only Black workers. So it meant all the difference in the world.

AS: Many of the League workers either themselves or their families had come from the South. Why is the South this important battleground in the class war?

WKF: What I think the League expresses is that there has always been multiracial struggle—there’s been Black working-class struggle but also multiracial struggle—in the South against the conditions of life there. There is union organizing in the South, despite Taft-Hartley, which said states can implement state-by-state right-to-work laws, which makes it almost impossible for unions to organize, so the South became the “solid South” of right-to-work. So both in terms of both working-class organizing and in terms of federal policy—economy, ecology, politics, and society, public institutions—the South is either a place where the working class breaks through or the capitalist class manages to control it and therefore the nation. And that’s why the South is such a battleground today, it’s emerging because the working class is in motion, and they know this is the place where it’s easiest for them to grab control back.

JS: The ruling class is once again relying on the fact that if they’re going to consolidate fascism in this country, they have to consolidate it in the South. And therefore they have to get rid of the Voting Rights Act, and they have to prevent unions from spreading across the South in this period where unions are really beginning to pick up again and beginning to organize.

AS: Tell me about the history of the League and its contacts with the PLO (Palestine Liberation Organization) and the Arab Workers Caucus (in the UAW in Dearborn, Michigan), especially given Israel’s genocide and the UAW’s divestment from Israel bonds.

JS: Over the last couple years, we’ve given a lot of thought to this too. We looked at ourselves as oppressed and exploited people—and Detroit and Dearborn was a special sort of area of the country. We had a bigger Middle Eastern population in Dearborn than any other place outside of the Middle East. And that was true because of the recruitment of international workers by the auto industry. They figured that cultural division might slow down the union process. But the fact was that we were working side by side with Middle Eastern folk who had migrated here to the United States and were part of our working-class brothers and sisters. When we learned that the UAW was buying Israeli bonds and that that was supporting the oppression of the Palestinian people, we reached out to our coworkers, and we even had delegations go to the Middle East and meet primarily with the PLO.

We realized it was our country, our government, that was sending all this money to Israel and soliciting our trade unions to use our pension funds, our money, to buy Israeli bonds. So not only did we develop good relations with them, but one of the wildcat strikes back in the day was a wildcat strike against the UAW continuing to buy those bonds. We didn’t appreciate our dues being used to support the oppression and exploitation of another set of oppressed and exploited people. That was the basis of our relationship, and we continued to have those kinds of relationships not only with the Palestinian people—we did the same thing with the Vietnamese people, and the Irish struggle against the British, the whole shebang of oppressed and exploited people—we tried to reach out to and let them know we were all fighting the same kind of fight, only on different fronts.

You have to return to the roots of the trade union movement and make your struggle […] a working-class issue, and any advancements, you want to be applied not only to the workers in that industry but also to the communities in which those workers live and to the section of society which those workers represent.

WKF: So internationalism was a big part of their working-class understanding of the world. It was Edna in our interviews who said what Jerome just said: We organized together because we lived side by side, in the same neighborhoods and worked together. So it was a very concrete unity, as well as an intellectual kind of unity, a political unity.

AS: What does the experience of the League contribute now to militant unionism?

JS: This is a war on the working class—it’s a war on the unions, so you’ve got to act like it’s a war—but it’s also a war on the working class as a whole. You have to return to the roots of the trade union movement and make your struggle, your contracts or whatever issue you’re fighting around, a working-class issue, and any advancements, you want to be applied not only to the workers in that industry but also to the communities in which those workers live and to the section of society which those workers represent. And so there has to be a working-class victory. And in order for there to be a working-class victory, you’ve got to mobilize and educate the working class as a whole.

That would be my message to the UAW. If they want this general strike in 2028 to actually happen and be a success, the mobilization for it has got to be a society, working-class-wide mobilization. When ‘28 comes, you might have those contracts that expire at the same time. But if you don’t have some secondary boycotts organized, if you don’t have some secondary supports mobilized around the logistics industry, then it will not be successful. So it has to be a community-wide effort if we’re going to make this general strike be an advancement for the working class in taking the offensive in this war.

WKF: The only other thing is that if it’s only about 10% of workers—and that’s workers who have jobs—who are unionized, then we’ve got to go back to our working-class roots. The trade union movement has an opportunity to really play a leadership role. But they’ve got to reach deep down to where the working class is, which is outside of the trade union movement, and figure out how to really play that role to build an organized hub of organizing.
