author: Helmut Weiss
title: Genua als Vorbild: Hafenarbeiter:innen weltweit im Widerstand gegen Militarisierung und Waffentransport
content:
Dossier




Der 

Streik der Hafenarbeiter von Genua gegen die Waffenlieferungen an die mörderische Saud-Bande und ihren Krieg gegen Jemen

 war eine Art Fanal, dass endlich etwas geschehen muss. Die Aktion der italienischen Docker steht in einer langen Tradition solcher Aktionen, mit denen bereits Waffenlieferungen nach Vietnam verhindert worden waren, aber auch Waffen an die Pinochet-Diktatur zu liefern wurde in Genua verhindert. Eine Tradition, die auch unter heutigen, schwierigen Bedingungen fortgesetzt werde, so sagt es Giacomo Marchetti, der zu den Organisatoren der Aktion gehörte im Gespräch mit David Broder 

„We Won’t Load Your Ships of Death – Italian dockers against Saudi war machine“ ursprünglich am 25. Mai 2019 im Jacobin Mag

 

, jetzt auf Europe Solidaire dokumentiert. Spätestens seit dem Ukraine-Krieg und Nahost-Konflikt hat sich der Wirderstand in den Häfen internalisiert – siehe dazu die Aktionen und 

die Liste der Länder-Meldungen/Dossiers

:







30. Oktober 2026: Gewerkschaften der Hafenarbeiter in mehr als 40 Häfen kündigen einen internationalen Tag der Streiks und Proteste gegen Krieg und Völkermord an 

 


„

Gewerkschaften, die die Beschäftigten in 40 Häfen in Europa und im Mittelmeerraum vertreten, rufen zu einem internationalen Aktionstag am 30. Oktober auf. Gewerkschaften der Hafenarbeiter in Frankreich, Griechenland, dem Baskenland, der Türkei, Marokko und Italien rufen für den ​„30. Oktober“ zu einem internationalen Aktionstag gegen Krieg und Militarisierung auf. Sie fordern ein Ende des ​„Völkermords am palästinensischen Volk“ und der ​„US-israelischen Angriffskriege im Nahen Osten und gegen den Iran“.


„Jede Gewerkschaft wird entsprechend den jeweiligen nationalen Gegebenheiten über die am besten geeignete Form der Mobilisierung entscheiden, ausgehend von Streikmaßnahmen und dem gemeinsamen Engagement, das Verursachen von Tod und Zerstörung zu verhindern“, heißt es in einer gemeinsamen Erklärung der Gewerkschaften, die am 31. Juli an das Workday Magazine und In These Times übermittelt wurde.


Gemeinsam vertreten die Gewerkschaften laut der Erklärung die Beschäftigten in 40 Häfen in Europa und im Mittelmeerraum. Ihr Aufruf zur Eskalation ging aus einem Treffen der Hafenarbeitergewerkschaften hervor, das im Mai in Istanbul stattfand. In der Erklärung wird zudem ​„volle Solidarität mit den Völkern Kubas, Venezuelas und des Sudans“ zum Ausdruck gebracht und erklärt, dass ​„Häfen nicht für den Transport von Waffen, Munition, militärischer Ausrüstung oder Truppen genutzt werden dürfen, die für Kriegsgebiete bestimmt sind.“


„Nein zur Kriegswirtschaft, zu den Aufrüstungsplänen der Regierungen und zum Vorhaben der EU, Häfen und strategische Infrastruktur zu militarisieren“, bekräftigen die Gewerkschaften in ihrer Erklärung. ​„Öffentliche Mittel müssen zur Deckung der sozialen Bedürfnisse der Menschen eingesetzt werden, nicht zur Finanzierung von Kriegen.“ Zu den Unterzeichnern gehören die CGT FNPD in Frankreich, die ENEDEP in Griechenland, die LAB im Baskenland, die LIMAN-IS in der Türkei, die ODT in Marokko sowie die ORSA Porti und die USB in Italien. (…)


Die Erklärung folgt auf zwei Generalstreiks in Italien im Herbst 2025 aus Solidarität mit den Palästinensern. Vor zehn Monaten versammelten sich etwa 60 Hafenarbeiter vor dem Gebäude der Hafenbehörde in Civitavecchia, einer kleinen italienischen Küstenstadt nordwestlich von Rom. Es war der 22. September 2025, und sie hatten ihre Arbeit früher am Tag niedergelegt und den Hafen lahmgelegt – als Teil eines Generalstreiks, mit dem sie gegen die Tatsache protestierten, dass die italienische Regierung der drittgrößte Waffenlieferant Israels ist. An der Stelle, an der sie standen, waren sie von etwa 600 Menschen umringt, die sie anfeuerten – Studenten, Lehrer, Eisenbahnarbeiter, Beschäftigte des öffentlichen Dienstes – eine beachtliche Menschenmenge für eine winzige Stadt

…“ engl. 

Artikel von Sarah Lazare vom 31. Juli 2026 in In These Times

 

 („Dockworkers Unions in Six Countries Announce Day of Strikes and Protests Against War and Genocide“, maschinenübersetzt), siehe Gewerkschaftsaufrufe:







Italien

: 30. Oktober 2026: Internationaler Aktionstag der Hafenarbeiter und Beschäftigten in den Häfen. Gegen Krieg und Militarisierung – Häfen für den Frieden und für menschenwürdige Arbeit. ital. 

Aufruf von USB

 




ver.di-Aktionstag gegen soziale Angriffe, Krieg und Militarisierung im Hamburger Hafen am 30.10.2026

 im Dossier: 

Nicht „nur“ Hamburger Hafen: Tor zum Tod in der Welt – Rüstungsexporte und Militärlogistik in deutschen Häfen










21 Häfen, sechs Länder: Europaweiter Kampftag der Hafenarbeiter mit Streiks und Protesten sowie Blockaden gegen Kriegsschiffe, für Arbeitssicherheit 







Kriegshäfen unter Beobachtung: Streiks und Proteste in mehr als 20 Häfen entlang des Mittelmeeres. Sie zeigen, dass die Kriegslogistik verwundbar ist – und wie




„Unter dem Motto »Die Hafenarbeiter arbeiten nicht für den Krieg!« protestierten am Freitag Zehntausende in über 20 Häfen Europas, vor allem am Mittelmeer, gegen die aktuellen Kriege, gegen die Militarisierungspolitik der EU und gegen die Nutzung der Häfen für Waffenlieferungen etwa nach ­Israel oder in die Ukraine. Das Zentrum des Aktionstags bildete Italien, wo die Basisgewerkschaft USB (­Unione Sindacale di Base) Arbeiter und Unterstützer in einem guten Dutzend der wichtigsten Häfen des Landes zu einem Hafenstreik mobilisieren konnte – von Genua über Palermo bis Triest. Proteste gab es unter anderem auch in Spanien, Griechenland und in der Türkei; in Deutschland wurde in Hamburg protestiert. In Marokko mussten geplante Kundgebungen aufgrund schwerer Unwetter abgesagt werden. Zu den Protesten aufgerufen hatten neben der USB noch vier weitere Gewerkschaften – LAB aus dem Baskenland, Enedep aus Griechenland, Liman-İş aus der Türkei und ODT aus Marokko.


In Italien konnte die USB neben den erfolgreichen Hafenstreiks noch weitere konkrete Erfolge vermelden. In Livorno gelang es mit einer Hafenblockade, ein Schiff der israelischen Reederei ZIM, das der USB zufolge Waffen geladen hatte, am Anlegen zu hindern; es musste vor der Küste warten. Zwei weitere ZIM-Schiffe konnten nicht, wie geplant, in die Häfen in Genua und Venedig einfahren und mussten in andere Häfen in Frankreich sowie in Slowenien ausweichen. Einem aus Israel kommenden Schiff der Schweizer Reederei MSC wurde die Einfahrt in den Hafen in Ravenna verwehrt; es drehte gleichfalls in Richtung Slowenien ab. Mit ihren Aktionen ist es der USB in der Vergangenheit bereits mehrfach gelungen, die Lieferung von Waffen nach Israel zu behindern; Lieferungen mussten aufwendig umgeleitet werden, was die Reedereien jeweils Zeit und viel Geld kostete. Zudem legen Aktionen wie diese auch offen, dass die Kriegslogistik verwundbar ist – und wie.


Einen weiteren konkreten Schritt vermeldete das autonome Hafenarbeiterkollektiv CALP (Collettivo Autonomo Lavoratori Portuali) in Genua. Wie dort anlässlich des Hafenstreiks berichtet wurde, bereitet CALP aktuell den Aufbau einer Beobachtungsstelle vor, die im Hafen »die Transparenz, die ethische Nachhaltigkeit und die Sicherheit der Hafenarbeiter« überwachen soll. Genua solle seinen Hafen offiziell zu einem »Hafen des Friedens« erklären, hieß es. Die Verbindung des Kampfes gegen den Krieg mit der Sicherheit der Arbeiter ist dabei alles andere als eine willkürliche Maßnahme, wie die USB anlässlich der Proteste am Freitag betonte

…“ 

Artikel von Jörg Kronauer in der jungen Welt vom 09.02.2026

 




21 Häfen, sechs Länder: Meilenstein der Koordination und Zusammenarbeit: Europaweiter Kampftag der Hafenarbeiter




„

Auf Initiative von Gewerkschaften aus Griechenland (Enedep), dem spanischen Baskenland (LAB), der Türkei (Liman-Is), Marokko (ODT) und Italien (USB) zum gemeinsamen Streiktag gegen Krieg entwickelt sich ein neues Niveau der Koordinierung und Kooperation der Hafenarbeiter international: „Hafenarbeiter arbeiten nicht für den Krieg!“ (…)


In Italien waren die Häfen in Palermo, Salerno, Civitavecchia, Genua, Livorno, Triest, Ravenna, Ancona, Bari, Crotone beteiligt. In Griechenland Piräus und Elefsina. In Spanien Bilbao und Pasaja. In der Türkei Antalya und Mursini. In Frankreich: Marseille und in Marokko: Tanger, Casablanca und Safi. Diese Streiks zeigten die führende Rolle der Arbeiterklasse im Kampf gegen die Vorbereitungen eines Dritten weltweiten imperialistischen Kriegs. In Italien zwangen die Streikposten das mit Waffen beladene Schiff „ZIM Virginia“ dazu, vor der Küste von Livorno zu ankern, da es nicht anlegen konnte. Das Gleiche galt für mehrere andere Schiffe. Am Freitagnachmittag wurden Streikversammlungen in einer Reihe von Häfen durchgeführt. In einer Erklärung betonte der USB-Gewerkschafter Jose Nivoi, dass ein solcher Streik beispiellos sei: „Es ist das erste Mal, dass Hafenarbeiter mit Forderungen mobilisieren, die nicht nur ‚eng‘ Arbeitsfragen, sondern mit Forderungen, die mit moralischen und politischen Fragen zusammenhängen. Ziel der Blockaden ist es, den Betrieb der Häfen zu beeinträchtigen, um deutlich zu machen, dass wir Arbeiter uns nicht zu Komplizen der Kriegswirtschaft machen lassen! (…) Bis heute dauert der Völkermord an den Palästinensern an! Wir erklären klar und deutlich, dass wir als Hafenarbeiter den Export von Waffen aus unseren Häfen nach Israel nicht zulassen werden, um diesen Völkermord zu unterstützen und zu verstärken!“ Er fügte hinzu, dass dieser Streik ein wichtiges Beispiel für alle Gewerkschaften sei, die sich an Initiativen zur Koordinierung der Hafenarbeiter beteiligt haben. Am Freitagmorgen wurden auch im Baskenland (Nordspanien) in den Häfen von Pasaja und Santurce (in Bilbao) Streikposten aufgestellt. In einem Beitrag betonte die Gewerkschaft LAB, die die Organisation des Streiks angeführt hatte, wie wichtig diese Mobilisierung in den großen Häfen des gesamten Mittelmeerraums gewesen sei.


Das Gleiche gilt für die Baustellen in Piräus und andere Arbeitsstätten. An den Kais 2 und 3, wo die Hafenarbeiter den Streik bewachen, bewegt sich kein Kran. Das Schiff „Faistos Pallas“ ist voll in der Hand der streikenden Seeleute und ihrer Gewerkschaft P.E.N.E.N. Die Beteiligung der Leiharbeiter in den Werften von Elefsina war durchweg hoch trotz der Versuche der Reeder, alle gegeneinander auszuspielen. Dutzende Gewerkschaften und Arbeiterorganisationen in Piräus, Thessaloniki, Patras und weiteren organisierten seit Wochen diese antimilitaristische und politische Aktion mit großem Erfolg. Respekt an alle. Die Sprecher der Gewerkschaften machten in den Versammlungen die ständig durchgeführt werden deutlich: „Täglich wächst die Armut in den Arbeiter- und Rentnerfamilien, in der ganzen Gesellschaft. Die Löhne sind am 15. des Monats aufgebraucht. Die Ursache liegt in der kapitalistischen Krise und dem Krieg, den sie vorbereiten

.“…“ 

Korrespondenten-Bericht vom 07.02.2026 auf rf-news.de

 




Die streikenden Hafenarbeiter halten die Kriegsschiffe auf




„

Die mit Waffen beladene ZIM Virginia liegt vor der Küste von Livorno, kann aber nicht anlegen: Der Streik der Hafenarbeiter der USB blockiert sie. Das Gleiche passiert gerade mit der ZIM New Zealand, die heute Morgen im Hafen von Genua erwartet wurde, und mit der ZIM Australia, die heute in Venedig und morgen in Ravenna anlegen sollte. Auch die MSC EAGLE III, die nach Israel unterwegs ist, gestern in Ravenna ankommen sollte und heute in Venedig erwartet wurde, hat ihre Pläne verschoben.


Dies sind die ersten greifbaren Ergebnisse des internationalen Streiks, den Hafenarbeiter aus verschiedenen Ländern für heute gegen Waffenhandel, Privatisierung der Kais und Militarisierung der Häfen organisiert haben.


Der Streik und die Demonstrationen, die ursprünglich in 21 Häfen im gesamten Mittelmeerraum und auch in Nordeuropa geplant waren, ziehen nun auch andere Hafenstädte wie Marseille und Barcelona mit ein und finden sogar jenseits des Atlantiks Unterstützung

…“ ital. 

USB-Meldung vom 6.02.2026

 




6. Februar 2026: Hafenarbeiter streiken gegen den Krieg! 

USB live vom internationalen Hafenstreik auf Youtube

 

 

 (ital.)










„Waffen nieder, Löhne rauf!”: Aktionstag am 6. Februar gegen Militarisierung und Krieg in mehr als 20 Häfen am Mittelmeer – und in Hamburg 







AUFRUF ZUM HANDELN – SOLIDARITÄT MIT DEM INTERNATIONALEN HAFENARBEITERSTREIK!




„

Am 6. Februar wird Hamburg seine Stimme gegen Krieg, Waffenlieferungen und Zerstörung erheben.




WAFFENLIEFERUNGEN STOPPEN ruft zu einer Massenkundgebung gegen den Krieg in Hamburg auf, die sich gegen wichtige Unternehmen und Institutionen richtet, die von Krieg, Militarisierung und Klimazerstörung profitieren.




Ich, @mo.anker ,bin Hafenarbeiter im Hamburger Hafen und Mitglied der Gewerkschaft ver.di und lade alle Bewegungen für Palästina, gegen Krieg und für Klimagerechtigkeit ein, sich solidarisch zusammenzuschließen. Dieser Aufruf schließt sich auch den Stimmen der Gewerkschaften und Hafenarbeiter an:




– Hafenarbeiter arbeiten nicht für den Krieg.




– Häfen dürfen nicht dazu benutzt werden, Kriege, Waffenlieferungen und Zerstörung zu schüren.




– Als organisierte Arbeitnehmer stehen wir für Frieden, internationale Solidarität und eine lebenswerte Zukunft.




Dies ist ein Aufruf an Arbeitnehmer, Aktivisten, Studenten, Klimagruppen, Friedensbewegungen und internationalistische Kollektive: Schließt euch uns an, seid sichtbar, seid laut, seid viele! (…) Als Hafenarbeiter wissen wir: Ohne Arbeitskraft bewegt sich nichts. Als Bewegung wissen wir: Ohne kollektives Handeln ändert sich nichts. (…) 

Bringt Fahnen, Transparente, eure Stimmen und Solidarität mit. Lassen uns zusammen Hamburg zu einem Ort des Widerstands machen!




#internationalsolidarity #dockworkersstrike #waffenlieferungenstoppen #armsembargonow #antiimperialism

“ 

Aufruf des Bündnisses „Waffenlieferungen Stoppen Hamburg“ auf Instagram

 







zur Kundgebung am 06.02.2026 vor Eurogate zum Schichtwechsel von 13.30 Uhr bis 14.30




Start um 13:00 Uhr: HAPAG LLOYD, Ballindamm 25 (Nähe U+S-Jungfernstieg) in HAMBURG/DEUTSCHLAND




Aufgerufen wird auch zur Kundgebung des Bündnisses „Waffenlieferungenstoppen!“ bei HHLA (ca.15.10 Uhr) und MSC (ca.15.45 Uhr).










„Waffen nieder, Löhne rauf!”




„

Interview mit Cinzia Della Porta über den Aktionstag gegen Militarisierung und Krieg in mehr als 20 Häfen am Mittelmeer – von Marokko über Italien bis in die Türkei.




ROM (Eigener Bericht) – Mit einem Aktionstag an diesem Freitag protestieren Arbeiter in mehr als 20 der größten Häfen am Mittelmeer gegen die Militarisierungspolitik der EU und gegen die Nutzung der Häfen für den Waffennachschub im Ukraine-Krieg und in Israel. Man setze sich gegen „die Umwandlung des Mittelmeers in einen Knotenpunkt für die Kriegsökonomie” zur Wehr, erläutert Cinzia Della Porta im Gespräch mit german-foreign-policy.com. Della Porta gehört dem Vorstand der italienischen Gewerkschaft Unione Sindicale di Base (USB) an, die an der Organisation des Aktionstags beteiligt ist. Die Häfen am Mittelmeer müssten „Orte des Friedens” sein, fordert die USB. Della Porta weist darauf hin, dass Arbeiter stets zu den ersten gehören, die „den Preis für den Krieg” zahlten, in Form zum Beispiel von Lohnkürzungen oder der Einschränkung gewerkschaftlicher Rechte; das seien „direkte Folgen der Kriegsökonomie”. Zudem würden etwa Hafenarbeiter, die Waffen verladen müssten, zu unfreiwilligen Komplizen in Kriegen, die sie ablehnten. Della Porta plädiert dafür, den „Widerstand gegen den Krieg mit sozialen Kämpfen um Löhne, öffentliche Dienstleistungen und Arbeiterrechte” zu verbinden

…“ 

Interview  vom 6.2.2026 auf german-foreign-policy

 

 – siehe hier unten die Aufrufe aus Italien zuvor

Nicht mit uns: Gewerkschaftsmitglieder schließen sich für den Frieden zusammen




Anfang Juni haben Hafenarbeiter in Europa Maßnahmen ergriffen und sich geweigert, Militärgüter für den Hafen von Haifa in Israel umzuschlagen. Solche Aktionen unterstreichen die wachsende Dringlichkeit, Kriege zu beenden und den Frieden zu wahren – und dürfen nicht kriminalisiert werden. Rechtmäßige Proteste und die Verweigerung des Transports von Militärausrüstung sind legitime Ausdrucksformen des Gewissens, die Schutz verdienen. 

In ganz Europa stellen sich Hafenarbeiter und andere Transportbeschäftigte gegen den Transport von Militärausrüstung und bekräftigen, dass Häfen und Verkehrsinfrastruktur nicht zur Unterstützung bewaffneter Konflikte genutzt werden dürfen. Diese Aktionen spiegeln eine breitere Weigerung wider, sich an Gewalt zu mitschuldig zu machen, sowie ein gemeinsames Bekenntnis zu internationaler Solidarität und humanitären Werten.




ETF bekräftigt ihr Engagement für Solidarität und Gerechtigkeit




Angesichts der eskalierenden globalen Konflikte zeigen Verkehrsbeschäftigte in ganz Europa außerordentlichen Mut und Gewissenhaftigkeit, indem sie gegen den Transport von Militärgütern vorgehen. Von Häfen bis zu Flughäfen setzen sich die Beschäftigten für die Verteidigung humanitärer Werte ein – und die Europäische Transportarbeiter-Föderation (ETF) 

steht fest an ihrer Seite

 

.


„Niemand sollte dafür bestraft werden, dass er sich gegen Gewalt einsetzt“, sagt ETF-Generalsekretärin Livia Spera. „Wir lehnen die Kriminalisierung von Verkehrsbeschäftigten, darunter auch Hafenarbeiter, die sich weigern, sich an Kriegen zu beteiligen, entschieden ab. Ihr Mut muss verteidigt und nicht unterdrückt werden.“




Was bedeutet das für den Verkehrssektor insgesamt?




Im Laufe der Geschichte haben Verkehrsbeschäftigte immer wieder die Hauptlast von Kriegen getragen. In jedem Konflikt gehören sie zu den ersten, die leiden – sie sind Gefahren, Störungen und Vertreibung ausgesetzt. 

Dennoch spielen Verkehrsbeschäftigte eine wichtige Rolle in der Gesellschaft, insbesondere in Krisenzeiten. Sie sind unverzichtbar für die Bereitstellung humanitärer Hilfe, Evakuierungen und die Lieferung lebenswichtiger Güter. In den letzten Monaten hat ihre Rolle jedoch über die Logistik hinausgewachsen und sie sind zu einer starken Stimme für den Frieden geworden. 

Dies wurde erneut in den jüngsten Konflikten deutlich, die unsere Welt erschüttert haben. Die Weigerung, sich an Gewalt zu beteiligen, unterstreicht die lobenswerte Entschlossenheit der Arbeiterklasse, sich gegen Regierungen zu stellen, die sich mitschuldig am Krieg machen.




Solidarität ist kein Verbrechen

(…) Auch die Stadtverwaltung hatte sich mit den Hafenarbeitern solidarisiert. »Wir sind davon überzeugt, dass es extrem wichtig ist, die Mobilisierung der Völker zu unterstützen, die es überall auf der Welt für den Frieden im Nahen Osten gibt, obwohl sie von der Politik und den Medien totgeschwiegen wird«, heißt es in einer Bekanntmachung. Wenige Stunden, nachdem die Gewerkschaften und die Genossenschaft der Hafenarbeiter den Boykott angekündigt hatten, wurde der Waffentransport von der Reederei ohne Angabe von Gründen abgeblasen. Und so verzichteten auch die Gewerkschaften auf ihre Aktion. »Die Hafenarbeiter von Ravenna«, erklärten sie daraufhin, »wissen sehr wohl, dass sie mit ihrem Akt für den Frieden zwischen dem israelischen und dem palästinensischen Volk in keiner Weise zur Lösung des Konflikts beigetragen konnten. Trotzdem meinen sie, dass die Aktion notwendig und unverzichtbar war. Die einzige Art, um sich dem Krieg friedlich zu widersetzen, ist es, aktiv dagegen Stellung zu beziehen – und das jedes Mal, wenn sich dazu eine Gelegenheit bietet.« Die italienischen Hafenarbeiter sind für ihre pazifistische und antifaschistische Einstellung bekannt

…“ 

Artikel von Anna Maldini, Rom, vom 26.05.2021 im ND online

Labour Against the Arms Trade auf Twitter

von Labour 4 Palestine

 










Italienische Hafenarbeiter:innen weigern sich Waffen nach Israel zu liefern 




„

In Livorno weigerten sich Arbeiter:innen ein Schiff zu entladen, das eine für Israel bestimmte Waffenlieferung transportiert. Sie zeigten damit ihre Solidarität mit den Palästinenser:innen, die gegen die israelische Besatzung um ihr Leben kämpfen. Am gestrigen Freitag erreichte die Asiatic Island den Hafen von Livorno, Italien. Dank des Berichts des Autonomen Kollektivs der Hafenarbeiter:innen Genuas und der Organisation „Weapon Watch“, erfuhren die Arbeiter:innen, die in der Basisgewerkschaft „Unione Sindacale di Base“ organisiert sind, dass das Schiff mit Waffen und Sprengstoff beladen war, die für das israelische Hafenbecken von Aschdod bestimmt waren. (…) Die Gewerkschaften der Hafenarbeiter:innen Italiens versuchen, das Eintreffen von Rüstungsgütern in Israel zu verhindern, indem sie mehr Informationen über die geplanten Lieferungen sammeln. Am Donnerstag erhielten sie einen Hinweis über die Ankunft dutzender militärischer Panzerfahrzeuge, die zur Verladung auf ein anderes Schiff, die Molo Italia, bereitstehen.

..“

.”

Repression gegen die Hafenarbeiter*innen in Genua: Hausdurchsuchungen und drohende Haftstrafen 




„… 

Am 22. Februar 2021 fanden auf Anordnung der Staatsanwaltschaft Hausdurchsuchungen bei fünf Genoss*innen des CALP statt. Die Anschuldigungen beziehen sich auf die Beteiligung der Angeklagten an antimilitaristischen Aktivitäten gegen den Waffenhandel im Hafen von Genua und auf ihre Teilnahme an antifaschistischen Aktionen als Teil der Gruppe Genova Antifascista. In einem Interview mit Dinamo Press beschreibt José Nivoi, einer der fünf Angeklagten und Mitglied der Basisgewerkschaft USB sowie des CALP, den Polizeieinsatz: „Gegen fünf Uhr morgens tauchten Agenten von DIGOS [Staatsschutz] bei einigen Arbeitern des Autonomen Kollektivs der Hafenarbeiter*innen auf und beschlagnahmten Computer, Mobiltelefone, Telefonkarten, politische Dokumente, Festplatten, USB-Speichersticks, kurz gesagt, alle möglichen Dinge, die sich auf antimilitaristische oder antifaschistische Aktivitäten beziehen könnten.“ Auch die Räume des CALPs auf den Docks wurden laut Nivoi durchsucht: „Hier hatten wir eine Niederlassung mit einem Fitnessraum darin, ein Büro für Meetings. Sie haben alles im Gebäude beschlagnahmt und uns faktisch geräumt“. Die Staatsanwaltschaft ermittelt nun wegen Angriffs auf die Verkehrssicherheit, Widerstand gegen die Staatsgewalt und Mitgliedschaft in einer kriminellen Vereinigung. Sollten die Angeklagten für letztere Straftat verurteilt werden, riskieren die fünf Genoss*innen von CALP und Genova Antifascista zwischen drei und sieben Jahre Haft. (…) Die gravierenden Vorwürfe haben schon jetzt Folgen für die Betroffenen, wie Novio beschreibt: „Wenn man dann vor Gericht kommt, sind die Vorwürfe nicht haltbar, aber bis zum Verfahren halten einen die Justizbehörden in einer Art Pattsituation, und wenn man irgendetwas tut, was mit dem Sicherheitserlass sanktioniert werden kann, bekommt man Hausarrest, Sonderüberbewachung oder sogar Haftstrafen.“ Tatsächlich handelt es sich bei der Sonderbewachung um die schwerwiegendste Präventivmaßnahme des italienischen Staates, die die betroffenen Personen „in Gefängniswärter*innen ihrer selbst transformiert“. Die Sonderüberbewachung dauert bis zu vier Jahre und ist verlängerbar. Vielerlei Auflagen gehen mit einher: U.a. muss man nachts zu Hause sein (das kann zu jeder Uhrzeit überprüft werden), der Wohnort darf nur mit polizeilicher Bewilligung verlassen werden und man darf nicht an öffentlichen Kundgebungen und Versammlungen teilnehmen. (…) Die Strategie der Staatsanwaltsschaft, die auf eine Anzeige der Delta-Agentur hin nun gegen CALP ermittelt, bestünde darin, „den Kopf der Gruppen von organisierten Arbeiter*innen abzutrennen, die nicht nur einen Streik wegen Streitigkeiten führen, sondern einen politischen. Seit dreißig Jahren gab es in Genua keinen politischen Streik mehr, der in der Lage war, ein Unternehmen zu blockieren.“ (…) Zur Finanzierung der zu erwartenden Prozesskosten können 

bei CALP Solidaritäts-Tshirts

 

 zum 10-jährigen Bestehen des Kollektivs bestellt werden

.“ 

Artikel von Jacqueline Andres vom 20. April 2021 als IMI-Standpunkt 2021/020

 




Interview zur Repression gegen Antimilitarismus in Italien: Repression gegen Hafenarbeiter*innen in Genua – Hausdurchsuchungen gegen erfolgreichen antimilitaristischen Protest in Genua 




„Mit Radio Corax machte Jacqueline Andres zwei Interviews zur Lange der Repression gegen Antimilitarismus in Italien. Im ersten Interview geht es um die aktuelle Repression, die einige des Autonomen Kollektivs der Hafenarbeiter*innen in Genua (CALP) erfahren. Diese streikten 2019, als ein mit Rüstungsgütern beladenen saudisches Frachtschiffs in den Hafen von Genua einlief. Nun verordnete die Staatsanwaltsschaft Hausdurchsuchungen und Prozesse werden demnächst anrollen. Gegen 45 Aktivit*innen wurde nun Anzeige erstattet – für 5 von ihnen wird subversive Vereinigung zum Zwecke des Terrorismus vorgeworfen…“

title: Mûsa O., di doza Îpek Erê de beraet kir
content:
Çawişê pispor ê berê Mûsa O. êrişa zayendî li Îpek Era 18 salî kiribû û 10 sal cezayê girtîgehê lê hatibû birîn. Mûsa O. bi tohmeta ku “bûye sedema xwekuştinê” dihat darizandin. Mûsa O. di dozê de beraet kir.




1emîn Dadgeha Cezê û Esliyê ya Êlihê di 22ê Cotmeha 2026an de biryar daye ku tu delîlek şênber nîne ku Mûsa O. bûye sedem ku Îpek Er xwe bikuje.







Çi bûbû?




Li navçeya Qubînê ya Êlihê, Î. E.ya 18 salî ya di 16ê Tîrmeha 2020an de hewl dabû xwe bikuje. Î. E. yê paşê aşkere kiribû ku Mûsa O. çawişê pispor tecawiz li wê kiriye. Î. E. ya ku li nexweşxaneyê dihate dermankirin, îro can daye.




Î. E. piştî ku xwestibû xwe bikuje û ew li nexweşxaneyê dihate dermankirin, malbata wê nameya wê dîtibû. Î. E. yê di nameya xwe de gotibû ku çawişê pispor Mûsa O.yî tecawiz lê kiriye.




Malbata Î. E. yê giliyê çawişê pispor kiribû û Mûsa O. heman rojê hatibû desteserkirin. Çawişê pispor di îfadeya xwe de ew tohmet qebûl nekiribûn.




Li gorî nûçeya Ajansa Mezopotamyayê Rapora Tipa Edlî aşkere kiribû ku Mûsa O. yî tecawizî Î. E. yê kiriye. Di encama vê rewşê de Mûsa O. yî îdia kiribû ku dema ew û Î. E. li Sêrtê hatine ba hev ew serxweş bûye.




Biryara “nepenîtiyê” ji bo dosyaya lêpirsînê hatibû dayîn. Çawişê pispor bi tohmeta ku “istismara zayendî ya xurt” kiriye şandibûn ber destê heyeda Dadweriya Silh û Cezayan a Nobedar a Sêrtê lê li vir bi şertê kontrola edlî serbest bûbû.




Malbata Î. E. yê ji bo alîkariya hiqûqî serî li Komeleya Mafên Mirovan a Êlihê dabûn.







(EMK/AY)

title: Şerda Mazlum: The process requires women's self-defence networks - Part Two
content:
YJA Star commander Şerda Mazlum Gabar spoke about Bêrîtan's life, personality and resistance, stressing that her legacy of resistance continues to place responsibilities on women today.




Part one of this interview can be read 

here

. 




What is the significance of women establishing their own defence forces in Rojava, Shengal and Rojhilat following the experience of YJA Star? What does this development mean for Kurdish women's shared understanding of self-defence?




Through the women's guerrilla struggle and its organisational identity, YJA Star, which embody women's historical dignity and responsibility, our Leadership provided Kurdish women, the Freedom Movement and its defence forces with a perspective on the self-organisation they needed and how free women's guerrilla struggle should be conducted. This perspective, developed by our Leadership, constitutes a fundamental approach to freedom in the struggle against all forms of domination.




Colonial systems regard the massacre and suppression of peoples, classes, genders and individuals struggling for freedom as their unquestionable right. To this end, they wage special warfare through a combination of military, political, social, cultural, economic, diplomatic and psychological methods.




As the women's defence forces of Kurdistan, we face the question of freedom both historically and in the present, in terms of national identity and gender. The genocidal policies imposed on Kurdistan and the Kurdish people, together with the policy of destroying society through the destruction of women, form the very basis of the existence of fascist colonial systems. For movements struggling against the system, however, resisting the destruction of women and society is the very reason for their existence. The ideology of women's freedom and Jineology, the science of women and life, emerged through the history, labour, heroism and consciousness of free women's guerrilla struggle in Kurdistan. Abdullah Öcalan further developed and gave concrete form to the perspective of Jineology on the basis of the accumulated knowledge and experience of free women's guerrilla struggle, which had been built through tremendous labour, effort and resistance in Kurdistan.




In fact, the perspectives on women developed by Öcalan during the 1990s provided an important foundation for the development of women's science. Through Jineology, Öcalan stated that Kurdish women, the Freedom Movement and its defence forces, YJA Star, could discover the knowledge needed to develop the form of social life that humanity requires. This historic responsibility both honoured Kurdish women and placed immense responsibilities upon them. As women guerrillas, we must redefine our tasks within the Peace and Democratic Society Process with an awareness of these historical and present-day responsibilities. Defining a reality correctly means recognising it and beginning to understand it. We need accurate definitions to better understand what we have done, what we need to do, what we have failed to accomplish and what we have done incorrectly. Only then can we do what is right and fulfil the tasks we have not yet accomplished.




The free women's defence forces established in Rojhilat, Rojava and Shengal, drawing inspiration from our YJA Star organisation, must continue to stand against every form of injustice, inequality and wrongdoing, as they have done throughout their history. They must seek ways to protect women, peoples, children, nature, life and society from a system that poisons them all, through ideological, social and political means. They must reflect deeply on these responsibilities and build networks of self-defence through diverse and creative methods.




Is it possible to say that threats and plans for attacks against the Kurdish people and women have ended with the beginning of the Peace and Democratic Society Process? How should the continuing threats against the organised structures of the Kurdish Freedom Movement, particularly in Rojava, Shengal and Rojhilat, be understood?




It would be naive to claim that threats or plans for attacks against the Kurdish people and women have ended with the beginning of the Peace and Democratic Society Process. Whether we reach a point where we can genuinely say this depends on our struggle.




Unfortunately, although two years have passed since the beginning of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, it is not possible to say that significant steps towards democratisation have been taken. Rather than speaking on behalf of the organised structures of the Kurdish people in Rojava, Shengal and Rojhilat, I would say this: Kurdish society needs to secure guarantees for its existence and freedom. The existence and freedom of the Kurdish people remain under threat. Of course, these guarantees cannot be secured solely through armed forces or armed struggle. The greatest and most effective deterrent force is an organised and conscious society. The people and women of Kurdistan must never, under any circumstances, be left without self-defence. To be without self-defence means being unable to guarantee not only a meaningful life, but even one's physical survival.




What kind of organisation and self-defence do the Kurdish people and women need at a time when political, social and cultural attacks continue alongside the possibility of war and conflict?




The struggle of the Kurdish people and women needs to develop a stronger philosophical, sociological and political foundation. At the same time, it is increasingly important to adopt a flexible, creative and dynamic approach to struggle based on a quantum-inspired way of thinking and acting. Our YJA Star guerrillas, who represent a distinctive experience both globally and in the Middle East, are not simply a force that takes up arms and engages in armed struggle. They are a movement that fundamentally questions established perceptions of women and men, as well as class-based and nationalist perspectives. Women's guerrilla struggle has gained its significance by organising itself around the theory of separation, the ideology of women's liberation and the principles of women's party organisation. These principles do not, of course, immediately create liberated individuals. However, they teach women to recognise themselves, maintain their independence and organise their lives through their own understanding and perspective. These are fundamental steps towards freedom.




Through our movement, women have learned to live independently of men, struggle under the most difficult conditions, organise their own lives, stand on their own feet and fight for their freedom. The way women are approached has become an important value and an established tradition. These achievements may seem ordinary to us now, but creating such a way of life and struggle in a region like Kurdistan represents an extremely important achievement and experience. The ability of women and men to remain together despite the historical contradictions between them, while developing relationships based on principles of freedom, is something that deserves to be properly understood.




As I have said, these developments do not mean that we have achieved complete liberation. Nevertheless, they represent advances on the path to freedom that must never be underestimated. Of course, we face difficulties in extending these achievements throughout society. There is a need to establish specific self-defence networks capable of bringing these advances into society, making them more widespread and enabling further progress. We must develop forms of organisation that are more focused and far-reaching, and establish structures capable of producing solutions quickly. It is also essential to create dedicated forms of organisation that put the projects developed by our women's movement into practice more effectively and respond to attacks against women arising from both macro-level and micro-level structures of power.




What message does Bêrîtan's action carry for the ongoing Peace and Democratic Society Process? What responsibilities does Bêrîtan remind women and society of in this process?




Bêrîtan's legacy can be examined and understood from many perspectives. Above all, it requires us to renew ourselves by reassessing and strengthening our relationship with Abdullah Öcalan and creating a deeper sense of meaning. Our commitment can only acquire real value when it is translated into powerful action. In this respect, it is important to question ourselves deeply: To what extent are we capable of taking action in life and struggle? How productive and creative are we, from ideology to politics and from politics to guerrilla struggle?




As militants participating in and advancing the freedom struggle, we must recognise the importance of maintaining a strong collective memory. Memory, in its deepest sense, means knowing oneself. All knowledge acquired without self-awareness is misleading. At a time when attempts are once again being made to deprive us of our memory, protecting it is undoubtedly possible through a strong commitment to the values of freedom and by putting those values into practice. A profound connection with freedom can only be achieved by protecting our own memory. By following comrade Bêrîtan's spirit and path of resistance, we can approach the current process and our responsibilities with the conviction and determination to put our strength into practice more effectively than ever before. We are facing attacks aimed at weakening and dismantling our movement. We must bring all our values of freedom to life, turning them into a force capable of overcoming these attempts to encircle and dismantle our movement through tremendous willpower, determination, conviction and struggle. Through the magnificence of resistance, we must put an end to all forms of surrender and betrayal, and advance towards freedom by remaining faithful to what it means to be human.




What role does YJA Star aim to play in the coming period after 33 years of experience? How do you see the future of women's armed organisation within the Peace and Democratic Society Process?




As you will have understood from my answers to the previous questions, YJA Star, the Free Women's Units, has never been merely a fighting force or an armed organisation. Over the past 33 years, we have created a living, vibrant history through blood, sweat, labour and the sacrifice of lives. New meaning is added to this history with each passing day. The significance of our STAR Free Women's Units continues to grow, particularly through the efforts of our women martyrs. In an age when meaninglessness and worthlessness are imposed on women and life itself, the conditions that led to the establishment of the STAR Free Women's Units, which embody a meaningful, dignified and free life, have not yet disappeared. Therefore, the reasons for their existence remain.




The STAR Free Women's Units emerged not as a cause of domination, injustice or the patriarchal mentality that poisons life and humanity, but as a consequence of these conditions. They will continue to exist for as long as injustice and inequality persist anywhere in the world. Our women's defence forces, which have included social objectives since their establishment, are also responsible for educating women, raising their awareness and organising them against attacks rooted in male domination.




Their most fundamental responsibility within the Peace and Democratic Society Process is to organise women's self-defence networks. Our essential task is to build these networks throughout society, weaving them together thread by thread, so that not a single woman remains unorganised.




There are also those who approach the Peace and Democratic Society Process in a superficial and simplistic manner. A considerable number of people treat it as just another process, as though it makes little difference whether it succeeds or fails.




We are going through a period that could be described as the last chance for the peoples of Kurdistan and Turkey. A last chance means reaching the edge of a cliff. At that point, either you seize the opportunity, spread your wings and take on a new essence and form, or you squander your final chance and fall to the bottom of the cliff. The Peace and Democratic Society Process developed by Abdullah Öcalan is a historic and strategic step. It must be met with an appropriate response.




If there are people among Turkey's ruling powers who genuinely love their homeland, who do not want to hand the country over to foreign powers and who want to protect it out of patriotism, they must first recognise the plans of those foreign powers and make proper use of the opportunity for a solution that now exists.




Until now, discussions have always centred on deadlock and problems. But it is now essential to move beyond discussion, develop practical solutions without waiting for anyone else, and ensure that these solutions become part of the lives of all women and society as a whole. A state founded on the understanding of a single nation and a single gender cannot solve any problem. On the contrary, it is itself the source of the problems. This nation-state kills its own children every day. Yes, human life and women's lives are treated as cheap, especially when the person concerned is Kurdish. The ideology of a single nation regards every difference as a potential criminal and therefore demands its elimination. Recognising human rights, children's rights and women's rights means understanding that life does not consist of a single colour or a single will. It means creating the conditions for people to live together on that basis. There can be no shared life in a place where some people are constantly oppressed while others oppress them, where some are always considered right and others wrong, and where some continually force others into submission. There can be no shared life or democratic relationships in a society where women are murdered with such brutality. But this situation is not inevitable. To ensure that it does not become our fate, we must establish our own organic forms of organisation and build communal structures to overcome this imposed uniformity, without waiting for the state. We must create organisations that defend our own rights and raise an outcry whenever the rights of others are violated, just as we would when our own rights are denied.




Only forces operating outside the state can develop collective wisdom and hearts that beat together for a better life. We must recognise the reality of the system behind the murder of a woman and establish a free and democratic way of life to prevent more women from being murdered or dying. We must demonstrate our own strength and determination to achieve this. We must be able to say no to what is imposed upon us. We must learn to live with the dignity of women who struggle for their identity and to face together all the difficulties that this entails. We must learn this so that we can put an end to the genocide of women. The attacks against women are themselves a form of genocide. They seek to eradicate the lineage of free women, to extinguish and destroy one of the most fundamental colours of life. If life is so beautiful and meaningful, why are women driven to suicide? Why are they subjected to harassment and rape? Why are they imprisoned for their entire lives in circumstances they never wanted? Why are they subjected to torture every day? We must recognise that this constitutes genocide against women and protect the essential, free and creative values of our heritage. We must take responsibility and truly grow in our understanding of the meaning of our times. My hope is that all of us will grow together in that understanding...

title: Özcan Yaman: No liberties, democracy or peace without free media
content:
Journalists took to the streets in several cities on Saturday, 24 October, to protest against the detention and imprisonment of journalists, the appointment of trustees to media outlets and access restrictions imposed on news websites and social media accounts.




The protests were organised following calls by the Dicle Fırat Journalists Association (DFG), the Mesopotamia Women Journalists Association, the Journalists' Union of Turkey (TGS), the Journalists Association of Turkey (TGC), the Press Council, the Confederation of Progressive Trade Unions of Turkey Press Workers' Union (DISK Basın-Iş), Haber-Sen and the Contemporary Journalists Association (ÇGD). Protesters demanded the release of imprisoned journalists and an end to interference with press freedom.




Journalists and members of the public gathered in front of the Bull Statue in Kadıköy, Istanbul, before marching to Kadıköy Pier Square, chanting slogans. They demanded the release of their colleagues, an end to the appointment of trustees and guarantees for the public's right to information.




ANF spoke to journalists who took to the streets against censorship about the attacks on press freedom and their ongoing struggle.




Karvar: ‘The government wants a media that speaks with one voice’




Journalist Rahime Karvar said censorship was not a new practice but had continued in various forms throughout history and in recent years. She said preventing journalists from carrying out their work was also an attack on the public's right to information.







 







Karvar said, “Preventing us from practising our profession also constitutes a serious attack on the peoples' right to information. There are discussions about an upcoming election. There is talk of the crisis deepening following the funding crisis. The government has taken no steps despite the ongoing Peace and Democratic Society Process and is therefore at the centre of criticism.




With all these developments taking place, silencing the press clearly shows that they want only one voice to be heard. The government wants a media that speaks with one voice. It wants a media that repeats only its own words and ensures that its message reaches the people. That is the purpose of today's attacks.”




‘Today's response is long overdue’




Rahime Karvar said the latest attacks on media organisations could not be viewed separately from past practices, recalling censorship targeting the Kurdish press and women's media outlets in particular.




Karvar said: “The closure of Halk TV and the appointment of a trustee to take control of it, the closure of T24, and the blocking of access to numerous accounts through the ‘My Family Is Safe’ operation, particularly targeting LGBTI+ issues… The sheer intensity of these measures suggests that we may have entered a new phase. We are talking about practices that have become easier to implement and increasingly entrenched.




But these practices are not unfamiliar to us. As women, we know them well. As Kurds, we know them well. Our television channels have been shut down before, and access to our news websites has been blocked. Today, to access any of our websites, we have to search for versions with numbers such as ‘45’, ‘55’ or ‘60’. Simply typing the name of a website is no longer enough.




That is why today's response is very important, but we can also say it is somewhat overdue. Those who previously remained silent, looked the other way or failed to take these attacks seriously because they were directed at a particular community or section of society are now horrified by what is happening.”




Karvar said journalists needed to strengthen their common grounds for struggle, adding that coming together should not be limited to street protests.




Karvar also said, “We will not find another way forward. Coming together must not be limited to the streets; we need to create new platforms. If the government attacks one area, journalists must find ways to unite elsewhere. With a tripod and a camera, we can defend the peoples' right to information and continue telling the truth.”




Karvar added that it was encouraging to see journalists and members of the public taking to the streets together.




Bahadır Özgür: ‘The construction of the regime and the dismantling of the press go hand in hand’




Journalist Bahadır Özgür, who was recently detained and subsequently released under judicial supervision, said he had not witnessed such a large demonstration for press freedom in a long time.




Özgür said the demonstration had attracted not only journalists but also many members of the public who came to support them. He described the attacks on the press as part of a broader political process: “Many people came to support journalists, not just journalists themselves. I think this is very important and encouraging. But it also shows something else: this is not simply a process in which individual journalists are detained or imprisoned, nor is it merely about news reporting.




The construction of the regime and the dismantling of the press have been going hand in hand for a long time. And it appears that, alongside the funding crisis, an all-out campaign to silence the press has begun. Any journalist colleague of ours could be detained or imprisoned on any pretext.




We must stop asking questions such as, ‘Why were they arrested? What did they say in their statement? What is the accusation? Did they publish a news report? Did they post a tweet?’ We need to move beyond these questions.”




‘The issue is not just press freedom’




Bahadır Özgür said the attacks on journalists also targeted the public's right to information and participation in political processes.




Özgür said, “I believe the government's aim, particularly as it comes under increasing pressure ahead of the elections, is to create a society that hears less and sees less. That is why this is not simply a matter of press freedom. I believe it is part of a broader political struggle aimed at abolishing the people's rights to information, to know, to vote and to stand for election.”




Özgür said all imprisoned journalists must be released and added: “If even one journalist remains in prison, none of us is free. That is how we see it. We want every single one of our colleagues released from prison.”




Yasin Akgül: ‘Every space in which we can work is being restricted’




Journalist and photojournalist Yasin Akgül, who was detained and imprisoned during the events of 19 March 2025, said journalists were facing increasing obstacles to carrying out their work.




Akgül said the spaces in which journalists could report, take photographs and write were becoming increasingly restricted, forcing them to take to the streets to make their voices heard.




Akgül said, “As a journalist and photojournalist, I find it increasingly difficult to work under constant pressure whenever I am taking photographs. We have already been detained and imprisoned because of such pressure in the past. That is why we are on the streets today, so that our colleagues do not have to experience the same thing.”




Özcan Yaman: ‘From Musa Anter to Metin Göktepe and Hakan Tosun’




Freelance journalist Özcan Yaman said censorship and repression of the press had a long history in Turkey, adding that journalists had faced not only restrictions on their reporting but also detention, torture and killings.







 







Yaman said, “In Turkey, alongside censorship, there have been years of repression, torture and killings targeting the press. All of these are part of our history. From Musa Anter to Metin Göktepe and Hakan Tosun…” and recalling attacks on journalists throughout the country's history.




Yaman said journalists had been left with no alternative but to take to the streets in response to the recent wave of undemocratic practices. He said, “The press has reached a point where, faced with so many undemocratic practices in recent times, it has found no other option but to take to the streets.”




‘Without the press, there can be no freedom, democracy or peace’




Özcan Yaman concluded by drawing attention to the relationship between press freedom, democracy and peace: “We do not know what else can be done from now on. But something must be done in this country. They talk about democracy, yet democracy has turned into autocracy. There is a struggle to break that autocracy. Without the press, there can be no freedom, no democracy and no peace. We need the press for peace and democracy…”

title: Sevda Karaca: War policies undermine unity and labour struggles - Part Three
content:
Sevda Karaca, Deputy Chair of the Labour Party (EMEP) and MP for Antep, answered ANF's questions about labour struggles and the struggle for peace.




Part one of this interview can be read 

here

 and part two 

here

. 




How do war policies undermine class solidarity between Turkish and Kurdish workers? You frequently visit workplaces and meet workers. Have you observed this in practice?




One of the most important realities we observe on the ground is that workers face very similar economic problems. Workers in Antep, Başpınar, metal factories and the logistics sector talk about inadequate wages, long working hours, workplace accidents, job insecurity and obstacles to trade union organising. Workers living in different cities and belonging to different identities share many of the same problems. But the existence of common problems does not automatically lead to a common struggle.




That requires organisation, trust and shared experiences. War policies and nationalist polarisation undermine precisely these foundations. The conflict of interests between workers and their employers is pushed into the background. Instead of being seen as a fellow worker demanding the same rights, another worker may be portrayed primarily as a representative of a particular identity. As a result, workers who should be standing together against their employers may begin to distrust one another.




Nationalist rhetoric can obscure the fact that Turkish and Kurdish workers in the same workplace are condemned to the same low wages, face the same occupational safety problems and experience the same pressure against trade union organising. This is precisely what weakens working-class unity.




However, it would not be enough to attribute this situation solely to nationalist propaganda. There must also be a genuine reckoning with workers' different identities and the inequalities they experience. We cannot build unity between Turkish and Kurdish workers simply by opposing nationalist propaganda. There can be no genuine unity if the Kurdish people's demands concerning their language, identity and democratic rights are ignored. Nor can there be a meaningful call for working-class unity that dismisses the national oppression experienced by Kurdish workers. Unity cannot be built on the expectation that one side will remain silent about its own problems.




The task of socialists is not to ignore these divisions but to establish a common foundation for struggle capable of overcoming them. Every experience in which workers organise together, defend one another's rights and struggle shoulder to shoulder for wages and trade union rights is valuable in this respect. But for economic unity to become lasting, we must also defend demands for equality and freedom. That is why it is so important for the working class in Kurdistan to develop an independent movement.




Workers, working people and poorer sections of society in the region must be able to participate in the process with their own demands and defend their right to have a say over wages, trade union rights, working conditions and their living environments. This is particularly important at a time when industrial investment is expected to increase as a result of the peace process and Kurdish regions are once again being viewed by capital as new areas of exploitation. We need to take this discussion much further.




‘Turkish workers must support the Kurdish people's demands’




Turkish workers and working people also have a responsibility to oppose the policies of their own ruling classes and support the Kurdish people's demands for peace, equality and democracy. This is necessary not only as an act of solidarity but also to defend the independent interests of their own class. Because in an environment where peoples are turned against one another, it becomes harder to develop a common struggle against capital.




However, this is not something that can happen simply because we call for it. We must raise and discuss this issue within every struggle. Indeed, these discussions are most possible among workers who are already engaged in struggle. We have repeatedly seen that every strike and every act of resistance provides an important opportunity for such discussions. From the Şık Makas resistance to strikes in Izmir, from the protests in Başpınar to workers' struggles in Kocaeli and Bursa, we make particular use of these opportunities to strengthen the need for resistance based on mutual understanding, building unity and preserving that unity. 




Strike bans and pressure on trade unions are justified on grounds of 'national security'. How can this mechanism be challenged?




How can workers defending their wages, working conditions and right to organise possibly constitute a threat to national security? Whose security, and what kind of security, is endangered when a worker goes on strike for a dignified life, a public sector worker demands their rights, or a people voices its democratic demands?




These questions are important because the government expands the concept of security to serve its own political interests and the needs of capital. Stopping production to oppose exploitation by employers, challenging the government's economic programme or demanding democratic rights for a section of society are all turned into security issues. In other words, what they call national security is actually about safeguarding the domination of hegemonic powers and capital. The interests of capital are thus presented as though they were identical to the common interests of society.




Strike bans are among the clearest examples of this mechanism. When workers seek to improve their rights through collective bargaining, their struggles can be halted on national security grounds. As a result, the right to strike, one of the working class's most important means of struggle, may continue to exist on paper while becoming impossible to exercise in practice. The struggle against this cannot be limited to legal challenges. Legal action is, of course, necessary. But other workplaces, trade unions and labour organisations must also develop a common response to strike bans. If a strike ban at one workplace is not recognised as a problem for the entire working class, it becomes easier for the government to continue using this mechanism.




We cannot create an artificial division between defending democratic rights and defending workers' rights. We must defend workers' right to organise, peoples' democratic demands and women's struggle for freedom at the same time. Because if we remain silent when some rights are suspended on security grounds, the collective strength needed to resist attacks on other rights will also have been weakened.




We have focused on war throughout our discussion. Can peace bring about unity among working people? Why is it so critical to build a comprehensive movement that directly connects opposition to war with the labour struggle?




There is a government approach that reduces a historical and political problem, rooted in the denial of the Kurdish nation and the violent suppression of a people's struggle for recognition and full equality of rights, to the question of 'terrorism' and the 'elimination of terrorism'.The Kurdish people have asserted their existence in the face of denial, demanding recognition and equal rights, only to encounter violence, massacres, repression and persecution. Yet the government continues to confine this entire historical struggle to the framework of terrorism. Whatever is said, it is clear that the government has never relaxed this position.




It is also evident that, for the government in the presidential palace, this process is connected to developments in the Middle East, calculations about strengthening Turkey's expansionist position in the region through cooperation with the United States, and ambitions for regional leadership. It also has the explicit objective of 'strengthening the domestic front'.




‘Criticism must not be mistaken for opposition to the peace process’




Identifying and discussing these realities, and therefore maintaining a clear-headed and critical position in debates about the process, must not be dismissed or labelled as opposition to the process. This is our historical responsibility, particularly as socialists.




Our criticisms, warnings and differing views are grounded above all in the Kurdish people's legitimate demands and interests, and in the unity of struggle and shared destiny between the oppressed Kurdish people and workers and working people of all nationalities against the ruling classes of the oppressor nation. They should therefore be understood as positions that contribute to the Kurdish people's struggle for peace, democracy and genuine equality of rights.




Discussions about peace can open the way for unity among working people, but that unity will not emerge automatically. We cannot assume that all inequalities will disappear once the guns fall silent.




Moreover, the government and capital have very different answers from those of the Kurdish people and the forces engaged in struggle to the question of what kind of country and what kind of Kurdish reality are envisaged once the guns fall silent. One development is particularly striking. 




Since discussions about the process began, representatives of the Kurdish capitalist class in the region, particularly those from chambers of industry and commerce in provinces such as Diyarbakır (Amed), Mardin and Van (Wan), have made numerous statements about the process and what needs to be done. Although many of these statements include democratic demands that few would oppose, the emphasis has largely been on the 'economic benefits of the process', the 'economic returns of peace', 'regional development' and claims that increased investment will bring prosperity to the region.




There is no doubt that Turkish capital is the principal force behind the plundering of Kurdistan. Kurdish capital is also seeking its share of that plunder. It is clear that Kurdish capital and Kurdish working people will not have the same interests or experience the same consequences when it comes to the destruction of forests, dams, new power plants, hydroelectric, geothermal and wind energy projects, and the expansion of mining exploration. We can also anticipate what awaits workers and working people in the region by looking at the conditions in factories that have spread to almost every province and district, particularly in the textile and mining sectors. Workers are condemned to wages at or below the minimum wage, deprived of organisation and job security, and forced to work under conditions resembling slavery. Those who rebel against these conditions and choose to organise and struggle face repression.




A recent statement to the press by Mehmet Kaya, President of the Diyarbakır Chamber of Commerce and Industry (DTSO), was particularly striking: “For the first time, Kurdish politics, which has largely been dominated by trade unions and strong working-class organisations, has produced a business community that moves alongside Kurdish politics.” This observation has its place in the context of a national movement. But our fundamental question is this: At a time when class interests are becoming just as important as national interests, how can the working class and working people of Kurdistan intervene in the process by organising their own independent class movement? How can they act in an organised manner, at least as effectively as the Kurdish capitalist class, make their voices heard, advance their demands and give the process their own class character in pursuit of a democratic, people-centred solution to the Kurdish national question?




To achieve this, we need to strengthen class organisations and the organised power of working people, while making their expectations and demands for peace more visible. This is precisely where we see our responsibility. It is a dual responsibility. Kurdish workers must organise as a class and become a central force in the process, including in relation to their national demands. At the same time, because this must be a common concern for the working class of all nationalities in this country, we must strengthen the foundations that enable Turkish workers to participate in the process.




This organised struggle requires mutual trust and a shared political will. As socialists, we still have considerable shortcomings when it comes to discussing these questions and establishing the foundations for such a struggle. But these are the principles underlying our objections, criticisms, assessments and the responsibilities we have taken upon ourselves.




What we need is more than simply bringing different struggles together. We must build a political movement capable of explaining the connections between why workers are becoming poorer, why women are condemned to insecure conditions and why peoples' democratic rights are being suppressed, while organising a common struggle against these problems.




It is also extremely important for workers and working people in Kurdistan to develop their own independent class movement. A peace process in which only political actors and business circles have a say will not automatically bring the demands of the working class onto the agenda. Workers must be able to participate in the process with their own demands concerning wages, trade union rights, working conditions, ecological destruction and the use of resources.




Turkish workers must also stop seeing the Kurdish people's struggle for equality and freedom as something separate from their own struggle. Opposing the policies of their own ruling classes and supporting the demands of Kurdish workers and working people are essential to developing a common class movement.




This is why connecting opposition to war with the labour struggle is so critical. If we limit our opposition to war to simply saying 'we want peace', we risk leaving intact the economic and political relationships that allow war to be perpetuated. But if we connect the demand for peace with workers' struggles over wages, the right to strike, tax justice, women's struggle for freedom and peoples' demands for equality, peace becomes a struggle that broad sections of society can embrace as part of their own lives.




It would therefore be a mistake to regard peace as a precondition for working-class unity. But working-class unity can lead to lasting peace. Unity among working people is not built by everyone thinking the same way. It is built on a foundation where differences and demands are recognised, common adversaries and shared interests are understood, and people also struggle for one another's rights. This is where the social strength needed for lasting peace emerges.




What responsibilities do those engaged in labour struggles and socialists have in achieving lasting peace, particularly at this stage?




The task facing socialists and labour organisations is not simply to present peace as a principle that must be defended, but to turn it into a demand for social struggle. To achieve this, we must first make visible the consequences of war policies in the lives of working people. We must expose the connections between war and poverty, militarism and strike bans, nationalist polarisation and divisions among workers, and patriarchal oppression and women's insecurity. But we cannot stop at simply explaining these connections.




We must create concrete opportunities for people to struggle together against these problems. Turkish and Kurdish workers organising together in a factory, workers from different sectors and workplaces taking a common stand against a strike ban, women workers organising for equal pay and working conditions free from violence, and defending the demand for peace alongside democratic rights are all parts of this struggle. These experiences enable people to see one another not merely as representatives of different identities, but as comrades in struggle who can build a common future.




We must make the consequences of war policies visible’




For socialists, the task goes beyond simply bringing these struggles together. We must develop a common political direction from the experiences of workers, women and oppressed peoples, connect economic demands with democratic rights, and create a foundation for organised struggle in which people defend not only their own interests but also one another's rights. Lasting peace can be strengthened through the struggle for a social order in which peoples have a say over their own destiny, working people can organise against exploitation, and women can live in equality and freedom. The task of socialists is to create the conditions for these struggles to come together around a common political direction.
