title: Sırbistan’da Öğrenci Listesi seçimden zaferle çıktı
content:
Sırbistan’da erken genel seçimde, 12 yıldır iktidarda olan Aleksandar Vucic’in öncülük ettiği liste yenilgiye uğradı. Cumhurbaşkanlığından istifa ederek başbakan adayı olan Vucic, “Öğrenci Listesi”nin seçimleri kazandığını kabul etti. Novi Sad’daki tren istasyonu faciasının ardından başlayan öğrenci protestoları, seçim sonuçlarıyla birlikte ülke siyasetinde yeni bir dönemin kapısını araladı.




Anadolu Ajansı’nın (AA) haberine göre, Sırp İlerleme Partisi (SNS) öncülüğündeki “Aleksandar Vucic-Birleşmiş Sırbistan” listesinin başbakan adayı Vucic, seçim sonuçlarının dış destekli bir sürecin ürünü olduğunu öne sürdü. Vucic, yenilgiyi kabul etmesine rağmen muhalefette mücadele etmeyi sürdüreceklerini söyledi.




2014’te başbakanlık görevine gelen Vucic, 2017 ve 2022’de iki kez cumhurbaşkanı seçildi. Seçime başbakan adayı olarak katılabilmek için cumhurbaşkanlığından istifa eden Vucic, böylece 12 yıllık iktidarının ardından siyasi geleceği açısından önemli bir yenilgi aldı.




Öğrenci protestoları seçim sonucunu etkiledi







Novi Sad kentindeki tren istasyonunda 1 Kasım 2024’te beton sundurmanın çökmesi sonucu 16 kişinin hayatını kaybetmesi, hükümete yönelik tepkileri büyüttü. Facianın ardından başlayan öğrenci protestoları, yaklaşık iki yıl boyunca devam ederek Vucic yönetimi üzerindeki baskıyı artırdı.




“Öğrenci Listesi-Öğrenciler Kazanıyor” sloganıyla erken genel seçime katılan öğrenci hareketi, iktidara karşı yükselen toplumsal tepkiyi seçimlere taşıdı.




Öğrenci Listesi adına zafer konuşması yapan akademisyen Radomir Saicic, oy kullananlara teşekkür etti ve geleceği inşa etmeye başlayacaklarını söyledi.




Geleneksel siyasi partilerden farklı bir örgütlenme biçimine sahip olan hareketin, seçim başarısını nasıl bir hükümet programına ve yönetim modeline dönüştüreceği ise belirsizliğini koruyor.




Öğrenci Listesi yüzde 52 oy aldı







Aleksandar Vucic







Sırbistan Özgür Seçimler ve Demokrasi Merkezi’nin (CeSID) açıkladığı resmi olmayan sonuçlara göre, oyların yüzde 56’sı sayıldığında Öğrenci Listesi yüzde 52, SNS öncülüğündeki Vucic’in listesi ise yüzde 39 oy aldı.




Ülkede kayıtlı 6,4 milyondan fazla seçmen, 250 sandalyeli Sırbistan Ulusal Meclisinin yeni üyelerini belirlemek için sandık başına gitti.




Sırbistan Devlet Seçim Komisyonu (RIK), yerel saatle 19.00 itibarıyla seçime katılım oranının yüzde 67,6 olduğunu açıkladı. Ülke medyası, katılımın rekor seviyeye ulaşabileceğini bildirdi. 2023’teki seçimlerde katılım oranı yüzde 58 olarak kaydedilmişti.




Seçim günü usulsüzlük iddiaları







Erken genel seçim sırasında bazı sandık merkezlerinde şiddet olayları yaşandı. Sırbistan medyası, maskeli grupların oy kullanılan merkezlerden çıkan kişilere sopalarla saldırdığını aktardı.




İçişleri Bakanlığı, Lazarevac’ta yaşanan olaylarda iki polisin yaralandığını, bazı kişilerin polise taş ve tehlikeli maddeler fırlattığını duyurdu.




Bazı sandıklarda usulsüzlük yapıldığı da öne sürüldü. Oy pusulalarının fotoğraflandığı ve birden fazla oy kullanılmasını önlemesi gereken sistemlerin gerektiği gibi işletilmediği yönünde iddialar gündeme geldi.




Başkent Belgrad’da sandıkların kapanmasına yakın saatlerde çok sayıda zırhlı polis aracının görülmesi de güvenlik önlemlerini gündeme taşıdı.




Vucic’in İsrail ile yakın ilişkileri




Vucic yönetimi, İsrail ile yakın ilişkileri nedeniyle de dikkat çekiyordu. Vucic, Sırbistan’ın İsrail ile ortaklaşa savaş dronları üreteceğini açıklamış, ülkenin askeri kapasitesini güçlendirmek amacıyla İsrail yapımı insansız hava araçlarına (İHA) yönelik yeni bir montaj fabrikasının açılışına katılmıştı.




Vucic, İsrail Başbakanı Binyamin Netanyahu’dan da “dostum” diye söz etmişti.




Seçim yenilgisi, Sırbistan’ın dış politikasının geleceği açısından da soru işaretleri yarattı. Yeni siyasi hareketin Avrupa Birliği (AB) üyelik süreci, Brüksel ve Washington ile ilişkiler, Rusya ve Çin’le bağlar ve Kosova meselesi konusunda nasıl bir tutum alacağı merak ediliyor.




Öğrenci Listesi’ni şimdi ne bekliyor?




euronews'in yer verdiği habere göre, Öğrenci hareketinin önündeki en önemli sınav, sokak protestolarıyla büyüttüğü toplumsal desteği yönetim kapasitesine dönüştürmek olacak.




Yeni yönetimin ekonomi, dış politika, enerji, güvenlik ve kamu maliyesi gibi alanlarda kararlar alması gerekecek. Yargının ve kamu kurumlarının bağımsızlığı, yolsuzlukla mücadele, kamu yayıncılığı ve seçim koşullarının iyileştirilmesi de yeni dönemin temel başlıkları arasında yer alacak.




Öğrenci Listesi’nin geleneksel siyasi partilerden farklı yapısının hükümet kurma sürecini nasıl etkileyeceği ve deneyimli kadrolarla nasıl bir çalışma ilişkisi geliştireceği henüz bilinmiyor.




Seçim sonucu, Sırbistan siyasetinde kuşak değişimi açısından da önemli bir gelişme olarak öne çıkıyor. Gençlerin öncülük ettiği bir hareket, yıllardır ülke siyasetini belirleyen iktidara karşı seçim zaferi elde etti.




Asıl sınav şimdi başlıyor




Öğrenci Listesi’nin seçim başarısı, Sırbistan’da değişim talebinin sandığa yansıdığını gösteriyor. Ancak protesto hareketinden hükümete geçiş, seçimleri kazanmaktan daha kapsamlı bir siyasi ve idari sorumluluk getiriyor.




Hareketin kurumlar arasında işbirliği kurması, ekonomik sorunlara çözüm üretmesi ve farklı toplumsal kesimlerin beklentilerine yanıt vermesi gerekecek.




Vucic’in yenilgisiyle birlikte siyasi ağırlığının ne ölçüde azalacağı ve SNS’nin muhalefette nasıl bir yol izleyeceği de önümüzdeki dönemde netleşecek.




Sırbistan’da seçim sonuçları, yerleşik siyasi düzene yönelik itirazın güçlü bir seçim başarısına dönüşebileceğini ortaya koydu. Bundan sonraki temel soru ise Öğrenci Listesi’nin bu desteği nasıl bir yönetim anlayışıyla karşılayacağı.




(EMK)

title: 27 de octubre. Asesoría de vivienda
content:
La Confederación Nacional del Trabajo (CNT) de Salamanca inaugurará el próximo 

martes 27 de octubre, a las 19:30 horas, su nueva Asesoría de Vivienda

, en un acto que tendrá lugar en el local sindical, situado en la avenida de Italia, 24-26.




La CNT de Salamanca pone en marcha una Asesoría de Vivienda como forma de contribuir a la lucha colectiva por este bien social esencial. El conflicto de la vivienda no es solo un tema de interés por el que los políticos, o aspirantes a serlo, hacen que se preocupan durante el periodo electoral; ellos simplemente buscan ganar votos o apoyos para alzarse a cotas más altas en su pelea por el poder.




El actual movimiento de vivienda está demostrando que organizándonos se consiguen avances, si bien, no es suficiente conseguir derechos o cambios legales favorables, pues estos derechos son claudicantes ya que quedan en manos del estado y los políticos que hacen las leyes.




Los derechos que realmente sirven a la gente son los que se ganan y mantienen con la lucha y fuerza colectiva, y se cumplen todos los días frente a quienes se opongan.




Esta es la propuesta genuinamente anarcosindicalista, la que al tiempo que pelea por las mejoras cotidianas, no ceja en la lucha social basada en la auto-organización y el apoyo mutuo entre iguales, mediante la acción directa donde las propias personas afectadas se unen sin jefes ni vanguardias, enfrentándose directamente, sin intermediarios, a quienes les explotan.










La entrada 

27 de octubre. Asesoría de vivienda

 se publicó primero en 

Confederación Nacional del Trabajo

.

title: 27 de octubre. Guía básica para huelguistas
content:
CNT Valladolid celebrará el próximo martes 27 de octubre, a las 19:30 horas, un acto informativo abierto bajo el título «Guía básica para huelguistas primerizos… y no tan primerizos».




La actividad tendrá lugar en la nueva sede del sindicato, situada en la calle La Merced, 6, y servirá para ofrecer información práctica sobre la huelga y resolver dudas de cara a la convocatoria de huelga general del 31 de octubre.




El encuentro se enmarca en la campaña por la huelga general, que busca unir las luchas de la clase trabajadora y reforzar la organización colectiva frente a la precariedad y los problemas laborales y de vivienda.

27 de octubre. Guía básica para huelguistas

author: Paul Gregoire
title: Allega Spender pushes to remove religious exemptions against LGBTIQ students, teachers
content:
The Sex Discrimination and Fair Work Amendment (Equality in Treatment in Religious Schools) Bill 2026, introduced on October 12, seeks to repeal the offending exemptions in federal sex discrimination law as well as removing the related provisions in federal workplace relations law. It also extends protections to associates of those who are captured under the current exemptions.

Section 38 of the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (SDA) makes it lawful for religious education institutions to discriminate against a teacher, student or contract worker due to their “sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, marital or relationship status or pregnancy”.

The proposal took centre stage in 2018, as the national religious freedoms debate took off prior to then-Coalition Prime Minister Scott Morrison shooting it down.

Morrison’s push to establish a religious freedoms regime in 2018 uncovered their existence. His years-long religious crusade was defeated after debate on these exemptions.

Labor PM Anthony Albanese promised to progress the reform in 2022, but changed his mind.

Spender, independent MP for Wentworth, is pushing popular reforms, despite far-right commentators claiming it as an attack on religious freedom.

“These exemptions have already been removed in state and territory law, to varying degrees, but there are no national standards,” Spender told NSW Parliament on October 12.

“The Australian Law Reform Commission’s 2024 review found that religious schools could still maintain their ethos without this exemption.

“At its heart, section 38 of the Sex Discrimination Act is repealed in its entirety and replaced with a far narrower provision,” Spender said in her second reading speech on her private member’s bill.

“Protections are also extended to a person’s associates ... This means a child cannot be treated differently just because she has two mums.”

The bill repeals the current provisions affecting students, teachers and contract workers in section 38, replacing it with a provision that allows institutions to preference staff based on faith in two ways — at their initial employment and in the promotion of senior leadership roles such as “principal, vice-principal, religious education teacher, chaplain” or any other comparable role.

The bill inserts section 7AAA into the SDA, which makes it unlawful to discriminate against an associate, such as a spouse or relative, of a person protected under the Act. It removes provisions that permitted discrimination based on sex, sexuality or gender.

It also repeals provisions in the Fair Work Act 2009 that extend discrimination into workplace agreements.

“But preferencing is not a licence to discriminate,” Spender said. “A school can choose a candidate because of their faith. It cannot fire someone because of their sexuality. Many students have wonderful, formative experiences at religious schools. Many LGBTQIA+ students come out to their friends and teachers in these schools and are accepted. But … this is not everyone’s experience.”

The exemptions in section 38 of the SDA relating to sexual orientation and gender identity, were inserted into the Act when a 2013 bill added anti-discrimination provisions into the law that related to sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex characteristics. The exemptions in respect of gay and transgender individuals joined pre-existing ones that permitted discrimination based on sex.

The October 2018 Ruddock review into religious freedoms recommended tightening these exemptions in federal law, which drew attention to and then condemnation of the laws.

While Morrison initially tried to downplay the outcry, he reversed course and promised to repeal the discriminatory measures targeting students. But Morrison, a Pentecostal, attempted to progress three versions of the Religious Freedoms Bill — two in 2019 and one in 2022 — and the removal of any exemptions was forgotten.

Each version of the religious freedoms legislation was increasingly watered down.

Three years of debate on these laws made it clear that his measures sought religious privileges.

The public debate over religious concerns is different to the present, with the conservative push to insert the controversial International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance definition of antisemitism into all levels of government to curb criticism of Israel and its genocide.

At the beginning of the decade, arch-conservative Christians were pushing to ensure that their religious beliefs trumped everyone else’s. The five-year-long religious freedoms debate came to an abrupt end in early 2022 when Morrison shelved the bill at the eleventh hour.

This was because five Liberal MPs crossed the floor to support an amendment by independent MP Rebekha Sharkie, which sought to make it unlawful to expel gay and trans students. Morrison was not prepared to allow this change for trans students.

Albanese promised to remove exemptions for students and teachers in the lead-up to the May 2022 election.

In March 2024, Labor had two draft laws — one to remove the exemptions and the other to progress religious discrimination protections. But as it did not receive Coalition support, both were dropped.

Spender told parliament that since 2016 there have been ten inquiries, more than 260 hearings and more than 70,000 submissions related to religious discrimination and the removal of the exemptions. She questioned why four years after federal Labor made a commitment, nothing had been done.

She said that while the removal of the exemptions will not encroach on the way in which religious educational institutions operate for the most part, the repeal of the law is necessary because, as it stands, the message it sends rings out “well beyond the school gate”. The existing laws say that discrimination against LGBTIQ people is permitted on some occasions.

“Australians expect equality in front of the law, not least from those institutions that are partly funded by taxpayers,” Spender added. “Getting this balance right is not easy, but our laws need to be applied fairly across our country. I think there is a practical and sensible pathway through this … that this parliament could unite around.”

[Paul Gregoire writes for Sydney Criminal Lawyers where this piece was first published.]

content:

Castellano

29 de octubre. Formación abierta Huelga 11N




Si tienes dudas sobre la convocatoria de huelga este 11 de noviembre, si quieres adherirte a la huelga pero no sabes cómo hacerlo en el trabajo, si quieres saber tus derechos para sumarte a este movimiento ¡esto te interesa!




El jueves 29 de octubre organizamos una formación abierta previa a la huelga general del 11N. No es necesario ser afiliado/a para asistir.




Además organizamos dos convocatorias (18h y 21h) para facilitar la asistencia.




¡Te esperamos en el local de la CNT en Granollers!







Català

11N: formació oberta




Si tens dubtes sobre la convocatòria de vaga aquest 11 de novembre, si vols adherir-te a la vaga però no saps com fer-ho a la feina, si vols saber els teus drets per sumar-te a aquest moviment això t’interessa!




Dijous 29 d’octubre organitzem una formació oberta prèvia a la vaga general del 11N. No cal ser afiliat/da per assistir.




A més organitzem dos convocatòries (18h i 21h) per facilitar l’assistència.




T’esperem al local de la CNT a Granollers!

author: Unknown
title: Cumhurbaşkanlığı Kabinesi bugün toplanıyor: Gündemde hangi konular var?
content:
Fotoğraf: Murat Çetinmühürdar/TCCB

Cumhurbaşkanlığı Kabinesi, bugün Cumhurbaşkanı ve AKP Genel Başkanı Tayyip Erdoğan başkanlığında Beştepe'deki sarayda toplanıyor. Toplantının ana gündemini fon krizi oluştururken, süreç, bölgesel gelişmeler ve ekonomi politikaları da ele alınacak.

Kabine toplantısında, tasfiyesine karar verilen yatırım fonlarına ilişkin yürütülen çalışmalar değerlendirilecek. Fon yatırımcılarına ara ödeme yapılmasını ve tasfiye sürecine ilişkin düzenlemeleri içeren 9 maddelik kanun teklifinin TBMM Genel Kurulunda kabul edilmesinin ardından atılacak adımlar görüşülecek. Cumhurbaşkanı Yardımcısı Cevdet Yılmaz'ın da tasfiye sürecindeki son duruma ilişkin Kabine üyelerine bilgi vermesi bekleniyor.

Toplantının bir diğer gündem maddesi, iktidarın "Terörsüz Türkiye" olarak adlandırdığı süreçte gelinen aşama olacak. Milli Dayanışma ve Bütünleşme Koordinasyon Kurulu tarafından oluşturulan alt komisyonların görev ve yetkileri ile Mecliste yürütülecek çalışmalar değerlendirilecek.

Dış politika başlığında ABD ile İran arasındaki görüşmeler ve çatışmaların son durumu ele alınacak. Rusya-Ukrayna savaşındaki gelişmeler, olası ateşkes görüşmeleri ve Gazze'deki süreç de gündemde olacak. Ayrıca Mekke İttifakı ile Libya'yla imzalanan deniz yetki alanları anlaşmasının değerlendirilmesi bekleniyor.

Kabine toplantısında enflasyonla mücadele ve fiyat istikrarına yönelik politikalar da görüşülecek. Orta Vadeli Program (OVP) kapsamında ekonomide atılması planlanan adımların ele alınması bekleniyor.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Labor Groups Seek to Put Demands on Agenda Ahead of Election
content:
TAIWAN HAS SEEN a number of labor demonstrations in recent weeks.

A strike by workers at iconic snack Kuai Kuai’s Zhongli factory came to an end after five days earlier this month. Kuai Kuai is an iconic snack best known for a superstition that keeping bags of it near machinery keeps them running smoothly. Kuai Kuai operates one factory in Taoyuan, but 130 out of 155 union members voted in favor of a strike after the company decided to relocate to Hsinchu.

The two sites are 39 kilometers from each other, meaning that the move is untenable for many workers. Workers were only informed of the land scale on September 1st. According to the Ministry of Labor, the move was not expected for another two years. The factory has operated in Zhongli since 1968, and 1/3rd of workers at Kuai Kuai have worked there for more than thirty years, despite the fact that their wages are near minimum wage.

Though workers initially voted only for a one-day strike, the action was later extended indefinitely. After the strike, workers won four months’ wages plus severance pay if they are reassigned in the Zhongli factory and eight months’ wages plus severance pay if they have to leave their jobs because of the planned reassignment to Hsinchu and resign by September 30, 2028. Workers with twelve years of experience under the labor pension system will receive a further 100,000 NT. Kuai Kuai has stated that it will not lay off workers for two years and that workers who are laid off afterward will receive two months’ wages.

Workers have accused the San-Ti Group that owns Kuai Kuai of perhaps having only acquired the company with an eye on selling its land to Advanced Semiconductor Engineering Inc. Originally, Kuai Kuai workers were only offered a 5% pay increase and verbal assurances that they would be relocated to the new factory. It is to be seen if acquiring land to sell it to technology companies is a tactic increasingly adopted in corporate acquisitions going forward.

To this extent, migrant worker groups have criticized Singaporean company Sheffield Green and Indonesian company PT Kepodang Makmur Sejahtera, both offshore wind manufacturers, of violating the contracts of Indonesian migrant workers. Specifically, despite being skilled workers as fitters, such workers signed contracts that promised pay of 48,000 NT per month, but were later only paid between 100 NT and 143 NT per month. Such groups demonstrated earlier this month.

Such workers were part of projects run by Taiwanese company Century Energy Co., Ltd., but Century Energy has skirted responsibility by stating that it had no responsibility over contracts signed between workers and foreign contractors under a “contract performance” system that allows the company to bring over foreign workers to be part of projects. Under this system, the Indonesian workers were paid less than the minimum salary in the Labor Standards Act.

In response to such criticism, the Ministry of Labor has stated that it will step up inspections. It is to be seen if this actually takes place.

Likewise, the May 1 Action Alliance–a coalition of labor groups–demonstrated outside of the Executive Yuan on October 13th to call for employers to increase the amount of money they contribute to worker pensions. The Action Alliance cited that the mandatory employer contribution rate had remained at 6% since the current pension system was introduced in 2005, though expectations were originally that the rate would increase. As such, calls by labor groups were for the contribution rate to increase to at least 12%.

Though Lai Ching-te had previously pledged to increase the contribution rate as a campaign pledge, there has not yet been action on the issue.

The demonstration was followed up by another demonstration on October 19th. Labor groups, including the Taoyuan Confederation of Trade Unions, Chunghwa Telecom Union, and other organizations, pledged to strike if their demands were not met, calling for higher wages and an increase in employer contributions to worker pensions.

It is to be if labor becomes a campaign issue ahead of elections next month, then. This does not look likely at present, unless candidates are seeking new issues to brand themselves with, but it can be expected that labor groups will seek to pressure the government on the matter.

title: No War Cargo Through Our Ports — No Support for Genocide (Maritime Union of Australia)
content:
A post shared by Maritime Union of Australia. (@maritime_union_australia)

The Maritime Union of Australia expresses its solidarity with dockworkers and port workers internationally who are organising under the slogan “International Day of Action of Dockworkers and Port Workers against war and militarisation” on a 30 October 2026 day of action. The MUA National Council endorse that Branches take measures to support these actions.

The MUA notes that port workers across Europe and the Mediterranean have called and organised coordinated international action against the use of ports and transport infrastructure for war. The MUA opposes loading weapons for war and genocide.

These actions have linked opposition to the genocide of the Palestinian people with opposition to the broader war economy, rearmament, and the transformation of civilian ports into logistical platforms for militarism.

The MUA believes ports belong to the people and to the workers who keep them operating.

They must not be turned into bases or supply chains for imperialist war, occupation or genocide. Public resources should be directed to jobs, communities, safety, wages and social need, not to militarisation, war cargo and the enrichment of arms manufacturers and shipping interests.

No war cargo through our ports.

author: labor4pal
title: SUNY BDS* Labor Alliance Call to UUP, GSEU, and RAU Leadership and Members
content:
A post shared by SUNY BDS (@sunybds)

SUNY BDS Labor Alliance Call to UUP, GSEU and RAU Leadership and Members

SUNY BDS* Labor Alliance, composed of United University Professions (UUP), Research Assistants Union (RAU), and Graduate Student Employees Union (GSEU) members, calls on our labor unions to show support for Palestinian liberation, take a stance against the US government’s facilitation of war and genocide in Palestine and the broader Middle East, and stand in solidarity with the international working class by adopting a clear anti-imperialist position.

Israel’s ongoing attacks against the Palestinians result in devastating loss and misery. According to official numbers, Israel has killed 46,707 Palestinians and injured over 110,265 as of January 15, 2025. However, according to numerous scientific studies and on-the-ground health professionals, the estimates of death tolls may be as high as 186,000, representing 7.9% of Gaza’s population. Additionally, 1.9 million people, virtually all of Gaza’s inhabitants, have been displaced, while 66% of all buildings have been damaged, 78% of which are completely destroyed, or severely or moderately damaged.

On January 31, 2024, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that Israel’s military engagement in Gaza constitutes a plausible genocide and insisted that the Israeli military immediately cease activities contributing to the destruction of Palestinian life and culture in Gaza. It has been established by multiple genocide scholars, historians and other experts that Israel’s activities in Gaza fit the definition of a genocide. Furthermore, Israel’s actions are made possible by the US. The US has provided Israel with more than $20 billion in military aid since October 7, 2023. ProPublica has revealed that the US government has continued sending aid to Israel, despite internal reporting by the US Agency for International Development (USAID) that Israeli interferes with “aid efforts, including killing aid workers, razing agricultural structures, bombing ambulances and hospitals, sitting on supply depots and routinely turning away trucks full of food and medicine.” US law itself makes it illegal to send weapons to countries that interfere with US-backed humanitarian aid. This USAID report was ignored by secretary of state Anthony Blinken in his address to Congress for more aid to Israel.

In this state of affairs, labor unions in the US face a historic responsibility. As SUNY BDS Labor Alliance, we reject the concept that labor unions are merely organizations of a narrow economic focus, whose only task is to bargain every few years and bureaucratically enforce contracts. Labor unions are organizations of the working class, and working class solidarity should not be limited either by workplace nor national borders. Labor unions historically have been and continue to be key institutions for workers to act collectively against exploitative and oppressive conditions, whether against wars, apartheid systems, or systemic racism and discrimination. The labor movement has a long history of solidarity with the struggle for liberation globally. From apartheid South Africa to the US civil rights movement, union members have marched, joined boycotts, lobbied politicians, and raised our collective voices to dismantle oppressive systems. We have refused our labor when it would further an amoral goal.

We thereby believe that standing against war, genocide, apartheid, and oppression are not exogenous matters for labor unions, these are integral aspects of the responsibilities and interests of workers who are now more internationally connected than ever. This is especially important for labor unions in countries like the US, whose corporations exploit cheap labor and resources all across the world, and facilitate war and genocide overseas. In this context, restricting our actions to incremental economic demands betrays international working-class solidarity and ignores the ways our collective structural power can challenge such affairs.

In line with these principles, scores of US labor unions are standing against Israel’s genocide, affirming Palestinian self-determination and calling for a ceasefire. On July 23, 2024, seven major US unions; Association of Flight Attendants (AFA), American Postal Workers Union (APWU), International Union of Painters (IUPAT), National Education Association (NEA), Service Employees International Union (SEIU), United Auto Workers (UAW), and United Electrical Workers (UE); which represent millions of workers, urged President Biden to end military aid to Israel.

Our labor unions reflect the diversity, in all senses, of the US public, whom the majority support an arms embargo against Israel.

It is past time that SUNY labor unions adopt a clear stance against genocide, ethnic cleansing, and apartheid in Palestine. Since the beginning of Israel’s genocide, SUNY system union members have been active participants of the SUNY BDS movement, and certain chapters and coalitions within our unions have been a driving force in organizing for Palestinian liberation. In terms of statewide commitment against genocide, though, SUNY unions have fallen behind many other examples. While individual chapters at Albany, Buffalo Center, Old Westbury, and Stony Brook issued unequivocal statements in support of the Palestinian people and their liberation, the statement endorsed by the UUP statewide Delegate Assembly made false moral equivalencies between the deliberate genocidal acts of the Israeli state and the acts of resistance against that genocide by the Palestinian people.

In 2023, GSEU issued in its chapters a poll that sought member approval for a ceasefire statement and for GSEU to partner with organizations on campuses that support Palestine. After overwhelming approval from membership in both instances, GSEU published a ceasefire statement that November. In May 2024, the Education Division of CWA 1104, to which RAU and GSEU belong, distributed a poll that asked its members to vote on whether the union “should join others in calling for SUNY, Fordham University, and the Research Foundation to divest from Israel.” At the end of the 3-day voting period, which lasted from May 7 to May 10, the union notified its membership that 87% of the participants voted in favor of divestment. However, it stated that “only about 4.6% of the bargaining unit members voted despite a long polling period. This makes it difficult for the Education Division to conclusively move forward as the result does not bear a representative sample.” A 3-day voting period is hardly a long polling period. We believe that the union should determine in advance a longer polling period, what percentage would indicate a representative sample, and varied methods for disseminating polls more widely. The union, though, noted that the results “indicate that there is a vocal interest in supporting such calls in the future, but to support those calls we will need more members to speak up and express interest.” This petition is just such a call.

We believe that these initiatives above in all our unions are simply not enough. As workers from various unions within the SUNY system, we are united in the SUNY BDS Labor Alliance, organizing to advance anti-imperialist, anti-war unionism and develop institutional support for Palestinian liberation within SUNY unions. The SUNY BDS call has already received the support of thousands of students, faculty and staff, alumni, community members and beyond, representing one of the most coordinated statewide movements in our education system for decades. On many SUNY campuses, both undergraduate and graduate student governments have advanced BDS resolutions, among them University at Albany, College of Environmental Science and Forestry (ESF), Binghamton University, Stony Brook University, Fashion Institution of Technology (FIT), and University at Buffalo.

It is past time that SUNY labor takes a collective stand against genocide as labor and with its primary institutions, our labor unions.

Thereby, as SUNY education workers, we demand:

UUP, RAU, and GSEU join the growing call from unions across the world to stop the genocide against Palestinians, and make a clear stance against the ongoing ethnic cleansing of Palestinians from their land.

UUP, RAU, and GSEU call for an end to the siege on Gaza and demand ongoing provision of humanitarian aid to Palestinians.

UUP, RAU, and GSEU call on the US government to act according to its own laws, particularly the Leahy law, to stop military aid to Israel.

UUP, RAU, and GSEU publicly declare support for the BDS (Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions) movement. We join the call for SUNY to adopt BDS measures.

UUP, RAU, and GSEU make earnest, clear effort for a visible display of the preceding institutional positions. This can be accomplished by placing their relative statements and value commitments in their website, sharing them with members, making social media posts, communicating this commitment as part of the union’s fundamental values when introducing the unions to new workers in orientations, prominently featuring them in its newsletters etc.

UUP, RAU, and GSEU internally ensure that our funding, dues, and investments follow BDS measures.

UUP, RAU, and GSEU strongly commit to supporting members who face retaliation in response to their support for Palestinian liberation.

UUP, RAU, and GSEU use our organizational capacities and resources to advance messaging and education initiatives against genocide and war, and which supports international solidarity and Palestinian liberation. This can include partnering officially with other campus organizations, hosting events, distributing messaging, devoting resources and organizing special committees within the unions in accordance with these purposes.

*SUNY BDS is proudly not affiliated with SUNY or NYS.

content:
El próximo sábado 31 de octubre, a las 18:00 horas, el Centro Social Anarquista (CSA) Boría Preta de Huesca acogerá la charla 

«Lucha de clases y vivienda: hacia la huelga general»

, con la participación de Genís Ferrero, militante de CNT y miembro del Centre d’Estudis Sindicals i Llibertaris, y Aitor Sarvisé, militante del Sindicato de Inquilinas de Zaragoza.




El encuentro abordará los retos de la clase trabajadora y la relación entre la lucha laboral y la lucha por la vivienda, bajo la pregunta: 

¿qué futuro nos espera a la clase trabajadora?




La actividad tendrá lugar en el CSA Boría Preta, situado en la avenida La Paz, 6, Huesca.




La entrada 

31 de octubre. Lucha de clases y vivienda

 se publicó primero en 

Confederación Nacional del Trabajo

.

author: Rafael Oliveira
title: Com “exército” de Janones, Lula consegue virada inédita e é reeleito presidente
content:
Nunca antes na história deste país, um candidato à presidência havia chegado ao segundo turno em desvantagem e revertido a posição.

 Aconteceu. Com 51,78% dos votos, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) está 

reeleito

 presidente do Brasil e vai exercer seu quarto mandato.




A virada improvável, que envolveu uma redução inédita na abstenção entre um turno e o outro (de 21,08% para 19,22%), tem relação direta com uma mobilização sem precedentes nas redes sociais – justamente o terreno em que a 

extrema direita

 deitou e rolou nos últimos anos.




A tomada das redes pelo campo progressista – que transbordou para as ruas, com as maiores manifestações da esquerda em décadas em todo o país – envolveu vários jovens parlamentares que subiram ao palanque do petista, como Ana Elisa, deputada federal eleita pelo PT em Minas Gerais aos 21 anos e Érika Hilton, reeleita pelo PSOL em São Paulo. Mas nenhuma figura se destacou tanto quanto a do deputado federal reeleito André Janones (Rede-MG) e seu canal do WhatsApp “Exército do Lula”, que soma quase 11 milhões de participantes.




Para os especialistas em comunicação e política ouvidos pela 

Agência Pública

, é consenso que a estratégia digital capitaneada por Janones foi central na histórica virada de Lula.




Jornalismo investigativo é antídoto contra a desinformação. Ajude a garantir informação acessível e gratuita para mais pessoas. Faça um Pix para 

contato@apublica.org

 ou doe em 

apoie.apublica.org

.




“O Janones entendeu a lógica das plataformas [digitais], no sentido de que não adianta só fazer conteúdo impulsionado e ou divulgado por influenciadores.

 O trabalho de formiguinha das pessoas para os seus grupos, das pessoas para as suas redes, é muito importante”, aponta Raquel Recuero, coordenadora do Laboratório de pesquisa MIDIARS (Mídia, Discurso e Análise de Redes Sociais) da Universidade Federal de Pelotas (UfPel).




A pesquisadora destaca que a estratégia conduzida por Janones também acertou ao gerar rejeição a Flávio – algo que a extrema direita vinha fazendo desde o início do terceiro mandato de Lula. “O que mobilizou foi a emoção, o medo de uma vitória de Flávio Bolsonaro [PL]. Não existe comparação com a campanha do primeiro turno. Foi uma campanha muito mais abrangente, digital, que chegou muito mais nas pessoas, já que, querendo ou não, o espaço do debate hoje é o digital”, diz.




Recuero destaca ainda a relevância da campanha digital em um cenário adverso para Lula no Congresso. “A mobilização é importante porque mostra que o presidente eleito tem força de mobilização, ou seja, tem apoio popular, isso pressiona o Congresso, pressiona as instituições. Mas vai ser um governo difícil”, afirma.




A pesquisadora Maria Paula Almada, codiretora executiva do Aláfia Lab e doutora em Comunicação e Cultura Contemporâneas pela Universidade Federal da Bahia (Ufba), destaca as circunstâncias em que a virada histórica ocorreu, com denúncias de interferência por parte da 

Meta

 e, de acordo com a pesquisadora, com “o ministro 

Kassio Nunes Marques

 agindo de maneira dúbia, muitas vezes juridicamente equivocada, favorecendo claramente um dos lados”.




“A gente viveu, pela primeira vez na história do Brasil, uma eleição das bolhas, em que a gente não tinha acesso ao que o outro lado estava consumindo e tomando como percepção da realidade”, diz Almada. 

“A gente sempre soube da importância das redes e sempre soube que a direita domina essa lógica, mas o papel dos algoritmos, das plataformas e o não acesso ao conteúdo que está sendo disseminado do outro lado é um fenômeno novo”

.




Para a pesquisadora, o fato de Lula ter ficado em segundo lugar em um primeiro turno morno, com uma esquerda desengajada, fez com que as pessoas começassem a se mobilizar, encarando um papel de “protagonistas”, com as missões desenvolvidas por Janones no canal de WhatsApp, o que foi central para reduzir a abstenção.




Tatiana Dourado, pesquisadora e professora do Programa de Pós-Graduação em Comunicação da PUC-Rio (PPGCOM PUC-Rio), destaca a importância da identificação na campanha vitoriosa de Lula. “O que vimos foi uma mobilização em larga escala, com milhões de pessoas acompanhando canais de WhatsApp e produzindo e compartilhando conteúdos virais que geravam identificação, ampliavam o alcance dessa onda e contribuíam para consolidar convicções de voto, que vão se reproduzindo por contágio”, descreve.




Ela aponta que essa identificação, para além do conteúdo racional, tem uma expressão emocional, que mobiliza afetos – e por isso é bem sucedida. “O canal de Janones, que chegou a superar 10 milhões de inscritos, foi a grande expressão desse fenômeno. 

Mais do que criar um canal, Janones conseguiu estabelecer pontes com públicos, com uso de uma linguagem bastante direta, emocional e popular, mobilizando afetos, estimulando o compartilhamento de mensagens e investindo com muita autenticidade na manutenção dessa onda”

, diz.




Dourado aponta que ainda é cedo para entender o quanto essa transformação da estratégia digital progressista irá se manter, mas destaca como a mobilização soube contrapor táticas que já eram usadas pelo campo bolsonarista nas redes. “Não vejo isso como uma transformação restrita à esquerda, mas como a articulação de diferentes atores em torno de uma oposição ao bolsonarismo, que se expressou tanto nas redes sociais quanto nas urnas. Ainda é difícil afirmar que essa capacidade de mobilização se tornou permanente, porque também depende de conjunturas políticas, redes de participação e condições específicas de engajamento”, pontua.

author: Bruno Fonseca
title: Lula é reeleito presidente do Brasil. Pela 4ª vez. Em virada histórica.
content:
Investigamos o que importa para os brasileiros além do que passa na campanha eleitoral. Leia mais reportagens como essa clicando 

aqui

.













Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) foi reeleito presidente do Brasil neste domingo, dia 25 de outubro de 2026. O resultado acontece em um dia de votação extremamente conturbado pela falta de ônibus para eleitores e a ampliação tardia do horário de votação.




A vitória de Lula é histórica: é a primeira vez no período democrático atual que um presidente é reeleito para um quarto mandato. Também é a primeira vez no período recente que um candidato à presidência que estava em segundo lugar no primeiro turno consegue virar o jogo e terminar em primeiro.




Outro fato histórico — e problemático — desde domingo foi a ampliação do horário de votação em duas horas. O presidente do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), Cristiano Zanin, 

tomou a decisão

 nos minutos finais da votação, após pedidos das campanhas de Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro para que a votação fosse ampliada. O presidente do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) Kassio Nunes Marques não ampliou o horário, apesar do Tribunal ter sido acionado muitas horas antes do fim das votações.




O pedido da campanha de Lula se baseou nas inúmeras denúncias de falta de transporte público para que a população votasse em várias cidades do Brasil. Ao longo do domingo, a 

Agência Pública

 

mostrou

 como a redução da oferta de ônibus dificultou o deslocamento dos eleitores.




Em São Paulo, a 

Pública

 

encontrou

 pontos de ônibus lotados e eleitores enfrentando trajetos muito mais longos que o habitual. Um eleitor, ouvido pela reportagem, levou mais de duas horas para percorrer um trajeto que normalmente faria em cerca de 40 minutos e chegou a temer não conseguir votar antes do encerramento previsto para as 17h.




A situação ocorreu apesar de uma determinação para que a cidade mantivesse 100% da frota equivalente à de um dia útil. A denúncia do PT apontou que os ônibus circulavam com cerca de 70% da frota total. A redução do transporte também afetou eleitores que conseguiram votar, mas enfrentavam dificuldades para retornar para casa.




Em Salvador, o problema foi ainda mais explícito. A Secretaria Municipal de Mobilidade confirmou que pelo menos 75 ônibus foram impedidos de sair das garagens depois que foram encontrados adesivos com o número de Lula nos veículos. A apuração do governo estadual chegou a identificar 252 ônibus parados em três garagens.




A redução da frota provocou a reação do TRE-BA. O presidente do tribunal determinou a prisão em flagrante do secretário municipal de Mobilidade, Pablo Souza, que está em Paris. O tribunal também determinou a retomada de 100% dos ônibus, sob pena de multa de R$ 1 milhão por hora.




O prefeito Bruno Reis, responsável pela administração municipal, é aliado da candidatura de Flávio Bolsonaro. No primeiro turno, Lula obteve 65,26% dos votos em Salvador, contra 27,03% de Flávio.




A situação em São Paulo tem paralelo com a de Salvador: Lula também foi o candidato que mais teve votos no 1º turno na cidade. O petista teve quase 300 mil votos a mais que Flávio Bolsonaro na capital paulista, que é o maior colegiado eleitoral do país. Lula se saiu melhor, além do centro da cidade, em bairros da periferia, em especial os mais distantes do centro.

author: Unknown
title: Ephéméride des luttes : 26 octobre
content:
Dans l'éphéméride des luttes du 26 octobre, ce sont les bois de Sivens qui marquent le paysage, mais aussi les mémoires, puisqu'un des nôtres n'en est pas ressorti. Ciao Rémi, on n'oublie pas.




1876 :

 A Berne en Suisse, ouverture du huitième congrès général de l'Internationale Anti-Autoritaire.




1884 :

 A Paris, parution de la 'Revue Anti-patriote Révolutionnaire'.




1905 :

 A Saint-Petersbourg, création du premier Soviet.




1974 :

 A New York, plusieurs attaques menées en tant que premières actions des Fuerzas Armadas de Liberación Nacional (FALN) pour exiger l'indépendance de Puerto Rico et la libération de prisonniers politiques portoricains. En six ans, ce groupe mènera plus de 100 actions de ce style.




1977 :

 En Italie, de nombreux attentats frappent des entreprises liées à l'économie allemande, continuant à marquer le coup de la mort des militant-e-s de la Fraction Armée Rouge dans la prison de haute sécurité de Stammheim quelques jours plus tôt.




1981 :

 A Londres, un soldat de l'armée britannique meurt alors qu'il tente de désamorcer une bombe placée dans Oxford Street par l'IRA Provisoire.




1983 :

 A Toulouse, le CLODO (Comité pour la Liquidation Ou la Destruction des Ordinateurs) incendie les bureaux de l'entreprise américaine Sperry Univac.




1989 :

 En Allemagne de l'Ouest, l'IRA abat un membre de la Royal Air Force anglaise.




2014 :

 A Sivens, mort de Rémi Fraisse au cours d'affrontements avec la police, alors que plusieurs milliers de personnes tentent de défendre la zone occupée contre la construction d'un barrage, revendiquée comme ZAD, de l'expulsion par les forces de l'ordre.




2016 :

 A Diyarbakir au Kurdistan turc, des affrontements très violents ont eu lieu entre la population et la police suite à 

l'arrestation de plusieurs maires

 Kurdes.




Voir également 

l'éphéméride anarchiste

 du 26 octobre.

author: April Holcombe
title: China’s forgotten miracle makers
content:
History has no parallel for modern China’s economic transformation. To what do we owe the China “miracle”, in which annual GDP growth averaged 9 percent over 40 years, wages up roughly tenfold in 30 years, and more high-speed rail built in ten years than the rest of the world in all time?

In the heyday of globalisation, people said China proved the magic of free markets and free trade. These days, people are more likely to attribute the country’s success to some special Chinese characteristic, such as its state-directed investment or its “Communist” dictatorship. 

These perspectives share in common a wilful or ignorant blindness to capitalism’s real wealth creators. Economic value comes neither from the market’s “invisible hand” nor the state’s “guiding hand”, but plain old everyday hands. The secret to China’s “miracle” is the not-so-miraculous condition of its working class.

Beginning in the 1990s, the greatest ever number of wage labourers was assembled through the collusion of profit-hungry foreign capital with millions of venal bureaucrats and their repressive state machine. Three hundred million people decamped from rural poverty to seek better lives in China’s cities, while urban compatriots in state-owned mines and mills lost their livelihoods through merciless privatisation.

China’s working class is legally stratified into “migrant” and “resident”, subject to the severest dictatorship of their bosses, and deprived of political rights to speak out or unionise. Apply hundreds of billions in Western and Taiwanese investments, lather, rinse, repeat for decades, and voilà! You have the most “miraculous” economic growth in capitalist history. 

China’s migrant workforce

We are used to hearing about how important migrants are to Western economies, but migration—the internal kind from village to city, not country-to-country—has been even more critical to China’s boom. In the 1990s, the government enticed young villagers with the prospect of independence, new experiences and better pay in newly established, deregulated Special Economic Zones with low wages and low taxes.

Lu Qingmin first left her family’s half-acre farm and came to Dongguan, a burgeoning megacity in the southern manufacturing heartland of the Pearl River Delta, in the early 2000s. Bosses preferred migrant women like her, considering them doubly docile. Writer Leslie Chang, in her 2008 book 

Factory Girls

, described Lu’s experiences at her first job in a Hong Kong-owned alarm clock factory:

“A day on the assembly line stretched from eight in the morning until midnight—thirteen hours on the job plus two breaks for meals—and workers labored every day for weeks on end. From the moment she entered the factory she wanted to leave.”

The Pearl River Delta opened wide to investment in such sweatshops, and American-style hyper-individualism flowed in with it. Self-help books, life-coaching gurus, pyramid schemes, talent markets, unregulated colleges: each refracted through the false prism of empowerment what migrant workers already felt in their bones: 

you are on your own

.

Hukou

: China’s internal visa system

Every migrant who left for the cities took the same thing with them: their rural 

hukou 

(户口), a residential registration that acts like an internal passport. Originally designed under Mao Zedong in 1958 to prohibit rural-to-urban movement altogether, the 

hukou 

household registration system was repurposed to create a pliant, defenceless workforce with second-class citizenship wherever it went.

Out-of-town 

hukou 

holders, also called the “floating population”, now represent just under half of the country’s workforce. Registered to villages far away, they are denied health insurance and pensions by the local government where they actually live. Many cities bar them from buying property, and local schools charge significant sums to teach their children. 

Think of them like the United States’ undocumented immigrants, who can get driver’s licences but not Social Security, who work in practically every key industry, but technically are not supposed to be there at all. Except there are now as many in China as the entire US population.

China does not offer the equivalent of America’s birthright citizenship: children inherit their parents’ 

hukou

 wherever they are born. Locked out by the prohibitive cost of urban schooling, tens of millions of “left behind” children grow up in the countryside with their grandparents, only seeing their parents once a year. 

The first generation of migrant workers (1992–2002) viewed themselves as temporarily itinerant farmers; the second (2003–15) identified as wage labourers from elsewhere. The third generation (2016–today) feel like urban natives except for the jarring fact of their 

hukou

. “Increasingly, if you walk around any cities in China, you won’t be able to tell who’s a migrant worker or not”, labour researcher Kevin Lin said. “There’s a pipeline from the technical vocational school into factories, but many others are college educated.”

Yet talk of 

hukou 

reform is just that; local governments simply save too much money by denying pensions, health care and education. As labour academic Eli Friedman explained in response to recent flowery statements by the State Council:

“Such a project [

hukou

 abolition] would need to be funded by taxes on the rich and capital. It could also drive up the cost of business and undermine China’s dominant export machine. It is precisely because deep 

hukou

 abolition entails profound fiscal and social reform that it has been quietly opposed, undermined, and diluted across the decades.”

Housing: the China dream?

Despite the headline figure of “90 percent home ownership” in China, between half and two-thirds of the migrant population are renting in cities far from the family home they “own”, according to a series of studies over the last decade.

“Urban villages” offer cheap, informally subdivided dwellings in once-rural outskirts now enveloped within city limits. Occupying a legal grey zone, residents in these neighbourhoods can face sudden eviction and demolition. Private developers build expensive new suburbs on the rubble, forcing migrants further out in cycles of gentrification familiar to residents of Sydney or New York City.

The Beijing city government went further in cleansing the whole capital of its “rat tribe”: people forced to rent out cellars, underground bunkers or even spaces inside walls. After a deadly fire killed nineteen people in 2017, officials launched an eviction drive of such ferocity that even Beijing’s urban residents, often seen as coldly indifferent to migrants’ plight, raised a public outcry. Many of the 120,000 evicted migrants had to sleep rough through the northern winter. The Communist Party made no dwellings available in the lavish gated communities or in the empty second properties owned by the city’s wealthiest residents. 

The factory dormitory system also lets companies extend labour hours and better monitor absenteeism, but workers cannot live with family, easily form relationships, or enjoy any privacy. Cramped quarters, however, can create stronger social bonds and explosive pressure, as in April 2014, when one retiring woman’s despair at finding that the Yue Yuen shoe factory had never paid into her social insurance triggered a ten-day strike of the entire complex’s 40,000 workers.

Rising wages and falling poverty

The most widespread defence of the Communist Party dictatorship is that, on its watch, 800 million people have been lifted out of absolute poverty. Undoubtedly, wages and living standards have risen sharply over the past 30 years. This is an inevitable, contradictory component of capitalist industrialisation, already analysed in Karl Marx’s 1861 work 

Capital

. Socialism requires workers’ democratic control over such explosions of new wealth to meet collectively determined needs. Instead, China has followed the same development path charted by anti-communist dictatorships in Singapore, South Korea and Taiwan.

For perspective, absolute poverty is a very low bar, since even rock-bottom wages are a lot of money for the poorest farming families. When one woman, Leiya, moved to Shenzhen in the early 2000s, she instantly became the family breadwinner. “She put together gift boxes for the factory’s clothing line, earning RMB 600 (US$70) a month, working from 8am to 2am”, Yuan Yang recounted in her 2024 book 

Private Revolutions

. “As a fifteen-year-old in the city, Leiya was already earning three times what the average farmer earned back home.”

Sending wages back to the village as remittances did most of the heavy lifting in raising living standards; it has similarly reduced absolute poverty in Pakistan, the Pacific Islands and the Philippines, as workers leave to be exploited in Australia or the Gulf monarchies. 

Industrialisation turned rural privation into something far more profitable and productive: urban wage labour. Figures for business profits, labour productivity and capital investment in China run rings around wage growth. This process of value extraction, which Marxists call exploitation, has benefited foreign investors, “Communist” bureaucrats and local billionaires and multi-millionaires. It has also buoyed a well-to-do middle class that is much more likely than the working masses to support China’s stabilising, profiteering dictatorship. 

Capitalist growth widened the wealth gap immeasurably faster than it reduced poverty. A 2022 report jointly produced by China’s Ministry of Finance and the World Bank found that the country’s Gini coefficient, a measure of income inequality, skyrocketed from 0.30 in the mid-1980s to 0.49 in 2008—that’s worse than the United States. China’s “semi-elasticity of poverty”, which measures the percentage reduction in the absolute poverty rate per percentage of GDP growth, was just 0.27. That means that, pound for pound, China reduced poverty 

less 

efficiently than Pakistan, South Africa or Indonesia.

Of course, there have been many, many more pounds. “More than the ability to translate growth into poverty reduction, it was China’s sustained fast growth that was unusual by international standards”, the report found. Eighty percent of all absolute poverty had been eliminated by 2008, over which time universal health care and social security had been utterly eviscerated.

Workers in state-owned enterprises

Over the same period, living standards for workers in state-owned enterprises (SOEs) also fell. Approximately 70 percent of SOEs were partially or completely privatised from 1990–2002, resulting in 60 million job losses. The resulting insecurity was a “big layoff stick waved over the head of any rebel workers”, wrote Fan Wendong, a militant distillery worker, in 

My Twenty Years in a State Enterprise

. Local bureaucrats, who once kept their jobs by hitting (or pretending to hit) production quotas, were now encouraged to get rich from the dirty work of mass sackings. The aim was not purely “efficiency”, but also to push managerial power even further out of workers’ reach. Fan wrote:

“Most of us were convinced that it was entirely possible that the factory could be run well if it wasn’t for the bureaucratic institutions ruining the operations. We workers never had the right to run our factories. All leadership positions in the enterprise were assigned top down, with the enterprise director post often filled by an inexperienced hand or even a crook.”

Company directors and party cadres forced workers to “buy into” the company before throwing them on the scrapheap, as Trotskyist Au Loong Yu described in a 2011 introduction to Fan’s book:

“Starting as a compulsory exercise to coerce workers into taking part in raising an enterprise’s capital, it would not be long before the enterprise would enter bankruptcy, perhaps by design, thus looting workers of their hard-earned savings in the process.”

Working hours: capitalism’s classic contradiction

The boom years, already pregnant with contradiction, gave way to slowdown. Over the past decade of declining wage growth, workers have raised their living standards only through inhuman, illegal and irrational amounts of overtime.

Inhuman because the average working week, at 48.2 hours or 9.64 hours per working day, is now the highest on record. The May 2026 figure from the National Bureau of Statistics is worse than the peak sweatshop era in 2005, and smashes contemporary averages for Japan, South Korea, and Vietnam of 36.6 hours, 37.9 hours and 41.5 hours, respectively. 

Illegal because the 2008 Labour Contract Law caps the working week at 44 hours. Yet bosses know that most workers cannot live without overtime. Suddenly implementing the 40-hour week is a new form of “disguised layoffs”, a claim made by 3,000 mostly women strikers at Shenzhen Yilisheng electronics factory in December 2025. What kind of system forces workers to strike for illegal overtime?

Irrational because hours in China are “polarising” between the overworked and underemployed, as the ILO details in its 2025 report 

Short Hours of Work, Long Hours of Work and Work Hours Mismatch in China’s Labour Market.

 Since a record 10 percent now work fewer than 20 hours weekly, the 42 percent who work “over 48 hours” includes tens of millions clocking 60, 70 and beyond. So 30 years of unparalleled economic development have not reduced the working day. Working-class life is still caught in the clutches of monstrous contradictions, condemned so long ago by Karl Marx in 

Capital

:

“Machinery in itself shortens the hours of labour, but when employed by capital it lengthens them. In itself, [machinery] lightens labour, but when employed by capital it heightens its intensity.”

Factory dictatorship

This heightened intensity shows up in brutal working conditions. Inside China’s gleaming new high-tech infrastructure—its modern offices, warehouses and factories—bosses have not stopped treating workers like absolute shit. 

Managers subject employees to verbal and even physical abuse, while docking pay for workplace infractions. A firm’s list of fineable offences can stretch to more than 100 behaviours and typically includes talking on the assembly line, using one’s phone, taking too long in the bathroom, production mistakes and taking too many sick days. 

Almost all factory workers suffer from work-related musculoskeletal disorders, but statistics cannot capture what migrant worker-poet Zheng Xiaoqiong could in her 2012 recollection of a 17-year-old workmate:

Fatiguehas become her only word of expression On the assembly lineher body is stiff and clumsy her joints acheher fingers are heavy like machines In her backlegs waist she has lost control of the indescribable painpressing her body like a rock 

With high turnover from stress and strain, bosses withhold workers’ first payment for two months as standard practice. Quitting before then means surrendering all wages, which some people still choose to do.

Labour law and trade unions: arms of the capitalist state

Most of the above violates the country’s 2008 Labor Contract Law. But the court system, expanded after a chilling crackdown on labour activism in 2015, is rigged against the workers. Bosses enjoy the upper hand in court as they do in life, winning 67 percent of unfair dismissal cases, according to a 2021 analysis of more than 2,000 rulings (employees win just 15 percent). Labour courts provide even less protection for those working without a contract, estimated at 85 percent of the 300 million in “flexible employment”. 

China’s official trade union movement is even more useless. The All-China Federation of Trade Unions is a government-controlled institution represented in workplaces by upper management. It has not endorsed a single strike since at least 1982, when the constitution removed the right to strike. During the 2010 Nanhai Honda dispute, a landmark struggle inaugurating China’s last strike wave, union officials led a hundred goons in physical clashes with picketing workers.

China’s unruliest subjects

The victimised, exploited Chinese working class is potentially the most powerful agent of change in world history. A lot of the Communist Party’s authoritarian rule is preoccupied with keeping this potential suppressed.

Hardline repression of strikes is neither practical nor wise. The state cannot expend resources and political legitimacy every year repressing thousands of labour protests. The party-state’s responsive flexibility, offering concessions in one hand and flashing the police baton in the other, is a source of great strength.

However, strike leaders are unfailingly, ruthlessly, single-mindedly identified, sacked and even arrested to prevent ongoing organising. Labour NGOs, which once helped educate and organise migrant workers, were smashed in 2015, with activists jailed and centres permanently closed. For China’s capitalist rulers, who still view comparatively low wages as their international competitive edge, the right to form independent trade unions is the reddest of red lines.

Partly a strategic adaptation to repression, partly a real feature of its atomisation, working-class struggles remain profoundly defensive and depoliticised. Strikes rarely raise overtly political slogans and mostly demand what they already have a legal right to. Of 240 recorded factory strikes in 2023, the 

China Labour Bulletin

 (which, under expanding state repression in Hong Kong, was forced to shut permanently in 2025) reported that 68 percent concerned unpaid wages. “Give us our blood and sweat wages!” is the most commonly heard chant.

This does not mean that strikes are tame. With safety in numbers, plenty of workers are willing to curse bosses, push on police lines, block highways and chant outside government or company buildings. 

In late November 2022, a riot shook Foxconn’s largest iPhone assembly complex in the city of Zhengzhou. The company’s COVID-zero “closed loop” system confined 200,000 people to work, eat and sleep in the factory. Pay frustrations and COVID fears resulted in a mass breakout attempt, with water cannon-wielding police fighting to hold back barricade-hurling crowds. Eventually, Foxconn, having lost US$7.4

 

billion in projected earnings, paid large bonuses to get the strikers to 

leave

. The pro-democracy White Paper protests began on a Shanghai street the very next day.

It is impossible to predict exactly when new waves of struggle will erupt from China’s working class. Yet the awesome power slumbering in its lap, the simmering frustration which here and there boils over in indignation, self-sacrificing courage and resourceful self-organisation, makes it all the more galling that some so-called leftists choose to support the country’s ruling party of exploiters instead.

China is home to 700 million workers. Those who hate capitalism must be able to look them in the face and call them—without caveat, hesitation or hypocrisy—our siblings in chains, our comrades in struggle, our world’s grandest hope for a new beginning.

author: Tom Sullivan
title: Review: Anti-Zionism: A Jewish History by Benjamin Moser
content:
Anti-Zionism: A Jewish History

 by US writer and Pulitzer Prize winner Benjamin Moser is a useful contribution to uncover the history of opposition to Zionism within modern Judaism. It traces the history of anti-Zionism from the late 19th Century through the lives of several anti-Zionist Jews across the Middle East, Latin America, Africa, Europe and the US.

Moser begins in the late 19th Century in the Russian Empire, where the deep oppression that the Jewish population faced led to a cultural Zionism that, among other things, sought to revive Hebrew. One of its leaders was Aaron Samuel Tamares. But around the same time, there was also a territorial, national, and racial Zionism being developed by figures like Theodor Herzl. Published in 1896, Herzl’s 

Der Judenstaat

 (The State of the Jews) gave a racial definition to Jewish people, as opposed to the then-dominant idea of Jews being a religious community. It also argued that European anti-semitism could never be eradicated and an independent Jewish state was therefore necessary.

In response to Herzl, the cultural Zionism of Tamares and many other rabbis quickly became an explicit anti-Zionism. They were among the first to criticise how Herzl’s Zionism reinforced the existing anti-semitism of the time by defining the Jewish population as a “race” and “foreign elements” in their own countries.

Tamares did not reject Jewish communities in Palestine despite being an anti-Zionist. But he ferociously opposed the establishment of a Jewish state. To him, such a project was inextricably linked to Western imperialism. He asked why the European powers “should make recompense for 

their 

wrongdoings by handing over foreign property, 

Ottoman

land”?’

When the British began that process with the establishment of the British Mandate after World War One, the Zionist movement remained on the fringes within the Jewish population as it had when Herzl published 

Der Judenstaat

. In 1917, for example, Zionist groups in England had no more than four thousand members between them.

Moser describes the early days of the British Mandate through Jacob Israel de Haan. When de Haan emigrated from the Netherlands to Palestine in 1919, he was among the most prominent Dutch Zionists. But after seeing the violence of the Zionist groups against the indigenous population of both the Palestinian Muslims and Orthodox Jews, he quickly became a leading figure of the Agudah, an anti-Zionist, Orthodox Jewish organisation.

De Haan’s articles were some of the first to document the growing Zionist domination of Palestine in the early 1920s. He explained “that no Arab is allowed to live in Tel Aviv. That no Arab is received in a Jewish hotel. That companies in their statutes decide that they can only employ Jews.”

De Haan quickly reached such prominence that 

Ha’aretz

 labelled him and other Agudah members “traitors” and “scum.” Such words helped fuel the violent attacks of Jewish settler groups against Agudah members to the point where, in 1924, a member of the Haganah, the main Zionist militia, assassinated him. The order was given by Yitzhak Ben-Zvi, later to become the second president of Israel. 

Moser then jumps to Egypt, focusing on Sadiq Saad, an Egyptian, anti-Zionist, Jewish leftist. One of Saad’s most important works was 

Palestine in the Claws of Colonialism, 

published in 1947 and detailing the apartheid-style system then already established. One of the book’s contributions was its coverage of the unique experience of the Palestinian peasantry. Unlike almost all other peasantries, when the Palestinians were expelled from their land, they were denied employment by the new owners of the land or in the cities. This came directly from the policies of the Palestine Foundation Fund, the World Zionist Organisation’s fundraising arm, which specifically stated in its loan contracts that the borrower “pledges to hire Jewish workers only.”

The book covers numerous other examples of prominent anti-Zionist Jewish individuals and groups. The chapters on the immediate post-World War Two period are particularly useful in understanding the rapid transformation of both Zionism and those opposed to it. The French New Left, for example, during the 1950s and 1960s suffered through a period of deep confusion that led many prominent figures to support a form of Zionism. Similarly, the chapter on Reform Judaism in the United States, which had opposed Zionism since the late 19th Century, shows how rapidly the political context changed from the late 1940s, as Moser writes:

“For Americans and other Westerners, the question of Israel’s legitimacy was, for the most part, no longer debated. The feeling that Israel was compensation for the Holocaust became so widespread that the anti-Zionists were mainly forgotten.” 

In barely half a century after Herzl’s 

Der Judenstaat

, support for a Jewish state in Palestine had grown from a fringe movement to a majority view within Western Judaism. And its key practical conclusion of turning Israel into an outpost of Western imperialism in the Middle East had won firm support among the Western ruling classes. 

Moser’s book is one of several in recent years from prominent anti-Zionist and Israel-critical Jewish writers that challenge mainstream narratives on Israel. Avi Shlaim’s 2023 memoir, 

Three Worlds: Memoirs of an Arab-Jew

, tells the story of his family’s expulsion from Iraq in the early 1950s. For generations his family had lived in Baghdad, a city where one-third of the population was Jewish during World War One, and Zionism was almost non-existent.

Shlaim documents how, after 1948, Israeli terrorists bombed several Jewish-owned businesses and a synagogue to foment racial tensions and force the Iraqi Jewish community to emigrate to Israel. At the time, “there had been no other attack on the Jewish community (in Iraq) in recent centuries,” according to Shlaim. From Israel’s founding in 1948 to the first bomb in 1950, only 126 Iraqi Jews had registered to emigrate. But once the attacks began thousands began to register. It took only a few years to put an end to two and a half millennia of Jewish presence in Mesopotamia.

When Shlaim’s family arrived in Israel in 1951, they faced extreme anti-semitism, this time from Israelis who denied them their right to be both Jewish 

and 

Arab. As Israel’s first prime minister, David Ben-Gurion, said “We do not want the Israelis to turn into Arabs.” 

Two other recent examples that focus on Jewish left-wing organisations are Molly Crabapple’s 

Here Where We Live Is Our Country: The Story Of The Jewish Bund

 and Benjamin Balthaser’s 

Citizens of the Whole World: Anti-Zionism and the cultures of the American Jewish left

.

Whilst reading Moser’s book, one cannot help but consider the changes in the Palestine movement over recent years. When Moser arrived at Brown University in the 1990s there was not “any real organized Palestinian presence.” Yet over recent years Ivy League universities have been some of the leading sites of pro-Palestinian resistance. Moser notes that one of the biggest barriers to the Palestine and anti-Zionist movement growing even bigger is the “lack of a tradition to fall back on.” His work, along with the others mentioned above, is an important contribution to re-building such a tradition.

author: Elliot Downes
title: NT government closes Darwin’s largest homelessness shelter
content:
Residents of Darwin’s largest homelessness shelter were evicted by the Northern Territory government on 12 October, and relocated to Batchelor, a town 100 kilometres away.

Yilli Short Stay Accommodation (YiSSA), which is run by Yilli Rreung Housing Aboriginal Corporation, was home to hundreds of people, mostly Aboriginal. Many have experienced domestic violence and are living with serious health conditions, including kidney conditions requiring dialysis. 

Residents from communities across the territory would stay at YiSSA while accessing medical care or other services in Darwin. Nearly 400 people were directly affected by the closure of the facility, including 160 children.

YiSSA’s closure will place more pressure on remaining homelessness services in Darwin. Meanwhile, the minority of residents transferred to the smaller facility in Batchelor will not have the same access to support networks, food, healthcare and education. Batchelor is a town with a population of around 500, a small health clinic and no public transport. 

The closure of a key homelessness service is particularly egregious given the Northern Territory has the highest rate of homelessness in the country. According to data released last year by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 

one in every 25 Territorians requires homelessness assistance

, and Aboriginal people make up 89 percent of those accessing homelessness services in the Northern Territory.

As the biggest landlord in the territory, the Northern Territory government is largely to blame for this situation. Territorians on the emergency public housing waiting list can expect to 

wait up to a decade for a roof over their head

. The government is also responsible for the apartheid-like conditions in Aboriginal town camps on the outskirts of places like Darwin and Alice Springs, as well as the overcrowding in remote communities.

The closure of YiSSA was announced by the ruling Country Liberal Party (CLP) in July. Ostensibly, it was due to a failure to secure a deal with Ausco, the owner of the buildings and other infrastructure on the Crown land site. But in reality, it was a political decision. 

After years of renting the demountable buildings, the government offered to buy them for $3 million—the equivalent of just one year’s rent. When this offer was rejected by Ausco, the federal government proposed to cover the cost of the purchase on the condition that Yilli Rreung continue running the service.

The CLP rejected the offer of federal funding, with Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro calling it a 

“waste of taxpayers’ hard-earned money”

. Yet it has cost 

$16.25 million to establish and fund the Batchelor facility

, run by Mission Australia.

The announcement of YiSSA’s closure sparked a campaign by the activist group, Justice Not Jails (JNJ). It culminated in a 200-strong rally outside of the Australian Homelessness Conference in Darwin just days before residents were to be evicted. 

Anna, an activist with JNJ, told 

Red Flag

 that the decision doesn’t make sense “unless you approach it from an ideological viewpoint. Some of the YiSSA residents have said that [the government] just don’t want Aboriginal people to have a nice, secure place to live.”

The YiSSA closure is symptomatic of a Trumpian government that has targeted Aboriginal people in particular. Since coming to power in 2024, the CLP have lowered the age of criminal responsibility to 10, reintroduced spit hoods in detention, and made it easier for Aboriginal children to be removed from their families and placed into long-term state care.

This has involved a significant expansion in the carceral state, with the prison population 

increasing by 24 percent between 2024 and 2025

, and the Finocchiaro government announcing earlier this year the construction of a new private prison in Darwin. 

The Northern Territory is one of the most incarcerated places in the world, 

second only to El Salvador

, with more than 1 percent of the entire population behind bars. Increasingly, this includes people on remand, who are awaiting trial or sentencing.

According to Anna, the next phase of the campaign will involve putting pressure on the federal Labor government. “There’s been a lot of disagreement between the CLP and Labor about what was actually promised. It’s all really immature and I think disrespectful to the people whose lives are actually being affected,” she told 

Red Flag. 

“The federal government obviously has the money. If they really wanted to do something, they could just purchase [land] and build a facility in Darwin.”

Despite social media posts critical of the YiSSA closure and promises of more consultation with Aboriginal communities, Labor has been in power in the Territory for the majority of the last 25 years and shares responsibility for the housing and incarceration crises. 

What the Northern Territory desperately needs is an organised left-wing force capable of mobilising the opposition to the closure of YiSSA and similar attacks by the Territory government, a force that can draw on the power of organised workers to make it impossible for governments to carry them through. A force willing to stand up to the criminals who run the capitalist system, who see human beings as dispensable if they’re not helping a business or landlord make money. The formation of the NT Socialists is an important step in that direction.

The petition against the YiSSA closure is available 

here
