title: Sevda Karaca: War policies undermine unity and labour struggles - Part Two
content:
Sevda Karaca, Deputy Chair of the Labour Party (EMEP) and MP for Antep, answered ANF's questions about labour struggles and the struggle for peace. 




Part one of this interview can be read 

here

.




Do war, conflict and the resulting militarism push poverty, insecurity and workers' demands out of the public agenda? How exactly are labour struggles weakened during periods when security-driven policies intensify?




The past 40 years have shown us that the effects of war are not confined to areas of armed conflict. War permeates every aspect of social life. Workers' demands for higher wages, the right to strike, women's struggle for equality and people's democratic demands can suddenly be pushed into the background by debates over 'national security', 'the survival of the state' or the 'domestic front'. Rather than answering the questions working people raise about its policies, the government attempts to bring them into line by presenting them with another supposed threat.




This mechanism has very concrete consequences. Strikes are postponed on national security grounds. Trade union organising faces repression. Democratic protests are portrayed as security threats. The conflict of interests between workers and their employers is treated as a security threat, with employers' interests presented as though they were the common interests of society as a whole. Moreover, under conditions of war, those who voice objections can easily be accused of failing to care about their country or their nation. It is workers, working people and poorer sections of society who pay the heaviest price for war. People face both economic devastation and the social consequences of war. Yet they are still expected to make sacrifices. Their questions about why their wages are insufficient, where public resources are being spent and why their rights are being restricted are often drowned out by nationalist rhetoric and growing chauvinism.




Opposition to war and the labour struggle are not two separate areas of struggle. Opposing war cannot be separated from defending workers' livelihoods, their right to strike and their freedom to organise. The political climate created by war restricts working people's ability to defend their rights. At the same time, struggles to protect those rights can become a force against the social consequences of war policies. What matters is that opposition to war must not be confined to a separate sphere, disconnected from the everyday demands of working people.




Opposing war is not a separate task from defending workers' livelihoods, their right to strike and their freedom to organise. On the contrary, to understand why these rights are constantly under threat, we must recognise the social role played by war and militarism.




‘Racism and chauvinism prevent people from coming together’




How can we build a movement for social peace by connecting opposition to war with demands for a higher minimum wage, tax justice, trade union rights and women's right to life?




First of all, we must not reduce peace to politicians sitting around a negotiating table, the silencing of guns or the signing of an agreement. These are, of course, important. But those responsible for war have spent decades using propaganda to legitimise it, dividing peoples and forcing the working class into artificial divisions. Social peace cannot be achieved, nor can peace take root throughout society, simply by bringing the opposing forces to the negotiating table.




War is also a major obstacle to bringing class struggles and broader social movements together. The racism, nationalism and chauvinism being fuelled prevent people, women and young people from uniting around common demands. For example, a worker in the defence industry may be subjected to terrible exploitation, yet that exploitation can be dismissed as an issue because their work is presented as service to the nation.




We must also remember that an atmosphere of war and conflict makes it easier to promote false answers to the question of who is responsible for the poverty, insecurity, discrimination and violence people experience every day. The real causes lie in the existing system and its political and economic representatives. Yet the ruling classes can easily point the finger at migrants, women or an oppressed nation instead.




Another decisive aspect of the struggle to establish lasting peace on a social foundation is discussing what kind of lives people will lead, what rights they will have and whose needs society's resources will serve.




For a worker, peace also means no longer having to worry about their child's future, earning a wage sufficient for a dignified life and not being dismissed for joining a trade union. For a woman, it means having control over her own life, not being left alone in the face of violence, receiving equal pay for equal work and not having to shoulder the burden of care alone. For Kurdish workers, it means all these things, together with recognition of their identity, language and democratic will, and guarantees of equal citizenship rights. 




Simply listing these demands alongside one another is not enough. We must establish the connections between them. Consider tax policies. Wage earners hand over a significant proportion of their income to the state through indirect taxes, while big capital benefits from various advantages. Workers seeking to organise in trade unions face pressure from employers. Women are concentrated in insecure jobs and carry out unpaid care work. The suppression of democratic rights through policies of conflict has severe consequences for economic and social life. Each of these issues, in different ways, raises the same questions: Whose interests are society's resources serving? Who makes the decisions? And who pays the price?




This discussion is sometimes conducted through misleading assumptions that peace will automatically bring greater prosperity, economic growth and regional development. We, too, expect that an end to the conflict will lead to more rapid industrialisation in Kurdish provinces and changes in their economic structures and conditions. But we must emphasise that this does not automatically mean prosperity, development, growth or employment, and that the consequences for capital will be different from those experienced by working people.




The economic and social consequences of the conflict in Kurdish provinces, control over resources and decisions about the region's future must also form part of this discussion. The economic benefits of peace, increased investment or regional development do not, in themselves, tell us how working people will live. We must also ask who will control new investments, under what conditions workers will be employed and who will receive the wealth created.




A movement for social peace can be built through common struggles in which workers, women, young people, the Kurdish people and all oppressed groups participate with their own demands. We are not talking about unity that requires anyone to abandon their demands. On the contrary, we are talking about unity in which different demands reinforce one another and every section of society sees the struggle for others' rights and freedoms as part of its own struggle.




How do economic destruction, dispossession and ecological devastation in conflict zones affect workers in western Turkey? Has this connection been sufficiently established?




We cannot say that this connection has been sufficiently established. The consequences of war are often treated as a problem confined to the geographical areas where the conflict takes place. Yet the economic, social and ecological consequences of war do not recognise borders. Conflict forces people from their land, homes and sources of livelihood. Agricultural production suffers, while livestock farming and local economies are severely affected.




One of the historical dimensions of the policies of denial and assimilation directed against the Kurdish people has been the control of the region's resources, its economic underdevelopment, the destruction of livelihoods and the forced displacement of its population. We must also consider today's debates over mining projects, dams, power plants and the exploitation of natural resources against this historical background. Control over Kurdistan's resources is not simply a question of regional development. It is a question of ownership, labour and decision-making power.




Who decides how land, water and forests are used? Who receives the economic benefits? Can local people have a say in decisions affecting their own living environments? These questions are directly connected to the working class. People who lose their livelihoods may be forced to seek work in other cities, often taking insecure and low-paid jobs. As workers are turned against one another on the basis of differences in identity, the gains of the working class as a whole are rolled back in favour of capital. Workers in Kurdish provinces, employed in sectors ranging from agriculture and mining to textiles and other industries, also face harsh working conditions, low wages and a lack of organisation.




If people's livelihoods are destroyed in one place, they may be forced to enter the labour market elsewhere under even harsher conditions. This increases the pressure to drive down wages and working conditions for all workers. Of course, this is not the only factor determining wages, but it is an important mechanism through which working people's employment and livelihoods become increasingly insecure. 




Ecological destruction cannot be regarded as a problem affecting only a particular region. The destruction of land, water, forests and shared living environments for the sake of capital accumulation deprives people of their livelihoods and their future. The destruction of agricultural land for mining in a village and the conditions that force workers in an industrial city to live and work in unhealthy environments are, in different ways, consequences of the same relations of production and ownership.




That is why simply telling Turkish workers to be concerned about what is happening in Kurdish provinces is not enough. We must demonstrate together how that destruction is connected to their own lives through economic relations. We must make the common interests of Turkish and Kurdish workers visible through their working and living conditions, rather than leaving them as an abstract appeal for brotherhood.




‘War fuels the growth of capital groups’




Is war merely a tool of political rule, or is it also a model of capital accumulation? Who pays the price for the resources allocated to the defence industry?




War is more than a tool used by governments to control society and consolidate their political power. It is also a major area of capital accumulation. Arms production, military technology, security and logistics contracts, energy resources and reconstruction activities are all areas involving substantial economic interests. Prolonged wars, or the constant emphasis on security threats, can increase the profits of capital groups operating in these sectors.




We must also examine the rhetoric of national pride surrounding Turkey's defence industry from this perspective. Of course, a country's technological capacity, production capabilities and independence in defence can be discussed. But the fundamental question is this: Who controls this production, what needs does it serve, and at what social cost? Which companies receive public resources, and under what conditions? Do these investments serve the common good of society or the profits of particular capital groups? Are defence and armament policies being used to turn the country into an instrument of imperialist powers' wars in the region, or to provide a foundation for the peoples of the region to build an equal, democratic and free life? These are crucial distinctions. 




Amid rhetoric about national security and becoming a powerful country in the region, workers see their wages eroded by inflation, pensioners struggle to make ends meet, and young people cannot afford housing. Yet the government presents these hardships as necessary sacrifices under conditions of war, constantly calling on people and society to make sacrifices. But whether the same sacrifices are being demanded of capital is not questioned. Wage earners bear a significant proportion of the tax burden, while people have almost no oversight of how public resources are used. Capital benefits both from the economic resources created by the people and from conditions in which pressure on labour intensifies.




The issue, therefore, is not simply the amount spent on defence. It is about who controls production and resources, how social needs are determined and to whom those making economic decisions are accountable. The struggle for peace must also raise these questions.




Beyond saying that 'war budgets increase poverty', what other factors cause war to deepen poverty?




If we explain the increase in poverty caused by war solely in terms of the share of the budget allocated to military expenditure, we miss a significant part of the problem. War also changes how people work, where they live, which rights they can exercise and how they can build their futures.




First, war destroys economic life and sources of livelihood. Agriculture, livestock farming and local production suffer, while people may be forced from their land, homes and jobs. Second, forced displacement and growing insecurity push people into low-paid employment. Third, security-driven policies suppress the very means through which workers can improve their wages and working conditions, including trade union organising and the right to strike.




Fourth, the weakening of democratic oversight during wartime, together with the marginalisation of questions about how public resources are used, makes it harder to challenge economic privileges. Fifth, the fear and polarisation created by war make it more difficult for workers to unite around their common problems. Working people living under similar conditions can be turned against one another on the basis of identity and nationality. 




We must also consider the burden placed on women. As livelihoods shrink, public services become inadequate and care needs increase, much of the resulting burden is met through women's unpaid labour. Women are pushed into harsher conditions in paid employment while also being forced to shoulder responsibilities at home. Conditions of war also lead to the normalisation of all forms of violence, while those fighting against violence are marginalised and portrayed as terrorists.




War, therefore, does not merely consume society's resources. It also strengthens the relationships and mechanisms that perpetuate poverty. That is why opposition to war must also include a struggle against all these mechanisms that determine working people's living conditions.

title: Şerda Mazlum: The process requires women's self-defence networks - Part One
content:
Bêrîtan (Gülnaz Karataş), one of the symbolic figures of the Kurdish women's freedom struggle, made history on 25 October 1992 with her self-sacrificing resistance against betrayal and surrender in South Kurdistan. Choosing freedom at the edge of a cliff, Bêrîtan became a symbol not only of resistance but also of women's determination to achieve freedom and continue their struggle.




YJA Star commander Şerda Mazlum Gabar spoke about Bêrîtan's life, personality and resistance, stressing that her legacy of resistance continues to place responsibilities on women today.




Mazlum said discussions in the Peace and Democratic Society Process must give way to concrete steps, pointing out that the freedom of the Kurdish people and women remains under threat. “The greatest and most effective deterrent force is an organised and conscious society,” she said, emphasising the need for women to strengthen their self-defence networks and for society to develop its own forms of organisation.




What were the conditions facing the Kurdish people, Kurdish women and the freedom guerrillas at the time of martyr Bêrîtan's self-sacrificing action? How should her action be understood in the context of those conditions?




Throughout human history, the struggle for human existence has continued despite every hardship, suffering and massacre. It may have been inadequate or incomplete at times, but the struggle to be human and to live a dignified life has always existed. As long as human beings continue to dominate one another, nature and life itself, this struggle will continue. The struggle to reach into the depths of history and recreate love, freedom, justice and labour in their true essence has always faced brutal attacks and attempts to suppress and destroy it. The price of rebelling against slavery and domination in pursuit of freedom has been immense. Across different places and periods, freedom has repeatedly been redefined and given meaning through these sacrifices. The history of every oppressed people, class and gender contains countless extraordinary examples of this. Our own history of freedom also possesses a profound and magnificent legacy of resistance. Among those at the forefront of this legacy is our comrade Bêrîtan, the embodiment of our dignity and freedom. As we mark the 34th anniversary of her martyrdom and enter the 35th year since her death, I commemorate our courageous and brave-hearted commander, comrade Bêrîtan, and, through her, all martyrs of freedom with love and gratitude. I bow respectfully before their memory and renew my promise to fulfil their aspirations for freedom.




Our encounter with freedom as women and Kurds, and our journey towards it, have not been easy. They have been forged through boundless labour, effort and struggle. Comrade Bêrîtan's self-sacrificing action became a breath of life for the Kurdish people and Kurdish women at that time. It revealed the truth that a free life could only be achieved through great resistance. In this sense, her action constitutes one of the fundamental building blocks of the Kurdistan revolution and the morality of freedom that has developed in Kurdistan. 25 October 1992 was the day when the meaninglessness and disgrace of betrayal were answered with the magnificent meaning and sacredness of resistance. It was the will, voice and action of a free and dignified woman against every form of degradation and surrender imposed upon her. Comrade Bêrîtan Hêvî assumed responsibility for a people and their history, acting with an awareness of what it meant to be a pioneer. She reversed the course of surrender and betrayal, halted the downward spiral, rejected every form of degradation imposed upon her and recreated life out of death. She understood what the moment demanded, followed the teachings of freedom and acted in a manner that reflected the spirit of her time.




Historic actions acquire their significance because, at the time and place in which they occur, they address the most vital and pressing problems facing society or offer solutions to them. Not every action marks a turning point or represents a leap into a new stage. Historic actions are distinguished from ordinary actions by the convergence of the right time, the right place and the capacity to bring about meaningful social change. Through these qualities, they become a spirit and a guiding path.




Comrade Bêrîtan and her action embody precisely such a spirit and such a path. There is no one who has not been moved by the historic photograph that immortalised comrade Bêrîtan's powerful yet graceful bearing. Her beauty could not be contained within the frame, and the depth of her heart seemed to overflow beyond it, leaving an indelible impression on all of us. Guerrilla life suited Bêrîtan, and Bêrîtan suited guerrilla life. Every word and sentence she wrote in her diary was distilled from suffering, hardship and the most beautiful moments of solidarity, becoming refined and acquiring profound meaning. Her participation in the freedom struggle was not something superficial or added on from the outside. It was a process of complete integration, of becoming inseparable from the struggle itself. The more she became one with the freedom struggle, the more beautiful and meaningful she became, while also enriching the struggle with her own meaning. Bêrîtan walked the path of liberation with her head held high and with dignity, remaining true to her word. Embracing Bêrîtan's spirit and path gave our movement the character of resisting under all circumstances and sustaining that resistance without interruption. Kurdish women certainly had a tradition of resistance in earlier uprisings. However, those acts of resistance and rebellion had not developed into an ideological and organised struggle for freedom and equality. Comrade Bêrîtan's spirit and path of resistance brought about a development in the women's struggle based on organisation and continuity. Through this path, the women's struggle advanced step by step towards the formation of an organised women's guerrilla force.




What message did Bêrîtan convey to the Kurdish people and women through her stance and action? What are the fundamental values that define Bêrîtan's legacy today?




An ideology and a commitment to freedom embraced even at the cost of one's life have the power to leave indelible marks on history. Humanity's struggle for freedom, which has continued for thousands of years and passed through different stages, has been engraved in history and in the collective memory of peoples through the martyrs who sacrificed their lives and the sacred blood shed for this cause. No amount of oppression or persecution has ever been able to erase that memory. Countless freedom fighters, known and unknown, who rebelled against the slavery, oppression and indignity imposed on much of humanity, refusing to submit or accept a meaningless existence, constitute the driving forces and enduring values of historical progress. In our age, dominant powers have used science and technology to make their policies of alienation, erasure of memory and destruction of identity increasingly sophisticated and deeply entrenched. Yet humanity can still speak of freedom, dignity, beauty and justice. This is thanks to the efforts made in pursuit of these ideals and the values created by the martyrs of freedom. Otherwise, humanity would long ago have been reduced to a mass of robots.




In this sense, the most decisive forces standing in the way of the ruling powers' objectives are the unwavering commitment to freedom, embraced even at the cost of life, the struggle to create meaning, and the mountain-hearted martyrs who lived with dignity. In the history of our struggle, the legacy of martyrdom extending from Haki, Mazlum, Egîd, Zîlan and Bêrîtan to the present day has been created by heroes who refused to bow to any form of oppression and accepted nothing less than a free life. Each of them represents an example of heroism, overcoming the most difficult paths of struggle by leading from the front and illuminating the way with both their minds and their hearts.




Bêrîtan, the rebellious daughter of Dersim and the embodiment of our dignity and freedom, became a legend through both her life and her martyrdom. Bêrîtan's cry for freedom from the edge of the cliff echoed everywhere, from South Kurdistan to the major cities of Turkey, reaching countless people and inspiring hundreds of young women and men. Bêrîtan deepened our awareness of the need to oppose the nationalist-chauvinist line, while strengthening our commitment to freedom, rebellion and the refusal to surrender. She was among those who understood the Leadership (Abdulah Öcalan) most profoundly and who, with her determined and persistent character, sought to put that understanding into practice. She had joined the struggle inspired by the image of Besê, who threw herself from a cliff during the Dersim uprising. Bêrîtan carried a deep love of history and her homeland in her heart. Following Besê's path and footsteps, she became a free spirit and a powerful mind capable of spreading its wings over the cliffs. All our martyrs and all the values of resistance created throughout the history of our struggle formed the foundation upon which YJA Star was built. Comrade Bêrîtan's path of self-sacrifice, her determination to persevere in guerrilla life and the pursuit of freedom, and her identity as a dignified and free woman who devoted herself entirely to the cause of liberation embody the values upon which YJA Star is founded. Reorganising and developing the struggle along Bêrîtan's path will be a historic step towards achieving victory and shaping a new way of life, as well as women and men, capable of fulfilling the need for freedom.




How has the women's armed organisation developed along Bêrîtan's path changed over the past 33 years? How should we assess the progress YJA Star has made since its establishment?




Every living phenomenon in nature passes through stages of change while maintaining an internal consistency with its purpose and way of life. This dialectic also applies to human societies and the institutions and concepts they create. Something that can no longer change has lost its vitality and is either dead or approaching death. The women's armed organisation that emerged in Kurdistan around clearly defined ideological objectives has also undergone a process of transformation in keeping with this dialectic of nature and society. Our free women's units linked the development of their national identity directly to the pursuit of freedom from the very beginning. They maintained this principle throughout every stage of their development. For this reason, they have consistently struggled against reactionary, traditional and dominant ideologies. The question was never confined to the Kurdish national struggle. Instead, the emphasis was on developing the principles of freedom and justice for Kurdish and women's identities, both of which had been subjected to denial and destruction, within the framework of socialist ideology. Developing the women's freedom struggle around these principles made significant contributions to struggles around the world, including socialist movements, and created an entirely new experience.




The emergence of women's armed organisation as such a distinctive and original experience within the historical and cultural context of the Middle East was primarily made possible by Öcalan, his constant questioning and creative approach, and the martyrs who devoted themselves selflessly to the path he set out. Öcalan expressed this very powerfully when he said, “A new world is being born around women.” The importance of this organisation is undoubtedly multidimensional, both in overcoming the problems women face and in creating personalities and identities capable of serving as models for society.




No matter how much dominant historical narratives have attempted to erase women, their history and their culture from collective memory, the more we learn about our own history, the more clearly we see that women's history is a living history that has never been completely erased from language or memory. This search and rediscovery have emerged, and continue to develop, through difficult struggles, evolutionary and revolutionary processes, and tremendous sacrifices. Despite the oppressive, destructive and annihilating nature of patriarchal ideology, there has always been a tradition of women's resistance that has persisted with all its vitality and diversity, even when it was unnamed or excluded from official records. Our martyrs, who represent our historical roots and stand as monuments to life and resistance, are among the most important forces illuminating the darkness created by a system of domination that has turned the contradictions within life, between women and men, and in nature into seemingly impossible knots. The more we understand our history, the more deeply we understand the present, strengthen our love for women and humanity, and take firmer steps towards the future and freedom.




Our courageous commander, comrade Bêrîtan, embodied extraordinary simplicity, honesty, sensitivity, courage, intellectual depth and a profound search for meaning. Both the nature of her action and her diaries reveal remarkable courage in the way she approached and interpreted herself, society and the circumstances of her time. Comrade Bêrîtan's dignified stance against betrayal and surrender deepened the women's freedom struggle, both in terms of individual development and organisational progress. The women's freedom struggle grew through this tradition of resistance. This was not simply because of the forms of action undertaken, but also because of the passion for freedom, love of humanity and depth of consciousness embodied in the characters of our martyrs. This is a love of freedom. It is a love that transcends ordinary forms of love, centred on freedom, love for society, being oneself, living a meaningful life, becoming a dignified woman and developing the consciousness needed for victory. It represents a transformation from women whose will has been suppressed by the dominant patriarchal system, who have been alienated from themselves and confined to narrow worlds, into free women who possess their own identities and willpower. These women become capable of developing solutions to problems ranging from social issues to questions of gender, embracing the creative and life-giving universe within themselves with profound love. Like many pioneering women throughout history, the women martyrs of our struggle represent this lineage of free women driven by love. They are symbols of the rebirth of the goddess.




At the present stage of our women's freedom struggle, living, struggling and developing an identity in the spirit of Zîlan and Bêrîtan will bring success. The keys to victory and freedom are hidden in their characters. What matters is that we listen to their hearts with our own hearts and understand their minds with our intelligence. Only then can we make freedom and victory a lived reality.




What role does YJA Star play today, not only as a military force but also in women's organisation and self-defence? What are the most important achievements of its 33 years of experience?




The free women's units in Kurdistan were never organised solely as a military force. The very purpose of establishing women's armed organisation was defined as building a world without armies. A world without armies means a world without domination, inequality or injustice. The aim of free women's guerrilla organisation is to create a model of free life. Our women's defence forces in Kurdistan were organised, first and foremost, as a force safeguarding the values created through 33 years of struggle, as well as our Leadership, our martyrs and our people. A force organised on these foundations must, above all, understand and embrace the immense responsibilities, sacrifices and moral obligations that this entails.




It is equally essential to reflect deeply on how these responsibilities can best be fulfilled and what must be done to achieve this. For our women's defence forces, interpreting the political and military developments of the current process as effectively as possible and developing strong responses to them carries both historical and immediate significance. Our Leadership has always entrusted the women's defence forces of Kurdistan with major responsibilities. For this reason, achieving success is a debt we owe to life itself. A militant approach capable of responding appropriately to the expectations of our people, our Leadership and the current process is essential. Conscious struggle, carried out with a clear understanding of one's responsibilities and in the service of the democratic society paradigm, is the fundamental principle for fulfilling the tasks and responsibilities of this period. If the Peace and Democratic Society Process is approached in this way, success will leave its mark on the destiny of the Kurdish people and women, and no force will be able to prevent it.

title: Tuğçe Tatari: Peace is an opportunity for the whole country
content:
Thirteen years after her previous visit, journalist Tuğçe Tatari travelled to Qandil once again during a peace process and met with Besê Hozat, Co-Chair of the Executive Council of the Kurdistan Communities Union (KCK).




Tatari spoke to ANF about her impressions of Qandil and the conference that the Women Side by Side group will organise on 31 October and 1 November under the theme “We Stand Side by Side, We Talk About the Future”.




You returned to Qandil after 13 years, once again during a peace process. What changes did you observe over that period? What had remained the same?




If you ask me what remained the same, it was nature. The colours and the light were the same. The natural light in the photographs I took 13 years ago was exactly the same as in the photographs taken this time. Apart from that, 13 years ago, life was lived outdoors. Now, new living spaces have been built inside the mountains, and people live in those spaces. Of course, it is difficult to picture what they are like. Colleagues who had visited before me had told me that they were growing plants inside and so on. But inevitably, you imagine very small, confined spaces and living arrangements that we are not accustomed to. That was not the case at all. They were enormous living spaces.




I was able to visit two communes: a press commune and a cultural commune. Through engineering work, they have created large living spaces inside the mountains, without windows. There are meeting areas, dining areas, kitchens, accommodation sections and rooms. That was undoubtedly the biggest change. On my previous visit, we had stayed outdoors, and I had slept in a tent. This time, they gave us one of the rooms inside, and we stayed there. That was quite a difference. In fact, it was a major change for me.




At the same time, although these large living spaces have been established, the emotional damage caused by the past decade of war, or rather, the period of conflict, and the sense of loss it has left behind were evident in almost every conversation. Because I stayed for several days, I had the opportunity to speak with many guerrillas. Everyone had stories marked by greater sadness. Most of their questions concerned the possibility of returning: ‘What will happen if we return?’, ‘Is Turkey ready for us to come back?’, ‘How do you see things?’ In fact, just as we are all watching the process with curiosity, wondering whether anything will happen, whether there will be developments and where the process will lead, they too are waiting there to see how it unfolds.




What was the mood among the guerrillas, as far as you could observe during your visit?




I cannot say there was a sense of hopelessness. It would be more accurate to say that the lack of concrete steps from Turkey was raising questions in their minds. They follow current developments closely, of course, through television, newspapers and other sources. They pay particular attention to statements coming from Turkey, especially those made on behalf of the state. In fact, the process does not seem to be moving forward at the moment. So, rather than expressing their own views, they want to hear what is happening here. As I said, they ask questions such as: ‘How is the process being viewed?’, ‘Why is there such difficulty in building public support for the process?’, ‘Looking at things from Turkey, do you see any possibility of the process succeeding?’ Beyond these questions, they are naturally wondering whether they will ever return. We said goodbye to one another with the thought that perhaps our next meeting would take place in Diyarbakır (Amed), Istanbul or Ankara.




In fact, like everyone else in Turkey, they are waiting to see what happens. But as people directly affected by the issue, whose futures depend to some extent on this process, their interest is naturally much more immediate. That applies to those in Europe, those in prison and those in Qandil. They are all directly concerned with the outcome. I would therefore say that their desire to understand what is happening in Turkey is much stronger.




What was the conviction that, as you mentioned in your article, became stronger during your time in Qandil? Could you elaborate on that?




Of course, I haven't written about Qandil itself yet. I've written about my interview with Besê Hozat. There is actually a great deal I want to write about Qandil. As I said, there were so many people to speak to, so much time for conversations, so many stories and so much suffering. There were injustices dating back to people's childhoods that could never be put right. Some had seen their fathers killed before their eyes. Others had seen their grandfathers tied to the back of armoured vehicles and dragged along the ground.




These were stories I had encountered in many interviews before, but this time I was hearing them from those in the mountains. People had told me similar stories in Şırnak (Şirnex) and Diyarbakır, in interviews with the Peace Mothers and in conversations with the children of murdered businesspeople.




I once again saw the Kurdish question in its entirety: how some people chose to go to the mountains, others pursued politics, and still others became Peace Mothers. Yet the rights violations they had experienced, and the forms of organisation and armed struggle that emerged from those violations, were closely connected and rooted in remarkably similar experiences. Certain questions need to be answered from the very beginning: Why did things reach this point? Why did these people go to the mountains? Why did they choose to fight, and why were they left feeling they had no other choice? I realised once again that this aspect of the issue needs to be explained much more clearly in Turkey.




There are people who have not seen their mothers, people who lost their fathers at a very young age. I was reminded once again how valuable it is to give these people a voice and make their stories heard.




When I went there 13 years ago, I already believed that peace was necessary. But now I have come to believe that we have reached a point where there is no alternative to peace. This is not a security issue, either for the people there or for those of us living in Turkey. It is a humanitarian issue, and resolving it requires a collective effort.




At a time when pressure on the media is increasing through various means, Ruşen Çakır from Medyascope visited Qandil before you, followed by İrfan Aktan from Spot Press Cooperative. You and your colleagues received both positive and negative criticism. However, the criticism directed at you differed from theirs in its sexist language. What do you think about this?




Just as Turkey has experienced ideological deterioration in many areas, there has also been a deterioration in attitudes towards women, journalism and freedom of expression.




Despite the advances of our time, women's presence in professional life and journalism has not progressed in a way that reflects the spirit of the age. If a society or a country is experiencing decay or collapse, it affects every area of life. 




To be perfectly clear, I don't let any of those criticisms bother me. If I did, I would have to become hesitant not only about going to Qandil but also about supporting peace and speaking out in favour of it. Almost everything I write attracts similar insults. I don't attach importance to them.




The reason is this: We are living in a period when the country has lost many of its rights in different areas, and humanity itself has suffered serious losses on many fronts. I am among those who believe that this peace is not only a gain for Kurds but also an opportunity for the country as a whole. I believe that everyone, collectively, from nationalists and secular nationalists to leftists, opposition supporters and those who support the regime, must embrace this process in one way or another. I believe it has now become a matter of vital importance.




If this peace process succeeds, it will create breathing space in the country and open a path towards the democracy that everyone says they want. That is why I defend peace openly and loudly, knowing full well the risks involved. Yes, that brings insults, but they don't matter.




The Kurdish Freedom Movement has been producing women leaders since 1993, and you met one of them, Besê Hozat, Co-Chair of the KCK Executive Council, in Qandil. How did you feel about this encounter as a woman?




That was actually something I kept thinking about throughout the journey and when we finally met. There are only two years between Besê Hozat and me. She is two years older than I am. We are two women who have come face to face from very different walks of life, with very different experiences and ways of existing in the world. Of course, as a woman, it is very difficult to encounter another woman in such a powerful position, with such a commanding presence, and not be affected by it. At the same time, journalism requires you to remain impartial and composed. But I inevitably found myself wondering what kind of choices she had made and how she had reached that position.




Ultimately, Kurdish society also has feudal structures. She is a woman who has reached a senior position by struggling against those structures, including within the organisation itself. Naturally, she is someone you cannot help but admire in that respect, and whose words you listen to with a sense of admiration.




Initially, I had the impression that she had a very stern personality, based on what I had seen of her in the media. So I was concerned about what our meeting would be like and how I would conduct an interview with someone who appeared so stern. But that was not my experience when we met. I did not find her nearly as stern as I had imagined. I do agree, however, that she becomes more forceful and uses stronger language when discussing political issues. In ordinary conversation, she was not like that.




The terrain there is difficult. I am a city person, and there were places where I could not walk as easily as they could. She held my hand and helped me. For me, moments like those made the encounter historic, not only professionally but also on a personal, human level.




Besê Hozat, Co-Chair of the KCK Executive Council, has criticised both the opposition and left-wing socialist circles. What role should women from different ideological backgrounds, who will come together at the ‘We Stand Side by Side, We Talk About the Future’ conference at the end of the month, play in this process? Where do women as a whole stand in it?




There was something Besê Hozat said during our interview: ‘How are we supposed to return to Turkey? When there is no breathing space, when women's freedom faces such serious problems, when a woman is murdered every day, when freedom of expression is so restricted and nobody feels safe in the country, how are we, as guerrillas, supposed to return and live there?’ For that to become possible, the country needs to democratise. At the very least, steps towards democratisation must begin so that the guerrillas can return to Turkey.




That is also the fundamental reason why the Women Side by Side group has come together and begun working collectively. We want to explore what ideas we can put forward and what work we can undertake to make this country more democratic. Yes, our primary concern is peace, but there are other issues connected to peace: women's freedom, democratisation, the struggle to make ends meet, economic slavery and children being made to work in Vocational Training Centres (MESEM). There are many issues that fall under the broader crisis of democracy. As women, we are trying to determine what we can do to make the country more democratic.




Our first step will be a two-day conference in Ankara on 31 October and 1 November. Women from different backgrounds, political perspectives and professions will come together to discuss peace and the many issues connected to it. These include racism, tolerance towards one another, coexistence and cultural deterioration. This will be our first collective initiative. Afterwards, we intend to continue through forums, meetings and perhaps fieldwork.




To return to Besê Hozat's words, as she explained in the interview, we have come together because we are all prepared to take responsibility and do whatever we can to make this country a more liveable place.




Finally, what motivated you to become one of the organisers behind the Women Side by Side initiative?




I have positioned myself ideologically as someone who seeks to protect Kurdish gains in this peace process. But beyond that, I agreed to join the organising group because, as I said, I believe this peace process is not simply about gains for Kurds or what Kurds stand to achieve. It is a matter of vital importance for Turkish society as a whole. I accepted because I believe every one of us must take responsibility.




We need to do something so that others will follow and our numbers will grow. Perhaps there are people I can encourage or whose attention I can attract. They might then begin to take an interest in the issue, and the number of people prepared to defend peace and take action for it could increase.




That is how I approach all the work I do in this field. At a time when freedom of expression is so severely restricted, journalism has become so uniform, and opposition journalism can only be practised within certain boundaries, it would be a tremendous achievement for me if I could show younger colleagues a way forward or give them courage.




At the same time, as I said, I believe that if we all contribute to this peace and work towards making it a reality, we will all benefit. The section of society we refer to as the Turkish left is distancing itself from this peace process. The Republican People's Party (CHP) and the circles we call the New Party are also keeping their distance. Yet the gains that emerge from this process could become gains shared by everyone.




There are very few areas left in Turkey where people can effectively struggle for change. But I believe that struggling for this peace process could open up breathing space once again. That is why I gladly accepted the invitation to join the organising group.




We need to make an appeal to all the peoples of Turkey. Your ethnicity, colour or language does not matter. What matters is recognising how closely connected these issues are and what achieving peace could make possible. We need to recognise that the mentality which persecuted Kurds yesterday is the same mentality persecuting İmamoğlu and his team today, and that the mentality which seized Kurdish municipalities in the past is the same one responsible for the problems we face today.




That is why people need to see the struggle for peace as a struggle for democracy. I want to invite everyone to struggle together, so that they can see this process not as sitting down at the negotiating table with a regime to bargain, but as an opportunity to secure meaningful gains.




Whether young or old, it does not matter who you are. For all of us, for our children and, more importantly, for future generations, we must embrace this process with determination, raise our voices and make ourselves heard.

title: Kurdish and Arab guerrillas pay tribute to commander Bêrîtan, a symbol of freedom for all women
content:
Bêrîtan (Gülnaz Karataş), one of the pioneering commanders of the women’s freedom struggle, was commemorated by Kurdish and Arab women guerrillas on the anniversary of her martyrdom. Drawing attention to Bêrîtan’s spiritual, military, and ideological role, the women guerrillas emphasized that her resistance occupies a historic place in the women’s freedom struggle.




The guerrillas stated that Bêrîtan’s path of resistance has shown all women in the Middle East the way to freedom, adding that her struggle continues to serve as a source of willpower, strength, and inspiration for women today.




Commander Bêrîtan is a symbol of resistance and freedom for all women




Guerrilla Bişenk Brûsk drew attention to the historical impact of Bêrîtan’s actions, stating that her resistance paved the way for the development of women’s military organization.







 







Guerrilla Brûsk said: “Martyr Bêrîtan represents willpower, strength, and morale for us. She was a woman who turned toward her own essence and refused to surrender to the enemy in the face of oppression and hardship. Following her sacrificial act, a women’s military organization developed. She showed us the way to understand both our own reality and the reality of the enemy.”




Bişenk Brûsk also stated that Bêrîtan’s modest and self-sacrificing character continues to be a source of energy and freedom for all her comrades.




Commander Bêrîtan, an inspiration for Arab women




Guerrilla Asya Amed, who is of Arab origin, stated that Bêrîtan’s stance transcended national boundaries and had also become a source of inspiration for Arab women.







 







Recalling how deeply she was moved when she watched a film about Bêrîtan’s life for the first time, Asya Amed said that Bêrîtan’s courage gives women hope and confidence.




Guerrilla Amed said: “When I watched the film about martyr Bêrîtan for the first time, I was deeply moved. She is a symbol of freedom not only for Kurdish women, but for all women. Her courage gives us hope and confidence. Her fearless stance shows that women can stand against obstacles under any circumstances.”




Asya Amed stated that, as an Arab guerrilla, she had pledged to uphold and follow Bêrîtan’s path of resistance and philosophy to the very end.

title: Рикардо Флорес Магон - Революция
content:
Автор

: Рикардо Флорес Магон

Название

: Революция

Дата

: 19 ноября 1910

Источник

: Regeneración




 Вот-вот упадёт вполне созревший плод внутреннего мятежа; плод горький для всех, кто возгордился положением, которое приносит почести, богатства и награды тем, кто основывает свои наслаждения на страдании и рабстве человечества; но плод сладкий и отрадный для всех, кто так или иначе ощутил на своём достоинстве копыта тех зверей, которые в одну ночь, длившуюся тридцать четыре года, крали, насиловали, убивали, обманывали, предавали, скрывая свои преступления под покровом закона и уклоняясь от кары под сенью официальной власти. 




 Кто боится Революции? Те же самые, кто её вызвал; те, кто своим гнётом или своей эксплуатацией народных масс довёл до того, что отчаяние овладело жертвами их подлостей; те, кто несправедливостью и грабежом возмутил совесть и заставил бледнеть от негодования честных людей земли. 




 Революция вот-вот разразится. Мы, столько лет следившие за всеми событиями общественной и политической жизни мексиканского народа, не можем обманываться. Симптомы грозного катаклизма не оставляют места сомнению в том, что нечто вот-вот возникнет и нечто вот-вот рухнет, что нечто воспрянет и нечто вот-вот падёт. Наконец, после тридцати четырёх лет позора, поднимет голову мексиканский народ, и наконец, после этой долгой ночи, обратится в развалины чёрное здание, чья тяжесть нас душила. 




 Сейчас уместно снова сказать то, что мы говорили так часто: нужно сделать так, чтобы это движение, вызванное отчаянием, не стало слепым движением того, кто делает усилие, чтобы сбросить с себя вес огромной ноши, – движением, в котором инстинкт почти полностью господствует над разумом. Мы, либертарии, должны позаботиться о том, чтобы это движение приняло направление, которое указывает Наука. Если этого не сделать, поднимающаяся Революция послужит лишь тому, чтобы заменить одного Президента другим Президентом, или, что то же самое, одного хозяина другим хозяином. Мы должны помнить, что нужно, чтобы у народа был хлеб, было жильё, была земля для обработки; мы должны помнить, что никакое Правительство, сколь бы честным оно ни было, не может декретировать отмену нищеты. Именно сам народ, именно голодные, именно обездоленные должны отменить нищету, в первую очередь вступив во владение землёй, которая по естественному праву не может быть прибрана к рукам несколькими, но является собственностью всякого человеческого существа. Невозможно предсказать, до какого предела дойдёт дело восстановления прав в грядущей Революции; но если мы, борцы доброй воли, несём намерение продвинуться по этому пути как можно дальше; если, берясь за винчестер, мы идём решительно не к возвышению очередного хозяина, но к восстановлению прав пролетариата; если мы несём на поле вооружённой борьбы стремление завоевать экономическую свободу, которая есть основа всех свобод, которая есть условие, без которого нет никакой свободы; если мы несём это намерение, мы направим грядущее народное движение по пути, достойному этой эпохи; но если из желания легко победить; если из стремления поскорее закончить борьбу мы уберём из наших устремлений тот радикализм, который делает их несовместимыми с устремлениями чисто буржуазных и консервативных партий, тогда мы совершим дело разбойников и убийц, ибо пролитая кровь послужит лишь тому, чтобы придать больше силы буржуазии, то есть касте, владеющей богатством, которая после победы снова наденет цепь на пролетариат, чьей кровью, чьей жертвой, чьим мученичеством она завоевала власть. 




 Итак, необходимо, пролетарии; необходимо, обездоленные, чтобы вы не обманывались. Консервативные и буржуазные партии говорят вам о свободе, о справедливости, о законе, о честном правительстве и говорят вам, что, если народ сменит людей, стоящих у Власти, на других, у вас будет свобода, будет справедливость, будет закон, будет честное правительство. Не давайте себя обмануть. Вам нужно, чтобы вам обеспечили довольство ваших семей и хлеб насущный; довольство семей не сможет дать вам никакое Правительство. Это вы сами должны завоевать эти блага, с самого начала вступив во владение землёй, которая есть первоисточник богатства, а землю не сможет дать вам никакое Правительство, – поймите это хорошо! – потому что закон защищает 

право

 тех, кто удерживает богатство; вы должны взять её сами, вопреки закону, вопреки Правительству, вопреки мнимому праву собственности; вы должны взять её во имя естественной справедливости, во имя права, которое имеет всякое человеческое существо – жить и развивать своё тело и свой разум. 




 Когда вы будете владеть землёй, у вас будет свобода, у вас будет справедливость, потому что свобода и справедливость не декретируются: они суть результат экономической независимости, то есть способности человека жить, не завися от хозяина, то есть пользоваться для себя и для своей семьи полным продуктом своего труда. 




 Итак, берите землю. Закон говорит, чтобы вы не брали, что она – частная собственность; но закон, который так говорит, был написан теми, кто держит вас в рабстве, и он настолько не отвечает общей потребности, что нуждается в поддержке силы. Если бы закон был результатом согласия всех, он не нуждался бы в поддержке полицейского, тюремщика, судьи, палача, солдата и чиновника. Закон был вам навязан, и на произвольные навязанные установления, опирающиеся на силу, мы, достойные люди, должны отвечать нашим бунтом.

author: Unknown
title: Duvara tutturulmak ya da duvarın içinde kalmak
content:
Bir bedene yer açmak ile onu bir mekana yerleştirmek aynı şey midir? Görünür olmak, hareket edebilmek anlamına gelir mi? Dilan Cudi Saruhan’ın 

Beden

 adlı yerleştirmesiyle Maurizio Cattelan’ın 

A Perfect Day

’i, bu soruları duvarın önünde yeniden kurar. Birinde canlı beden dışarıdan sabitlenir; diğerinde beden imgesi, kendisini kuşatan yüzeyle aynı maddede oluşur. Duvar her iki yapıtta da varlığın yerini belirler. Fakat o yerin içinde nasıl kalındığı değişir.




Şeritlerin merkezde yoğunlaşıp çevreye yayılması, iki çalışma arasında çarpıcı bir görsel yakınlık yaratır. Bu benzerlik, doğrudan etkilenmenin kanıtı değildir. Karşılaştırmayı verimli kılan, benzer düzenlerin farklı toplumsal deneyimler içinde ürettiği ayrımdır: bedenin hareketini durdurmak ile sınırı bedenin içine yerleştirmek arasındaki ayrım.




Saruhan’ın figürü cenin formunda kendi üzerine kapanmıştır. Başı gövdesine yaklaşır, uzuvları merkezde toplanır; beden, dışarıya açılmak yerine kendi içine çekilir. Bu duruşu yalnızca sıkışmanın sonucu saymak, figürün kendini koruma hareketini gözden kaçırır. Ancak korunmanın daralarak mümkün oluşu da başlı başına bir sorudur. Beden burada hem sığınak hem sığınılandır.




Kuşatan ile kuşatılan




Beden’de oluklu karton şeritler merkezde düğümlenerek hacim kazanır, kenarlarda uzayıp seyrelir. Figürün çevresini izlerken bir noktadan sonra bedeni mi, onu içine alan dokuyu mu gördüğümüz belirsizleşir. Çünkü kuşatan ile kuşatılan aynı maddeden yapılmıştır. Karton, figürün çevresindeki engel olduğu kadar onun varlık koşuludur. Sınırı kaldırdığımızda altında özgürleşmeyi bekleyen, önceden tamamlanmış bir beden bulacağımızdan emin olamayız.




Cenin formu bu maddesel ortaklığı daha da yoğunlaştırır. Başın eğilmesi, gövdenin kıvrılması ve uzuvların içe çekilmesi, bedeni kendi sınırları içinde yeniden toplar. Anne rahmini çağrıştıran bu biçimde korunma ile kuşatılma birbirine yaklaşır. Yine de burada güvenli bir başlangıca dönüşten söz etmek güçtür. Figür, onu taşıyan dokunun içinde saklanırken aynı dokunun baskısını da taşır. Bir sığınağın ne zaman kapatılma mekânına dönüştüğünü, formun içinden sorar.




Cattelan’ın 1999 tarihli 

A Perfect Day

’inde ise galerici Massimo De Carlo, yapışkan bantlarla kendi galerisinin duvarına sabitlenmiştir. Yüzü, giysisi ve ayakkabıları, kuşatmanın içindeki kişinin kimliğini görünür tutar. Düşey gövde ayakta durma hâlini anımsatır; fakat ayaklar yere değmez. Bedenin ağırlığını taşıma işi zeminden bantlara aktarılmıştır. Başın yana düşüşü, bu duruşun kişinin kendi dengesiyle sürdürülemediğini açığa çıkarır (MASSIMODECARLO, 1999; Phillips, t.y.).










Maurizio Cattelan, A Perfect Day, 1999. Massimo De Carlo’nun yapışkan bantlarla galeri duvarına sabitlendiği eylemin fotoğrafik belgesi. Görsel kaynağı: Phillips, yapıt kaydı, lot 23.










Duruşun izleyicide bıraktığı iz




Cattelan’ın bedeni dışarıdan tutulur; Saruhan’ın bedeni kendi üzerine kapanır. Birinde düşeyliğin dayanağı alınmış, diğerinde bedenin kapladığı alan daralmıştır. Bu ayrım, bakışın yönünü de değiştirir. De Carlo’nun açıkta kalan yüzü bizi belirli bir kişiye götürürken Saruhan’ın yüzü dokunun içinde geri çekilir. Karşılaştığımız, portresinden tanıyabileceğimiz bir kişi kadar, duruşunu kendi bedenimizde yoklayabileceğimiz bir varlık hâlidir.




Görmek, burada bedenden bağımsız bir etkinlik değildir. Merleau-Ponty’nin bedensel algı yaklaşımıyla düşünüldüğünde, izleyici gördüğü duruşu kendi hareket olanakları içinden kavrar (Merleau-Ponty, 2012). Cattelan’ın karşısında kendi ayaklarının yere bastığını fark edebilir; Saruhan’ın figürüne bakarken dizlerini kendine çekmeyi, başını eğmeyi, omuzlarını daraltmayı hatırlayabilir. Cenin formunun tanıdıklığı, bu yakınlığı güçlendirir. Bununla birlikte tanıdıklık, bütün izleyicilerin aynı duyguyu yaşayacağı anlamına gelmez.




Saruhan’ın kapanan bedeninde özdeşlik, yüz benzerliğinden önce bir korunma jesti üzerinden kurulabilir. Kendi kırılganlığımızı o kıvrımın içinde düşünürüz. Fakat “Ben de böyle kıvrılabilirim” demek ile “Ben de aynı kapatılmayı yaşadım” demek arasında aşılması kolay olmayan bir mesafe vardır. Yakınlık, başkasının tarihini kendimize mal etme hakkı vermez. Bakışın sorumluluğu, bu mesafeyi koruyarak yaklaşabilmektir.










Görsel 3. Dilan Cudi Saruhan, Beden, 2026. Oluklu karton ve sünger. 










Yandan bakışta figür duvardan öne çıkar; karşıdan bakışta dokunun içine çekilir. Bakış yer değiştirdikçe beden de görünürlük kazanır ya da kaybolmaya yaklaşır. Duvarın içinde kalmak, burada yalnızca bir tema değil, görmenin koşuludur. Bu okuma, yapıtın farklı açılardan çekilmiş fotoğraflarına dayanmaktadır.




Sınırın bedenin içine yerleşmesi




Cattelan’da sergilenen kişinin galerici olması rastlantısal değildir. Sanatçının görünürlüğünü sağlayan aracı, bu kez sanatçının belirlediği yerde görünür olur. Sanat alanındaki iktidar ilişkisi, galericinin bedeni üzerinden geçici olarak tersine çevrilir. Bourdieu’nün kültürel üretim alanı yaklaşımı, bu jesti sanatçı ile galerici arasındaki karşılıklı bağımlılık içinde düşünmeye imkân verir (Bourdieu, 1993). Eylemin fotoğrafının edisyonlu yapıt olarak dolaşıma girmesi ise ironinin sanat piyasasının içinde işlemeyi sürdürdüğünü gösterir (Artsy, t.y.).




Saruhan’ın figüründe kapanma başka bir süre taşır. Sanatçı, cezaevi sonrasında devam eden hareket ve seyahat kısıtlamalarının içerisi ile dışarısı arasındaki ayrımı belirsizleştirdiğini anlatır (Saruhan, 2026). Bu deneyim, yapıtı biyografinin resimli açıklamasına indirgemez; mekânın bedende nasıl sürdüğünü düşünmeye açar. Foucault’nun disiplin çözümlemesinin işaret ettiği gibi, sınır yalnızca dışarıdan engellemez; davranışın ve duruşun içine de yerleşebilir (Foucault, 1995). Cenin formunda içe kapanmış figür, bu bakımdan, duvarın önündeki bir bedenden fazlasını düşündürür: duvarı içinde taşımaya başlayan bir bedeni.




Kartonun ambalaj olarak taşıma ve koruma işlevi de bu okumaya katılır. Korunmaya ihtiyaç duyan form, kendisi de kırılgan bir maddeden oluşmuştur. Onu dışarıdan sarıp sağlamlaştıran güvenli bir kabuk yoktur. Koruyucu ile korunanın ortak kırılganlığı vardır. Şeritlerin çevreye dağılması bu kapalılığı bütünüyle mühürlemez; fakat açıklığı hemen özgürlük diye adlandırmak da mümkün değildir. Kenarlarda çözülme sürerken merkezde beden hâlâ kendi üzerine kapanmaktadır.




Cenin imgesini yalnızca yeniden doğuşun vaadi olarak okumak, yapıtın gerilimini erkenden yatıştırır. Buradaki kapanış, henüz açılmamış bir hayat kadar, açılmak için yeterli yer bulamayan bir varlığı da düşündürür. Bedenin geleceğini bizim yerimize tamamlayan bir umut anlatısına ihtiyaç yoktur. Figür seçilebilir durumdadır; çevresine karışmış, fakat silinmemiştir. Varlığını sürdürmesi, kuşatmanın tamamlanamadığı yeri gösterir.




İki yapıtın karşılaşması böylece benzerlikten ayrılığa açılır. Cattelan’da bantların kaldırılmasıyla duvardan ayrılabilecek canlı bir kişi vardır. Saruhan’da kuşatmayı bedenden ayırmak, bedenin kendisini de çözebilir. Birinde hareket askıya alınır; diğerinde sınır, varlığın dokusuna karışır. İzleyici için soru, kendisini hangi bedene daha yakın hissettiğinden önce, o bedenin hareket edemediği yerde kendisinin nasıl hareket edebildiğidir. Görünürlük özgürlük değildir. Bir bedene yer açmak, onu seyredilebilir kılmaktan fazlasını ister.




Güncel Not: Dilan Cudi Saruhan’ın 

Bir İhtimal Gökyüzü

 başlıklı kişisel sergisi, 22 Eylül–21 Kasım 2026 tarihleri arasında Depo / Tütün Deposu’nda izlenebilir. Cezaevi öncesinde, cezaevinde ve sonrasında üretilen işleri bir araya getiren sergi, bedenin mekânla ilişkisine ve kısıtlı koşullarda süren yaratım olanaklarına odaklanıyor. Sergi metni Günseli Baki’ye; küratöryel çalışma Bahar Saruhan, Delal Eken, Rozelin Akgün ve Y. Cemre Gürbüz’e ait.

title: All power to the people is something we build
content:
General Strike U.S. describes a phase where a movement has built something beyond capitalism, is ready to withdraw, is ready to sustain that withdrawal and has material power behind it. We don't disappear after disruption, the speaker says. We govern what we build, a dual and contending power becoming real power. All power to the people is something actually being built and committed to.

author: radical.guide
title: Power is the capacity to act
content:
General Strike U.S. and The Panther Party defines power as something you can hold: the ability to define a phenomenon and make it act in the desired manner. Political power backed by the ability to enact a political consequence is real, and any proclamation without that backing is words on paper. The aim is the capacity of the people to affect their material conditions directly, to protect ourselves and make the things we need.

title: Joyeux anniversaire à l'AIF
content:
Depuis 2021, au Myanmar, l'armée birmane a de nouveau repris le pouvoir par un coup d'État. 


Ancienne colonie britannique, le pays a ensuite essuyé plusieurs décennies de contrôle par l'armée birmane (Tatmadaw) avant d'avoir un début de transition démocratique en 2015. Cette séquence démocratique, loin d'être parfaite, comme tous les régimes politiques, a vite été balayée par la reprise du pouvoir par l'armée officielle du Myanmar.




 

 

 

 




Depuis 5 ans donc, des groupes armés rebelles s'organisent et font face à cette hégémonie. Ils sont nombreux et tentent de faire front commun contre la Tatmadaw et ses alliées (Chine et Russie).




La semaine dernière on célébrait l'anniversaire de l'

AIF

 (Front internationaliste antifasciste)

 qui a été fondé en octobre 2024 dans un village à la périphérie de la ville de Falam au Myanmar, alors que des internationalistes aux côtés de révolutionnaires locaux se préparaient à ce qui allait devenir la bataille de cinq mois pour libérer Falam.




 

 

 

 




L'

AIF

 combat dans l'état de 

CHIN

, dans la partie ouest du Myanmar, et aux côtés de groupes armés camarades. L'

AIF

 participe à la formation de camarades venus de différentes région du pays, mais aussi à des internationalistes venus du monde entier.




En unissant nos luttes, nous renforçons le front toujours plus large contre le fascisme. 

 


La lutte au Myanmar s'inscrit dans une révolution plus globale des peuples pour leur autodétermination. 


Et ce combat est plus que présent au cœur de l'internationalisme, emplis d'enjeux économiques et de jeux d'alliances notamment avec la chine : vente d'armes, nouvelles routes et corridor économiques, Etc.

author: Unknown
title: Liberté pour Jülide, Non à son extradition !
content:
Communiqué du comité de soutien de Tours pour Yülide Yacizi




Depuis le 4 août, Jülide Yazıcı, notre camarade communiste, militante, autrice pour la revue turque Teori ve Politika et réfugiée politique en France depuis 10 ans, est détenue en Albanie à la suite d'une demande d'extradition émise par les autorités turques par le biais d'une utilisation abusive des notices rouges d'

INTERPOL

.




Depuis plus de dix ans, Jülide milite pour des causes justes en Turquie et en Europe. 


En France, et plus précisément à Tours, Jülide participe à différents cadres militants : le collectif Solidarité Palestine 37, les ateliers populaires anti-impérialiste et l'Union pour la Reconstruction Communiste.


En Turquie, Jülide fait l'objet de poursuites dans un contexte de répression du mouvement kurde et de ses soutiens. Les faits qui lui sont reprochés sont qualifiés de «

 

soutien logistique

 

» au 

PKK

 par les autorités turques, qui les inscrivent dans le cadre de la lutte antiterroriste. Nous dénonçons le recours routinier à cette qualification pour criminaliser les engagements politiques et réprimer les solidarités avec le peuple kurde. Nous exprimons notre entière solidarité avec Jülide.





Après deux mois d'incertitude, la décision en première instance a été prise ce mercredi 21 octobre : l'Albanie acte l'extradition de Jülide vers la Turquie. Cette décision de première instance n'est pas définitive dans la mesure où Jülide va faire appel, faire valoir ses droits les plus fondamentaux. Néanmoins, cette décision profondément politique a été prise dans un contexte où le juge prétendait refuser toute considération politique. Ce dernier arguant à l'avocat de Jülide que son argumentaire basé sur le droit d'asile européen n'était pas à appliquer en Albanie, État qui prétend adhérer à l'Union Européenne, État signataire de la convention de Genève de 1951 sur le droit d'asile. 


Malgré ces dispositions juridiques, la justice albanaise a acté, en première instance, l'extradition de notre camarade. 


Nous ne pouvons pas accepter les faits tels qu'ils nous sont présentés. Invoquant son refus de traiter politiquement l'affaire, le juge a pourtant émis une décision profondément politique : il a admis lui-même «

 

s'en remettre au ministère de la justice albanais

 

» qui, ici, n'est que le porte parole de la volonté de l'État turc, et ce, au mépris du droit européen auquel l'Albanie prétend adhérer. 





La France, dans ce contexte, joue un rôle majeur, et jusqu'ici, insuffisant. Quand le juge et le ministère de la justice albanais reçoivent des pressions de l'État turc, la France se contente du minimum : la protection consulaire, c'est-à-dire rendre visite à Jülide en prison et être présent lors des séances devant le juge. Or, la France est le pays qui a accordé le statut de réfugiée à Jülide, et, par la même, lui a fourni les documents nécessaires pour voyager. Le statut de réfugiée politique de Jülide oblige la France. Il apparaît aberrant que l'État français accorde aux réfugiés les documents nécessaires pour voyager hors de l'Union européenne sans leur garantir sa protection

 

!





À l'heure où le pouvoir autoritaire d'Erdoğan fait clairement pression sur la justice albanaise pour qu'elle aille dans son sens, nous, militants progressistes en France, appelons notre État à assumer le rôle qu'il a choisi de porter en accordant le statut de réfugiée à Jülide. Nous continuerons ainsi la lutte afin d'intensifier le rapport de force, jusqu'à ce que l'État français assume véritablement son rôle. Actuellement, une personne bénéficiant du statut de réfugiée politique, et donc de la protection de l'état français, en procédure de naturalisation, est détenue illégitimement en Albanie. 





Notre camarade n'est pas seule, nous continuerons de nous mobiliser, partout, jusqu'à sa libération. Nous appelons les autorités françaises a assurer la protection qui lui est due, à agir diplomatiquement, politiquement, pour permettre la libération de Jülide et enrayer ce simulacre de procédure judiciaire initié par l'État turc. 


Nous lutterons et nous obtiendrons sa libération

 

!




Liberté pour Jülide, Non à son extradition

 

!

 

 

 

 

 

 

 Article d'origine sur 

La Gabarre

author: Unknown
title: Ephéméride des luttes : 25 octobre
content:
L'éphéméride des luttes du 25 octobre sert à ne pas oublier nos camarades, les luttes qui ont été menées, parce que celles qui vivent aujourd'hui sont aussi faites de la même matière, de celle qui pousse à la révolte.




1806 :

 Naissance à Bayreuth en Bavière de Max Stirner, théoricien de l'individualisme anarchiste.




1878 :

 En Espagne, l'anarchiste Juan Oliva Moncasi tente d'abattre le roi d'Espagne Alphonse XII.




1884 :

 A Paris, parution du journal '

Terre et Liberté

'.




 

 

 

 




1920 :

 Dans la prison de Brixton en Angleterre, l'Irlandais du Nord Terence MacSwiney meurt au terme de 74 jours de grève de la faim.




1928 :

 A Montevideo (Uruguay), "

les anarchistes catalans, Jaime Tadeo Peña, Agustin Garcia Capdevilla, Pedro Boadas Rivas et des argentins Antonio et Vicente Moretti braquent le bureau de change Messina. Ils s'emparent d'un butin de 4 000 pesos mais dans la violence de l'attaque tuent trois personnes dont le directeur de l'agence, un employé et un chauffeur de taxi. La fusillade nourrie blesse également trois autres personnes et mobilise alors la police uruguayenne sur la piste des anarchistes qui seront arrêtés le 9 novembre

".




Repris de l'éphéméride anarchiste (lien plus bas)




1956 :

 A Budapest, on est encore dans la révolution et de grandes émeutes sont en cours contre l'entrée des chars soviétiques dans la ville.




1977 :

 - En Allemagne, Irmgard Moeller, la seule survivante des quatre prisonnier-e-s de la RAF en prison à Stammheim, est de nouveau capable de parler. Elle dit avoir été éveillée jusqu'à tard dans la nuit, avoir entendu deux coups de feu puis s'être évanouie et avoir été traînée en-dehors de sa cellule, où elle s'est réveillée couverte de sang. Elle écarte toute hypothèse de suicide.




 

 

 

 

 A Rome, trois attentats sont commis contre des concessionnaires automobiles allemands.


Par ailleurs, deux molotov sont lancés sur un magasin Volkswagen en réaction à la mort de plusieurs membres de la Fraction Armée Rouge dans les prisons allemandes quelques jours plus tôt.

 A Turin, les Brigades Rouges tirent six coups de feu dans les jambes du conseiller de la Démocratie Chrétienne (DC, le parti au pouvoir depuis l'après-guerre) Antonio Cocozzello.

 A Trento, une charge de dynamite explose contre un concessionnaire Volkswagen et deux cocktails molotov sont lancés dans le jardin du directeur de l'entreprise allemande Brinkmann.

 A Potenza, la voiture du maire et la maison d'un conseiller régional (tous les deux appartenant à la DC) sont attaquées au molotov.




2016 :

 A Limoges, une voiture de police 

est incendiée

 à deux ans de la mort de Rémi Fraisse et en soutien aux proches d'Adama Traoré.




Voir aussi 

l'éphéméride anarchiste

 du 25 octobre.
