title: Using it/its as pronouns is the reclamation of a slur.
content:
fyshiebusiness

:

oupydogcity

:

lavenderfoxboy-deactivated20240

:

i wish there was more it/its positivity that wasn’t just “hell yeah look at you go funky little goblins/otherwordly beings/freaks/objects”

this is really important actually i wanted to link one of my fav tweets on this subject :>

This is just weird to me because when I hear it/it’s in reference to sapient beings I think of people being treated as objects. People being dehumanized. The past uses of the word for slaves and prisoners who were treated as subhuman.

I’m pretty sure there are very few people who think about it referring to rocks instead of mountains in that context. 

People who use it/it’s are allowed to choose that for themselves but I think they should always remember that the word in association with humans specifically comes with baggage.




Using it/its as pronouns is the reclamation of a slur. 

And before people go police it: no, this is not a slur that only one specific demographic can reclaim. Any group that’s been unpersoned has at some point been called it. ‘It’ is the universal slur for unpersoning a person. 

As usually with the reclamation of a slur, most of the people using it/its are not particularly concerned with being appealing to the majority. They’re doing their own thing, They use the word freaks affectionately for themselves and their friends. 

So we can expect “hell yeah look at you go funky little freaks” to be the dominant form of it/its expression for quite a while, until the slur gets so fully reclaimed that people more concerned with respectability start calling themselves it/its and trying to distance themselves from the deliberate freaks and polishing what it/its can mean. OP might be an early participant in that attempt at mainstreaming it/its.

author: Amanda Audi
title: Vorcaro orquestrou venda de bens da Igreja Lagoinha e prometeu expansão de R$ 100 milhões
content:
Uma fungada forte próxima ao microfone para não restarem dúvidas sobre o nível de emoção e uma caprichada na voz embargada: “Ô, Daniel, que o senhor te dê sabedoria, te cubra, te guarde, que ele nos guie e guie você nesse momento a voz de Deus, sempre”. Outra fungada. “É no mundo todo, Dani. É no mundo todo que tá acontecendo, é muito forte, irmão”. E outra fungada. A voz chorosa mineira é do pastor André Valadão, líder da Igreja Lagoinha Global. Essa emoção toda é uma resposta a uma felicitação de aniversário que também faria você chorar.







“Deus me incomodou para uma ação junto contigo. Vou colocar 100mm de reais de doação para abrir novas igrejas”, disse, sem rodeios, ninguém menos que Daniel Vorcaro, então dono do Banco Master e de um sem número de empresas. “Queria que pensasse e orasse e depois me passasse um plano pra implementarmos”, instruiu naquele 16 de abril de 2024.



















Depois das prisões de Vorcaro em novembro de 2025 e março de 2026, quando o escândalo Master-BRB já estava em todas as manchetes, Valadão reconheceu que os dois se conhecem há décadas, mas 

frisou

 que o relacionamento dos dois se restringia à igreja e não envolvia negócios. Conversas interceptadas pela Polícia Federal (PF) no âmbito da Operação Compliance Zero, às quais a 

Agência Pública

 teve acesso, contam outra história.




Em meio a orações, viagens em jatos executivos, convites para Fórmula 1 e declarações de amor (há pelo menos 44 “eu te amo”), os diálogos entre o banqueiro e o pastor revelam uma intrincada rede de influência e a proteção de Vorcaro em círculos de poder evangélicos. Os diálogos entre “Dede” e “Dan Dan”, ou “Dani”, como se chamavam mostram que a relação passava longe de se restringir a doações, mas envolvia também conselhos sobre a gestão dos ativos da Igreja Lagoinha e formas inteligentes de aproveitar o potencial de operações financeiras e imobiliárias na própria rede de igrejas, com especial preocupação em continuar evitando impostos no ecossistema que, segundo Valadão, deve movimentar R$ 1 bilhão até 2030.




As mensagens do WhatsApp do ex-banqueiro mostram uma intensa troca de aconselhamento – espiritual, no caso de Valadão, e financeiro, do lado de Vorcaro. Com muitas citações a Deus e a Jesus, eles faziam articulações com lideranças da direita para viabilizar negócios de interesse comum e contornar crises de imagem – como no 

episódio

 em que Vorcaro pediu a intervenção de Valadão para falar com o deputado Nikolas Ferreira (PL-MG) após uma postagem que enfureceu o banqueiro. É a pedido de Valadão que Nikolas busca “Dani” para se desculpar e diz que nem teria falado se soubesse que o negócio era dele.



















A troca de favores tem duas vias. Em pelo menos dois episódios, Valadão pede ajudas, condicionando o atendimento a se “Deus tocasse no coração” do amigo. Apenas nos eventos de virada de ano da Lagoinha, o toque divino solicitado foi de US$ 350 mil e US$ 450 mil, em 2023 e 2024. Não há registros na mensagens se os gloriosos depósitos chegaram a abençoar as referidas celebrações.







Vende-se e aluga-se




No site vinculado à Igreja da Lagoinha, há 14 imóveis à venda em três municípios mineiros. A avaliação apresentada ao público é de R$ 38,2 milhões no conjunto de prédios comerciais e até fazendas para hospedagem com lazer. O que quem visita o catálogo da Lagoinha desconhece é que a ideia de vender os bens da rede de igrejas partiu do ex-dono do Banco Master.










“Uma das coisas que eu estou pensando é de internacionalizar os bens da Lagoinha toda, sabe? Porque o dinheiro nos EUA, o crédito é muito fácil, né, muito menos juros, né. O juros tá alto hoje, mas ainda assim é baixo. Então seria um ministério sem fins lucrativos, 

non for profit

 americano, que detém bens no mundo todo, Europa, África, Brasil, Estados Unidos também, Canadá. Tô fazendo essa mudança, sabe”, conta animadamente André Valadão, em áudio enviado a Vorcaro, que responde:  “Acho excelente ideia”.







 “Como você me aconselhou, eu coloquei vários bens nossos à venda”, continua o pastor. “Tem um pessoal que me procurou também pra gente, tipo, criar um fundo com a quantidade de bens que a gente tem da Lagoinha, sabe? Mas eu acho que, como a maioria deles a gente nem paga imposto, acho que fazer um fundo, coisa assim, podia acabar sendo pior, né? Não sei o que você me aconselha a respeito”, indaga. “Fundo não é vantagem pra você. Legal é fazer base USA e virar global mesmo”, recomenda o empresário, enquanto falam do interesse de acionar advogados “de fora”.







A imunidade tributária das igrejas no Brasil bebe na fonte da Inglaterra moderna, que visava proteger os templos dado seu trabalho de acolhimento de doentes e desempregados, como explica o jurista Francisco Tenório, autor do livro “Direito das Igrejas”: “No Brasil, o artigo 150, inciso VI alínea b, prevê que é proibido instituir imposto sobre ‘entidades religiosas e templos de qualquer culto, inclusive suas organizações assistenciais e beneficentes’. […] Basta a igreja ter um CNPJ regular, e a fiscalização sobre as igrejas, na prática, é inexistente. Além do que, esse benefício constitucional não exige nenhuma contrapartida da igreja, como deveria ser devido a história de origem da imunidade como contrapartida pelo labor social.”




A ideia do fundo referente aos bens da Lagoinha continuou sendo uma grande questão nas conversas entre Valadão e Vorcaro. O pastor diz ao amigo que está levantando quanto as igrejas de sua rede pagam de aluguel, na intenção de negociar imóveis com as próprias afiliadas. A ideia era criar um fundo imobiliário voltado para a aquisição e construção de imóveis próprios, convertendo o custo do aluguel pago pelas igrejas em amortização de patrimônio.




“Acho que deve ser um valor relevante e certo todo mês, às vezes dá pra acessar possibilidade de compra de imóveis e as igrejas pagarem direto, mas em compra do imóvel semelhante ao invés de aluguel”, disse Valadão. “O valor que pagamos talvez conseguiríamos de alguma formar um fundo para até construir prédio próprio e alugar para as igrejas. Ou comprar algo semelhante… ?” Vorcaro rebate que no Brasil não haveria fundo “com apetite pra isso.”



















O jurista Francisco Tenório explica que, mesmo em imóvel alugado, igrejas não pagam IPTU, por exemplo, e que bens de luxo de líderes religiosos, se ocultados em nome da igreja, seriam um caminho para a sonegação. Quanto aos fundos imobiliários envolvendo templos, o advogado desconhece planos semelhantes no Brasil, mas explica que esta seria uma forma de transformar um ativo imobiliário em capital com liquidez imediata e classifica a ideia de “escandalosa”. “Condenaria perpetuamente a membresia a ser inquilina e pagar aluguel dos templos que foram adquiridos com seus dízimos e ofertas. Moralmente essa conduta é absurda e inaceitável”, opina.










 




A igreja ter imóveis alugados gerando renda que é revertida para os fins da própria igreja não tem problema algum. Agora, criar FII com templos é outra questão. […] Seria um atestado de que a igreja deixou o conceito bíblico de comunidade de salvos, lavados e remidos pelo sangue de Jesus para se tornar uma corporação capitalista cuja finalidade é dinheiro e poder para seus ‘donos’.”




Francisco Tenório

 

jurista e autor de “Direito das Igrejas”

 










Clava Forte Bank, a fintech cristã que caiu quando Vorcaro foi preso




A inadimplência de instituições religiosas e o controle sobre sua própria rede de afiliadas fez André Valadão investir, contra a recomendação de Vorcaro, na primeira fintech cristão do país. Entre a primeira conversa entre os dois sobre o assunto e a inauguração do Clava Forte Bank se passaram menos de oito meses até a inauguração da iniciativa, em 31 de julho de 2024. A fintech se definia como “um banco para impulsionar os projetos do Reino de Deus”. O site da iniciativa ofertava serviços de contas digitais, cartões, maquininhas, financiamentos, seguros, marketplace e programas de cashback.



















Fazia tempo que Valadão tinha interesse em seguir os passos do amigo em negócios bancários e meios de pagamento. Em 2019, ele usou um culto para promover um cartão de crédito consignado com a marca “Fé”, voltado a pensionistas e aposentados. Na época, chamou o cartão “uma coisa de Deus”. Pegou tão mal que o projeto foi engavetado.




A ideia do Clava Forte Bank – o nome vem do trecho do hino nacional – foi mencionada na conversa com Vorcaro pela primeira vez em 9 de dezembro de 2023, quando Valadão convidou o amigo a patrocinar um show na virada daquele ano na Lagoinha de Orlando. “Ano que vem eu quero lançar um banco interno também da Lagoinha, principalmente para os pastores e para a igreja, não pro público diretamente primeiro”, disse em áudio.




Meses depois, em abril de 2024, o pastor pede orientação jurídica do amigo sobre um sistema para unir o sistema financeiro das igrejas do seu grupo, que estimava movimentar R$ 300 a 350 milhões internamente. Em vários momentos, Valadão diz temer “perder o foco” da igreja frente às possibilidades financeiras, ao mesmo tempo em que se mostra deslumbrado com a chance de aumentar as posses da Lagoinha. “Ano que vem vamos dobrar, se Deus quiser”, complementou. “Até 2030 fato só brasil vms passar de 1B ano. em ano de jesus.” Segundo Valadão, o negócio do banco era um negócio dele e da esposa, e “não da igreja”.



















Dias antes da inauguração do Clava Forte, em 23 de julho de 2024, ele anunciou ao amigo o “sistema ‘pay’ próprio Lagoinha Global” junto com a empresa de pagamentos Dock. O público estimado era de 2 a 4 mil clientes. Mas, em seguida, demonstra como o projeto poderia crescer: “só no ecossistema da Lagoinha hoje tem : igrejas, pastores, funcionários, livrarias, seminário (só hoje, 12 mil alunos ativos), fundação oasis filantrópica que recebe recursos federais… tipo tudo que envolve o mundo da Lagoinha pra dentro do CLAVA.”




Meses depois, Valadão pede ajuda a Vorcaro sobre pacotes de serviços para acoplar no sistema e de FIDC – tipo de investimento em renda fixa que compra dívidas de empresas que têm a receber no futuro. “Depois me explica o que precisa”, responde o ex-banqueiro. Em 17 de setembro, ele pede para falar com o amigo sobre alguns assuntos, entre eles “a fintech, que por sinal tá indo super bem e sem dúvida é algo que pode ficar grande demais”. Os dois fazem duas ligações que duram 15 minutos.




O sistema do Clava Forte Bank 

saiu do ar

 logo após a primeira prisão de Daniel Vorcaro no âmbito da operação Compliance Zero, no Aeroporto Internacional de Guarulhos (SP), enquanto se preparava para embarcar em um jato particular com destino a Dubai, em 18 novembro de 2025. Com o sistema da fintech fora do ar desde o dia 21, Valadão 

justificou

 a indisponibilidade como uma manutenção temporária para evitar ataques hackers.



















Vorcaro foi preso numa investigação a respeito de suspeita de fraudes bancárias, emissões irregulares de Certificados de Depósito Bancário (CDBs) e títulos de crédito falsos pelo Banco Master, que chegou a ser comprado pelo Banco de Brasília (BRB). Paralelamente, uma outra polêmica passou a ligar o Clava Forte Bank, Valadão e Vorcaro. Durante os trabalhos da Comissão Parlamentar Mista de Inquérito (CPMI) do INSS, o deputado federal Rogério Correia (PT-MG) apontou o ecossistema da Lagoinha e a fintech cristã como possíveis envolvidas no escândalo dos descontos indevidos nas contas de aposentados.




“Eu tenho comprovações de que tanto o Vorcaro como o Pastor [Fabiano] Zettel [cunhado de Vorcaro], André Valadão e a Clava Forte Bank também receberam recursos que vieram de pessoas aposentadas. Nós precisamos investigar isso, fazer a quebra [de sigilo], para ver se isso era dízimo ou se era lavagem de dinheiro”, sintetizou Correia.




O Congresso acabou apontando ainda a proximidade entre André Valadão e Felipe Machado Gomes, presidente de uma das associações suspeitas da fraude no INSS e já investigado no STF por organização criminosa e lavagem de dinheiro. Conhecido por sua vida de luxo, Gomes é amigo de Valadão e foi um dos patrocinadores do réveillon da Lagoinha de 2024 – o mesmo em que o pastor pediu para Vorcaro ajudar com o que Deus tocasse o seu coração.



















O sonho de US$ 20 milhões em Orlando




Em 14 de julho de 2024, Vorcaro avisa Valadão que iria fazer um bate e volta para jantar em Miami e chamou o amigo para ir junto no avião e dormir na casa dele. Os dois fazem uma breve ligação de voz. Em seguida, o pastor envia fotos de um terreno à venda em Orlando, que descreve como “inacreditável”. Ele passa uma foto de anúncio com a oferta de US$ 10,8 milhões e diz que o lugar fica “no miolo” da cidade, em uma região comparável aos bairros nobres Savassi ou Lourdes, em Belo Horizonte – os dois são mineiros.




“Dede, vamos pra cima.” O pastor diz que estaria disposto a vender um terreno que tinha na capital mineira para comprarem o terreno juntos. “Aquele valor que te falei tá comprometido”, responde o banqueiro, mencionando os R$ 100 milhões que prometeu doar à igreja, e esclarece os cálculos: “Você tem que ver como melhor usar. São 20mm usd [US$ 20 milhões]”.




“Faria a sede aqui com esses 20 com certeza. A compra e a construção”, responde Valadão. “Então vamos fazer”, resume Vorcaro. O pastor responde com 38 emojis de “aos prantos”, com um de “mãos em prece” no meio. “Se for isso que Deus colocar no seu coração, pra gente montar proposta aqui, você me fala que proposta que eu faço. Dani, você não tá entendendo”, ele continua com mais emojis “aos prantos”, antes de encaminhar mensagens do corretor do terreno e fotos feitas com inteligência artificial para simular o uso do terreno.







Dois dias depois, o ex-banqueiro tranquiliza o amigo: “Pode seguir com a aquisição. Eu tô já movimentando. Pra te mandar o recurso”. Ao que o pastor responde com um textão de gratidão sem limites e doses de “Amém Dani” e “Tô aqui Dani”.




O assunto voltou em 31 de julho. Valadão relata que, se assinar o contrato, teria que depositar US$ 200 mil [cerca de R$ 1 milhão] em cinco dias. Vorcaro não respondeu. Segue-se mais uma leva de mensagens melosas de Valadão, enfatizando que o amigo é um “escolhido de Deus” que “nada nem ninguém vai derrubar”. E continua pedindo por um telefonema: “Tô sempre à disposição com telefone na mão.” Vorcaro só respondeu quando Valadão anunciou que um processo que respondia por 

homofobia

 havia sido arquivado. “Que showwwwwww. Parabéns!!!”, disse.




Em 15 de agosto, Valadão cobra uma resposta. “Dani sobre o terreno estamos finalizando e precisamos de 200k de dólares pra amarrar a proposta … e prosseguir com 

due diligence

 de até 80 dias para ter toda liberação da prefeitura para o projeto ou não”, escreveu. Até o dia 17 de setembro, os dois trocam dados de contas e instruções, como um modelo de “

proof of funds

”, que Vorcaro se compromete a preencher com os dados de suas empresas para viabilizar a compra do terreno para a igreja do amigo. O valor indicado é de US$ 11,8 milhões, o que, considerando o sinal de US$ 200 mil, sugere um compromisso de compra de US$ 12 milhões – aproximadamente R$ 60 milhões.



















Dois meses após os últimos pontos discutidos sobre a aquisição, Daniel Vorcaro foi preso pela primeira vez, em novembro de 2025. Quase um ano depois, o 

anúncio do terreno

 na S Apopka Vineland Road, em Orlando, na Flórida, segue no ar, ainda sem dono.




O próspero caso da Lagoinha Belvedere




André Valadão e Daniel Vorcaro não discutiram aquisições apenas no exterior e nem todos os negócios discutidos deixaram de sair do papel. Em um dos contatos entre os amigos, eles discutiram sobre um imóvel em frente ao BH Shopping, em Belo Horizonte (MG). O espaço seria destinado à instalação de uma igreja ligada a Fabiano Zettel, cunhado de Vorcaro. “Segunda feira vou em BH com Zettel ver o imóvel da Jorlan, em frente o BH shopping para ser a igreja dele. Será lindo. 4 mil lugares”, escreveu Valadão. Mais tarde, a unidade seria transformada na Lagoinha Belvedere, liderada por Zettel, e na mira do Conselho de Controle de Atividades Financeiras (Coaf).
















Unidade da Lagoinha Belvedere em Belo Horizonte foi construída no espaço onde antes funcionava uma concessionária de veículos




Zettel é apontado pela Polícia Federal como um dos principais operadores financeiros de Vorcaro. De acordo com as investigações, ele intermediava pagamentos, organizava transferências e participava da estruturação de contratos que teriam sido utilizados para justificar repasses financeiros.




Conversas às quais a 

Pública

 teve acesso mostram que Zettel recebia ordens de Vorcaro para movimentar grandes quantias, além de lembrar o cunhado de despesas que iam desde IPTU a dívidas milionárias. Embora os diálogos entre os dois tratassem predominantemente de questões financeiras, as mensagens analisadas não mostram solicitações de Vorcaro para que Zettel realizasse repasses especificamente a Valadão — apesar das doações expressivas que o empresário teria feito ao líder religioso.




Em 2018, Valadão celebrou o casamento de Fabiano Zettel com Natália Vorcaro, irmã do ex-controlador do Banco Master. A relação entre os dois pastores e Vorcaro, no entanto, envolvia outros familiares e projetos, como mostra o Relatório de Informações Financeiras 140.515, do Coaf, ao qual a 

Pública

 teve acesso.
















Fabiano Zetel e a esposa, que também é irmã de Vorcaro. André Valadão e a esposa. A imagem foi encaminhada por André Valadão a Daniel Vorcaro. A troca de mensagem foi obtida pela Polícia Federal após quebra de sigilo do celular de Vorcaro




Segundo o documento, a unidade Belvedere tinha um faturamento presumido de R$ 950 mil por ano. No entanto, a igreja recebeu, entre dezembro de 2024 e dezembro de 2025, um total de R$ 57,1 milhões, em movimentações classificadas com atípicas pelo órgão regulador de finanças.




Chama a atenção que o pastor líder da Lagoinha Belvedere, Fabiano Zettel, cunhado de Daniel Vorcaro, por exemplo, tenha feito 26 operações, totalizando R$ 19,2 milhões para a unidade, fechada após a prisão de Zettel, em março deste ano, na mesma operação Compliance Zero que prendeu o ex-dono do Banco Master.




A igreja também recebeu doações da ordem de R$ 101,6 mil de Fabíola Vorcaro, ex-esposa do banqueiro, em sete operações; de R$ 120 mil, em quatro operações de Henrique Vorcaro, pai de Daniel; e outros R$ 22 mil, em 11 operações de Luiz Phillipi Machado de Moraes Mourão, ninguém menos que o “Sicário” de Vorcaro, seu braço operacional nas operações do Master, que morreu no hospital enquanto estava custodiado.




Além das movimentações envolvendo a Lagoinha Belvedere, Zettel também aparece ligado a movimentações consideradas atípicas quanto à empresa Super Empreendimentos e Participações, que já foi dirigida pelo cunhado de Vorcaro e tem movimentações imobiliárias e financeiras investigadas pela PF. Segundo o Coaf, R$ 19,693 milhões foram movimentados em operações suspeitas no mês de junho de 2022.




A 

Pública

 procurou André Valadão, Daniel Vorcaro, Fabiano Zettel e a Igreja Lagoinha para esclarecer os questionamentos apontados na reportagem. Até o momento da publicação, apenas a defesa de Vorcaro respondeu, informando que não iria comentar o assunto. Em caso de manifestação, este espaço será atualizado.



















Conexões onipresentes




Com bateria social quase ilimitada, acesso que vai de pequenos empresários a jogadores de futebol e ministros do STF, Daniel Vorcaro passou a alimentar fantasias de vários gêneros no imaginário popular do brasileiro. Mas pouca gente lembra que antes de ser preso investigado por fraude, e antes disso um rico banqueiro, Vorcaro era apresentador de um programa de música gospel na Rede Super, o Supersônica, da emissora de TV que pertence à Lagoinha – logo, ligada ao amigo André Valadão.




Em 2022, Bolsonaro visitou a Lagoinha em Orlando, onde Valadão prega. O pastor fez uma oração pelo ex-presidente. Naquele ano, a emissora havia recebido R$ 217 mil do governo federal. Ao longo do mandato do ex-presidente, a emissora 

recebeu

 R$ 756 mil pagos por campanhas de comunicação. O pastor já disse não ser bolsonarista, mas já compartilhou posicionamentos ideológicos com o ex-presidente. Valadão também tem laços estreitos com bolsonaristas expoentes, como Nikolas Ferreira e Fábio Faria, e até já foi cicerone para o blogueiro Allan dos Santos, foragido nos Estados Unidos. Já Vorcaro, já disse explicitamente apoiar a direita, como revelou a 

Pública

.




A Rede Super é um ativo da Lagoinha obtido por meio de uma parceria antiga com a família Vorcaro. O pai de Daniel, Henrique Vorcaro, frequentava os cultos de Márcio Valadão, pai de André Valadão. Segundo a 

revista piauí

, os conselhos do pastor foram tão importantes para o empresário que, ao obter sucesso com a corretagem de imóveis, passou a dar gordas doações para a igreja – que usou a verba para comprar a emissora em 1997.




Lagoinha ontem e hoje




A igreja “da parede preta” ou “que tem área VIP”. As opções de organização e a estética reformada da Igreja Batista da Lagoinha, que bebe na fonte da australiana Hillsong Church, podem fazer parecer que a organização é uma espécie de novidade que vem ganhando projeção, mas ela foi fundada em 1957, em Belo Horizonte.




A força da organização levou, ainda nos anos 1990, Ana Paula Valadão, irmã de André, a lançar a banda gospel Diante do Trono – que se tornou um sucesso de vendas e projetou a Lagoinha de uma igreja regional para uma potência nacional.





































Imagem do interior da Igreja Batista da Lagoinha. As imagens foram encaminhada por André Valadão a Daniel Vorcaro. A troca de mensagem foi obtida pela Polícia Federal após quebra de sigilo do celular de Vorcaro




A expansão para o resto do país e até unidades internacionais veio também com a adoção das paredes escuras, que buscava priorizar a visibilidade de paredes de LED e projeções de luz para conquistar um público mais jovem com a estética de espetáculo. Já a segregação de celebridades, políticos e convidados dos pastores, que geram polêmica na unidade Alphaville – onde também há estacionamentos privativos, entradas exclusivas e camarim com bufê – sempre foi negada pelos pastores.




O próprio André Valadão, aliás, diz não ser adepto de área VIP, mas de eventuais “assentos reservados, 20, 30, sei lá” para seus convidados. “Nada além do normal”.




A nova geração de Valadões e Vorcaros parece seguir o mesmo caminho da amizade que, de tempos em tempos, impulsionou os negócios ligados à Lagoinha. Stella, filha de Daniel, estuda com um filho de André. Os dois dançaram juntos a valsa na festa de 15 anos da menina, que não contou com Diante do Trono como atração musical, mas com um show exclusivo do DJ Alok.




A relevância da Lagoinha é inegável, com uma influência que chega ao Supremo Tribunal Federal: foi Fábio Faria, hoje casado com Patrícia Abravanel, filha de Silvio Santos, quem apresentou Daniel Vorcaro ao ministro Alexandre de Moraes. Além disso, a reunião que o dono do Master participou com o ministro André Mendonça também foi organizado por membros da igreja. Uma história de poder, fé e fraternidade de uma congregação que nos próximos meses completa 70 anos.

title: Construction Workers' Union, an model for independent unionism
content:
The idea of independent trade unions operating outside the established confederations has long been debated in Turkey. Criticism of existing unions has also led to the establishment of independent organisations in particular sectors.




The debate has been driven by accusations that unions fail to defend workers' rights, cooperate with employers and pay their officials high salaries. Against this backdrop, one union has attracted attention for adopting a different approach.




Founding members killed in massacres




The Construction Workers' Union (Insaat-Is) has distinguished itself through its organising efforts in a sector where trade union activity has historically been limited in Turkey. Operating in the construction industry, which has largely been neglected by trade union confederations, Insaat-Is works in a sector where working conditions make collective bargaining negotiations difficult and maintaining a stable membership has never been possible. Since its official establishment in 2014, the union has become known not only for its trade union struggles but also for its activities in other areas.




The union emerged from discussions and organising efforts prompted by a question raised during a workers' resistance at the Sapphire Tower construction site in 2010: “Why don't construction workers have a union?” The union has also attracted attention for its stance on wider social and political developments. One of its founding members, Ethem Sarısülük, was shot and killed by police in Ankara during the Gezi Resistance.




Six other founding members, Serdar Ben, Tekin Arslan, Erol Ekici, Tayfun Benol, Ismail Kızılçay and Gökmen Dalmaç, were killed in the ISIS attack on a peace rally outside Ankara Train Station on 10 October 2015. The union's history includes several significant workers' struggles in recent years, including the Emaar resistance, the Third Airport resistance and the Financial Centre protests. Insaat-Is has also drawn attention through its solidarity efforts in earthquake-affected regions, as well as statements and campaigns organised during the resistance in Kobanê and Sur.




The union's activities intensified following the Ankara Train Station Massacre. Insaat-Is continued its work with an approach that differed from conventional forms of trade union struggle.




The Construction Workers' Union organising coordinators Anıl Deniz Gider and Yunus Özgür, together with union executive Ekrem Ekşi, spoke to ANF about the union's history, its experiences of struggle and its approach to trade union organising.







 







‘We lost six comrades in Ankara, but we knew we could carry on their work’




Yunus Özgür pointed out that the idea of independent trade unionism emerged at a time when conventional trade union structures had reached their limits. He continued: “The idea of independent trade unionism emerged at a time when the traditional trade union movement in Turkey was no longer sufficient and could no longer respond to the problems and organising needs of the working class.




Why the construction sector? Following the organising efforts of figures such as İsmet Demir in the construction industry during the 1970s and 1980s, neither the Turkish revolutionary movement nor the trade union confederations undertook any significant organising work in this sector. For the confederations, construction is an extremely difficult sector to organise, and the chances of securing a collective bargaining agreement are less than one in a thousand. In other words, there are virtually no membership dues to be collected.”




Özgür explained that the founding idea behind Insaat-Is emerged during the resistance at the Sapphire construction site. He also highlighted the importance of Serdar Ben, one of the union's founding members, who was widely known as Maviş: “The process essentially began with Mustafa's resistance at the Sapphire construction site in 4th Levent. Maviş had a profound influence on both the trade union movement and the revolutionary movement in Turkey. Our comrade Serdar, in particular, pioneered a new path despite the trade union confederations.




Our union representatives who attended the 10 October rally were there not primarily to support a particular peace policy, but to stand alongside the oppressed Kurdish people. We lost six of our representatives there, although calling them representatives feels rather strange. We lost six comrades who had built this union from nothing, who had created it from the ground up and who carried all its accumulated experience.




10 October was a traumatic event for the entire revolutionary opposition and society. For us, the trauma was particularly profound because we lost six of our founding members.”




Yunus Özgür recalled that the union organised its first major resistance following the Ankara Train Station Massacre at the Emaar construction site.




He said, “The trauma continued to affect us afterwards, but we threw ourselves into the struggle without hesitation. We told ourselves, ‘We are going to carry this work forward. A banner has been left in our hands.’ The organising work that Maviş and our other comrades had begun at the first Emaar construction site had remained unfinished.




At Emaar, we both found a way to ease our grief and gained confidence in our ability to carry on the struggle. We told ourselves, ‘We lost six comrades, but we can carry their legacy forward.’ Despite all our shortcomings and weaknesses, we came to believe that we could do justice to the work they had begun.”




‘The union was built through immense sacrifices and hard work’




Anıl Deniz Gider, an organising specialist with Insaat-Is, recalled that another founding member of the union was Ethem Sarısülük, who was killed by police during the Gezi Resistance.







 







Gider said, “The establishment of the Construction Workers' Union  was never simply about setting up a table and a few chairs and organising workers within a narrow framework. From the outset, the union pursued an approach that directly addressed wider social issues. The foundations of this union were laid through immense sacrifices and tremendous effort. Ethem Sarısülük, who fought on the barricades in Ankara and lost his life during the Gezi Resistance; Duran Baysal, one of our founders who was working on the construction of a mosque in Diyarbakır (Amed) in 2014; and Hasan Oğuz, the European coordinator of the Revolutionary Construction Workers' Union (Dev Yapı-Iş), who contracted Covid-19 while working at a construction site during the pandemic and died following a heart attack, are among the symbolic figures of this struggle. We continue this struggle as a generation carrying forward the banner left to us by the comrades who made these sacrifices.”




‘The interests of the working class took priority through joint struggle’




One of the union's most significant struggles was the resistance at Istanbul's Third Airport construction site. Tens of thousands of construction workers participated in the protests, which attracted attention in Turkey and internationally. Workers also faced police detentions and arrests during the resistance.




Anıl Deniz Gider described the events: “The Third Airport construction site, which had been designated as a pilot area, was an enormous project employing between 30,000 and 40,000 workers. Around 300 to 350 workers had lost their lives in workplace killings, while companies operating under the IGA consortium were responsible for serious violations of workers' rights. On the morning of 14 September, adverse weather conditions, delays to shuttle buses and workers being transported in severely overcrowded vehicles became the final straw, triggering a mass uprising.




Union officials at the construction site were singled out as targets. Nearly 2,700 workers were detained in a single night. Helicopters and riot-control vehicles (TOMAs) were deployed during the operations, which resulted in the arrest and imprisonment of union officials. Although those imprisoned were released after approximately two and a half to three months, convictions were subsequently handed down in the cases brought against them. The resistance received extensive coverage in the Turkish and international press, bringing the exploitation of construction workers into the public spotlight.”




Gider also discussed the resistance at the Istanbul Financial Centre, which represented a different approach to trade union struggle. He explained that Insaat-Is had achieved significant gains by joining forces with the Revolutionary Construction Workers' Union, another union operating in the same sector, in a form of cooperation rarely seen among trade unions.




Gider said, “The Istanbul Financial Centre project involved a rotating workforce of more than 30,000 workers and received investment from institutions such as the Turkish Wealth Fund and Emlak Konut. Insaat-Is joined forces with Dev Yapı-Is, setting aside concerns about institutional influence and membership numbers to prioritise the interests of the working class. The two unions launched a joint campaign under a shared banner with the slogan ‘Enough Is Enough’. This united approach to struggle continued in the reconstruction efforts carried out in earthquake-affected regions following the earthquakes of 6 February.”




Anıl Deniz Gider stressed that the union rejected the prevailing model of trade unionism and continued: “We maintain an uncompromising stance against yellow unionism, bureaucratic management within trade union confederations, exorbitant salaries and excessive spending of membership dues. Given the nature of construction sites, we have adopted an approach based on direct, legitimate and militant struggle rather than allowing ourselves to become trapped in bureaucracy. We have fought for workers' rights through protests, occupations and, when necessary, radical actions such as blocking traffic on the Bosphorus Bridge.”




‘We went beyond workers’ rights to put social solidarity into practice’







 







Anıl Deniz Gider stressed that the Construction Workers' Union carried out activities extending far beyond conventional trade unionism and challenged that traditional approach. He explained that the union had organised a solidarity campaign following the Kobanê Resistance.




Gider said, “Insaat-Is did not limit its activities to defending workers' rights but also developed significant forms of solidarity across society. Through the ‘Lay a Brick’ campaign, we contributed to the construction of a health centre in Kobanê and sent a delegation to the region. During the Sur Resistance, we called on our members not to work at construction sites involved in the destruction of the area. During the pandemic, we organised food parcel distributions. This solidarity initiative later developed into a Workers' Cooperative in cooperation with local farmers.




Following the earthquakes of 6 February, the Solidarity Search and Rescue Team was formally established with the participation of construction workers, students, women and teachers. Through training programmes and practical exercises, the team began carrying out activities across Turkey.”




Ekrem Ekşi, one of the union's executives, explained that the concept of independent trade unionism represented a rejection of trade union bureaucracy and yellow unionism.




Ekşi said, “Insaat-Is has a trade union approach that serves no interests other than those of the working class. It opposes approaches that divide the struggle into separate sectors and reduce the demands of the working class to localised and partial issues. In this sense, independent trade unionism means pursuing a path independent of the dominant political approach. The union's practices, its response to social developments and its activities within the construction sector clearly demonstrate this.




The bourgeoisie's approach is based on dividing the struggle of the working class and undermining collective resistance whenever workers come together and their struggles gain strength. By dividing workers into sectors and creating distinctions between permanent and temporary workers, it places various obstacles in the way of working-class mobilisation. Independent trade unionism maintains that developing a line of struggle free from this political approach is the principal means through which the working class can achieve its fundamental interests. Through its activities, Insaat-Is has consistently sought to carry forward this tradition.”




‘We showed that workers hold the power to liberate themselves’




Ekrem Ekşi stressed that the union's organising efforts were not confined to workplace struggles but extended into wider society. He continued: “One of the fundamental principles on which we cannot compromise is that our struggle must not be limited to the construction sector. Today, working-class struggles are emerging in many different areas, and joining forces with these struggles is entirely consistent with the union's fundamental approach. This understanding is also why we participate in militant trade union networks and have transformed our union premises into a centre of solidarity with working people.




Our union premises are not simply a place where construction workers gather or where issues concerning the sector are discussed. On the contrary, they are a space where people come together in solidarity to confront problems affecting their neighbourhoods, local communities and working people across Turkey. They are a practical expression of the understanding that working people can achieve liberation only through their own collective efforts. As part of this approach, we organise cinema days for children at the union premises. University students and people from various grassroots organisations also participate in these activities, sharing responsibilities on an equal footing and working together to make them possible. Our primary goal in the coming period is to expand this struggle based on solidarity and strengthen the bonds that bring people together.”

title: Biçer: Humanitarian and legal steps needed for ill prisoners
content:
Rights violations against sick prisoners continue to increase in prisons. Obstacles to accessing healthcare, delays in hospital transfers and the failure to release seriously ill prisoners are threatening prisoners' right to life.




Sebahat Biçer, an executive of the Federation of Associations for Solidarity with Prisoners' Families (MED TUHAD-FED), spoke to ANF about the rights violations faced by ill prisoners.




‘Urgent steps must be taken regardless of discussions on the peace process’




Sebahat Biçer pointed out that despite ongoing political discussions about the peace process, no concrete progress had been made in prisons. She stressed that releasing sick prisoners was a humanitarian necessity that should not be subject to political bargaining.




Biçer described the lack of progress in prisons and the deep anxiety experienced by prisoners' families: “Yes, that is correct. This peace process has been discussed for more than two years, but so far there has been no progress whatsoever regarding prisons. In fact, regardless of the process, sick prisoners should be released as soon as possible. This is a humanitarian necessity. Yet we have sick prisoners whose coffins could be carried out of prison at any moment. We have prisoners with stage-four cancer. We have sick prisoners who cannot meet their basic needs or sustain their lives independently. Unfortunately, no solution has been found for any of them. Families are deeply worried, and the condition of our friends in prison is deteriorating with each passing day.”







 







‘Even those who have completed their sentences are held hostage and threatened’




Sebahat Biçer said prisoners whose health was deteriorating were being subjected to pressure by prison administrations, including those who had completed their sentences but had not been released.




Biçer said: “Take Önder Poyraz, for example. He uses a wheelchair and cannot meet any of his basic needs, including bathing. His fellow prisoners take care of his needs, yet he is still being held in prison. Similarly, nothing is being done even for seriously ill prisoners who have completed 30 years in prison and should have been released. Although they have served their sentences, they are not being released.




We have prisoners with stage-four cancer who are approaching the end of their lives. They should be spending their final days with their families, but instead they are being held hostage in prison. Looking at the current process, unfortunately, no measures have been taken to address either their situation or that of prisoners whose releases have been postponed. They are being held entirely at the discretion of prison administrations. They are now being threatened with statements such as, ‘We will keep you here until the very end. You will leave in a coffin.’ Our friends are being held hostage under increasingly severe conditions of isolation, accompanied by such threats.”




‘They are beaten on their way to treatment, and violations are covered up’




Biçer described the conduct of prison officials and incidents of physical violence against prisoners being taken for medical treatment.




She said: “As I mentioned, prison administrations and even guards make threats, saying things like, ‘We will always prevent your release.’ One of these sick prisoners is Devrim Ayık. He has a colon condition and is completely blind in one eye. Even with glasses, he can only see up to one metre ahead with his other eye. He is beaten while being taken for medical treatment and severely beaten again on his return to prison. Attempts are being made to cover up what happened. His family noticed his condition during a prison visit and began pursuing the matter. Many others are being subjected to similar treatment.




Recently, our friend Celal Yıldırım in Urfa also suffered a heart attack, and his condition is deteriorating with each passing day. Yet they are deliberately keeping these prisoners behind bars. They are not being released for political reasons. Our friends are being detained even though they have completed their sentences.




We will not abandon this struggle. We will stand by our friends until the very end and be their voice outside prison. We will also continue to stand alongside their families.”




‘There are nearly 400 ill prisoners, 180 of them seriously ill’




Sebahat Biçer provided figures on the overall situation in prisons, criticised the authorities' indifference and called on the state to take concrete action. Biçer said: “There are currently nearly 400 ill prisoners, 180 of whom are seriously ill. These are people whose conditions are so severe that they cannot sustain their lives independently. Unfortunately, the authorities have turned a deaf ear and are taking no action whatsoever. Humanitarian steps must be taken regardless of the peace process.




There is a process underway, but the steps are always being taken by one side. The state must now take a step as well, beginning with sick prisoners. If a seriously ill prisoner with stage-four cancer or another terminal illness were released, they would simply be lying in bed beside their family. These are people who are no longer capable of carrying out any activities. The state is acting on political considerations. It continues its policy of intimidation and repression by keeping sick prisoners behind bars, which is why it refuses to release them.”




‘Transfers far from families and inadequate treatment are policies of intimidation’




Biçer criticised the continued detention of seriously ill prisoners in facilities far from their families and the restrictions imposed on their access to healthcare.




Biçer concluded: “Similarly, requests to transfer sick prisoners are not being granted. There are seriously ill prisoners being held far away from their families. One of them is Botan Kars. He is being held in Van (Wan) Prison, while his family lives in Diyarbakır (Amed). Despite repeatedly requesting a transfer closer to his family, the authorities have refused. His mother has stage-four cancer and cannot travel to visit him. This is also a policy of intimidation and repression.




The medical treatment provided to prisoners is seriously inadequate. There are major shortages of medication. They are either not taken to hospital at all or are beaten while being taken there. They are subjected to demands for searches inside their mouths. Families also face severe pressure when they visit prisons, while sick prisoners receive only partial and inadequate treatment, often limited to painkillers and other medication intended merely to relieve symptoms. Neither seriously ill prisoners nor other sick prisoners are being provided with comprehensive medical treatment.”

title: Mihemed: We will continue our struggle for constitutional recognition of Kurdish in Syria
content:
Reactions continue in Rojava Kurdistan to the Damascus transitional government's decision concerning the Kurdish language. On 17 October 2026, the Initiative for the Constitutional Recognition of Kurdish and Its Adoption as an Official Language in Syria was announced in Qamishlo. Hesen Mihemed, a member of the initiative, spoke about its activities, aims and objectives.




Hesen Mihemed said there was an urgent need for such an initiative today. He said, “We worked to establish this initiative because our aim was to secure official status for our language. For the past 15 years, students in Rojava have generally been reading, writing and receiving their education in Kurdish, their mother tongue. Unfortunately, under the latest decision, the Syrian Minister of Education has allocated only a few hours, three hours in total, to Kurdish. Even if some other subjects, such as philosophy, mathematics and history, can also be taught in Kurdish, this is unfortunately not enough.




The Kurdish people are an indigenous people, as stated in Article 13 of the Syrian presidential decree. Kurds have rights as Syrian citizens. They must be able to speak, read and receive education in their own language. Unfortunately, however, there has recently been a retreat from these rights. That is why our initiative seeks recognition of Kurdish as an indigenous language alongside Arabic and aims to secure its official status. Just as Arabs can study and receive education in their own language, Kurds must also be able to receive education in theirs. This is why we considered it important to establish such an initiative.”




‘Efforts to secure official status for Kurdish will continue’




Hesen Mihemed stressed that efforts to secure official recognition of Kurdish would continue. Mihemed said: “Kurdish must be permanently recognised as an official language in Syria's future constitution. We will carry out our work towards this goal. They acknowledge that Kurdish is an indigenous language and that Kurds are Syrian citizens. But if the rights verbally acknowledged for Kurds are not reflected in practice and enshrined in the constitution, it cannot truly be said that those rights have been recognised. In such circumstances, there can be no genuine justice regarding Kurdish rights. That is why we are making these efforts. There are human rights organisations, civil society organisations and institutions such as the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) and the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF). There are organisations that defend the right of every people to speak and receive education in their own language, particularly when it comes to children's education.




We believe that if we continue our efforts, maintain our activities and pursue our work with determination, we can secure our rights. We will establish relations with legal organisations, international institutions and all organisations working on children's rights and issues concerning children. We will also maintain contact with national institutions working in education and language teaching, as well as civil society organisations, intellectuals and individuals concerned with the rights of peoples. Our aim is to establish relations with every organisation working on language rights. We have already established contacts with international and civil society organisations both inside and outside Syria. We contacted and visited them before formally establishing and launching the initiative. We met with representatives of Assyrians, Armenians, Chaldeans and other communities. We developed relations with individuals and institutions representing different peoples.




We explained that we are a civil initiative, that we are not affiliated with any political party and that our work is peaceful. Our objective is to ensure that Kurdish is permanently recognised as an official language in Syria's future constitution. We do not want division. Demanding official status for one language does not mean diminishing or eliminating another language, nor does it mean dividing the country. On the contrary, it represents richness and diversity. In many countries around the world, education is provided in two, three, four or even five languages. We want this to be possible in our own country as well. We are asking for support in this regard. The people we met told us that they supported us, that they could join the initiative and that Kurds were entitled to this right. They also expressed their willingness to become part of the initiative.”




‘Multilingual education does not divide a country; it enriches it’




Hesen Mihemed stressed that multilingualism did not mean dividing a country but, on the contrary, represented a source of richness and diversity. Mihemed continued: “There will be no division in Syria over language or education. What we are demanding is constitutional protection for Kurdish. This would enrich both education and the country's culture. We want to carry out activities towards this goal and raise awareness among all the peoples around us. Allowing people to receive education in their mother tongue and recognising their languages as official languages in the constitution does not mean dividing the country. Nor does it mean weakening another language or diminishing the position of the language spoken by the majority in Syria. Take Arabic, for example. Granting Kurdish official status would not represent a loss for Arabic. On the contrary, it would enrich the country.




This would improve education, mutual understanding and linguistic diversity. One of our objectives is to make our voices heard by all relevant institutions and individuals. We are trying to reach organisations concerned with children's rights and education in the mother tongue. So far, we have managed to reach some individuals and organisations, particularly those outside Syria. Unfortunately, we have not yet been able to reach everyone or every organisation because our initiative was established only recently. Nevertheless, we are continuing our efforts to make our voices heard as widely as possible. The countries and organisations concerned have signed conventions recognising that children should be able to speak, learn and receive education in their mother tongue. Every child should be able to speak, learn and receive education in their own language. Speaking and receiving education in one's mother tongue is a right belonging to all citizens and peoples.




Syria signed a convention in 1993 concerning children's right to speak their mother tongue and the right of all peoples to receive education in their own languages. That is why we will work to reach the relevant institutions. They should also support us. We hope our efforts will succeed. I want to ask a question: Education is provided in five languages in Switzerland, two in Canada and four or five in South Africa. Have these countries been divided? Has multilingual education posed a threat to them? On the contrary, it has helped foster solidarity and equality in these countries. It has encouraged meaningful dialogue and mutual understanding between different communities and peoples. This is a form of richness. It helps develop cultural understanding between people.




Our demands are being misinterpreted. Our call for Kurdish to be constitutionally protected and recognised as an official language certainly does not mean that we want separation or to break away part of the country. Nor do we want to diminish the importance of Arabic as an official language of the state. Quite the opposite. We want Kurdish people to be able to speak, read and receive education in their own language, just as Arab people can speak, read and receive education in theirs. This creates richness and strengthens solidarity between peoples. As an initiative, we want to make one thing clear: Nobody should be afraid. We do not want separation or division, and we do not want to diminish the importance of any other language. We are simply demanding the right of a people to receive education in their own language.”




‘The Kurdish people must protect their language’




Mihemed said the establishment of the initiative had attracted considerable attention. He also said: “Everyone believes that the time has come for the Kurdish people to receive education in their mother tongue. Martyrs, students and teachers have made tremendous efforts towards this goal. Significant work has been carried out through activities organised in support of Kurdish, initiatives both inside and outside the country, and the many relationships established over the years. All these efforts have received support, and people have openly expressed their solidarity. We now want to carry out this work on an institutional basis and strive to secure official status for Kurdish. As an initiative, we have also visited Kurdish political parties. We met with all parties without discrimination because we are a neutral, civil, independent and peaceful initiative. Everyone should join this initiative, support it and contribute to our work. That is why we visited different political parties in Syria individually and invited them to participate. Kurdish is not the language of any particular group. It is the common language of the entire Kurdish people.




That is why we want to set politics aside and carry out this work as independent individuals. Our aim is for the initiative to achieve meaningful results and for Kurdish to be recognised as the language of the entire Kurdish people. We have therefore tried to bring everyone together. We hope that Kurdish parties will unite around the language issue through this initiative and that they will also be able to act together on other matters. We have worked to involve everyone in the initiative and secure their support. The vast majority of parties have expressed their support. They told us that our work and struggle were valuable and that they would join us. As an initiative, we call on the Kurdish people to take responsibility for their own future. Before turning to other institutions, we want the Kurdish people themselves, together with all sections of society, including political groups, intellectuals and academics, to fulfil their responsibilities. We expect everyone, including students, teachers and families, to take responsibility in this regard. Our hope is that the Kurdish people will protect their language. Today is a day of struggle to secure constitutional guarantees for Kurdish and ensure that it becomes a permanent official language in Syria's future constitution. This requires effort, hard work, resistance and struggle.




We hope that all families will send their children to school to receive education in their mother tongue. We also call on existing relevant institutions and those responsible for children and education to support us Together, we can make Kurdish an official language in the Syria of the future. We want a diverse, multilingual Syria founded on equality. Our hope is that, by working together, we can ensure that the Kurdish people also secure their rights.”

title: Sevda Karaca: War policies undermine unity and labour struggles - Part One
content:
Sevda Karaca, Deputy Chair of the Labour Party (EMEP) and MP for Antep, answered ANF's questions about labour struggles and the struggle for peace.




Karaca said, “War permeates every aspect of social life. Workers' demands for higher wages, the right to strike, women's struggle for equality and people's democratic demands can suddenly be pushed into the background by debates over 'national security', 'the survival of the state' or the 'domestic front'. The racism, nationalism and chauvinism being fuelled also prevent people, women and young people from coming together around shared demands.”




Karaca stressed that Turkish workers also had a responsibility to oppose the policies of their own ruling classes and support the Kurdish people's demands for peace, equality and democracy. She added, “This is necessary not only as an act of solidarity but also to defend the independent interests of their own class. Because in an environment where peoples are turned against one another, it becomes harder to develop a common struggle against capital.”




How do you assess the current state of the labour struggle in Turkey? Is it sufficient, and where does it fall short?




One of the greatest contradictions in Turkey's labour struggle is this: workers' anger is growing, working and living conditions are deteriorating, and individual pockets of resistance are continuing and spreading. Yet this accumulation of struggle has not developed into an effective nationwide class movement or an independent political force representing the working class.




Workers in textiles, metalworking, logistics, mining and the service sector are engaged in fierce struggles over wages, working conditions and trade union rights across industrial regions with very different characteristics throughout the country. They continue to resist despite the threat of dismissal, pressure from employers, obstacles to trade union organising and the corruption of the trade union bureaucracy.




These struggles show us that the working class has not surrendered. However, the experience gained in one factory or one struggle is not being carried over sufficiently to other workplaces, sectors and cities. Resistance often remains confined to individual workplaces and struggles to develop into a collective class consciousness and political force.




What do you attribute these difficulties to?




We cannot attribute these shortcomings to a lack of willingness among workers to struggle. The limitations imposed by trade union bureaucracy, the lack of organisation, fear of unemployment, increasingly precarious employment and political repression are significant obstacles. But socialists and labour organisations must also confront their own responsibilities. Exposing workers' problems and voicing their legitimate demands is not enough. We must establish connections between these problems, bring struggles together, help workers develop confidence in their own strength and link economic demands to a political programme.




The connection between economic and political struggle does not emerge automatically. What we need today is to unite the fragmented experiences of the working class around a common struggle. We must ensure that workers have a say not only in confronting the employers in their own factories, but also in challenging the economic and political system that determines their working and living conditions. The working class needs to organise itself as a force capable of shaping society as a whole. We need to develop a strategy of struggle that transforms workers' scattered anger into collective strength, builds political action out of everyday experiences and enables the working class to shape society according to its own demands and objectives.




Are socialists sufficiently self-critical? Is enough thought being given to why poorer sections of society turn to ruling parties?




The government does not merely control economic resources and the institutions of the state. It also intervenes in people's everyday lives, their sense of belonging, their expectations and their relationships of trust. It creates the everyday, consistent and long-term mechanisms needed to sustain this influence. We cannot explain the political choices of a worker or a poor family solely in terms of economic interests.




People also make political choices based on belonging, trust, identity, solidarity and expectations for the future. Through the networks of everyday relationships it has established among working people, the government controls not only material resources but also the power to shape what society regards as a problem and whom people trust. Confronted with this hegemonic relationship, correctly identifying the problem is not enough. We must also question how we reach workers and working people in their everyday lives and which of their experiences we are able to transform into a common struggle.




‘

We must return to the old principles of organising’




Which of the everyday, consistent and long-term mechanisms of engagement established by the government do we possess? Socialists do not have these material resources at their disposal. For socialist organisations that lack the power, money and resources available to the government, there is ultimately no substitute for consistent work rooted directly in workers' living and working environments, work that does not lose its direction regardless of circumstances, together with perseverance and determination. This is how we can build lasting foundations within everyday life that respond to people's sense of belonging and their expectations. Perhaps I can give an example from Antep. This is essentially what we are trying to do there. We insist on working in working-class neighbourhoods, at the grassroots, where such efforts often remain unseen and unrecognised. This work has taken concrete shape in the workers' resistance struggles in Başpınar. Our efforts are fundamentally aimed at giving working people's struggles an organised foundation. This is not work that attracts attention on social media or is loudly advertised. It requires accepting the demanding task of long-term organising rather than seeking short-term results.




This is the only way to become an organised force rooted in the everyday lives of working people in industrial areas that are regarded as government strongholds, where every mechanism of its hegemony is deployed.




We must become part of people's everyday lives, learn alongside them, develop shared solutions rather than arrive with ready-made answers to their problems, and build political consciousness out of these experiences. For the Labour Party, one of our central challenges is to go beyond being a party that says the right things. We must become a political force that workers trust through struggle, where they make decisions collectively and recognise their own strength.




But something else is even more important to us. Socialists know that the fundamental task is to strengthen the organised power of the working class. The growth of socialist organisations and the growth of the working class's political power are not the same thing. That is why I sometimes disagree with assessments on social media that measure socialist parties by their membership numbers and similar indicators. An organisation's membership may increase. Its visibility on social media may grow. It may win more votes in elections. But none of these, on their own, can measure whether the working class is becoming a historical political subject.




In periods of severe repression, discussions about turning workers and working people into an organised force tend to focus largely on finding new methods and approaches. I disagree with this. In periods such as these, when fear and political and economic repression become increasingly ruthless, we need to return to the old, time-tested methods of organising. Rather than searching for some magical 'new' form of organisation, we need to return to much older principles of organising.




Working-class organising is not glamorous. Spending years building an organisation in a workplace or a working-class neighbourhood is no easy task in a country where the aggression of the one-man regime constantly forces us to respond immediately to one attack after another. Winning a worker's trust or spending years building a lasting organisation in a neighbourhood is not highly visible work. In this climate of repression, it cannot be. Unfortunately, in an atmosphere of left-wing populism where visibility is sometimes valued more highly than becoming deeply rooted in workers' lives, discussions can proceed on entirely the wrong basis. It seems almost characteristic of our times to shy away from the long and demanding nature of organising working people, and to regard forceful rhetoric as more important than devoting time and effort to a street, a factory or three politically conscious workers in that factory. What I mean by time-tested knowledge is precisely this: revolutionary politics is built not so much on these visible displays, but on the often unseen labour of organising.




No matter how high poverty and hunger rates rise, how much anger repression generates, or how clearly the nature of the government becomes apparent to broad sections of society, social struggles will not develop automatically unless we become deeply involved in them as an organising force. Nor will it be possible to transform spontaneous eruptions of anger into purposeful political struggles. Those spontaneous outbursts will eventually subside. The conditions that gave rise to them will either be addressed by the system to some extent or, more often, become normalised in the minds of millions as circumstances that simply have to be accepted. The existing order will find a way to preserve itself.




We have seen numerous examples of this at different moments, from the Gezi resistance to the events surrounding 19 March. Transforming social energy from immediate reactions into lasting organisation requires time, effort and patience. Rather than constantly trying to respond to every new issue the government places on the agenda, our priority must be to build the foundations for sustained struggle. If we are to respond to attacks, our response must emerge from those organised foundations. We must concentrate our efforts in the vital centres of working-class life. Working-class neighbourhoods and industrial areas must be our priority. Only in this way can 'working people' cease to be an abstract expression and become a concrete political subject, conscious of their class position and shared interests. This requires persistence.




‘We must strengthen people's capacity to act collectively’




At the stage we have reached, repression and oppression may be presented as the only reality, and each new wave of attacks may leave people feeling overwhelmed, wondering how they can possibly respond to everything. Yet the issues at stake, and the foundations for resisting them, have actually become clearer. Whatever the government does, it cannot completely exclude people from politics in Turkey.




We can see how essential organisation is if people are to play a decisive role in political life. In recent years, we have repeatedly been told that everything depends on a leader, a saviour, the ballot box or electoral campaigns. Politics has increasingly been discussed as though it were simply a matter of the performance of professional politicians, party leaders and MPs. Yet these approaches have repeatedly proved ineffective. We must strengthen what really matters: people's capacity to act collectively through organisation. Political organisation is one of our most fundamental challenges. It is not simply about expanding political parties. It also means building women's associations deeply rooted in neighbourhoods, initiatives established by residents against local drug gangs, parents' groups fighting for free school meals, villagers coming together to protect their living environments, and students organising dormitory committees, corridor by corridor, because there is no hot water in their accommodation. We need to devote time and effort to strengthening these forms of organisation.




One of the most decisive factors in this period is ideological clarity and understanding. For nearly 50 years, not only in our country but across the world, we have repeatedly heard claims that ideologies are dead, that they destroy freedoms, and that politics is essentially a matter of pragmatism. The Justice and Development Party's (AKP) attempts to co-opt opposition politicians in order to divide and weaken the opposition, the lack of a political programme that may appear left-wing but is essentially rooted in liberalism, and the tendency to regard positions that remain within the existing system and fundamentally serve capital as preferable under conditions of repression all demonstrate how important ideological clarity and consistency become when political struggles intensify.




Professor Cangül Örnek made an observation recently that I agree with: for the first time in many years, the political situation in Turkey has become remarkably clear. There is no longer any political force that people can rely on other than their own capacity to organise and act. Perhaps for the first time since the military coup of 12 September 1980, we are living through a historical period that offers considerable opportunities to strengthen opposition to capital. Today, people are experiencing enormous anger towards capital, but that anger has not yet become fully politicised. We must give it a political direction and prevent it from being absorbed back into the existing system. This is also what we are seeing internationally, from France to Albania.




We are confronted with a brutal labour regime that condemns the working class to ruthless working conditions and extremely low wages, attempts to discipline workers through the fear of unemployment, and traps people in lives stripped of dignity. The scale, consequences and cruelty of poverty are frequently discussed, but there is very little discussion of the means of struggle. There is only diagnosis! It is not enough to define injustice, lawlessness and inequality solely through the government's most prominent attacks. General statements about justice and the rule of law are ineffective unless they are grounded in clear, fundamental demands that working people can embrace.




The subjects of opposition politics are not merely those who are politically active in some way and face repression because of it. The real subjects of opposition politics are the exploited and the oppressed. Politics that neglects this reality has no prospect of expanding its influence or bringing about change.
