author: Unknown
title: 17 octobre de feu à Marseille
content:
Récit de la première journée de l'époque post-contemporaine dans la plus belle ville du monde.




Quoi dire après une telle journée ? 


Prenons le temps de nous rappeler de tout ce qui s'est passé dans notre ville.




A l'aube, 5h30, sur le site industriel d'Eurolinks, fabricant de maillons utilisés dans les mitraillettes de l'armée coloniale contre les Palestiniens installé à Château-Gombert, une centaine de manifestant.es commence la journée avec un blocage en soutien au peuple palestinien !




 

 

 

 




D'autres ont decidé de commencer la journée avec un tour de vélo vers les beaux quartiers de Marseille. Après des premiers jets de gaz lacrymogènes au rond-point du Prado, jeunes et gilets jaunes remontent l'avenue du Prado vers Castellane en déposant des poubelles sur la route - il est même pas 8h, et voilà, premier blocage d'une longue journée !




De là, les hostilités se deplacent vers la Préfecture, à la gare, aux Reformés... il est 8h30 et on compte bien plus que 1000 personnes dans les rues du centre-ville. Une partie de la manif sauvage descend la Canebière et prend la direction du Vieux Port, les CRS positionnés devant le commissariat de Noailles se prennent des jets de projectiles, notamment de bouteilles de verre.




 

 

 

 




Avec une partie des manifestants restée aux Réformés, les CRS ont désormais des foules devant mais aussi derrière eux et... se font nasser ! Des manifestants tirent des feux d'artifice sur les CRS et déscellent des pavés, le poste de police municipale de la Canebière est pris pour cible et termine absolument saccagé.




 

 

 

 




Un peu avant 10h, on se sert : SFR et JD Sports dans la rue Saint-Férreol sont les premiers magasins pillés. A partir de maintenant, tout se passe en même temps - la police est définitivement dépassée et ne se relèvera pas avant tard dans la nuit.




 

 

 

 




Blocage au Vieux-Port, pillages dans tout l'hyper-centre marseillais, puis... plusieurs dizaines de manifestant.es se sont amusé.es avec une petite balade dans la mairie ! En criant "c'est la Révolution, on prend la Bastille", ils décorent les murs avec des graffitis et renversent le buste de Marianne !




 

 

 

 




 

 

 

 




Dans tout ce bordel, plusieurs dizaines de personnes ont réussi à forcer une des grilles d'accès du Centre Bourse, côté Belsunce. Des personnes font leurs chourses également rue Paradis - le luxe pour toustes ! Rolex, Longchamp, Hermès... Partout, des sacs Foot Locker, des caddies avec tout ce qu'il faut pour une fois, des arbres à chats et enceintes sur scoots et trottinettes, meme une voiture sans plaque d'immatriculation pour charger les trouvailles.




 

 

 

 




En haut de la Canebière, une free party est improvisée par un DJ, on chante : "

la jeunesse emmerde le Front national !

" Et l'autoroute A7 est bloquée, dans les deux sens, ça danse sur le béton. Un air de liberté souffle dans la ville. Le soir, à la Plaine, ça partage le champagne et ça distribue des Air Max, ça fête et ça danse autour d'un feu digne de Carnaval, sous l'oeil des crevé des caméras incendiées !




Mais un bilan de cette journée ne peut pas être fait sans parler de la violence policière et des nombreuses victimes qui ont perdu un oeil, ou sont parties à l'hôpital avec le crâne ouvert à cause des grenades envoyées par les bleus.




Nous appelons à soutenir également les victimes de la répression policière et judiciaire déchainée - plus de 2400 personnes ont été interpellées en France, dont 74 adultes et 27 mineurs à Marseille. Une soixantaine a déjà été jugé cette semaine avec des peines hyper sévères. Pour savoir comment les soutenir, 

lisez cet article de la Legal Team.

.

author: Unknown
title: Emir: SPK, 455 bin 758 mağdurun hakkını gasbedenlere kalkan olma derdinde
content:
Yeni Parti Grup Başkanvekili Murat Emir, "Suçüstü yakalanan Sermaye Piyasası Kurulu (SPK), gece yarısı önergesini aklamak için bugün panikle bir duyuru yayımlamış ama kendi kendini ele vermiş. Onca manipülasyon olurken koltuğunda oturup seyreden SPK yönetimi, şimdi kelime oyunlarıyla 455 bin 758 mağdurun hakkını gasbeden gece yarısı önergesine kalkan olma derdinde" dedi.

Emir, SPK'nın "Takas kesinliği ve PBLK husularına ilişkin basın duyurusu" başlıklı açıklamasına sosyal medya hesabından tepki gösterdi. SPK'nın kendini ele verdiğini söyleyen Emir, şunları kaydetti: "Suçüstü yakalanan SPK, gece yarısı önergesini aklamak için bugün panikle bir bir duyuru yayımlamış ama kendi kendini ele vermiş. SPK duyurusunda 'Sermaye Piyasası Kanunu 79. maddesine göre takas talimat ve işlemleri tasfiye halinde dahi geri alınamaz ve iptal edilemez ama PBLK’da bekleyen satış talimatları takasın başladığı anlamına gelmez' diyor. O zaman size sormak isterim; kanunun 79. maddesi sadece tamamlanmış işlemleri değil, açıkça 'takas talimatlarını' da koruma altına alıyor. Yatırımcının payını TEFAS İşlem Blokaj Alt Hesabına (PBLK) alıp bloke koymak takas sürecini başlatmak değilse nedir? AKP’nin gece yarısı önergesinde tam 4 defa 'ilgili fonun temerrüdü' yazarken, SPK bugünkü duyurusunda 'temerrüt' kelimesini neden sansürleyip metinden tamamen çıkardı? Çünkü ortada doğmuş bir nakit borcu olmadan temerrüt olmayacağını kendileri de çok iyi biliyor. Madem PBLK’daki 250 bin mağdur zaten alacaklı değil ve doğal olarak fon pay sahibi sayılıyordu, o zaman dün gece mahkeme yolunu kapatmak için neden apar topar kanuna madde eklediniz? Onca manipülasyon olurken koltuğunda oturup seyreden SPK yönetimi, şimdi kelime oyunlarıyla 455 bin 758 mağdurun hakkını gasbeden gece yarısı önergesine kalkan olma derdinde."

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Unknown
title: TBMM Başkanı Kurtulmuş: Süreç planlandığı gibi ilerliyor, hiçbir şey geç kalmıyor
content:
Ankara - Türkiye Büyük Millet Meclisi (TBMM) Başkanı Numan Kurtulmuş, Türkiye’yi ziyaret eden Lüksemburg Temsilciler Meclisi Başkanı Claude Wiseler ile düzenlediği ortak basın toplantısında, çözüm sürecine ilişkin değerlendirmelerde bulundu.

Sürecin Türkiye’nin en önemli sorunlarından birinin çözümüne yönelik yürütüldüğünü vurgulayan Kurtulmuş, Meclis’teki siyasi partilerin katılımıyla hazırlanan raporun kabul edilmesini demokratik açıdan önemli bir başarı olarak nitelendirdi.

Kurtulmuş, sürecin planlandığı şekilde ilerlediğini belirterek, Meclis bünyesinde kurulması öngörülen izleme kuruluna ilişkin siyasi partilerle görüşmelerin sürdüğünü ve kurulun önümüzdeki günlerde oluşturulacağını açıkladı.

Kurtulmuş şunları söyledi; "Bir taraftan örgütün silahsızlanması, fesih sürecinin devam ettiği; bir taraftan da bu sürecin özellikle uygulamada nasıl seyredeceğine ilişkin oluşturulan üst kurulun çalışmalarına devam etmesi zaten planlandığı gibi gidiyor. Bunun bir ayağı da Türkiye Büyük Millet Meclisi ayağıdır. Biz başından itibaren bir iddiada bulunuyoruz: Bu model özgün bir modeldir ve Türkiye modelidir. Bu modelin nasıl işlediği, bu sürecin nasıl yönetildiğine ilişkin asla dışarıdan bir göz olmayacak. Asla üçüncü bir göz işin içerisine müdahil olamayacaktır. Milletin tamamı adına Meclis bütün farklılıklarıyla, partileriyle bu süreci yönetecek”

Meclis'te de yasanın gerektirdiği izleme kurulu kurulacağını belirten Kurtulmuş; “Önümüzdeki günlerde bu kurulu kurarız. Nasıl olacağı ile ilgili olarak siyasi partiler ile zaten yasanın çıktığının ertesi gününden itibaren müzakerelerimizi yapıyoruz. Önümüzdeki günlerde bu konu ete kemiğe bürünür. Ben bir şey söylemiştim, onu bilerek söyledim: Her şey kendi yolunda tıkır tıkır işliyor. Hiçbir şey geç kalmıyor. Böylesine önemli bir konuda herkes üzerine düşen sorumluluğu yerine getirsin. Kimse bir diğerine ödev vermeye kalkmasın. Terör örgütü silahsızlanma sürecini sürdürecek ve bunu sonlandıracak. Siyaset üstüne düşen sorumluluğu şimdiye kadar yaptığı gibi bundan sonra da başarıyla yapacak ve inşallah bu süreç tıkır tıkır işleyecektir, sonlanacaktır. Milletimizin bu konuda büyük bir beklentisi ve büyük bir desteği vardır. Kimse bu desteği boşa çıkaracak sözlerin içerisinde olmasın” dedi.

Mekke Ortak Savunma Anlaşması'nda sürecin nasıl işleyeceğinin sorulması üzerine ise Kurtulmuş, "Mekke Anlaşması bildiğiniz gibi Türkiye, Pakistan ve Suudi Arabistan'ın uzlaşmaya vardığı bir anlaşma. Cumhurbaşkanlığı'ndan bu konuyla ilgili yasa teklifi bize geldiği zaman ben de hemen bunu Türkiye Büyük Millet Meclisi'ne, önce komisyona, sonra da Genel Kurula geçecek. Dolayısıyla önce komisyonda tartışılacak. Komisyonda kabul edilirse Türkiye Büyük Millet Meclisi Genel Kuruluna gelecek ve Türkiye Büyük Millet Meclisi'nde yapılan müzakereler sonrasında da kabul edilirse yasalaşacak. Süreç budur, usul budur ve her şey usulüne uygun bir şekilde işliyor" ifadesini kullandı.

Lüksemburg Temsilciler Meclisi Başkanı Claude Wiseler ise "Son dönemde özellikle başta Fransa olmak üzere Avrupa'nın birçok başkentinde artan şiddetli protestoları görüyoruz, dikkat çekiyor. Bununla birlikte Avrupa'daki bu artan tansiyonu, artan gerilimi nasıl değerlendiriyorsunuz? Ayrıca bu gelişmelerin Avrupa'nın siyasi ve toplumsal geleceğine etkileri hakkında ne düşünüyorsunuz" sorusunu şöyle yanıtladı:

"İlk olarak, şimdi Lüksemburg'da böyle bir gerilim yok hâlihazırda. Toplum olarak barış, huzur içerisinde yaşıyoruz kendi ülkemizde, Lüksemburg sınırları içerisinde. Yani Lüksemburg'la ilgili bir soru değil ama tabii ki diğer ülkelerde gerçekleşen durumlar, tabii ki ekonomik durum, buna yönelik baskılar; tabii ki işte petrol fiyatlarının, bazı ülkelerdeki konut fiyatlarının artıyor olması sosyal anlamda birçok soruna neden oluyor ve bunlar da tabii ki bazı ülkelerde bu şekilde daha belki şiddetli bir şekilde vuku buluyor. Bunun tabii ki ülkelerin siyasetlerine etkisi var. Başka ülkelerin siyasetlerine de etkisi olabilir ama daha ziyade ülkelere münferit bakmak gerekiyor. Ve bu sorunların tabii ki çözülmesi için ekonomik olarak, sosyal olarak çalışmak gerekecektir."

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Jenny Brown
title: Tampa TSA Union Averted   Privatization Disaster
content:
TSA agents noticed something was up. “We started seeing people around the airport that you wouldn’t normally see, people in suits,” said Mark Harris, Transportation Security Officer and union steward in Tampa, Florida.  




That’s when he realized the airport was a target for the TSA privatization program he had been reading about—the $13 billion Gold+ program. Harris, and his union Government Employees (AFGE) Local 556, swung into action. 




Transportation Security Administration workers have been winning battles lately. Twice in two years the Trump administration has tried to cancel their union contract, and twice it has been stopped by the courts. Now things are mostly back to normal, with the contract in force and grievances being processed.




But Gold+ would undermine the union by outsourcing TSO jobs to private companies. As the dimensions of the plan became clear, Harris said his co-workers “felt like they had been kicked in the gut. You know, everything that they had worked for, their federal pension, careers, everything.”




Tampa is a model airport that consistently ranks at the top in customer satisfaction. That’s why TSA picked it for the Gold+ privatization effort, Harris said. “They don’t want to give it to a poor airport or a failing airport. That would be disastrous for TSA, right?”




DOWN THE RABBIT HOLE




Harris first became aware of Gold+ from 

Against Giants

, a website maintained by an ex-TSA agent. As he went down a research rabbit hole, a fellow steward took on some of his union work so he could focus. 




Harris, a former police detective, was able to ferret out government documents to back up the union’s case. The agency “seemed like they were trying to do it under the cover of darkness,” he said. The program wasn’t officially acknowledged until July 21, and even then AFGE had to sue to get documents.




Although TSA insisted that the private jobs would pay the same, Harris found that they were saying the opposite to prospective contractors. He found that staff and wage cuts were essential to the program.




When confronted, TSA officials told the workers they didn’t know what the private companies would pay, but also reassured them that their pay wouldn’t change. “That kind of got me… We’re not being truthful about this, right?” Harris said.




The local’s president, Chris Finlay, had worked at a smaller airport at Sanford, Florida, where a private security company came in. At first they hired people at their former pay, but after a few weeks, “they brought them all in one by one. They said, sorry, we can no longer pay you that. We can only pay you this starting pay,” Harris said.




PRESSURE POINTS




The union figured out who would be deciding on Gold+ in Tampa—the airport’s board of directors—and then organized pressure from workers and the community.




The union argued that if privatization came in, salaries would be cut and that would affect local businesses: TSOs wouldn’t take their families out to dinner, or to a football game. If TSOs had to suddenly relocate, it would depress housing prices. Harris created pre-written letters from business owners, airport workers, and others, and union members asked everyone they knew to send the letters.  




For workers, the stakes were clear, Harris said. When jobs are privatized, “we know there’s no union protections. But when you work for Homeland Security, when you work for TSA, it’s a career.”




That career was hard-won. Airports used a patchwork of private security companies until TSA was founded in 2001. But it was the union that built TSO jobs into sustainable ones, by winning first union representation and then a contract in 2011. Finally in 2023, TSA workers were included in the federal pay schedule. AFGE now represents 47,000 TSA workers. 




Local 556 leadership met with the mayors of Tampa and neighboring St. Petersburg, along with congressional representatives. Airport workers raised questions and objections at in-person town hall meetings with TSA and airport leadership. 




Finally, on August 24, Tampa airport leaders decided not to adopt the program. It was apparently a fatal blow—TSA cancelled the entire project right after Tampa’s decision. Private companies had already advertised jobs for the contracts they anticipated.




The union expects the push for privatization 

to continue

, but workers definitively won this round.

author: Unknown
title: Ümit Özlale, Taha Çakmak'a sordu: Kamu kaynaklarıyla fondan erken çıkışlar finanse edildi mi?
content:
Yeni Parti İzmir Milletvekili Ümit Özlale, fon vurgunu soruşturmasında iki özel kalem personeli gözaltına alınan, kendisi de istifa eden eski Türkiye Sigorta Genel Müdürü Taha Çakmak’a, Karayipler’deki Artsmrkts Ltd, Londra’daki GildenCrest ve İsviçre’deki Century City Securities üzerinden hesabına veya menfaatine işlem yapılıp yapılmadığını sordu. Kişisel yatırımlarıyla yönettiği şirketlerin fon yatırımları arasında çıkar çatışması bulunup bulunmadığını soran Özlale, Türkiye Sigorta ve Türkiye Hayat ve Emeklilik kaynakları ile BES fonlarından TERA ve bağlantılı kuruluşlara yapılan yatırımların açıklanmasını istedi.

Özlale'nin sosyal medya hesabından yaptığı açıklamalar ve gündeme taşıdığı sorular şöyle:

"Taha Çakmak’ın kamu kaynaklarıyla kişisel yatırımlarının yolları kesişti mi? Taha Çakmak, fon vurgunundaki en kritik isimlerden biri ve sahibi bu ülkenin vatandaşları olan Türkiye Sigorta ile Türkiye Hayat ve Emeklilik’in geçen haftaya kadar genel müdürüydü. Daha önce de BDDK ve Türkiye Cumhuriyet Merkez Bankası (TCMB) Başkan Yardımcılığı gibi en kritik makamlarda oturdu. Cebimizdeki 50 TL’lik banknotlarda imzası bulunan bir isimdi. Bugün ise Taha Çakmak’ın özel kalem personelleri Fahri Uğur ve Hakan Eryılmaz aynı fon ve hisse soruşturması kapsamında gözaltına alındı.

Kamuoyunu aydınlatmak için Çakmak’a ve yetkililere şu soruları yöneltiyoruz: BDDK’de üst düzey yöneticiyken TERA Yatırım’da kendi adınıza, BDDK’deki resmi e-posta adresinizin kayıtlı olduğu bir müşteri hesabı açtınız mı? TERA Yatırım, Londra merkezli GildenCrest (Tera Europe) veya bunlarla bağlantılı kuruluşlarda kendi adınıza ya da başkası üzerinden kullandığınız yatırım hesaplarınız oldu mu? Görev yaptığınız dönemde Türkiye Sigorta ve Türkiye Hayat ve Emeklilik’in kendi kurumsal kaynaklarından ve yönettikleri bireysel emeklilik (BES) fonlarından TERA’ya veya bağlantılı fonlara toplam ne kadar para yatırıldı? Bu yatırımların kararını kim verdi? Bugün gözaltına alınan özel kalem personelleriniz Fahri Uğur ve Hakan Eryılmaz’ın bu süreçteki rolü ve talimat trafiği nedir? Yatırım komitesi kararlarını ve risk değerlendirme raporlarını açıklayacak mısınız?

Türkiye Sigorta ve Türkiye Hayat ve Emeklilik bu yatırımlara karar verirken sizin de aynı fonlarda veya bu fonların aldığı hisselerde yatırımınız var mıydı? Varsa kendi mali çıkarınızın da bulunduğunu yöneticilere ve denetçilere bildirdiniz mi? Bu kararların alınmasına katıldınız mı, yoksa karar sürecinin dışında mı kaldınız? Karayipler’deki Saint Vincent adasında kurulu Artsmrkts Ltd hesabında bugün özel kalemlerinizin gözaltına alındığı soruşturmada geçen Vişne Madencilik ve TERA/Hedef hisseleriyle aynı sepette 15,5 milyon lot Türkiye Sigorta pozisyonu taşındığından haberiniz oldu mu? Daha anlaşılır soralım: Maslak’tan yönetilen Artsmrkts, Londra’daki GildenCrest ve İsviçre’deki Century City Securities ile herhangi bir hesap, para transferi, yatırım veya talimat ilişkiniz oldu mu? Bu kuruluşlar üzerinden sizin hesabınıza ya da menfaatinize işlem yapıldı mı?

Yönettiğiniz kamu bağlantılı şirketler bu fonlara para yatırırken siz kendi hesaplarınızdaki fonları veya hisseleri satıp paranızı çektiniz mi? Şirketlerin para yatırdığı tarihlerle sizin satış yapıp para çektiğiniz tarihleri karşılaştırmalı olarak açıklayacak mısınız? Bu kurumsal yatırımların karşılığında hangi varlıklar alındı, kimlerin fon iade talepleri ödendi? Kamu şirketlerinin yatırdığı 100 milyon TL’nin fonda batık kalırken sizin ve diğer imtiyazlı yatırımcıların fondan erken çıkışını (nakde dönmesini) finanse edip etmediği araştırıldı mı? TERA ve bağlantılı fonlara yapılan yatırımlar konusunda risk birimleri veya denetçiler sizi uyardı mı? Uyardılarsa hangi önlemleri aldınız? Önlem alınmadıysa neden alınmadı? Türkiye Sigorta’nın bilançosunun açıklanmasının ertelendiği ve 4 milyar TL’lik geri alım maliyeti oluştuğu yönündeki iddialar doğru mu? Doğruysa bu gelişmelerin söz konusu yatırımlarla bağlantısı nedir ve sorumluluğu kim taşıyor?”

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Caitlyn Clark
title: Interview: How We Beat Back Nonunion Subcontracting at Kroger
content:
After more than six months fighting against Kroger’s use of non-union subcontractors, members of Food and Commercial Workers (UFCW) Local 700 in Indiana won a 

victory

 in August, when Kroger announced it would be ending the Retail Odyssey direct store delivery (DSD) program entirely.




This means more hours for union members—thanks to those who organized to enforce the contract, file grievances, and educate their co-workers. In this interview conducted by Caitlyn Clark of the reform group Essential Workers for Democracy, shop stewards Andrea Reynolds and Kristen Jackson explain how they did it.




Essential Workers for Democracy: What is Retail Odyssey and why is it a problem? 




Andrea Reynolds:

 Retail Odyssey is a nonunion third-party contractor that solely services Kroger stores. Normally RO does things like rearranging a store layout or auditing whether products are displayed the way the brand wants.




A few months ago, the Kroger Central Division here in Indiana developed a new program utilizing RO employees to stock direct store delivery vendor items on weekends. [

DSD items are delivered straight to the store by the supplier, rather than coming through a Kroger warehouse.

]




Why is this a problem? Kroger has employees who need hours. This isn't “extra help.” Kroger wants to phase nonunion third parties into the stores to cut hours of its union employees. If we don't speak up, it will only get worse. We’ve seen this happen already with cut fruit vendors, outdoor floral products, floor cleaning, and gift cards, just to name a few. 




How did you and your co-workers start taking on Retail Odyssey?

 




Reynolds:

 We immediately started gathering as much accurate information as we could and passing it along to our co-workers. We shared information in our Facebook group and we shared flyers with our co-workers.




We wanted them to know why this was a problem and what they could do about it. The company wants us to think that third parties are there to make our jobs easier. But time and time again, we see our hours cut and wonder why. 




We also passed along the feedback of our vendors. Their products were being damaged, mixed with other vendors, and stocked incorrectly. 




Kristen Jackson:

 Although in the pharmacy, I am not as impacted, my union brothers and sisters are. As a steward, I try my best to let others know what is wrong with RO taking our work.




I walked around and talked to my co-workers about what the RO workers were allowed to stock. I told them if they saw them, to please take pictures, talk to the RO workers, and be nice.













By having a standardized report form, members could make sure grievances were airtight.










How did you collect information to file grievances? How did you make sure grievances got filed and processed?




Reynolds:

 Retail Odyssey was scheduled to work Friday through Sunday, noon to 6 p.m. I had a lot of conversations with members I knew were normally there during those hours.




I instructed them to take photos, make note of the day, time, duration of stocking, what non-vendor products were stocked, and anyone who witnessed it. We had them send this info to our stewards or trusted employees who could contact our union rep.




Every week after the grievance was filed, we messaged our reps asking for status of the grievance. We didn't want it to fall through the cracks.




Jackson:

 I just went up to the RO workers, introduced myself as a steward, and let them know I would be taking pictures of them and why. I explained, “I'm not against you having a job. I'm here to document Kroger violating our contract.”




The RO workers were understanding, and would tell me that the manager told them to stock our product and let me file the grievances. The RO worker at my store location would tell me exactly what he stocked, so I could file the grievances effectively. We filed three grievances at my location. 




What advice would you give to anyone dealing with non-union subcontracting?




Reynolds:

 Document, document, document! You need to prove there was a contract violation.




Talk with your co-workers about how to document. Contact your rep. Don't hesitate to ask for help from a steward or a trusted member.




You have power in your numbers. The more members speaking up, the better! We filed so many grievances in six months that the third-party DSD program has officially ended. When we fight, we win. 			




Andrea Reynolds and Kristen Jackson are UFCW Local 700 shop stewards in Kokomo and Zionsville, Indiana. Caitlyn Clark is the director of Essential Workers for Democracy.

author: Chris Walker
title: Prosecutors Filed Over 900 Cases of “Pregnancy-Related Crimes” Since Dobbs
content:
Most of the charges being brought stem from laws that were never meant to apply to pregnancy.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

A new report has found that, in the years following the Supreme Court’s overturning of abortion rights established in Roe v. Wade, hundreds of people have been charged with crimes related to their pregnancies.

Reproductive rights nonprofit Pregnancy Justice documented at least 902 cases of such charges in the three years after the court’s Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health decision. The data suggests that more cases likely exist, since the research only covers the period from the summer of 2022 through 2025, and doesn’t include instances where people were charged over the past year.

Most of the charges being brought against pregnant people relate to their actions while pregnant, pregnancy loss, or births, Pregnancy Justice noted in its report. The cases are primarily based on long-existing criminal statutes, not new abortion ban laws, with 876 of the 955 charges documented relating to allegations of child neglect, endangerment, or abuse.

While the report notes that 23 states charged people with pregnancy-related crimes during that three-year period, a majority of the cases were in just three states — South Carolina (381 cases), Oklahoma (222), and Alabama (204).

These charges included claims from prosecutors that individuals were abusing drugs or other substances during their pregnancies; failed to provide an adequate amount of prenatal care for their fetus or infant; and attempted to obtain, obtained, or even merely researched abortion services.

What’s more, prosecutors overwhelmingly charged pregnant people under statutes that allow them to obtain convictions without proving that there was any actual harm to a fetus or infant. According to the report, close to 95 percent of the cases involved such charges.

“These numbers show that the criminalization of pregnancy in this country is not some distant or hypothetical consequence of abortion bans,” said Lourdes A. Rivera, president of Pregnancy Justice. “It is already happening.”

Law enforcement is using laws that were never intended to apply to pregnancy to investigate, arrest, and punish women, and it’s only getting worse since the overturning of Roe. Pregnant people deserve health care, support, and dignity — not handcuffs.

Beyond criminal charges that pregnant people have faced, abortion bans and other restrictions on reproductive health care have also led to deadly outcomes in the years since the Dobbs decision.

A ProPublica report from last month, for example, found around 200 documented instances of people dying from ectopic pregnancies from 2020-2025 — a rate that is about double what it had been in the preceding six-year period.

The report noted that doctors, perhaps concerned that their action could be viewed as illegal by their state governments, may be hesitating to offer treatment when an ectopic pregnancy occurs. Such pregnancies, in which a fertilized egg implants outside the uterus, often in a fallopian tube, are in no way viable and can often lead to life-threatening complications.

In an op-ed for Truthout in the spring of 2025, Lauren Rankin, reproductive rights author and journalist, wrote: “Under abortion bans, the life of the pregnant person is a secondary concern.”

“Doctors are afraid of being prosecuted for treating a potentially life-threatening health issue; someone facing a miscarriage is afraid of being prosecuted for flushing the toilet; and a teenager and her mother were imprisoned because she didn’t know where else to turn for an abortion in her state,” Rankin said, discussing real-life examples of how abortion restrictions have detrimentally affected people’s lives.

“This isn’t an accident, but an intentional byproduct of overturning Roe and ending the constitutional right to an abortion,” Rankin added. “Ending Roe was meant to ripple far beyond abortion — it was meant to erode the personhood of pregnant people, to eradicate their full-fledged autonomy and ability to determine the course of their own lives. When you reduce someone to less than a person in the eyes of the state, criminalization is never far behind.”

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Jen Fifield
title: Ballot Rejections Soared in Rural Counties After USPS Cost-Cutting Measures
content:
The rates of primary ballots rejected for arriving late this year doubled or tripled in some areas compared to 2022.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

In early August, election workers north of Spokane, Washington, went across the street to the post office to check for late mail-in ballots. It was three days after the primary and they were expecting no more than a few dozen.

Instead, their mailbox was brimming with envelopes — more than 500 of them, each a vote that wouldn’t count. The sight was “jarring,” said Auditor Lori Larsen, a Republican who oversees voting in Stevens County.

Across the region, other election officials were getting similar jolts. In the 11 predominately rural counties in eastern Washington, nearly 2,000 ballots came in late, compared to about 600 in 2022, the previous midterm primary.

In recent weeks, concerns about mail-in voting disruptions have focused almost entirely on President Donald Trump’s now-shelved plan to sharply restrict who can vote by mail.

But a ProPublica data analysis shows that delays resulting from the U.S. Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures have endangered the validity of ballots cast in rural areas, not only in Washington, but across the country.

Over the past three years, as mail volume continued to plummet and annual deficits ballooned, the Postal Service started consolidating the processing of first-class mail at larger regional plants instead of at smaller hubs closer to local post offices. Then, in a little-noted switch that mostly took effect after the 2024 election, the agency cut the frequency of mail pickups in half at many post offices 50 miles or more from these processing plants, from twice daily to once.

The changes often added a day or more to delivery time and, most importantly for ballots, pushed back postmarking, which doesn’t happen until mail reaches the regional centers.

In this year’s primary, the effects of the cuts were clearest in five states that make detailed data on mail-in ballots available: Washington, California, Ohio, North Carolina and Oregon. All have or recently had grace periods allowing ballots to count if they come in after Election Day as long as they’re postmarked by the deadline.

In these states, the number of ballots rejected for arriving late soared in counties affected by the service changes compared to 2022, ProPublica’s analysis showed.

Rejection rates in counties where services were cut doubled or tripled from what they were four years ago, dwarfing any increases in counties where postal pickups remained as they were, our analysis showed. In urban Spokane, for example, the number of ballots rejected for being late actually dropped this year.

Across the five states, the delays have had the most substantial effect in areas that voted for Trump in 2024, ProPublica’s analysis shows. In Washington, Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, a Democrat, said he sees the service changes directed by Republican appointees leading the Postal Service as a way to undermine mail-in voting.

“I don’t think they realized how much it was going to affect their voter base,” he said, adding that Washington has “a lot of rural Republican voters.”

Postal Service leaders say such delays are less likely in the Nov. 3 general election because of “extraordinary measures” the agency puts into place for these votes, when there’s typically far more turnout. They have circulated a memo to the nation’s more than 30,000 post offices saying that for the 10 days before the election, managers should separate completed ballots from other first-class mail and deliver those intended for local election offices the day they come in.

At an Oct. 15 news conference, Postal Service leaders emphasized the agency’s longstanding recommendation that voters mail ballots back at least a week before their states’ deadlines, while defending the agency’s ability to fast-track ballots through the system.

“We work to identify and address issues quickly,” said Amber McReynolds, chair of the Postal Service board of governors, “so ballots can continue to move swiftly from election offices to voters and from voters back to election offices.”

Election consultants, researchers and former Postal Service officials told ProPublica that the guidance for the upcoming vote gave more detailed directions on how to expedite ballots. They said they hoped the agency’s special measures would limit delays, but some said mistakes were likely.

“I don’t think we can say with any kind of conviction that there will be no ballots rejected,” said Tammy Patrick, chief programs officer of the National Association of Election Officials. “It isn’t a question of ‘if,’ but a question of ‘how many.’”

A pilot program instituting the delivery changes in 18 regions before the 2024 election ran into problems. An audit by the Postal Service’s inspector general found that agency staff in these areas sometimes didn’t handle ballots correctly, mainly because instructions weren’t clearly communicated. (A Postal Service spokesperson said “learnings from the pilot” have been applied as the program has expanded.)

After this year’s primary, reports by media outlets noted that mail-in ballot rejection rates were higher than in the past, but ProPublica’s analysis shows these increases were directly connected to Postal Service changes. Research published in September by the Brookings Institution also found this connection, projecting that if the pattern held in the general election, tens of thousands of mail-in ballots could be rejected.

At least seven closely contested congressional districts — including Washington’s 3rd, California’s 22nd and North Carolina’s 11th — are in areas that were affected by service changes in the primary, ProPublica found.

Elena Patel, who conducted the Brookings analysis, said service changes may still imperil mail-in votes in the general election.

“I think there remain risks to ballots,” she said, adding that the Postal Service’s plan for the general election “depends on flawless execution.”

Mail-in voting has become more popular over the last decade, with many states broadening access to it during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Nearly 1 in 3 Americans voted this way in 2022 and 2024. Trump himself frequently votes by mail, and in recent weeks has started to encourage his supporters to do so as well, though he has claimed without evidence that the process is rife with fraud.

The Postal Service has mostly ensured the timely delivery of hundreds of millions of ballots, even as mail volume overall has dropped 50% from its high in 2006.

When Louis DeJoy was appointed postmaster general in spring 2020, he inherited an $81 billion operating deficit and rapidly took steps such as eliminating overtime to reduce costs, under pressure from Trump and others in his administration. (DeJoy did not respond to questions from ProPublica.)

The NAACP sued that August, alleging the measures could affect mail-in votes in that year’s general election. Courts ordered DeJoy to reverse some of the cuts and the Postal Service agreed to implement special procedures to ensure ballots weren’t delayed. The Postal Service has continued following those procedures since.

Still, DeJoy went forward with a 10-year restructuring plan designed to save the agency billions. It ended evening pickups from some post offices, often in rural areas. Trucks serving these places travel long distances and at times were mostly empty. This part of the plan — called regional transportation optimization, or RTO — was projected to eventually save the Postal Service $4 billion a year.

The agency announced the national rollout of the RTO plan in 2024, but DeJoy agreed to pause it leading up to that year’s November election, leaving only about 4,000 ZIP codes in the pilot project affected by the service changes.

In January 2025, the Postal Regulatory Commission, which oversees the Postal Service, warned that moving forward with the plan would be disruptive to rural communities and might not save as much money as expected. The Postal Service rolled out the reductions anyway, extending the changes to almost 20,000 ZIP codes to date. Officials said they expect the system to be fully implemented within two years.

This January, the agency put out a statement saying the transportation cuts would mean it took longer for mail, including ballots, to be postmarked and delivered. But the Postal Service didn’t specify which voters would be affected by the slowdowns and which wouldn’t.

Though the delay from RTO is often only a day, mail can be delayed longer if it’s deposited in a mailbox after the daily pickup time, or just before Sunday or a holiday.

A Postal Service spokesperson said the agency told election officials that RTO would change schedules and reemphasized the need for voters to get their ballots in the mail at least a week ahead of time. Election officials in Washington said the Postal Service wasn’t direct enough about the fact that the changes would lead to delays in delivering and postmarking ballots.

“What they said was, ‘We are going to change the way we do postmarks,’” said Hobbs, Washington’s secretary of state. “That was it.”

Patel, the Brookings analyst and a former Postal Regulatory Commission employee, said that more direct communication to voters could have helped change their behavior. “That’s the part that I think has not been super transparent about the whole process,” she said.

Many of the areas that saw a spike in late ballots were in Western states, which were the earliest and most enthusiastic adopters of expanded mail-in voting.

In 2004, Washington became the second state to start conducting all-mail elections, in which every eligible voter automatically receives a mail-in ballot. Most residents vote by putting their ballots in drop boxes. Still, in 2024, about 33% put them in the mail.

In the 30 mostly rural Washington counties most affected by RTO, the percentage of ballots postmarked late more than tripled compared to the 2022 primary, ProPublica found.

In Garfield County, in southeastern Washington, 19 ballots — nearly 1 in 10 cast — had late postmarks this year. In 2022, only a single ballot was postmarked late. In Pend Oreille County, in northeast Washington along the Idaho panhandle, 6% of ballots were rejected for arriving late, compared to 1% in the 2022 primary.

“It was pretty awful telling people we couldn’t count their votes,” said Marianne Nichols, Pend Oreille’s longtime auditor. “They were quite upset because they felt like, ‘Why? This was in the mailbox on election day, the post office picked it up and had it.’ They felt like it should have counted.”

In Stevens County, the percentage of ballots rejected for having a late postmark jumped to 8%, from 1% in 2022.

Steve Hutkins, a retired professor who analyzes the effect of Postal Service changes on Savethepostoffice.com, also found that places in Washington with RTO had more ballot rejections during local elections earlier this year for school board and other measures. The patterns “set off the alarm bells,” he said.

Stuart Holmes, the state’s director of elections, said he reached out to Postal Service officials to find out what had happened, but got few answers and no specifics on delays related to RTO, which were a “total surprise,” he said.

Election officials in California and Oregon also reported thousands more ballots rejected for arriving late during their primaries. Counties affected by RTO, including Kern County, California, had substantially higher rates of ballots rejected for mail-related reasons, ProPublica found.

Kern County’s assistant registrar of voters, Laura Cantu, said election officials are urging rural voters to use drop boxes to cast their ballots in the general election.

The expansion of RTO had a similar effect in North Carolina and Ohio, where the rates of late ballots were about twice as high in counties affected by the restructuring as rates in counties that weren’t. Since 2022, these states have also eliminated grace periods in which ballots postmarked by Election Day could count even if they arrived later. Voters unused to the tighter deadlines also could have contributed to an increase in late ballots.

ProPublica didn’t find any association between RTO and higher rates of late ballots in Wisconsin, even though clerks reported delays involving mail-in ballots cast in its state election, held this spring. (Other Postal Service changes may have contributed to the delays.)

Wisconsin’s data does not distinguish ballots sent by mail from those cast in drop boxes or in person, making it impossible to definitively measure rejection rates just for ballots returned by mail. Election researchers said Wisconsin’s deadline for mail ballots, which must come into election offices by 8 p.m. on Election Day, also probably had an effect.

“If you know that you don’t have a grace period, it probably affects voter behavior,” said Patel, the Brookings researcher.

Recent Postal Service audits have found that RTO-related changes had saved the agency about $2.8 billion by the end of fiscal year 2025 — less money than expected — and are slowing down all first-class mail, not just ballots. Residents of rural areas are waiting longer for everything from prescriptions to bills, a report published in September by the Postal Service’s inspector general said.

A Postal Service spokesperson still defended the plan, both for financial reasons and to adjust to the changing marketplace. “These savings are both significant and necessary,” he said.

In the lead-up to Nov. 3, the agency’s plan is to route ballots meant for local election offices to a nearby postal facility or directly to their destination. They shouldn’t go to regional plants, which the Postal Service says should minimize delays.

Larsen, the Stevens County auditor, is encouraging Washington voters to deposit their ballots in drop boxes rather than relying on the mail. Since the primary, she’s increased the number of red, white and blue drop boxes that sit outside government buildings from seven to 12. Near each box, there’s a large sign encouraging people to take selfies when they vote and send the photos to Larsen.

In prior years, Larsen said, she avoided telling voters how or when to vote, concerned they might regret choices they made if critical information later emerged about the candidates. That’s no longer uppermost in her mind.

“Now we are more concerned that we get your ballot,” she said.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

author: Sara Luterman
title: Nursing Home Residents Have a Right to Vote — Despite What Trump CMS Agency Says
content:
The Nursing Home Reform Act of 1987 requires facilities to support their residents in exercising their rights.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Cindy Napolitan and her daughter Melissa have multiple sclerosis, a degenerative condition in which the immune system attacks the brain, spinal cord and nerves. They have lived together at a nursing home in Mesquite, Texas, for nine years. In previous elections, Cindy and Melissa Napolitan voted by mail, but this year they took an unusual step: They voted in person. They worried their mail-in ballots — and even their in-person votes — may not be counted.

“I’ve never worried like this before. I’ve never worried that I don’t have the proper ID. I’ve never worried that somebody is going to intimidate me. Will I encounter somebody that’s going to threaten me or make me feel less than? So yeah, I’m very worried, and I shouldn’t be,” Cindy Napolitan said. “I shouldn’t have to be worried about stuff like that. This is the 19th Amendment. I’m allowed to vote.”

Nursing home residents are guaranteed the right to vote. Around two-thirds of all nursing home residents in the United States are women, making aging and long-term care gendered issues.

There is no data on how many nursing home residents exercise that right. Cindy, 70, and Melissa Napolitan, 48, at least, feel like they’ve had good experiences with voting at their facility. Cindy Napolitan, in particular, has worked with the activities coordinator to organize rides to the polls for her, her daughter and other interested residents.

“We are scheduled to go on the first day of early voting. So in case there are any issues that we come across, we still have time to rectify the situation and be allowed to vote,” Cindy Napolitan said.

Cindy and Melissa Napolitan are more concerned this year than in previous years about government interference and voter suppression. Their fears are not unfounded: Experts and advocates for the rights of nursing home residents, older adults and people with disabilities are worried too.

In July, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services rescinded previous guidance affirming that nursing home residents have the right to vote.

“The memo does not alter the underlying law. Nursing homes are governed by the Nursing Home Reform Act of 1987 and its implementing regulations,” said Nina Kohn, a professor at Syracuse University and expert on elder law. “That law still requires facilities to support their residents in exercising their rights as Americans.”

The memo also emphasized voter fraud in nursing homes, specifically around mail-in ballots. For years, President Trump has disparaged mail-in ballots, insisting without evidence that fraudulent votes by mail had a role in his loss during the 2020 presidential election. His comments have led to some states restricting who can use a mail-in ballot and in what contexts.

According to experts, including Kohn, there is no evidence that voter fraud is a serious or widespread problem in nursing homes. Instead, Kohn is concerned about the chilling effect that it may have on residents’ rights.

“The language in the memo itself is intimidating, and it may understandably make staff think that they could face criminal prosecution or be in some other form of legal trouble if they help residents vote,” Kohn said.

Cindy and Melissa Napolitan do everything together — and on Monday, they voted together. They are also roommates at the facility; most people living in nursing homes are assigned roommates who are strangers.

“Unlike other people that have roommates that don’t get along, I’m very lucky and fortunate that I have somebody that loves me and I love her,” Cindy Napolitan said.

This is the second time Cindy and Melissa Napolitan have voted in person since entering a nursing home. The first time was during the 2024 presidential election.

“I’ve been checking my status weekly to make sure that I haven’t been dropped off the voter rolls, making sure my daughter and I don’t have some sort of issue that says that we can’t vote,” Cindy Napolitan said.

People living in nursing homes and other long-term care facilities face specific barriers. Some residents may need assistance filling out their ballots because they lack the movement or dexterity to hold a pen or press buttons on a computer screen. People with dexterity or coordination issues may also be unable to produce the same signature twice.

“With some forms of voting, some states will use your ID to verify your signature. If your signature looks different than the one on your ID, your ballot might get thrown out. Or there is a ballot hearing process, so you could be notified of that and able to fix it, but it is a bunch of extra steps that impact disabled voters at higher rates,” said Alexia Kemerling, director of Accessible Democracy for the nonpartisan American Association of People with Disabilities.

An increasing number of states now require voters to show some form of photo identification. This can also be a problem for many nursing home residents because they may no longer have a driver’s license. They also may no longer have passports because they aren’t traveling internationally. States have other forms of identification, but getting them can involve complex paperwork and multiple trips.

Some states will accommodate voters in nursing homes and other facilities so they can acquire state identification that isn’t a driver’s license.

“My license expired, and so I had to apply for an identification card. I had to coordinate with them to come here instead of going to the DMV because I wasn’t about to do that. I didn’t know how long I would have to sit there. I didn’t have a ride,” Melissa Napolitan said. “They came and took our pictures, and filled out all the forms for us.”

Kemerling objects to the idea that this somehow renders nursing home residents and other people with disabilities incapable of making an independent choice.

“In the disability community, we don’t necessarily mean that independence means doing something alone. Independence is having control over how something is done,” Kemerling said. “Just because you need someone to assist you as part of the voting process does not mean that you are giving up your choice.”

There are steps nursing home residents and their families can take to advocate for their rights. Lori Smetanka is the executive director of the National Consumer Voice for Quality Long Term Care, which advocates on behalf of people living in nursing homes and assisted living facilities. Her organization produces a fact sheet for nursing home residents enumerating their rights and how they can advocate for themselves.

“For the generation of people that are living in long-term care facilities, it’s largely an older population of people,” Smetanka said. “It’s very important to them to exercise their right to vote. When we talk with residents, it is very important to them. Some of them have really advocated very heavily for themselves in order to be able to do that.”

Smetanka emphasized that it is not only up to residents and their families to advocate for their rights.

“If the resident has the ability to raise the questions about it, they certainly should be doing that, Smetanka said. “Families should be asking, but staff should be asking too — ‘What can we do to help you vote this year? Who is interested in voting? How can we get the requirements in place so you can cast your ballots?’” At some facilities, voting may not be on staff’s radar, despite the legal requirements.

Cindy Napolitan has been active in advocating for her right to vote, as well as the rights of her fellow residents, and she encourages others who are able to do the same.

“I’m very vocal and very into advocating for our residents here and making sure that they’re all able to vote,” Cindy Napolitan said. “I’m the one that will start telling our activity director that there’s a deadline for filing to become a registered voter. There’s a deadline to file for a mail-in ballot, and I’m usually the one that makes sure that those things get done.”

When asked what she wants people to understand most about voting in nursing homes, Melissa Napolitan pushed back against the insinuation that nursing homes are hotbeds of voter fraud and that she and her peers don’t have their own opinions.

“I think that people maybe don’t take the time to realize that people in nursing homes aren’t just here waiting to die,” Melissa Napolitan said.

title: «No Data Center»: maxi scritta di Extinction Rebellion sull’edificio in cui dovrebbe sorgere il più grande data center d’Italia
content:
Riceviamo e pubblichiamo il comunicato stampa di Extinction Rebellion Torino.







22 ottobre 2026, Moncalieri (Torino) – 

Extinction Rebellion ha realizzato delle enormi scritte “No Data Center” sullo stabilimento dismesso dell’ex Ilte e appeso uno striscione con la frase “Fermare l’ecocidio”. Una protesta per denunciare l’impatto ambientale, sanitario e sociale dei data center e di quello che potrebbe diventare il più grande impianto del Paese. «In un mondo che sta collassando, non c’è spazio per altre strutture ecocide»




“No Data Center”. È l’enorme scritta realizzata da Extinction Rebellion sulla facciata dello stabilimento ex-Ilte di Moncalieri, alle porte di Torino, edificio al centro dell’iter per la realizzazione di quello che potrebbe diventare il 

più grande data center

 d’Italia. Accanto alla scritta principale, visibile anche dall’autostrada e da Moncalieri, una seconda scritta “Stop Tech Fascism” (Stop tecno-fascismo) è stata realizzata sulla facciata laterale e uno striscione srotolato su una terza facciata con scritto “Fermare l’ecocidio”.




«Lasciamo qui questo messaggio affinché sia visibile ovunque e serva da monito a tutte le amministrazioni»,

 spiega Extinction Rebellion. 

«Un data center di queste dimensioni ha impatti ambientali, sanitari e sociali pericolosissimi ed è incompatibile con qualsiasi obiettivo climatico. In un mondo che sta collassando e in cui il costo della vita sta soffocando la maggioranza della popolazione, non c’è spazio per investimenti miliardari per strutture ecocide».

 Al centro della protesta ci sono gli enormi consumi energetici e idrici dei data center, oltre ai possibili effetti sociali e sanitari. Un impianto come quello ipotizzato a Moncalieri, da 527 megawatt e 4,5 miliardi di euro, consumerebbe tanta energia 

quanto tutte le famiglie

 piemontesi. A ciò si aggiunge l’acqua necessaria a raffreddare i server, in una regione alle prese con una siccità cronica, che ad agosto ha 

avviato le procedure

 per chiedere lo stato di calamità naturale per l’emergenza idrica. Anche i refrigeranti identificati come soluzione al consumo d’acqua possono in realtà comportare rischi: 

molti contengono

 PFAS, le cosiddette «sostanze chimiche eterne», che si disperdono nell’ambiente e si accumulano nel corpo umano. Un problema che il Piemonte conosce bene: a Spinetta Marengo, nell’Alessandrino, la produzione di PFAS dello stabilimento Solvay 

ha già esposto

 gli abitanti alla contaminazione, e queste stesse sostanze 

sono state rilevate

 anche nell’acqua potabile di oltre 70 comuni del torinese. In ultimo, i data center sono diventati veri e propri 

bersagli militari strategici

 negli ultimi anni, trasformando le infrastrutture digitali e l’Intelligenza Artificiale in nuovi teatri di guerra.




«Moltiplicare queste enormi infrastrutture è folle: significa aumentare la pressione sulle risorse naturali e la dipendenza dai combustibili fossili, proprio quando la crisi climatica impone di azzerare le emissioni e contenere i consumi»,

 aggiunge Extinction Rebellion. Nel 

rapporto «Energy and AI»

 del 2025 dell’Agenzia Internazionale dell’Energia (IEA), la domanda dei maxi data center è infatti indicata come uno dei motori della crescita della produzione elettrica da gas e carbone fino alla fine del decennio. Lo stesso assessore regionale all’Ambiente, Matteo Marnati, ha ammesso che le rinnovabili non basteranno e ha annunciato che 

chiederà al governo

 di escludere i consumi dei data center dal calcolo degli obiettivi di decarbonizzazione. Durante un convegno all’Ordine degli Avvocati di Torino 

ha poi dichiarato

 che per alimentarli «è imprescindibile pensare all’energia nucleare». 

«Le scelte del governo e della Regione sono surreali: prima creano il problema, poi impongono una soluzione che ne genera un altro, ancora più grave, spacciandola per inevitabile»,

 replica Extinction Rebellion.




Il progetto del più grande data center di Italia ha già incontrato i primi ostacoli: a ottobre il sindaco di Moncalieri lo 

ha definito

 «non accoglibile», anche se il Comune ha tempo fino a fine mese per la decisione. Per questo la protesta è andata in scena proprio sullo stabilimento: mentre l’iter prosegue, la scritta resterà lì, visibile a tutti. Intanto i cittadini del posto 

hanno lanciato

 una raccolta firme per fermare il progetto. La richiesta di Extinction Rebellion è netta: fermare il maxi data center, bonificare l’area e restituirla alla comunità. 

«Al posto di altro cemento e di una nuova struttura energivora, si avvii un percorso partecipato per rinaturalizzare l’area o destinarla all’emergenza abitativa»,

 conclude il movimento.
