title: The Student Revolt in France Spreads : Moving Forward with Rage and Solidarity
content:
October 17 marked one of the fiercest days of mass protest in recent French history. Scenes of ferocious resistance unfolded throughout the day, not only in Paris but in 


Bordeaux

, 


Dijon

, 

Marseille

, 

Nancy

, and dozens of other cities across the country. Some observers have described the day’s events as 

more explosive

 than the 

Yellow Vest movement

 of 2018-19—and the rebellion shows no sign of slowing.




How did we get here? Courageous high school students 

have been protesting for weeks

 against abominable conditions in schools, the rise of the extreme right, and the bleak prospects they face in a world dominated by technocrats and tech barons. Alongside growing anti-government protests from 

Albania

, 

Italy

, 

Spain

, and beyond in recent days, the French student rebellions may herald the emergence of a new wave of global struggle.




In this article, our correspondent from Paris explains the context behind the youth rebellion, tracks the movement’s growth over the two weeks leading up to October 17 and the government’s failed attempts to repress or to pacify it, and clarifies the stakes moving forward.




Stay tuned for a full report on the uprising of October 17 and the ongoing rebellions across France and beyond.







 




Thousands gather to protest police violence and support the students in revolt (Nantes, October 6, 2026)













This update on the student unrest in France picks up where we ended 

our previous report

, on the eve of the national call to take the streets on October 6, 2026.




The stakes were high on this crucial day of action. It was critical to show massive solidarity with the high school students fighting like hell against the empty future looming on their horizon. The day presented an ideal opportunity to expand the scope of the current movement by joining forces to resist the authoritarian state power that has been growing stronger every day.




The following article provides further context and analysis to understand the current situation in France, along with reports on what went down in the streets over these last rebellious weeks.




Background: The 

Banlieues

 and the Enemy Within




When governments or powerful institutions feel threatened, they often strive to reaffirm their authority by inventing scapegoats to hold responsible for all supposed misfortunes. By invoking the menace of an “enemy within,” politicians can shift blame for systemic problems that have resulted from their own actions onto a specific category of individuals. In France, the most common targets are the residents of the 

banlieues

, the impoverished suburbs on the outskirts of Paris and other cities.




At the beginning of the student blockades, the movement remained limited to a handful of high schools in these Parisian suburbs. In response, President Emmanuel Macron and his ministers decided to react quickly and do everything in their power to silence this emerging wave of youth protest. Due to the location of the first blockades, authorities believed that they could act more freely and repress the unrest with impunity, since these specific territories have been targeted for generations by all government administrations across political lines.




The condition of the 

banlieues

, which remain populated by descendants of the French Empire’s colonized subjects, reflects France’s ongoing role as a 

neocolonial power

 that continues to exploit African territories. Consider the disastrous 

oil project

 in Uganda orchestrated by the France-based multinational company TotalEnergies, or the 

corruption case

 involving the French far-right business tycoon Vincent Bolloré and his bribery and money laundering schemes across West African ports.




French governments and corporations have no scruples about extracting enormous wealth from African countries. This neocolonial pillaging fuels France’s position as the 

seventh richest country

 in the world today, according to the IMF. Yet despite these astronomical profits, the nation refuses to address the problems facing its post-colonial population and their descendants within its national territory.




At the twilight of France’s colonial empire, decades of occupation and racist violence had created political and economic instability across northern and western Africa. As a result, waves of migrants began leaving their countries to come to France for work in the 1950s. Upon arriving, they continued to face systemic colonial racism, relegated to the economic margins and second-class citizenship. This cheap workforce ended up gathering on the outskirts of major cities, living in makeshift neighborhoods and slums like those of 

Nanterre

 on the western edges of Paris.







 




Shantytown in the Parisian suburb of Nanterre in the 1960s










Over the following decades, urban development projects replaced these slums with massive apartment blocks into which immigrant families and low-income workers were relocated. Today, these areas are known as the 

banlieues

 (the suburbs). In mainstream French political discourse, authorities and journalists invoke the 

banlieues

 as a derogatory term that embodies all the supposed flaws of our modern society.




The 

banlieues

 also offer areas of experimentation for law enforcement. Politicians ranging from moderate to reactionary have long considered these suburbs “lawless areas” whose young residents pose a threat to the ruling order. In response, the French state consistently harasses and represses these populations to instill fear and obedience and to force them to adapt to its laws. This targeted violence reproduces old colonial strategies within the territory of the nation. For example, the “state of emergency,” developed as legal tool in former French colonies for crowd control, was first used within the borders of France in the 

banlieues

.




Past governments pushed law enforcement to increase the pressure in the suburbs, invoking the “war on drugs” and defense of their sacrosanct “democracy.” They invested in new weapons and equipment, which specific police units experimented with freely in the streets of the 

banlieues

 to test their usefulness in repressing popular mobilization. These racist police forces operate with impunity in these territories and consider every person they encounter a potential threat. As a result, numerous young people of color have been abused, injured, or killed at the hands of police, such as Zyed Benna and Bouna Traoré in 

2005

, Adama Traoré in 

2016

, and more recently, Nahel Merzouk in 

2023

.




In the face of such contemptuous violence from the French state and its armed henchmen, it is inevitable that people would organize on a grassroot level to defend themselves and counterattack against these intolerable conditions. It is simply a question of dignity and survival. Historically, the 

banlieues

 have been the settings of intense riots and confrontations with police forces, often leading to massive property destruction and arsons.




In this context, it is not a coincidence that the student blockades first emerged in these suburbs, nor that the government decided without hesitation to send in heavily equipped police forces to repress them. This response is only a logical extension of the long legacy of colonial racism directed against part of the population. The French state continues to consider working-class people and the children of immigrants as the biggest threat to its stability. Therefore, to maintain its crumbling power structure by any means necessary, its solution is to constantly terrorize these youths to contain their rebellious energy.







 




The repressive technologies used by police against students and protesters today were tested out on the populations of the 

banlieues

 (Lyon, October 6, 2026)










Keeping the Rage Alive




After more than a week of intense confrontations and blockades throughout France, it became clear that curbing the ungovernable student movement had become the number one priority of the current ruling order.




Nevertheless, the movement refused to be intimidated by the brutal repression implemented by authorities. Instead, it paid tribute in its own way to the 

Yellow Vest

 unrest that began in 2018 by rebranding its own key days of actions as “Acts.” This framework of successive mobilizations, each building on the last, maintained the pressure on politicians and law enforcement by providing regular opportunities to take the streets in massive demonstrations on a national scale.




While these national days of action appeared once or twice per week, this doesn’t mean that nothing happened the rest of the week. On the contrary, multiple forms of action—blockades, sit-ins, direct confrontations with police forces, property destruction, arsons, and more—continued to take place daily across multiple cities throughout France. This plurality of tactics, combined with the courage and determination of numerous teenagers throughout the past weeks, has enabled the unrest to last this long.







 




Clouds of tear gas in Rennes (October 6, 2026)










Act III: October 6, 2026




On the morning of Tuesday, October 6, students gathered in front of their high schools and universities to block access. This time, due to the state’s escalation of violence against the youth demonstrations over the previous days, parents and teachers decided to join the students and assembled with them in front of schools. Through their presence, they hoped to prevent intensifying repression from police forces.




For the most part, their strategy appears to have worked. Reports from different blockades during the morning mentioned that on the whole, tensions were not as high as on previous days. Nevertheless, some locations saw police officers attempting to break through the lines of some parents and teachers who were protecting students or using pepper-spray to disperse protesters.




It is difficult to confirm whether the less brutal state response that morning resulted from police reluctance due to the presence of adults among students, or from specific orders coming from government officials. After the increasing number of injuries inflicted on students over the preceding days, the government may have instructed its armed forces to be more careful while dealing with student blockades, especially with parents and teachers joining them.







 




Parents and teachers on the front line to defend their children and students (Bordeaux, October 6, 2026)










While parents and teachers joining their students on the front lines during these morning actions may have discouraged a more violent response from the state, their presence in the blockades may also have helped authorities to regain some partial control in the streets. The presence of such authority figures can play a role in discouraging rebellious behavior among young people. In the days to come, the success of the unrest may depend in part on whether students can receive support from adults while maintaining their own autonomy and momentum.




That same morning, as the first demonstrations were taking place in Lille, Lyon, Marseille, Bordeaux, Nantes, and other cities, some university students blocked their campuses to join the movement. Around noon, as people converged at the Place de la République for the Paris demonstration, authorities announced that 891 of the country’s 3700 high schools were either partially or completely closed, including 250 just in the Paris region. Contrary to the official announcements made by the government, the movement was gaining rather than losing momentum.




The Paris demonstration was scheduled to depart from Place de la République in the direction of Place de la Nation. The 3.3-kilometer pathway connecting these two major squares in eastern Paris has frequently been the scene of social movement marches and intense clashes with police forces. This time, however, we learned beforehand that police units had received orders to keep their distance from demonstrators and to not be “visible” to prevent escalating tensions. The government appeared to have adapted its law enforcement strategy for the day in response to mounting criticisms of its repression of the students since the beginning of the movement.




Before the official departure time of the procession, the square was already so packed that thousands of demonstrators had begun walking down the boulevard towards La Nation to make space for more people to join. The flow of individuals passing through Place de la République seemed endless. Massive numbers of high school and university students, teachers and other educational workers were joined by leftist organizations, trade unions, and other supporters, as well as some radicals and anarchists. The feeling among the crowds was festive, impassioned, and full of determination.




As the crowd approached Place de la Nation, the atmosphere gradually changed. Police units in riot gear were blocking adjacent streets preventing anyone from entering or exiting the procession. Marchers erected a makeshift barricade and set it ablaze in the middle of the boulevard, while several targets had their front windows smashed and their offices ransacked. After weeks of brutal attacks on the protesting students, this escalation of tactics reflected the justified rage and desire to take the offensive that many demonstrators felt.




At this point, intense confrontations with police forces began at Place de la Nation. Riot police and 

BRAV-M special units

 encountered showers of stones and projectiles thrown by courageous rioters, while the rest of the crowd of protesters that did not physically take part showed their support by chanting the classic “

Tout le monde déteste la police

” (“Everyone hates the police”) and shouting, “

ACAB

”.




Police forces used tear gas, stun grenades and rubber bullets to attempt to disperse the thick crowds entering La Nation. But people stayed, continuing to demonstrate and hanging out amid the joyful chaos. At times, officers charged demonstrators in order to snatch and arrest specific individuals, while determined individuals counterattacked them head-on and without respite. The solidarity experienced during these moments was a breath of fresh air among the thick clouds of tear gas.




At the end of the day, despite the false reassurances of the authorities in the mainstream media, the third national day of action was a clear victory for the movement. The objective of gathering masses of people in the streets to join forces with the students had been achieved. According to unions and organizations, at least 450,000 demonstrators participated across France, around one fourth in Paris. As usual, authorities announced much 

lower numbers

, estimating around 250,000 total demonstrators. Moreover, to reassure the nation of its control over the situation, the government’s Ministry of the Interior announced that 488 individuals had been arrested during the day, raising the total of arrests since the beginning of the movement to an unprecedented number of 6547.




These figures illustrate the escalation of authoritarian law enforcement doctrine in France. By comparison, during the first 26 days of the Yellow Vest movement, French police recorded around 12,000 arrests, an average of 460 each day. Eight years later, these 

figures

 have been dramatically surpassed. As of October 6, 2026, approximately 935 arrests had taken place every single day since the beginning of the movement.




Despite these disturbing figures reflecting growing mass arrests, the student movement did not back down. Their persistence in the streets shows their determination to continue fighting, not only to improve the 

conditions in their schools

 but to challenge the living hell the French authorities are drawing tighter around us every day.







 




Students building a barricade in front of their high school (Paris, October 8, 2026)










Act IV: October 8, 2026




Two days after this impressive mobilization in the streets, student unions issued another call for mass convergence in the streets to maintain pressure on the government. As they had done for nearly two weeks, students from all over the country woke up early to meet in front of their schools, build makeshift barricades, and block the main entrances.




By 8:00 am, hundreds of high schools remained blocked in different cities. In the Paris region alone, about 145 schools were either closed, blocked or experiencing some sort of disruption. The Ministry of Education announced that 224 schools were completely closed and 151 partially closed. Authorities used these figures to once again claim that the movement was losing momentum, since “94% of high schools in France were completely or partially open” on this Thursday morning.




On this new day of action, a demonstration was scheduled to take place in Paris during the afternoon. However, the city’s Police Prefecture refused to approve the initial route requested by student unions. Instead, authorities only allowed students and protesters to converge and gather at Place de la Bastille, an ideal location for 

kettling

 large crowds of individuals by closing all access to the square.




Nevertheless, an estimated 

25,000 students and other demonstrators

 gathered at La Bastille, while demonstrations also took place in Lille, Lyon, Marseille, Nantes, Rennes, Toulon, and other cities.




After several uneventful hours in the plaza, confusion began to spread among demonstrators, as no one knew where to leave the demonstration with police units holding their lines in front of every potential exit. The crowd simmered as people moved from one street to another seeking a way to escape from this trap.




Unsurprisingly, this stressful situation led to clashes with law enforcement. As the sun set, tensions between protesters and police escalated. To “clear the square,” police forces carried out repeated violent charges and shot tear gas canisters, rubber bullets, and sting ball grenades at demonstrators. Courageous rioters answered by shooting fireworks and throwing paving stones, glass bottles, and other projectiles. Authorities struggling to disperse the remaining protesters deployed a water cannon. Reports suggested that several individuals were injured in the clashes that afternoon. While the last groups of demonstrators were still resisting police attacks at La Bastille and in the nearby streets, other demonstrators attempted to regroup at Place de la Nation, but were rapidly surrounded by officers.







 




Riot police units attempt to clear out 

La Bastille

 (Paris, October 8, 2026)










At the end of the day, the government 

announced

 that 71,500 people had participated in the afternoon demonstrations across the country, including 25,000 in Paris. 55,000 took part in actions in front of high schools, of whom only some joined the afternoon processions and gatherings. Officials reported 504 arrests on October 8.




But government statistics should be interpreted with extreme caution. For example, authorities claimed that since the beginning of the movement on September 17, 215 students, 85 teachers and education staff members, and 800 police officers had been injured. These figures seem dubious, given the unlikelihood that heavily equipped police officers would receive injuries at far higher rates than mostly unarmed high school students and other protesters. As always during protest movements, the war of numbers offers authorities a useful tool to build their narrative and justify their actions.




Repressions and Concessions: The State Tries to Undermine Solidarity




In the face of this increasing wave of solidarity with students and boiling anger against government inaction and 

police violence

, the Macron administration desperately attempted to keep up appearances while deploying strategies to divide the movement and regain control.




During a speech to the National Assembly on October 6, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu reiterated the need to deploy large numbers of law enforcement officers in the streets to counter the “violence” spread by the student movement. This shows the government’s willingness to legitimize the use of brutal force against the nation’s teenagers without second-guessing its policies or even admitting the existence of “police violence”.




All sorts of media outlets have widely reported how students have been insulted, assaulted, brutalized, and injured by police forces since the beginning of the movement. In response, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez 

stated

 that law enforcement actions have been carried out with “the utmost proportionality” and that he refused to apologize for any of the state’s actions since the emergence of the movement.







 




Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, who is in charge of the management of public order in response to the students protest movement (Paris, October 7, 2026)










In the same breath, without a hint of shame for its glaring hypocrisy, the government also 

announced

 that the use of stun grenades by police against the student movement would be suspended until further notice, following the tragic 

loss of a hand by young protestor

 on October 5. Such decisions refute the government’s own narrative of “proportionality,” as they are well aware that they are targeting teenagers with military weapons intended to cause physical or mental injury, if not death. This hypocrisy, while not surprising, remains infuriating.




Hoping to divert attention from the protestors’ demands, the government also announced its decision to accelerate discussions regarding the voting of a bill named “

casseurs-payeurs

.” This new repressive measure was first proposed last May in the aftermath of the riots and lootings that followed the victory of the PSG (the Parisian football team) during the final game of the Champions League. Its aim is simple: to make the families of suspected rioters pay for damages they allegedly caused. This law, a favorite proposal of the extreme right for years, would force any individual who knowingly took part in a group that committed violence, theft, or damage to pay up to 10,000€ [over $11,000] each towards repairs.




But the law goes beyond restitution into criminalizing participation in nearly any public resistance. Authorities will not have to prove that a specific individual broke anything; simply belonging to a group of “rioters” will suffice to find someone guilty. Any time a person decides to remain in the streets after police ordered a crowd to disperse, they would become “co-responsible” for whatever happens next. For minors, their parents would have to pay the actions of their children. And to make sure money can be extracted from the rebellious poor, the law allows authorities to garnish money directly from potential housing benefits and family allowances. In short, this law once again targets low-income individuals and families perceived as threats to the ruling order, as well as anyone who would dare to defy authority.




Beyond these repressive measures, the government also scrambled to find “solutions”—i.e., distractions—to end the crisis. During his speech, Lecornu also insisted that the government, via the Ministry of Education, had implemented tools for high school students to take part in some sort of national survey where they can express their frustrations and make requests to improve the educational system. Such strategy of watered-down participatory democracy was also used during the Yellow Vest movement to divide demonstrators and weaken their collective force. First, the French government represses students in cold blood; then it asks them for “constructive” dialogue.




Lecornu explained that by the end of the month, the government would study and work to address all the demands received by students via their official platforms to provide concrete solutions to the current crisis in the educational system. He also promised to improve “ParcourSup,” the online platform with which students list their “wishes” and apply to different post-secondary education options. He also announced that until the end of the week, each high school has been asked by the Ministry of Education to cancel half a day of classes in order to create some space and time for “a period of internal democracy” during which students and teachers could exchange about what should be changed within the school. This isn’t the first time that 

the language of “democracy”

 has been used as a tool for counterinsurgency.




Similarly, on October 8 Education Minister Édouard Geffray made a new promise to 

provide

 3000 extra teachers, while welcoming student unions and organizations to contribute their views on the current situation in hopes of reaching a political agreement to end the demonstrations as soon as possible. These promises and calls for dialogue show the Macron government’s strategy to pacify the situation by partially answering some of the main demands made by student movement—while ratcheting up repression in the streets to maintain power on their own terms.




National media have reported that tens of thousands of demands were already made by students through these official platforms. Nonetheless, it seems to us that, so far, doing so has not stopped them from continuing to be present in the streets. Even students who may participate in such official channels recognize that their collective power to disrupt the status quo, not the government’s pacifying gestures, remains the source of their genuine power and voice.




So far, the student movement has resisted cooptation by political opportunists and trade unions. However, its success and widespread public support render it a tempting target for those who would attempt to control it or hitch it to other agendas. University student unions and their spokespeople form part of the movement, and some leftist politicians and their followers actively support it. However, none of them have yet been able to speak on behalf of all its participants, nor to control the diversity of tactics that have flourished within it.




Finally, the existing solidarity within the ranks of students is admirable. As we 

reported previously

, teenagers face vastly different realities depending on the geographical areas where they live and study. The claim of the French school system to promote equal opportunity and reward merit rather than class and geographic background is simply a lie, in the face of the structural inequalities that flourish within capitalism and the educational system designed to reinforce it. Nevertheless, while high-school students in the suburbs were facing violent repression from police forces, students from wealthier districts and prestigious universities joined the struggle by blocking or occupying their schools in solidarity. Numerous students explained that although they are well aware that they do not experience the same difficulties as their counterparts living in the 

banlieues

, they could not remain passive in the face of such police violence and injustice against their counterparts.







 




Students blocking the Hélène-Boucher high school. The sign reads: “Fewer cops, more money.” (Paris, October 6, 2026)










Onward Together Against Their World




Following another intense week of actions and protests, the Ministry of Justice 

announced

 on Friday, October 9 that since the beginning of the movement, more than 6800 people have been taken into custody, 86% of whom are minors. So far, 21 individuals have been held in jail while awaiting trial.




At the eve of a new weekend, the government continued to promote the narrative that the movement was declining and the situation was progressively coming back under control, trumpeting the decreasing number of blocked high schools as evidence. But despite the mainstream media’s faithful adherence to this story, students remained unsatisfied by the government’s response and determined not to give up the fight. Far from feeling defeated, they issued a new call to take to the streets on Tuesday, October 13.




Act V: October 13, 2026




As the next day of action dawned, blockades and clashes with law enforcement forced the closure of about 200 high schools. Over the previous days, that number had held steady, showing that a significant core of high school students remained willing to fight for what they think is right.




But what changed dramatically on this day compared to the previous acts is that a large number of universities decided to join the movement all at once. Around noon, the organization 

Union étudiante

 announced to the media that 90% of the seventy French universities were blocked or completely closed. This massive involvement of university students during the fifth act of the student unrest would prove to be a critical development.







 




The sign reads: “High-school students maimed, shot in the eye, drowned, or toothless. University students outraged.” (Rennes, October 6, 2026)










As the movement expanded and gained in strength, the counterrevolutionary backlash against it from both the government and the grassroots extreme right increased in turn. The growing number of blockades at universities over these days led to a surge in fascist attacks intended to intimidate protesters in cities such as Paris and Lille.




As usual, the first marches throughout France took place in the morning. In Paris, the official demonstration was announced for 2:00 pm. This time, the itinerary validated by authorities changed from the classic Place de la République to La Nation. Demonstrators would be storming the southern and western parts of the city, departing from Place d’Italie and reaching Invalides, not far from the Ministry of Education and Matignon, the official residence of the Prime Minister. This route evoked sweet memories from another famous student movement that took place in France 

20 years ago

, during which intense riots took place once demonstrators reached Invalides. Another unofficial call went out summoning protestors to meet in front of City Hall. This unauthorized procession was finally granted the right to walk through the streets of Paris to reach its destination not far from the other demonstration.




On the afternoon of the 13th, police forces changed their tactics and drew up very close to the demonstrators, moving at the front of the procession. Before participants could join the march, they were subject to search by the police. Officers attempted to confiscate as many anti-police signs as possible. However, this strategy to muzzle public opinion against the police’s violent behavior proved unsuccessful, as thousands of protesters took pleasure in chanting the classic anti-police slogans in unison during the march.




As demonstrators approached their final destination, tensions with law enforcement escalated. Near Invalides, some motivated protesters attempted to continue their afternoon march towards Matignon, but were quickly stopped and pushed back by lines of police near Place Vauban.




It was here that intense confrontations unfolded over the next several hours. Police deployed water cannons and blanketed the square with tear gas in order to disperse the crowd. What demonstrators didn’t yet know yet was that other police units had surrounded them and stood ready to kettle them if needed in order to arrest specific individuals. During the clashes, rioters set a BMW SUV on fire and looted a nearby wine store.







 




Street confrontations at 

Place Vauban

 (Paris, October 13, 2026)










Later that night, the government stated that 161,500 people demonstrated during the fifth act of the student movement, while the student unions claimed a total turnout of 480,000. Officials estimated 41,500 demonstrators in Paris. Further demonstrations took place in Nantes, Lens, Strasbourg, Bordeaux, Marseille and Lyon, where some confrontations with police forces and property destruction took place towards the end of the march.




By the end of the day, arrest figures had shot up further. 7950 individuals had been taken into police custody since the beginning of the student protests, 85% of whom were minors. To date, 2735 criminal cases had been filed, 2190 of which involved minors, and 26 individuals were placed in pretrial detention, including 9 minors.




Looking Forward: Will the Unrest Survive the Holidays?




As the first school holidays of the year approached, many students wondered whether their month-long mobilization would survive the two-week break from classes. Their worries were understandable; it is well known that holidays have often taken the wind out of the sails of many social movements, in France and beyond.




This is why, for days, high-school students have continuously called to take the street on Saturday, October 17, 2026. This call, massively shared online for weeks, suggests a resurgence of 

the Yellow Vest movement

 that launched in 2018. Rebellious high schoolers hoped that university students, Yellow Vesters, and other angry protesters would be able to merge with the movement to expand this social and political unrest in new directions.







 




We haven’t been defeated yet. (Paris, October 13, 2026)










Meanwhile, the government continued to find itself in a bind over the 

crisis

, despite its pathetic attempts to defuse the uproar through dialogue with student unions and organizations. After weeks of insisting that the movement was losing steam, now they are acknowledging that the level of militancy and determination coming from protesters has progressively increased over the previous days of action. They feared the potential outcome of the October 17 demonstrations—and as we have seen, their fears were justified.




With the fateful date approaching and tension building, important questions remained. Will other demographics decide to join the movement by also revolting against the government and their current living conditions, as authorities fear? Will we live up to the expectations of high school students and the courageous precedent they have set? Will we be able to unleash hell?







 




Will the student movement be able to unleash hell? (Paris, October 6, 2026).

title: PJAK calls on Iran to disclose Xalid Berzincî’s whereabouts
content:
The Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK) issued a written statement after losing contact with its member Xalid Berzincî following his detention by the Iranian regime. PJAK held the Iranian regime directly responsible for Berzincî’s fate, calling for an end to the policy of enforced disappearances and demanding clarification of his situation.




According to the statement, Berzincî was detained by regime forces on July 9, 2026, in the village of Ûçtepe, near Bokan. PJAK emphasized that no clear or reliable information has been provided about his whereabouts or legal status since his detention.




PJAK stated that the Iranian regime’s refusal to disclose Berzincî’s fate has raised serious concerns about his health and the conditions of his detention.




“The Iranian regime is directly responsible for the fate of Xalid Berzincî. The regime must put an end to its policy of enforced disappearances,” the statement said.




Emphasizing that the Iranian regime is responsible for protecting Berzincî’s life, physical health, and safety, PJAK stated that the authorities must immediately disclose information about his place of detention, health condition, and legal status.




The statement stressed that leaving questions about Berzincî’s situation unanswered and withholding information is unacceptable, issuing the following call:




“Any failure to provide clear answers regarding our comrade’s situation, or any concealment of information, is unacceptable. The Iranian regime bears direct responsibility for the consequences of any negligence or practices that violate fundamental standards of humanity. The concealment of our comrade’s fate must end, and his situation must be clarified as soon as possible.”

title: Two women killed in Sulaymaniyah and Mardin
content:
Two women have died in Sulaymaniyah in South Kurdistan and in Mardin in North Kurdistan. Kîjan Bûrhan was shot by her father and succumbed to her severe injuries, while Remziye Damar was found dead in her home under unexplained circumstances.




Kîjan Bûrhan was shot by her father in Sulaymaniyah on Monday evening. The 30-year-old woman was struck by three bullets. She was taken for medical treatment in critical condition but died from her injuries on Tuesday afternoon.




Meanwhile, Remziye Damar was found lifeless in her home in the village of Boxazîyê in Kızıltepe district. Emergency services arrived following a call for assistance and confirmed her death. Her body was taken to the forensic medicine department of Kızıltepe State Hospital for an autopsy. Following the completion of the examinations, Damar was laid to rest in her home village of Boxazîyê.

author: Unknown
title: South African women condemn death sentence against Varisheh Moradi, call for an end to executions
content:
Abahlali baseMjondolo (AbM), one of the largest grassroots movements to emerge in South Africa following the end of apartheid, issued a message of solidarity with Kurdish political prisoner Varisheh Moradi. Women members of the movement condemned the Iranian regime’s renewed death sentence against Moradi, issued on October 14, 2026, and called for the execution to be halted.




In a visual message featuring numerous AbM members, the movement called on the Iranian regime to end its policies of repression and executions targeting Kurds. The message demanded the immediate release of Varisheh Moradi and all other political prisoners, while expressing solidarity with the women’s freedom struggle in Kurdistan through the slogan “Jin Jiyan Azadî” (Woman, Life, Freedom).










https://1649452211.rsc.cdn77.org/20261020214855_2026-10-20-pretoria-guney-afrikali-kadinlar-werise-muradiye-idam-cezasina-karsi-cikti_1.mp4













Background




Varisheh (also Warisha) Moradi, also known as Ciwana Sine, a member of the East Kurdistan Free Women’s Society (KJAR) from Sanandaj, Kurdistan Province, was arrested by the Ministry of Intelligence on 1 August 2023 at the entrance to Sanandaj upon her return from Kermanshah, Kermanshah Province, where she had been involved in political and organisational activities.




She spent the first 13 days of her detention in the detention centre of this security institution in Sanandaj, and was then transferred to Ward 209 of Evin Prison in Tehran.




During this period, she was subjected to pressure and threats to make forced confessions, and on 26 December 2023, after five months of solitary confinement, she was transferred to the women’s ward of Evin Prison.




On 10 October 2024, coinciding with the World Day Against the Death Penalty, Moradi went on a 20-day hunger strike in Tehran’s Evin Prison to protest the issuing and execution of death sentences by the Islamic Republic of Iran.




Due to digestive complications following the hunger strike, she was transferred to a medical facility outside the prison, and returned after spending one night under care.




The death penalty, handed down by Judge Abolghassem Salavati, followed two court hearings on 16 June and 5 October 2024, and the death sentence was formally notified to Moradi’s lawyers on 10 November 2024.




During the court hearings, Moradi was denied the right to defend herself, and the judge barred her lawyers from presenting a defence.




Additionally, the lawyers, who had previously been prevented from reviewing the case file, were only allowed a few hours to review the case after the second hearing.




Moradi’s death sentence contradicts an earlier indictment that referred to Article 288 of the Islamic Penal Code, which provides for a maximum sentence of 15 years’ imprisonment. However, in an illegal ruling, Judge Salavati cited Article 287, which allows for the imposition of the death penalty in cases where individuals are involved in armed rebellion against the Islamic Republic.




Additionally, in October 2024, Moradi and several other female political prisoners in Evin’s women’s ward were sentenced

 

to six months in prison by the Second Criminal Court of the Qods Judicial Complex in Tehran, presided over by Judge Abolfazl Ameri, on charges of “disturbing prison order”.




Moradi’s case has been referred to Branch Nine of the Supreme Court and is currently under review following her appeal against the death sentence.




Moradi is being denied access to vital medical care despite suffering from serious health conditions, including a herniated cervical disc and spinal canal stenosis.




In March 2024, Moradi was examined by a neurologist and both the specialist and the medical team at Evin Prison recommended immediate surgery. However, prison authorities have so far refused to allow her transfer to a hospital. Her condition has since worsened, leading to numbness and chronic pain in her right hand.




The political prisoner also developed gastrointestinal issues following a 20-day hunger strike in October 2024, for which she received no medical care for several months. It was only after mounting pressure from international human rights organisations that she was taken to a medical centre outside the prison for examination and treatment about two months ago.

author: Brad Reed
title: FCC Chair Brendan Carr Threatens Broadcasters Over Poll Coverage
content:
A Democratic strategist points out that “it’s not illegal to tell the American people that Trump is a failed president.”

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Federal Communications Commission Chairman Brendan Carr on Wednesday threatened broadcasters that cover what he described as “fake polls,” which he said hurt “voter turnout and enthusiasm.”

In a social media post, Carr attacked news outlets for “amplifying or airing these polls without regard to basic journalistic ethics and without informing the public that those polls lack a scientific, accurate, or even real basis.”

Carr did not provide a single specific example of a “fake” opinion poll, nor did he name a broadcaster who has promoted one. President Donald Trump, who nominated Carr to head the FCC, has repeatedly decried polls as “fake” as they’ve shown his approval ratings at record lows.

Later in the post, Carr hinted that the FCC would take direct action against broadcasters for informing their viewers about opinion polls.

“The FCC takes these issues seriously,” said Carr. “Broadcasters are prohibited by the terms of their federal licenses from engaging in news distortion or promoting broadcast hoaxes. It is important that broadcasters comply with their public interest obligations.”

Carr’s post drew a swift rebuke from Democratic FCC commissioner Anna Gomez.

“Pollsters who intentionally mislead the public should answer for it,” wrote Gomez, “but broadcasters who report publicly available polling data should never be punished when a poll is wrong. FCC rules on news distortion or hoaxes do not apply to a station that reports this data in good faith.”

Steve Herman, former White House bureau chief at Voice of America, wrote in a social media post that Carr’s assertions about “news distortion” are “stretching specific regulations far beyond their legal definitions,” as “the FCC can’t mandate how a broadcaster contextualizes a poll.”

“The FCC threatening broadcasters for airing specific political data is a chilling content-based restriction on speech,” Herman added, “which federal courts subject to extreme judicial review and the commission would almost certainly lose such cases, according to First Amendment scholars.”

Former TV meteorologist Chris Gloninger predicted that Carr’s post would have a chilling effect on local news stations.

“Holy shit, this is dangerous,” Gloninger wrote. “Two weeks before an election, the FCC chair is threatening broadcaster licenses over polls he calls ‘fake.’ No GM will risk that, so polls vanish.”

Mark Jacob, former metro editor at the Chicago Tribune, called Carr “anti-free-speech” for “threatening to punish news outlets that publish polls showing Trump’s deep unpopularity.”

“We are sliding into a dictatorship,” Jacob said, “and it would be helpful if major media would do their duty and warn the public.”

Adam Klasfeld, editor-in-chief at All Rise News, described Carr as the president’s “censorship czar” who is warning news outlets against “the dissemination of data disfavored by the state.”

Princeton historian Kevin Kruse argued Carr’s threats warranted his impeachment and removal from office.

“The president shouting ‘fake news’ is bad enough,” wrote Kruse, “but the FCC commissioner threatening to punish broadcasters for promoting ‘fake news’ like ‘the president is historically unpopular’ is so much worse.”

Carr’s post drew ridicule from Democratic strategist Adam Parkhomenko, who informed the FCC chair that “it’s not illegal to tell the American people that Trump is a failed president.”

Max Steele, senior director of communications at gun safety advocacy organization Everytown, similarly ridiculed Carr.

“It is ILLEGAL to say the brave and smart President Trump is at historic polling lows!!!” he wrote sarcastically.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Simon Feisthauer Fournet
title: Dispatch From Paris: Student-Led Protests Spread, Despite Brutal Policing
content:
Weeks of student-led demonstrations have spread nationwide, with arrests, reports of police brutality, and restrictions.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Paris, France — The march on the iconic Place de la République in the French capital had barely begun when riot police — known as the Compagnies républicaines de sécurité, or CRS — fired tear gas in the square. The demonstration on October 17, 2026, had been officially declared to the Paris prefecture, which banned the longer route organizers planned through the center of the city but allowed a march departing from the square. Even so, police launched tear gas that incapacitated the 400 musicians of the Orchestre du Nouveau Monde, an activist classical ensemble that had played at earlier high school protests and came to perform again.

The heavy police presence did not deter protesters who dressed the statue of Marianne, a figure personifying the French Republic, at the center of the square in a giant yellow vest — a reference to the “yellow vest” protest movement that began in 2018 over rising fuel prices and cost of living and has recently joined forces with the French high schoolers’ protests. An inscription on the statue read: “2026, the police mutilate high schoolers.”

Similar crowds filled cities and towns across France. Organizers counted about 800,000 people among the protesters while authorities reported 550,000. Officials had expected far fewer, about 200,000, and Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez later conceded the state had been caught off guard.

The movement began in early September with blockades at high schools in France’s overseas territories — where students denounced decaying buildings, unfilled teaching posts and shrinking budgets — and then spread to underserved Paris suburbs and the rest of the country, in part through social media.

The police sometimes used force to contain and arrest students who were protesting and blocking off their schools. By October 1, the Collectif d’action judiciaire, a group of lawyers defending arrested students, said police in the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis had pressured, blackmailed, and even beaten detained high schoolers. Several cases of police wounding students have been reported.

Unions, student organizations, and activist groups joined the movement, tying the school-related grievances to frustrations with the cost of living and anger at the government in a general convergence of struggles.

Daniel, 29, said French mainstream media tended to ignore the students’ demands, which is why the movement started on social media. “It breaks the dialogue, so it has to go through social media, where a freer thought for young people in general can emerge,” he said.

He argued that the French government in recent years has ignored every democratic channel, from the left’s win in the 2024 legislative elections after the National Assembly was dissolved by President Emmanuel Macron to citizen petitions against laws passed without debate.

“All of that creates a break between two parts of society, the elites in power and the rest of society, with those elites telling us, essentially, ‘you lot don’t understand anything, you’re idealists,’” he said.

Videos of police brutality shared on social media brought Éric, 32, into the streets on October 17, he said, adding that he was impressed by the scale of the Gen Z mobilization: “It took very little time to mobilize this many young people, and that’s impressive.”

With at least 1,400 arrests, 3,000 businesses robbed, and several public buildings set ablaze that day, media coverage in France and abroad has generally focused on looting and arson on the margins on the protests, which some organizers and independent media have denounced, pointing to escalation from the police and anger built up over weeks of heavy-handed repression against students.

For Éric, the anger has been building for years. “Everything that has been done since the Macron era, such as the abolition of the TV license fee [a tax that funded public broadcasting] that brought the public service to its knees, with the rest of the media largely owned by far right billionaires — we’ve reached a critical point in the history of France and of Macron’s two terms, and it’s catastrophic,” he said.

The French online media outlet StreetPress reported about 50 cases of police violence from the weekend so far, which include a 17-year-old in Saint-Étienne whose hand was torn off by a police grenade and a 17-year-old in Mulhouse who lost sight in her left eye.

The French government in recent days banned public gatherings in some cities, installed local curfews, and announced that the police will step up its response to any further demonstrations and call in army reinforcements.

The movement shows no sign of slowing, with more actions planned throughout the week, ahead of another protest on October 24.

“This government’s policy of extreme austerity isn’t necessary; we’re told there’s no other solution, but that’s not the case,” said Éric, who wants to continue rallying for students’ demands and against the high cost of living. “The proof is that other European countries have adopted different solutions that, while certainly not perfect, have proven way more effective than those last 10 years of Macron’s administration.”

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Aldrey Olegario
title: Políticos têm rede ‘paralela’ na Meta sem declarar ao TSE
content:
Investigamos o que importa para os brasileiros além do que passa na campanha eleitoral. Leia mais reportagens como essa clicando 

aqui

.













Candidatos nas eleições deste ano estão usando uma estratégia em comum: 

além das contas oficiais nas redes sociais com milhões de seguidores que foram declaradas ao Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), muitos têm uma rede paralela de perfis de apoio que copiam parte do conteúdo das páginas dos políticos.

 Esse “exército alternativo” turbina o alcance, com menções cruzadas e postagens iguais feitas quase ao mesmo tempo.




Segundo a 

Agência Pública

 apurou, 

Flávio Bolsonaro, que disputa a presidência, tem ao menos sete perfis de apoio não declarados ao TSE com mais de 100 mil seguidores cada. Juntos eles reúnem mais de 2,5 milhões de seguidores.

 Para se ter uma comparação, o principal perfil oficial de Flávio declarado ao TSE tem 14,8 milhões.




Além de fazerem propaganda com o número de urna do candidato, essa rede de perfis de apoio divulga links para grupos oficiais de Bolsonaro e o @ oficial de Flávio.




Algumas delas postam o mesmo conteúdo com minutos de diferença. Isso aconteceu no último final de semana, quando uma conta de apoio com mais de 770 mil seguidores publicou o mesmo corte da entrevista de Flávio para a Rede Globo com minutos de diferença, indicando o perfil oficial.





































O mesmo corte da entrevista à Globo foi divulgado pelo perfil oficial de Flávio e uma das páginas de apoio com minutos de diferença. A única diferença foi a inclusão de letterings




Os perfis de Flávio não são recentes. A maioria deles foi criada em 2022 ou fim de 2023, quando Lula tomou posse. Do outro lado da disputa, André Janones, deputado federal (Rede-MG) e a principal cabeça por trás da estratégia digital de Lula (PT) no segundo turno, também tem uma página de apoio no Instagram que não foi declarada ao TSE nem por Lula, nem pelo deputado. Nesse caso, o perfil de Janones foi criado em 6 de outubro deste ano, quando o político afirmou que a sua conta oficial estava sendo alvo de perseguição por grupos bolsonaristas e corria risco de ser derrubada. No vídeo, ele assume a criação da página.




O perfil de apoio de Janones traz um link tanto para o @ oficial do político, quanto para o de Lula. Com 1,6 milhão de seguidores, a página também divulga o canal de WhatsApp do “Exército de Lula”, onde são compartilhadas as diretrizes para engajar a favor do candidato.




A 

Pública

 apurou com especialistas em direito eleitoral que explicam que 

ter uma conta de apoio não configura um crime, porém, há limites para o que essas contas podem fazer – e que ficam mais difíceis de serem fiscalizados pela falta de transparência das plataformas.




Como a 

Pública

 já 

mostrou

, a Meta deixou anúncios pagos com dinheiro estrangeiro circularem sem rótulo de conteúdo político nestas eleições, o que impede saber quem pagou pelos anúncios e quais postagens foram impulsionadas. A 

Pública

 também 

revelou

 que a plataforma não tem sido transparente nos critérios que usa para ampliar ou derrubar o alcance de contas.




A advogada Caroline Lacerda, doutora em Direito Eleitoral pela Universidade de Brasília, explica que as campanhas exploram essas contas paralelas de forma estratégica. Um dos motivos é contornar a regra do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral que impede as plataformas de recomendarem os perfis oficiais dos candidatos políticos para os usuários. As páginas de apoio não estão sujeitas a essa limitação.




“A regra de não recomendação cria um incentivo evidente para que as campanhas terceirizem o alcance em perfis paralelos”, explica ela. “As páginas de apoio funcionam, na prática, como caminho alternativo para furar o bloqueio de recomendação dos perfis oficiais. Isso é lícito quando a página é espontânea e sem dinheiro por trás.”




O advogado Fernando Neisser reforça que as publicações em contas de apoio não podem ser impulsionadas através de pagamento. 

“Por não serem contas oficiais da campanha, elas não precisam ser informadas ao TSE. Por outro lado, essas contas não podem fazer impulsionamento pago de absolutamente nenhum conteúdo eleitoral”,

 diz.




É aí que a falta de transparência da Meta dificulta a fiscalização. Só é possível saber se houve algum pagamento não declarado através de uma investigação – como o 

procedimento

 aberto a pedido da Procuradoria Federal dos Direitos do Cidadão (PFDC) contra a empresa – ou se a própria Meta identificar alguma irregularidade, e decidir combatê-la.




Com base na decisão do TSE de que pessoas físicas não podem pagar para promover conteúdos eleitorais,

 a Meta decidiu, por exemplo, remover três publicações de conteúdo eleitoral de uma página no Facebook em apoio ao candidato Flávio Bolsonaro com 13,7 mil seguidores.

 Os posts, que circularam nos meses de agosto e outubro deste ano, receberam pagamento para ampliar seu alcance – o que é uma conduta proibida e está sujeita à multa de R$ 5 mil a R$ 30 mil. 




“Perfis de apoio devem ter identificação de seus autores, e devem ser de pessoas físicas. Qualquer outra forma de propaganda eleitoral pode ser caracterizada como irregular, sujeita à remoção do conteúdo eleitoral e até da conta inteira. Se for um caso reiterado, consistente e articulado, poderá configurar abuso de poder midiático”, afirma Luiz Scarpino, especialista em Direito Eleitoral.




A reportagem questionou o TSE sobre os achados da apuração, que respondeu que “não se manifesta sobre casos concretos, que podem vir a ser objeto de análise pela Justiça Eleitoral”.




A 

Pública

 procurou as assessorias de Flávio e Janones e dos demais políticos citados na matéria. O espaço segue aberto para respostas.







Campopiano e Pavanato também mobilizam rede de apoio paralela




Além de Flávio e Janones, dois campeões de voto do PL em São Paulo também têm perfis que parecem operar em rede: o segundo deputado federal mais votado do país, Lucas Pavanato, e a deputada estadual que teve mais votos no Brasil, Eduarda Campopiano.




Campopiano tem ao menos sete contas de apoio, além do perfil que foi informado ao TSE. Juntos, esses perfis têm cerca de 1,8 milhão de seguidores, mais da metade dos 3,2 milhões que ela tem no perfil oficial atualmente.

 Essa rede de perfis que se declaram “de apoio” à política atuam em rede, um marcando o outro, e muitos divulgam na bio o número de urna de Campopiano, além de divulgar links que direcionam para o instagram oficial e para a comunidade oficial da candidata. 




Lacerda explica que esse comportamento é considerado válido desde que essa seja uma iniciativa orgânica e espontânea vinda dos próprios usuários. “Se a campanha pede para alguém criar a página, dirige o conteúdo ou paga por ela, a iniciativa é da campanha, não da pessoa”, ressalta.




A falta de transparência nas plataformas também dificulta saber quem é o verdadeiro dono de um perfil. 

“O que prova a existência de uma conta fantasma oficial da campanha é, se houver suspeita suficiente, entrar com ação, obter a quebra dos metadados de acesso daquela conta e identificar que aquele login está sendo feito pela equipe oficial da campanha”

, explica Neisser. Fora isso, o que resta é observar o padrão de atividade dos perfis para identificar indícios de irregularidade.




No maior perfil de apoio a Campopiano, com 847 mil seguidores, há publicações feitas em collab – isto é, em conjunto – com a conta oficial do chefe de gabinete e coordenador de campanha de Campopiano, David Itiúba.

 Como explica Scarpino, ao envolver o núcleo operativo da campanha, esse tipo de relação corre o risco de ser considerada irregular. 




“Pode ser que esses perfis nasçam independentes, mas se tais páginas de apoio venham, em algum momento, a tangenciar o núcleo da campanha, passariam a merecer o mesmo tipo de restrição como comunicação à Justiça Eleitoral, tal como ocorreu no canal do Janones”, explica ele.




O canal Exército do Lula, organizado pelo deputado federal André Janones, foi suspenso por decisão do TSE e só voltou ao ar no dia 14 de outubro, após o político registrá-lo no TSE, conforme 

determinação

 do presidente da corte, Kassio Nunes Marques.




Já Lucas Pavanato tem ao menos cinco contas dedicadas à sua campanha, diferentes da principal declarada ao TSE. Segundo o levantamento, esses perfis juntos têm mais de 230 mil seguidores.




Ao todo, o levantamento encontrou outros políticos que também têm contas ativas de apoio não declaradas à Justiça Eleitoral. A maioria, 66%, foi de políticos do PL, seguidas de 22% de partidos como o MDB, PSD, PSDB, União, Podemos e 11% de candidatos diretamente ligados ao governo, de partidos como o próprio PT, o PSOL, PSB, PDT, dentre outros.

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Video game helps Inuit youth learn mental wellness strategies
content:
When Letia Kalluk wrote her song 

Maana

 for a contest in the Northwest Territories, she did not know it would eventually be featured in a game that aims to improve the mental wellness of Inuit youth.




In 

Virtual Qaggiq

, billed as the first Inuit-designed video game for mobile devices, the Inuktitut song plays alongside videos of elders.




“The lyrics go something like, ‘A wise man told me that you’re still young. You have a lot to live for. You haven’t seen the whole world yet,’” said Kalluk, who is from Arctic Bay, in an interview.




“It’s really good for [youth] to hear music in their own language. It’s been very fulfilling for me as an artist to contribute to that.”




York University researchers, Inuit youth and cultural advisers started developing the game in 2022.




It follows Alaasua, the main character, through seven quests that pair Inuit cultural activities with mental wellness strategies, said project co-ordinator Yogita Singh.




In one quest, mythical creatures tempt Alaasua to drink spoiled water while she gathers fresh water and ice. Players learn to resist the temptation and manage stress without turning to substance use, Singh said.
















The soundtrack includes a rap track by Kinngait artist Iola Oshoweetok, a drumming instrumental by Kimmirut artist Leo Temela, and throat-singing tracks by Yellowknife duo Tiffany Kuliktana Ayalik and Kayley Inuksuk Mackay, also known as Piqsiq.




The game’s testing phase took place from October 2025 to July, with 276 Inuit youth from 21 communities in Nunavut and 16 other communities across Canada taking part, Singh said.




Participants completed a 39-question wellness questionnaire before and after playing, with in-person workshops held in Arctic Bay, Kinngait, Pangnirtung, Iqaluit, Baker Lake and Ottawa.




Others tested the game from home, Singh said.




“Youth felt they had learned strategies to help themselves cope better with negative thoughts, make themselves feel better and feel more comfortable asking for help, for example, when they feel a bad mood coming on,” said Yvonne Bohr, the project’s principal investigator at York University. 




“Usually, it takes a while for lessons to sink in, but the fact that there were changes even right afterward is very encouraging,” she added. 
















Researchers also found no negative changes in participants’ wellness after playing the game.




Kalluk said she helped translate 12 interviews with elders from Arctic Bay, Kinngait, Baker Lake and Pangnirtung, which can be accessed by players in the digital qaggiq, or traditional meeting space within the game.




“There are a few videos that talk about fishing, going out hunting, as well as mental health aspects. An elder’s point of view is very important, and it’s important to have these kinds of resources readily available for youth,” said Kalluk. 




The team is working to make the game available on iPads and is in discussion with the territorial Education Department about using it in schools.




Singh said the hope is to make 

Virtual Qaggiq

 available in early 2027 on iPhone and Android devices.
















“It makes me feel very proud as an Inuk to be part of something like this, something so groundbreaking for our youth in Nunavut,” Kalluq said.

author: Chris Walker
title: Acton Says Ramaswamy Exploited Her Estranged Mother for Political Gain
content:
Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton accused her mother’s then-husband of sexual assault when she was a child.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Democratic candidate for Ohio governor Amy Acton has responded to a political ad produced by her Republican opponent Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign, which features her mother — whom she’s been estranged from for decades — describing Acton as a liar.

The ad is being widely criticized as distasteful because Acton accused her mother and her then-stepfather of abuse and sexual assault when she was just a child.

In the ad, Donna Arthur, Acton’s mother, is shown speaking directly into the camera about her daughter, whom she has not seen since 1978, when Acton was just 12 years old.

“Amy has a serious problem. She is a liar,” Arthur says. “She’s lied her entire life. My daughter needs help.”

The ad doesn’t mention why Arthur believes her daughter is a liar, and it leaves out all relevant information about their estrangement.

Acton alleges that she was the victim of sexual abuse by Arthur’s now-deceased husband when she was between the ages of 10 and 12. Acton has also recalled being unhoused at one point while living with her mother and stepfather.

She later told her father about the abuses, and a grand jury indicted her stepfather. Her mother and stepfather then fled the state to avoid prosecution, Acton has recounted.

The ad did not indicate who paid for or produced it. Though the Ramaswamy campaign had initially avoided taking responsibility for the ad, it has now admitted they made the commercial. What’s more, the campaign intends to spend an additional $4 million to continue airing it.

The campaign defended the ad in a statement.

“We don’t know what happened between Amy and her mother, who first spoke about Amy in 2020, but we know that Amy Acton is a serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of before deciding who to entrust as governor,” the Ramaswamy campaign said.

On Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance came to Ramaswamy’s defense.

“Whether the ad was appropriate or not is not really my concern,” Vance said in response to a reporter’s question, saying he was more focused on the election’s outcome.

“Have the opinion you want to have on that ad,” Vance continued, adding that he was “disgusted” at members of his own party “whining” about the contents of the ad.

Acton has condemned Ramaswamy for the ad in a statement posted on Facebook.

“Between the ages of 10 and 12, I was sexually abused by her husband, while my birth mother did nothing to protect me. … I’ve always known that she was deeply sick and unwell, and it’s sad to see Vivek Ramaswamy exploit her all for his own political gain,” Acton said.

I know what it feels like to be a child who is hungry, frightened, and uncertain of what tomorrow will bring. I know what it means to feel powerless and to depend on the courage and compassion of others to find a way forward. Those experiences shaped my values, my compassion, and my belief that every person deserves to be safe, to be heard, and to have a fair chance at a better life. They are part of what led me to become a doctor, to dedicate my life to public service, and to fight for people who too often feel forgotten or left behind.

Acton’s brother, Phillip Stearns, has also blasted the ad.

“It’s not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at twelve years old from our birth mother’s husband into a political talking point,” Stearns said in a statement, adding that the commercial is a “desperate, disgusting attack” that “reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core – a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants.”

The race between Acton, a physician and former director of the Ohio Department of Health, and Ramaswamy, an ally of President Donald Trump, is a tight one. According to an average of polling data compiled by FiftyPlusOne, Acton is currently leading the contest, garnering around 49 percent of support in the state, while Ramaswamy receives 44.5 percent.
